shelves.title: Probiotics for childhood gastroenteritis: two big blinded trials, both null
shelves.question: Do probiotics help children with acute gastroenteritis seen in the emergency department?
shelves.mesh: Gastroenteritis · Probiotics · Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus · Lactobacillus helveticus · Double-Blind Method · Child, Preschool · Infant · Diarrhea · Vomiting · Treatment Failure · Acute Disease
shelves.balance: Two countries, two different products, about 1,900 children — the probiotic didn't shorten or soften the illness. It is still the first thing parents reach for.

cards.headline: PROGUT (Freedman 2018): a combination probiotic did not soften gastroenteritis in Canadian children.
cards.summary: Moderate-to-severe gastroenteritis 26.1% probiotic vs 24.7% placebo, OR 1.06 — null.
cards.people: 886 children, 6 Canadian pediatric EDs
cards.result: Moderate-to-severe gastroenteritis 26.1% probiotic vs 24.7% placebo, OR 1.06 — null
cards.watchOut: One product combination at one dose; the null answers for this preparation in ED-presenting children, and its twin trial with a different product (Reference 2) found the same. Product tested: a combination of Lactobacillus rhamnosus R0011 and L. helveticus R0052, as named in the publication.
cards.source: Freedman SB et al., N Engl J Med 2018 (PMID 30462939 · NCT01853124)

cards.headline: Schnadower 2018: Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG did not soften gastroenteritis in US children.

shelves.title: Fluid boluses in sick children: FEAST
shelves.question: In children with severe infection and impaired perfusion, do fluid boluses save lives — or cost them?
shelves.mesh: Fluid Therapy · Shock · Infections · Critical Illness · Resuscitation · Child
shelves.balance: The reflex bolus — the first thing every trainee reaches for in a shocked child — killed children who would have lived without it. The caveat matters: this was care without ventilators or ICU backup; the trial convicts the unmonitored bolus there and cautions everywhere.

cards.headline: FEAST (Maitland 2011): the fluid bolus killed children who would have lived without it.
cards.summary: 48-hour mortality — albumin bolus 10.6% , saline bolus 10.5% , no-bolus control 7.3% ; RR for any bolus vs control 1.45 (1.13–1.86) ; the excess mortality persisted at 4 weeks.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial — unblinded (fluid resuscitation cannot be blinded)
cards.people: 3,141 children in Uganda, Kenya, and Tanzania
cards.result: 48-hour mortality — albumin bolus 10.6% , saline bolus 10.5% , no-bolus control 7.3% ; RR for any bolus vs control 1.45 (1.13–1.86) ; the excess mortality persisted at 4 weeks.
cards.watchOut: A resource-limited setting — largely malaria and sepsis, no mechanical ventilation or ICU backup; the result convicts the unmonitored bolus there and cautions everywhere, and does not by itself settle bolus care in a fully supported PICU.
cards.source: Maitland K et al., N Engl J Med 2011 (PMID 21615299 · ISRCTN69856593)

shelves.title: One dose of ondansetron in the pediatric ED
shelves.question: In children with gastroenteritis and dehydration in the emergency department, does one oral dose of ondansetron reduce vomiting and the need for IV rehydration?
shelves.mesh: Gastroenteritis · Ondansetron · Antiemetics · Vomiting · Dehydration · Fluid Therapy · Double-Blind Method · Child · Child, Preschool · Infant · Administration, Oral · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: One dissolvable tablet cut vomiting by more than half and halved IV starts — a more comfortable child and a needle avoided, honestly a symptom-tier benefit, with no claim it changes where the illness ends.

cards.headline: Freedman 2006: one ondansetron dose halved vomiting and IV starts in children with gastroenteritis.
cards.summary: Vomiting 14% ondansetron vs 35% placebo, RR 0.40 ; IV rehydration 14% vs 31% , RR 0.46 ; hospitalization and return visits not significantly different.
cards.people: 215 children, pediatric emergency department
cards.result: Vomiting 14% ondansetron vs 35% placebo, RR 0.40 ; IV rehydration 14% vs 31% , RR 0.46 ; hospitalization and return visits not significantly different.
cards.watchOut: a symptom/process-tier benefit — comfort and IV avoidance, not a hard outcome; single trial, shelved by developer’s exception.
cards.source: Freedman SB et al., N Engl J Med 2006 (PMID 16625009)

shelves.title: Second-line drugs for status epilepticus in children
shelves.question: After benzodiazepines fail in convulsive status epilepticus, which second-line drug stops the seizure?
shelves.mesh: Status Epilepticus · Anticonvulsants · Levetiracetam · Phenytoin · Valproic Acid · Benzodiazepines · Double-Blind Method · Emergency Service, Hospital · Treatment Outcome · Adolescent · Child · Child, Preschool · Infant
shelves.balance: No winner. The blinded trial calls the three drugs equal, and the open-label trial agrees — choose by availability, preparation, and side effects, not by hope.

cards.headline: ESETT (Kapur 2019): levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, valproate — a three-way tie.
cards.summary: Seizure cessation with improved consciousness at 60 minutes — levetiracetam 47% , fosphenytoin 45% , valproate 46% ; the trial stopped early for futility — no drug was going to win.
cards.type: randomized, double-blind trial (Bayesian adaptive design; stopped early when futility criteria were met)
cards.people: 384 patients, children and adults, emergency departments
cards.result: Seizure cessation with improved consciousness at 60 minutes — levetiracetam 47% , fosphenytoin 45% , valproate 46% ; the trial stopped early for futility — no drug was going to win.
cards.watchOut: equivalence at these doses in this design; it answers “which of the three,” not dosing or third-line care.
cards.source: Kapur J et al., N Engl J Med 2019 (PMID 31774955 · NCT01960075)

cards.headline: EcLiPSE (Lyttle 2019): levetiracetam vs phenytoin — no significant difference, and it was open-label.
cards.summary: Seizure cessation 70% levetiracetam vs 64% phenytoin; median time to cessation 35 vs 45 minutes , HR 1.20 (0.91–1.60), p=0.20 — not significant.
cards.people: 286 children treated, UK and Ireland emergency departments
cards.result: Seizure cessation 70% levetiracetam vs 64% phenytoin; median time to cessation 35 vs 45 minutes , HR 1.20 (0.91–1.60), p=0.20 — not significant.
cards.watchOut: open-label — treating teams knew the drug; read alongside the blinded ESETT (Reference 1), which found the same tie.

shelves.title: Cooling the hypoxic newborn: two trials
shelves.question: In term infants with hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, does cooling for 72 hours, started in the first hours of life, reduce death or disability?
shelves.mesh: Hypoxia-Ischemia, Brain · Asphyxia Neonatorum · Hypothermia, Induced · Cerebral Palsy · Developmental Disabilities · Nervous System Diseases · Infant, Newborn
shelves.balance: One trial hit its endpoint and one missed it, and the pair together is the honest story: cooling became standard because the babies who were cooled more often survived intact — not because either trial was a clean win.

cards.headline: Shankaran 2005: whole-body cooling cut death or disability from 62% to 44%.
cards.summary: Death or moderate/severe disability 44% (45/102) hypothermia vs 62% (64/103) control, RR 0.72 (0.54–0.95), P=0.01; death alone 24% vs 37%, RR 0.68 (0.44–1.05), P=0.08; cerebral palsy among survivors 19% vs 30%, RR 0.68 (0.38–1.22).
cards.type: randomized controlled trial — unblinded (cooling cannot be blinded)
cards.people: 239 eligible infants (primary-outcome data for 205), US NICHD network
cards.result: Death or moderate/severe disability 44% (45/102) hypothermia vs 62% (64/103) control, RR 0.72 (0.54–0.95), P=0.01; death alone 24% vs 37%, RR 0.68 (0.44–1.05), P=0.08; cerebral palsy among survivors 19% vs 30%, RR 0.68 (0.38–1.22).
cards.watchOut: the primary endpoint was met; mortality alone was not significantly reduced, and disability was measured at 18–22 months, not school age.
cards.source: Shankaran S et al., N Engl J Med 2005 (PMID 16221780)

cards.headline: TOBY 2009: the same composite missed — but cooled babies more often survived intact.
cards.summary: Death or severe disability — RR 0.86 (0.68–1.07), P=0.17, NOT significant (42 deaths + 32 severe disability cooled vs 44 + 42 control); survival without neurologic abnormality — RR 1.57 (1.16–2.12), P=0.003; among survivors, cerebral palsy RR 0.67 (0.47–0.96), P=0.03.
cards.type: randomized controlled trial — unblinded (cooling cannot be blinded)
cards.people: 325 infants (163 cooled, 162 control), UK-led
cards.result: Death or severe disability — RR 0.86 (0.68–1.07), P=0.17, NOT significant (42 deaths + 32 severe disability cooled vs 44 + 42 control); survival without neurologic abnormality — RR 1.57 (1.16–2.12), P=0.003; among survivors, cerebral palsy RR 0.67 (0.47–0.96), P=0.03.
cards.watchOut: read with Card 1 — the two trials point the same way with different precision; cooling’s case rests on the pattern, not on either P value alone.
cards.source: Azzopardi DV et al., N Engl J Med 2009 (PMID 19797281 · ISRCTN89547571)

shelves.title: Caffeine for apnea of prematurity: the CAP trial and its long arc
shelves.question: Does caffeine for apnea of prematurity help very-low-birth-weight infants — in the NICU, and as they grow?
shelves.mesh: Apnea · Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia · Caffeine · Central Nervous System Stimulants · Cerebral Palsy · Developmental Disabilities · Follow-Up Studies · Infant, Newborn · Infant, Premature · Infant, Very Low Birth Weight · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Caffeine got preterm babies off oxygen sooner, and at 18 months fewer of them had died or were disabled — a benefit that had faded to non-significance by age 5. One trial, shelved by developer's exception, with its whole arc printed.

cards.headline: CAP 2006: caffeine cut bronchopulmonary dysplasia from 47% to 36%.
cards.summary: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (oxygen at 36 weeks) 36% caffeine vs 47% placebo, adjusted OR 0.63 (0.52–0.76); death, brain injury on ultrasound, and necrotizing enterocolitis did not differ significantly.
cards.people: 2,006 infants, international NICUs
cards.result: Bronchopulmonary dysplasia (oxygen at 36 weeks) 36% caffeine vs 47% placebo, adjusted OR 0.63 (0.52–0.76); death, brain injury on ultrasound, and necrotizing enterocolitis did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: a short-term lung outcome; the disability question needed the follow-ups (Reference 2) — and caffeine became universal NICU practice on this trial.
cards.source: Schmidt B et al., N Engl J Med 2006 (PMID 16707748 · NCT00182312)

cards.headline: The CAP follow-ups: an 18-month disability benefit that faded by age 5.
cards.summary: At 18–21 months, death or disability 40.2% caffeine vs 46.2% placebo, adjusted OR 0.77 (0.64–0.93), P=0.008 — cerebral palsy 4.4% vs 7.3%, cognitive delay 33.8% vs 38.3%; at 5 years, death or disability 21.1% vs 24.8%, adjusted OR 0.82 (0.65–1.03), P=0.09 — no longer significant, with cognitive impairment similar (4.9% vs 5.1%).
cards.type: prespecified follow-up analyses of the Card 1 cohort at 18–21 months and at 5 years
cards.people: 1,869 children with outcome data at 18–21 months; 1,640 at 5 years
cards.result: At 18–21 months, death or disability 40.2% caffeine vs 46.2% placebo, adjusted OR 0.77 (0.64–0.93), P=0.008 — cerebral palsy 4.4% vs 7.3%, cognitive delay 33.8% vs 38.3%; at 5 years, death or disability 21.1% vs 24.8%, adjusted OR 0.82 (0.65–1.03), P=0.09 — no longer significant, with cognitive impairment similar (4.9% vs 5.1%).
cards.watchOut: follow-ups of one trial, not new evidence — the early neuro benefit was real and it attenuated; both halves of that sentence belong on the card.
cards.source: Schmidt B et al., N Engl J Med 2007 (PMID 17989382) and JAMA 2012 (PMID 22253394)

shelves.title: Fluids in childhood DKA: the PECARN trial
shelves.question: In children with diabetic ketoacidosis, do the rate and the sodium content of IV fluids affect brain injury?
shelves.mesh: Diabetic Ketoacidosis · Brain Edema · Brain Injuries · Fluid Therapy · Rehydration Solutions · Sodium Chloride · Infusions, Intravenous · Drug Administration Schedule · Glasgow Coma Scale · Child · Child, Preschool · Adolescent · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: For a generation, fear of cerebral edema throttled fluids in childhood DKA. The largest randomized test of that fear — fast versus slow, full versus half saline — found nothing: brain outcomes were the same at every speed and every salt.

cards.headline: PECARN FLUID (Kuppermann 2018): fast or slow, saline or half-saline — no difference in brain outcomes.
cards.summary: Glasgow Coma Scale below 14 during treatment in 3.5% of episodes overall and clinically apparent brain injury in 0.9% — with NO significant differences among the four arms in GCS decline, brain injury, memory scores at 2–6 months, or IQ; protocol adherence was excellent and the crossover-excluded re-analysis was also null.
cards.type: randomized 2×2 factorial trial (13 PECARN emergency departments)
cards.people: 1,389 DKA episodes in 1,255 children
cards.result: Glasgow Coma Scale below 14 during treatment in 3.5% of episodes overall and clinically apparent brain injury in 0.9% — with NO significant differences among the four arms in GCS decline, brain injury, memory scores at 2–6 months, or IQ; protocol adherence was excellent and the crossover-excluded re-analysis was also null.
cards.watchOut: children with GCS ≤11 at presentation were excluded — the sickest brains are outside this evidence; “no difference found” within the rates tested, not a licence for unlimited speed.
cards.source: Kuppermann N et al., N Engl J Med 2018 (PMID 29897851 · NCT00629707)

shelves.title: Replacing sugary drinks in children and teenagers: works while it lasts
shelves.question: Does replacing sugar-sweetened drinks with sugar-free drinks slow weight gain in children and teenagers?
shelves.balance: Replacing sugary drinks with sugar-free ones slowed weight gain while the substitution lasted; the effect faded once the intervention stopped. A maintenance problem, not a one-time fix. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE — modest and maintenance-dependent.

cards.headline: DRINK: sugar-free drinks in identical cans slowed weight gain over 18 months — while the swap lasted
cards.summary: BMI z-score rose 0.02 vs 0.15 SD units; weight gain 6.35 vs 7.37 kg over 18 months.
cards.people: 641 children aged 5–12; 18 months of sugar-free vs sugared drinks in identical cans
cards.result: BMI z-score rose 0.02 vs 0.15 SD units; weight gain 6.35 vs 7.37 kg.
cards.watchOut: Genuinely blinded — the drinks came in identical masked cans, rare for a diet trial. The benefit is a slower rise in weight, not weight loss.
cards.source: de Ruyter et al. (DRINK). N Engl J Med. 2012;367:1397–1406. PMID 22998340 · NCT00893529.

cards.headline: Ebbeling 2012: ahead at 1 year, caught up by 2 — the gap closed when the deliveries stopped
cards.summary: BMI change at 2 years was not significant (−0.3, P=0.46); at 1 year the intervention group was ahead (BMI difference −0.57, P=0.045; weight −1.9 kg, P=0.04).
cards.people: 224 overweight or obese adolescents; home delivery of noncaloric drinks with counseling vs control
cards.result: Primary endpoint, BMI change at 2 years, was not significant (−0.3, P=0.46); at 1 year the intervention group was ahead (BMI difference −0.57, P=0.045; weight −1.9 kg, P=0.04), a gap that closed after deliveries stopped.

shelves.title: Zinc for acute diarrhea in young children
shelves.question: Does oral zinc shorten acute diarrhea in young children?
shelves.balance: Zinc shortens episodes and cuts prolonged diarrhea in young children in low-income settings — two double-blind trials and a very large community trial agree, and this is the basis of the WHO recommendation. But a hospital-based trial in India found no effect, so the benefit is not universal: it tracks with deficiency-prone, community populations. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE — consistent benefit in community, low-income settings; not shown in every setting.

cards.headline: Sazawal 1995: zinc cut the risk of continued diarrhea by 23% in young children in New Delhi
cards.summary: Risk of continued diarrhea was 23% lower with zinc (95% CI 12–32%); episodes lasting more than 7 days were 39% fewer when zinc was started within 3 days.
cards.people: 937 children aged 6–35 months in New Delhi; zinc or placebo with standard care
cards.result: Risk of continued diarrhea was 23% lower with zinc (95% CI 12–32%); episodes lasting more than 7 days were 39% fewer when zinc was started within 3 days.
cards.watchOut: A community population in a setting where zinc deficiency is common — the setting the benefit tracks with (see Card 4).
cards.source: Sazawal et al. N Engl J Med. 1995;333:839–844. PMID 7651474 · no registry ID (pre-registration era).

cards.people: 684 children aged 6 months to 2 years at a Dhaka hospital with acute watery diarrhea of 3 days or less and some dehydration; zinc (with or without vitamin A) for 15 days vs controls

cards.headline: Patel 2009 — the dissenting trial: no difference in diarrhea duration at a Nagpur hospital
cards.summary: Mean diarrhea duration was 63.7 hours with no significant differences across the groups. The expected benefit of zinc was not observed here.
cards.people: 808 children aged 6–59 months at a Nagpur hospital with acute diarrhea; zinc, zinc plus copper, or placebo with standard treatment
cards.result: Mean diarrhea duration was 63.7 hours with no significant differences across the groups. The expected benefit of zinc was not observed here.

shelves.balance: In bronchiolitis, almost nothing beaten in a trial beats supportive care. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE — for the negative claims.

shelves.title: Acute otitis media: do antibiotics beat placebo in young children?
shelves.question: Do antibiotics beat placebo in young children with acute otitis media?
shelves.mesh: Otitis Media · Amoxicillin · Amoxicillin-Potassium Clavulanate Combination · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Child, Preschool · Infant · Humans
shelves.balance: In strictly diagnosed otitis media in children under 3, amoxicillin or amoxicillin-clavulanate roughly halves treatment failure; about 1 child in 5 treated gets diarrhea or rash. Where diagnosis is loose, the advantage shrinks toward a number-needed-to-treat of about 11–20. Developer’s verdict: LIKELY.

shelves.title: After a first febrile UTI: does antibiotic prophylaxis prevent recurrences?
shelves.question: After a first febrile urinary tract infection, does antibiotic prophylaxis prevent recurrences?
shelves.mesh: Urinary Tract Infections · Vesico-Ureteral Reflux · Trimethoprim, Sulfamethoxazole Drug Combination · Antibiotic Prophylaxis · Recurrence · Child · Humans
shelves.balance: Continuous low-dose prophylaxis halves recurrences while a child takes it — about 13% vs 24% in the largest trial — but has not been shown to prevent kidney scarring, and the recurrences that break through are far more often drug-resistant. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE–LIKELY — population-dependent.

shelves.mesh: Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infections · Antibodies, Monoclonal · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Palivizumab · Infant · Humans

shelves.title: Probiotics to prevent necrotizing enterocolitis in preterm infants
shelves.question: Do probiotics prevent necrotizing enterocolitis in preterm infants?
shelves.mesh: Enterocolitis, Necrotizing · Probiotics · Infant, Premature · Infant, Very Low Birth Weight · Infant, Newborn · Humans
shelves.balance: The answer depends on the strain. Two Taiwanese trials of specific combinations or single strains found less death-or-NEC; a large UK trial of Bifidobacterium breve BBG-001 found nothing, and a Turkish Lactobacillus sporogenes trial found nothing. There is no class effect to claim. Developer’s verdict: MAYBE (weak evidence).

shelves.title: Magnesium sulfate before preterm birth: protecting the baby’s brain
shelves.question: Does magnesium sulfate given before preterm birth protect the baby’s brain?
shelves.mesh: Magnesium Sulfate · Cerebral Palsy · Infant, Premature · Obstetric Labor, Premature · Pregnancy · Female · Humans
shelves.balance: Magnesium given to the mother before early preterm birth lowers moderate-to-severe cerebral palsy in survivors — 1.9% vs 3.5% in the largest trial — without lowering death. The benefit claim rests on that secondary outcome; the one older high-dose tocolytic-era trial pointed the other way. Developer’s verdict: LIKELY.

shelves.title: Febrile seizures: can medicine at fever onset stop the next one?
shelves.question: Can medicine at fever onset stop the next febrile seizure?
shelves.mesh: Seizures, Febrile · Diazepam · Ibuprofen · Acetaminophen · Diclofenac · Child, Preschool · Humans
shelves.balance: Antipyretics do not prevent febrile-seizure recurrence — three randomized trials agree, including one where recurrence was 23.4% with antipyretics and 23.5% with placebo. Intermittent diazepam works, but at the price of sedation in about a third of children. Developer’s verdict: LIKELY — for the antipyretic negative.

shelves.title: More time outdoors: does it delay myopia in children?
shelves.question: Does more time outdoors delay myopia in children?
shelves.mesh: Myopia · Schools · Recreation · Child · Humans
shelves.balance: Adding outdoor time at school reduced new myopia onset in all three randomized studies — by about 9 percentage points over three years in the largest — without slowing progression in children already myopic. The claim is reduced onset in schoolchildren, not protection for any one child. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE–LIKELY.

cards.result: Three-year cumulative myopia incidence 30.4% vs 39.5% (a 9.1-point absolute difference; 23% relative reduction); progression in children already myopic was no different.

shelves.title: Cooling the newborn brain after oxygen deprivation (HIE)
shelves.question: Does cooling a term or near-term newborn with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy improve outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Hypoxia-Ischemia, Brain · Hypothermia, Induced · Infant, Newborn · Humans
shelves.balance: Cooling a term or near-term newborn with moderate-to-severe hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy to about 33.5 °C for 72 hours lowers death or major disability — 44% vs 62% in the first big trial. shelves.title: Rotavirus vaccination: efficacy where the burden is, and where it isn’t
shelves.question: How well does rotavirus vaccination prevent severe disease — where the burden is, and where it isn’t?
shelves.mesh: Rotavirus Infections · Rotavirus Vaccines · Gastroenteritis · Infant · Humans
shelves.balance: Two large vaccine programs prevent most severe rotavirus disease. Efficacy against severe disease is highest in wealthy settings (85–98% relative) and lower in high-mortality settings (about 42–61% relative) — but because baseline risk is so much higher there, the number of severe cases prevented per 100 vaccinated children is larger, not smaller. Developer’s verdict: LIKELY.

shelves.title: Peanut oral immunotherapy: desensitization is LIKELY — net benefit only POSSIBLE, because the treatment itself causes the reactions it guards against
shelves.question: Does peanut oral immunotherapy protect children with peanut allergy — and what does the protection cost?
shelves.mesh: Peanut Hypersensitivity · Desensitization, Immunologic · Allergens · Arachis · Immune Tolerance · Quality of Life · Humans · Child
shelves.balance: This is the shelf Shelf #1's prevention index points to ('Food allergy — preventing reactions'), and its split stamp is the honest summary of a genuinely two-sided literature. Desensitization is LIKELY and large: two-thirds of 4–17-year-olds tolerated a 600 mg challenge after AR101 vs 4% on placebo (PALISADE, Card 1), and starting at age 1–3 produced desensitization in 71% and — uniquely — remission after avoidance in 21% (IMPACT, Card 2). Net benefit is only POSSIBLE, because the harm side is at full weight on Card 3: across 12 trials, OIT increased anaphylaxis (RR 3.12, relative; +15.1 points absolute) and epinephrine use, and did not improve quality of life. The therapy trades accidental-exposure risk for scheduled, treatment-caused reactions; whether that trade serves a given child depends on their exposure risk, reaction history, and family — which is why the stamp refuses to collapse the two halves into one word. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: PALISADE (Vickery 2018): 67.2% vs 4.0% tolerated a 600 mg peanut challenge after AR101 — desensitization proven in ages 4–17, NOT shown at 18+
cards.summary: 551 participants aged 4–55, all reacting at ≤100 mg of peanut protein at entry: among the 496 aged 4–17, 67.2% on AR101 vs 4.0% on placebo could ingest ≥600 mg without dose-limiting symptoms at the exit challenge (difference 63.2 points [53.0–73.3]; P<0.001), and reaction severity at exit was lower. Efficacy was not shown in participants 18 or older. The burden side, at full weight: adverse events touched >95% of the active group during treatment; moderate events in 59.7% vs 44.4%, severe events in 4.3% vs 0.8%. Desensitization — protection while taking the drug daily — is what this trial proved; it is not a cure, and it is not remission.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (PALISADE), N Engl J Med 2018. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT02635776.
cards.people: 551 participants aged 4 to 55 years with peanut allergy who reacted at a challenge dose of 100 mg or less of peanut protein; the primary efficacy population was the 496 participants aged 4 to 17 (372 active, 124 placebo), treated with escalating doses then 300 mg daily for approximately 24 weeks. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: Of the participants aged 4 to 17, 250 of 372 (67.2%) on active treatment vs 5 of 124 (4.0%) on placebo ingested a dose of 600 mg or more of peanut protein without dose-limiting symptoms at the exit food challenge (difference 63.2 percentage points [53.0–73.3]; P<0.001). During the exit challenge, maximum symptom severity was moderate in 25% (active) vs 59% (placebo) and severe in 5% vs 11%. During the intervention period, adverse events affected more than 95% of participants aged 4–17; events were graded mild in 34.7% (active) vs 50.0% (placebo), moderate in 59.7% vs 44.4%, and severe in 4.3% vs 0.8%. Efficacy was not shown in participants 18 years of age or older.
cards.watchOut: PALISADE's endpoint is a supervised challenge, not real-world reaction prevention — the trial shows a raised threshold while on daily therapy, in the age band 4–17 only. The treatment itself causes allergic reactions in nearly everyone who takes it; whether that trade is worth it is the shelf's actual question, and Cards 2 and 3 exist to keep this card's big percentage honest.

cards.headline: IMPACT (Jones 2022): starting before age 4 — desensitization 71% vs 2%, and remission after 6 months off therapy 21% vs 2%
cards.summary: 146 children aged 12 to <48 months, reactive to ≤500 mg of peanut protein: after 134 weeks of peanut OIT (2,000 mg daily), desensitization on a 5,000 mg challenge was 71% (68/96) vs 2% (1/50) (risk difference 69% [59–79]); after 26 weeks of avoidance, remission was 21% (20/96) vs 2% (1/50) (risk difference 19% [10–28], P=0.0021) — and remission clustered in the youngest children with the lowest starting peanut IgE. A significant share of the desensitized children had already lost their 5,000 mg tolerance by week 160. The harm ledger: dosing reactions in 98% vs 80% , and 35 moderate dosing events were treated with epinephrine in 21 OIT participants .
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (IMPACT, Immune Tolerance Network), Lancet 2022 — five US academic centres; 134 weeks of treatment then 26 weeks of avoidance. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT03345160.
cards.people: 146 children aged 12 to younger than 48 months (median age 39.3 months [IQR 30.8–44.7]) who reacted to 500 mg or less of peanut protein at entry challenge: 96 assigned to peanut oral immunotherapy, 50 to placebo. The record does not state a sex split.
cards.result: At week 134, 68 (71% [61–80]) of 96 participants on peanut OIT vs 1 (2% [0.05–11]) of 50 on placebo met the primary outcome of desensitisation (risk difference 69% [59–79]; P<0.0001); the median cumulative tolerated dose was 5,005 mg vs 5 mg. After avoidance, 20 (21% [13–30]) of 96 vs 1 (2%) of 50 met remission criteria (risk difference 19% [10–28]; P=0.0021); the median tolerated dose at week 160 was 755 mg vs 0 mg. Younger age and lower baseline peanut-specific IgE predicted remission. Most participants (98% OIT vs 80% placebo) had at least one dosing reaction, predominantly mild to moderate and more frequent on OIT; 35 OIT dosing events with moderate symptoms were treated with epinephrine in 21 participants.
cards.watchOut: IMPACT is the strongest argument for early OIT and the clearest statement of its limits, in one trial: start at 1–3 years and a fifth of children are still non-reactive six months after stopping — but four-fifths are not, protection decays measurably within those 26 weeks, and the protocol itself required epinephrine for moderate reactions in over a fifth of treated toddlers. Remission here means passing a challenge after avoidance, not a guarantee against future reactions.
cards.source: Jones SM et al. Efficacy and safety of oral immunotherapy in children aged 1–3 years with peanut allergy (the Immune Tolerance Network IMPACT trial): a randomised placebo-controlled study. Lancet. 2022;399:359–371. cards.headline: PACE meta-analysis (Chu 2019): the harm side at full weight — anaphylaxis RR 3.12 (relative), epinephrine use RR 2.21, quality of life NOT improved
cards.summary: Across 12 randomized trials (1,041 patients; median age 8.7 years), peanut OIT vs avoidance/placebo increased anaphylaxis risk ( RR 3.12 [1.76–5.55] , relative; absolute risk difference 15.1%, high-certainty), anaphylaxis frequency (incidence rate ratio 2.72; RD 12.2%), and epinephrine use ( RR 2.21 [1.27–3.83] , relative; RD 4.5%). Serious adverse events rose (RR 1.92, RD 5.7%, moderate-certainty). Passing a supervised challenge — the surrogate for protection — was far more likely (RR 12.42; RD 36.5%, high-certainty). And the outcome families feel daily, quality of life, was not different between groups (low-certainty). The reviewers' conclusion is carded verbatim in spirit: regimens 'considerably increase allergic and anaphylactic reactions over avoidance or placebo, despite effectively inducing desensitisation.'
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 randomized trials (PACE — Peanut Allergen immunotherapy, Clarifying the Evidence), Lancet 2019; GRADE-assessed. Registered with PROSPERO (CRD42019117930), as stated in the record; the record carries no ClinicalTrials.gov databank entry.
cards.people: 12 randomized trials with 1,041 patients with peanut allergy (median age across trials 8.7 years [IQR 5.9–11.2]) comparing oral immunotherapy with allergen avoidance or placebo. No pooled sex split is stated in the record.
cards.result: Oral immunotherapy vs no oral immunotherapy increased anaphylaxis risk (RR 3.12 [1.76–5.55], I²=0%, risk difference 15.1%, high-certainty), anaphylaxis frequency (incidence rate ratio 2.72 [1.57–4.72], RD 12.2%, high-certainty), and epinephrine use (RR 2.21 [1.27–3.83], RD 4.5%, high-certainty), similarly during build-up and maintenance. Serious adverse events increased (RR 1.92 [1.00–3.66], RD 5.7%, moderate-certainty), as did vomiting (RR 1.79), angioedema (RR 2.25), and upper-respiratory reactions (RR 1.36). Passing a supervised challenge was more likely with OIT (RR 12.42 [6.82–22.61], RD 36.5%, high-certainty). Quality of life was not different between groups (low-certainty).
cards.watchOut: PACE is why this shelf carries a split stamp. The trials' primary currency — passing a food challenge — is a surrogate; on the outcomes that happen in kitchens and schoolyards, OIT as trialed caused more anaphylaxis and more epinephrine use than avoidance did, and did not measurably improve quality of life. A family choosing OIT is buying a raised reaction threshold with daily dosing reactions as the price; this card exists so that price is never quoted second-hand or softened.

shelves.title: Milk oral immunotherapy: most children can be desensitized — remission is fragile, reactions are part of the treatment, and nature resolves many cases anyway
shelves.question: A child is allergic to cow's milk. Does feeding tiny, rising doses of milk under supervision free them — or just trade avoidance for a treatment that itself causes reactions?
shelves.mesh: Milk Hypersensitivity · Desensitization, Immunologic · Milk · Immune Tolerance · Immunoglobulin E · Humans
shelves.balance: Milk OIT desensitizes: about six in ten treated children in the early trials could drink a full serving of milk, against fewer than one in ten controls (Reference 1) — graded POSSIBLE as a single grade. Three cautions ride on the same shelf. The protection is rented, not owned: two to eight weeks after stopping a successful course, only about a third of patients in the World Allergy Organization's synthesis still tolerated milk (Reference 2). The treatment causes the disease's own events — anaphylaxis and epinephrine use are far more frequent on OIT than on avoidance (Reference 2). And the comparison is never against nothing: in a large referral cohort, milk allergy resolved on its own in 19% of children by age 4 and 79% by age 16 (Reference 3), so some of every OIT cohort's 'successes' were going to happen anyway. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: Milk OIT desensitizes most children (Yeung 2012, Cochrane): a full serving tolerated by 62% vs 8% — with symptoms in nearly everyone treated
cards.summary: Five small randomized trials, 196 children with IgE-mediated cow's-milk allergy: 62% of the milk-OIT group (66 of 106) could tolerate a full serving of milk (~200 mL) vs 8% of controls (7 of 90) — RR 6.61 [3.51–12.44], a relative effect printed beside its absolute rates. Another 25% on OIT could manage a partial serving vs none on control. The cost side is not incidental: 97 of 106 treated children had at least one symptom during treatment (most local and mild), and for every 11 children treated, one needed intramuscular epinephrine. No included study checked whether tolerance survived a period off therapy — that question belongs to Card 2.
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomized controlled trials (Yeung 2012, CD009542). Systematic review — no registry number applies.
cards.people: 196 children with IgE-mediated cow's-milk allergy across five trials (106 OIT, 90 control), each trial using a different protocol; the reviewers rated the overall quality of evidence low.
cards.result: Sixty-six patients (62%) in the MOIT group were able to tolerate a full serving of milk (about 200 mL) compared to seven (8%) of the control group (RR 6.61, 95% CI 3.51 to 12.44). In addition, 27 (25%) in the MOIT group could ingest a partial serving of milk (10 to 184 mL) while none could in the control group (RR 9.34, 95% CI 2.72 to 32.09). None of the studies assessed patients following a period off immunotherapy. Adverse reactions were common (97 of 106 MOIT patients had at least one symptom), although most were local and mild; for every 11 patients receiving MOIT, one required intramuscular epinephrine.
cards.watchOut: Five small trials, five different protocols, low-quality evidence — 'milk OIT' in 2012 was a family of recipes, not a standardized treatment. Desensitization measured at a challenge while still dosing says nothing about the child who stops; and a 1-in-11 epinephrine rate during treatment is the number a family should hear before the 62%.

cards.headline: After stopping, tolerance usually evaporates — and OIT multiplies anaphylaxis and epinephrine use (WAO DRACMA systematic review 2022)
cards.summary: The World Allergy Organization's updated synthesis (13 randomized trials, 109 observational studies) found low-certainty evidence that OIT with unheated cow's milk raised the chance of consuming ≥150 mL (RR 12.3 [5.9–26.0], relative). But 2–8 weeks after discontinuing a successful course, tolerance persisted in only 36% of patients (range 20–91%). The harm ledger is quantified: anaphylaxis occurred at 60 times the rate on avoidance (rate ratio 60.0 [15–244]; moderate-certainty evidence — about 5 more anaphylactic reactions per person per year), epinephrine use at 35 times the rate (rate ratio 35.2 [9–136.5]; high-certainty), gastrointestinal symptoms RR 6.9 [1.6–30.9], and eosinophilic-esophagitis-like reactions are part of the treated picture. Desensitization is real; so is the reaction burden that buys it.
cards.type: Systematic review for the World Allergy Organization DRACMA guideline update (Bognanni 2022). Systematic review — no registry number applies; the review protocol was registered on the Open Science Framework (10.17605/OSF.IO/AH2DT), as stated in its record.
cards.people: Patients with IgE-mediated cow's-milk allergy in 13 randomized trials and 109 observational studies published between 2010 and 2021.
cards.result: Low-certainty evidence that OIT with unheated cow's milk, compared with elimination diet alone, increased the likelihood of being able to consume ≥150 mL of cow's milk in controlled settings (RR 12.3, 95% CI 5.9 to 26.0; risk difference 25 more per 100) and to accidentally ingest a small amount (≥5 mL; RR 8.7, 95% CI 4.7 to 16.1). Two to eight weeks after discontinuation of successful OIT, tolerance persisted in only 36% (range 20%–91%). OIT increased anaphylaxis frequency (rate ratio 60.0, 95% CI 15 to 244; moderate evidence) and epinephrine use (rate ratio 35.2, 95% CI 9 to 136.5; high certainty), gastrointestinal symptoms (RR 6.9, 95% CI 1.6 to 30.9), and respiratory symptoms.
cards.watchOut: Rate ratios of 60 and 35 are relative measures on a low baseline — the review's own absolute translation, about 5 extra anaphylactic reactions per person-year of treatment, is the figure to quote to families. The 36% persistence figure pools protocols stopped for different lengths of time; the 20–91% range is the honest part. The longest follow-up of the original trial cohorts (Keet 2013, JACI; PMID 23806635) is a letter whose PubMed record prints no abstract, so this shelf cards no numbers from it.

cards.headline: The context card: milk allergy often resolves on its own (Skripak 2007) — 19% by age 4, 79% by age 16 in a referral cohort
cards.summary: In 807 children with IgE-mediated cow's-milk allergy followed at a referral center, tolerance developed in 19% by age 4 years, 42% by age 8, 64% by age 12, and 79% by age 16 . The prognosis was worse than older studies had suggested, and the peak cow's-milk IgE level strongly predicted who would persist (P<0.001), as did coexisting asthma and allergic rhinitis. This card is the shelf's denominator: any uncontrolled claim that OIT 'cured' a group of children must first subtract the children who were going to outgrow the allergy untreated.
cards.type: Natural-history cohort study (Skripak 2007) — observational, labeled as such. No registry number applies.
cards.people: 807 patients with IgE-mediated cow's-milk allergy at a referral center; tolerance defined as passing a challenge or no reactions in the past 12 months with cow's-milk IgE <3 kU/L.
cards.result: Rates of resolution were 19% by age 4 years, 42% by age 8 years, 64% by age 12 years, and 79% by 16 years. Patients with persistent allergy had higher cow's-milk IgE levels at all ages; the peak IgE level was highly predictive of outcome (P < .001). Coexisting asthma (P < .001) and allergic rhinitis (P < .001) were also significant predictors of persistence.
cards.watchOut: A referral population is sicker than the average allergic toddler — community resolution rates are likely faster, which strengthens rather than weakens this card's point. Natural history also cuts the other way for the persistent minority: a child whose milk IgE stays high is exactly the child for whom waiting is not a plan, and the one OIT trials should be enrolling.

shelves.title: Egg oral immunotherapy: desensitization is LIKELY — sustained unresponsiveness after stopping is only POSSIBLE, and the gap between the two is the shelf
shelves.question: Egg is in everything. Can oral immunotherapy free a child with egg allergy — and does the freedom survive stopping the treatment?
shelves.mesh: Egg Hypersensitivity · Desensitization, Immunologic · Eggs · Immunoglobulin E · Immunoglobulin G · Humans
shelves.balance: The NEJM trial (Reference 1) draws the line this shelf is built on: after 22 months of egg OIT, 75% of children passed a 10 g egg-white challenge while on therapy — but after 4–6 weeks off it, only 28% still passed. Desensitization is common; remission is the minority outcome. Longer treatment buys more remission: by year 4 of the same program (Reference 2), 50% had achieved sustained unresponsiveness, and those who had were eating egg freely years later. The reactions along the way were mostly oral and gastrointestinal, with mild symptoms in over half of children still dosing in years 3–4. Quote the two numbers together — 75% and 28% — or do not quote either. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: Burks 2012 (NEJM): 75% desensitized at 22 months — 28% still unresponsive after 4–6 weeks off therapy
cards.summary: Fifty-five children aged 5–11 with egg allergy, randomized to egg-white powder OIT (n=40) or placebo (n=15). After 10 months, 55% of the OIT group passed a 10 g oral food challenge vs 0% on placebo ; after 22 months, 75% were desensitized . Those who passed then stopped OIT and avoided egg for 4–6 weeks: at 24 months, 28% (11 of 40) passed again and were classed as having sustained unresponsiveness — and every one of them was still eating egg at 30 and 36 months. The desensitization–remission gap (75% → 28%) is printed in the headline because it is the finding families most need and summaries most often omit.
cards.type: Double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial (Burks 2012, NEJM; CoFAR). Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT00461097.
cards.people: 55 children, 5 to 11 years of age, with egg allergy: 40 received oral immunotherapy with egg-white powder, 15 placebo.
cards.result: After 10 months of therapy, none of the children who received placebo and 55% of those who received oral immunotherapy passed the oral food challenge and were considered desensitized; after 22 months, 75% of children in the oral-immunotherapy group were desensitized. In the oral-immunotherapy group, 28% (11 of 40 children) passed the oral food challenge at 24 months, after 4 to 6 weeks off therapy, and were considered to have sustained unresponsiveness. At 30 months and 36 months, all children who had passed the challenge at 24 months were consuming egg. Small skin-prick wheal diameters and increases in egg-specific IgG4 were associated with passing the 24-month challenge.
cards.watchOut: The placebo arm is small (15 children), so its 0% pass rate is a coarse anchor. The record's abstract does not tabulate adverse-event rates; symptoms during long-term dosing are quantified in the follow-up (Reference 2). And 'sustained unresponsiveness' here means passing a challenge after 4–6 weeks off therapy — a stricter test than still-dosing desensitization, a looser one than lifelong tolerance.

cards.headline: Four years of egg OIT (Jones 2016): sustained unresponsiveness rises to 50% — longer treatment converts desensitization into remission for some
cards.summary: The long-term extension of the Burks trial (same registry): of 40 children treated with egg OIT for up to 4 years, 20 (50.0%) achieved sustained unresponsiveness by year 4 , up from 27.5% at 2 years. At follow-up questionnaires after the study ended, 68% (LFQ-1) and 64% (LFQ-2) of the OIT group were eating unbaked and baked egg vs 18% and 25% of the placebo group — and 100% of those who had achieved SU and completed follow-up were eating all forms of egg. The cost across years 3–4: mild symptoms in 54.5% of the 22 children still dosing . Duration is the lever — remission accrues slowly, and half the cohort still had not reached it at four years.
cards.type: Long-term follow-up of a randomized placebo-controlled trial (Jones 2016, JACI; CoFAR). Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT00461097.
cards.people: Children with egg allergy, 5–18 years: egg OIT (n=40) for up to 4 years, or placebo (n=15) for 1 year or less; long-term follow-up questionnaires after study conclusion and 1 year later.
cards.result: Of 40 eOIT-treated subjects, 20 (50.0%) demonstrated sustained unresponsiveness by year 4. For those still dosing during years 3 and 4, mild symptoms were present in 12 (54.5%) of 22 subjects. At follow-up, more eOIT subjects (LFQ-1, 23/34 [68%]; LFQ-2, 21/33 [64%]) were consuming unbaked and baked egg versus placebo (LFQ-1, 2/11 [18%], P=.006; LFQ-2, 3/12 [25%], P=.04). Of subjects achieving SU, 18 (90%) of 20 completed the LFQ, with 18 (100%) of 18 reporting consumption of all forms of egg. SU was associated with higher IgG4 values (P=.001), lower egg skin-prick scores (P=.0002), and a lower median baseline egg-specific IgE to total IgE ratio (1.1% vs 2.7%, P=.04).
cards.watchOut: After year 1 the placebo group left the blinded comparison, so the year-4 figures are a treated cohort's trajectory, not a randomized contrast — and the denominators shrink as the committed remain (34 and 33 questionnaire respondents). The biomarker associations (IgG4, skin tests, IgE ratio) are markers of who reached SU, not yet a selection rule for who should start.

shelves.title: Early introduction of allergenic foods: in high-risk infants, feeding peanut early prevents the allergy — for the general population the proof is thinner
shelves.question: For decades the advice was delay. Do the randomized trials say feeding allergenic foods early — peanut, egg — prevents food allergy instead?
shelves.mesh: Peanut Hypersensitivity · Egg Hypersensitivity · Food Hypersensitivity · Arachis · Eczema · Infant · Humans
shelves.balance: LEAP (Reference 1) is the strongest prevention result in this library's allergy wing: in infants with severe eczema or egg allergy, eating peanut from infancy cut peanut allergy at age 5 from 13.7% to 1.9% in the skin-test-negative stratum — and the protection persisted through a full year of complete avoidance (Reference 2). EAT (Reference 3) asked the general-population question and its intention-to-treat answer was null; early introduction worked only in the families who actually managed it, which in an unselected population was the minority. PETIT (Reference 4) extends the principle to heated egg in infants with eczema, at the price of more hospital admissions in the egg group. Prevention is the correct word on this shelf: these trials prevented allergy from developing; they treated nothing. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: LEAP (Du Toit 2015, NEJM): peanut allergy at age 5 — 1.9% with early consumption vs 13.7% with avoidance in the skin-test-negative stratum
cards.summary: 640 infants aged 4–11 months with severe eczema, egg allergy, or both, randomized to consume peanut regularly or avoid it until age 5. Among the 530 infants with a negative peanut skin-prick test at entry, peanut allergy at 60 months: 1.9% (consumption) vs 13.7% (avoidance) , P<0.001 — an 11.8-point absolute difference. Among the 98 with a positive test (1–4 mm wheal), the same direction: 10.6% vs 35.3% , P=0.004. There was no significant difference in serious adverse events. This is a true prevention trial — the outcome is an allergy that never developed.
cards.type: Randomized, controlled prevention trial (LEAP; Du Toit 2015, NEJM). Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT00329784.
cards.people: 640 infants at high risk (severe eczema and/or egg allergy), enrolled at 4–11 months and assigned by baseline peanut skin-prick result: 530 with no measurable wheal and 98 with a 1–4 mm wheal in the intention-to-treat population.
cards.result: Among the 530 infants in the intention-to-treat population who initially had negative results on the skin-prick test, the prevalence of peanut allergy at 60 months of age was 13.7% in the avoidance group and 1.9% in the consumption group (P<0.001). Among the 98 participants who initially had positive test results, the prevalence was 35.3% in the avoidance group and 10.6% in the consumption group (P=0.004). There was no significant between-group difference in the incidence of serious adverse events. Increases in peanut-specific IgG4 occurred predominantly in the consumption group.
cards.watchOut: The population is the fence: these were screened, high-risk infants enrolled after skin testing — the result licenses early introduction in that setting, not unsupervised home feeding of a baby who has already reacted to peanut. The design was open-label (families knew the assignment), with an independently assessed endpoint. The general-population version of this question is Card 3, and it did not answer the same way.

cards.headline: LEAP-On (2016): after 12 months of complete peanut avoidance, the protection held — 4.8% vs 18.6% at age 6
cards.summary: LEAP's participants were followed after the main trial: all were instructed to avoid peanut completely for 12 months, to age 6. Peanut allergy at 72 months remained far less prevalent in the early-consumption group: 4.8% (13 of 270) vs 18.6% (52 of 280) , P<0.001. In the consumption group the rate barely moved during the avoidance year (3.6% at 60 months to 4.8% at 72 months, P=0.25), with three new cases in each group. Early consumption had induced something durable — not a desensitization that needed daily feeding to survive.
cards.type: Prospective follow-up study of a randomized trial (LEAP-On; Du Toit 2016, NEJM). Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT01366846.
cards.people: 556 of 628 eligible LEAP participants (88.5%) enrolled in the follow-up; 550 (98.9%) had complete primary-outcome data. Adherence to the avoidance year was 90.4% in the peanut-avoidance group and 69.3% in the peanut-consumption group.
cards.result: Peanut allergy at 72 months was significantly more prevalent among participants in the peanut-avoidance group than among those in the peanut-consumption group (18.6% [52 of 280 participants] vs 4.8% [13 of 270], P<0.001). Three new cases of allergy developed in each group; after 12 months of avoidance there was no significant increase in the prevalence of allergy among participants in the consumption group (3.6% [10 of 274] at 60 months and 4.8% [13 of 270] at 72 months, P=0.25). Participants in the consumption group continued to have higher peanut-specific IgG4 and IgG4:IgE ratios.
cards.watchOut: Durability is shown for 12 months of avoidance, not for a childhood — the record itself states that longer-term effects are not known. The consumption group's lower adherence to the avoidance year (69.3%) would, if anything, bias against the persistence finding.
cards.source: Du Toit G et al. Effect of avoidance on peanut allergy after early peanut consumption. N Engl J Med. 2016;374(15):1435–1443. PMID 26942922 · NCT01366846 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1514209

cards.headline: EAT (Perkin 2016, NEJM): the general-population trial was NULL on intention-to-treat — 5.6% vs 7.1%, P=0.32 — positive only per-protocol
cards.summary: 1,303 exclusively breast-fed infants from the general population, randomized at 3 months to early introduction of six allergenic foods (peanut, cooked egg, cow's milk, sesame, whitefish, wheat) or standard introduction (~6 months). The primary intention-to-treat result was null: food allergy to one or more of the six foods between 1 and 3 years developed in 5.6% of the early group (32 of 567) vs 7.1% of the standard group (42 of 595), P=0.32. In the per-protocol analysis the early group did better (any food allergy 2.4% vs 7.3%, P=0.01; peanut 0% vs 2.5%, P=0.003; egg 1.4% vs 5.5%, P=0.009), and consuming ≥2 g per week of peanut or egg-white protein tracked with lower allergy — but per-protocol here means the families who actually sustained six new foods in a young infant's diet, a self-selected minority. The intervention was safe; achieving it was the problem.
cards.type: Randomized trial (EAT — Enquiring About Tolerance; Perkin 2016, NEJM). Registry verified against the record's own databank: ISRCTN14254740.
cards.people: 1,303 exclusively breast-fed infants from the general population (not selected for eczema or allergy risk), enrolled at 3 months of age; primary-outcome data in 567 (early) and 595 (standard).
cards.result: In the intention-to-treat analysis, food allergy to one or more of the six intervention foods developed in 7.1% of the standard-introduction group (42 of 595) and 5.6% of the early-introduction group (32 of 567) (P=0.32). In the per-protocol analysis, the prevalence of any food allergy was significantly lower in the early-introduction group (2.4% vs 7.3%, P=0.01), as was peanut allergy (0% vs 2.5%, P=0.003) and egg allergy (1.4% vs 5.5%, P=0.009); there were no significant effects for milk, sesame, fish, or wheat. The early introduction of all six foods was not easily achieved but was safe.
cards.watchOut: This card is why the shelf splits its grade. LEAP's effect was proven in high-risk infants with a single food and high adherence; EAT shows the same idea diluted across six foods in an unselected population dissolving into non-adherence. Policy built on EAT alone would promise what its own primary analysis did not deliver; policy built on LEAP alone over-generalizes a high-risk result. Both errors are available; the shelf declines both.
cards.source: Perkin MR et al. Randomized trial of introduction of allergenic foods in breast-fed infants. N Engl J Med. 2016;374(18):1733–1743. PMID 26943128 · ISRCTN14254740 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1514210

cards.headline: PETIT (Natsume 2017, Lancet): heated egg from 6 months cut egg allergy at 1 year — 8% vs 38% — in infants with eczema; admissions 10% vs 0%
cards.summary: 147 Japanese infants aged 4–5 months with eczema, randomized to stepwise heated-egg powder (50 mg/day from 6–9 months, then 250 mg/day to 12 months) with aggressively controlled eczema, or placebo. Egg allergy confirmed by open oral food challenge at 12 months: 8% (5 of 60) in the egg group vs 38% (23 of 61) on placebo — RR 0.221 [0.090–0.543] (relative), P=0.0001; a 30-point absolute difference. The trial was stopped early after a scheduled interim analysis showed the difference. The harm line is printed, not footnoted: hospital admissions occurred in 10% of the egg group (6 of 60) vs none on placebo, P=0.022 .
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (PETIT; Natsume 2017, Lancet). The record's abstract states registration with the UMIN Clinical Trials Registry, number UMIN000008673; the record carries no databank entry.
cards.people: 147 infants 4–5 months of age with eczema at two Japanese centers (73 egg, 74 placebo); 121 in the primary analysis population. Eczema was aggressively treated and maintained in both arms.
cards.result: In the primary analysis population, five (8%) of 60 participants had egg allergy in the egg group compared with 23 (38%) of 61 in the placebo group (risk ratio 0.221 [95% CI 0.090–0.543]; P=0.0001). The trial was terminated on the basis of a scheduled interim analysis of 100 participants (4 [9%] of 47 vs 18 [38%] of 47; RR 0.222 [0.081–0.607]; P=0.0012). The only difference in adverse events between groups was admissions to hospital (six [10%] of 60 in the egg group vs none in the placebo group; P=0.022).
cards.watchOut: Early stopping inflates effects — trials halted at a random high point overestimate, so a 30-point difference from 121 analyzed infants should be read as 'large, imprecisely known.' The admissions signal (10% vs 0%) is the counterweight, and the reason early egg introduction in eczematous infants belongs in a protocol, not a kitchen experiment. One country, one food preparation (heated egg), and eczema aggressively controlled in both arms — all three are part of the intervention.

shelves.title: Omalizumab for multiple food allergies: one pivotal trial raises the reaction threshold while dosing continues — it is not tolerance
shelves.question: For a patient allergic to peanut and at least two other foods, can an anti-IgE antibody — with no allergen ingestion at all — raise the dose it takes to trigger a reaction?
shelves.mesh: Food Hypersensitivity · Omalizumab · Peanut Hypersensitivity · Desensitization, Immunologic · Anti-Allergic Agents · Humans
shelves.balance: One trial carries this shelf, and the shelf says so: OUtMATCH stage 1 (Reference 1) randomized 180 patients and showed that 16–20 weeks of omalizumab let 67% tolerate a 600 mg peanut challenge vs 7% on placebo, with concordant threshold-raising for cashew, milk, and egg. On that basis the FDA approved omalizumab for food allergy in February 2024. The fences are printed in the same size of type: the drug raises the reaction threshold only while dosing continues — it induces neither tolerance nor remission — and avoidance plus epinephrine carriage continue unchanged. What happens over years of dosing, or after stopping, this trial does not say. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: OUtMATCH stage 1 (Wood 2024, NEJM): tolerated ≥600 mg peanut protein — 67% on omalizumab vs 7% on placebo [single pivotal trial]
cards.summary: Persons aged 1–55 allergic to peanut and at least two other trial foods (reacting at entry to ≤100 mg of peanut protein and ≤300 mg of the others) received omalizumab or placebo every 2–4 weeks for 16–20 weeks, dosed by weight and IgE level. The analysis population was the 177 children and adolescents (118 omalizumab, 59 placebo). Primary endpoint — ingesting ≥600 mg of peanut protein in a single dose without dose-limiting symptoms: 67% (79 of 118) vs 7% (4 of 59) , P<0.001. The key secondary thresholds moved together: cashew ≥1,000 mg in 41% vs 3% ; milk 66% vs 10% ; egg 67% vs 0% (all P<0.001). Safety endpoints did not differ between the groups except more injection-site reactions on omalizumab.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial — stage 1 of OUtMATCH (Wood 2024, NEJM). Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT03881696. SINGLE-PIVOTAL-TRIAL flag: this shelf's claim rests on this one trial.
cards.people: 180 persons underwent randomization of 462 screened; the analysis population consisted of 177 children and adolescents (1 to 17 years of age). The screened population ran from 1 to 55 years. The first 60 completers entered a 24-week open-label extension.
cards.result: A total of 79 of 118 participants (67%) receiving omalizumab met the primary end-point criteria, as compared with 4 of 59 participants (7%) receiving placebo (P<0.001). Results for the key secondary end points were consistent (cashew, 41% vs 3%; milk, 66% vs 10%; egg, 67% vs 0%; P<0.001 for all comparisons). Safety end points did not differ between the groups, aside from more injection-site reactions in the omalizumab group.
cards.watchOut: A raised threshold is a margin of safety against accidental exposure — protection against a bite, not a serving. Nobody in this trial was made tolerant: stop the antibody and the IgE it was holding down is still there, so avoidance and epinephrine carriage continue — the trial's design assumes both. The trial measured supervised challenge thresholds at week 16–20; the multi-year, real-kitchen reaction rate is the outcome that matters and is not yet in any record carded here.

shelves.title: Malaria vaccines: R21 prevents most first-year episodes; RTS,S a third over four years — mortality untested
shelves.question: Do malaria vaccines (RTS,S and R21) protect young children against malaria?
shelves.mesh: Africa South of the Sahara · Child, Preschool · Humans · Immunization, Secondary · Infant · Malaria Vaccines · Malaria, Falciparum
shelves.balance: Two large phase 3 programmes agree that malaria vaccines work against illness: R21/Matrix-M prevented 75% of first clinical episodes at seasonal sites and 68% at perennial sites over 12 months (4,878 children); RTS,S/AS01 prevented 36.3% of episodes over four years with a booster, and 32.2% of severe malaria — an effect that vanished without the booster (1.1%). Neither trial was powered for mortality, and this shelf claims none. Proposed grade: POSSIBLE for episode prevention. Tier C — built Nov 8, 2026 and held for the developer’s personal verdict; no approval stamp is claimed for this shelf.

cards.headline: RTS,S/AS01 phase 3 final results (2015, The Lancet): a third fewer malaria episodes with a booster — severe malaria protection modest and booster-dependent
cards.summary: 8,922 children (5–17 months) and 6,537 young infants (6–12 weeks) at 11 centres in 7 sub-Saharan African countries, randomised to three RTS,S doses plus a booster (R3R), three doses plus a comparator booster (R3C), or control. In children, over a median 48 months, vaccine efficacy against clinical malaria was 36.3% [31.8–40.5] with the booster and 28.3% [23.3–32.9] without. Against severe malaria in children: 32.2% [13.7–46.9] with the booster, and 1.1% [−23.0 to 20.5] without it — the severe-disease claim rests on the fourth dose. In young infants, efficacy against clinical malaria was 25.9% [19.9–31.5] with the booster.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, controlled phase 3 trial (final analysis), Lancet 2015. Registry ID from the record’s own text: NCT00866619.
cards.people: 8,922 children aged 5–17 months and 6,537 young infants aged 6–12 weeks at 11 centres in seven sub-Saharan African countries; median follow-up 48 months (children) and 38 months (infants) after dose 1.
cards.result: Compared with 9,585 episodes of clinical malaria in children in the control group, 6,616 episodes occurred in the booster group (vaccine efficacy 36.3%, 95% CI 31.8–40.5) and 7,396 in the non-booster group (28.3%, 23.3–32.9). Compared with 171 children who experienced at least one episode of severe malaria in the control group, 116 children did so in the booster group (32.2%, 13.7 to 46.9) and 169 in the non-booster group (1.1%, −23.0 to 20.5). In young infants, efficacy against clinical malaria was 25.9% (19.9–31.5) with the booster.
cards.watchOut: The honest summary of RTS,S is ‘partial, waning, booster-dependent’: a third off clinical episodes is a large absolute gain where children suffer repeated malaria, and a modest relative one; protection against severe malaria — the outcome closest to mortality — was statistically fragile without the booster and absent in the non-booster arm’s point estimate. The trial was not powered for mortality, and no mortality result is claimed on this shelf.

cards.headline: R21/Matrix-M phase 3 (Datoo 2024, The Lancet): 75% efficacy at seasonal sites, 68% at perennial sites, over the first year
cards.summary: 4,878 children aged 5–36 months received a first dose across five sites in four African countries (Burkina Faso, Kenya, Mali, Tanzania), randomised 2:1 to R21/Matrix-M (three doses, then a booster at 12 months) or a licensed rabies vaccine. Twelve-month vaccine efficacy against a first clinical malaria episode was 75% [71–79] at the seasonal-transmission sites and 68% [61–74] at the standard (perennial) sites , with similar efficacy against multiple episodes. The vaccine was well tolerated — injection-site pain (18.6%) and fever (46.7%) the most frequent events; serious adverse events did not differ between groups and there were no treatment-related deaths .
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised, controlled phase 3 trial, Lancet 2024. Registry ID from the record’s own text: NCT04704830.
cards.people: Children aged 5–36 months at five sites in four African countries with seasonal or perennial transmission; 4,878 received a first dose (3,434 assigned R21/Matrix-M, 1,705 control in the randomised set), with the modified per-protocol population 51.9% male.
cards.result: 12-month vaccine efficacy was 75% (95% CI 71–79; p<0.0001) at the seasonal sites and 68% (61–74; p<0.0001) at the standard sites for time to first clinical malaria episode; efficacy against multiple clinical malaria episodes was similar (75% at seasonal sites). The vaccine was well tolerated, with injection site pain and fever as the most frequent adverse events; the number of adverse events of special interest and serious adverse events did not significantly differ between the vaccine groups, and there were no treatment-related deaths.
cards.watchOut: A stronger first-year number than RTS,S — with the comparison fenced: different sites, seasons, ages and follow-up (12 months here versus four years for the RTS,S final analysis), so the two trials’ percentages are not a head-to-head. Efficacy beyond the first year, severe-malaria and mortality effects, and performance as transmission falls are the open questions the ongoing trial and rollout data must answer; the primary report’s follow-up is short by design.

cards.headline: Reading the malaria vaccine evidence together: real protection against illness, severe-disease evidence still thin — a Tier C shelf
cards.summary: Two vaccines, one consistent shape: both prevent a substantial share of clinical malaria episodes in young African children — RTS,S about a third over four years with a booster, R21 about 70–75% over its first year — and both records thin out exactly where the stakes rise. Severe malaria: RTS,S shows 32% efficacy only with the booster and none without; R21’s primary report is a first-year, episode-based readout. Mortality: neither trial was powered for it, and this shelf claims none — which is why a shelf about preventing a disease that kills children sits in Tier C awaiting the developer’s own verdict on how its claims are worded. The deployment case for these vaccines rests on episode burden, severe-disease signals and modelling beyond these records; the carded claim is narrower, and deliberately so.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study. This card states why this shelf is Tier C and what would strengthen it.
cards.people: The populations of Cards 1 and 2: children aged 6 weeks to 36 months in malaria-endemic sub-Saharan Africa, across 16 trial sites in eight countries.
cards.result: The evidence establishes clinically meaningful protection against clinical malaria episodes for both vaccines, with R21’s first-year efficacy the higher. It establishes severe-malaria protection only partially (RTS,S, booster-dependent) and mortality protection not at all within these records. Longer R21 follow-up and post-introduction effectiveness data are the records that would change this shelf.
cards.watchOut: Do not let the episode efficacy figures (36%, 75%) be quoted as lives saved: the distance between episodes prevented and deaths prevented is exactly the distance this shelf declines to cross without a record.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cards 1–2 on this shelf (PMID 25913272; PMID 38310910).

shelves.title: Fluoride varnish and sealants in children
shelves.question: In children and adolescents, do fluoride varnish and pit-and-fissure sealants prevent dental caries compared with placebo, no treatment, or each other?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Child · Dental Caries · Dentition, Permanent · Fluorides, Topical · Humans · Mouth, Edentulous · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Tooth, Deciduous
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — Two Cochrane reviews of randomised trials, both rated moderate quality, support each intervention against doing nothing: fluoride varnish prevented 43% (relative) of the caries increment in permanent teeth and 37% (relative) in primary teeth, and resin-based sealants cut the relative odds of occlusal caries sharply at 2 years, with absolute benefits that grow with baseline caries risk. Head-to-head, which of the two is better is unresolved (very low certainty). Effects come mostly from older, higher-caries populations, so absolute benefit in a low-caries, fluoridated population will be smaller. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: Fluoride varnish: about two-fifths of the caries increment prevented, in both dentitions
cards.summary: Cochrane, fluoride varnish (13 trials, permanent teeth): the prevented fraction — the treatment–control difference as a share of the control increment, a relative measure — was 43% [30–57]; for primary teeth, 37% [24–51]. Moderate-quality evidence in both dentitions.
cards.people: 22 trials randomising 12,455 children and adolescents up to 16 years (9,595 in the analyses); mean age and sex distribution not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: The pooled prevented fraction — a relative measure, the treatment–control difference expressed as a percentage of the control-group caries increment — was 43% (95% CI 30% to 57%; p < 0.0001) for permanent tooth surfaces (13 trials) and 37% (95% CI 24% to 51%; p < 0.0001) for primary tooth surfaces (10 trials). The abstract pools no single absolute caries increment, so no absolute number of surfaces saved can be stated. Little information on adverse effects or acceptability was available.
cards.watchOut: Evidence rated moderate quality but built mainly on high risk-of-bias studies with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 75% permanent, 59% primary); a relative prevented fraction overstates what a low-caries population gains in absolute terms.
cards.source: Marinho VC et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2013 Jul 11. PMID 23846772. Registry ID: none in the PubMed record — this is a Cochrane review, not a trial.

cards.headline: Resin sealants vs none: large relative effect at 2 years, absolute gain depends on baseline risk
cards.summary: Cochrane, resin sealants versus none: caries in first permanent molars at 24 months, relative odds 0.12 [0.08–0.19], maintained at 48–54 months (0.21) — a large relative effect whose absolute value depends entirely on the child’s baseline risk, as the review’s own scenario shows.
cards.people: 38 trials involving 7,924 children and adolescents aged 5 to 16 years; the resin-sealant-vs-no-sealant comparison at 24 months covered children aged 5 to 10 years (1,548 randomised, 1,322 evaluated in 7 trials); sex distribution not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: Resin-based sealant versus no sealant prevented caries in first permanent molars at 24 months (relative odds OR 0.12, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.19; moderate-quality evidence), with the effect maintained at 48–54 months (relative OR 0.21, 95% CI 0.16 to 0.28). In absolute terms, from the review's own scenarios: if 16% of control surfaces decayed over 24 months (160 per 1,000), sealant reduced this to 5.2%; if 40% decayed (400 per 1,000), sealant reduced it to 6.25%. Glass ionomer sealant versus no sealant was inconclusive (very low-quality evidence). Only 4 trials assessed adverse events; none were reported.
cards.watchOut: Five of the seven 24-month trials were published in the 1970s, outcome assessors cannot be blinded in sealant trials (rated high risk of bias throughout), and trials rarely reported participants' background fluoride exposure or baseline caries prevalence.
cards.source: Ahovuo-Saloranta A et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2017 Jul 31. PMID 28759120. Registry ID: none in the PubMed record — this is a Cochrane review, not a trial.

cards.headline: Sealant vs varnish head-to-head: no reliable winner
cards.summary: Head-to-head, sealant versus varnish: relative odds 0.67 [0.37–1.19], very low certainty — the reviewers could not say which is better. Nobody has proven a winner.
cards.people: 11 trials with 3,374 participants aged 5 to 10 years at trial start; sex distribution not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: Resin-based sealant versus fluoride varnish for caries in first permanent molars at 2–3 years: relative odds OR 0.67 (95% CI 0.37 to 1.19; 4 studies, 1,683 children evaluated) — the reviewers were uncertain which is better, rating this very low certainty. One split-mouth trial (92 children) favoured resin sealant plus varnish over varnish alone at 2 years (relative OR 0.30, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.55), also very low certainty. Five trials (1,801 participants) reported no adverse events from either intervention over 1–9 years.
cards.watchOut: Very low certainty throughout, with high heterogeneity (I² = 84%) in the main comparison; the review noted 14 studies ongoing in 2020 whose results could firm this up — the 2024–2026 sweep found no new large head-to-head trial reporting a decisive result.
cards.source: Kashbour W et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2020 Nov 4. PMID 33142363. Registry ID: none in the PubMed record — this is a Cochrane review, not a trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: both beat doing nothing; the choice between them is a delivery decision, not a proven efficacy gap
cards.summary: Both beat doing nothing on moderate-quality randomised evidence; between them, the choice is a delivery decision (cost, setting, retention), not a proven efficacy gap. POSSIBLE.
cards.people: No new participants — synthesis of the three verified cards above.
cards.result: Stamp: POSSIBLE. Fluoride varnish and resin-based sealants each prevent caries in children versus placebo or no treatment, on moderate-quality randomised evidence; the absolute payoff is largest where baseline caries risk is highest (sealant scenario: 400 decayed surfaces per 1,000 untreated falling to about 63 per 1,000 sealed at high baseline risk, versus 160 falling to 52 per 1,000 at lower risk).

shelves.title: Dental amalgam safety — Children's Amalgam Trial
shelves.question: In children needing dental restorations, does dental amalgam, compared with resin composite, cause adverse neuropsychological, neurobehavioral or renal effects?
shelves.mesh: Child · Dental Amalgam · Dental Caries · Female · Humans · Kidney Function Tests · Longitudinal Studies · Male · Mercury · Mercury Poisoning · Neuropsychological Tests · Resin Cements · Volatilization
shelves.balance: LIKELY: two independent large randomized safety trials in children — the New England Children's Amalgam Trial and the Casa Pia trial in Lisbon — found higher urinary mercury with amalgam but no statistically significant differences in IQ, memory, visuomotor, neurobehavioral or renal outcomes over 5 to 7 years. Very small effects cannot be ruled out, and follow-up does not extend into adult life. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: New England Children's Amalgam Trial: no IQ, memory, visuomotor or renal difference at 5 years
cards.summary: New England Children’s Amalgam Trial (534 children, JAMA 2006): urinary mercury higher with amalgam (0.9 vs 0.6 µg/g creatinine), but 5-year IQ change differed by 1.0 point [−0.6 to 2.5] — no significant difference in IQ, memory, visuomotor function or urinary albumin. Very small effects cannot be ruled out; none were found.

shelves.title: Silver diamine fluoride for caries arrest
shelves.question: Does professionally applied silver diamine fluoride (SDF), mainly 38% SDF, arrest active dentine caries, especially in children's primary teeth, compared with no treatment, fluoride varnish or glass ionomer?
shelves.mesh: Cariostatic Agents · Child · Dental Care · Dental Caries · Fluorides, Topical · Humans · Quaternary Ammonium Compounds · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Silver Compounds · Sodium Fluoride · Tooth Remineralization
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: SDF arrested a high proportion of dentine caries in trials (meta-analytic proportion 65.9%, 95% CI 41.2% to 90.7%, for 38% SDF; trial arrest rates 79% to 91% depending on application frequency), and it outperformed no treatment in early controlled work. Certainty is held at POSSIBLE because the 2024 Cochrane review, across 29 RCTs, rated the arrest evidence low to very uncertain and noted all studies were at high risk of bias and staining was poorly reported. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.result: Meta-analysis of five papers using 38% silver diamine fluoride to arrest dentine caries gave an overall proportion of arrested dentine caries of 65.9% (95% CI 41.2% to 90.7%; p<0.001).
