shelves.title: Zambia’s CHAP trial: a penny-a-day antibiotic that cut child HIV deaths by 43% (relative) — country 41
shelves.question: In HIV-infected children in a high-resistance, pre-ART-era setting, does daily co-trimoxazole prophylaxis reduce mortality?
shelves.mesh: AIDS-Related Opportunistic Infections · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Antibiotic Prophylaxis · Child · Double-Blind Method · HIV Infections · Humans · Survival Rate · Trimethoprim, Sulfamethoxazole Drug Combination · Zambia
shelves.balance: One trial carries this shelf, and it is a strong one: 541 Zambian children randomised double-blind, mortality 28% vs 42% (HR 0.57 [0.43–0.77]), consistent across ages and CD4 counts, stopped early by its safety board, in the very setting — high bacterial resistance, no ART — where sceptics expected the drug to fail. Zambia is a not-yet-covered country, so the developer’s country exception applies: one strong RCT may card. The grade is LIKELY, not the top tier, precisely because there is one trial: the benefit’s direction is secure, its size in an ART-era cohort is not something this trial can price. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: CHAP trial (Chintu 2004, The Lancet): daily co-trimoxazole cut mortality in Zambian children with HIV — deaths 28% vs 42%, HR 0.57
cards.summary: 541 children randomised (534 HIV-positive children analysed) at University Teaching Hospital, Lusaka, Zambia — double-blind, placebo-controlled, in a setting with high bacterial resistance to co-trimoxazole. After median follow-up of 19 months: deaths 74 (28%) on co-trimoxazole vs 112 (42%) on placebo — HR 0.57 [0.43–0.77], P=0.0002 , a 43% relative mortality reduction (14 percentage points absolute). Grade 3/4 adverse events: 6% vs 7% . The data and safety monitoring committee recommended stopping the trial early, in October 2003, because of the benefit.
cards.type: Double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial, The Lancet 2004. Pre-registration-era trial: the record carries no registry ID, and none is printed.
cards.people: 541 children aged 1–14 years with clinical features of HIV infection, enrolled in Lusaka, Zambia; seven were subsequently identified as HIV-negative and excluded, leaving 534 in the analysis. This was the pre-ART era: these children were not receiving antiretroviral therapy.
cards.result: After median follow-up of 19 months, 74 children (28%) in the co-trimoxazole group and 112 (42%) in the placebo group had died (hazard ratio 0.57; 95% CI, 0.43 to 0.77; P=0.0002). The benefit applied in children followed beyond 12 months (HR 0.48 [0.27–0.84]) and was consistent across all ages and baseline CD4 counts (tests for heterogeneity all non-significant). Grade 3 or 4 adverse events occurred in 16 children (6%) on co-trimoxazole vs 18 (7%) on placebo; a single low neutrophil count was more frequent on co-trimoxazole (6% vs 3%, P=0.06). Pneumocystis was identified in only one of 73 nasopharyngeal aspirates from children with pneumonia — the drug’s benefit in this setting ran mainly through bacterial infections, not PCP.
cards.watchOut: One trial, one country, one era — the three fences are real. The children were diagnosed clinically, before ART existed for them; in a modern ART-treated cohort the absolute benefit would very likely be smaller, and this trial cannot measure it. Early stopping for benefit tends to flatter effect sizes, though with 186 deaths and a confidence interval ending at 0.77 the qualitative conclusion is not fragile. The shelf rests on the developer’s country exception (a not-yet-covered country may card on one strong RCT) — stated openly, not hidden.

cards.headline: The objection CHAP was built to answer: local bacteria were already highly resistant to co-trimoxazole — and prophylaxis worked anyway
cards.summary: No trial of co-trimoxazole prophylaxis in HIV had been done where bacterial resistance to the drug was already high — Zambia was exactly that place, and the reasonable fear was that a cheap drug the local bacteria had beaten would prevent nothing. The trial’s answer: mortality fell by the same margin seen in low-resistance settings. The authors’ conclusion, printed on the record: children with clinical features of HIV infection should receive co-trimoxazole prophylaxis in resource-poor settings irrespective of local resistance to the drug .
cards.type: Context card — the trial’s stated rationale and interpretation, from the CHAP record itself (PMID 15555666). No new study.
cards.people: The same Lusaka cohort as Card 1: children aged 1–14 with clinical features of HIV infection, in a region documented to have high levels of bacterial resistance to co-trimoxazole.
cards.result: The background of the record states the gap directly: no trials of co-trimoxazole prophylaxis for HIV-infected adults or children had been done in areas with high levels of bacterial resistance to the antibiotic. CHAP was designed to fill it, and its result (Reference 1) showed the mortality benefit intact. The finding travelled: the trial became a principal evidence base for the WHO/UNAIDS/UNICEF recommendation of co-trimoxazole prophylaxis for children with HIV in resource-poor settings.
cards.watchOut: Resistance is a moving quantity, measured in particular places at particular times; a 2004 Zambian answer does not certify 2026 resistance patterns anywhere, including Zambia. What the card establishes is narrower and more useful: high measured resistance at the population level did not, in the event, predict prophylaxis failure — because much of what prophylaxis prevents is not captured by a single resistance percentage.

cards.headline: Reading CHAP alone: what one stopped-early Zambian trial can carry — and the country-exception fence around this shelf
cards.summary: A single double-blind trial, 186 deaths , HR 0.57 [0.43–0.77] , consistent across age and CD4 strata, stopped early by its own safety board, with adverse events balanced (6% vs 7%). By this library’s ordinary rules a benefit shelf wants two randomised trials; Zambia enters under the developer’s country exception — a not-yet-covered country may rest on one strong RCT — and the grade stops at LIKELY rather than the library’s top tier for the same reason: there is no second trial to catch this one if it is wrong about magnitude.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study. This card reads Card 1 together with the library’s gates and states the fence.
cards.people: The population of Card 1: HIV-infected children aged 1–14 in Lusaka, Zambia, pre-ART era, followed a median of 19 months.
cards.result: The direction and rough size of the mortality benefit are about as secure as a single trial can make them: hard primary outcome, blinded design, narrow confidence interval, no subgroup contradicting it. What one trial cannot do is price the benefit in a different era — with ART available, with different resistance, in adults (a separate question with its own literature, not carded here). A modern replication or an ART-era trial would either confirm the transfer or redraw it; until one reports, the shelf says what this trial showed, where it showed it.
cards.watchOut: Do not cite this shelf as ‘co-trimoxazole saves lives in HIV, full stop’ — cite it as what it is: in untreated HIV-infected Zambian children in 2001–2003, daily prophylaxis prevented roughly one death in seven over about a year and a half (42% to 28%), in a high-resistance setting, at a cost of pennies per day.

shelves.title: Reduced-osmolarity oral rehydration solution
shelves.question: Does reduced-osmolarity ORS beat the standard WHO formulation for acute diarrhoea?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Bicarbonates/therapeutic use · Cholera/complications · Dehydration/etiology/therapy · Diarrhea/complications · Fluid Therapy/methods · Glucose/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY: In the Hahn systematic review of 15 randomised trials (2,397 children), reduced-osmolarity ORS was associated with fewer unscheduled intravenous infusions than standard WHO ORS (odds ratio 0.61, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.81 — a ratio inside the 0.5-2.0 band, printed with its absolute-outcome context: in three trials no child needed unscheduled infusion at all), with lower stool output and less vomiting (odds ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.92) and no significant difference in hyponatraemia. A primary trial points the same way (treatment failure 1% versus 8% in the Santosham trial, as reported). The cholera-specific Cochrane review is the caution: in cholera, reduced-osmolarity ORS brought more biochemical hyponatraemia (risk ratio 1.67, 95% CI 1.09 to 2.57) with no significant difference in need for unscheduled intravenous infusion and no symptomatic hyponatraemia or deaths reported — in 718 participants, a small total experience. Zinc as an adjunct for childhood diarrhoea lives at #207 and probiotics at #141; neither is carded here.

cards.headline: Hahn review: reduced-osmolarity ORS meant fewer unscheduled IV infusions (odds ratio 0.61), less stool output and less vomiting in children
cards.summary: Hahn review (15 trials, 2,397 children): fewer unscheduled IV infusions on reduced-osmolarity ORS (odds ratio 0.61 [0.47 to 0.81]) — inside the band, printed with its absolute context.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
cards.people: 15 randomised controlled trials including 2,397 randomised patients — children admitted to hospital with dehydration associated with diarrhoea. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In a meta-analysis of 9 trials for the primary outcome, reduced-osmolarity rehydration solution was associated with fewer unscheduled intravenous infusions compared with standard WHO rehydration solution (odds ratio 0.61, 95% confidence interval 0.47 to 0.81); three trials reported that no patients required unscheduled intravenous infusion. Stool output was lower in the reduced-osmolarity group (standardised mean difference in the log scale -0.214, 95% CI -0.305 to -0.123; 13 trials) and vomiting was less frequent (odds ratio 0.71, 0.55 to 0.92; 6 trials). Six trials sought hyponatraemia, with events in three studies, but no significant difference between the two arms.
cards.watchOut: The headline odds ratio (0.61) sits inside the 0.5-2.0 band this library does not treat as solid on its own; the stamp rests on the concordance of the infusion, stool-output and vomiting outcomes and the primary trial below, not on that ratio alone. The same authors' Cochrane version of this review (PMID 11869639) is the same evidence base and is deliberately not carded separately.

cards.headline: Santosham 1996: reduced-osmolarity ORS cut stool output by 36% in the rehydration phase, with treatment failure 1% versus 8%
cards.summary: Santosham 1996: stool output 36% lower in relative terms; treatment failure 1% vs 8% ; vomiting 17% vs 33%.
cards.people: 190 boys aged 1 to 24 months admitted to hospital in Cairo, Egypt, with acute diarrhoea and signs of dehydration, randomised to reduced-osmolarity ORS (245 mmol/L; sodium and glucose 75 mmol/L each) or standard WHO ORS (311 mmol/L).
cards.result: During the rehydration phase, mean stool output was 36% lower in relative terms (95% confidence interval, 1% to 100%) in the reduced-osmolarity group, and vomiting was less frequent (17% versus 33%, as reported in the record). Treatment failure (need for unscheduled intravenous fluids) occurred in 1% of the reduced-osmolarity group versus 8% of the standard group, as reported. During the maintenance phase, stool output, intake, duration of diarrhoea, and weight gain were similar. Mean serum sodium at 24 hours was lower with reduced-osmolarity ORS (134 versus 138 mEq/L; p<0.001) but within the normal range in both groups, and the development or worsening of hyponatraemia did not differ.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial in boys only, aged 1-24 months, with non-cholera diarrhoea; the record's relative-risk labelling for vomiting and treatment failure is internally inconsistent in direction, so this card prints the reported percentages (17% versus 33%; 1% versus 8%) rather than those ratios.

cards.headline: In cholera, reduced-osmolarity ORS brought more biochemical hyponatraemia (risk ratio 1.67) and no clear infusion advantage
cards.summary: In cholera, the caution: more biochemical hyponatraemia (risk ratio 1.67 ) and no clear infusion advantage.
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised controlled trials
cards.people: For glucose-based reduced-osmolarity ORS, 7 trials (718 participants) — adults and children with acute diarrhoea due to cholera. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Biochemical hyponatraemia (serum sodium <130 mmol/L) was more common with reduced-osmolarity ORS (risk ratio 1.67, 95% CI 1.09 to 2.57; 465 participants, 4 trials); for severe biochemical hyponatraemia (<125 mmol/L) the difference was not significant (risk ratio 1.58, 95% CI 0.62 to 4.04). No trials reported symptomatic hyponatraemia or death. There was no statistically significant difference in the need for unscheduled intravenous infusion. In two trials examining rice-based ORS, duration of diarrhoea was shorter in the reduced-osmolarity group (weighted mean difference -16.85 hours, 95% CI -21.22 to -12.48; 102 participants).
cards.watchOut: This is the record the topic file cited as the general reduced-osmolarity Cochrane review; on its own record it is cholera-specific (Murphy et al., CD003754) — see the summary's gate corrections. Its hyponatraemia signal is biochemical only, in a small total trial experience (718 participants), and the review itself urges caution where monitoring is difficult.

cards.summary: The better default for non-cholera diarrhoea (LIKELY), with a biochemical caution in cholera.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: a 15-trial systematic review (2,397 children), one 190-child primary trial, and a cholera-specific Cochrane review (7 trials, 718 participants).
cards.result: For children with acute (non-cholera) diarrhoea, reduced-osmolarity ORS reduces unscheduled intravenous infusions (odds ratio 0.61, with concordant stool-output and vomiting benefits and a 1% versus 8% treatment-failure split in the primary trial) without a hyponatraemia penalty in that population. cards.watchOut: Do not merge the cholera and non-cholera records into one safety statement: the hyponatraemia signal belongs to cholera, the infusion benefit is best shown in non-cholera childhood diarrhoea.

shelves.title: Amblyopia in children: patching vs atropine penalisation
shelves.question: In moderate amblyopia in children under 7, is atropine penalisation of the sound eye as effective as patching — and how much patching is enough?
shelves.mesh: Amblyopia/therapy · Atropine/therapeutic use · Mydriatics/therapeutic use · Ophthalmic Solutions · Patient Compliance · Sensory Deprivation · Visual Acuity/physiology
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two PEDIG randomised trials settle both halves. Atropine and patching improved acuity by a similar amount at 6 months (3.16 vs 2.84 lines; mean difference 0.034 logMAR, clinically inconsequential), so either is an appropriate initial treatment for moderate amblyopia at age 3 to under 7. And 2 hours of daily patching matched 6 hours at 4 months (2.40 lines gained in each group) when combined with 1 hour of near activities — less patching is enough for moderate disease.

cards.headline: PEDIG 2002: atropine matched patching for moderate amblyopia at 6 months (3.16 vs 2.84 lines gained)
cards.summary: PEDIG 2002: atropine matched patching at 6 months ( 2.84 vs 3.16 lines gained; difference 0.034 logMAR).
cards.people: 419 children younger than 7 years with moderate amblyopia (visual acuity 20/40 to 20/100), assigned to patching or atropine penalisation of the sound eye. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Acuity in the amblyopic eye improved by 3.16 lines with patching and 2.84 lines with atropine from baseline to 6 months; improvement was initially faster with patching, but the 6-month difference was small (mean difference 0.034 logMAR units; 95% CI 0.005 to 0.064). Acuity of 20/30 or better and/or improvement of 3 or more lines was reached by 79% (patching) and 74% (atropine). Both treatments were well tolerated; atropine scored slightly higher on parental acceptability, and more atropine patients had reduced sound-eye acuity at 6 months, which did not persist with further follow-up.
cards.watchOut: Moderate amblyopia only (20/40 to 20/100) in children aged 3 to under 7: the equivalence does not extend to severe amblyopia or older children, and patching's faster early gain may matter where follow-up is uncertain.
cards.source: Pediatric Eye Disease Investigator Group. A randomized trial of atropine vs. patching for treatment of moderate amblyopia in children. Arch Ophthalmol. 2002;120(3):268-78. PMID: 11879129. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a pre-registration-era trial (2002).

cards.headline: PEDIG 2003: 2 hours of daily patching matched 6 hours at 4 months (2.40 lines gained in each group)
cards.summary: PEDIG 2003: 2 hours of daily patching matched 6 hours at 4 months ( 2.40 lines gained in each group).
cards.people: 189 children younger than 7 years with moderate amblyopia (visual acuity 20/40 to 20/80), assigned to 2 hours or 6 hours of daily patching, each combined with at least 1 hour per day of near visual activities during patching. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Improvement in amblyopic-eye acuity from baseline to 4 months averaged 2.40 lines in each group (P=.98). Four-month acuity of at least 20/32 and/or improvement of 3 or more lines was achieved by 62% of patients in each group (P>.99).

cards.headline: Synthesis: either penalisation method works, and 2 hours of patching is enough for moderate amblyopia — LIKELY
cards.summary: Either penalisation method works, and 2 hours of patching is enough for moderate amblyopia — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: PEDIG atropine-vs-patching trial (419 children) and PEDIG patching-regimens trial (189 children).
cards.result: Both comparisons landed on near-identity: 0.034 logMAR between atropine and patching at 6 months, and exactly 2.40 lines gained on 2 versus 6 hours of patching at 4 months. For moderate amblyopia in children aged 3 to under 7, the choice between atropine and patching can follow family preference and acceptability, and the patching prescription can start at 2 hours with near activities.
cards.watchOut: Both trials predate trial-registration norms and enrolled moderate disease only; severe amblyopia, older children and glasses-alone (refractive adaptation) strategies are outside this shelf.

shelves.title: Low-dose atropine to slow childhood myopia
shelves.question: Does low-dose atropine (0.01–0.05%) slow myopia progression in children, at what concentration, and with what rebound on stopping?
shelves.mesh: Accommodation, Ocular/physiology · Administration, Ophthalmic · Atropine/administration & dosage · Axial Length, Eye · Disease Progression · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Muscarinic Antagonists/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Atropine slows progression in a concentration-dependent way across two randomised programmes. LAMP (438 children, placebo-controlled) found 1-year spherical-equivalent change of -0.27 D on 0.05%, -0.46 D on 0.025%, -0.59 D on 0.01% and -0.81 D on placebo, with axial elongation ordered the same way. ATOM2 (400 children, no concurrent placebo arm) found 2-year progression of -0.30 D (0.5%), -0.38 D (0.1%) and -0.49 D (0.01%), with 0.01% nearly free of accommodation and pupil effects. Neither carded abstract reports what happens on stopping, so the drafted question's rebound half is not answered by the carded records and is not claimed.

cards.headline: LAMP 2019: atropine slowed myopia in a dose-dependent way — 1-year change -0.27 D on 0.05% vs -0.81 D on placebo
cards.summary: LAMP: 1-year progression was dose-ordered — −0.27 D on 0.05% atropine vs −0.81 D on placebo.
cards.people: 438 children aged 4 to 12 years with myopia of at least -1.0 D and astigmatism of -2.5 D or less, randomised 1:1:1:1 to 0.05%, 0.025% or 0.01% atropine eye drops or placebo, once nightly to both eyes for 1 year. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Mean spherical-equivalent change after 1 year was -0.27±0.61 D (0.05%), -0.46±0.45 D (0.025%), -0.59±0.61 D (0.01%) and -0.81±0.53 D (placebo) (P<0.001), with mean axial-length increase of 0.20±0.25, 0.29±0.20, 0.36±0.29 and 0.41±0.22 mm respectively (P<0.001). Accommodation amplitude fell most at 0.05% (-1.98 D) and least at 0.01% (-0.26 D, similar to placebo's -0.32 D); pupil size rose with concentration. Visual acuity and vision-related quality of life were not affected in any group, and the authors identify 0.05% as the most effective of the three concentrations over 1 year.
cards.watchOut: One year is short for a childhood-long treatment, and LAMP's first phase cannot answer durability or rebound after stopping — later LAMP phases are not carded here.
cards.source: Yam JC et al. Low-Concentration Atropine for Myopia Progression (LAMP) Study: A Randomized, Double-Blinded, Placebo-Controlled Trial of 0.05%, 0.025%, and 0.01% Atropine Eye Drops in Myopia Control. Ophthalmology. 2019;126(1):113-124. PMID: 30514630. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: ATOM2 2012: 0.01% atropine retained most of the effect of higher doses over 2 years (-0.49 D vs -0.30 D on 0.5%) with negligible side effects
cards.summary: ATOM2: 0.01% atropine kept most of the effect over 2 years ( −0.49 D vs −0.30 D on 0.5%) with negligible side effects.
cards.type: Single-centre, double-masked randomised trial (no concurrent placebo arm)
cards.people: 400 children aged 6–12 years with myopia of at least -2.0 D and astigmatism of -1.50 D or less, randomised 2:2:1 to 0.5%, 0.1% or 0.01% atropine once nightly to both eyes for 2 years. The abstract does not state mean age.

shelves.title: Retinopathy of prematurity: anti-VEGF injection vs laser
shelves.question: For stage 3+ retinopathy of prematurity, does intravitreal bevacizumab (or ranibizumab) beat laser ablation, by zone of disease?
shelves.mesh: Angiogenesis Inhibitors/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Bevacizumab · Infant, Newborn · Infant, Premature · Intravitreal Injections
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY — bevacizumab over laser for zone I recurrence · POSSIBLE — ranibizumab benefit: BEAT-ROP (150 infants) found recurrence requiring retreatment in 4% of bevacizumab eyes versus 22% of laser eyes (P=0.002), with the significant effect in zone I disease (P=0.003) and not zone II (P=0.27). RAINBOW (225 infants) found treatment success in 80% on ranibizumab 0.2 mg versus 66% on laser, but the odds ratio of 2.19 (95% CI 0.99 to 4.82; p=0.051, a relative measure inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band's neighbourhood and not significant) supports only POSSIBLE. Both trials were too small to settle systemic safety of anti-VEGF in preterm infants.

cards.headline: BEAT-ROP 2011: bevacizumab cut recurrence from 22% to 4% of eyes, with the benefit in zone I disease
cards.summary: BEAT-ROP: bevacizumab cut recurrence to 4% vs 22% of eyes (P=0.002) — significant in zone I (P=0.003), not zone II.
cards.type: Prospective, controlled, randomised, stratified multicentre trial
cards.people: 150 infants (300 eyes) with zone I or zone II posterior stage 3+ retinopathy of prematurity (stage 3 with plus disease), randomised to intravitreal bevacizumab (0.625 mg) or conventional laser therapy, bilaterally; 143 infants survived to 54 weeks' postmenstrual age and the 7 who died were excluded from the primary-outcome analysis. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Retinopathy recurred in 4 infants in the bevacizumab group (6 of 140 eyes [4%]) versus 19 infants in the laser group (32 of 146 eyes [22%], P=0.002). The treatment effect was significant for zone I disease (P=0.003) but not zone II (P=0.27), with recurrence counted before 54 weeks' postmenstrual age. Peripheral retinal vessel development continued after bevacizumab, whereas laser permanently destroyed the peripheral retina.
cards.watchOut: The authors state plainly that the trial was too small to assess safety — systemic anti-VEGF exposure in preterm infants is the open question this shelf cannot close — and the zone split means the headline does not apply to zone II disease.

shelves.title: Optical myopia control: multifocal and dual-focus contact lenses
shelves.question: Do multifocal or dual-focus soft contact lenses slow myopia progression and axial elongation in children versus single-vision lenses?
shelves.mesh: Contact Lenses, Hydrophilic/adverse effects · Disease Progression · Linear Models · Myopia/rehabilitation · Ohio · Refraction, Ocular · Sample Size
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two double-masked randomised trials agree. BLINK (294 children) found high-add (+2.50 D) multifocal lenses slowed 3-year progression to -0.60 D versus -1.05 D on single-vision lenses (difference 0.46 D) and slowed eye growth (0.42 vs 0.66 mm), while medium-add lenses sat in between. The MiSight dual-focus trial (144 children) found 3-year progression of -0.51 D versus -1.24 D on single-vision lenses and axial growth of 0.30 versus 0.62 mm. The drug option (low-dose atropine) is Shelf #614 — a different intervention, not re-carded here.

cards.headline: BLINK 2020: high-add multifocal lenses slowed 3-year progression to -0.60 D vs -1.05 D on single-vision lenses
cards.summary: BLINK: high-add multifocal lenses slowed 3-year progression to −0.60 D vs −1.05 D on single-vision lenses.
cards.type: Double-masked randomised clinical trial (two optometry schools)
cards.people: 294 children aged 7 to 11 years with -0.75 to -5.00 D myopia and under 1.00 D astigmatism, randomised to high add power (+2.50 D; 98), medium add power (+1.50 D; 98) or single-vision (98) soft contact lenses; 292 (99%) were analysed (mean age 10.3 [SD 1.2] years; 177 [60.2%] female; mean spherical equivalent -2.39 [1.00] D).
cards.result: Adjusted 3-year myopia progression was -0.60 D (high add), -0.89 D (medium add) and -1.05 D (single vision): differences of 0.46 D (95% CI 0.29 to 0.63) for high add versus single vision, 0.30 D (0.13 to 0.47) for high versus medium add, and 0.16 D (-0.01 to 0.33) for medium add versus single vision. Adjusted mean eye growth was 0.42, 0.58 and 0.66 mm respectively (high add vs single vision difference -0.23 mm, -0.30 to -0.17). The authors note that further research is needed to understand the clinical importance of the observed differences.
cards.watchOut: Progression was slowed, not stopped, and the medium-add versus single-vision difference (0.16 D) had a confidence interval crossing zero — the proven dose is the high add power.
cards.source: Walline JJ et al. Effect of High Add Power, Medium Add Power, or Single-Vision Contact Lenses on Myopia Progression in Children: The BLINK Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2020;324(6):571-580. PMID: 32780139. Registry ID: NCT02255474, from the record's databank fields.

cards.summary: MiSight: dual-focus lenses slowed 3-year progression by 0.73 D and axial growth by 0.32 mm vs single-vision lenses.
cards.type: Randomised, double-masked clinical trial (four sites, four countries)
cards.people: 144 myopic children aged 8 to 12 years (spherical equivalent -0.75 to -4.00 D; astigmatism under 1.00 D) with no prior contact-lens experience, randomised to MiSight 1-day dual-focus lenses or Proclear 1-day single-vision lenses on a daily-disposable basis; 109 (75.5%) completed the trial (53 test, 56 control). cards.result: Over 3 years, unadjusted change in spherical equivalent refraction was -0.51±0.64 D (MiSight) versus -1.24±0.61 D (control) (P<.001) — 0.73 D (59%) less progression — and mean axial-length change was 0.30±0.27 versus 0.62±0.30 mm (P<.001), 0.32 mm (52%) less growth. No serious ocular adverse events were reported; four asymptomatic corneal infiltrative events were observed (one test, three control).
cards.watchOut: A quarter of enrolled children did not complete the trial, and the percentages (59%/52%) are relative reductions on small absolute dioptre changes — the absolute differences (0.73 D; 0.32 mm over 3 years) are the figures to quote.

cards.headline: Synthesis: optical myopia control works — high-add multifocal and dual-focus lenses both slow progression — LIKELY
cards.summary: Optical myopia control works — both designs slow progression — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: BLINK (294 children, 3 years) and the MiSight trial (144 children, 3 years).
cards.result: Two lens designs, two trials, the same finding over the same horizon: roughly 0.5–0.7 D less progression and 0.23–0.32 mm less axial growth over 3 years versus single-vision correction. Whether that dioptre sparing converts into fewer high-myopia complications decades later is not something either trial measured.
cards.watchOut: Contact-lens wear in children carries its own hygiene and infection burden, which neither abstract quantifies beyond MiSight's four infiltrative events — the shelf supports efficacy, not a blanket recommendation for every child.

shelves.title: Probiotics (L. reuteri) for infant colic
shelves.question: Does Lactobacillus reuteri DSM 17938 reduce crying time in breastfed infants with colic versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Colic/therapy · Feces/microbiology · Infant, Newborn · Limosilactobacillus reuteri · Infant Behavior · Limosilactobacillus reuteri/metabolism · Probiotics/adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — breastfed infants · MAYBE (weak evidence) — formula-fed infants: The trials genuinely disagree, and feeding type explains most of it. Savino 2010 (50 exclusively breastfed infants) found crying fell to a median 35 versus 90 minutes/day by day 21. Sung 2014 (167 breastfed and formula-fed infants) found the probiotic group cried or fussed 49 minutes MORE than placebo at one month (P=0.02), driven by fussing in formula-fed infants. The individual-participant meta-analysis of all four double-blind trials (345 infants) found 25.4 minutes less crying/fussing at day 21 overall and treatment success almost twice as likely (incidence ratio 1.7, relative), with the effect dramatic in breastfed infants (number needed to treat 2.6) and insignificant in formula-fed infants, for whom the data were insufficient. Hence POSSIBLE for breastfed infants from a pooling anchored by one small positive trial against a larger null, and MAYBE (weak evidence) for formula-fed infants.

cards.headline: Savino 2010: in exclusively breastfed colicky infants, L. reuteri cut median crying to 35 vs 90 minutes/day by day 21
cards.summary: Savino 2010: in exclusively breastfed colicky infants, L. reuteri cut median crying to 35 vs 90 minutes/day by day 21.
cards.people: 50 exclusively breastfed colicky infants diagnosed by modified Wessel's criteria, randomly assigned to L. reuteri DSM 17938 (10^8 colony-forming units daily) or placebo for 21 days; 46 completed the trial (25 probiotic, 21 placebo); the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Daily crying times (median [interquartile range], minutes/day) were 370 (120) versus 300 (150) at day 0 (P=0.127) and 35.0 (85) versus 90.0 (148) at day 21 (P=0.022) in the L. reuteri and placebo groups respectively. Responders (a 50% reduction in crying time from baseline) were significantly more frequent with L. reuteri on days 7 (20 vs 8; P=0.006), 14 (24 vs 13; P=0.007) and 21 (24 vs 15; P=0.036). Faecal lactobacilli increased and Escherichia coli and ammonia fell in the probiotic group only. There were no differences in weight gain, stooling frequency, constipation or regurgitation, and no adverse events related to the supplementation were observed.
cards.watchOut: Fifty infants, one centre, exclusively breastfed — the population most favourable to the probiotic. Its medians carry wide interquartile ranges, and it cannot speak for formula-fed infants, where the larger trial found no benefit.
cards.source: Savino F et al. Lactobacillus reuteri DSM 17938 in infantile colic: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Pediatrics. 2010;126(3):e526-e533. PMID: 20713478. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Sung 2014: in a broad community sample, L. reuteri did not help — the probiotic group cried or fussed 49 minutes MORE than placebo at one month (P=0.02)
cards.summary: Sung 2014: in a broad community sample, L. reuteri did not help — the probiotic group cried or fussed 49 minutes MORE than placebo at one month.
cards.people: 167 breastfed and formula-fed infants aged under 3 months meeting Wessel's criteria for crying or fussing, from a community-based sample in Melbourne, Australia, randomised to oral L. reuteri DSM 17938 (1 × 10^8 colony-forming units daily, 85) or placebo (82) for one month; 127 (76%) were retained to the primary outcome; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At one month, the probiotic group cried or fussed 49 minutes more per day than the placebo group (95% CI 8 to 90 minutes; P=0.02), mainly reflecting more fussing, especially in formula-fed infants. The groups were similar on all secondary outcomes, including sleep duration, maternal mental health, family functioning and quality of life, and no study-related adverse events occurred. The authors conclude the findings differ from previous smaller trials of selected populations and do not support a general recommendation for probiotics to treat colic.
cards.watchOut: A quarter of infants were not retained to the primary outcome, and crying fell steadily in both groups — colic resolves with time, so any uncontrolled experience of this probiotic will look better than it is. The significant difference here ran AGAINST the probiotic. BioGaia Sweden supplied the investigational product and placebo at no cost, as named in the publication's full text.

cards.headline: Sung 2018 (individual-participant meta-analysis): benefit concentrated in breastfed infants — 25.4 minutes less crying at day 21 overall, NNT 2.6 in breastfed, insignificant in formula-fed
cards.summary: Sung 2018 (individual-participant meta-analysis): benefit concentrated in breastfed infants (NNT 2.6); insignificant in formula-fed.
cards.type: Individual participant data meta-analysis of double-blind randomised trials
cards.people: Four double-blind trials involving 345 infants with colic (174 probiotic, 171 placebo), published by June 2017, comparing oral L. reuteri DSM 17938 with placebo; the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: The probiotic group averaged less crying and/or fussing time than placebo at all time points (day 21 adjusted mean difference in change from baseline −25.4 minutes [95% CI −47.3 to −3.5]) and was almost twice as likely to experience treatment success at all time points (day 21 adjusted incidence ratio 1.7 [95% CI 1.4 to 2.2] — a relative figure). Intervention effects were dramatic in breastfed infants (number needed to treat for day 21 success 2.6 [95% CI 2.0 to 3.6]) but insignificant in formula-fed infants, for whom there were insufficient data to draw conclusions. The authors recommend L. reuteri for breastfed infants with colic and call for further research in formula-fed infants.
cards.watchOut: Four trials and 345 infants is a small evidence base for an individual-participant pooling, and two of its trials are carded above with opposite results — the pooled breastfed estimate leans heavily on small selected trials like Savino's. The incidence ratio of 1.7 sits inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band on its own; the absolute minute differences are the sturdier figures.

cards.summary: Feeding type splits the shelf — POSSIBLE in breastfed infants, MAYBE (weak evidence) in formula-fed.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Savino 2010 (50 breastfed infants), Sung 2014 (167 mixed-fed infants) and Sung 2018 (four trials, 345 infants pooled).

The split stamp prices that honestly — POSSIBLE where the signal is, MAYBE (weak evidence) where it is absent. shelves.title: Acid suppression for infant reflux and irritability
shelves.question: Do proton-pump inhibitors improve crying/irritability attributed to gastro-oesophageal reflux in infants versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: 2-Pyridinylmethylsulfinylbenzimidazoles/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions · Gastroesophageal Reflux/drug therapy · Lansoprazole · Proton Pump Inhibitors/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Anti-Ulcer Agents/therapeutic use · Cross-Over Studies
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): Two double-blind, placebo-controlled trials agree that proton-pump inhibitors do not reduce infant crying or irritability attributed to reflux. Orenstein 2009 (162 infants) found identical responder rates for lansoprazole and placebo (54% in each group) — and significantly more serious adverse events, particularly lower respiratory tract infections, with lansoprazole (10 vs 2 infants; P=0.032). Moore 2003 (30 infants, crossover) confirmed the mechanism and the disconnect: omeprazole cut oesophageal acid exposure (reflux index −8.9% vs −1.9%; P<0.001) yet irritability improved with time regardless of treatment, with no difference between omeprazole and placebo. The drug does what it is sold to do to acid; it does not do what it is prescribed to do to crying.

cards.headline: Orenstein 2009: lansoprazole was no better than placebo for infant GERD symptoms (responders 54% in both groups) — with more serious infections on the drug (10 vs 2)
cards.summary: Orenstein 2009: lansoprazole was no better than placebo for infant reflux symptoms (responders 54% in both groups ) — with more serious infections on the drug (10 vs 2).
cards.people: 162 infants aged 1 to 12 months with symptoms attributed to gastroesophageal reflux disease persisting despite at least one week of nonpharmacologic management, randomised to lansoprazole or placebo for four weeks (81 per group in the responder analysis); the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Of 216 infants screened, 162 were randomised; responders (a ≥50% reduction in feeding-related crying) numbered 44 of 81 (54%) in EACH group — identical for lansoprazole and placebo. No significant lansoprazole–placebo differences were detected in any secondary efficacy measures or analyses. During double-blind treatment, 62% of lansoprazole-treated infants experienced one or more treatment-emergent adverse events versus 46% of placebo recipients (P=0.058). Serious adverse events, particularly lower respiratory tract infections, occurred in 12 infants and significantly more frequently with lansoprazole than placebo (10 vs 2; P=0.032).
cards.watchOut: Symptoms were 'attributed to' reflux by clinical impression rather than proven acid-related in every infant — but that is exactly the population in practice, and the harm signal (respiratory infections) is the part prescribers least expect from a drug given for crying.

cards.summary: Moore 2003: omeprazole slashed acid exposure but not irritability — crying fell with time on both treatments.

shelves.title: Bracing for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (BrAIST)
shelves.question: Does rigid bracing prevent curve progression to the surgical threshold in adolescent idiopathic scoliosis — and is there a dose (hours worn) response?
shelves.mesh: Braces/adverse effects · Disease Progression · Intention to Treat Analysis · Logistic Models · Propensity Score · Spinal Curvatures/pathology,therapy · Spine/pathology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: BrAIST is one trial programme — a randomised cohort nested in a larger preference cohort — and it was stopped early for efficacy. Across both cohorts, treatment success (reaching skeletal maturity without progression to 50 degrees) was 72% with bracing versus 48% with observation (propensity-adjusted odds ratio 1.93, relative — inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band); in the randomised intention-to-treat analysis alone, success was 75% versus 42% (odds ratio 4.11, relative). Hours worn mattered: success rose significantly with longer daily brace wear (P<0.001). A single trial programme, half of it non-randomised, caps the stamp at POSSIBLE despite the dose-response.

cards.headline: BrAIST 2013: bracing kept 72% of high-risk adolescents from the surgical threshold vs 48% observed — and more hours worn meant more success
cards.summary: BrAIST 2013: bracing kept 72% of high-risk adolescents from the surgical threshold vs 48% observed — and more hours worn meant more success.
cards.type: Multicentre trial with randomised and preference cohorts (stopped early for efficacy)
cards.people: 242 patients with typical bracing indications (age, skeletal immaturity and degree of scoliosis putting them at risk of progression to surgery): 116 randomly assigned to bracing or observation and 126 who chose between them; patients in the bracing group were instructed to wear the brace at least 18 hours per day; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary outcomes were curve progression to 50 degrees or more (treatment failure) and skeletal maturity without that degree of progression (treatment success). In the combined randomised and preference cohorts, the rate of treatment success was 72% after bracing versus 48% after observation (propensity-score-adjusted odds ratio for treatment success 1.93; 95% CI 1.08 to 3.46 — a relative figure, inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band, with the absolute rates 72% vs 48% beside it). In the intention-to-treat analysis of the randomised cohort, success was 75% among patients assigned to bracing versus 42% assigned to observation (odds ratio 4.11; 95% CI 1.85 to 9.16 — relative). There was a significant positive association between hours of brace wear and treatment success (P<0.001). The trial was stopped early owing to the efficacy of bracing.
cards.watchOut: Half the analysed patients chose their own treatment, early stopping tends to inflate effects, and the combined-cohort odds ratio of 1.93 sits inside the library's 0.5–2.0 'not solid on its own' band — the randomised-cohort analysis and the dose-response carry the claim, and a single trial programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
cards.source: Weinstein SL et al. Effects of bracing in adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis. N Engl J Med. 2013;369(16):1512-1521. PMID: 24047455. Registry ID: NCT00448448, from the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: ADHD in children: stimulant medication and the MTA strategy trial
shelves.question: For childhood ADHD, how do stimulants compare with behavioural treatment and their combination — acutely (MTA) and in preschool children (PATS)?
shelves.mesh: Anxiety Disorders/epidemiology · Attention Deficit Disorder with Hyperactivity/drug therapy,therapy · Behavior Therapy/methods · Central Nervous System Stimulants/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Combined Modality Therapy · Community Mental Health Services · Comorbidity
shelves.balance: LIKELY: For core ADHD symptoms in school-age children, carefully managed medication beat intensive behavioural treatment and routine community care over 14 months in the MTA trial (579 children): the combined and medication-management groups improved significantly more than behavioural treatment and community care, and combined treatment did not significantly beat medication management alone on core symptoms — though it edged ahead on several non-core outcomes (oppositional symptoms, internalising symptoms, social skills, parent–child relations, reading). In preschoolers (PATS, Greenhill 2006), immediate-release methylphenidate given three times daily reduced symptoms significantly at 2.5, 5 and 7.5 mg doses versus placebo, with smaller effect sizes (0.4–0.8) than in school-age children and only 21% of preschoolers reaching the MTA remission criterion on their best dose. These are 14-month and short-term findings; neither trial answers what years of treatment do.

cards.headline: MTA 1999: over 14 months, medication management and combined treatment beat behavioural treatment and community care for ADHD symptoms; combined did not beat medication alone on core symptoms
cards.summary: MTA 1999: over 14 months, medication management and combined treatment beat behavioural treatment and community care for ADHD symptoms; combined did not beat medication alone on core symptoms.
cards.people: 579 children with ADHD, Combined Type, aged 7 to 9.9 years, assigned to 14 months of medication management (titration then monthly visits), intensive behavioural treatment (parent, school and child components), the two combined, or standard community care; the abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: All four groups showed sizable reductions in symptoms over time, with significant differences in degree of change. For most ADHD symptoms, children in the combined-treatment and medication-management groups showed significantly greater improvement than those given intensive behavioural treatment and community care. Combined and medication management did not differ significantly on any direct comparison for core symptoms, but in several instances (oppositional/aggressive symptoms, internalising symptoms, teacher-rated social skills, parent–child relations and reading achievement) combined treatment proved superior to intensive behavioural treatment and/or community care while medication management did not. The study medication strategies were superior to community care even though two thirds of community-treated children received medication during the study.
cards.watchOut: A 14-month strategy trial from 1999: 'medication management' meant protocolised titration and monthly review, not a routine prescription, and the trial does not address outcomes after treatment stops or over years.
cards.source: MTA Cooperative Group. A 14-month randomized clinical trial of treatment strategies for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Arch Gen Psychiatry. 1999;56(12):1073-1086. PMID: 10591283. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a pre-registration-era trial.

cards.headline: PATS 2006: methylphenidate worked in preschoolers at 2.5–7.5 mg three times daily, but effect sizes (0.4–0.8) were smaller than in school-age children
cards.summary: PATS 2006: methylphenidate worked in preschoolers at 2.5–7.5 mg three times daily, but effect sizes (0.4–0.8) were smaller than in school-age children.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial programme (double-blind crossover-titration followed by a placebo-controlled parallel phase)
cards.people: Preschool children aged 3 to 5.5 years with ADHD: 303 enrolled in the Preschool ADHD Treatment Study, 165 randomised into the crossover-titration trial and 114 into the later parallel placebo-controlled phase; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, significant decreases in ADHD symptoms were found on immediate-release methylphenidate at 2.5 mg (P<0.01), 5 mg (P<0.001) and 7.5 mg (P<0.001) three times daily, but not at 1.25 mg (P<0.06). The mean optimal total daily dose was 14.2 ±8.1 mg/day (0.7 ±0.4 mg/kg/day). In the parallel phase, only 21% of children on best-dose methylphenidate and 13% on placebo achieved the MTA-defined categorical remission criterion set for school-age children. Effect sizes (0.4–0.8) were smaller than those cited for school-age children on the same medication.
cards.watchOut: Preschoolers responded less completely than older children and needed weight-based doses three times a day; this record reports the efficacy phases of a 70-week programme, and growth and long-term safety monitoring belong to its later reports, not this card.

cards.headline: Synthesis: medication is the stronger lever on core symptoms at both ages — LIKELY for the short-to-medium term
cards.summary: Medication is the stronger lever on core symptoms at both ages — LIKELY for the short-to-medium term.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: MTA 1999 (579 children aged 7–9.9) and PATS 2006 (303 preschoolers enrolled).
cards.result: In school-age children, MTA's protocolised medication management (and its combination with behavioural treatment) produced significantly greater core-symptom improvement than intensive behavioural treatment alone or community care over 14 months; in preschoolers, PATS showed the same drug class beating placebo in double-blind phases, with smaller effects (0.4–0.8) and a best-dose remission rate of 21% versus 13% on placebo. Two randomised programmes at two ages earn LIKELY — bounded to symptom control while treated. Combined treatment's extra value sits in non-core outcomes, per MTA's own comparisons. Fluoxetine for adolescent depression lives on Shelf #224 and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial licenses claims about long-term academic, occupational or safety outcomes; the shelf's claim ends where the trials end (14 months in MTA; the controlled phases in PATS).

shelves.title: Early behavioural intervention for autism
shelves.question: Does intensive early behavioural intervention (Early Start Denver Model; parent-mediated communication therapy) improve cognition, language, or symptom severity in young autistic children?
shelves.mesh: Analysis of Variance · Autistic Disorder/diagnosis,therapy · Behavior Therapy/methods · Child Development/physiology · Cognition/physiology · Developmental Disabilities/etiology,prevention & control · Early Diagnosis
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two randomised trials of two different models both found gains, but each carries a ceiling. ESDM (Dawson 2010) randomised only 48 toddlers: after two years the ESDM group had improved 17.6 IQ standard-score points versus 7.0 in the community-intervention group, maintained adaptive-behaviour growth, and was more likely to shift diagnosis from autism to pervasive developmental disorder–not otherwise specified. PACT (Pickles 2016 long-term follow-up of 152 children) found a parent-mediated communication therapy reduced autism symptom severity across the trial and follow-up period (effect size 0.55, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.91; P=0.004), though the follow-up-only difference was not significant (0.70, −0.05 to 1.47) and there was no language-composite difference at follow-up (0.15, −0.23 to 0.53). Small numbers and one follow-up analysis keep the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Dawson 2010 (ESDM): two years of the Early Start Denver Model improved IQ by 17.6 points vs 7.0 with community intervention in toddlers
cards.summary: Dawson 2010 (ESDM): two years of the Early Start Denver Model improved IQ by 17.6 points vs 7.0 with community intervention in toddlers.
cards.people: 48 children diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder between 18 and 30 months of age, randomly assigned to the Early Start Denver Model (a developmental and applied-behaviour-analytic intervention delivered by trained therapists and parents for two years) or referral to community providers for commonly available intervention; the abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: Two years after entering intervention, the ESDM group had on average improved 17.6 standard-score points (1 SD: 15 points) on IQ compared with 7.0 points in the comparison group relative to baseline. The ESDM group maintained its rate of growth in adaptive behaviour compared with a normative sample of typically developing children, while the comparison group showed greater delays in adaptive behaviour over the two years. Children receiving ESDM were also more likely to experience a change in diagnosis from autism to pervasive developmental disorder, not otherwise specified, than the comparison group. The authors describe this as the first randomised trial to demonstrate efficacy of a comprehensive developmental behavioural intervention for toddlers with ASD on cognitive and adaptive behaviour.
cards.watchOut: Forty-eight children in one programme: a large effect in a small single trial is exactly the pattern that later trials usually shrink, and the comparison was heterogeneous community care, not a matched-intensity control.
cards.source: Dawson G et al. Randomized, controlled trial of an intervention for toddlers with autism: the Early Start Denver Model. Pediatrics. 2010;125(1):e17-e23. PMID: 19948568. Registry ID: NCT00090415, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Pickles 2016 (PACT follow-up): parent-mediated communication therapy reduced symptom severity across six years (effect size 0.55), with no language advantage at follow-up
cards.summary: Pickles 2016 (PACT follow-up): parent-mediated communication therapy reduced symptom severity across six years (effect size 0.55), with no language advantage at follow-up.
cards.type: Long-term follow-up of a randomised controlled trial
cards.people: 152 children aged 2–4 years with core autism randomised in the Preschool Autism Communication Trial to a parent-mediated social communication intervention or treatment as usual; 121 (80%) were traced and assessed at a median 5.75 years from the original trial endpoint (59 of 77 PACT, 62 of 75 treatment-as-usual); mean age at follow-up 10.5 years (SD 0.8); the abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: The group difference in autism symptom severity (Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule comparative severity score, log-odds effect size) was 0.64 (95% CI 0.07 to 1.20) at the treatment endpoint and 0.70 (−0.05 to 1.47) at follow-up, giving an overall reduction in symptom severity over the whole trial and follow-up period (effect size 0.55, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.91; P=0.004). Child initiations in parent interaction were greater with PACT at follow-up on the study-wide analysis (effect size 0.33, 0.11 to 0.57; P=0.004). There were no group differences in the expressive-receptive language composite at follow-up (effect size 0.15, −0.23 to 0.53). The authors describe these as the first results showing long-term symptom reduction after a randomised trial of early intervention in autism.
cards.watchOut: The follow-up-point estimate alone is not significant (confidence interval −0.05 to 1.47); the significant figure pools endpoint and follow-up, one in five families was lost, and language — the outcome parents most often ask about — showed no difference.
cards.source: Pickles A et al. Parent-mediated social communication therapy for young children with autism (PACT): long-term follow-up of a randomised controlled trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: early intervention helps, with the size and durability still uncertain — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Early intervention helps, with the size and durability still uncertain — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Dawson 2010 (48 toddlers, therapist-and-parent ESDM) and Pickles 2016 (152 children in PACT, parent-mediated, followed to about age 10).
cards.result: Two different delivery models in two countries both beat their controls on their headline developmental outcomes: ESDM on IQ gain (17.6 vs 7.0 standard points over two years) and PACT on symptom severity across six years (pooled effect size 0.55, P=0.004). The ceilings are equally clear: ESDM's trial held 48 children, and PACT's follow-up-only severity estimate and its language outcome were null. A small intensive trial plus a long-term follow-up with mixed horizons support POSSIBLE — early behavioural intervention does something real, and neither record can price it precisely.
cards.watchOut: Do not merge the two models into one claim: ESDM is intensive therapist-delivered treatment in toddlers; PACT is parent-mediated communication therapy. Their shared ground is direction, not dose or mechanism.

shelves.title: Nocturnal enuresis: alarm therapy vs desmopressin
shelves.question: In childhood nocturnal enuresis, does an enuresis alarm produce more durable dryness than desmopressin — and what does each do while used?
shelves.mesh: Absorbent Pads · Case-Control Studies · Deamino Arginine Vasopressin/therapeutic use · Electrodes · Enuresis/drug therapy,prevention & control · Nephrology/methods · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: LIKELY: The Cochrane synthesis of alarm trials (55 trials, 3,152 children) and an 18-trial network meta-analysis (1,649 children) draw the same picture from opposite ends. While used, about two thirds of children become dry on an alarm (relative risk of failure 0.38 versus no treatment, relative); nearly half of those who persist remain dry after the alarm stops, versus almost none after no treatment. Desmopressin may act faster, but alarms were more effective by the end of a treatment course (relative risk 0.71, relative) and clearly more durable afterwards (failure or relapse 18% vs 67% in the limited head-to-head data; network analysis: relapse much lower with alarm monotherapy than desmopressin monotherapy). Combinations topped the network rankings for initial response, but the alarm is the durability play — at the price of weeks of family effort.

cards.headline: Glazener 2005 (Cochrane): alarms made about two thirds of children dry during use and beat desmopressin by the end of treatment and after it
cards.summary: Glazener 2005 (Cochrane): alarms made about two thirds of children dry during use (relative risk of failure 0.38, relative) and beat desmopressin by the end of treatment and after it.
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised and quasi-randomised trials (Cochrane)
cards.people: 55 trials involving 3,152 children with nocturnal enuresis, of whom 2,345 used an alarm (mostly audio alarms); trials searched to 22 November 2004; the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Compared with no treatment, about two thirds of children became dry during alarm use (relative risk for failure 0.38, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.45 — relative). Nearly half who persisted with alarm use remained dry after treatment finished, compared with almost none after no treatment (relative risk of failure or relapse 45/81 [55%] vs 80/81 [99%]; relative risk 0.56, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.68 — relative, with the absolute rates beside it). Although desmopressin may have a more immediate effect, alarms appeared more effective by the end of a course of treatment (relative risk 0.71, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.99 — relative) with limited evidence of greater long-term success (failure 4/22 [18%] vs 16/24 [67%]; relative risk 0.27, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.69 — relative). Alarms also beat tricyclics during treatment (relative risk 0.73) and afterwards. Adding overlearning or dry-bed training further reduced relapse; penalties for wet beds appeared counter-productive, and electric-shock alarms were unacceptable. The review notes many trials were poor quality.
cards.watchOut: A 2005 review of often poor-quality, small trials: the durability advantage over desmopressin rests on very small numbers (22 vs 24 children in the long-term comparison), which is why the network analysis is carded beside it.
cards.source: Glazener CM et al. Alarm interventions for nocturnal enuresis in children. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2005;(2):CD002911. PMID: 15846643. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.type: Network meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
cards.people: 18 randomised trials with 1,649 participants with paediatric monosymptomatic nocturnal enuresis, comparing desmopressin, alarm, desmopressin plus alarm, and desmopressin plus an anticholinergic agent; literature searched to 1 March 2018; the abstract does not state mean age.

cards.summary: Desmopressin is the fast, temporary tool; the alarm is the durable one — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Glazener 2005 (55 trials, 3,152 children) and Song 2019 (18 trials, 1,649 children).
cards.result: Both syntheses agree on the trade: alarms get about two thirds of children dry during use (relative risk of failure 0.38 vs no treatment, relative) and keep nearly half of persisters dry afterwards, while desmopressin's effect is quicker but fades on stopping — alarms beat it by the end of treatment (relative risk 0.71, relative) and on later relapse in both analyses. shelves.title: Kawasaki disease: IVIG, aspirin dose, and added steroids for high-risk children
shelves.question: Does adding corticosteroids to IVIG prevent coronary artery abnormalities in high-risk Kawasaki disease — and does IVIG regimen (single high dose) matter?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Inflammatory Agents/therapeutic use · Aspirin/therapeutic use · Coronary Artery Disease/prevention & control · Coronary Vessel Anomalies/prevention & control · Drug Therapy, Combination · Immunoglobulins/therapeutic use · Mucocutaneous Lymph Node Syndrome/drug therapy
shelves.balance: PROPOSED stamp, pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C — coronary-outcome benefit claims): Split: POSSIBLE — single high-dose IVIG · POSSIBLE — added prednisolone in severe disease. Newburger 1991 (549 children) found a single 2 g/kg IVIG infusion beat four daily 400 mg/kg infusions on coronary abnormalities at two weeks (relative prevalence 1.94 for the four-day regimen versus single, relative; absolute rates not printed in the abstract) with faster fever resolution — though the seven-week comparison was not significant (1.84, 95% CI 0.89 to 3.82). RAISE (Kobayashi 2012; 248 children with severe Kawasaki disease in Japan) found adding prednisolone to IVIG cut coronary artery abnormalities from 23% to 3% (risk difference 0.20) during the study period. Each claim rests on a single trial — and RAISE enrolled risk-score-selected Japanese children in an open-label design — so both halves are POSSIBLE, and the shelf is Tier C because its claims are cardiovascular-outcome benefits.

cards.headline: RAISE 2012: adding prednisolone to IVIG cut coronary artery abnormalities from 23% to 3% in severe Kawasaki disease
cards.summary: RAISE 2012: adding prednisolone to IVIG cut coronary artery abnormalities from 23% to 3% in severe Kawasaki disease. (Tier C — coronary-outcome claim; PROPOSED pending the developer's verdict.)
cards.people: 248 patients with severe Kawasaki disease at 74 hospitals in Japan, randomly assigned to intravenous immunoglobulin (2 g/kg over 24 hours) plus aspirin 30 mg/kg per day (123) or the same regimen plus prednisolone 2 mg/kg per day given over 15 days after C-reactive protein normalised (125); the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The incidence of coronary artery abnormalities during the study period was significantly lower in the IVIG plus prednisolone group than in the IVIG group (four patients [3%] vs 28 patients [23%]; risk difference 0.20, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.28; P<0.0001). Serious adverse events were similar between groups: in the prednisolone group two patients had high total cholesterol and one had neutropenia; in the IVIG group one had high total cholesterol and another a non-occlusive thrombus. The authors conclude that adding prednisolone improves coronary artery outcomes in severe Kawasaki disease in Japan and call for study in a mixed ethnic population.
cards.watchOut: Open-label (with blinded endpoint assessment), single trial, and a risk-score-selected Japanese population: 'severe' was defined by Japanese risk scoring that performs differently in other ethnic groups, so the 3% vs 23% gap should not be transplanted untested into unselected or non-Japanese cohorts.
cards.source: Kobayashi T et al. Lancet. 2012;379(9826):1613-1620. PMID: 22405251. Registry ID: UMIN000000940 (University Hospital Medical Information Network), stated in the record's abstract; the MEDLINE record carries no databank SI field.

cards.headline: Newburger 1991: a single 2 g/kg IVIG infusion beat four daily doses on coronary abnormalities at two weeks and settled fever faster
cards.summary: Newburger 1991: a single 2 g/kg IVIG infusion beat four daily doses on coronary abnormalities at two weeks (relative prevalence 1.94, relative) and settled fever faster; the abstract prints no absolute prevalences, so none is claimed.
cards.people: 549 children with acute Kawasaki syndrome, assigned to gamma globulin as a single infusion of 2 g/kg over 10 hours or as daily infusions of 400 mg/kg for four consecutive days; both groups received aspirin (100 mg/kg per day through the 14th day of illness, then 3 to 5 mg/kg per day); the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The relative prevalence of coronary abnormalities, adjusted for age and sex, among patients on the four-day regimen compared with the single-infusion regimen was 1.94 (95% CI 1.01 to 3.71 — relative) two weeks after enrolment and 1.84 (95% CI 0.89 to 3.82 — relative) seven weeks after enrolment; the abstract does not print the absolute prevalence in each group, so none is claimed here. Children on the single-infusion regimen had lower mean temperatures while hospitalised (day 2, P<0.001; day 3, P=0.004), a shorter mean duration of fever (P=0.028), and laboratory indexes of inflammation that moved more rapidly towards normal; lower IgG levels on day 4 were associated with a higher prevalence of coronary lesions (P=0.005). Adverse effects occurred in 2.7% of children overall (including new or worsening congestive heart failure in nine children) and were similar between groups and transient. The ratio 1.94 sits inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band's edge and its seven-week counterpart is non-significant, so the regimen claim is stated modestly.
cards.watchOut: A 1991 trial from the era when the four-day regimen was standard: the two-week endpoint favoured the single dose, the seven-week endpoint did not reach significance, and aspirin dosing in the trial (100 mg/kg/day) is higher than many current protocols — the shelf answers the infusion question, not modern aspirin dose.

cards.headline: Synthesis: single high-dose IVIG is the backbone; added steroids help high-risk children — split POSSIBLE, PROPOSED (Tier C)
cards.summary: Single high-dose IVIG is the backbone; added steroids help high-risk children — split POSSIBLE, PROPOSED (Tier C).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Newburger 1991 (549 children, IVIG regimen) and RAISE 2012 (248 children with severe disease, added prednisolone).
cards.result: The regimen question and the intensification question have one trial each. Single-infusion IVIG beat divided dosing on the early coronary endpoint (relative prevalence 1.94 for the four-day regimen, relative) with faster defervescence (Newburger), and in risk-selected severe disease, adding prednisolone to that backbone produced the large absolute gap of 3% vs 23% in coronary abnormalities (RAISE). Neither has a confirmatory second trial on its own question, so both halves are POSSIBLE, and because both claims are coronary-outcome benefits the whole shelf is Tier C: the stamp is proposed pending the developer's personal verdict.
cards.watchOut: Do not generalise RAISE beyond its entry gate: its benefit was shown in Japanese children scored as severe/high-risk, and applying steroids to all Kawasaki presentations goes beyond the tested population.

shelves.title: Childhood functional constipation: polyethylene glycol vs lactulose
shelves.question: Is PEG more effective than lactulose (or other osmotic laxatives) for functional constipation in children?
shelves.mesh: Cathartics/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Constipation/drug therapy,physiopathology · Defecation/drug effects · Drug Administration Schedule · Electrolytes/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Encopresis/drug therapy · Lactulose/adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind randomised trials support polyethylene glycol on both sides of the comparison. Against lactulose head-to-head (Voskuijl 2004, 100 children), treatment success at eight weeks was 56% with PEG 3350 versus 29% with lactulose, with less abdominal pain, straining and pain at defecation on PEG (though a worse taste). Against placebo (Nurko 2008, 103 children), PEG 3350 at 0.2–0.8 g/kg/day produced successful treatment in 73–77% versus 42% on placebo (P<0.04), with the authors recommending a starting dose of 0.4 g/kg/day; the highest dose brought more abdominal pain and faecal incontinence. Two blinded trials, two comparators, one direction — LIKELY.

cards.headline: Voskuijl 2004: PEG 3350 doubled treatment success versus lactulose at eight weeks (56% vs 29%)
cards.summary: Voskuijl 2004: PEG 3350 doubled treatment success vs lactulose at eight weeks ( 56% vs 29% ).
cards.people: 100 patients aged 6 months to 15 years with paediatric functional constipation, treated for eight weeks after faecal disimpaction with PEG 3350 (Transipeg, 2.95 g/sachet) or lactulose (6 g/sachet), with children aged six and over starting at two sachets a day; 91 patients (49 male) completed the study; the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Defecation frequency rose significantly in both groups (PEG 3350: 3 to 7 per week; lactulose: 3 to 6 per week) and encopresis frequency fell in both (PEG: 10 to 3 per week; lactulose: 8 to 3 per week), with no significant between-group difference on those frequencies. Successful treatment (defecation frequency ≥3/week and encopresis ≤1 every two weeks) was nevertheless significantly higher with PEG (56%) than lactulose (29%). PEG patients reported less abdominal pain, straining and pain at defecation, but bad taste significantly more often. Doses used were PEG 3350 0.26 (SD 0.11) g/kg versus lactulose 0.66 (0.32) g/kg.
cards.watchOut: An eight-week trial in one Dutch programme using the Transipeg formulation: success is a composite of stool frequency and soiling, and nine of 100 children did not complete — long-term maintenance and other PEG formulations are outside this record.
cards.source: Voskuijl W et al. PEG 3350 (Transipeg) versus lactulose in the treatment of childhood functional constipation: a double blind, randomised, controlled, multicentre trial. Gut. 2004;53(11):1590-1594. PMID: 15479678. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Nurko 2008: PEG 3350 beat placebo at every dose (successful treatment 73–77% vs 42%); 0.4 g/kg/day was the recommended start
cards.summary: Nurko 2008: PEG 3350 beat placebo at every dose (successful treatment 73–77% vs 42% ); 0.4 g/kg/day was the recommended start.
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, dose-ranging trial
cards.people: 103 children with functional constipation (mean age 8.5 ±3.1 years) randomised after a one-week run-in to placebo or PEG 3350 at 0.2, 0.4 or 0.8 g/kg/day for two weeks, all receiving behaviour modification; the abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: Successful treatment response (≥3 bowel movements in the second week) occurred in 77%, 74% and 73% of the 0.2, 0.4 and 0.8 g/kg/day groups respectively, versus 42% on placebo (P<0.04). Bowel movements increased significantly (P<0.001) and straining improved (P<0.05) at the PEG doses; stool consistency improved significantly at 0.4 g/kg/day or higher (P<0.001). There was more abdominal pain and faecal incontinence at 0.8 g/kg/day. PEG 3350 was well tolerated overall, and the authors recommend a starting dose of 0.4 g/kg/day.
cards.watchOut: A two-week, dose-ranging trial: it proves short-term efficacy and calibrates the starting dose, but says nothing about months of maintenance, which is how the drug is actually used — that duration evidence sits with the eight-week lactulose comparison carded above.

shelves.title: Probiotics to prevent antibiotic-associated diarrhoea in children
shelves.question: Do probiotics given with antibiotics prevent antibiotic-associated diarrhoea in children — and does strain/dose decide it?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Diarrhea/etiology,prevention & control · Infant, Newborn · Probiotics/therapeutic use · Diarrhea/chemically induced,prevention & control · Feces/enzymology · Glucuronidase/metabolism
shelves.balance: LIKELY: The Cochrane prevention review (Guo 2019; 33 trials, 6,352 children) found antibiotic-associated diarrhoea in 8% of probiotic children versus 19% of controls (pooled risk ratio 0.45, relative — at or beyond the library's ≤0.5 solidity threshold — with a number needed to treat of 9), and the benefit survived an extreme-plausible intention-to-treat re-analysis (12% vs 19%; risk ratio 0.61, relative). Dose decided it: high-dose probiotics (≥5 billion CFU/day) performed better (number needed to treat 6), while low-dose studies were compatible with no effect in the intention-to-treat analysis. No serious adverse events were attributed to probiotics in the 24 reporting trials. The carded primary trial (Arvola 1999, Lactobacillus GG) matches the pooled pattern: diarrhoea in 5% versus 16% on placebo.

cards.headline: Guo 2019 (Cochrane): probiotics halved antibiotic-associated diarrhoea in children (8% vs 19%; risk ratio 0.45, relative; NNT 9) — with high dose doing the work
cards.summary: Guo 2019 (Cochrane): probiotics halved antibiotic-associated diarrhoea in children ( 8% vs 19% ; risk ratio 0.45, relative; NNT 9) — with high dose (≥5 billion CFU/day) doing the work.
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials (Cochrane)
cards.people: 33 studies with 6,352 participants aged 0 to 18 years receiving antibiotics, comparing probiotics (Bacillus, Bifidobacterium, Clostridium butyricum, Lactobacilli, Lactococcus, Leuconostoc, Saccharomyces or Streptococcus species, alone or combined) with placebo, active prophylaxis or no treatment; searches ran to 28 May 2018; risk of bias was high in 20 studies and low in 13; the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: In complete-case results from all 33 trials, the incidence of antibiotic-associated diarrhoea after five days to 12 weeks was 8% (259/3232) in the probiotic group versus 19% (598/3120) in the control group (risk ratio 0.45, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.56; I²=57%; number needed to treat for benefit 9, 95% CI 7 to 13; moderate-certainty evidence). Under an extreme-plausible intention-to-treat analysis accounting for losses to follow-up (1–46% across 19 studies), the benefit persisted (12% [436/3551] vs 19% [664/3468]; risk ratio 0.61, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.77; I²=70%). High-dose probiotics (≥5 billion CFU/day) were more effective than low dose (interaction P=0.01): in high-dose studies in the extreme-plausible analysis, incidence was 13% (278/2218) versus 23% (503/2207) (risk ratio 0.54, 95% CI 0.42 to 0.70), giving a number needed to treat of 6 (95% CI 5 to 9) on the complete-case high-dose figures, while low-dose studies gave 8% (97/1155) versus 13% (133/1059) (risk ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.46 to 1.01). None of the 24 trials reporting adverse events (4,415 participants) reported any serious adverse event attributable to probiotics, and mean diarrhoea duration was shortened by almost one day (mean difference −0.91 days; low-certainty evidence).
cards.watchOut: Twenty of 33 trials were at high risk of bias and strains were pooled across eight genera — the review supports a class-and-dose claim (high dose prevents AAD), not a guarantee for any single named product at any dose.
cards.source: Guo Q et al. Probiotics for the prevention of pediatric antibiotic-associated diarrhea. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2019;4(4):CD004827. PMID: 31039287. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Arvola 1999: Lactobacillus GG cut diarrhoea during antibiotics from 16% to 5% in children treated for respiratory infections
cards.summary: Arvola 1999: Lactobacillus GG cut diarrhoea during antibiotics from 16% to 5% in children treated for respiratory infections.
cards.people: 119 children from 2 weeks to 12.8 years of age (mean 4.5 years) receiving oral antibiotics for acute respiratory infections at clinics in Tampere, Finland, with no antibiotics in the previous three months and no gastrointestinal disorders, randomised to Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (2 × 10^10 colony-forming units in capsules twice daily during antibiotic treatment) or identical placebo; 167 were invited and 48 were lost to follow-up before the final population; the abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: The incidence of diarrhoea (at least three watery or loose stools per day for at least two consecutive days) within two weeks of starting antimicrobial therapy was 5% in the Lactobacillus GG group and 16% in the placebo group (chi-square 3.82; the abstract's text is truncated at that statistic, and no P value or confidence interval is printed in the record, so none is claimed here). Most gastrointestinal symptoms (80%) occurred during the first two weeks of follow-up, and parents kept daily symptom diaries with stool frequency and consistency recorded for three months.
cards.watchOut: A single-strain, single-centre-era trial with heavy early attrition (48 of 167 invited children did not reach the analysed population) and an abstract that truncates its own statistics — carded as the named-strain illustration of the Cochrane pattern, not as stand-alone proof.
