shelves.title: Rituximab for childhood steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome
shelves.question: In children with frequently relapsing/steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome, does rituximab prolong relapse-free survival versus placebo (Iijima) or versus low-dose mycophenolate (RITURNS)?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies, Monoclonal, Murine-Derived/adverse effects,therapeutic use · B-Lymphocytes/drug effects · Drug Therapy, Combination · Glucocorticoids/therapeutic use · Immunosuppressive Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Lymphocyte Count
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised trials, in complementary populations, both found rituximab prolonging relapse-free survival: Iijima 2014 in complicated frequently relapsing / steroid-dependent disease (median relapse-free period 267 vs 101 days; hazard ratio 0.27, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.53 — a relative measure at the strong end, outside the 0.5–2.0 caution band) and the 2025 JSKDC10 trial in uncomplicated disease (median 285 vs 81 days; 3-year cumulative relapse-free survival 38% vs 9% on follow-up). The third named comparison, RITURNS (rituximab versus low-dose mycophenolate), is fenced in the synthesis: its PubMed and Europe PMC records carry only a one-sentence description with no results figures, so no figure from it is printed on this shelf.

cards.headline: Iijima 2014: rituximab more than doubled the relapse-free period in complicated childhood FRNS/SDNS — median 267 vs 101 days, relative hazard 0.27
cards.summary: Iijima 2014: rituximab more than doubled the relapse-free period in complicated childhood FRNS/SDNS — median 267 vs 101 days , relative hazard 0.27.
cards.people: Children and young people aged 2 years or older at nine centres in Japan, with childhood-onset (diagnosed at 1–18 years) complicated frequently relapsing or steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome, in remission after treatment of a relapse at screening: 52 randomised, 48 received the assigned intervention (24 rituximab 375 mg/m2 once weekly for 4 weeks, 24 placebo), followed for 1 year; all received standard steroid treatment for the screening relapse and stopped immunosuppressants by day 169. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The median relapse-free period was significantly longer with rituximab (267 days, 95% confidence interval 223 to 374) than with placebo (101 days, 70 to 155; hazard ratio 0.27, 0.14 to 0.53; p<0.0001 — a relative measure). Ten patients (42%) in the rituximab group and six (25%) in the placebo group had at least one serious adverse event (p=0.36). The authors conclude rituximab is an effective and safe treatment for childhood-onset, complicated FRNS and SDNS.
cards.watchOut: Small (48 treated) and single-country, in complicated disease with high prior treatment exposure: the effect size is large, but the population is the severe end of the syndrome, which is why the uncomplicated-disease trial below matters.

cards.headline: JSKDC10 2025: in uncomplicated childhood FRNS/SDNS, rituximab stretched the median relapse-free period to 285 vs 81 days
cards.summary: JSKDC10 2025 (found by the currency sweep and carded): in uncomplicated childhood FRNS/SDNS, rituximab stretched the median relapse-free period to 285 vs 81 days.
cards.type: Multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial with a follow-up study after B-cell recovery
cards.people: Children with childhood-onset uncomplicated frequently relapsing or steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome (no prior glucocorticoid-sparing immunosuppressive agents): 43 randomised, 40 received the intervention (18 rituximab 375 mg/m2, maximum 500 mg, once weekly for 2 weeks; 22 placebo). cards.result: The relapse-free period during the 1-year trial was significantly longer with rituximab than placebo (median 285 vs 81 days; p<0.001). Infusion reactions were more frequent with rituximab (p<0.001), with no difference in overall adverse-event incidence between groups. cards.headline: Synthesis: two placebo-controlled trials agree across the severity range — LIKELY; the mycophenolate head-to-head is fenced, unfigured
cards.summary: Two placebo-controlled trials agree across the severity range — LIKELY; the mycophenolate head-to-head (RITURNS) is fenced by name, unfigured, because its records carry no results figures.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Iijima 2014 (48 treated, complicated disease) and JSKDC10 2025 (40 treated, uncomplicated disease).
cards.result: The medians tell one story twice: 267 vs 101 days in complicated disease (relative hazard 0.27) and 285 vs 81 days in uncomplicated disease, with a 3-year relapse-free survival of 38% vs 9% after a single course in the newer trial. Rituximab delays relapse in both populations; it does not cure the syndrome, since relapses followed B-cell recovery in both programmes. The drafted shelf's third comparison — RITURNS (Basu 2022, rituximab versus low-dose mycophenolate mofetil, PMID 33616641) — is NOT carded with figures: its PubMed record and its Europe PMC record both carry only a one-sentence description of the trial and no results, so under this library's figure rule nothing from it is printed here; the active-comparator question remains open on this shelf until a figure-bearing record is carded.
cards.watchOut: Both carded trials are Japanese and small; infusion reactions were more frequent with rituximab in the 2025 trial, and serious adverse events were numerically more frequent with rituximab in Iijima 2014 (42% vs 25%, p=0.36).

shelves.title: Obesity pharmacotherapy in adolescents: semaglutide and liraglutide
shelves.question: In adolescents with obesity, how much weight do once-weekly semaglutide and daily liraglutide lose versus placebo, on top of lifestyle therapy?
shelves.mesh: Pediatric Obesity/drug therapy,therapy · Weight Loss/drug effects · Healthy Lifestyle · Body Mass Index · Anti-Obesity Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Administration, Cutaneous · Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind, placebo-controlled trials in adolescents aged 12 to <18 years point the same way: once-weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg changed BMI by -16.1% versus +0.6% on placebo at 68 weeks (STEP TEENS), and daily liraglutide 3.0 mg beat placebo on BMI standard-deviation score by an estimated -0.22 at 56 weeks (Ellipse), with 43.3% versus 18.7% achieving at least 5% BMI reduction. Gastrointestinal adverse events were more common on both drugs (62% vs 42% semaglutide; 64.8% vs 36.5% liraglutide), and weight tended to return after liraglutide was stopped. No cardiovascular-outcome claim is made on this shelf.

cards.headline: STEP TEENS: once-weekly semaglutide changed BMI by -16.1% versus +0.6% on placebo at 68 weeks in adolescents with obesity
cards.summary: STEP TEENS: once-weekly semaglutide changed BMI by −16.1% vs +0.6% on placebo at 68 weeks in adolescents with obesity.
cards.people: 201 adolescents aged 12 to <18 years with obesity (BMI at or above the 95th percentile), or overweight with at least one weight-related condition; all but one participant had obesity; 180 (90%) completed treatment. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Mean BMI change at week 68 was -16.1% with semaglutide versus +0.6% with placebo (estimated difference -16.7 percentage points, 95% CI -20.3 to -13.2; P<0.001). Weight loss of at least 5% occurred in 95 of 131 (73%) on semaglutide versus 11 of 62 (18%) on placebo (estimated odds ratio 14.0, relative). Waist circumference and cardiometabolic risk factors (glycated haemoglobin, lipids except HDL cholesterol, alanine aminotransferase) improved more with semaglutide. Gastrointestinal adverse events: 62% versus 42%; cholelithiasis in 5 participants (4%) on semaglutide versus none on placebo; serious adverse events 11% versus 9%.
cards.watchOut: BMI and weight are surrogate outcomes over 68 weeks in a manufacturer-funded trial; there are no hard-outcome or long-term post-treatment data on this card, and gallbladder events appeared only in the semaglutide arm.

shelves.title: Minimally invasive surfactant therapy in preterm infants: OPTIMIST-A and NINSAPP
shelves.question: In preterm infants on CPAP with respiratory distress, does giving surfactant through a thin catheter without intubation reduce death or bronchopulmonary dysplasia versus sham or standard intubation-based administration?
shelves.mesh: Biological Products/administration & dosage · Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia/prevention & control · Continuous Positive Airway Pressure · Infant, Newborn · Infant, Premature · Infant, Premature, Diseases/mortality · Phospholipids/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C — the composite includes death): Split — POSSIBLE that thin-catheter surfactant reduces intubation and days of ventilation (NINSAPP: intubation 74.8% vs 99.0%); MAYBE (weak evidence) that it reduces death or bronchopulmonary dysplasia, because both trials missed that primary — OPTIMIST-A: death or BPD 43.6% vs 49.6% (relative risk 0.87, relative; P=.10), with death itself 10.0% vs 7.8%; NINSAPP: survival without BPD 67.3% vs 58.7% (absolute difference 8.6%, P=.20). FENCE: this shelf asks how surfactant is GIVEN to infants already on CPAP; the delivery-room CPAP-first versus early-intubation strategy question is home on Shelf #421 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: OPTIMIST-A: minimally invasive surfactant therapy did not significantly reduce death or BPD (43.6% vs 49.6%; P=.10)
cards.summary: OPTIMIST-A: minimally invasive surfactant therapy did not significantly reduce death or BPD ( 43.6% vs 49.6% ; P=.10); the death component was 10.0% vs 7.8%.
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial with sham control, blinded clinicians and outcome assessors
cards.people: 485 preterm infants of 25 to 28 weeks' gestation on CPAP requiring FiO2 of 0.30 or more within 6 hours of birth, at 33 tertiary neonatal units: 241 assigned to MIST (poractant alfa 200 mg/kg via thin catheter) and 244 to sham treatment; median gestational age 27.3 weeks; 241 (49.7%) female.
cards.result: Death or physiological BPD at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age occurred in 105 infants (43.6%) on MIST versus 121 (49.6%) on sham (risk difference -6.3%, 95% CI -14.2% to 1.6%; relative risk 0.87, relative, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.03; P=.10). Death before 36 weeks did not differ: 10.0% versus 7.8% (relative risk 1.27, relative). BPD among survivors was lower with MIST: 81 of 217 (37.3%) versus 102 of 225 (45.3%) (relative risk 0.83, relative; P=.03). Serious adverse events: 10.3% versus 11.1%. The relative risk of 0.87 sits inside the 0.5–2.0 band and is not solid evidence of benefit on its own.
cards.watchOut: The primary composite was null and the confidence interval cannot exclude a clinically important effect in either direction; the BPD-in-survivors component is a secondary, survivor-restricted analysis, and the death component pointed the other way.

cards.summary: NINSAPP: LISA did not significantly raise survival without BPD ( 67.3% vs 58.7% ; P=.20), but cut intubation and major complications.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two trials, two null primaries on death or BPD — the ventilation-sparing effect is the firmer ground (PROPOSED, Tier C)
cards.summary: Two trials, two null primaries on death or BPD — the ventilation-sparing effect is the firmer ground — Split: POSSIBLE · MAYBE (weak evidence), Tier C.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: OPTIMIST-A (485 infants, 25–28 weeks, sham control) and NINSAPP (211 infants, 23–27 weeks, intubation control).
cards.result: Neither trial significantly improved its death-or-BPD primary (OPTIMIST-A 43.6% vs 49.6%, relative risk 0.87 relative; NINSAPP survival without BPD 67.3% vs 58.7%, P=.20), and OPTIMIST-A's death component was 10.0% versus 7.8%. The consistent signal is process-level: less intubation (74.8% vs 99.0% in NINSAPP) and fewer ventilation days. The stamp is therefore split and PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict, because the composite contains death. This shelf is fenced against Shelf #421 (CPAP-first strategy): no trial from that shelf is carded here.

shelves.title: Step-up therapy for childhood asthma: BADGER and TREXA
shelves.question: In children whose asthma is uncontrolled on low-dose inhaled steroids, which step-up works best — and can rescue steroid replace daily control in mild persistent asthma?
shelves.mesh: Acetates/administration & dosage · Administration, Inhalation · Administration, Oral · Adrenergic beta-Agonists/administration & dosage · Albuterol/administration & dosage,analogs & derivatives · Androstadienes/administration & dosage · Asthma/complications,drug therapy,ethnology,physiopathology
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY that, for children uncontrolled on low-dose inhaled corticosteroid (ICS), adding a long-acting beta-agonist (LABA) is the step-up most likely to give the best response (BADGER: relative probability 1.6 versus leukotriene-antagonist step-up and 1.7 versus ICS step-up, relative) — though nearly every child had a differential response and many did best on another option. POSSIBLE that, in mild persistent asthma, rescue beclomethasone with albuterol is an effective step-down versus albuterol alone (TREXA: exacerbations 35% vs 49%, not significant at P=0.07; treatment failure 8.5% vs 23%, P=0.024), while daily ICS remained the most effective exacerbation prevention (28% vs 49%; P=0.03) at a cost of 1.1 cm less linear growth.

cards.headline: BADGER: LABA step-up was most likely to be the best response in children uncontrolled on low-dose ICS
cards.summary: BADGER: LABA step-up was most likely to be the best response in children uncontrolled on low-dose ICS (relative probability 1.6 ).
cards.type: Randomised, blinded, triple-crossover trial (each child received all three step-ups in random order)
cards.people: 182 children aged 6 to 17 years with asthma uncontrolled on fluticasone 100 micrograms twice daily; 165 were evaluated for differential response. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: A differential response to the three 16-week step-ups occurred in 161 of 165 evaluated children (P<0.001). LABA step-up (fluticasone plus salmeterol) was most likely to be the best response: relative probability 1.6 (95% CI 1.1 to 2.3; P=0.004) versus leukotriene-receptor-antagonist step-up and 1.7 (95% CI 1.2 to 2.4; P=0.002) versus doubling the ICS dose — both relative measures inside the 0.5–2.0 band's upper region, printed as relative. Better baseline Asthma Control Test scores predicted a better LABA response; many children nonetheless did best on ICS or LTRA step-up.
cards.watchOut: A crossover 'best response' composite (exacerbations, control days, FEV1) is not a hard-outcome ranking, and the trial's own message is heterogeneity: the winning step-up differed by child, so monitoring and adjustment matter more than a universal order.

cards.result: The two trials answer different rungs of the ladder: BADGER ranks step-ups when control is lost (LABA most likely best, relative probability 1.6–1.7, relative), and TREXA shows daily ICS is the strongest exacerbation prevention in mild disease (28% vs 49%) while rescue ICS plus albuterol cuts treatment failure versus albuterol alone (8.5% vs 23%) without the 1.1 cm growth penalty of daily dosing. shelves.title: Preventive drugs for paediatric migraine: the CHAMP trial
shelves.question: Do amitriptyline or topiramate prevent migraine in children and adolescents better than placebo?
shelves.mesh: Amitriptyline/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Anticonvulsants/therapeutic use · Fatigue/chemically induced · Fructose/adverse effects,analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use · Linear Models · Migraine Disorders/drug therapy · Paresthesia/chemically induced
shelves.balance: LIKELY the null: In CHAMP — a large double-blind, placebo-controlled trial stopped early for futility — neither amitriptyline (52% achieving at least a 50% relative reduction in headache days) nor topiramate (55%) beat placebo (61%) over 24 weeks, and both drugs caused more adverse events than placebo. A single very large, futility-stopped null trial carries LIKELY for the null, per the library's stated reasoning for large single null trials. FENCE: this CHAMP is the paediatric-migraine trial; the CHAMPION carbetocin trial carded on Shelf #416 is a different study sharing a similar acronym.

cards.headline: CHAMP: neither amitriptyline (52%) nor topiramate (55%) beat placebo (61%) for paediatric migraine prevention — stopped for futility
cards.summary: CHAMP: neither amitriptyline ( 52% ) nor topiramate ( 55% ) beat placebo ( 61% ) for paediatric migraine prevention — stopped for futility.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (2:2:1 allocation), stopped early for futility at planned interim analysis
cards.people: 361 children and adolescents aged 8 to 17 years with migraine randomised; 328 in the primary efficacy analysis (132 amitriptyline 1 mg/kg/day, 130 topiramate 2 mg/kg/day, 66 placebo). The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: The primary outcome — a relative reduction of 50% or more in headache days over the last 28 days of the 24-week trial versus baseline — occurred in 52% on amitriptyline, 55% on topiramate and 61% on placebo (amitriptyline vs placebo P=0.26; topiramate vs placebo P=0.48; amitriptyline vs topiramate P=0.49). There were no significant differences in headache-related disability, headache days, or completion. Adverse events were more frequent on active drugs: fatigue 30% versus 14% and dry mouth 25% versus 12% (amitriptyline); paraesthesia 31% versus 8% and weight loss 8% versus 0% (topiramate). Three amitriptyline patients had serious adverse events of altered mood; one topiramate patient attempted suicide.
cards.watchOut: A single trial — but a large, NIH-funded, futility-stopped one; the high placebo response (61%) is itself the lesson, and the result does not exclude benefit from other preventive classes not tested here.
cards.source: Powers SW et al. Trial of Amitriptyline, Topiramate, and Placebo for Pediatric Migraine. N Engl J Med. 2017;376(2):115-124. PMID: 27788026. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT01581281, from the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: Vitamin D in pregnancy to delay offspring asthma and wheeze: VDAART and COPSAC
shelves.question: Does high-dose vitamin D supplementation during pregnancy reduce asthma or recurrent or persistent wheeze in the child by age 3?
shelves.mesh: Asthma/epidemiology,prevention & control · Cholecalciferol/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Dietary Supplements · Fetal Blood/chemistry · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Trimester, Third/blood · Recurrence
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): Each trial was null alone on its primary — VDAART: asthma or recurrent wheeze by age 3 in 24.3% versus 30.4% (hazard ratio 0.8, relative, 95% CI 0.6 to 1.0; P=.051); COPSAC: persistent wheeze in 16% versus 20%, not statistically significant. Any pooled positivity rests on combining two individually null trials, and the hazard ratio of 0.8 sits inside the 0.5–2.0 band that is not solid evidence on its own — so the shelf prints MAYBE (weak evidence) for any delay or reduction in offspring wheeze. Wording follows the developer's standard: delay/risk-reduction, never prevention.

cards.headline: VDAART: prenatal vitamin D 4400 IU/day — offspring asthma or recurrent wheeze 24.3% vs 30.4% (P=.051), not significant
cards.summary: VDAART: prenatal vitamin D 4400 IU/day — offspring asthma or recurrent wheeze 24.3% vs 30.4% (P=.051), not significant.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (3 US centres)
cards.people: 876 pregnant women aged 18 to 39 years at high risk of having children with asthma, randomised at 10 to 18 weeks' gestation (440 to 4400 IU/day total vitamin D, 436 to 400 IU/day); 806 infants were included in the 3-year outcome analyses. Mean age is as stated in the eligibility band; the abstract does not state a mean age or the infants' sex mix.
cards.result: Asthma or recurrent wheeze by age 3 occurred in 98 of 405 children (24.3%) in the 4400-IU group versus 120 of 401 (30.4%) in the 400-IU group (hazard ratio 0.8, relative, 95% CI 0.6 to 1.0; P=.051 — not significant, and inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band). Maternal third-trimester 25-hydroxyvitamin D of at least 30 ng/mL was achieved by 74.9% versus 34.0% of checked women (P<.001).
cards.watchOut: The trial may have been underpowered, as its authors state; the population was selected for high asthma risk, and the endpoint is parental report of physician-diagnosed asthma or recurrent wheeze, not a hard outcome.

cards.headline: COPSAC: vitamin D3 2800 IU/day in pregnancy did not significantly reduce persistent wheeze in offspring (16% vs 20%)
cards.summary: COPSAC: vitamin D3 2800 IU/day in pregnancy did not significantly reduce persistent wheeze in offspring ( 16% vs 20% ).
cards.people: 623 women recruited at 24 weeks of pregnancy (315 assigned to vitamin D3 2400 IU/day plus usual-care 400 IU/day, 308 to placebo plus 400 IU/day); follow-up of 581 children was completed to age 3 years. The abstract does not state mean age or the children's sex mix.
cards.result: Persistent wheeze in the first 3 years was diagnosed in 47 children (16%) in the vitamin D3 group versus 57 (20%) in the control group — not a statistically significant reduction, and any relative effect sits inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band. shelves.title: Influenza vaccination in pregnancy: protection for mother and infant
shelves.question: Does vaccinating pregnant women against influenza protect their infants in the first months of life?
shelves.mesh: Bangladesh/epidemiology · Infant, Newborn · Influenza Vaccines/adverse effects,immunology · Influenza, Human/epidemiology,immunology,prevention & control · Pneumococcal Vaccines/immunology · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Trimester, Third
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials in different settings found maternal influenza vaccination protects young infants who are too young to be vaccinated themselves — Bangladesh (Zaman): laboratory-confirmed influenza in infants 6 versus 16 cases, vaccine effectiveness 63% (relative), with febrile respiratory illness reduced by 29% (relative) in infants and 36% (relative) in mothers; South Africa (Madhi): vaccine efficacy 48.8% (relative) in infants not exposed to HIV and 50.4% (relative) in HIV-uninfected mothers. Effects are partial, not complete, protection.

cards.headline: Zaman (Bangladesh): maternal influenza vaccination — infant laboratory-confirmed influenza vaccine effectiveness 63% (relative)
cards.summary: Bangladesh: maternal influenza vaccination — infant laboratory-confirmed influenza vaccine effectiveness 63% (relative) .
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (influenza vaccine versus pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine control)
cards.people: 340 mothers in Bangladesh assigned to inactivated influenza vaccine or 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine during pregnancy, with mothers and infants observed to 24 weeks after birth (August 2004 to December 2005). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Laboratory-confirmed influenza in infants: 6 cases in the influenza-vaccine group versus 16 in the control group (vaccine effectiveness 63%, relative, 95% CI 5 to 85). Respiratory illness with fever occurred in 110 versus 153 infants (vaccine effectiveness 29%, relative, 95% CI 7 to 46). Among mothers, respiratory illness with fever was reduced by 36% (relative, 95% CI 4 to 57).
cards.watchOut: Small case counts (6 vs 16 confirmed infant cases) make the 63% estimate imprecise (CI 5 to 85), and the control was an active pneumococcal vaccine rather than placebo; one setting, one era of influenza circulation.
cards.source: Zaman K et al. Effectiveness of maternal influenza immunization in mothers and infants. N Engl J Med. 2008;359(15):1555-1564. PMID: 18799552. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT00142389, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Madhi (South Africa): influenza vaccine efficacy 48.8% (relative) in infants and 50.4% (relative) in HIV-uninfected mothers
cards.summary: South Africa: influenza vaccine efficacy 48.8% (relative) in infants and 50.4% (relative) in HIV-uninfected mothers.
cards.type: Two double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trials of trivalent inactivated influenza vaccine
cards.people: 2,116 pregnant women not infected with HIV and 194 pregnant women infected with HIV in South Africa (2011–2012), with infants evaluated to 24 weeks after birth. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Among HIV-uninfected participants, the attack rate for RT-PCR-confirmed influenza in placebo recipients and their infants was 3.6%; rates in vaccine recipients were 1.8% (mothers) and 1.9% (infants), giving vaccine efficacy of 50.4% (relative, 95% CI 14.5 to 71.2) and 48.8% (relative, 95% CI 11.6 to 70.4). Among HIV-infected women, attack rates were 17.0% on placebo versus 7.0% on vaccine (vaccine efficacy 57.7%, relative, 95% CI 0.2 to 82.1). Vaccine was immunogenic in both cohorts, and newborns of vaccine recipients had higher haemagglutination-inhibition titres.
cards.watchOut: Protection is partial (about half of confirmed influenza), the HIV-infected cohort was small (194 women) with a very wide efficacy interval, and efficacy varies by season and strain match — neither is stated beyond these trials' seasons.

shelves.title: Short-course antibiotics for childhood urinary tract infection (SCOUT)
shelves.question: In children with UTI who have improved by day 5, is stopping at 5 days as good as continuing to 10?
shelves.mesh: Duration of Therapy · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Bacteriuria/drug therapy · Urinary Tract Infections/drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: In SCOUT, the single large randomised trial, stopping antibiotics at 5 days in children who had already improved produced more treatment failures than continuing to 10 days (4.2% vs 0.6%; absolute difference 3.6%) and non-inferiority was not established — yet the absolute failure rate on the short course was low, which is why the trial's authors call 5 days a reasonable option for improvers. A single pivotal trial caps this shelf at POSSIBLE. Fenced in the synthesis: the 2025 INDI-UTI trial asks an individualised-duration question in febrile UTI, a different population.

cards.headline: SCOUT: 5-day therapy failed more often than 10-day (4.2% vs 0.6%) in children improved by day 5 — non-inferiority not met
cards.summary: SCOUT: 5-day therapy failed more often than 10-day ( 4.2% vs 0.6% ) in children improved by day 5 — non-inferiority not met.
cards.type: Randomised clinical non-inferiority trial (standard course versus placebo for days 6–10)
cards.people: 664 randomised children aged 2 months to 10 years with UTI who had shown clinical improvement after 5 days of antimicrobials, at outpatient clinics and emergency departments of 2 children's hospitals (639 female, 96%; median age 4 years).
cards.result: Treatment failure (symptomatic UTI at or before the day 11–14 follow-up visit) occurred in 14 of 336 children (4.2%) on short-course therapy versus 2 of 328 (0.6%) on standard-course therapy (absolute difference 3.6%, upper bound of the 95% CI 5.5%). Short-course children were more likely to have asymptomatic bacteriuria or a positive urine culture at or by first follow-up. There were no differences in UTI after the first follow-up visit, adverse events, or gastrointestinal colonisation with resistant organisms.
cards.watchOut: A single trial, and its population is pre-selected improvers — the result does not apply to children still symptomatic at day 5, to febrile infants, or to complicated UTI; the trade-off is 3.6 extra failures per 100 against 5 fewer antibiotic days.

shelves.title: Anxiety disorders in children and adolescents: CBT, sertraline, or both (CAMS)
shelves.question: In childhood anxiety disorders, how do cognitive behavioural therapy and sertraline compare alone and combined versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Anxiety Disorders/therapy · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Combined Modality Therapy · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Sertraline/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: In CAMS, the single large randomised trial, combination therapy responded best (80.7% much or very much improved), ahead of CBT alone (59.7%) and sertraline alone (54.9%), each superior to placebo (23.7%). A single pivotal trial caps this shelf at POSSIBLE despite the trial's size and internal consistency across its categorical and dimensional outcomes. Adverse events, including suicidal ideation, were no more frequent on sertraline than on placebo, and no child attempted suicide.

cards.headline: CAMS: combination therapy responded in 80.7%, versus 59.7% CBT, 54.9% sertraline and 23.7% placebo
cards.summary: CAMS: combination therapy responded in 80.7% , versus 59.7% CBT, 54.9% sertraline and 23.7% placebo.
cards.people: 488 children aged 7 to 17 years with a primary diagnosis of separation anxiety disorder, generalised anxiety disorder, or social phobia, assigned to 14 sessions of CBT, sertraline (up to 200 mg/day), both, or placebo drug. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Children rated very much or much improved on the Clinician Global Impression–Improvement scale: 80.7% combination (P<0.001 vs placebo), 59.7% CBT (P<0.001), 54.9% sertraline (P<0.001), 23.7% placebo. Combination therapy was superior to both monotherapies (P<0.001); CBT and sertraline were equivalent to each other on the Pediatric Anxiety Rating Scale pattern. Adverse events, including suicidal and homicidal ideation, were no more frequent with sertraline than placebo; no child attempted suicide. Insomnia, fatigue, sedation and restlessness were less frequent with CBT than with sertraline.
cards.watchOut: A single trial with a 12-week horizon and clinician-rated response as the headline; CBT here was a specific 14-session protocol, and the placebo arm received pill placebo without an attention-matched therapy control.
cards.source: Walkup JT et al. Cognitive behavioral therapy, sertraline, or a combination in childhood anxiety. N Engl J Med. 2008;359(26):2753-2766. PMID: 18974308. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT00052078, from the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: High-flow oxygen for infants with bronchiolitis: PARIS and PARIS-2
shelves.question: Does early high-flow nasal oxygen reduce treatment escalation in infants with bronchiolitis versus standard low-flow oxygen — and does it shorten hospital stay in children with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure?
shelves.mesh: Bronchiolitis/therapy · Infant, Newborn · Infant, Premature · Infant, Premature, Diseases/therapy · Intensive Care Units · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Length of Stay
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY that high-flow oxygen reduces escalation of care in infants with bronchiolitis treated outside intensive care (PARIS: 12% vs 23%; risk difference -11 percentage points), without shortening hospital stay — and LIKELY that, in children aged 1 to 4 years with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, early high-flow does NOT shorten stay: PARIS-2 found stay was longer on high-flow (median 1.77 vs 1.50 days) with more ICU admissions (12.5% vs 6.9%). FENCE: nebulised therapies and steroids in bronchiolitis are home on Shelf #252; high-flow is a support modality, not a nebulised drug, and no #252 trial is carded here.

cards.headline: PARIS: high-flow oxygen cut escalation of care in bronchiolitis from 23% to 12%, without shortening stay
cards.summary: PARIS: high-flow oxygen cut escalation of care in bronchiolitis from 23% to 12% , without shortening stay.
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, controlled trial (open-label; rescue high-flow permitted in the standard arm)
cards.people: 1,472 infants younger than 12 months with bronchiolitis needing supplemental oxygen, treated outside intensive care: 739 assigned to high-flow and 733 to standard oxygen therapy. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Escalation of care due to treatment failure occurred in 87 of 739 infants (12%) on high-flow versus 167 of 733 (23%) on standard therapy (risk difference -11 percentage points, 95% CI -15 to -7; P<0.001). There were no significant differences in duration of hospital stay or duration of oxygen therapy. Pneumothorax occurred once in each group (<1%). Of the 167 standard-therapy infants with treatment failure, 102 (61%) responded to rescue high-flow therapy.
cards.watchOut: Escalation is a clinician-judged composite in an unblinded trial, and the standard arm's rescue pathway means the trial tests early versus rescue high-flow as much as high-flow versus none; stay and oxygen duration were unchanged.
cards.source: Franklin D et al. A Randomized Trial of High-Flow Oxygen Therapy in Infants with Bronchiolitis. N Engl J Med. 2018;378(12):1121-1131. PMID: 29562151. Registry ID: ANZCTR: ACTRN12613000388718, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: PARIS-2: early high-flow lengthened hospital stay in children 1–4 years with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (1.77 vs 1.50 days)
cards.summary: PARIS-2: early high-flow lengthened hospital stay in children 1–4 years with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure ( 1.77 vs 1.50 days ).
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised clinical trial (therapy unmasked; investigators blinded until data lock)
cards.people: 1,567 children aged 1 to 4 years admitted with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure at 14 Australian and New Zealand hospitals; 1,517 (97%) in the primary analysis (median age 1.9 years; 732, 46.7%, female): 753 allocated to high-flow and 764 to standard oxygen in the analysed set as reported.
cards.result: Length of hospital stay was longer with high-flow: median 1.77 days (IQR 1.03–2.80) versus 1.50 days (IQR 0.85–2.44) (adjusted hazard ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.75 to 0.92; P<.001 — a relative measure, with the absolute medians beside it). Length of oxygen therapy was also longer (median 1.07 vs 0.75 days; adjusted hazard ratio 0.78, relative). ICU admission: 94 (12.5%) on high-flow versus 53 (6.9%) on standard oxygen (adjusted odds ratio 1.93, relative). One death occurred, in the high-flow group. Four of 9 prespecified secondary outcomes showed no significant difference.
cards.watchOut: A different population from PARIS (older children, mixed AHRF causes, not bronchiolitis alone) — the two trials must not be averaged; why stay lengthened (weaning practice, monitoring intensity) is not established by the trial.
cards.source: Franklin D et al. shelves.title: Donor human milk versus preterm formula when mother's own milk is unavailable
shelves.question: In extremely preterm infants fed no or insufficient mother's own milk, does donor human milk reduce necrotising enterocolitis versus preterm formula — and at what growth cost?
shelves.mesh: Enterocolitis, Necrotizing/prevention & control · Gestational Age · Infant Formula · Infant Nutritional Physiological Phenomena · Infant, Newborn · Infant, Premature · Infant, Premature, Diseases/prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The trial base is small and old. The largest single randomised trial (Schanler) found no difference between donor milk and preterm formula in late-onset sepsis and/or necrotising enterocolitis (NEC), with slower weight gain on donor milk; the Cochrane synthesis of 12 trials (1,879 infants) found formula feeding raised NEC risk versus donor milk (typical relative risk 1.87, relative; risk difference 0.03) while formula-fed infants grew faster in hospital, with no effect on all-cause mortality or neurodevelopment — moderate-certainty evidence, hence POSSIBLE. Mother's own milk outperformed both substitutes in Schanler.

cards.headline: Schanler: donor milk offered little short-term advantage over preterm formula as a substitute for mother's own milk
cards.summary: Donor milk offered little short-term advantage over preterm formula as a substitute for mother's own milk in the largest single trial.
cards.people: 243 extremely premature infants (<30 weeks' gestation) whose mothers intended to breastfeed: 70 received only mother's own milk (reference group), 81 donor human milk and 92 preterm formula when mother's milk supply became insufficient. The abstract does not state mean age (a neonatal population) or the sex mix.
cards.result: There were no differences between the donor-milk and formula groups in late-onset sepsis and/or NEC, other infection-related events, hospital stay, or deaths. Donor-milk infants received greater milk intake and more nutritional supplements but gained weight more slowly than formula infants; 17 infants (21%), all in the donor-milk group, were switched to formula for poor weight gain. Compared with both substitute groups, the mother's-own-milk group had fewer episodes of late-onset sepsis and/or NEC and total infection-related events and a shorter hospital stay.
cards.watchOut: A single, small (243 infants), 2005 trial; the headline comparison is null, and the mother's-milk reference group was not randomised — its advantage is observational within the trial and must not be read as a randomised effect.
cards.source: Schanler RJ et al. Randomized trial of donor human milk versus preterm formula as substitutes for mothers' own milk in the feeding of extremely premature infants. Pediatrics. 2005;116(2):400-406. PMID: 16061595. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — pre-registration-era trial.

cards.headline: Quigley (Cochrane): formula versus donor milk — NEC relative risk 1.87 (relative) with formula, faster growth with formula, no mortality difference
cards.summary: Cochrane review: formula versus donor milk — NEC relative risk 1.87 (relative) with formula, faster growth with formula, no mortality difference.
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised and quasi-randomised trials
cards.people: 12 trials with 1,879 preterm or low-birth-weight infants comparing formula (term or nutrient-enriched preterm) with donor breast milk, as a supplement to maternal milk or as sole diet; only the 5 most recent trials used nutrient-fortified donor milk. The abstract does not state a pooled mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Formula feeding increased necrotising enterocolitis (typical relative risk 1.87, relative, 95% CI 1.23 to 2.85; risk difference 0.03, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.05; number needed to treat for one additional harmful outcome 33; 9 studies, 1,675 infants). Formula-fed infants grew faster in hospital: weight gain mean difference 2.51 g/kg/day (95% CI 1.93 to 3.08), linear growth 1.21 mm/week, head growth 0.85 mm/week. There was no evidence of an effect on all-cause mortality, long-term growth, or neurodevelopment. GRADE certainty was moderate for NEC, mortality, growth and neurodevelopmental disability.
cards.watchOut: Most included trials were funded by formula companies, most lacked blinding, four had allocation-concealment concerns, and growth meta-analyses had high heterogeneity; the NEC relative risk of 1.87 sits inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band — the absolute risk difference (0.03) is the firmer figure.

shelves.title: School-based childhood obesity prevention: WAVES and IDEFICS
shelves.question: Do school-delivered obesity-prevention programmes change children's weight — the UK WAVES trial (null on its BMI primary) and the eight-country European IDEFICS intervention?
shelves.mesh: Body Mass Index · England · Outcome and Process Assessment, Health Care · Pediatric Obesity/prevention & control · School Health Services/organization & administration · Cluster Analysis · Community Health Services/organization & administration
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): Two very large school-based cluster trials found these programmes did not change children's weight trajectory. WAVES (54 UK primary schools, 1467 pupils aged 5–6) found no significant effect on BMI z score at 15 months (−0.075, CI including zero) or 30 months (−0.027), and no significant effects on diet, activity or psychological measures. IDEFICS (more than 16,000 children aged 2–9.9 years in eight European countries) found no intervention effects on parent-reported diet, sedentary behaviour or physical activity overall. Two large independent nulls, on the outcomes the programmes themselves chose, carry LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — for programmes of this intensity, delivered through schools alone.

cards.headline: WAVES 2018: a school and family healthy-lifestyle programme did not prevent childhood obesity — BMI z-score differences were null at 15 and 30 months
cards.summary: WAVES (2018): a school and family healthy-lifestyle programme did not prevent childhood obesity — BMI z-score differences were null at 15 and 30 months.
cards.type: Cluster randomised controlled trial in 54 primary schools, follow-up to 30 months
cards.people: 1467 year-1 pupils aged 5 and 6 years in 54 UK primary schools in the West Midlands (28 control schools, 778 pupils at randomisation), cluster-randomised to a 12-month healthy eating and physical activity programme (daily extra 30 minutes of school activity, a six-week Aston Villa football club skills programme, family activity signposting, termly cooking workshops) or usual practice; outcome data on 1287 pupils (87.7%) at 15 months and 1169 (79.7%) at 30 months.
cards.result: The mean BMI z score was non-significantly lower in the intervention arm at 15 months (mean difference −0.075 [95% confidence interval −0.183 to 0.033], P=0.18, baseline-adjusted) and at 30 months (−0.027 [−0.137 to 0.083], P=0.63). There was no statistically significant difference between groups for other anthropometric, dietary, physical activity, or psychological measurements, including assessment of harm. The authors conclude schools are unlikely to impact the childhood obesity epidemic with such interventions without wider support across multiple sectors and environments.
cards.watchOut: A null for this programme at this intensity in this setting — not proof no school intervention can work; but it is a large, blinded-outcome-assessment trial, and its null is the result the field must answer, not explain away.

cards.summary: IDEFICS (2015): across eight European countries and more than 16,000 children, the community-and-school intervention produced no overall effects on weight-related behaviours.
cards.type: Cluster-controlled trial (intervention and control communities in each of eight countries), 2-year follow-up
cards.people: More than 16,000 children aged 2 to 9.9 years in intervention and control communities in eight European countries, exposed for about 2 years to a culturally adapted intervention delivered through the community, schools/kindergartens and families; behaviours were measured by parent-completed questionnaires at baseline and follow-up; the abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: The pan-European analysis revealed no significant time-by-condition interaction effects for boys or girls — no intervention effects on parent-reported water, soft drink and fruit juice intake; fruit and vegetable intake; TV viewing and other sedentary behaviours; daily physical activity; or parent-child relationship measures (F = 0.0 to 3.3, all p > 0.05). shelves.title: Water, sanitation and handwashing for child diarrhoea and growth: WASH Benefits
shelves.question: Do household water-quality, sanitation, and handwashing interventions — alone or combined with nutrition — reduce diarrhoea and improve linear growth in young children, in the twin WASH Benefits cluster trials in Bangladesh and Kenya?
shelves.mesh: Bangladesh/epidemiology · Child Development/physiology · Child Nutritional Physiological Phenomena · Cluster Analysis · Diarrhea/epidemiology,prevention & control · Hand Disinfection · Pregnancy
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — WASH reduces diarrhoea in Bangladesh · LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — WASH alone does not improve growth, and Kenya found no diarrhoea benefit either. The twin WASH Benefits cluster trials (Bangladesh: 5551 pregnant women, 720 clusters; Kenya: 8246 women, 702 clusters) tested water quality, sanitation and handwashing, alone and combined with nutrition. In Bangladesh, sanitation, handwashing, combined WASH and the nutrition-containing arms each cut 7-day diarrhoea prevalence to about 3.5% versus 5.7% in controls (prevalence ratios 0.60–0.69), while water treatment alone did not (0.89). In Kenya, no intervention reduced diarrhoea. In both trials, only the nutrition arms (counselling plus lipid-based supplements) improved length-for-age — WASH itself never did, in either country, at high measured adherence in Bangladesh.

cards.headline: WASH Benefits Bangladesh 2018: sanitation, handwashing and combined WASH cut diarrhoea prevalence to ~3.5% vs 5.7% — but only nutrition improved growth
cards.summary: WASH Benefits Bangladesh (2018): sanitation, handwashing and combined WASH cut diarrhoea prevalence to about 3.5% vs 5.7% — but only nutrition improved growth.
cards.type: Cluster randomised controlled trial (720 clusters, seven arms), outcomes at 1 and 2 years
cards.people: 5551 pregnant women in 720 clusters in rural Bangladesh, block-randomised to chlorinated drinking water (698), upgraded sanitation (696), handwashing promotion (688), combined water+sanitation+handwashing (702), nutrition counselling plus lipid-based nutrient supplements (699), combined WASH+nutrition (686), or control (1382); diarrhoea data were available for 14,425 children and length-for-age data for 4584 children at year 2; adherence was high in all intervention groups.
cards.result: Against a control 7-day diarrhoea prevalence of 5.7% (200 of 3517 child-weeks), prevalence was lower with sanitation (3.5% [61 of 1760]; prevalence ratio 0.61 [95% CI 0.46–0.81]), handwashing (3.5% [62 of 1795]; 0.60 [0.45–0.80]), combined WASH (3.9% [74 of 1902]; 0.69 [0.53–0.90]), nutrition (3.5% [62 of 1766]; 0.64 [0.49–0.85]) and combined WASH+nutrition (3.5% [66 of 1861]; 0.62 [0.47–0.81]) — relative ratios printed beside their absolute rates; water treatment alone was not significantly lower (4.9% [90 of 1824]; 0.89 [0.70–1.13]). For growth, versus a control length-for-age Z score of −1.79, children were taller at year 2 only in the nutrition group (mean difference 0.25 [0.15–0.36]) and the combined WASH+nutrition group (0.13 [0.02–0.24]); no WASH-only arm improved linear growth, and combined WASH added nothing over single interventions for diarrhoea.
cards.watchOut: Diarrhoea was caregiver-reported over 7 days in an unblinded trial — exactly the outcome most vulnerable to courtesy bias in intervention households — and prevalence ratios of 0.60–0.69 sit inside this library's 0.5–2.0 caution band; the growth null for WASH, the trial's harder outcome, faced no such bias and is the more trustworthy half of the result.
cards.source: Luby SP et al. Effects of water quality, sanitation, handwashing, and nutritional interventions on diarrhoea and child growth in rural Bangladesh: a cluster randomised controlled trial. Lancet Glob Health. 2018;6(3):e302-e315. PMID: 29396217. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the abstract prints a malformed registration string ('NCC01590095') and the MEDLINE record carries no databank SI field.

cards.headline: WASH Benefits Kenya 2018: no intervention reduced diarrhoea, and again only nutrition improved growth
cards.summary: WASH Benefits Kenya (2018): no intervention reduced diarrhoea, and again only nutrition improved growth.
cards.type: Cluster randomised controlled trial (702 clusters, eight arms including active and passive controls), outcomes at 1 and 2 years
cards.people: 8246 pregnant women in 702 clusters in rural Kenya, block-randomised to active control (1919), passive control (938), water (904), sanitation (892), handwashing (917), combined WASH (912), nutrition (843), or combined WASH+nutrition (921); diarrhoea data for 6494 children and length-for-age data for 6583 children at year 2; adherence exceeded 70% at year 1 for sanitation, handwashing and nutrition but fell below 25% by year 2 for handwashing and water.
cards.result: None of the interventions reduced diarrhoea prevalence compared with the active control. For growth, versus an active-control length-for-age Z score of −1.54, children were taller at year 2 in the nutrition group (mean difference 0.13 [95% CI 0.01–0.25]) and the combined WASH+nutrition group (0.16 [0.05–0.27]); the individual water, sanitation and handwashing arms and combined WASH had no effect on linear growth. The authors conclude the interventions might have been more efficacious with higher adherence or in an environment with lower baseline sanitation coverage.
cards.watchOut: The Kenyan null may be an adherence story (water and handwashing adherence collapsed by year 2) or a setting story (high baseline coverage) — the trial cannot fully separate them, which is why the diarrhoea discordance between the twin trials keeps the Bangladesh result at POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY.

cards.headline: Synthesis: WASH did not grow children in either country; its diarrhoea benefit appeared in one of two settings — split stamp
cards.summary: WASH did not grow children in either country; its diarrhoea benefit appeared in one of two settings — Split: POSSIBLE · LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: WASH Benefits Bangladesh (5551 women, 720 clusters) and WASH Benefits Kenya (8246 women, 702 clusters) — twin trials, one protocol family, discordant diarrhoea results.
cards.result: The growth answer is consistent and two-trial strong: WASH-only arms improved length-for-age in neither country (LIKELY, the null), while nutrition counselling plus supplements did in both (+0.25 and +0.13 Z in Bangladesh arms; +0.13 and +0.16 in Kenya). The diarrhoea answer splits by setting: prevalence ratios of 0.60–0.69 for most arms in Bangladesh, nothing in Kenya (POSSIBLE). Treating diarrhoea that has already happened (oral rehydration) is drafted as Shelf #588 and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Both trials delivered household-level behaviour-change packages, not infrastructure: the nulls judge promotion-plus-simple-hardware, not piped water or sewerage, and should never be quoted against infrastructure investment.

shelves.title: The second dengue vaccine: TAK-003 (Qdenga) in the TIDES trial
shelves.question: Does the live attenuated tetravalent TAK-003 vaccine prevent virologically confirmed dengue and dengue hospitalisation in children and adolescents — including in baseline-seronegative children?
shelves.mesh: Americas/epidemiology · Antibodies, Neutralizing/blood · Antibodies, Viral/blood · Asia/epidemiology · Dengue/epidemiology,immunology,prevention & control · Dengue Vaccines/adverse effects,immunology · Dengue Virus/immunology,isolation & purification
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One large phase 3 programme (TIDES, ~20,000 children and adolescents in endemic countries). Efficacy against virologically confirmed dengue was 80.9% in the first year (0.5 vs 2.5 cases per 100 person-years), with 95.4% efficacy against dengue leading to hospitalisation; by 4.5 years the cumulative efficacy had waned to 61.2% against confirmed dengue and 84.1% against hospitalised dengue. In baseline-seronegative participants, cumulative efficacy was 53.5% against confirmed dengue and 79.3% against hospitalised dengue, with efficacy shown against DENV-1 and DENV-2 but NOT observed against DENV-3 (and too few DENV-4 cases to judge) — a narrower seronegative profile than its predecessor's harm pattern, but not a clean all-serotype bill. Serious adverse events were similar (3.1% vs 3.8% initially; 5.0% vs 5.9% in the long-term phase) and no death was judged vaccine-related. One programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. The first dengue vaccine (CYD-TDV/Dengvaxia) and its serostatus lesson live on Shelf #448 and are not re-carded here.

cards.headline: TIDES primary 2019: TAK-003 was 80.9% efficacious against virologically confirmed dengue and 95.4% against dengue leading to hospitalisation in the first year
cards.summary: TIDES 2019: TAK-003 was 80.9% efficacious against virologically confirmed dengue and 95.4% against dengue hospitalisation.
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised, placebo-controlled trial (part 1 of an ongoing trial)
cards.people: 20,071 healthy children and adolescents aged 4–16 years in dengue-endemic regions of Asia and Latin America given at least one dose of TAK-003 or placebo (2:1, two doses 3 months apart); 19,021 (94.8%) received both doses and formed the per-protocol set. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: Overall vaccine efficacy against virologically confirmed dengue in the safety population was 80.9% (95% CI 75.2 to 85.3), with 78 cases among 13,380 vaccine recipients (0.5 per 100 person-years) vs 199 among 6,687 placebo recipients (2.5 per 100 person-years) — a relative measure with its absolute rates printed. Per-protocol efficacy was 80.2% (73.3 to 85.3), and efficacy against dengue leading to hospitalisation was 95.4% (88.4 to 98.2; 5 vs 53 hospitalisations). In the 27.7% of the per-protocol population seronegative at baseline, efficacy was 74.9% (57.0 to 85.4; 20 vs 39 cases). Efficacy trends varied by serotype. Serious adverse events occurred in 3.1% (vaccine) and 3.8% (placebo).
cards.watchOut: First-year, per-protocol-flavoured results from a single programme: the serotype variation visible even here is the thread the long-term follow-up (card below) pulls on, and first-year efficacy is the high-water mark, not the durable estimate.
cards.source: Biswal S et al. Efficacy of a Tetravalent Dengue Vaccine in Healthy Children and Adolescents. N Engl J Med. 2019;381(21):2009-2019. PMID: 31693803. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02747927, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: TIDES 4.5-year 2024: cumulative efficacy waned to 61.2% against confirmed dengue and 84.1% against hospitalised dengue; in seronegative participants, no efficacy was observed against DENV-3
cards.summary: TIDES 4.5-year 2024: cumulative efficacy waned to 61.2% against confirmed dengue and 84.1% against hospitalised dengue.
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial — long-term (4.5-year) follow-up report of TIDES
cards.people: 20,099 participants aged 4–16 years at 26 centres in eight dengue-endemic countries, assigned 2:1 to two doses of TAK-003 (13,401) or placebo (6,698); 20,071 received at least one dose (50.5% male) and 18,257 (91.0%) completed about 4.5 years of follow-up after the second dose.
cards.result: Of 27,684 febrile illnesses, 1,007 were virologically confirmed dengue (560 placebo, 447 vaccine), 188 requiring hospitalisation (142 placebo, 46 vaccine). Cumulative vaccine efficacy was 61.2% (95% CI 56.0 to 65.8) against confirmed dengue and 84.1% (77.8 to 88.6) against hospitalised confirmed dengue — relative measures. In baseline-seronegative participants, efficacy was 53.5% (41.6 to 62.9) and 79.3% (63.5 to 88.2), respectively; efficacy was shown against all four serotypes in seropositive participants, but in seronegative participants only against DENV-1 and DENV-2 — it was not observed against DENV-3, and low incidence precluded evaluation against DENV-4. In the long-term phase, serious adverse events were reported in 5.0% of vaccine and 5.9% of placebo recipients; 17 deaths (11 vaccine, 6 placebo) were reported, none judged vaccine-related.
cards.watchOut: The seronegative DENV-3 gap is an absence-of-efficacy finding, not the demonstrated enhancement harm that sank Dengvaxia's seronegative use — but with follow-up still ongoing and DENV-4 untested in seronegatives, the honest summary is 'protected against some serotypes, unproven against others,' in exactly the group where the predecessor vaccine caused harm.

shelves.title: Mass azithromycin and child mortality in Africa (MORDOR)
shelves.question: Does biannual mass distribution of azithromycin reduce mortality in preschool children in high-mortality settings?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Azithromycin/therapeutic use · Child Mortality/trends · Communicable Disease Control · Communicable Diseases/mortality · Drug Resistance, Bacterial
shelves.balance: Split stamp — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C; the claim is child mortality itself): POSSIBLE for the MORDOR claim — in 1,533 communities across Niger, Malawi and Tanzania, biannual azithromycin to children 1–59 months gave an annual mortality of 14.6 vs 16.5 deaths per 1,000 person-years, 13.5% lower in relative terms (95% CI 6.7 to 19.8) — a relative effect inside this library's 0.5–2.0 caution band, heterogeneous by country (Niger 18.1% lower; Malawi 5.7% and Tanzania 3.4%, both non-significant) and largest at 1–5 months of age (24.9% lower). The PRET secondary analysis points the same way but weakly (biannual vs annual distribution: mortality rate ratio 0.81, 0.66 to 1.00; P=0.07 — not significant, and not a placebo comparison). MAYBE (weak evidence) for the narrowed infant strategy — the MIRAMA trial in Burkina Faso (302,668 children reached, ages 1–11 months only) found NO mortality difference (2.6 vs 2.5 per 1,000 person-years; incidence rate ratio 1.04, 0.75 to 1.46). Antibiotic resistance is the standing cost: MORDOR's own abstract defers the resistance evaluation, and any implementation claim must carry it.

cards.headline: MORDOR 2018: biannual mass azithromycin lowered preschool mortality by 13.5% in relative terms — 14.6 vs 16.5 deaths per 1,000 person-years
cards.summary: MORDOR 2018: biannual mass azithromycin lowered preschool mortality by 13.5% in relative terms (14.6 vs 16.5 deaths per 1,000 person-years).
cards.people: 1,533 communities in Malawi, Niger and Tanzania assigned to four twice-yearly mass distributions of oral azithromycin (~20 mg/kg) or placebo to children aged 1–59 months identified in twice-yearly censuses; 190,238 children at baseline and 323,302 person-years monitored; mean distribution coverage 90.4%.
cards.result: The overall annual mortality rate was 14.6 deaths per 1,000 person-years in azithromycin communities (9.1 Malawi, 22.5 Niger, 5.4 Tanzania) and 16.5 per 1,000 person-years in placebo communities (9.6, 27.5, 5.5) — mortality was 13.5% lower in relative terms (95% CI 6.7 to 19.8; P<0.001). By country the relative reductions were 18.1% in Niger (10.0 to 25.5), 5.7% in Malawi (−9.7 to 18.9) and 3.4% in Tanzania (−21.2 to 23.0) — only Niger's was significant. The largest effect was at 1–5 months of age (24.9% lower; 10.6 to 37.0). Serious adverse events within a week of dosing were uncommon and did not differ between groups. The authors state any implementation policy would need to strongly consider antibiotic resistance, whose evaluation was ongoing.
cards.watchOut: The headline is a relative 13.5% on a ratio of 0.865 — inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library does not treat as solid on its own — and it averages three countries, in two of which the effect was not significant; the absolute difference is 1.9 deaths per 1,000 person-years, in settings with very high baseline mortality, which may not travel to lower-mortality settings.

cards.summary: PRET secondary analysis 2018: biannual vs annual distribution — mortality rate ratio 0.81 (P=0.07), non-significant.
cards.type: Prespecified secondary analysis of a cluster-randomised trial (PRET, Niger)
cards.people: 48 Nigerien communities randomised to annual treatment of everyone (24) or biannual treatment of children under 12 (24) for 3 years with single-dose oral azithromycin for trachoma; this analysis covers children aged 6 months to under 5 years, among whom 404 deaths occurred.
cards.result: The mortality rate was 35.6 deaths per 1,000 person-years (231 deaths) in the annual arm and 29.0 per 1,000 person-years (173 deaths) in the biannual arm: a mortality rate ratio of 0.81 (95% CI 0.66 to 1.00; P=0.07) — not significant. For infectious-cause deaths the ratio was 0.73 (0.57 to 0.94; P=0.02). No adverse events were reported. The authors note the trial was neither designed nor powered to detect a mortality effect and that bias cannot be excluded.
cards.watchOut: A secondary analysis comparing two active schedules (no placebo arm) in one trachoma-endemic, high-mortality area: supportive of MORDOR's direction, evidentially weak on its own — it is carded as the topic's specified companion and labelled accordingly.

cards.headline: MIRAMA 2026 (Burkina Faso): mass azithromycin narrowed to infants 1–11 months did NOT reduce mortality — 2.6 vs 2.5 deaths per 1,000 person-years (incidence rate ratio 1.04)
cards.summary: MIRAMA 2026: narrowed to infants 1–11 months, mass azithromycin did NOT reduce mortality (2.6 vs 2.5 deaths per 1,000 person-years).
cards.type: Double-masked, cluster-randomised, placebo-controlled trial integrated into a Child Health Days platform
cards.people: Primary-healthcare-centre catchment areas (CSPS) in Burkina Faso randomised 2:1 to biannual azithromycin or placebo for children aged 1–11 months, delivered with vitamin A through Child Health Days: 201,709 children in 303 CSPS received azithromycin and 100,959 in 158 CSPS received placebo, with 85% overall treatment coverage, September 2021 to January 2024.
cards.result: Mortality rates were 2.6 deaths per 1,000 person-years (95% CI 2.1 to 3.1) in the azithromycin arm and 2.5 (1.8 to 3.2) in the placebo arm — no significant difference (incidence rate ratio 1.04, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.46; P=0.80). Sixteen non-serious adverse events and no serious adverse events were recorded. The authors conclude the strategy can be scaled and integrated into existing programmes but did not demonstrate a mortality effect, and that policy should consider treating the larger age group up to 5 years.
cards.watchOut: A null in the age band MORDOR suggested was most responsive — but MIRAMA treated only 1–11-month-olds (MORDOR's largest subgroup effect was at 1–5 months within a 1–59-month programme) and Burkina Faso's baseline infant mortality here (2.5 per 1,000 person-years) is far below MORDOR-Niger's; the trial refutes the narrow targeting, not the whole strategy.
cards.source: Yago-Wienne F et al. cards.summary: A real but modest and setting-dependent mortality effect for the broad age band; the infant-only version failed — Split, Tier C, proposed only.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: MORDOR (1,533 communities, placebo-controlled), the PRET secondary analysis (48 communities, active-comparator) and MIRAMA (461 CSPS clusters, placebo-controlled, infants only).
cards.result: The pattern across the shelf: where baseline mortality is very high and the whole 1–59-month band is treated, mortality fell by 1.9 deaths per 1,000 person-years (14.6 vs 16.5; 13.5% relative); where the programme was narrowed to infants in a lower-mortality setting, nothing happened (2.6 vs 2.5 per 1,000 person-years; ratio 1.04). cards.watchOut: Do not quote MORDOR's 13.5% without 'relative', the absolute rates, and the country split (only Niger significant); and do not quote it at all for an infant-only programme after MIRAMA.

shelves.title: Honey for acute cough in children (Cochrane evidence)
shelves.question: Does honey relieve acute cough in children better than no treatment, diphenhydramine, dextromethorphan or placebo — across the Cochrane review's randomised trials and the blinded Cohen trial?
shelves.mesh: Albuterol/therapeutic use · Antitussive Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Apitherapy/adverse effects,methods · Bromelains/therapeutic use · Bronchodilator Agents/therapeutic use · Cough/therapy · Dextromethorphan/adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The 2018 Cochrane review (6 randomised trials, 899 children aged 12 months to 18 years) graded the evidence moderate-certainty that honey reduces cough frequency more than no treatment (mean difference −1.05 points on a 7-point scale, 95% CI −1.48 to −0.62; 2 studies, 154 children) or placebo (−1.62, −3.02 to −0.22; 2 studies, 402 children), low-certainty that it beats diphenhydramine (−0.57, −0.90 to −0.24; 1 study, 80 children), and low-certainty that it makes little or no difference versus dextromethorphan (−0.07, −1.07 to 0.94; 2 studies, 149 children). Most children were treated for a single night. Shelf-face caution: honey must never be given to infants under 12 months (infant botulism risk) — every trial and the review itself start at 12 months. NOTE: the topic file's printed anchor (PMID 22419319) is the 2012 version of this review; the 2018 update (PMID 29633783) is carded instead — see summary.md.

cards.headline: Cochrane (Oduwole) 2018: honey probably beats no treatment and placebo on cough frequency, matches dextromethorphan, and may beat diphenhydramine
cards.summary: Cochrane (Oduwole) 2018: honey probably beats no treatment and placebo on cough frequency (mean difference −1.05 on a 7-point scale), matches dextromethorphan, and may beat diphenhydramine. (The 2018 update is carded; the topic's printed anchor was its superseded 2012 version.)
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials (update of reviews published in 2014, 2012 and 2010)
cards.people: Six randomised controlled trials involving 899 children aged 12 months to 18 years with acute cough in ambulatory settings, comparing honey alone or with antibiotics against no treatment, placebo, honey-based cough syrup or other over-the-counter cough medicines. The abstract does not state a pooled mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: On 7-point Likert scales (lower = better relief), honey probably reduces cough frequency better than no treatment (mean difference −1.05, 95% CI −1.48 to −0.62; 2 studies, 154 children; moderate-certainty evidence) or placebo (−1.62, −3.02 to −0.22; 2 studies, 402 children; moderate-certainty). Honey may have a similar effect to dextromethorphan (MD −0.07, −1.07 to 0.94; 2 studies, 149 children; low-certainty) and may be better than diphenhydramine (MD −0.57, −0.90 to −0.24; 1 study, 80 children; low-certainty). Giving honey for up to three days is probably more effective than placebo or salbutamol for cough symptoms; beyond three days it probably had no advantage over salbutamol or placebo. Gastrointestinal symptoms occurred in 12% on honey versus 11% on placebo (risk ratio 1.91, 1.12 to 3.24 — relative; 2 studies, 402 children; moderate-certainty); nervousness, insomnia and hyperactivity occurred in 7 children (9.3%) on honey versus 2 (2.7%) on dextromethorphan (RR 2.94, 0.74 to 11.71; low-certainty).
cards.watchOut: Two of the six studies were at high risk of performance and detection bias (hard to blind a food), most treatment lasted one night, and the review's own bottom line is measured: 'probably relieves cough symptoms to a greater extent than no treatment, diphenhydramine, and placebo' — not a strong endorsement. Children under 12 months are outside every included trial. The pooled trials used different preparations; no single product was tested — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Oduwole O et al. Honey for acute cough in children. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2018;4(4):CD007094. PMID: 29633783. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Cohen 2012: a single bedtime dose of three honeys improved nocturnal cough more than a date-extract placebo in 300 children
cards.summary: Cohen 2012: a single bedtime dose of three honeys improved nocturnal cough more than a date-extract placebo in 300 children — a constituent trial of the review, labelled as such, not independent confirmation.
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled study (single nocturnal dose)
cards.people: 300 children aged 1 to 5 years with upper respiratory tract infections, nocturnal cough and illness duration of 7 days or less, from 6 general paediatric community clinics, given a single 10 g dose of eucalyptus honey, citrus honey, labiatae honey or placebo (silan date extract) 30 minutes before bedtime. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: In all three honey groups and the placebo group there was significant improvement from the night before treatment to the night of treatment; the improvement was greater in the honey groups on the parent-rated measures (cough frequency, cough severity, bothersome nature of cough, and child and parent sleep quality), and parents rated the honey products higher than the silan date extract for symptomatic relief. The record's abstract reports this comparison qualitatively and prints no numeric score differences, so none are reproduced here.
cards.watchOut: One night, one dose, parent-reported outcomes, and a placebo (date extract) that is itself sweet and viscous — the design most vulnerable to expectation effects in this literature, and a constituent trial of the Cochrane review carded above, not independent confirmation of it. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.result: The honest summary is the review's own: honey probably relieves cough symptoms more than no treatment, diphenhydramine and placebo, may make little or no difference versus dextromethorphan, and has mainly been tested for a single night. shelves.title: Less amoxicillin for childhood pneumonia: CAP-IT and SAFER
shelves.question: For children with community-acquired pneumonia sent home on amoxicillin, is less enough — a lower dose for three days (CAP-IT), and five days versus ten (SAFER) — without more re-treatment or complications?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Amoxicillin/administration & dosage · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage · Community-Acquired Infections/drug therapy · Drug Administration Schedule · Duration of Therapy · Patient Discharge
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two noninferiority RCTs on two continents answer the same less-is-more question. CAP-IT (824 children, 2×2 factorial) found lower-dose amoxicillin noninferior to higher dose (re-treatment 12.6% vs 12.4%) and 3 days noninferior to 7 days (12.5% vs 12.5%), both within the 8% margin. SAFER (281 children) found 5 days of high-dose amoxicillin noninferior to 10 days for clinical cure (88.6% vs 90.8% per protocol). Two blinded/factorial trials converging carry LIKELY, with the severity caveat on both cards.

cards.headline: CAP-IT (Bielicki 2021): lower dose and 3 days were both noninferior — re-treatment 12.6% vs 12.4% and 12.5% vs 12.5%
cards.summary: CAP-IT (2021): lower dose and 3 days were both noninferior — re-treatment 12.6% vs 12.4% and 12.5% vs 12.5% .
cards.people: 824 children aged 6 months and older with clinically diagnosed community-acquired pneumonia, treated with amoxicillin on discharge from emergency departments and inpatient wards of 28 UK hospitals and 1 in Ireland; 814 received at least one dose (median age 2.5 years; 52% male); primary outcome available for 789 (97%).
cards.result: Clinically indicated antibiotic re-treatment within 28 days: lower dose 12.6% versus higher dose 12.4% (difference 0.2%, 1-sided 95% CI −∞ to 4.0%), and 3-day 12.5% versus 7-day 12.5% (difference 0.1%, −∞ to 3.9%) — both noninferior against the 8% margin, with no significant interaction (P=.63). The only significant secondary differences were longer cough with 3 days (median 12 vs 10 days) and more sleep disturbed by cough. In the severe-CAP subgroup the lower-dose difference was 3.8% (upper confidence limit 10%), so noninferiority was not shown within that subgroup. Registry ID: ISRCTN76888927, stated in the record's abstract; the MEDLINE record carries no databank SI field.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority against a generous 8% margin, in children well enough to be discharged — not a licence to shorten treatment for severe or inpatient pneumonia; the severe subgroup is exactly where the data thin out.
cards.source: Bielicki JA et al. Effect of Amoxicillin Dose and Treatment Duration on the Need for Antibiotic Re-treatment in Children With Community-Acquired Pneumonia: The CAP-IT Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2021;326(17):1713-1724. PMID: 34726708. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the registry ID ISRCTN76888927 is stated in the record's abstract.

cards.summary: SAFER (2021): 5 days of high-dose amoxicillin was noninferior to 10 days — cure 88.6% vs 90.8% per protocol.

shelves.title: Laparoscopic versus open pyloromyotomy for pyloric stenosis
shelves.question: In infants with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, does laparoscopic pyloromyotomy match open surgery on complications while speeding recovery?
shelves.mesh: Laparoscopy/methods · Laparotomy/methods · Pyloric Stenosis/diagnostic imaging,surgery · Pylorus/diagnostic imaging,surgery · Ultrasonography · Enteral Nutrition · Infant, Newborn
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two prospective randomised trials agree. St Peter (200 infants) found no difference in operating time, time to full feeding or length of stay, but fewer emesis episodes and fewer analgesia doses with laparoscopy. Hall's double-blind multicentre trial (180 infants, stopped early for benefit) found faster full enteral feeding (median 18.5 vs 23.9 hours) and shorter postoperative stay (33.6 vs 43.8 hours) with laparoscopy, with similar vomiting and complications. A surgical question is unblindable for the operator by nature; outcome assessment in Hall was blinded. Two concordant RCTs carry LIKELY.

cards.headline: St Peter 2006: no difference in operating time, feeding or stay — but less emesis and less analgesia with laparoscopy
cards.summary: St Peter (2006): no difference in operating time, feeding or stay — but less emesis and less analgesia with laparoscopy.
cards.people: 200 infants with ultrasound-proven pyloric stenosis, enrolled April 2003 to March 2006, randomised to open or laparoscopic pyloromyotomy with identical postoperative pain management, feeding schedule and discharge criteria. The abstract does not state mean age (infants).
cards.result: There were no significant differences in operating time, time to full feeding, or length of stay. The laparoscopic group had significantly fewer emesis episodes and fewer doses of analgesia. One mucosal perforation and one incisional hernia occurred in the open group; one laparoscopic case was converted to open late in the study. Wound infection occurred in 4 open versus 2 laparoscopic patients (P=0.68). The abstract gives no incomplete-pyloromyotomy counts, and none are printed here.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre trial from a high-volume laparoscopic unit — its equivalence on time and stay may not transfer to low-volume centres; cosmetic benefit is asserted by the authors as likely, not measured in the abstract.
cards.source: St Peter SD et al. Open versus laparoscopic pyloromyotomy for pyloric stenosis: a prospective, randomized trial. Ann Surg. 2006;244(3):363-70. PMID: 16926562. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a pre-registration-era surgical trial (2006).

cards.headline: Hall 2009: double-blind multicentre trial — full feeds at 18.5 versus 23.9 hours and discharge at 33.6 versus 43.8 hours with laparoscopy
cards.summary: Hall (2009, double-blind): full feeds at 18.5 vs 23.9 hours and discharge at 33.6 vs 43.8 hours with laparoscopy.
cards.type: Multicentre, international, double-blind, randomised controlled trial (participants, parents and nursing staff blinded; stopped early on the data monitoring committee's recommendation for benefit)
cards.people: 180 infants with pyloric stenosis at six tertiary paediatric surgical centres (93 open, 87 laparoscopic), randomised June 2004 to May 2007 with minimisation for age, weight, gestational age, bicarbonate, feeding type, symptom duration and centre. The abstract does not state mean age (infants).

shelves.title: Gut-directed hypnotherapy for functional abdominal pain in children
shelves.question: Does gut-directed hypnotherapy produce lasting remission of functional abdominal pain or irritable bowel syndrome in children versus standard medical care — and does a standardised self-exercise version on CD retain the effect?
shelves.mesh: Abdominal Pain/psychology,therapy · Diet Therapy · Hypnosis · Irritable Bowel Syndrome/psychology,therapy · Pain Measurement · Patient Education as Topic · Abdominal Pain/therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Therapist-delivered gut-directed hypnotherapy beat standard medical care decisively at 1 year in Vlieger's trial (treatment success 85% vs 25%), and Rutten's noninferiority trial then showed home-based CD self-exercises were noninferior to individual therapist treatment at 1 year (success 62.1% vs 71.0%). Two RCTs of one intervention family, the second testing the scalable form of the first, carry LIKELY. Behavioural therapy is unblindable by nature; both trials are labelled as such.

cards.headline: Vlieger 2007: hypnotherapy success 85% versus 25% with standard care at 1 year (P<.001)
cards.summary: Vlieger (2007): hypnotherapy success 85% vs 25% with standard care at 1 year (P<.001).
cards.people: 53 children aged 8–18 years with functional abdominal pain (31) or irritable bowel syndrome (22), randomised to gut-directed hypnotherapy (6 sessions over 3 months) or standard medical therapy with 6 sessions of supportive therapy; pain scored in weekly diaries at baseline, during therapy, and 6 and 12 months after therapy. Sex mix is not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: Pain intensity scores fell from 13.5 to 1.3 with hypnotherapy versus 14.1 to 8.0 with standard care; pain frequency scores fell from 13.5 to 1.1 versus 14.4 to 9.3 — hypnotherapy significantly superior on both (P<.001). At 1-year follow-up, successful treatment was accomplished in 85% of the hypnotherapy group and 25% of the standard-care group (P<.001).
cards.watchOut: Small (53 children), single-programme trial with an unusually large effect — the size of the gap is itself a reason the shelf needs its second trial, and unblinded self-reported pain is the outcome throughout.
cards.source: Vlieger AM et al. Hypnotherapy for children with functional abdominal pain or irritable bowel syndrome: a randomized controlled trial. Gastroenterology. 2007;133(5):1430-6. PMID: 17919634. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a pre-registration-era trial report (2007).
