shelves.title: Dupilumab for atopic dermatitis in adolescents, and in children under six
shelves.question: Does dupilumab clear skin and itch in the age bands the adult trials did not enrol — adolescents with uncontrolled moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis, and children aged six months to under six years, each against placebo with background topical therapy?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Inflammatory Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Canada · Conjunctivitis/chemically induced,epidemiology · Dermatitis, Atopic/diagnosis,drug therapy · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Administration Schedule
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two phase 3 placebo-controlled trials in distinct age bands both met their primary endpoints. In adolescents (251 patients), EASI-75 at week 16 was 41.5% (every-2-weeks dosing) and 38.1% (every-4-weeks) versus 8.2% with placebo. In children 6 months to under 6 years (162 patients, with low-potency topical corticosteroids), clear-or-almost-clear skin (IGA 0–1) was 28% versus 4% and EASI-75 was 53% versus 11%. Conjunctivitis was the consistent excess adverse event in both. Two blinded trials in two age bands carry LIKELY. Adult dupilumab lives on Shelf #374 and is not re-carded here.

shelves.title: A vitamin A capsule on day one of life: the three Neovita trials disagree
shelves.question: Does a single early neonatal dose of vitamin A reduce mortality in infancy — in India, where the largest trial found a borderline benefit; in Ghana and Tanzania, where it did not?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Capsules · Dietary Supplements · Diterpenes · Drug Combinations · India/epidemiology · Infant Mortality
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (no consistent mortality benefit) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, because the headline outcome is infant mortality itself): Three parallel double-blind trials under one WHO-coordinated programme family randomised about 99,000 newborns to a single 50,000 IU vitamin A dose or placebo. India found mortality to 6 months of 29.2 versus 32.3 per 1000 (risk ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.00 — a relative figure at the edge of significance); Ghana found 24.5 versus 21.8 per 1000 (relative risk 1.12) and Tanzania 26 versus 24 per 1000 (risk ratio 1.10) — both point estimates on the harm side. All three ratios sit inside the 0.5–2.0 band the library treats as not solid on its own. Two nulls and one borderline positive do not make a policy: POSSIBLE that there is no general benefit, with any real effect confined, at most, to the more deficient setting. Vitamin A in older preschool children lives on Shelf #199 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Neovita India (Mazumder 2015): mortality 29.2 versus 32.3 per 1000 (relative risk ratio 0.90, CI 0.81 to 1.00) — a borderline benefit
cards.summary: Neovita India (2015): mortality 29.2 vs 32.3 per 1000 (risk ratio 0.90 relative, CI 0.81 to 1.00) — a borderline benefit.
cards.people: 44,984 neonates in Haryana, India, randomised within 72 hours of birth to oral vitamin A (retinol palmitate 50,000 IU plus vitamin E) (22,493) or placebo (vitamin E alone) (22,491), identified through a population surveillance programme; primary outcome mortality between supplementation and 6 months of age. Sex mix is as randomised; the abstract reports no significant interaction with sex (p=0.409).
cards.result: Between supplementation and 6 months, 656 infants died in the vitamin A group versus 726 in the placebo group (29.2 per 1000 vs 32.3 per 1000; difference −3.1 per 1000, 95% CI −6.3 to 0.1; risk ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.00 — a relative figure, absolute rates beside it). The exception to good tolerability was a small excess of transient bulging fontanelle (205 vs 80 confirmed cases; risk ratio 2.56, 1.98 to 3.32). The authors describe their population as one where vitamin A deficiency is a moderate public health problem.
cards.watchOut: The interval touches 1.00 — this is the weakest form of 'positive', and its own authors say it must be viewed with the sister trials. Tier C proposed.

shelves.title: Adding CBT to an SSRI in adolescent depression: ADAPT and IMPACT
shelves.question: Once an adolescent with major depression is on an SSRI with routine specialist care, does adding cognitive behaviour therapy improve outcomes (ADAPT) — and among psychological therapies, is CBT better than short-term psychoanalytical psychotherapy or a brief psychosocial intervention (IMPACT)?
shelves.mesh: Antidepressive Agents/therapeutic use · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy/methods · Combined Modality Therapy · Depressive Disorder/therapy · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Major Depressive Disorder/psychology,therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY (no added or superior effect): ADAPT (208 adolescents) found adding CBT to an SSRI plus routine care changed nothing — the primary treatment effect at 12 weeks was −0.64 points (95% CI −2.54 to 1.26; P=0.50), with no difference on any secondary measure and no protective effect on suicidal thinking. IMPACT (470 adolescents) found CBT and short-term psychoanalytical psychotherapy indistinguishable from each other and neither superior to a brief psychosocial intervention through 86 weeks. Two large pragmatic trials, unblindable by nature, converging on equivalence carry LIKELY. Suicidal behaviour was monitored in both trials and no mortality claim is made. The TADS trial is already carded (Shelf #224 territory) and is fenced, not re-carded.

cards.headline: ADAPT (Goodyer 2007): adding CBT to an SSRI plus routine care improved nothing by 28 weeks (treatment effect −0.64; P=0.50)
cards.summary: ADAPT (2007): adding CBT to an SSRI plus routine care improved nothing by 28 weeks (treatment effect −0.64; P=0.50).
cards.people: 208 adolescents aged 11–17 with moderate to severe major or probable major depression who had not responded to a brief initial intervention, at 6 outpatient clinics in Manchester and Cambridge; 103 received an SSRI and routine care, 105 received an SSRI, routine care and CBT; adolescents with suicidality, depressive psychosis or conduct disorder were included; follow-up to 28 weeks. Sex mix is not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: At 12 weeks the treatment effect on the primary outcome (Health of the Nation Outcome Scales for Children and Adolescents) was −0.64 (95% CI −2.54 to 1.26, P=0.50); longitudinally there was no difference on the primary (average effect 0.001, −1.52 to 1.52; P=0.99) or any secondary outcome. Suicidal thoughts and self-harm decreased on average in both groups, with no evidence of a protective effect of CBT. By 28 weeks 57% were much or very much improved and 20% remained unimproved.
cards.watchOut: A trial of CBT added to drug treatment in non-responders to a brief intervention — it does not test CBT alone, CBT first, or fluoxetine itself (Shelf #224). Registry ID: ISRCTN83809224, from the record's databank fields.
cards.source: Goodyer I et al. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and routine specialist care with and without cognitive behaviour therapy in adolescents with major depression: randomised controlled trial. BMJ. 2007;335(7611):142. PMID: 17556431. Registry ID: ISRCTN: ISRCTN83809224.

cards.headline: IMPACT (Goodyer 2017): CBT and psychoanalytical therapy were equal to each other — and neither beat a brief psychosocial intervention
cards.summary: IMPACT (2017): CBT and psychoanalytical therapy were equal to each other — and neither beat a brief psychosocial intervention.
cards.type: Multicentre, pragmatic, observer-blind, randomised controlled superiority trial
cards.people: 470 adolescents aged 11–17 with DSM-IV major depressive disorder at 15 NHS child and adolescent mental health clinics in England, randomised to brief psychosocial intervention (158), CBT (155) or short-term psychoanalytical psychotherapy (157); 465 in the intention-to-treat population; primary outcome self-reported depression symptoms (Mood and Feelings Questionnaire) at weeks 36, 52 and 86. Sex mix is not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: Depression symptoms did not differ between CBT and short-term psychoanalytical therapy at weeks 36, 52 or 86 (treatment effects 0.179, 0.307 and 0.578; all p>0.74), and neither therapy was superior to the brief psychosocial intervention at any point (effects −3.234, −2.806 and −1.898; p=0.061, 0.065 and 0.219). Median sessions differed (6 brief, 9 CBT, 11 psychoanalytical) over similar total treatment durations. Physical adverse events and total intervention costs did not differ between groups. Registry ID: ISRCTN83033550, stated in the record's abstract; the MEDLINE record carries no databank SI field.
cards.watchOut: Equivalence here is among three active therapies delivered in routine CAMHS — not evidence that therapy does nothing, and not a comparison with drug treatment. Observer-blind only; patients and clinicians knew allocation.
cards.source: Goodyer IM et al. Cognitive behavioural therapy and short-term psychoanalytical psychotherapy versus a brief psychosocial intervention in adolescents with unipolar major depressive disorder (IMPACT): a multicentre, pragmatic, observer-blind, randomised controlled superiority trial. Lancet Psychiatry. 2017;4(2):109-119. PMID: 27914903. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the registry ID ISRCTN83033550 is stated in the record's abstract.

cards.headline: Synthesis: more therapy, or fancier therapy, added nothing measurable — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: more therapy, or fancier therapy, added nothing measurable in these trials — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: ADAPT (208 adolescents) and IMPACT (470 adolescents).
cards.result: Two different questions, one shape of answer: adding CBT to an SSRI-plus-routine-care package did not improve outcomes (ADAPT), and among therapies, brand-name treatments did not beat a briefer psychosocial intervention over 86 weeks (IMPACT). What the trials support is good routine specialist care with an SSRI where indicated, and patient choice among therapies — not escalation by addition. Fluoxetine efficacy and safety live on Shelf #224; TADS stays home there.
cards.watchOut: Do not read these nulls as 'CBT doesn't work' — neither trial had a no-treatment arm; both compared active packages.
cards.source: Synthesis of Goodyer I et al. BMJ. 2007. PMID: 17556431; Goodyer IM et al. Lancet Psychiatry. 2017. PMID: 27914903. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Cutting the tongue-tie: frenotomy and breastfeeding
shelves.question: Does dividing a tongue-tie improve breastfeeding — maternal nipple pain and feeding scores in a neonatal sham-controlled trial, and breastfeeding continuation in a trial of early frenotomy for mild-to-moderate tongue-tie?
shelves.mesh: Breast Feeding/adverse effects · Infant, Newborn · Lingual Frenum/abnormalities,surgery · Mouth Abnormalities/complications,surgery · Nipples/pathology · Pain/diagnosis,etiology,prevention & control · Pain Measurement/methods
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE for immediate symptomatic benefit — in Buryk's sham-controlled trial (58 neonates), frenotomy improved nipple pain significantly more than sham (P<.001) and breastfeeding scores improved (P=.029), though pain also fell after the sham procedure; MAYBE (weak evidence) for objective breastfeeding continuation — in Emond's pragmatic trial (107 infants with mild-to-moderate tongue-tie), early frenotomy produced no difference in the primary LATCH-based outcome at 5 days or in breastfeeding measures at 8 weeks, though maternal self-efficacy improved and 44 of the comparison group crossed over to frenotomy after day 5, which thins the comparison. Two small trials with different designs and different outcome types earn a split, not a single stamp.

cards.headline: Buryk 2011: frenotomy beat sham on nipple pain (P<.001) and feeding scores (P=.029) — immediately
cards.summary: Buryk (2011): frenotomy beat sham on nipple pain (P<.001) and feeding scores (P=.029) — immediately.
cards.type: Randomised, single-blinded, controlled trial (sham procedure comparison)
cards.people: 58 neonates with difficulty breastfeeding and significant ankyloglossia, enrolled over 12 months and assigned to frenotomy (30) or a sham procedure (28), assessed by nipple-pain scale and the Infant Breastfeeding Assessment Tool before and after the intervention, at 2 weeks, and over 1 year of follow-up. Sex mix is not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: Both groups had significantly decreased pain scores after the intervention, but the frenotomy group improved significantly more than the sham group (P<.001). Breastfeeding scores significantly improved in the frenotomy group (P=.029) with no significant change in the control group. The abstract reports P values without the underlying score values, and no score values are printed here. All but 1 parent in the sham group elected frenotomy by the 2-week follow-up, preventing further between-group comparisons.
cards.watchOut: Tiny trial, immediate outcomes, and a visible placebo effect on pain (the sham group improved too) — the honest claim is a short-term symptomatic one. Near-total crossover ends the experiment after the first assessment.
cards.source: Buryk M et al. Efficacy of neonatal release of ankyloglossia: a randomized trial. Pediatrics. 2011;128(2):280-8. PMID: 21768318. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT00967915.

cards.headline: Emond 2014: early frenotomy for mild-to-moderate tongue-tie did not improve the objective feeding score at 5 days
cards.summary: Emond (2014): early frenotomy for mild-to-moderate tongue-tie did not improve the objective feeding score at 5 days.
cards.type: Randomised, parallel-group, pragmatic trial (outcome assessors blinded)
cards.people: 107 term infants under 2 weeks old with mild or moderate tongue-tie whose mothers were having difficulties breastfeeding, at a large UK maternity hospital, randomised to early frenotomy (55) or standard breastfeeding support (52); primary outcome breastfeeding at 5 days (LATCH score), final assessment at 8 weeks. Sex mix is not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: Intention-to-treat analysis showed no difference in the primary outcome (Latch, Audible swallowing, nipple Type, Comfort, Hold score) at 5 days. Frenotomy did improve the tongue-tie itself and increased maternal breastfeeding self-efficacy. Bottle feeding rose by 15.5% in the comparison group versus 7.5% in the intervention group by day 5. After the 5-day clinic, 44 of the comparison group requested frenotomy; by 8 weeks only 6 (12%) were breastfeeding without one, and there were no differences between groups in breastfeeding measures or infant weight at 8 weeks. No adverse events were observed.
cards.watchOut: Mild-to-moderate tongue-tie only — not Buryk's significant ankyloglossia — and mass crossover (44 of 52) means the 8-week 'no difference' compares a treated group with a mostly-treated group. The bottle-feeding difference is a secondary signal, not the primary outcome.
cards.source: Emond A et al. Randomised controlled trial of early frenotomy in breastfed infants with mild-moderate tongue-tie. Arch Dis Child Fetal Neonatal Ed. 2014;99(3):F189-95. PMID: 24249695. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this trial report's record carries no databank registry field.

cards.headline: Synthesis: pain relief now is plausible; proven continuation benefit is not — split stamp
cards.summary: Synthesis: pain relief now is plausible; proven continuation benefit is not — split POSSIBLE / MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Buryk 2011 (58 neonates, significant tongue-tie, sham-controlled) and Emond 2014 (107 infants, mild-to-moderate tongue-tie, pragmatic).
cards.result: The two trials are often quoted as opposites; they answer different questions. Buryk supports an immediate effect on pain and feeding scores in significant tongue-tie. Emond, in milder cases, found no objective feeding-score gain from doing it early — while mothers mostly chose it anyway and felt more confident. Breastfeeding promotion and support generally live on Shelf #665 (PROBIT) and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Quote Buryk for immediate symptoms in significant ankyloglossia only; quote Emond whenever early frenotomy is proposed as proven to extend breastfeeding in mild cases.
cards.source: Synthesis of Buryk M et al. Pediatrics. 2011. PMID: 21768318; Emond A et al. Arch Dis Child Fetal Neonatal Ed. 2014. PMID: 24249695. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Ultrasound for the newborn hip: the UK Hip Trial and the screening trial
shelves.question: Does ultrasonography in the diagnosis and management of developmental hip dysplasia reduce late surgery and improve outcomes versus clinical examination-based management — and does screening all newborns with ultrasound beat selective screening?
shelves.mesh: Costs and Cost Analysis · Hip Dislocation, Congenital/diagnostic imaging,economics,surgery · Infant, Newborn · Splints/economics · Ultrasonography · United Kingdom · Hip Dislocation, Congenital/diagnostic imaging,epidemiology,therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Ultrasound changes management more than outcomes. In the UK Hip Trial (629 infants with clinical hip instability), ultrasound guidance halved nothing but did reduce abduction splinting (relative risk 0.78) with identical radiographic abnormality at 2 years (21 children in each group; relative risk 1.00) and similar surgery (6.7% vs 7.9%). In the Norwegian screening trial (11,925 newborns), general ultrasound screening raised the treatment rate (3.4% vs 2.0% selective and 1.8% none) while late subluxation/dislocation fell only non-significantly (0.3 vs 0.7 vs 1.3 per 1000). Two RCTs showing process effects without proven outcome benefit earn POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: UK Hip Trial (Elbourne 2002): ultrasound cut splinting (relative risk 0.78) but hips at 2 years were identical (21 versus 21 children)
cards.summary: UK Hip Trial (2002): ultrasound cut splinting (RR 0.78 relative) but hips at 2 years were identical ( 21 vs 21 children).
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial (33 centres, UK and Ireland)
cards.people: 629 infants with clinical hip instability recruited from 33 centres, randomised to ultrasonographic hip examination (314) or clinical assessment alone (315); primary outcome appearance on hip radiographs by 2 years; radiographic information available for 91% by 12–14 months and 85% by 2 years. Sex mix is not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: By age 2, subluxation, dislocation or acetabular dysplasia were identified on one or both hips of 21 children in each group (relative risk 1.00, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.80 — a relative figure). Fewer children in the ultrasonography group had abduction splinting in the first 2 years (relative risk 0.78, 0.65 to 0.94; p=0.01). Surgical treatment was required by 21 infants (6.7%) versus 25 (7.9%) (0.84, 0.48 to 1.47). One child (ultrasound) and four (no ultrasound) were not walking by 2 years. Ultrasound costs were higher (£42 vs £23 per infant); total hospital costs were lower but not significantly.
cards.watchOut: A management trial in infants already flagged by clinical screening — not a population-screening trial. Its proven gain is fewer babies splinted, a harm-and-burden outcome, not better hips. Pre-registration-era trial; no registry ID in the record's databank fields.
cards.source: Elbourne D et al. Ultrasonography in the diagnosis and management of developmental hip dysplasia (UK Hip Trial): clinical and economic results of a multicentre randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2002;360(9350):2009-17. PMID: 12504396. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a pre-registration-era trial (2002).

cards.headline: Rosendahl 1994: screening every newborn raised treatment to 3.4% versus 1.8% with no screening — late cases fell only non-significantly
cards.summary: Rosendahl (1994): screening every newborn raised treatment to 3.4% vs 1.8% with no screening — late cases fell only non-significantly.
cards.people: 11,925 newborn infants allocated to general ultrasound screening, selective ultrasound screening (risk factors or clinical findings only), or no ultrasound screening, in addition to clinical examination; infants were at least 27 months old at the study's conclusion, and those with risk factors had hip radiographs at 4.5 months. The abstract does not state mean age (newborns).
cards.result: General ultrasound screening produced a higher treatment rate than selective or no screening (3.4% vs 2.0% and 1.8%, P<.0001), and a higher follow-up rate for nonconclusive early findings among untreated infants (13%, 1.8% and 0% respectively; P<.0001). The prevalence of late subluxation or dislocation was 0.3 per 1000 with general screening versus 0.7 (selective) and 1.3 (no screening), but the differences were not statistically significant (P=.11, test for trend). The authors conclude the effect on late cases was at best marginal despite considerably increased diagnostic and therapeutic effort.
cards.watchOut: 1994 technology and practice; the late-case endpoint — the one screening exists to prevent — rests on very small event counts (per-1000 rates), so the trial can exclude a large effect only loosely. Pre-registration-era trial; no registry ID in the record's databank fields.
cards.source: Rosendahl K et al. Ultrasound screening for developmental dysplasia of the hip in the neonate: the effect on treatment rate and prevalence of late cases. Pediatrics. 1994;94(1):47-52. PMID: 8008537. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a pre-registration-era trial (1994).

cards.summary: Synthesis: ultrasound finds more, treats more, and proves less than its advocates claim — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: UK Hip Trial (629 infants with clinical instability) and Rosendahl 1994 (11,925 newborns).
cards.result: Used to guide management of an unstable hip, ultrasound reduces unnecessary splinting without worse hips at 2 years. shelves.title: Live attenuated versus inactivated influenza vaccine in young children
shelves.question: In infants and young children, does the intranasal live attenuated influenza vaccine prevent culture-confirmed influenza better than the injected inactivated vaccine — and what did it show on wheezing, the safety signal that fenced its youngest age band?
shelves.mesh: Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Influenza Vaccines/adverse effects · Influenza, Human/epidemiology,prevention & control · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Respiratory Sounds · Vaccines, Attenuated/adverse effects · Administration, Intranasal
shelves.balance: LIKELY: In Belshe's double-blind head-to-head trial (7,852 children completing the study per protocol, aged 6–59 months), live attenuated vaccine produced 54.9% fewer cases of culture-confirmed influenza than inactivated vaccine in relative terms (153 vs 338 cases; P<0.001), against matched and drifted strains alike. A second placebo-controlled trial in vaccine-naive children under 3 (Bracco Neto 2009) confirms the live vaccine's own efficacy (73.5% for two doses against antigenically similar strains). The fence is safety in the youngest: wheezing and hospitalisation signals at 6–11 months are why the authors themselves limit their endorsement to children 12–59 months without asthma or wheezing history. Two RCTs carry LIKELY for efficacy in the licensed age band.

cards.headline: Belshe 2007: 54.9% fewer culture-confirmed influenza cases with live attenuated vaccine (153 versus 338 cases) — with a wheeze signal at 6–11 months
cards.summary: Belshe (2007): 54.9% fewer culture-confirmed influenza cases (relative) with live attenuated vaccine (153 vs 338 cases) — with a wheeze signal as the fence.
cards.people: Children 6 to 59 months of age without a recent wheezing episode or severe asthma, randomised 1:1 to cold-adapted trivalent live attenuated intranasal vaccine or trivalent inactivated vaccine; safety data available for 8,352 children and 7,852 completed the study per protocol; influenza-like illness was culture-monitored through the 2004–2005 season. Sex mix is not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: There were 54.9% fewer cases of culture-confirmed influenza with live attenuated vaccine than with inactivated vaccine in relative terms (153 vs 338 cases, P<0.001 — a relative figure, case counts beside it), for antigenically well-matched and drifted viruses alike. Among previously unvaccinated children, wheezing within 42 days of dose 1 was more common with live attenuated vaccine at 6–11 months (3.8% vs 2.1%, P=0.076; 12 more episodes), and all-cause hospitalisation in that age group was higher (6.1% vs 2.6%, P=0.002). The authors conclude live attenuated vaccine should be a highly effective, safe option for children 12 to 59 months without a history of asthma or wheezing.
cards.watchOut: One season (2004–2005), one formulation era — efficacy against that season's strains does not guarantee the same margin in poorly matched seasons; and the trial's own safety fence (under 12 months, wheeze history) is part of the result, not a footnote.
cards.source: Belshe RB et al. Live attenuated versus inactivated influenza vaccine in infants and young children. N Engl J Med. 2007;356(7):685-96. PMID: 17301299. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT00128167.

cards.headline: Bracco Neto 2009: in vaccine-naive children under 3, two doses of live attenuated vaccine were 73.5% efficacious against similar strains versus placebo
cards.summary: Bracco Neto (2009): in vaccine-naive children under 3, two doses of live attenuated vaccine were 73.5% efficacious against similar strains.
cards.people: Influenza vaccine-naive children aged 6 to under 36 months, randomised in year 1 to 2 doses of live attenuated vaccine, 1 dose, excipient placebo, or saline placebo; in year 2, live-vaccine recipients received 1 dose and placebo recipients saline placebo (with one treatment-allocation error block, disclosed in the abstract). Total enrolment is not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: In year 1, vaccine efficacy versus placebo against antigenically similar strains was 73.5% (2 doses) and 57.7% (1 dose). In year 2, single-dose efficacy was 73.6% and 65.2% in children who had received 2 and 1 doses in year 1, and 57.0% in children who received 2 doses in year 1 and placebo in year 2 — protection persisted through a second season without revaccination. Seroconversion was significantly higher with 2 doses than 1 in year 1. Safety and tolerability were consistent with previous studies, and reactogenicity was similar between placebo groups.
cards.watchOut: A placebo comparison, not a head-to-head: it establishes that the live vaccine works in the youngest children, while Belshe's wheeze and hospitalisation signals in the same age band are why working is not the same as recommended there. A year-2 allocation error affected one block and is disclosed by the authors.
cards.source: Bracco Neto H et al. Efficacy and safety of 1 and 2 doses of live attenuated influenza vaccine in vaccine-naive children. Pediatr Infect Dis J. 2009;28(5):365-71. PMID: 19395948. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT00192400.

cards.headline: Synthesis: better efficacy than the injection, fenced by wheeze under 12 months — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: better efficacy than the injection, fenced by wheeze under 12 months — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Belshe 2007 (7,852 children per protocol) and Block 2009 (vaccine-naive children under 3).
cards.result: The live intranasal vaccine beat the injected vaccine head-to-head (153 vs 338 confirmed cases) and beat placebo in the naive youngest children (73.5% efficacy, two doses). High-dose influenza vaccine in older adults (Shelf #321) and influenza vaccination in pregnancy (Shelf #875) are different populations and are not re-carded here.

shelves.title: Helmet therapy for positional skull deformation: the HEADS null
shelves.question: Does a cranial remoulding helmet improve head shape in infants with positional plagiocephaly or brachycephaly versus the natural course — or is it an expensive, uncomfortable treatment for a self-correcting shape?
shelves.mesh: Cephalometry · Child Development · Cohort Studies · Craniosynostoses/therapy · Head Protective Devices · Parents/psychology · Physical Therapy Modalities
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): In the single randomised trial (HEADS; 84 infants aged 5–6 months with moderate-to-severe positional skull deformation), six months of helmet therapy changed head shape no more than the natural course — plagiocephaly change-score difference −0.2 (95% CI −1.6 to 1.2; P=0.80) and brachycephaly 0.2 (−1.7 to 2.2; P=0.81) at 24 months, with full recovery in 26% versus 23% (odds ratio 1.2). All parents reported one or more side effects. A single small trial caps the null at POSSIBLE, but its intervals are narrow enough to exclude a large shape benefit, and the authors discourage helmets as standard treatment for healthy infants.

cards.headline: HEADS (van Wijk 2014): helmet and natural course changed head shape equally (−0.2 and 0.2 difference scores; P=0.80 and 0.81)
cards.summary: HEADS (2014): helmet and natural course changed head shape equally (P=0.80 and 0.81).
cards.type: Pragmatic, single-blinded, randomised controlled trial nested in a prospective cohort
cards.people: 84 infants aged 5 to 6 months with moderate to severe positional skull deformation, born after 36 weeks' gestation, without muscular torticollis, craniosynostosis or dysmorphic features, at 29 Dutch paediatric physiotherapy practices, randomised to helmet therapy (42) or natural course (42) for 6 months, with blinded primary outcome assessment at 24 months. Sex mix is not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: Change in skull shape from baseline to 24 months was equal between groups: plagiocephaly (oblique diameter difference index) mean difference −0.2 (95% CI −1.6 to 1.2, P=0.80) and brachycephaly (cranioproportional index) 0.2 (−1.7 to 2.2, P=0.81). Full recovery was achieved in 10 of 39 infants (26%) with helmet therapy and 9 of 40 (23%) with natural course (odds ratio 1.2, 0.4 to 3.3; P=0.74 — a relative figure, absolute rates beside it). Secondary outcomes included ear deviation, facial asymmetry, motor development and parental satisfaction and anxiety; all parents reported one or more side effects. The authors discourage helmet use as standard treatment given equal effectiveness, side effects and high costs.
cards.watchOut: Only 84 infants and one helmet protocol in one health system — but the null is on the trial's own precise anthropometric measure, not a soft outcome; the trial's protocol record (PMID 22776627) is not carded, because a protocol carries no results.

shelves.title: Deworming a million preschool children: DEVTA
shelves.question: Does deworming every six months with albendazole, given to a whole population of preschool children, reduce mortality or improve growth?
shelves.mesh: Adjuvants, Immunologic/administration & dosage · Albendazole/administration & dosage · Anthelmintics/administration & dosage · Child Mortality/trends · Cluster Analysis · Diterpenes · Feces/parasitology
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, ruled at build: mortality was the programme's headline outcome and was not reduced): DEVTA (about 1 million preschool children in 72 administrative blocks in north India, 5 years) found deaths per child-care centre of 3.00 versus 3.16 (mortality ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.02 — a relative figure inside the caution band, consistent with no effect), absolute risks of dying between ages 1 and 6 of roughly 2.5% versus 2.6%, and no weight effect (difference 0.04 kg) despite halving worm-egg prevalence (16% vs 36%). The Cochrane synthesis of 51 trials concurs: no effect on mortality (low certainty), height, haemoglobin, cognition or school performance, with any weight effect confined to two decades-old study areas. A mega-trial null plus a concordant synthesis carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). DEVTA's companion vitamin A report (PMID 23498849) is already carded on the vitamin A shelves and is fenced here as background, not re-carded.

cards.headline: DEVTA (Awasthi 2013): mortality ratio 0.95 (CI 0.89 to 1.02) and no weight gain — deworming a million children changed neither
cards.summary: DEVTA (2013): mortality ratio 0.95 (CI 0.89 to 1.02) and no weight gain — deworming a million preschool children changed neither.
cards.type: Cluster-randomised trial (72 administrative blocks; 8,338 village child-care centres; 5 calendar years)
cards.people: About 1 million preschool children in the catchment areas of Integrated Child Development Service centres in north India, in blocks cluster-allocated to 6-monthly albendazole 400 mg, vitamin A, both, or neither (open control); the albendazole contrast is 36 versus 36 blocks, with 11 mass-treatment days, estimated albendazole compliance 86%, and 25,000 deaths at ages 1.0–6.0 years recorded as the primary outcome. In the worm/weight survey sample, children were standardised to age 4.0 years, 50% male.
cards.result: Deaths per child-care centre at ages 1.0–6.0 years over 5 years were 3.00 (SE 0.07) with albendazole versus 3.16 (SE 0.09) control (mortality ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.02; p=0.16 — a relative figure), suggesting absolute risks of dying between ages 1 and 6 of roughly 2.5% versus 2.6%. Weight at ages 3.0–6.0 was 12.72 kg versus 12.68 kg (difference 0.04 kg, −0.14 to 0.21; p=0.66), while nematode egg prevalence was 16% versus 36% — the treatment killed worms without changing the outcomes that justified it. No specific cause of death was significantly affected.
cards.watchOut: A lightly infected population (most infection was light) — the null governs mass treatment where worm burdens resemble DEVTA's, not treatment of heavily infected or symptomatic individual children, which is ordinary clinical care and untested here. Open control design. Tier C proposed.

cards.summary: Cochrane deworming synthesis (2019): across 51 trials, regular deworming did not improve growth, haemoglobin or cognition.

shelves.title: Therapeutic hypothermia after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in children (THAPCA-OH)
shelves.question: In comatose children after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, does therapeutic hypothermia (33.0 °C) vs therapeutic normothermia (36.8 °C) improve survival with good neurobehavioural outcome at 12 months?
shelves.mesh: Hypothermia, Induced/adverse effects · Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest/complications,mortality,therapy · Treatment Outcome · Humans · Child · Adolescent · Infant · Male · Female
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, survival is the primary claim): One multicentre randomised trial (THAPCA-OH, 295 children randomised at 38 children's hospitals) found no significant benefit of hypothermia at 33.0 °C over normothermia at 36.8 °C: survival with a good neurobehavioural outcome (Vineland VABS-II ≥70) at 12 months was 20% versus 12% among the 260 evaluable children with good baseline function (relative likelihood 1.54 relative, 95% CI 0.86 to 2.76; P=0.14), change in VABS-II did not differ significantly (P=0.13), and 1-year survival was 38% versus 29% (relative likelihood 1.29 relative, 0.93 to 1.79; P=0.13), with similar infection, serious arrhythmia, blood-product use and 28-day mortality. The point estimates lean toward hypothermia but the intervals are wide and cross no-effect in both directions — this is an imprecise null, which is why the stamp is POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) rather than LIKELY, and why the card prints the favourable point estimates rather than burying them. This shelf is out-of-hospital arrest only; the in-hospital companion trial is a different population and is not carded here.

cards.headline: THAPCA-OH 2015: hypothermia did not significantly improve survival with good function at 12 months (20% vs 12%; P=0.14) or 1-year survival (38% vs 29%; P=0.13)
cards.summary: THAPCA-OH 2015: hypothermia did not significantly improve survival with good function at 12 months (20% vs 12%; P=0.14) or 1-year survival (38% vs 29%; P=0.13)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial (38 children's hospitals; two targeted temperature strategies)
cards.people: 295 comatose children older than 2 days and younger than 18 years who remained unconscious after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, randomised within 6 hours of return of circulation to therapeutic hypothermia (target 33.0 °C) or therapeutic normothermia (target 36.8 °C); the primary outcome was evaluated in the 260 patients with evaluable data and a pre-arrest VABS-II score of at least 70. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in the primary outcome — survival at 12 months with a VABS-II score of 70 or higher — between hypothermia (20%) and normothermia (12%) (relative likelihood 1.54 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.86 to 2.76; P=0.14). Among all evaluable patients, the change in VABS-II score from baseline to 12 months was not significantly different (P=0.13), and 1-year survival was 38% in the hypothermia group versus 29% in the normothermia group (relative likelihood 1.29 relative, 0.93 to 1.79; P=0.13). The groups had similar incidences of infection and serious arrhythmias, similar use of blood products, and similar 28-day mortality. The authors conclude hypothermia did not confer a significant benefit in survival with a good functional outcome at 1 year.
cards.watchOut: Both headline estimates favour hypothermia numerically (20% vs 12%; 38% vs 29%) in a trial too small to resolve differences of that size — the correct reading is 'unproven', not 'disproven'. The comparator was actively maintained normothermia (36.8 °C), not unmanaged care, so the trial does not test cooling against fever-permitting usual care.
cards.source: Moler FW et al. Therapeutic hypothermia after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in children. N Engl J Med. 2015. PMID: 25913022. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00878644, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Racecadotril for acute watery diarrhoea in children
shelves.question: In young children with acute watery diarrhoea, does racecadotril vs placebo, both with oral rehydration, reduce stool output and diarrhoea duration?
shelves.mesh: Antidiarrheals/therapeutic use · Diarrhea/drug therapy,therapy · Fluid Therapy · Acute Disease · Humans · Child, Preschool · Double-Blind Method
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Salazar-Lindo 2000, 135 hospitalised boys aged 3–35 months in Peru) found racecadotril added to oral rehydration reduced 48-hour stool output by 46% relative (92±12 vs 170±15 g/kg; P<0.001), total stool output (157±27 vs 331±39 g/kg; P<0.001), and median diarrhoea duration (28 hours versus 72 hours in rotavirus-positive and 52 hours in rotavirus-negative placebo patients; P<0.001), with lower oral rehydration intake and only mild transient adverse effects in seven treated children. The relative reduction is labelled relative; the absolute outputs are printed beside it. A single trial, in boys only, in one country, nearly three decades old, caps at POSSIBLE however clean its result.

cards.headline: Salazar-Lindo 2000: racecadotril cut 48-hour stool output by 46% relative (92 vs 170 g/kg) and shortened diarrhoea (median 28 vs 52–72 hours) in hospitalised boys
cards.summary: Salazar-Lindo 2000: racecadotril cut 48-hour stool output by 46% relative (92 vs 170 g/kg) and shortened diarrhoea (median 28 vs 52–72 hours) in hospitalised boys
cards.people: 135 boys aged 3 to 35 months with watery diarrhoea of five days' duration or less, treated in hospital with racecadotril (1.5 mg/kg orally every eight hours) or placebo, in addition to oral rehydration solution; 73 of the boys had rotavirus infections. No girls were enrolled, as the record states.
cards.result: The mean (±SE) 48-hour stool output was 92±12 g per kilogram in the racecadotril group and 170±15 g per kilogram in the placebo group (P<0.001), a 46% relative reduction. Total stool output was 157±27 versus 331±39 g/kg (P<0.001). The median duration of diarrhoea was significantly less in the racecadotril group (28 hours regardless of rotavirus status) than in the placebo group (72 and 52 hours, respectively, for rotavirus-positive and rotavirus-negative patients) (P<0.001). Oral rehydration solution intake was significantly lower in the racecadotril group (P<0.001). Racecadotril was well tolerated; only seven patients taking it had adverse effects, all mild and transient.
cards.watchOut: Boys only, one Peruvian hospital population, stool output as the primary endpoint: the trial shows less fluid loss and shorter diarrhoea, not fewer complications or deaths, and says nothing directly about girls, outpatients, or non-watery diarrhoea.
cards.source: Salazar-Lindo E et al. Racecadotril in the treatment of acute watery diarrhea in children. N Engl J Med. 2000. PMID: 10944563. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Oral prednisolone for preschool children with acute virus-induced wheeze
shelves.question: In preschool children admitted with acute virus-induced wheezing, does a short course of oral prednisolone vs placebo shorten hospital stay?
shelves.mesh: Glucocorticoids/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Respiratory Sounds · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Child · Child, Preschool · Double-Blind Method · Female
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): One large double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Panickar 2009, 700 children aged 10–60 months presenting to three English hospitals with viral wheeze) found no benefit from a 5-day course of oral prednisolone on the primary outcome — duration of hospitalisation 11.0 hours on prednisolone versus 13.9 hours on placebo (ratio of geometric means 0.90 relative, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.05) — nor on time to physician sign-off for discharge, Preschool Respiratory Assessment Measure scores, albuterol use, 7-day symptom scores, or adverse events. A large, clean null in exactly the population where the practice was widespread carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). The population was mild-to-moderate wheeze, as the authors scope it — this shelf does not answer severe or hypoxic episodes.

cards.headline: Panickar 2009: prednisolone did not shorten hospital stay in preschool viral wheeze (11.0 vs 13.9 hours; ratio 0.90 relative, interval crossing 1) and helped no secondary outcome
cards.summary: Panickar 2009: prednisolone did not shorten hospital stay in preschool viral wheeze (11.0 vs 13.9 hours; ratio 0.90 relative, interval crossing 1) and helped no secondary outcome
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (three hospitals, England)
cards.people: 700 children between 10 months and 60 months presenting with an attack of wheezing associated with a viral infection, randomised to a 5-day course of oral prednisolone (10 mg daily for children 10–24 months; 20 mg daily for older children) or placebo; 687 children were included in the intention-to-treat analysis (343 prednisolone, 344 placebo). The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in the duration of hospitalisation between the placebo group and the prednisolone group (13.9 hours vs 11.0 hours; ratio of geometric means 0.90 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.77 to 1.05) or in the interval between admission and sign-off for discharge by a physician. There was no significant difference for any secondary outcome (Preschool Respiratory Assessment Measure score, albuterol use, 7-day symptom score) or in the number of adverse events. The authors conclude that in preschool children presenting to hospital with mild-to-moderate wheezing associated with viral infection, oral prednisolone was not superior to placebo.
cards.watchOut: The scoping matters: these were mild-to-moderate episodes with a median stay under a day. The null should not be extended to severe wheeze, hypoxia, intensive care, or to school-age asthma exacerbations, where corticosteroid evidence is a different literature.

shelves.title: Oral propranolol for infantile haemangioma
shelves.question: In infants with infantile haemangioma requiring treatment, does oral propranolol vs placebo achieve complete or near-complete resolution?
shelves.mesh: Hemangioma/drug therapy · Adrenergic beta-Antagonists/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Propranolol/therapeutic use · Humans · Infant · Female · Double-Blind Method
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trials agree. The large adaptive phase 2–3 trial (Léauté-Labrèze 2015, 460 infants aged 1–5 months with proliferating haemangioma requiring systemic therapy) selected 3 mg/kg/day for 6 months at interim analysis and found successful treatment (complete or near-complete resolution at week 24, blinded central photographic assessment) in 60% on that regimen versus 4% on placebo (P<0.001), with 88% of the selected-regimen group improved by week 5 versus 5% on placebo; known propranolol adverse events (hypoglycaemia, hypotension, bradycardia, bronchospasm) occurred infrequently without significant difference from placebo, and 10% of successes needed systemic retreatment in follow-up. The smaller earlier trial (Hogeling 2011, 40 children aged 9 weeks to 5 years, 2 mg/kg/day) found growth stopped by week 4 and significantly greater reductions in volume, redness and elevation. Two blinded trials, a very large effect on the large trial's primary endpoint, earn LIKELY.

cards.headline: Léauté-Labrèze 2015: propranolol 3 mg/kg/day for 6 months achieved complete or near-complete resolution in 60% vs 4% on placebo
cards.summary: Léauté-Labrèze 2015: propranolol 3 mg/kg/day for 6 months achieved complete or near-complete resolution in 60% vs 4% on placebo
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, adaptive, phase 2–3 trial
cards.people: 460 infants aged 1 to 5 months with proliferating infantile hemangioma requiring systemic therapy, randomised to placebo or one of four propranolol regimens (1 or 3 mg of propranolol base per kilogram per day for 3 or 6 months); 456 received treatment. A preplanned interim analysis of the first 188 patients completing 24 weeks selected the 3 mg/kg/day for 6 months regimen for the final efficacy analysis.
cards.result: The frequency of successful treatment (complete or nearly complete resolution of the target hemangioma at week 24, by independent centralised blinded evaluation of standardised photographs) was higher with the selected regimen than with placebo (60% vs 4%, P<0.001). A total of 88% of patients on the selected regimen showed improvement by week 5, versus 5% on placebo. A total of 10% of patients in whom treatment was successful required systemic retreatment during follow-up. Known adverse events associated with propranolol (hypoglycemia, hypotension, bradycardia, and bronchospasm) occurred infrequently, with no significant difference in frequency between the placebo group and the propranolol groups.
cards.watchOut: An adaptive design: the headline 60% versus 4% compares the regimen chosen because it looked best at interim against placebo, which inflates the apparent precision of that specific dose-duration claim — though an effect of this size is not an artefact of selection. The trial enrolled haemangiomas judged to need systemic therapy, not the many lesions safely left alone.

cards.summary: Hogeling 2011: propranolol 2 mg/kg/day stopped haemangioma growth by week 4 and reduced volume, redness and elevation versus placebo (40 children)
cards.people: 40 children between 9 weeks and 5 years of age with facial infantile haemangiomas or haemangiomas in sites with potential for disfigurement, randomly assigned to oral propranolol or placebo solution 2 mg/kg per day divided three times daily for 6 months, with baseline electrocardiogram, echocardiogram and laboratory evaluation and monitoring of heart rate, blood pressure and blood glucose at each visit.
cards.result: Haemangioma growth stopped by week 4 in the propranolol group. Significant differences in the percent change in volume were seen between groups, with the largest difference at week 12. Significant decreases in redness and elevation occurred in the propranolol group at weeks 12 and 24 (P=.01 and .001, respectively). No significant hypoglycemia, hypotension, or bradycardia occurred. shelves.title: Extending initial prednisolone treatment in childhood nephrotic syndrome
shelves.question: In children with a first episode of steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome, does extending initial prednisolone beyond the standard course vs standard duration reduce relapses?
shelves.mesh: Nephrotic Syndrome/drug therapy · Prednisolone/administration & dosage · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage · Recurrence · Humans · Child · Child, Preschool · Double-Blind Method
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): One double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial designed to separate duration from dose (Teeninga 2013, 150 children in 69 Dutch hospitals) gave both groups the same cumulative prednisolone dose (approximately 3,360 mg/m²) over either 3 months of prednisolone followed by 3 months of placebo, or 6 months of prednisolone. With median follow-up of 47 months, relapses occurred in 77% of the 3-month group and 80% of the 6-month group; frequent relapses (45% vs 50%), eventual maintenance or other immunosuppression (50% vs 59%), steroid dependence and adverse effects did not differ significantly. The trial's own interpretation — earlier apparent benefits of longer regimens most likely reflected higher cumulative dose, not duration — is the shelf's balance point. One well-designed trial carrying the exact comparison earns LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for duration extension at equal dose; it does not test higher cumulative doses. Distinct from #739 (rituximab for established steroid-dependent disease).

cards.headline: Teeninga 2013: extending prednisolone from 3 to 6 months at equal cumulative dose did not reduce relapses (77% vs 80%) over a median 47 months
cards.summary: Teeninga 2013: extending prednisolone from 3 to 6 months at equal cumulative dose did not reduce relapses (77% vs 80%) over a median 47 months
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (69 hospitals, the Netherlands)
cards.people: 150 children aged 9 months to 17 years presenting with a first episode of nephrotic syndrome, randomly assigned to 3 months of prednisolone followed by 3 months of placebo (74) or 6 months of prednisolone (76); both groups received equal cumulative doses of approximately 3,360 mg/m². Among the 126 children who started trial medication, 62 were in the 3-month group and 64 in the 6-month group; median follow-up was 47 months.
cards.result: Relapses occurred in 48 (77%) of 62 patients who received 3 months of prednisolone and 51 (80%) of 64 patients who received 6 months. Frequent relapses occurred with similar frequency (45% versus 50%). There were no statistically significant differences in eventual initiation of prednisolone maintenance and/or other immunosuppressive therapy (50% versus 59%), steroid dependence, or adverse effects. The authors conclude that extending initial treatment from 3 to 6 months without increasing cumulative dose did not benefit clinical outcome, and that previous findings favouring prolonged regimens most likely resulted from increased cumulative dose rather than treatment duration.
cards.watchOut: The equal-dose design is the point and the limit: this trial refutes duration extension achieved by tapering the same total dose more slowly. It does not refute regimens that genuinely give more prednisolone in total — those carry their own toxicity question, untested here.
cards.source: Teeninga N et al. Extending prednisolone treatment does not reduce relapses in childhood nephrotic syndrome. J Am Soc Nephrol. 2013. PMID: 23274956. shelves.title: Adenotonsillectomy vs watchful waiting for childhood obstructive sleep apnoea (CHAT)
shelves.question: In children aged 5–9 with obstructive sleep apnoea, does early adenotonsillectomy vs watchful waiting improve neurobehavioural outcomes and polysomnography?
shelves.mesh: Sleep Apnea, Obstructive/surgery · Adenoidectomy · Tonsillectomy · Polysomnography · Cognition · Humans · Child · Child, Preschool
shelves.balance: SPLIT — POSSIBLE for polysomnographic and symptom benefit / LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for the primary neuropsychological outcome: One large randomised trial (CHAT, Marcus 2013, 464 children aged 5–9 years) split cleanly by outcome type. The primary outcome — change in attention and executive function (Developmental Neuropsychological Assessment) — did not differ significantly (mean improvement 7.1±13.9 with early adenotonsillectomy vs 5.1±13.4 with watchful waiting; P=0.16), from baselines already close to the population mean of 100. Secondary outcomes favoured surgery: significantly greater improvements in behaviour, quality of life and symptoms, and normalisation of polysomnographic findings in 79% versus 46%. A single trial with a null primary endpoint and positive secondary endpoints is exactly a split stamp: the operation demonstrably fixes the sleep study and symptoms, and demonstrably did not fix the cognitive measure the trial was powered on.

cards.headline: CHAT 2013: adenotonsillectomy normalised polysomnography in 79% vs 46% but did not significantly improve the primary attention/executive-function score (P=0.16)
cards.summary: CHAT 2013: adenotonsillectomy normalised polysomnography in 79% vs 46% but did not significantly improve the primary attention/executive-function score (P=0.16)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (early surgery vs watchful waiting with supportive care; unblinded)
cards.people: 464 children aged 5 to 9 years with the obstructive sleep apnea syndrome (without prolonged oxyhemoglobin desaturation, as the record scopes it), randomly assigned to early adenotonsillectomy or watchful waiting; polysomnographic, cognitive, behavioural and health outcomes were assessed at baseline and at 7 months. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: The primary outcome — the attention and executive-function score on the Developmental Neuropsychological Assessment (scores 50 to 150, higher better) — started close to the population mean of 100 in both groups and did not differ significantly in change (mean [±SD] improvement 7.1±13.9 in the early-adenotonsillectomy group and 5.1±13.4 in the watchful-waiting group; P=0.16). In contrast, there were significantly greater improvements in behavioral, quality-of-life, and polysomnographic findings and significantly greater reduction in symptoms with surgery. Normalization of polysomnographic findings occurred in 79% of the surgery group versus 46% of the watchful-waiting group. The authors conclude surgery did not significantly improve attention or executive function but did reduce symptoms and improve secondary outcomes, providing evidence of beneficial effects of early adenotonsillectomy.
cards.watchOut: Unblinded surgery with parent-reported secondary outcomes invites expectation bias on exactly the outcomes that were positive, while the blinded-scored primary was null — that asymmetry is why the cognitive claim stays a null and the symptom claim stays at POSSIBLE. Also note 46% of watchful-waiting children normalised their sleep study spontaneously within 7 months.

shelves.title: Vitamin A supplementation for morbidity and mortality in children 6 months–5 years
shelves.question: In children aged 6 months to 5 years in low-income settings, does periodic high-dose vitamin A vs placebo reduce all-cause mortality?
shelves.mesh: Vitamin A/administration & dosage · Dietary Supplements · Child Mortality · Vitamin A Deficiency · Humans · Child · Child, Preschool · Female · Male
shelves.balance: SPLIT — POSSIBLE for a mortality benefit in vitamin-A-deficient populations / LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for the largest trial — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality is the primary claim): The randomised record genuinely conflicts. DEVTA (Awasthi 2013, cluster-randomised, about 1 million preschool children in north India) found no significant mortality reduction from 6-monthly retinol (mortality ratio 0.96 relative, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.03; P=0.22; absolute risks about 2.5% vs 2.6% between ages 1 and 6 years), despite halving severe deficiency. The earlier Nepal trial (West 1991, 28,630 children, double-masked, placebo-controlled) found a 30% relative mortality reduction (relative risk 0.70 relative, 0.56 to 0.88). DEVTA's own interpretation threads the needle: pooling DEVTA with eight previous randomised trials gives a weighted average mortality reduction of 11% relative (95% CI 5 to 16) — reliably contradicting no-effect, and reliably contradicting the 20–30% reductions once expected. Any single-grade stamp would misrepresent this record; the split, with the pooled 11% relative figure and its absolute context, is the honest balance. Distinct from #1164 (the DEVTA deworming question).

cards.headline: DEVTA 2013: 6-monthly vitamin A did not significantly reduce preschool mortality in ~1 million Indian children (mortality ratio 0.96 relative; P=0.22)
cards.summary: DEVTA 2013: 6-monthly vitamin A did not significantly reduce preschool mortality in ~1 million Indian children (mortality ratio 0.96 relative; P=0.22)
cards.type: Cluster-randomised trial (72 administrative blocks, north India; open control)
cards.people: Pre-school children in the catchment areas of 8,338 state-staffed village child-care centres (under-5 population about 1 million) in 72 administrative blocks, cluster-allocated to 6-monthly vitamin A (200,000 IU retinyl acetate), albendazole, both, or neither, over 5 years with 11 mass-treatment days for children then aged 6–72 months; the vitamin A analysis compares 36 retinol-allocated versus 36 control blocks, monitoring about 25,000 deaths at ages 1.0–6.0 years. Estimated compliance with supplements was 86%.
cards.result: Deaths per child-care centre at ages 1.0–6.0 years were 3.01 in retinol blocks versus 3.15 in control blocks (absolute reduction 0.14 [SE 0.11]; mortality ratio 0.96 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.89 to 1.03; P=0.22), suggesting absolute risks of death between ages 1.0 and 6.0 years of approximately 2.5% (retinol) versus 2.6% (control). No specific cause of death was significantly affected. The supplement demonstrably worked biochemically: among surveyed children, mean plasma retinol was one-sixth higher (0.72 vs 0.62 µmol/L) and severe deficiency was halved (retinol <0.35 µmol/L: 6% vs 13%), as was Bitot's spots (1.4% vs 3.5%). The authors state DEVTA contradicts the expectation of a 20–30% mortality reduction but cannot rule out a more modest effect, and that meta-analysis of DEVTA plus eight previous trials yields a weighted average mortality reduction of 11% relative (95% CI 5 to 16; P=0.00015).
cards.watchOut: DEVTA's open control and block-level analysis are design facts, and its mortality ratio interval (0.89 to 1.03 relative) excludes the large benefits of the older trials in its own population — the conflict with the earlier record is the finding, not a defect to be averaged away silently.
cards.source: Awasthi S et al. Vitamin A supplementation every 6 months with retinol in 1 million pre-school children in north India: DEVTA, a cluster-randomised trial. Lancet. 2013. PMID: 23498849. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00222547, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: West 1991 (Nepal): vitamin A reduced preschool child mortality by 30% relative (relative risk 0.70 relative, 0.56 to 0.88) in a double-masked placebo-controlled community trial
cards.summary: West 1991 (Nepal): vitamin A reduced preschool child mortality by 30% relative (relative risk 0.70 relative, 0.56 to 0.88) in a double-masked placebo-controlled community trial
cards.type: Randomised, double-masked, placebo-controlled community trial (randomisation by administrative ward, rural Nepal)
cards.people: 28,630 children aged 6–72 months in rural Nepal, an area representative of the Gangetic flood plain of South Asia; supplemented children received 60,000 retinol equivalents every 4 months and controls received identical capsules containing 300 retinol equivalents; the trial, planned for 2 years, was discontinued after 12 months.
cards.result: After 12 months, the relative risk of death in the vitamin-A-supplemented compared with the control group was 0.70 — a relative measure — (95% CI 0.56 to 0.88), equivalent to a 30% relative reduction in mortality. The reduction was present in both sexes (relative risk for boys 0.77 relative; for girls 0.65 relative), at all ages (range of relative risks 0.83 to 0.50 relative), and throughout the year (0.76 to 0.67 relative). The reduction was not affected by acute nutritional status as measured by arm circumference. The authors conclude periodic community vitamin A delivery can greatly reduce child mortality in developing countries.

shelves.title: Buccal dextrose gel for neonatal hypoglycaemia (Sugar Babies)
shelves.question: In at-risk newborn infants with hypoglycaemia, does buccal 40% dextrose gel plus feeding vs placebo gel plus feeding reduce treatment failure and NICU admission?
shelves.mesh: Glucose/administration & dosage · Hypoglycemia/drug therapy · Blood Glucose/drug effects · Gels · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Female · Double-Blind Method
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Sugar Babies, Harris 2013, single tertiary centre in New Zealand) found buccal 40% dextrose gel 200 mg/kg plus feeding reduced treatment failure (blood glucose under 2.6 mmol/L (≈47 mg/dL) after two treatment attempts) from 24% to 14% (relative risk 0.57 relative, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.98; P=0.04) in 237 analysed at-risk babies who became hypoglycaemic, with no serious adverse events. A single-centre, single-trial result on a biochemical-process endpoint (treatment failure, not brain injury or NICU admission as a powered outcome) caps at POSSIBLE; the topic question's NICU-admission limb is not answered by this record and the balance does not claim it.

cards.headline: Sugar Babies 2013: dextrose gel reduced treatment failure for neonatal hypoglycaemia (14% vs 24%; relative risk 0.57 relative; P=0.04)
cards.summary: Sugar Babies 2013: dextrose gel reduced treatment failure for neonatal hypoglycaemia (14% vs 24%; relative risk 0.57 relative; P=0.04)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (single tertiary centre, New Zealand)
cards.people: 514 at-risk babies aged 35–42 weeks' gestation and younger than 48 hours old were enrolled; 242 (47%) became hypoglycaemic and were randomised to 40% dextrose gel 200 mg/kg or placebo gel, each plus feeding, with randomisation stratified by maternal diabetes and birthweight; five babies were randomised in error, leaving 237 for analysis (118 dextrose, 119 placebo).
cards.result: Dextrose gel reduced the frequency of treatment failure — defined as a blood glucose concentration of less than 2.6 mmol/L (≈47 mg/dL) after two treatment attempts — compared with placebo (16 [14%] vs 29 [24%]; relative risk 0.57 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.33 to 0.98; P=0.04). No serious adverse events were noted. Three babies (3%) in the placebo group each had one blood glucose concentration of 0.9 mmol/L (≈16 mg/dL); no other adverse events took place. The authors conclude dextrose gel is inexpensive and simple to administer and should be considered for first-line treatment of hypoglycaemia in late preterm and term babies in the first 48 hours after birth.
cards.watchOut: The P value is 0.04 on a single-centre trial with a confidence interval reaching 0.98 relative — a fragile margin — and 'treatment failure' is a glucose-threshold endpoint: the trial does not show less NICU admission, less intravenous dextrose exposure overall, or better neurodevelopment, and its authors' 'should be considered first-line' recommendation runs slightly ahead of a one-trial record, which this shelf notes rather than repeats as its own claim.
cards.source: Harris DL et al. Dextrose gel for neonatal hypoglycaemia (the Sugar Babies Study): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet. 2013. PMID: 24075361. shelves.title: Daily emollient from birth to prevent eczema in high-risk infants (BEEP)
shelves.question: In newborn infants at high risk of eczema, does daily whole-body emollient for the first year vs standard skin care prevent eczema by age 2?
shelves.mesh: Eczema/prevention & control · Emollients/therapeutic use · Dermatitis, Atopic · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Humans · Female · Follow-Up Studies
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): One large pragmatic multicentre randomised trial (BEEP, Chalmers 2020, 1,394 term newborns at high risk of eczema in the UK) found no evidence that daily emollient for the first year prevented eczema at age 2 (23% vs 25%; adjusted relative risk 0.95 relative, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.16; P=0.61; adjusted risk difference −1.2 percentage points, −5.9 to 3.6), with other eczema definitions supporting the primary analysis — and a harm signal in the other direction: more skin infections per child in year 1 in the emollient group (mean 0.23 vs 0.15; adjusted incidence rate ratio 1.55 relative, 1.15 to 2.09). Adherence was good (74–88% across the year), so this is a genuine null, not a compliance failure. A large clean null carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). The question's 'prevent' wording is the trial's own framing for eczema onset; no diabetes-onset claim is involved.

cards.headline: BEEP 2020: daily emollient in the first year did not prevent eczema at age 2 (23% vs 25%; P=0.61) and increased skin infections (rate ratio 1.55 relative)
cards.summary: BEEP 2020: daily emollient in the first year did not prevent eczema at age 2 (23% vs 25%; P=0.61) and increased skin infections (rate ratio 1.55 relative)
cards.type: Multicentre, pragmatic, parallel-group randomised controlled trial (12 hospitals and four primary care sites, UK)
cards.people: 1,394 term newborns (at least 37 weeks' gestation) at high risk of eczema (at least one first-degree relative with parent-reported eczema, allergic rhinitis, or asthma diagnosed by a doctor), randomly assigned to daily emollient (Diprobase cream or DoubleBase gel) for the first year plus standard skin-care advice (693) or standard skin-care advice only (701); outcome data at age 2 were collected for 598 and 612 infants respectively. Adherence in the emollient group was 88% at 3 months, 82% at 6 months and 74% at 12 months among those with questionnaire data.
cards.result: At age 2 years, eczema (UK working party criteria) was present in 139 (23%) of 598 infants in the emollient group and 150 (25%) of 612 in the control group (adjusted relative risk 0.95 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.78 to 1.16; P=0.61; adjusted risk difference −1.2%, −5.9 to 3.6). Other eczema definitions supported the primary analysis. The mean number of skin infections per child in year 1 was 0.23 (SD 0.68) in the emollient group versus 0.15 (0.46) in the control group (adjusted incidence rate ratio 1.55 relative, 1.15 to 2.09). The authors conclude there is no evidence daily emollient in the first year prevents eczema in high-risk children, with some evidence of increased skin infection risk, and that families with eczema, asthma or allergic rhinitis should not use daily emollients to try to prevent eczema in their newborn.
cards.watchOut: The tested products were two specific emollients applied daily to the whole body; the null governs that strategy. It does not address emollient treatment of established eczema, which is a different question with different evidence.
cards.source: Chalmers JR et al. Daily emollient during infancy for prevention of eczema: the BEEP randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2020. PMID: 32087126. Registry ID: ISRCTN21528841, stated in the record's abstract (none in the databank fields). shelves.title: Antibiotics-first vs appendicectomy for uncomplicated acute appendicitis in children
shelves.question: In children with acute non-perforated appendicitis, does non-operative antibiotic treatment vs appendicectomy avoid surgery without increasing perforation or complications?
shelves.mesh: Appendicitis/complications,drug therapy,surgery · Appendectomy · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Acute Disease · Humans · Child · Adolescent
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): The paediatric randomised record is one pilot trial (Svensson 2015, 50 children at a Swedish centre, 1-year follow-up) designed to test feasibility and safety, not efficacy. Of 24 children randomised to antibiotics, 22 (92%) had initial resolution of symptoms; two had appendicectomy during primary treatment and one more at 9 months for recurrent appendicitis, while six further children had appendicectomies for recurrent abdominal pain (five) or parental wish (one) — none of those six specimens showed appendicitis. Overall 62% of the antibiotic group had not had an appendicectomy at follow-up; all 26 surgical children had histopathologically confirmed appendicitis with no significant complications in the surgery group. A 50-child pilot can show a strategy is feasible; it cannot show it is equivalent, safer, or perforation-neutral — hence MAYBE (weak evidence), the weakest stamp in this batch. Adult APPAC and CODA evidence must not be imported as paediatric evidence, and this shelf does not do so.

cards.headline: Svensson 2015 (pilot, 50 children): 92% of antibiotic-treated children resolved initially and 62% avoided appendicectomy at 1 year; no complications signal in either arm
cards.summary: Svensson 2015 (pilot, 50 children): 92% of antibiotic-treated children resolved initially and 62% avoided appendicectomy at 1 year; no complications signal in either arm
cards.type: Pilot randomised controlled trial (single centre, Sweden)
cards.people: 50 children with imaging-confirmed acute nonperforated appendicitis who would normally have had emergency appendectomy, randomised to non-operative treatment with antibiotics (24) or surgery (26), with 1 year of follow-up. The abstract does not state ages or sex mix beyond the paediatric frame.
cards.result: All children in the surgery group had histopathologically confirmed acute appendicitis, and there were no significant complications in this group. In the non-operative group, two of 24 patients had appendicectomy within the primary antibiotic treatment period and one patient after 9 months for recurrent acute appendicitis. Another six patients had an appendicectomy for recurrent abdominal pain (five) or parental wish (one) during follow-up; none of these six had appendicitis on histopathological examination. Twenty-two of 24 patients (92%) treated with antibiotics had initial resolution of symptoms; of these, only one (5%) had recurrence of acute appendicitis during follow-up. Overall, 62% of patients had not had an appendicectomy during follow-up. The authors conclude the pilot suggests non-operative treatment is feasible and safe and that further investigation is warranted.
cards.watchOut: Fifty children cannot exclude an increase in perforation or complications — the outcomes the topic question asks about — and 'feasible and safe' in a pilot's conclusion means 'no disaster in 24 children', not demonstrated safety. Five of the later appendicectomies were for pain without appendicitis, which also shows the diagnostic uncertainty families live with under a non-operative strategy.
cards.source: Svensson JF et al. Nonoperative treatment with antibiotics versus surgery for acute nonperforated appendicitis in children: a pilot randomized controlled trial. Ann Surg. 2015. cards.summary: Synthesis: a promising feasibility signal and nothing stronger — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: Svensson 2015 (50 children with nonperforated appendicitis).
cards.result: The pilot justifies a definitive paediatric trial; it does not justify a practice claim. What it establishes: most antibiotic-treated children (22 of 24) settle, most (62%) still have their appendix a year later, and true recurrence was rare (1 of 22). What it cannot establish is comparative safety — the question that decides whether antibiotics-first should replace an operation with a near-zero major-complication rate in this trial's own surgical arm.

shelves.title: Internet-based CBT for adolescents with chronic fatigue syndrome (FITNET)
shelves.question: In adolescents with chronic fatigue syndrome, does internet-based cognitive behavioural treatment vs care as usual increase recovery (school attendance and fatigue) at 6 months?
shelves.mesh: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy/methods · Fatigue Syndrome, Chronic/diagnosis,therapy · Internet · Adolescent · Humans · Female · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One open-label randomised trial (FITNET, Nijhof 2012, 135 adolescents aged 12–18 at one Dutch tertiary centre) found internet-based CBT markedly superior to usual care on all three dichotomised primary outcomes at 6 months: full school attendance 75% versus 16% (relative risk 4.8 relative, 95% CI 2.7 to 8.9), absence of severe fatigue 85% versus 27% (relative risk 3.2 relative, 2.1 to 4.9), and normal physical functioning 78% versus 20% (relative risk 3.8 relative, 2.3 to 6.3), all P<0.0001, with no serious adverse events reported. The effects are very large — which, in a single unblinded trial with self-reported outcomes and a heterogeneous 'usual care' comparator, is itself a reason for caution rather than a higher stamp: expectation and engagement effects cannot be separated from treatment effects in this design. One trial, one country, one centre: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: FITNET 2012: internet CBT gave 75% full school attendance vs 16% on usual care, 85% vs 27% free of severe fatigue at 6 months
cards.summary: FITNET 2012: internet CBT gave 75% full school attendance vs 16% on usual care, 85% vs 27% free of severe fatigue at 6 months
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (open label; one tertiary treatment centre, the Netherlands)
cards.people: 135 adolescents aged 12–18 years with chronic fatigue syndrome, assigned 1:1 to the FITNET internet-based CBT programme (68) or usual care (67); 67 and 64 respectively were analysed. Primary outcomes (school attendance, fatigue severity, physical functioning) were assessed at 6 months by computerised questionnaires; thereafter all patients were offered FITNET if needed.
cards.result: FITNET was significantly more effective than usual care for all dichotomised primary outcomes at 6 months: full school attendance 50 (75%) versus 10 (16%) (relative risk 4.8 — a relative measure — 95% CI 2.7 to 8.9; P<0.0001); absence of severe fatigue 57 (85%) versus 17 (27%) (relative risk 3.2 relative, 2.1 to 4.9; P<0.0001); and normal physical functioning 52 (78%) versus 13 (20%) (relative risk 3.8 relative, 2.3 to 6.3; P<0.0001). No serious adverse events were reported. The authors conclude FITNET is a readily accessible and highly effective treatment whose results justify broader implementation.
cards.watchOut: Relative risks of 3–5 on subjective, self-reported outcomes in an unblinded trial against an undefined 'usual care' mix are the classic signature of a result that will shrink on replication. The authors' implementation recommendation is printed in the result; this shelf's stamp (POSSIBLE) is deliberately more cautious than the paper's conclusion, because the design cannot exclude large non-specific effects.
cards.source: Nijhof SL et al. Effectiveness of internet-based cognitive behavioural treatment for adolescents with chronic fatigue syndrome (FITNET): a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2012. shelves.title: Family-based treatment vs adolescent-focused therapy for anorexia nervosa
shelves.question: In adolescents with anorexia nervosa, does family-based treatment vs individual adolescent-focused therapy improve remission?
shelves.mesh: Anorexia Nervosa/psychology,therapy · Family Therapy · Psychotherapy · Adolescent · Humans · Female · Male · Follow-Up Studies
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised trial (Lock 2010, 121 adolescents aged 12–18 at Stanford and the University of Chicago) comparing 24 outpatient hours over 12 months of family-based treatment (FBT) with adolescent-focused therapy (AFT) found no difference in full remission at end of treatment, but FBT significantly superior on full remission at both 6- and 12-month post-treatment follow-up; FBT was also superior for partial remission and BMI percentile at end of treatment, though not at follow-up, and for Eating Disorder Examination change at end of treatment only. The trial's abstract reports these findings without printing the remission percentages, and none are supplied here from outside the record — the card states the pattern exactly as the record gives it. A single trial whose advantage appears after treatment ends, on a categorical outcome whose rates the abstract does not quantify, earns POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Lock 2010: FBT and AFT tied on full remission at end of treatment; FBT significantly superior at 6- and 12-month follow-up
cards.summary: Lock 2010: FBT and AFT tied on full remission at end of treatment; FBT significantly superior at 6- and 12-month follow-up
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (two US academic centres; 24 outpatient treatment hours over 12 months in each arm)
cards.people: 121 participants aged 12 through 18 years with a DSM-IV diagnosis of anorexia nervosa (excluding the amenorrhea requirement), treated at Stanford University and the University of Chicago between April 2005 and March 2009, and assessed at baseline, end of treatment, and 6 and 12 months post-treatment. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: Full remission was defined as normal weight (≥95% of expected for sex, age and height) plus a mean global Eating Disorder Examination score within 1 SD of published means. There were no differences in full remission between treatments at end of treatment; at both the 6- and 12-month follow-up, FBT was significantly superior to AFT on this measure. FBT was significantly superior for partial remission at end of treatment but not at follow-up; BMI percentile at end of treatment was significantly superior for FBT but not at follow-up; Eating Disorder Examination change was greater with FBT at end of treatment with no difference at follow-up. The record's abstract does not print the remission percentages, and this card does not import them from elsewhere.
cards.watchOut: The pattern — parity at end of treatment, divergence afterwards — is favourable to FBT but is also the pattern most vulnerable to differential follow-up and post-treatment care; with one trial and no effect sizes in the abstract, the margin of FBT's advantage cannot be sized from this record.
