shelves.title: CBT, sertraline, and combination for paediatric OCD (POTS I & POTS II)
shelves.question: In children/adolescents with OCD, does CBT, sertraline, or their combination vs placebo reduce OCD severity?
shelves.mesh: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder/therapy · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Sertraline/therapeutic use · Combined Modality Therapy · Humans · Child · Adolescent · Female · Male
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two linked randomised trials from the same programme answer the initial-treatment and the augmentation questions. POTS I (2004, 112 patients aged 7–17, masked, three US academic centres) found combined CBT plus sertraline, CBT alone and sertraline alone all superior to pill placebo on CY-BOCS change (P=.001, .003 and .007 respectively); combined treatment was superior to each monotherapy on the continuous outcome (P=.008 vs CBT; P=.006 vs sertraline) while remission rates (CY-BOCS ≤10) were 53.6% combined, 39.3% CBT alone, 21.4% sertraline alone and 3.6% placebo — with the combined-versus-CBT remission difference itself not significant (P=.42) and sertraline alone not significantly different from placebo on remission (P=.10), both printed on the card because they qualify the headline. POTS II (2011, 124 SRI partial responders) found adding full CBT to medication management produced a 68.6% response rate versus 30.0% for medication management alone and 34.0% for medication management plus brief CBT instructions (which did not beat medication alone, P=.72). Two trials, concordant that CBT is the active ingredient and combination is the strongest start, earn LIKELY. Distinct from #877 (CAMS anxiety disorders).

cards.headline: POTS I 2004: combined CBT+sertraline, CBT alone and sertraline alone all beat placebo on CY-BOCS; remission 53.6% / 39.3% / 21.4% / 3.6%
cards.summary: POTS I 2004: combined CBT+sertraline, CBT alone and sertraline alone all beat placebo on CY-BOCS; remission 53.6% / 39.3% / 21.4% / 3.6%
cards.type: Balanced, masked randomised controlled trial (three US academic centres)
cards.people: 112 outpatients aged 7 through 17 years with a primary DSM-IV diagnosis of OCD and a Children's Yale-Brown Obsessive-Compulsive Scale (CY-BOCS) score of 16 or higher, recruited September 1997 to December 2002, randomised to CBT alone, sertraline alone, combined CBT and sertraline, or pill placebo for 12 weeks; 97 (87%) completed treatment. Outcomes were rated by an independent evaluator masked to treatment.
cards.result: Intent-to-treat analyses showed a statistically significant advantage over placebo for combined treatment (P=.001), CBT alone (P=.003) and sertraline alone (P=.007) on CY-BOCS change. Combined treatment was superior to CBT alone (P=.008) and to sertraline alone (P=.006), which did not differ from each other; site differences emerged for CBT and sertraline but not for combined treatment. Clinical remission (CY-BOCS ≤10) rates were 53.6% (95% CI 36% to 70%) for combined treatment, 39.3% (24% to 58%) for CBT alone, 21.4% (10% to 40%) for sertraline alone and 3.6% (0% to 19%) for placebo. The combined remission rate did not differ significantly from CBT alone (P=.42) but differed from sertraline alone (P=.03) and placebo (P<.001); CBT alone differed from placebo on remission (P=.002) whereas sertraline alone did not (P=.10). The three active treatments were acceptable and well tolerated, with no evidence of treatment-emergent harm to self or others.
cards.watchOut: The authors' conclusion (start with combination or CBT alone) is supported on symptom change; on the harder remission endpoint, combination's edge over good CBT alone was not significant and sertraline alone's edge over placebo was not significant either — both facts belong beside any summary that quotes the 53.6% headline.

cards.summary: POTS II 2011: adding full CBT to medication management doubled response in SRI partial responders (68.6% vs 30.0%); brief CBT instructions did not (34.0%)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (three US academic medical centres)
cards.people: 124 paediatric outpatients aged 7 to 17 years with OCD as a primary diagnosis and a CY-BOCS score of 16 or higher despite an adequate SRI trial, enrolled 2004–2009, randomly assigned to medication management only (42), medication management plus instructions in CBT (42), or medication management plus full CBT (42; 14 concurrent CBT sessions), over 12 weeks.
cards.result: In the primary intention-to-treat analysis, 68.6% (95% CI 53.9% to 83.3%) in the medication-management-plus-CBT group were responders (≥30% CY-BOCS improvement), significantly better than 34.0% (18.0% to 50.0%) in the plus-instructions group and 30.0% (14.9% to 45.1%) in the medication-management-only group (P<.01 for both pairwise comparisons). The plus-instructions strategy was not statistically superior to medication management only (P=.72). Number needed to treat for one additional responder with full CBT versus medication management alone was estimated at 3.
cards.watchOut: POTS II answers the augmentation question in partial responders — a different population from POTS I's initial treatment — and shows the dose of CBT matters: handing families CBT instructions inside medication visits did not work, which is a service-design finding as much as a drug finding.

cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: POTS I (112 patients, initial treatment) and POTS II (124 patients, SRI partial responders).

shelves.title: Advance provision of emergency contraception for adolescents
shelves.question: In adolescent women, does advance provision of emergency contraception vs standard access change EC use, unprotected sex, or pregnancy/STI risk behaviour?
shelves.mesh: Contraceptives, Postcoital/administration & dosage,supply & distribution · Contraception Behavior · Adolescent · Female · Humans · Health Knowledge, Attitudes, Practice
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised trial (Gold 2004, 301 sexually active young women aged 15–20 at an urban Pittsburgh adolescent clinic — note the record's age range extends beyond adolescence, printed on the card) found advance provision of emergency contraception (EC) was not associated with more unprotected intercourse or less condom or hormonal contraception use over 6 months; at 1 month the advance group reported nearly twice as much EC use (15% vs 8%; P=0.05) and began EC significantly sooner after unprotected intercourse (11.4 vs 21.8 hours; P=0.005), though EC use no longer differed at 6 months (8% vs 6%; P=0.54). Condom use in the past month at 6 months was actually higher in the advance group (77% vs 62%; P=0.02), while use at last intercourse did not differ. The reassurance claim (no risk compensation) rests on self-reported behaviour in one trial from 1997–2002, before modern EC formulations and access routes: POSSIBLE. This is an access/behaviour question, distinct from #244 (EC drug efficacy).

cards.headline: Gold 2004: advance EC did not increase unprotected sex or reduce condom/hormonal contraception; EC was used earlier (11.4 vs 21.8 hours) and more at 1 month
cards.summary: Gold 2004: advance EC did not increase unprotected sex or reduce condom/hormonal contraception; EC was used earlier (11.4 vs 21.8 hours) and more at 1 month
cards.type: Randomised trial (urban hospital-based adolescent clinic, Pittsburgh; monthly telephone follow-up for 6 months)
cards.people: 301 predominantly minority, low-income, sexually active young women aged 15–20 years not using long-acting contraception, enrolled June 1997 to June 2002, randomised to receive emergency contraception in advance or instruction on how to obtain it; behaviours were self-reported in monthly 10-minute telephone interviews. (The topic frames the population as adolescents; the record's enrolled range is 15–20 years.)
cards.result: At both 1- and 6-month interviews there were no differences between advance-EC and control groups in reported unprotected intercourse within the past month or at last intercourse. At 6 months, more advance-EC participants reported condom use in the past month than controls (77% vs 62%, P=0.02), but not at last intercourse (83% vs 78%, P=0.34). Hormonal contraception use did not differ in the past month (44% vs 53%, P=0.19) or at last intercourse (48% vs 58%, P=0.20). At the first follow-up, the advance group reported nearly twice as much EC use as controls (15% vs 8%, P=0.05), but not at the final follow-up (8% vs 6%, P=0.54). Advance-group participants began EC significantly sooner (11.4 hours vs 21.8 hours, P=0.005).
cards.watchOut: All outcomes are self-reported behaviour with no pregnancy or STI endpoints measured, in a single clinic population two decades ago; 'no increase in reported unprotected intercourse' is weaker evidence than a measured pregnancy outcome would be, and the EC-use advantage had washed out by 6 months.
cards.source: Gold MA et al. The effects of advance provision of emergency contraception on adolescent women's sexual and contraceptive behaviors. J Pediatr Adolesc Gynecol. 2004. PMID: 15050984. shelves.title: First- vs second-generation antipsychotics in early-onset schizophrenia (TEOSS)
shelves.question: In adolescents with early-onset schizophrenia/schizoaffective disorder, do risperidone or olanzapine vs molindone improve response?
shelves.mesh: Antipsychotic Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Schizophrenia/drug therapy · Molindone/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Risperidone · Olanzapine · Humans · Adolescent · Child · Double-Blind Method
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): One double-blind multisite randomised trial (TEOSS, Sikich 2008, 119 youth randomised, 116 treated) found no significant efficacy difference over 8 weeks between the first-generation agent molindone and the second-generation agents risperidone and olanzapine in early-onset schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder: response rates were 50% (molindone), 46% (risperidone) and 34% (olanzapine), with no significant difference in the magnitude of symptom reduction. The harms differed by drug and are part of the claim: olanzapine and risperidone produced significantly greater weight gain; olanzapine showed the greatest weight-gain risk plus significant increases in fasting cholesterol, LDL, insulin and liver transaminases; molindone produced more self-reported akathisia. A single trial with response-rate intervals too wide to prove equivalence caps at POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the correct claim is 'no demonstrated superiority', not 'proven equal'.

cards.headline: TEOSS 2008: response rates did not differ significantly between molindone (50%), risperidone (46%) and olanzapine (34%); second-generation agents caused more weight gain and metabolic harm
cards.summary: TEOSS 2008: response rates did not differ significantly between molindone (50%), risperidone (46%) and olanzapine (34%); second-generation agents caused more weight gain and metabolic harm
cards.people: 119 youth with early-onset schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder randomly assigned to olanzapine (2.5–20 mg/day), risperidone (0.5–6 mg/day), or molindone (10–140 mg/day plus 1 mg/day benztropine); 116 received at least one dose and were analysed. The record's MeSH places the population across Child and Adolescent categories; the abstract does not state a mean age.
cards.result: No significant differences were found among treatment groups in response rates — molindone 50%, olanzapine 34%, risperidone 46% (response defined as a CGI improvement score of 1 or 2 plus at least a 20% reduction in PANSS total score after 8 weeks) — or in the magnitude of symptom reduction. Olanzapine and risperidone were associated with significantly greater weight gain. Olanzapine showed the greatest risk of weight gain and significant increases in fasting cholesterol, low-density lipoprotein, insulin, and liver transaminase levels. Molindone led to more self-reports of akathisia. The authors conclude risperidone and olanzapine did not demonstrate superior efficacy over molindone, and that the weight and metabolic findings raise public-health concerns given widespread second-generation use in youth.
cards.watchOut: With roughly 40 patients per arm, the response-rate differences (34% to 50%) are compatible with chance and with clinically meaningful differences in either direction; the trial's contribution is the absence of demonstrated second-generation superiority plus a differentiated harm profile, not proof the drugs are interchangeable for an individual patient.

cards.summary: Synthesis: no efficacy case for defaulting to second-generation agents in early-onset schizophrenia — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)

cards.result: In the one head-to-head randomised test, the older drug matched the newer ones on response (50% vs 46% and 34%) while the newer ones — olanzapine above all — carried the heavier metabolic price. shelves.title: Text-message vaping-cessation programme for adolescents
shelves.question: In adolescent e-cigarette users, does a tailored text-message quit programme vs assessment-only control increase abstinence?
shelves.mesh: Text Messaging · Vaping/adverse effects,epidemiology,therapy · Smoking Cessation/methods,statistics & numerical data · Electronic Nicotine Delivery Systems · Adolescent · Humans · Double-Blind Method
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One double-blind randomised trial (Graham 2024, 1,503 US adolescents aged 13–17 who vaped and wanted to quit, recruited via social media) found self-reported 30-day point-prevalence abstinence at 7 months of 37.8% with the interactive text programme versus 28.0% with assessment-only control (relative risk 1.35 relative, 95% CI 1.17 to 1.57; P<0.001), with missing responses coded as vaping, a 70.8% follow-up rate, and no evidence that quitters switched to combustible tobacco. The topic file quoted abstinence of '~24% vs ~19%' for this shelf — those are the figures of the companion YOUNG-ADULT trial (Graham 2021, PMID 33999133: 24.1% vs 18.6%), not of the adolescent trial; the card prints the adolescent trial's own 37.8% vs 28.0%, and the young-adult trial is fenced in the synthesis as a different age group. One trial, self-reported abstinence without biochemical verification, in motivated volunteers: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Graham 2024 (adolescents): text programme raised 7-month abstinence to 37.8% vs 28.0% (relative risk 1.35 relative) in 1,503 teen vapers
cards.summary: Graham 2024 (adolescents): text programme raised 7-month abstinence to 37.8% vs 28.0% (relative risk 1.35 relative) in 1,503 teen vapers
cards.type: Parallel, two-group, double-blind, individually randomised clinical trial (US; social-media recruitment; follow-up at 1 and 7 months)
cards.people: 1,503 US residents aged 13 to 17 years (average age 16.4 years, SD 0.8; 50.6% female, 42.1% male, 7.4% nonbinary/other) who reported past-30-day e-cigarette use, wanted to quit within 30 days, and owned a mobile phone with an active text plan; 76.2% vaped within 30 minutes of waking. Intervention participants (759) received the automated interactive text programme plus monthly assessment texts; assessment-only controls (744) received only the retention/assessment texts. The 7-month follow-up rate was 70.8%.
cards.result: Self-reported 30-day point-prevalence abstinence from vaping at 7 months (intention-to-treat, missingness coded as vaping) was 37.8% (95% CI 34.4% to 41.3%) in the intervention group and 28.0% (24.9% to 31.3%) in the control group (relative risk 1.35 — a relative measure — 95% CI 1.17 to 1.57; P<0.001). No baseline variables moderated the treatment-outcome relationship. There was no evidence that adolescents who quit vaping transitioned to combustible tobacco products.
cards.watchOut: Abstinence is self-reported (no biochemical verification) in a sample of volunteers already motivated to quit, and the 'assessment-only' control still received monthly texts about vaping — an active minimal intervention that makes the absolute quit rates (28% even in controls) ungeneralisable to unselected school populations.
cards.source: Graham AL et al. A Vaping Cessation Text Message Program for Adolescent E-Cigarette Users: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2024. PMID: 39110436. shelves.title: Dating Matters: comprehensive teen dating-violence prevention
shelves.question: In middle-school students, does the multi-component Dating Matters programme vs standard health education reduce dating-violence perpetration and victimisation?
shelves.mesh: Intimate Partner Violence/prevention & control,statistics & numerical data · Adolescent Behavior/psychology · Health Education · Humans · Adolescent · Child · Female · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One longitudinal cluster-randomised trial (Niolon 2019, 46 middle schools in high-risk urban neighbourhoods in four US cities; analysis sample 2,349 students who had dated) found the multi-component Dating Matters model outperformed the standard-of-care curriculum (Safe Dates, itself an evidence-based programme) on three of four self-reported outcomes, averaged across sixth-to-eighth grade: teen dating-violence perpetration 8.43% lower, victimisation 9.78% lower, and use of negative conflict-resolution strategies 5.52% lower (all relative differences as the record reports them), with no significant effect on positive relationship behaviours. Effects of this size on self-reported behaviour, from one cluster trial whose schools had 71% retention (lost schools were replaced and independently re-randomised — a design awkwardness printed on the card), support POSSIBLE. The comparator was an active evidence-based curriculum, not nothing, which strengthens the comparative claim while shrinking its expected size. Note the programme's own 'prevention' framing is retained from the record; no diabetes-onset claim is involved.

cards.headline: Dating Matters RCT 2019: perpetration 8.43% lower and victimisation 9.78% lower than the Safe Dates standard curriculum across middle school (self-reported)
cards.summary: Dating Matters RCT 2019: perpetration 8.43% lower and victimisation 9.78% lower than the Safe Dates standard curriculum across middle school (self-reported)
cards.type: Longitudinal cluster-randomised controlled trial (46 middle schools, four US cities)
cards.people: 46 middle schools in high-risk urban neighbourhoods in four US cities were randomised to Dating Matters (classroom programmes for grades 6–8, parent training, educator training, a youth communications programme, and local health-department capacity activities) or standard of care (the evidence-based Safe Dates curriculum in eighth grade). Students were surveyed in fall and spring of grades 6–8 (2012–2016); the analysis sample comprised 2,349 students from schools implementing for over 2 years who started sixth grade in fall 2012 or 2013 and had dated (mean age 12 years; 49% female; 55% Black non-Hispanic, 28% Hispanic, 17% other). School retention was 71%; schools lost to follow-up were replaced with new schools, independently randomised.
cards.result: Latent panel models showed significant programme effects for three of four outcomes: Dating Matters students reported 8.43% lower teen dating-violence perpetration, 9.78% lower teen dating-violence victimisation, and 5.52% lower use of negative conflict-resolution strategies, on average across time points and cohorts, than standard-of-care students. There were no significant effects on positive relationship behaviours. The percentages are the record's own relative-effect figures; the abstract does not print the underlying absolute perpetration or victimisation rates, and none are supplied here.
cards.watchOut: All outcomes are adolescent self-reports of behaviour and attitudes collected by survey — the measurement most vulnerable to a programme teaching students what the desirable answers are. The mid-trial replacement of lost schools, and an analysis restricted to schools implementing for over 2 years and students who had dated, further soften the comparison; the honest claim is 'better than an already evidence-based curriculum on reported behaviour', at modest size.
cards.source: Niolon PH et al. An RCT of Dating Matters: Effects on Teen Dating Violence and Relationship Behaviors. Am J Prev Med. 2019. PMID: 31128957. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01672541, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: CBT for insomnia (internet and group formats) in adolescents
shelves.question: In adolescents with insomnia, does CBT-I (internet or group) vs waiting list improve sleep?
shelves.mesh: Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders/diagnosis,psychology,therapy · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy/methods · Internet · Psychotherapy, Group · Adolescent · Humans · Female · Male · Netherlands
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised trial (de Bruin 2015, 116 adolescents meeting DSM-IV insomnia criteria, mean age 15.6 years, in the Netherlands) found both guided internet CBT-I and group CBT-I (six weekly sessions each) significantly improved sleep efficiency, sleep onset latency, wake after sleep onset and total sleep time versus waiting list at post-treatment, on both actigraphy and sleep logs, with improvements maintained at 2-month follow-up, medium-to-large effect sizes, and significantly decreased insomnia complaints and chronic sleep-reduction symptoms. The record's abstract reports significance and effect-size ranges without printing the group means, and none are invented here. A waiting-list comparator (which controls for time but not attention or expectation), one trial, and a 2-month horizon cap the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: de Bruin 2015: internet and group CBT-I both significantly improved actigraphic and logged sleep versus waiting list, maintained at 2 months
cards.summary: de Bruin 2015: internet and group CBT-I both significantly improved actigraphic and logged sleep versus waiting list, maintained at 2 months
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (three arms; Amsterdam, the Netherlands)
cards.people: 116 adolescents (mean age 15.6 years, SD 1.6; 25% male) meeting DSM-IV criteria for insomnia, randomised to guided internet therapy, group therapy, or waiting list. CBT-I comprised six weekly sessions (psychoeducation, sleep hygiene, restriction of time in bed, stimulus control, cognitive therapy, relaxation); group therapy ran in groups of 6–8 with two trained sleep therapists, and internet therapy was guided self-help with written therapist feedback. Sleep was measured with actigraphy and sleep logs for 7 days at baseline, post-test and 2-month follow-up.
cards.result: Adolescents in both internet and group CBT-I, compared with waiting list, improved significantly on sleep efficiency, sleep onset latency, wake after sleep onset, and total sleep time at post-test, and improvements were maintained at follow-up; most improvements appeared in both objective (actigraphy) and subjective (log) measures. Insomnia complaints and symptoms of chronic sleep reduction also decreased significantly in both treatment conditions. Effect sizes for improvements ranged from medium to large, and a greater proportion of treated participants showed high end-state functioning and clinically significant improvement. There were small differences between internet and group therapy, with comparable endpoints. The abstract does not print the numerical group means for the sleep outcomes, and this card reports the findings as the record states them.
cards.watchOut: A waiting-list control cannot separate CBT-I's specific effect from attention, structure and expectation — the standard inflation in psychotherapy trials — and 2 months is the whole of the follow-up. The absence of printed means in the record means anyone quoting exact minutes of improvement is quoting beyond this abstract.
cards.source: de Bruin EJ et al. Efficacy of Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia in Adolescents: A Randomized Controlled Trial with Internet Therapy, Group Therapy and A Waiting List Condition. Sleep. 2015. PMID: 26158889. Registry ID: ISRCTN33922163, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Interpersonal Psychotherapy–Adolescent Skills Training (IPT-AST) for depressive symptoms in school adolescents
shelves.question: In school adolescents with subthreshold depressive symptoms, does IPT-AST vs group counselling prevent or reduce depressive symptoms?
shelves.mesh: Depression/prevention & control · Psychotherapy/methods · Psychotherapy, Group · Counseling · Adolescent · Humans · Female · Male
shelves.balance: SPLIT — POSSIBLE for symptom reduction / LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for onset of depression diagnoses: One randomised trial (Young 2016, 186 adolescents with elevated depressive symptoms in schools) found IPT-AST delivered by research staff produced significantly greater improvements in self-reported depressive symptoms and evaluator-rated overall functioning than group counselling delivered by school counsellors, from baseline to 6-month follow-up — but NO significant difference between the conditions in onset of depression diagnoses, the outcome the word 'prevention' actually refers to. The balance therefore splits: a modest symptom benefit over an active, session-matched comparator (POSSIBLE, one trial, and confounded by deliverer — research staff versus school counsellors — as the card notes), and no demonstrated prevention of depressive disorder (the treatment made no difference on diagnoses, in a trial with limited power for that outcome). This is a subthreshold-symptom programme, distinct from depression treatment (#1145).

cards.headline: Young 2016: IPT-AST improved depressive symptoms and functioning more than group counselling, but did not differ on onset of depression diagnoses
cards.summary: Young 2016: IPT-AST improved depressive symptoms and functioning more than group counselling, but did not differ on onset of depression diagnoses
cards.type: Randomised trial (indicated prevention design; school-based; 6-month follow-up)
cards.people: 186 adolescents with elevated depression symptoms, randomised to receive IPT-AST delivered by research staff or group counselling (GC) delivered by school counsellors; the two programmes were matched on frequency and duration of sessions. Outcomes were rates of change in depressive symptoms and overall functioning (hierarchical linear modelling) and rates of depression diagnoses (Cox regression) from baseline to the 6-month follow-up. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Adolescents in IPT-AST showed significantly greater improvements in self-reported depressive symptoms and evaluator-rated overall functioning than GC adolescents from baseline to the 6-month follow-up. However, there were no significant differences between the two conditions in onset of depression diagnoses. Both intervention conditions demonstrated significant improvements in symptoms and functioning. The authors describe IPT-AST's benefits over school-counsellor groups as modest, note the clinical utility is at least short-term, and call for longer follow-up, particularly on preventing depression onset. The abstract does not print effect sizes for the symptom differences, and none are supplied here.
cards.watchOut: Two confounds ride on the comparison: IPT-AST was delivered by research staff and GC by school counsellors, so programme and deliverer effects cannot be separated; and the headline outcome that justifies calling this 'prevention' — new depression diagnoses — was null. Any summary saying IPT-AST 'prevents depression' overclaims this record.

cards.headline: Synthesis: fewer symptoms than ordinary school groups, no proven prevention of disorder — SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: fewer symptoms than ordinary school groups, no proven prevention of disorder — SPLIT
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: Young 2016 (186 adolescents with elevated depressive symptoms).
cards.result: IPT-AST is a reasonable, modestly superior alternative to usual school group counselling for adolescents already showing symptoms (symptom and functioning gains to 6 months), and it is not — on this record — a demonstrated way to stop depression from starting (diagnoses: no difference). shelves.title: Telephone reminder/recall to raise adolescent immunisation
shelves.question: In adolescents due immunisations or preventive visits, does telephone reminder/recall vs usual care increase uptake?
shelves.mesh: Reminder Systems/statistics & numerical data · Telephone · Immunization/statistics & numerical data · Preventive Health Services/statistics & numerical data · Adolescent · Humans · Female · Male
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): One randomised trial (Szilagyi 2006, 3,006 adolescents aged 11–14 in four urban US primary care practices, 18 months) found an intensive audiotaped telephone reminder/recall system largely ineffective: at study end the intervention group had slightly higher completed hepatitis B coverage (62% vs 57.8%; P=.02), well-child visit rates were identical (53% vs 54%), and impact on other vaccinations was minimal. The authors' own analysis locates the failure: contact information — 71% of study subjects with a single stable telephone number had a well-child visit, versus 25% of those with multiple or changed numbers. A process intervention whose single trial shows one significant vaccine among several, null visits, and a mechanism defeated by phone-number churn earns MAYBE (weak evidence) that telephone reminder/recall, as implemented here, raises adolescent uptake. Modern text/electronic reminder systems are a different intervention and are not covered by this record.

cards.headline: Szilagyi 2006: intensive telephone reminder/recall barely moved adolescent immunisation (hepatitis B 62% vs 57.8%) and did not move preventive visits (53% vs 54%)
cards.summary: Szilagyi 2006: intensive telephone reminder/recall barely moved adolescent immunisation (hepatitis B 62% vs 57.8%) and did not move preventive visits (53% vs 54%)
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial (four urban primary care practices; 18 months)
cards.people: Adolescents aged 11 to 14 years in four urban primary care practices, randomised within practices to the reminder/recall intervention (1,496) or control (1,510); the intervention group received audiotaped telephone reminders about a scheduled or needed immunisation or well-child visit, with households called weekly if there was no response and telephone numbers updated weekly; controls received standard care. Baseline demographics and immunisation and visit rates were similar between groups.
cards.result: The intervention was largely ineffective in improving immunisation or well-child visit rates. At the end of the study, the intervention group had slightly higher hepatitis B coverage (3 vaccinations) (62% vs 57.8%; P=.02), well-child visits were the same (53% and 54%), and impact on other vaccinations was minimal. The effect was equivalent across demographic subgroups. The major limiting factor was inaccurate telephone numbers: 71% of study subjects with a single telephone number throughout the study had a well-child visit versus 25% of study subjects with multiple or changed telephone numbers and 54% of controls (P<.001). The authors conclude the intensive system was only minimally successful, largely owing to changed or inaccurate telephone numbers.
cards.watchOut: One significant result (hepatitis B series completion) among multiple vaccine and visit outcomes invites a multiple-comparisons reading; and the trial is from 2006 landline/mobile-transition practice — it convicts this telephone implementation in this population, not reminder systems in general.
cards.source: Szilagyi PG et al. Effect of telephone reminder/recall on adolescent immunization and preventive visits: results from a randomized clinical trial. Arch Pediatr Adolesc Med. 2006. PMID: 16461871. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.summary: Synthesis: reminder/recall by telephone, as tested, mostly failed on contact data — MAYBE (weak evidence)

shelves.title: Early nasal CPAP vs intubation at birth in very preterm infants
shelves.question: In very preterm infants, does starting nasal CPAP vs intubation/ventilation in the delivery room reduce death or bronchopulmonary dysplasia?
shelves.mesh: Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia/epidemiology,prevention & control · Continuous Positive Airway Pressure/adverse effects · Female · Gestational Age · Humans · Infant Mortality · Infant, Newborn · Infant, Premature · Intubation, Intratracheal · Male
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, death in the primary composite): Two large randomised trials agree that early CPAP does not significantly reduce death or bronchopulmonary dysplasia. COIN (Morley 2008, 610 infants born at 25–28 weeks) found death or BPD at 36 weeks in 33.9% on CPAP versus 38.9% with intubation (odds ratio 0.80 relative, 95% CI 0.58 to 1.12; P=0.19). SUPPORT (Finer 2010, 1,316 infants born at 24–27 weeks) found death or BPD in 47.8% with CPAP versus 51.0% with intubation/surfactant (relative risk 0.95 relative, 0.85 to 1.05). CPAP did reduce intubation (46% intubated in the first 5 days in COIN), halved surfactant use, and reduced ventilation days and postnatal steroid use — real process gains — at a cost of more pneumothorax in COIN (9% vs 3%; P<0.001). The composite-outcome claim is a LIKELY null; the strategy's value is avoiding intubation, not preventing death or BPD.

cards.headline: COIN 2008: early CPAP did not significantly reduce death or BPD at 36 weeks (33.9% vs 38.9%), but halved surfactant use — with more pneumothorax (9% vs 3%)
cards.summary: COIN 2008: early CPAP did not significantly reduce death or BPD at 36 weeks (33.9% vs 38.9%), but halved surfactant use — with more pneumothorax (9% vs 3%)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (multicentre, Australia/New Zealand and international)
cards.people: 610 infants born at 25–28 weeks' gestation, assigned at 5 minutes after birth to nasal CPAP (307) or intubation and ventilation (303). The abstract does not state mean birth weight or sex mix.
cards.result: At 36 weeks' gestational age, 33.9% of CPAP infants had died or had bronchopulmonary dysplasia versus 38.9% with intubation (odds ratio favouring CPAP 0.80 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.58 to 1.12; P=0.19). At 28 days, death or need for oxygen therapy was lower with CPAP (odds ratio 0.63 relative, 0.46 to 0.88; P=0.006), with little difference in overall mortality. In the CPAP group 46% were intubated during the first 5 days and surfactant use was halved; pneumothorax occurred in 9% versus 3% (P<0.001), and the CPAP group had fewer days of ventilation.
cards.watchOut: The 28-day secondary outcome favours CPAP while the 36-week primary composite does not reach significance — the shelf's stamp follows the primary outcome, and the pneumothorax excess is part of the bargain, not a footnote.
cards.source: Morley CJ et al. Nasal CPAP or intubation at birth for very preterm infants. N Engl J Med. 2008. PMID: 18272893. Registry ID: Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry 12606000258550, stated in the record's abstract (no databank registry field in the record). cards.headline: SUPPORT 2010 (CPAP arm): death or BPD 47.8% with early CPAP vs 51.0% with intubation/surfactant (relative risk 0.95) — less intubation, fewer ventilation days
cards.summary: SUPPORT 2010 (CPAP arm): death or BPD 47.8% with early CPAP vs 51.0% with intubation/surfactant (relative risk 0.95) — less intubation, fewer ventilation days
cards.type: Randomised, multicentre trial with a 2-by-2 factorial design (the CPAP comparison; the oxygen-target comparison is Shelf #1381)
cards.people: 1,316 infants born between 24 weeks 0 days and 27 weeks 6 days of gestation, assigned to intubation and surfactant within 1 hour of birth or to CPAP initiated in the delivery room with a protocol-driven limited-ventilation strategy; infants were simultaneously randomised to one of two oxygen-saturation targets. The abstract does not state sex mix for this comparison.
cards.result: Rates of death or bronchopulmonary dysplasia (oxygen requirement at 36 weeks) did not differ significantly: 47.8% with CPAP versus 51.0% with surfactant (relative risk with CPAP 0.95 relative, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.05, adjusted for gestational age, centre and familial clustering). With BPD defined as any supplemental oxygen at 36 weeks, rates were 48.7% versus 54.1% (relative risk 0.91 relative, 0.83 to 1.01). CPAP infants less frequently required intubation or postnatal corticosteroids (P<0.001), required fewer days of mechanical ventilation (P=0.03), and were more likely to be alive and free of mechanical ventilation by day 7 (P=0.01). Other adverse neonatal outcomes did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: A factorial trial: these infants are the same population as the oxygen-target report carded on Shelf #1381 (same registry number) — the two shelves answer different randomised questions and must not be pooled as separate populations.
cards.source: Finer NN et al. Early CPAP versus surfactant in extremely preterm infants. N Engl J Med. 2010. PMID: 20472939. shelves.title: Oxygen-saturation target range in extremely preterm infants (SUPPORT)
shelves.question: In extremely preterm infants, does a lower SpO2 target (85–89%) vs higher target (91–95%) affect death, retinopathy of prematurity, or BPD?
shelves.mesh: Continuous Positive Airway Pressure · Female · Hospital Mortality · Humans · Infant Mortality · Infant, Newborn · Infant, Premature/blood · Intubation, Intratracheal · Male · Oximetry · Oxygen/administration & dosage,blood
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for the composite · LIKELY for the trade-off — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality): In SUPPORT's oximetry comparison (Carlo 2010, 1,316 infants born at 24–27 weeks), the composite of severe retinopathy of prematurity or death before discharge did not differ significantly between the lower (85–89%) and higher (91–95%) saturation targets (28.3% vs 32.1%; relative risk 0.90 relative, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.06; P=0.21) — but the components moved in opposite directions: death before discharge was HIGHER with the lower target (19.9% vs 16.2%; relative risk 1.27 relative, 1.01 to 1.60; P=0.04) while severe retinopathy among survivors was substantially LOWER (8.6% vs 17.9%; relative risk 0.52 relative, 0.37 to 0.73; P<0.001). A composite that hides a mortality increase behind a retinopathy decrease must not be stamped as a simple null: the trade-off itself is the finding. The wider BOOST/NeOProM family is named in the topic file as supporting this direction but was not pinned trial-by-trial at build, so this shelf rests on SUPPORT alone and says so.

cards.headline: SUPPORT oximetry 2010: lower saturation target — composite null (28.3% vs 32.1%), but death before discharge higher (19.9% vs 16.2%) and severe retinopathy lower (8.6% vs 17.9%)
cards.summary: SUPPORT oximetry 2010: lower saturation target — composite null (28.3% vs 32.1%), but death before discharge higher (19.9% vs 16.2%) and severe retinopathy lower (8.6% vs 17.9%)
cards.type: Randomised trial with a 2-by-2 factorial design (the oxygen-target comparison; the CPAP comparison is Shelf #1380)
cards.people: 1,316 infants born between 24 weeks 0 days and 27 weeks 6 days of gestation, randomised to an oxygen-saturation target of 85–89% or 91–95%; all infants were also randomised to CPAP or intubation/surfactant. The abstract does not state the sex mix for this comparison.
cards.result: Rates of severe retinopathy of prematurity or death did not differ significantly (28.3% lower target vs 32.1% higher target; relative risk 0.90 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.76 to 1.06; P=0.21). Death before discharge occurred more frequently with the lower target (19.9% vs 16.2%; relative risk 1.27 relative, 1.01 to 1.60; P=0.04), whereas severe retinopathy among survivors occurred less often (8.6% vs 17.9%; relative risk 0.52 relative, 0.37 to 0.73; P<0.001). There were no significant differences in other adverse events. The authors conclude that the increase in mortality is a major concern.
cards.watchOut: The mortality difference is a component of a null composite, tested among many outcomes — but it is mortality, in the direction opposite to the retinopathy gain, and later trials in this family pointed the same way; it cannot be waved away as a chance subgroup.
cards.source: Carlo WA et al. Target ranges of oxygen saturation in extremely preterm infants. N Engl J Med. 2010. PMID: 20472937. cards.summary: Synthesis: the lower target trades lives for eyes — a split verdict, not a null

shelves.title: Prophylactic indomethacin in extremely-low-birth-weight infants (TIPP)
shelves.question: In extremely-low-birth-weight infants, does prophylactic indomethacin vs placebo improve survival without neurodevelopmental impairment, despite reducing severe intracranial haemorrhage?
shelves.mesh: Blindness/prevention & control · Cerebral Palsy/prevention & control · Cognition Disorders/prevention & control · Ductus Arteriosus, Patent/prevention & control · Humans · Indomethacin/therapeutic use · Infant, Newborn · Infant, Very Low Birth Weight · Intracranial Hemorrhages/prevention & control
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, death/impairment composite): The single large trial (TIPP, Schmidt 2001, 1,202 infants with birth weights 500–999 g) found prophylactic indomethacin did NOT improve the primary long-term outcome: death or survival with impairment at a corrected age of 18 months occurred in 47% on indomethacin versus 46% on placebo (odds ratio 1.1 relative, 95% CI 0.8 to 1.4; P=0.61). The short-term pharmacology worked exactly as expected — patent ductus arteriosus fell from 50% to 24% (odds ratio 0.3 relative; P<0.001) and severe periventricular/intraventricular haemorrhage from 13% to 9% (odds ratio 0.6 relative; P=0.02) — and none of it converted into better survival without impairment. A 1,200-infant blinded trial whose long-term confidence interval centres on no effect carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for the outcome that matters, and this shelf is the library's cleanest neonatal example of a surrogate win that is not a patient win.

cards.headline: TIPP 2001: indomethacin prophylaxis halved PDA (24% vs 50%) and cut severe IVH (9% vs 13%) but did not improve survival without impairment at 18 months (47% vs 46%)
cards.summary: TIPP 2001: indomethacin prophylaxis halved PDA (24% vs 50%) and cut severe IVH (9% vs 13%) but did not improve survival without impairment at 18 months (47% vs 46%)
cards.people: 1,202 infants with birth weights of 500 to 999 g (extremely low birth weight), randomly assigned soon after birth to indomethacin 0.1 mg/kg or placebo intravenously once daily for three days; primary-outcome data were available for 574 infants assigned to indomethacin and 569 assigned to placebo. The abstract does not state sex mix.
cards.result: Of infants with primary-outcome data, 271 of 574 (47%) assigned to indomethacin died or survived with impairments (cerebral palsy, cognitive delay, deafness or blindness at a corrected age of 18 months), versus 261 of 569 (46%) on placebo (odds ratio 1.1 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.8 to 1.4; P=0.61). Indomethacin reduced patent ductus arteriosus (24% vs 50%; odds ratio 0.3 relative; P<0.001) and severe periventricular/intraventricular haemorrhage (9% vs 13%; odds ratio 0.6 relative; P=0.02). No other short- or long-term outcomes (including hydrocephalus, seizure disorder, microcephaly, chronic lung disease, necrotising enterocolitis, retinopathy) were altered.
cards.watchOut: The trial's own conclusion is the watch-out: reducing ultrasound-detected haemorrhage and ductus closure are intermediate wins that did not translate into children surviving unimpaired — quoting the IVH figure without the 18-month composite misstates this trial.
cards.source: Schmidt B et al. Long-term effects of indomethacin prophylaxis in extremely-low-birth-weight infants. N Engl J Med. 2001. PMID: 11430325. shelves.title: Systemic hydrocortisone to prevent BPD in preterm infants (PREMILOC vs SToP-BPD)
shelves.question: In extremely/very preterm ventilated infants, does low-dose hydrocortisone vs placebo improve survival without BPD?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Inflammatory Agents/administration & dosage · Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia/prevention & control · Double-Blind Method · Female · France · Humans · Hydrocortisone/administration & dosage · Infant, Extremely Premature · Infant, Newborn · Male · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE (early start) · POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) (later start) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, survival in the composite): The two trials differ mainly in TIMING, and their results differ with it. PREMILOC (Baud 2016, 523 infants born before 28 weeks, hydrocortisone started within 24 hours of birth for 10 days) found survival without BPD at 36 weeks in 60% on hydrocortisone versus 51% on placebo (adjusted odds ratio 1.48 relative, 95% CI 1.02 to 2.16; P=0.04; number needed to treat 12, with a very wide interval of 6 to 200) — with a sepsis signal in the 24–25-week subgroup (40% vs 23%). SToP-BPD (Onland 2019, 372 ventilator-dependent infants, hydrocortisone started at 7–14 days for a 22-day course) found death or BPD in 70.7% versus 73.7% (adjusted risk difference −3.6%, −12.7% to 5.4%; P=0.54) — no composite benefit, though death at 36 weeks alone was lower (15.5% vs 23.7%; P=0.048) among 29 secondary outcomes, and hyperglycaemia requiring insulin was more common (18.2% vs 7.9%). Discordant trials on different schedules get a split stamp keyed to timing, not an average.

cards.headline: PREMILOC 2016: hydrocortisone from the first day of life improved survival without BPD (60% vs 51%; adjusted OR 1.48) — with a sepsis signal at 24–25 weeks
cards.summary: PREMILOC 2016: hydrocortisone from the first day of life improved survival without BPD (60% vs 51%; adjusted OR 1.48) — with a sepsis signal at 24–25 weeks
cards.type: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre randomised trial (21 French NICUs; sequential analytical design)
cards.people: 523 extremely preterm infants born at less than 28 weeks of gestation, enrolled by 24 hours after birth and randomly assigned to intravenous low-dose hydrocortisone (256; 1 mg/kg/day divided twice daily for 7 days, then 0.5 mg/kg/day for 3 days) or placebo (267); 255 and 266 respectively were analysed after one consent withdrawal in each group.
cards.result: Survival without bronchopulmonary dysplasia at 36 weeks of postmenstrual age occurred in 153 of 255 infants (60%) on hydrocortisone versus 136 of 266 (51%) on placebo (odds ratio adjusted for gestational-age group and interim analyses 1.48 — a relative measure — 95% CI 1.02 to 2.16; P=0.04); the number needed to treat for one additional BPD-free survival was 12 (95% CI 6 to 200). Overall sepsis rates did not differ significantly, but in the subgroup born at 24–25 weeks sepsis was higher with hydrocortisone (30 of 83 [40%] vs 21 of 90 [23%]; sub-hazard ratio 1.87 relative, 1.09 to 3.21; P=0.02). Gastrointestinal perforation and other adverse events did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: A just-significant primary result (lower confidence bound 1.02) from a sequential design stopped on its own stopping rule, with the NNT interval running from 6 to 200 — a real but fragile benefit, and the youngest infants paid a sepsis price.
cards.source: Baud O et al. cards.headline: SToP-BPD 2019: hydrocortisone started at 7–14 days did not improve death or BPD (70.7% vs 73.7%; P=0.54)
cards.summary: SToP-BPD 2019: hydrocortisone started at 7–14 days did not improve death or BPD (70.7% vs 73.7%; P=0.54)
cards.type: Double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised trial (19 NICUs, Netherlands and Belgium)
cards.people: 372 preterm infants with a gestational age under 30 weeks and/or birth weight under 1,250 g who were ventilator-dependent between 7 and 14 days of life (mean gestational age 26 weeks; 55% male), randomised to a 22-day course of systemic hydrocortisone (cumulative dose 72.5 mg/kg; 182) or placebo (190); 371 completed the trial.
cards.result: Death or BPD at 36 weeks of postmenstrual age occurred in 128 of 181 infants (70.7%) on hydrocortisone versus 140 of 190 (73.7%) on placebo (adjusted risk difference −3.6%, 95% CI −12.7% to 5.4%; adjusted odds ratio 0.87 relative, 0.54 to 1.38; P=0.54). Of 29 secondary outcomes, death at 36 weeks was lower with hydrocortisone (15.5% vs 23.7%; risk difference −8.2%, −16.2% to −0.1%; P=0.048) while BPD among survivors was numerically higher (55.2% vs 50.0%; P=0.31). Hyperglycaemia requiring insulin was more frequent with hydrocortisone (18.2% vs 7.9%). The authors conclude these findings do not support hydrocortisone for this indication.
cards.watchOut: The lower death rate is one significant result among 29 secondary outcomes in a null trial — exactly the pattern multiplicity produces — and it is offset on the same page by numerically more BPD; it is reported here because mortality is Tier C, not because it rescues the trial.

shelves.title: Erythropoietin for neuroprotection in extremely preterm infants (PENUT)
shelves.question: In extremely preterm infants, does high-dose erythropoietin vs placebo reduce death or severe neurodevelopmental impairment?
shelves.mesh: Brain/diagnostic imaging · Child, Preschool · Double-Blind Method · Erythropoietin/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Infant · Infant, Extremely Premature · Infant, Newborn · Male
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, death in the primary composite): The single large trial (PENUT, Juul 2020, 941 infants born at 24–27 weeks) found high-dose erythropoietin, started within 24 hours of birth and continued through 32 weeks of postmenstrual age, did not reduce death or severe neurodevelopmental impairment at 2 years: 26% versus 26% (relative risk 1.03 relative, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.32; P=0.80). There were no significant differences in retinopathy, intracranial haemorrhage, sepsis, necrotising enterocolitis, BPD, death, or serious adverse events. A near-1,000-infant double-blind trial with a point estimate of 1.03 is a definitive test of the regimen as given, and the preclinical/phase-2 promise behind it does not survive it: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: PENUT 2020: high-dose erythropoietin did not reduce death or severe neurodevelopmental impairment at 2 years (26% vs 26%; relative risk 1.03)
cards.summary: PENUT 2020: high-dose erythropoietin did not reduce death or severe neurodevelopmental impairment at 2 years (26% vs 26%; relative risk 1.03)
cards.people: 941 infants born at 24 weeks 0 days to 27 weeks 6 days of gestation, assigned within 24 hours of birth to erythropoietin (1,000 U/kg intravenously every 48 hours for six doses, then 400 U/kg subcutaneously three times weekly through 32 completed weeks of postmenstrual age) or placebo (saline, then sham injections); 741 infants (376 erythropoietin, 365 placebo) were included in the per-protocol efficacy analysis. The abstract does not state sex mix.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in death or severe neurodevelopmental impairment at 22 to 26 months of postmenstrual age: 97 children (26%) on erythropoietin versus 94 (26%) on placebo (relative risk 1.03 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.81 to 1.32; P=0.80). Severe impairment was defined as severe cerebral palsy or a Bayley-III composite motor or cognitive score below 70. There were no significant differences in retinopathy of prematurity, intracranial haemorrhage, sepsis, necrotising enterocolitis, bronchopulmonary dysplasia, death, or serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: The headline analysis is per-protocol (741 of 941 randomised); the abstract's framing is nonetheless unambiguous and no outcome layer favours erythropoietin. This null is about this high-dose regimen started at birth — it does not test erythropoietin for anaemia of prematurity, a different question.
cards.source: Juul SE et al. A Randomized Trial of Erythropoietin for Neuroprotection in Preterm Infants. N Engl J Med. 2020. PMID: 31940698. shelves.title: Sustained lung inflation vs standard positive-pressure ventilation at preterm birth (SAIL)
shelves.question: In extremely preterm infants needing resuscitation at birth, does sustained inflation vs intermittent positive-pressure ventilation reduce bronchopulmonary dysplasia or death?
shelves.mesh: Asphyxia Neonatorum/physiopathology,therapy · Bradycardia/therapy · Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia/etiology · Female · Functional Residual Capacity · Gestational Age · Heart Rate · Hospital Mortality · Humans · Infant · Infant Mortality · Infant, Extremely Premature
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference, with an early-harm signal) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, death in the primary composite plus an early-mortality signal): The single trial (SAIL, Kirpalani 2019) was stopped early after enrolling 426 of a planned 600 infants, following a prespecified review of adverse outcomes. Sustained inflation did not reduce BPD or death at 36 weeks (63.7% vs 59.2%; adjusted risk difference +4.7%, 95% CI −3.8% to 13.1%; P=0.29) — and death within the first 48 hours was significantly HIGHER with sustained inflation (7.4% vs 1.4%; adjusted risk difference +5.6%, 2.1% to 9.1%; P=0.002), with blinded adjudication judging most of the excess early deaths possibly attributable to the resuscitation. Early stopping truncates the evidence, capping the null at POSSIBLE; the harm signal is part of the stamp, not an aside.

cards.headline: SAIL 2019: sustained inflation did not reduce BPD or death (63.7% vs 59.2%) and early deaths were higher (7.4% vs 1.4% within 48 hours); trial stopped early
cards.summary: SAIL 2019: sustained inflation did not reduce BPD or death (63.7% vs 59.2%) and early deaths were higher (7.4% vs 1.4% within 48 hours); trial stopped early
cards.type: Unmasked, randomised clinical trial (18 NICUs, 9 countries) — stopped early after a prespecified adverse-outcome review
cards.people: 460 infants of 23 to 26 weeks' gestational age requiring resuscitation at birth for inadequate respiratory effort or bradycardia were randomised (mean gestational age 25.3 weeks; 50.2% female); 426 (215 sustained inflation, 211 standard ventilation) completed the trial, against a planned enrolment of 600. The intervention was up to two sustained inflations at a peak pressure of 25 cm H2O for 15 seconds via T-piece and mask, versus standard intermittent positive-pressure ventilation.
cards.result: The primary outcome, BPD or death at 36 weeks of postmenstrual age, occurred in 137 infants (63.7%) in the sustained-inflation group versus 125 (59.2%) with standard resuscitation (adjusted risk difference 4.7%, 95% CI −3.8% to 13.1%; P=0.29). Death at less than 48 hours occurred in 16 infants (7.4%) versus 3 (1.4%) (adjusted risk difference 5.6%, 2.1% to 9.1%; P=0.002); blinded adjudication found an imbalance in early deaths possibly attributable to resuscitation (11 of 16 vs 1 of 3). Of 27 secondary efficacy outcomes, 26 showed no significant difference. The authors conclude the findings do not support sustained inflations in extremely preterm infants, while noting early termination limits definitive conclusions.
cards.watchOut: An unmasked delivery-room intervention with a mortality imbalance in the first 48 hours: resuscitation trials cannot blind the team, so adjudication and the prespecified stopping review carry the weight here — both pointed against the intervention.
cards.source: Kirpalani H et al. shelves.title: Aggressive vs conservative phototherapy in extremely-low-birth-weight infants
shelves.question: In ELBW infants, does aggressive vs conservative phototherapy reduce neurodevelopmental impairment without increasing mortality?
shelves.mesh: Bayes Theorem · Bilirubin/blood · Birth Weight · Developmental Disabilities/epidemiology,etiology,prevention & control · Female · Humans · Hyperbilirubinemia, Neonatal/complications,therapy · Infant Mortality · Infant, Extremely Low Birth Weight/blood · Infant, Newborn · Male · Phototherapy/adverse effects,methods
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE (less impairment) · POSSIBLE (unresolved mortality concern in the smallest infants) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality signal): The single large trial (Morris 2008, 1,974 infants with birth weight ≤1,000 g) found aggressive phototherapy lowered peak bilirubin (7.0 vs 9.8 mg/dL) but did NOT significantly reduce the primary composite of death or neurodevelopmental impairment (52% vs 55%; relative risk 0.94 relative, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.02; P=0.15). The impairment component alone was significantly lower (26% vs 30%; relative risk 0.86 relative, 0.74 to 0.99), while death was numerically higher overall (24% vs 23%; relative risk 1.05 relative, 0.90 to 1.22) and, in the preplanned 501–750 g subgroup, 39% versus 34% (relative risk 1.13 relative, 0.96 to 1.34) — a subgroup signal whose interval includes no effect, set against 13% versus 14% in the 751–1,000 g subgroup. Neither half of this split may be quoted without the other.

cards.headline: Morris 2008: aggressive phototherapy reduced neurodevelopmental impairment (26% vs 30%) but not death-or-impairment (52% vs 55%), with a mortality signal at 501–750 g (39% vs 34%)
cards.summary: Morris 2008: aggressive phototherapy reduced neurodevelopmental impairment (26% vs 30%) but not death-or-impairment (52% vs 55%), with a mortality signal at 501–750 g (39% vs 34%)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (NICHD Neonatal Research Network, multicentre); outcome assessors unaware of treatment assignment
cards.people: 1,974 infants with extremely low birth weight (≤1,000 g), randomly assigned at 12 to 36 hours of age to aggressive or conservative phototherapy thresholds; the primary outcome (death or neurodevelopmental impairment) was determined for 91% of infants. The abstract does not state sex mix.
cards.result: Aggressive phototherapy significantly reduced mean peak serum bilirubin (7.0 vs 9.8 mg per deciliter; P<0.01) but not the primary outcome: death or neurodevelopmental impairment occurred in 52% versus 55% (relative risk 0.94 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.87 to 1.02; P=0.15). Neurodevelopmental impairment alone was reduced (26% vs 30%; relative risk 0.86 relative, 0.74 to 0.99). Death occurred in 24% versus 23% (relative risk 1.05 relative, 0.90 to 1.22). In preplanned subgroups, death rates were 13% versus 14% for birth weight 751–1,000 g and 39% versus 34% (relative risk 1.13 relative, 0.96 to 1.34) for 501–750 g. The authors conclude the impairment reduction may be offset by increased mortality among infants weighing 501 to 750 g.
cards.watchOut: The impairment benefit and the mortality worry come from decomposing a null composite — legitimate here because both components were prespecified and the subgroup was preplanned, but neither component alone is the trial's primary answer.
cards.source: Morris BH et al. Aggressive vs. conservative phototherapy for infants with extremely low birth weight. N Engl J Med. 2008. PMID: 18971491. shelves.title: Early inhaled budesonide to prevent BPD (NEuroSIS)
shelves.question: In extremely preterm infants, does early inhaled budesonide vs placebo prevent bronchopulmonary dysplasia?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia/prevention & control · Budesonide/administration & dosage · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Gestational Age · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage · Humans · Infant, Extremely Premature · Infant, Newborn
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE (BPD reduction) · POSSIBLE (unresolved mortality concern) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality signal): The single trial (NEuroSIS, Bassler 2015, 863 infants born at 23–27 weeks) found early inhaled budesonide reduced bronchopulmonary dysplasia (27.8% vs 38.0%; relative risk 0.74 relative, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.91; P=0.004), while the primary composite of death or BPD only bordered on significance (40.0% vs 46.3%; relative risk 0.86 relative, 0.75 to 1.00; P=0.05) because death was numerically HIGHER with budesonide (16.9% vs 13.6%; relative risk 1.24 relative, 0.91 to 1.69; P=0.17). The trial's own conclusion states the BPD advantage may have been gained at the expense of increased mortality. A BPD-only headline for this shelf would misstate the trial; the split is the record.

cards.headline: NEuroSIS 2015: inhaled budesonide cut BPD (27.8% vs 38.0%) but death was numerically higher (16.9% vs 13.6%); the death-or-BPD composite was borderline (P=0.05)
cards.summary: NEuroSIS 2015: inhaled budesonide cut BPD (27.8% vs 38.0%) but death was numerically higher (16.9% vs 13.6%); the death-or-BPD composite was borderline (P=0.05)
cards.people: 863 infants born at 23 weeks 0 days to 27 weeks 6 days of gestation, randomly assigned within 24 hours of birth to inhaled budesonide or placebo, continued until oxygen and positive-pressure support were no longer required or 32 weeks of postmenstrual age; adequate primary-outcome data were available for 437 infants assigned to budesonide and 419 assigned to placebo. The abstract does not state sex mix.
cards.result: Death or bronchopulmonary dysplasia at 36 weeks occurred in 175 of 437 infants (40.0%) on budesonide versus 194 of 419 (46.3%) on placebo (relative risk stratified by gestational age 0.86 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.75 to 1.00; P=0.05). BPD alone was lower with budesonide (27.8% vs 38.0%; relative risk 0.74 relative, 0.60 to 0.91; P=0.004); death occurred in 16.9% versus 13.6% (relative risk 1.24 relative, 0.91 to 1.69; P=0.17). Fewer budesonide infants required surgical closure of a patent ductus arteriosus (relative risk 0.55 relative; P=0.004) or reintubation (relative risk 0.58 relative; P=0.03); other neonatal illnesses and adverse events were similar. The authors conclude the BPD advantage may have been gained at the expense of increased mortality.
cards.watchOut: The mortality interval (0.91 to 1.69) includes substantial harm and no reassurance; a non-significant mortality excess inside a positive lung trial is precisely the pattern this library's Tier C flag exists to keep visible.
cards.source: Bassler D et al. Early Inhaled Budesonide for the Prevention of Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia. N Engl J Med. 2015. PMID: 26465983. shelves.title: Buprenorphine vs morphine for neonatal abstinence syndrome (BBORN)
shelves.question: In infants with neonatal abstinence syndrome needing pharmacotherapy, does sublingual buprenorphine vs oral morphine shorten treatment?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Administration, Sublingual · Analgesics, Opioid/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Buprenorphine/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Neonatal Abstinence Syndrome/drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One single-centre, double-blind, double-dummy trial (BBORN, Kraft 2017, 63 term infants with neonatal abstinence syndrome) found sublingual buprenorphine markedly shortened treatment: median duration of treatment 15 days versus 28 days on oral morphine, and median hospital stay 21 versus 33 days (P<0.001 for both). Adjunctive phenobarbital was needed by 15% versus 23% (P=0.36), and adverse-event rates were similar. The effect is large and internally clean, but 63 infants at one site is a pilot-scale evidence base for a change in standard neonatal practice: POSSIBLE, pending multicentre confirmation.

cards.headline: BBORN 2017: buprenorphine roughly halved treatment duration (median 15 vs 28 days) and hospital stay (21 vs 33 days) versus morphine in NAS
cards.summary: BBORN 2017: buprenorphine roughly halved treatment duration (median 15 vs 28 days) and hospital stay (21 vs 33 days) versus morphine in NAS
cards.type: Single-site, double-blind, double-dummy randomised clinical trial
cards.people: 63 term infants (≥37 weeks of gestation) exposed to opioids in utero who had signs of the neonatal abstinence syndrome, randomly assigned to sublingual buprenorphine (33) or oral morphine (30); infants whose symptoms were not controlled at the maximum opioid dose received adjunctive phenobarbital. The abstract does not state sex mix.
cards.result: The median duration of treatment was significantly shorter with buprenorphine than with morphine (15 days vs 28 days), as was the median length of hospital stay (21 days vs 33 days) (P<0.001 for both comparisons). Adjunctive phenobarbital was administered in 5 of 33 infants (15%) on buprenorphine and 7 of 30 (23%) on morphine (P=0.36). Rates of adverse events were similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: Medians from 63 infants at a single site: length-of-stay outcomes are partly practice-pattern outcomes (weaning protocols, discharge thresholds), so the day-counts may travel less well than the direction of effect.
cards.source: Kraft WK et al. Buprenorphine for the Treatment of the Neonatal Abstinence Syndrome. N Engl J Med. 2017. PMID: 28468518. shelves.title: Oral sucrose analgesia for neonatal procedural pain
shelves.question: In newborns undergoing heel lance/venepuncture, does oral sucrose vs water/placebo reduce validated pain scores?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Analgesics/administration & dosage · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Infant, Premature · Pain/physiopathology,prevention & control · Pain Measurement · Punctures/adverse effects · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Sucrose/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The evidence is many small blinded randomised trials, summarised in the Cochrane review carded here (Stevens 2016; 74 studies, 7,049 infants) — carded explicitly AS a systematic review, because no single primary trial anchors this question and the gate permits a labelled review card only with that status disclosed. Pooled results consistently favoured sucrose on validated pain scores: for heel lance, the Premature Infant Pain Profile (PIPP) was lower with sucrose plus non-nutritive sucking at 30 seconds (weighted mean difference −1.70, 95% CI −2.13 to −1.26; 3 studies, 278 infants; graded high-quality evidence by the review) and at 60 seconds (−2.14, −3.34 to −0.94); for venipuncture, 2 mL of 24% sucrose gave a PIPP weighted mean difference of −2.79 (−3.76 to −1.83). Most other analyses were graded low- or moderate-quality, and every endpoint is a pain score or crying measure — a surrogate with no demonstrated downstream outcome benefit: POSSIBLE, surrogate-only, as flagged in the topic file.

cards.headline: Stevens 2016 (Cochrane review of 74 RCTs, 7,049 infants): sucrose reduced validated pain scores for heel lance and venipuncture — labelled review card, no single primary trial
cards.summary: Stevens 2016 (Cochrane review of 74 RCTs, 7,049 infants): sucrose reduced validated pain scores for heel lance and venipuncture — labelled review card, no single primary trial
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (Cochrane Neonatal) — carded explicitly as a review, per the library's review-card rule
cards.people: 74 randomised trials enrolling 7,049 term or preterm neonates (postnatal age up to 28 days after reaching 40 weeks postmenstrual age) receiving sucrose for procedural pain, against controls including no treatment, water, glucose, breast milk, breastfeeding, local anaesthetic, pacifier, positioning/containing or acupuncture. Only a few studies could be combined in each meta-analysis.
cards.result: There was high-quality evidence (the review's GRADE assessment) for sucrose (24%) with non-nutritive sucking or 0.5 mL oral sucrose in preterm and term infants: PIPP score 30 seconds after heel lance, weighted mean difference −1.70 (95% CI −2.13 to −1.26; I²=0%; 3 studies, n=278); PIPP at 60 seconds, −2.14 (−3.34 to −0.94; 2 studies, n=164). For venipuncture, 2 mL of 24% sucrose before the procedure gave a PIPP weighted mean difference of −2.79 (−3.76 to −1.83; 1 study, 213 infants across 2 groups). For most other analyses the review graded the evidence low or moderate quality, with substantial heterogeneity in doses, comparators and measures across the 74 trials.
cards.watchOut: This is a review card, not a trial: pooled pain-score differences of 1.7–2.8 points on a composite scale are surrogate effects measured over seconds-to-minutes, and the review cannot show that sucrose analgesia changes any downstream clinical outcome. Effect sizes vary by dose, procedure and comparator.
cards.source: Stevens B et al. Sucrose for analgesia in newborn infants undergoing painful procedures. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2016. PMID: 27420164. shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The pinned anchor (Michelson 2002, 171 children and adolescents aged 6–16) is a 6-week double-blind trial in which once-daily atomoxetine was superior to placebo on investigator, parent and teacher ratings, with a treatment effect size of 0.71 and discontinuations for adverse events under 3% in both groups. cards.result: Outcomes among atomoxetine-treated patients were superior to placebo as assessed by investigator, parent, and teacher ratings; the treatment effect size was 0.71, similar to previous twice-daily atomoxetine studies. Parent diary ratings suggested drug-specific effects were sustained late in the day. Discontinuations due to adverse events were low (less than 3%) for both treatment groups, and no serious safety concerns were observed. The abstract reports no numerical rating-scale scores, so this card prints none.
cards.watchOut: An abstract without effect magnitudes on the actual scales: the 0.71 effect size is a standardised measure, and anyone quoting point improvements for this trial is quoting beyond this record. Six weeks is also a short window for a chronic condition.

shelves.title: Guanfacine extended-release for ADHD (non-stimulant)
shelves.question: In children/adolescents with ADHD, does guanfacine XR vs placebo reduce ADHD symptoms?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Attention Deficit Disorder with Hyperactivity/diagnosis,drug therapy · Child · Delayed-Action Preparations/administration & dosage · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Guanfacine/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The pinned anchor (Biederman 2008, 345 patients aged 6–17) is an 8-week double-blind fixed-dose trial in which all three guanfacine extended-release doses beat placebo on the ADHD Rating Scale IV total score: least-squares mean changes of −16.18 (2 mg), −16.43 (3 mg) and −18.87 (4 mg) versus −8.48 on placebo, with concordant improvements on hyperactivity/impulsivity and inattention subscales and global measures. The price is the alpha-agonist profile — headache, somnolence, fatigue, upper abdominal pain and sedation were the commonest treatment-emergent events, with small blood-pressure, pulse and ECG changes the authors judged not clinically meaningful. The topic file labels the question DOUBLE-A, but only this trial was pinned and verified at build, so the shelf rests on one carded trial: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Biederman 2008: guanfacine XR at 2–4 mg improved ADHD Rating Scale scores by −16 to −19 points vs −8.5 on placebo over 8 weeks; somnolence and sedation the main harms
cards.summary: Biederman 2008: guanfacine XR at 2–4 mg improved ADHD Rating Scale scores by −16 to −19 points vs −8.5 on placebo over 8 weeks; somnolence and sedation the main harms
cards.type: Multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled, fixed-dosage escalation study
cards.people: 345 patients aged 6 to 17 years with ADHD, randomly assigned to guanfacine extended release 2 mg (87), 3 mg (86) or 4 mg (86) once daily, or placebo (86), for 8 weeks. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: Least-squares mean changes from baseline in ADHD Rating Scale IV total scores were −16.18 (2 mg), −16.43 (3 mg) and −18.87 (4 mg), compared with −8.48 on placebo — significant in all guanfacine groups, as were the hyperactivity/impulsivity and inattentiveness subscales and the Clinical Global Impression of Improvement, Parent's Global Assessment and Conners' short-form ratings. The most commonly reported treatment-emergent adverse events were headache, somnolence, fatigue, upper abdominal pain, and sedation. Small to modest changes in blood pressure, pulse rate, and electrocardiogram parameters were observed but were not clinically meaningful.
cards.watchOut: An 8-week trial with a flat dose-response (2 mg nearly matches 4 mg on the primary score while sedation rises with the drug class) — the record supports starting low; it does not support dose escalation as a route to more benefit.

shelves.title: Comprehensive Behavioral Intervention for Tics (CBIT) in Tourette disorder
shelves.question: In children with Tourette disorder, does CBIT (habit-reversal-based behaviour therapy) vs supportive therapy/education reduce tic severity?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Behavior Therapy · Child · Female · Humans · Male · Severity of Illness Index · Tourette Syndrome/therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The pinned anchor (Piacentini 2010, 126 children aged 9–17) is an observer-blind randomised trial in which eight sessions of comprehensive behavioural intervention over 10 weeks reduced Yale Global Tic Severity Scale scores more than supportive therapy and education (24.7 to 17.1 vs 24.6 to 21.1; difference between groups 4.1 points, 95% CI 2.0 to 6.2; effect size 0.68), with a positive-response rate of 52.5% versus 18.5% (number needed to treat 3), low attrition (9.5%), tic worsening in 4%, and 87% of responders maintaining benefit at 6 months. The topic file also names a separate adult behaviour-therapy trial; it was not pinned at build, so this shelf rests on the paediatric trial alone and does not import the adult result: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Piacentini 2010: CBIT cut tic severity more than supportive therapy (YGTSS difference 4.1 points) with a 52.5% vs 18.5% response rate
cards.summary: Piacentini 2010: CBIT cut tic severity more than supportive therapy (YGTSS difference 4.1 points) with a 52.5% vs 18.5% response rate
cards.people: 126 children aged 9 through 17 years with impairing Tourette or chronic tic disorder as a primary diagnosis, recruited December 2004 to May 2007 and randomly assigned to 8 sessions over 10 weeks of comprehensive behavioural intervention (61) or supportive therapy and education (65); responders received 3 monthly booster sessions and were reassessed at 3 and 6 months.
cards.result: Behavioural intervention produced a significantly greater decrease on the Yale Global Tic Severity Scale (from 24.7 [95% CI 23.1 to 26.3] to 17.1 [15.1 to 19.1]) than the control treatment (24.6 [23.2 to 26.0] to 21.1 [19.2 to 23.0]) (P<0.001; difference between groups 4.1, 95% CI 2.0 to 6.2; effect size 0.68). Significantly more children receiving behavioural intervention were rated very much or much improved on the Clinical Global Impressions–Improvement scale (52.5% vs 18.5%; P<0.001; number needed to treat 3). Attrition was low (12 of 126, 9.5%); tic worsening was reported by 4% of children (5 of 126). Treatment gains were durable, with 87% of available responders to behaviour therapy exhibiting continued benefit 6 months after treatment.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is supportive therapy/education, not an attention-matched sham — families' and children's effort and expectation are part of what was tested, which is fair for a behavioural intervention but caps how 'specific' the effect can be claimed to be. Participants cannot be blinded in behaviour therapy; the trial's protection is observer blinding.

shelves.title: Risperidone for irritability in autism
shelves.question: In children with autism and serious behavioural problems, does risperidone vs placebo reduce irritability/aggression?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Antipsychotic Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Autistic Disorder/drug therapy,psychology · Child · Child Behavior/drug effects · Child, Preschool · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The pinned anchor (RUPP Autism Network, McCracken 2002, 101 children aged 5–17 with autism and severe tantrums, aggression or self-injury) is an 8-week double-blind trial in which risperidone reduced the Aberrant Behavior Checklist Irritability score by 56.9% versus 14.1% on placebo (P<0.001), with a positive-response rate of 69% versus 12% (P<0.001), and benefit maintained at 6 months in two thirds of initial responders. The harms are on the same card: mean weight gain 2.7 kg versus 0.8 kg in eight weeks (P<0.001), plus more increased appetite, fatigue, drowsiness, dizziness and drooling. A large short-term effect with a real metabolic price, from one carded trial (the topic file's DOUBLE-A label rests on the wider programme, not pinned at build): POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: RUPP 2002: risperidone cut irritability scores by 56.9% vs 14.1% on placebo and tripled-plus response (69% vs 12%) — with 2.7 kg weight gain in 8 weeks
cards.summary: RUPP 2002: risperidone cut irritability scores by 56.9% vs 14.1% on placebo and tripled-plus response (69% vs 12%) — with 2.7 kg weight gain in 8 weeks
cards.type: Multisite, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Research Units on Pediatric Psychopharmacology Autism Network)
cards.people: 101 children (82 boys and 19 girls; mean age 8.8 [SD 2.7] years) aged 5 to 17 years with autistic disorder accompanied by severe tantrums, aggression, or self-injurious behaviour, randomly assigned to risperidone 0.5 to 3.5 mg per day (49) or placebo (52) for eight weeks.
cards.result: Risperidone produced a 56.9% reduction in the Irritability subscale score versus a 14.1% decrease on placebo (P<0.001). The positive-response rate (at least a 25% decrease in Irritability plus a rating of much or very much improved on the Clinical Global Impressions–Improvement scale) was 69% (34 of 49) versus 12% (6 of 52) (P<0.001). Risperidone was associated with an average weight gain of 2.7 (SD 2.9) kg versus 0.8 (SD 2.2) kg on placebo (P<0.001); increased appetite, fatigue, drowsiness, dizziness, and drooling were each more common with risperidone (P<0.05 for each). In two thirds of children with a positive response at eight weeks (23 of 34), benefit was maintained at six months. The authors note the short trial limits inferences about adverse effects such as tardive dyskinesia.
cards.watchOut: Eight weeks, 2.7 kg: the weight trajectory in growing children is the central long-term problem with this drug class, and the trial's own authors flag that harms like tardive dyskinesia cannot be assessed in a trial this short. The benefit claim is for severe behaviour in autism — not for core autism symptoms.
cards.source: McCracken JT et al. Risperidone in children with autism and serious behavioral problems. N Engl J Med. 2002. PMID: 12151468. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields (pre-registration-era trial).
