shelves.title: Parent-mediated communication intervention (PACT) in preschool autism
shelves.question: In preschool children with autism, does parent-mediated communication-focused therapy vs treatment as usual improve child social-communication outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Adaptation, Psychological · Adult · Age Factors · Attention · Autistic Disorder/classification,psychology,therapy · Child Behavior · Child Language · Child, Preschool · Communication
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) on the child outcome the question asks about · POSSIBLE on dyadic interaction: The question asks whether the intervention improves CHILD social-communication outcomes, and the pivotal trial's answer on its own primary outcome is no. PACT (Green 2010, 152 children aged 2 years to 4 years 11 months) found autism symptom severity at 13 months reduced by 3.9 points on PACT versus 2.9 on treatment as usual — a between-group effect size of −0.24 (95% CI −0.59 to 0.11), not significant — and the authors state they cannot recommend adding PACT to treatment as usual for reducing autism symptoms. What DID improve, significantly, were measures of the interaction itself: parental synchronous response (effect 1.22, 0.85 to 1.59), child initiations with the parent (0.41, 0.08 to 0.74), with shared attention borderline (0.33, −0.02 to 0.68). The South Asian adaptation (PASS, Rahman 2016, 65 children aged 2–9) replicated the dyadic pattern delivered by non-specialist workers — parental synchrony effect size 1.61 and child initiation 0.99 — while mutual shared attention was REDUCED (−0.70), a negative effect not seen in PACT. Interventions that change how parents and children interact without demonstrably changing the child's measured symptoms earn exactly this split.

cards.headline: PACT 2010: primary child outcome null — symptom severity effect −0.24 (95% CI −0.59 to 0.11) — while parent–child interaction measures improved clearly
cards.summary: PACT 2010: primary child outcome null — symptom severity effect −0.24 (95% CI −0.59 to 0.11) — while parent–child interaction measures improved clearly
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (three UK specialist centres)
cards.people: 152 children with core autism, aged 2 years to 4 years and 11 months, randomly assigned to the parent-mediated Preschool Autism Communication Trial intervention plus treatment as usual (77) or treatment as usual alone (75); primary outcome was autism symptom severity (ADOS-G social-communication algorithm total) at 13 months, analysed by intention to treat.
cards.result: At 13 months, symptom severity had fallen by 3.9 points (SD 4.7) with PACT and 2.9 (SD 3.9) with treatment as usual — a between-group effect size of −0.24 (95% CI −0.59 to 0.11) after adjustment — not statistically significant. Treatment effects were positive for parental synchronous response to the child (1.22, 0.85 to 1.59), child initiations with the parent (0.41, 0.08 to 0.74), and parent–child shared attention (0.33, −0.02 to 0.68). Effects on directly assessed language and adaptive functioning in school were small. The authors conclude: on the basis of these findings, they cannot recommend the addition of PACT to treatment as usual for the reduction of autism symptoms, though a clear benefit was noted for parent–child dyadic social communication.
cards.watchOut: The trial's authors decline to recommend their own intervention for the primary aim — that sentence, not the positive secondary outcomes, is the headline. Dyadic measures are rated from the interactions the intervention directly trains, so improvement there is partly a measure of treatment receipt.
cards.source: Green J et al. Parent-mediated communication-focused treatment in children with autism (PACT): a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2010. PMID: 20494434. cards.type: Single-blind randomised trial (two centres: Goa, India, and Rawalpindi, Pakistan) — feasibility and effectiveness of an adapted parent-mediated intervention
cards.people: 65 children aged 2–9 years with autism spectrum disorder, randomly assigned to 12 sessions of the Parent-mediated intervention for Autism Spectrum Disorder in South Asia (PASS) plus treatment as usual (32) or treatment as usual alone (33), delivered by non-specialist health workers; 26 of 32 (81%) completed the intervention. Primary outcome was quality of parent–child interaction (Dyadic Communication Measure for Autism) at 8 months.
cards.result: After adjustment, the primary outcome favoured PASS for parental synchrony (adjusted mean difference 0.25 [95% CI 0.14 to 0.36]; effect size 1.61 [0.90 to 2.32]) and initiation of communication by the child with the parent (0.15 [0.04 to 0.26]; effect size 0.99 [0.29 to 1.68]), but time in mutual shared attention was reduced (−0.16 [−0.26 to −0.05]; effect size −0.70 [−1.16 to −0.23]). The authors describe the results as showing the feasibility of adapting and task-shifting the intervention to low- and middle-income settings, replicating PACT's positive dyadic effects with one negative effect not reported previously.
cards.watchOut: A 65-child feasibility-scale trial whose primary outcome is again the trained interaction itself, with one dyadic measure moving the wrong way; it establishes deliverability in LMICs, not child symptom benefit.
cards.source: Rahman A et al. Effectiveness of the parent-mediated intervention for children with autism spectrum disorder in south Asia in India and Pakistan (PASS): a randomised controlled trial. Lancet Psychiatry. 2016. PMID: 26704571. Registry ID: ISRCTN79675498, from the record's databank fields. cards.summary: Synthesis: parents interact differently; children's measured symptoms did not significantly change — SPLIT
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: PACT 2010 (152 preschool children, UK) and PASS 2016 (65 children, India and Pakistan).
cards.result: Across both trials the consistent finding is dyadic: parents become more synchronous and children initiate more with the parent. The inconsistent-to-absent finding is the one the shelf's question asks about — child social-communication symptom change — which was null on PACT's primary outcome (−0.24, CI crossing zero) and not PASS's outcome at all. Families may value the dyadic gains; the record does not support promising symptom reduction.
cards.watchOut: Later long-term follow-up reports of PACT exist in the literature; they are not carded here, and this shelf's verdict rests on the trials' prespecified primary endpoints as published in the carded reports.

shelves.title: Community speech and language therapy for preschool speech/language delay
shelves.question: In preschool children with primary speech/language delay, does community speech and language therapy vs watchful waiting/deferred therapy improve language outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Analysis of Variance · Chi-Square Distribution · Child, Preschool · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Infant · Language Development Disorders/therapy · Language Therapy/methods · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): The single trial (Glogowska 2000, 159 preschool children in 16 Bristol community clinics) compared routine community speech and language therapy with 12 months of watchful waiting and found little evidence of benefit: of four quantitative language measures, only auditory comprehension significantly favoured therapy (adjusted difference in means 4.1, 95% CI 0.5 to 7.6; P=0.025), while expressive language (1.4, −2.1 to 4.8), phonology error rate (−4.4, −12.0 to 3.3), language development (0.1, −0.4 to 0.6) and improvement on the trial entry criterion (odds ratio 1.3 relative, 0.67 to 2.4) were all non-significant. At the end of the trial 70% of ALL children still had substantial speech and language deficits. One positive secondary measure among five, in one community trial of therapy as routinely delivered, supports POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for routine provision as tested — and the authors' own call to reconsider the timing, nature and intensity of such therapy is printed on the card.

cards.headline: Glogowska 2000: community speech and language therapy vs watchful waiting — only 1 of 5 outcomes (auditory comprehension) favoured therapy; 70% of all children still substantially impaired at 12 months
cards.summary: Glogowska 2000: community speech and language therapy vs watchful waiting — only 1 of 5 outcomes (auditory comprehension) favoured therapy; 70% of all children still substantially impaired at 12 months
cards.type: Pragmatic randomised controlled trial (16 community clinics, Bristol, UK)
cards.people: 159 preschool children with appreciable speech or language difficulties who met criteria for admission to speech and language therapy, randomised to routine therapy or 12 months of watchful waiting; four quantitative speech/language measures were assessed at 6 and 12 months, plus a binary improvement variable on the trial entry criterion. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Improvement in auditory comprehension was significant in favour of therapy (adjusted difference in means 4.1, 95% CI 0.5 to 7.6; P=0.025). No significant differences were observed for expressive language (1.4, −2.1 to 4.8; P=0.44), phonology error rate (−4.4, −12.0 to 3.3; P=0.26), language development (0.1, −0.4 to 0.6; P=0.73), or improvement on the entry criterion (odds ratio 1.3 — a relative measure — 0.67 to 2.4; P=0.46). At the end of the trial, 70% of all children still had substantial speech and language deficits. The authors conclude the study provides little evidence for the effectiveness of speech and language therapy compared with watchful waiting over 12 months, and that providers should reconsider the appropriateness, timing, nature, and intensity of such therapy in preschool children.
cards.watchOut: A null for therapy AS ROUTINELY DELIVERED at community intensity in 2000 — not a proof that no form, dose or subgroup targeting of therapy can work; the authors themselves direct future research at more specific provision to subgroups. Equally, the one significant measure does not rescue routine provision.
cards.source: Glogowska M et al. Randomised controlled trial of community based speech and language therapy in preschool children. BMJ. 2000. PMID: 11030677. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields (pre-registration-era trial). shelves.title: Intensive remedial reading instruction for severe reading disability / dyslexia
shelves.question: In children with severe reading disability, does intensive phonologically-based remedial instruction improve reading achievement vs standard provision?
shelves.mesh: Awareness · Child · Dyslexia/therapy · Education, Special · Educational Status · Female · Florida · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — with a correction to the topic file on the card's face: the question as drafted asks about intensive instruction VERSUS STANDARD PROVISION, but the pinned trial (Torgesen et al.) contains NO standard-provision or untreated control arm. Sixty children with severe reading disabilities were randomised between TWO intensive instructional programmes (differing in depth of phonemic-awareness and phonemic-decoding instruction), each delivering 67.5 hours of one-to-one tuition over 8 weeks. Both programmes produced very large gains in generalised reading skills (growth effect sizes of 4.4 and 3.9 relative to the children's previous 16 months in learning-disability resource rooms — a within-child historical comparison, not a randomised contrast), stable over 2 years, with accuracy and comprehension reaching the average range while reading RATE remained severely impaired for most children; 40% no longer needed special-education services within a year. The two approaches were not differentially effective. So the record supports: intensive one-to-one phonologically based instruction is followed by large, durable gains — POSSIBLE, on an uncontrolled-for-this-question design. It does not randomise the 'versus standard provision' comparison. CORRECTION: the topic file dates this paper 2004; the record is the Journal of Learning Disabilities, 2001 (the study's later reports are separate publications).

cards.headline: Torgesen 2001: two intensive reading programmes both produced large durable gains (growth effect sizes 4.4 and 3.9 vs prior resource-room progress) — but there was no standard-provision control arm, and reading rate stayed severely impaired
cards.summary: Torgesen 2001: two intensive reading programmes both produced large durable gains (growth effect sizes 4.4 and 3.9 vs prior resource-room progress) — but there was no standard-provision control arm, and reading rate stayed severely impaired
cards.type: Randomised comparison of two active instructional programmes (no untreated/standard-provision control), with 2-year follow-up
cards.people: 60 children with severe reading disabilities, randomly assigned to two instructional programmes incorporating principles of effective instruction but differing in depth and extent of phonemic-awareness and phonemic-decoding instruction; all children received 67.5 hours of one-to-one instruction (two 50-minute sessions daily for 8 weeks). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Both instructional programmes produced very large improvements in generalised reading skills that were stable over a 2-year follow-up. Compared with the growth in broad reading ability made during the children's previous 16 months in learning-disabilities resource rooms, growth during the intervention produced effect sizes of 4.4 for one intervention and 3.9 for the other. Average scores on reading accuracy and comprehension were in the average range at the end of follow-up, but measures of reading rate showed continued severe impairment for most children. Within 1 year of the intervention, 40% of children were no longer in need of special education services. The two methods were not differentially effective for children entering with different levels of phonological ability; the best predictors of long-term growth were resource-room teacher ratings of attention/behaviour, general verbal ability, and prior levels of component reading skills.
cards.watchOut: The headline effect sizes (4.4, 3.9) compare intervention growth with the same children's prior progress — a historical, within-child yardstick vulnerable to maturation, regression to the mean and selection (children were referred at their worst). No randomised standard-provision group exists in this record, so the shelf's 'versus standard provision' framing is answered only indirectly. The topic file's 2004 date is also corrected here: the record is 2001.
cards.source: Torgesen JK et al. Intensive remedial instruction for children with severe reading disabilities: immediate and long-term outcomes from two instructional approaches. J Learn Disabil. 2001. PMID: 15497271. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Botulinum toxin A for lower-limb spasticity in cerebral palsy
shelves.question: In children with spastic cerebral palsy, does botulinum toxin A injection vs placebo/usual care reduce spasticity and improve function?
shelves.mesh: Botulinum Toxins, Type A/therapeutic use · Cerebral Palsy/complications · Child · Child, Preschool · Disability Evaluation · Double-Blind Method · Electromyography · Humans · Injections, Intramuscular · Leg
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The pinned anchor (Bjornson 2007, 33 children with spastic diplegia, mean age 5.5 years, Gross Motor Function Classification System levels I–III) is a randomised, double-masked, placebo-controlled trial of botulinum toxin A 12 U/kg into both gastrocnemius muscles, evaluated across all five rehabilitation domains. The physiology moved: electromyographic spasticity fell significantly at 3 weeks, viscoelastic spasticity measures at 8 weeks, and dorsiflexion range increased at 12 weeks. Function moved late and partly: performance goals improved at 12 weeks and maximum voluntary torque and gross motor function at 24 weeks — but there were NO significant differences in satisfaction with performance goals, energy expenditure, Ashworth scores, or adverse effects. The topic file's balance line is exactly right and is adopted: benefit is proven mainly on tone and physiology, with functional gains limited and inconsistent: POSSIBLE. The topic file's 'multiple RCTs' framing is fenced in the synthesis — only this trial was pinned at build.

cards.headline: Bjornson 2007: BoNT-A reduced measured spasticity (EMG at 3 weeks, viscoelastic at 8 weeks) and improved some function at 24 weeks — but Ashworth scores and family satisfaction did not differ from placebo
cards.summary: Bjornson 2007: BoNT-A reduced measured spasticity (EMG at 3 weeks, viscoelastic at 8 weeks) and improved some function at 24 weeks — but Ashworth scores and family satisfaction did not differ from placebo
cards.people: 33 children with spastic diplegia (mean age 5.5 years; Gross Motor Function Classification System levels I–III), receiving either botulinum toxin A 12 U/kg or placebo saline injections into bilateral gastrocnemius muscles; outcomes were measured at baseline and at 3, 8, 12, and 24 weeks. The abstract does not state the sex mix or per-group numbers.
cards.result: Significant decreases in the electromyographic representation of spasticity were documented 3 weeks after botulinum toxin A treatment; a significant decrease in viscoelastic aspects of spasticity was present at 8 weeks, and subsequent increases in dorsiflexion range were documented at 12 weeks. Improvement was found in performance goals at 12 weeks and in maximum voluntary torque and gross motor function at 24 weeks for the botulinum toxin A group. There were NO significant differences between groups in satisfaction with performance goals, energy expenditure, Ashworth scores, or frequency of adverse effects. The authors describe the safety profile of 12 U/kg as excellent and note that communication is needed to ensure realistic expectations of treatment.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-three children, one muscle group, one dose: the trial is powered for physiology, not for the functional and satisfaction outcomes families actually buy the injections for — and on the commonest clinical tone scale (Ashworth) it found no difference at all.
cards.source: Bjornson K et al. Botulinum toxin for spasticity in children with cerebral palsy: a comprehensive evaluation. Pediatrics. 2007. PMID: 17606561. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Maternal choline supplementation in pregnancies with heavy alcohol exposure (fetal alcohol spectrum)
shelves.question: In heavy-drinking pregnant women, does choline supplementation vs placebo mitigate prenatal alcohol effects on infant growth and cognition?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Alcohol Drinking/drug therapy,epidemiology · Birth Weight/drug effects,physiology · Choline/administration & dosage · Cognition/drug effects,physiology · Dietary Supplements · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorders/epidemiology,prevention & control · Pregnancy
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): The single trial (Jacobson 2018, 69 heavy-drinking pregnant women in Cape Town, South Africa, randomised in mid-pregnancy to 2 g/day choline or placebo until delivery) is described by its own authors as exploratory, and its abstract reports directions rather than figures: infants of choline-treated mothers were more likely to meet the criterion for eyeblink conditioning at 6.5 months (the primary outcome), showed considerable catch-up growth in weight and head circumference at 6.5 and 12 months after both groups were small at birth, and had higher novelty-preference scores (better visual recognition memory) at 12 months; within the choline arm, maternal adherence strongly predicted eyeblink performance. No percentages, effect sizes or P values appear in the record's abstract, so none are printed on the card. Sixty-nine mothers, one population, an adherence-dependent signal and no quantified effects: MAYBE (weak evidence). Nothing on this shelf should be read as making continued heavy drinking safe — the intervention was tested as mitigation alongside ongoing exposure, in women who continued to drink.

cards.headline: Jacobson 2018: choline in pregnancy was associated with better infant eyeblink conditioning, catch-up growth and recognition memory — an exploratory 69-woman trial whose abstract prints no effect sizes
cards.summary: Jacobson 2018: choline in pregnancy was associated with better infant eyeblink conditioning, catch-up growth and recognition memory — an exploratory 69-woman trial whose abstract prints no effect sizes
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial (exploratory, per the authors)
cards.people: 69 Cape Coloured (mixed ancestry) heavy drinkers in Cape Town, South Africa, recruited in mid-pregnancy and randomly assigned to a daily oral dose of 2 g choline or placebo from enrolment until delivery. The primary outcome, eyeblink conditioning (EBC), was assessed at 6.5 months; somatic growth was measured at birth, 6.5 and 12 months, and recognition memory and processing speed (Fagan Test of Infant Intelligence) at 6.5 and 12 months.
cards.result: Infants born to choline-treated mothers were more likely to meet criterion for conditioning on EBC than the placebo group; within the choline arm, the degree of maternal adherence to the supplementation protocol strongly predicted EBC performance. Both groups were small at birth, but choline-treated infants showed considerable catch-up growth in weight and head circumference at 6.5 and 12 months. At 12 months, infants in the choline arm had higher novelty preference scores, indicating better visual recognition memory. The authors call this an exploratory study — the first to provide evidence that a high dose of choline given early in pregnancy can mitigate adverse effects of heavy prenatal alcohol exposure on EBC, postnatal growth, and cognition in human infants. No numerical effect sizes are stated in the record's abstract, and none are printed here.
cards.watchOut: The adherence gradient inside the choline arm cuts both ways: it supports a dose relationship, but it also means the effect concentrates in women who took the supplement reliably — the group least comparable to the placebo arm. With 69 participants and unquantified outcomes, this is a hypothesis-strengthening result, not a supplementation recommendation.
cards.source: Jacobson SW et al. Efficacy of Maternal Choline Supplementation During Pregnancy in Mitigating Adverse Effects of Prenatal Alcohol Exposure on Growth and Cognitive Function: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Clinical Trial. Alcohol Clin Exp Res. 2018. PMID: 29750367. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: a biologically plausible mitigation signal at exploratory strength — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: a biologically plausible mitigation signal at exploratory strength — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: Jacobson 2018 (69 heavy-drinking pregnant women, Cape Town).
cards.result: Choline supplementation during pregnancy was associated with better infant conditioning, growth catch-up and recognition memory after heavy alcohol exposure, consistent with the animal literature the authors cite. cards.watchOut: This shelf must never be summarised as 'choline protects the baby if you drink': the trial tested mitigation of harm in women who continued heavy drinking despite recruitment into care, and showed partial, exploratory signals only.

shelves.title: Memantine for dementia/cognition in adults with Down syndrome (MEADOWS)
shelves.question: In adults over 40 with Down syndrome, does memantine vs placebo improve cognition or function?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Alzheimer Disease/drug therapy · Cognition/drug effects · Dementia/drug therapy,etiology · Double-Blind Method · Down Syndrome/complications,psychology · Female · Humans · Male · Memantine/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): The single trial (MEADOWS, Hanney 2012, 173 adults over 40 with Down syndrome, with and without dementia) found memantine did not improve cognition or function over 52 weeks: both groups declined, and adjusted differences numerically favoured PLACEBO on all three outcomes — DAMES score difference −4.1 (95% CI −13.1 to 4.8), adaptive behaviour scale part I −8.5 (−20.1 to 3.1), part II 2.0 (−7.2 to 11.3), all non-significant. Serious adverse events occurred in 11% on memantine versus 7% on placebo (P=0.33), and deaths from serious adverse events in 5 versus 4 participants (P=0.77). The intervals are wide enough that a modest benefit is not excluded, capping the null at POSSIBLE; the authors' conclusion — memantine is not an effective treatment in this group, and Alzheimer's-drug efficacy does not transfer by assumption — is the shelf's position.

cards.headline: MEADOWS 2012: memantine did not improve cognition or function in adults over 40 with Down syndrome — adjusted differences numerically favoured placebo on every outcome
cards.summary: MEADOWS 2012: memantine did not improve cognition or function in adults over 40 with Down syndrome — adjusted differences numerically favoured placebo on every outcome
cards.type: Prospective randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (four learning-disability centres, UK and Norway)
cards.people: 173 adults (over 40 years) with karyotypic or clinically diagnosed Down syndrome, with and without dementia, randomly allocated to memantine (88; 72 [82%] with DAMES data and 75 [85%] with adaptive behaviour data at 52 weeks) or placebo (85; 74 [87%] and 73 [86%]) for 52 weeks. Primary outcomes were change in cognition and function (DAMES scores and Adaptive Behaviour Scale parts I and II).
cards.result: Both groups declined in cognition and function, and rates did not differ between groups for any outcome. After adjustment for baseline score, differences between groups were −4.1 (95% CI −13.1 to 4.8) in DAMES scores, −8.5 (−20.1 to 3.1) in ABS part I scores, and 2.0 (−7.2 to 11.3) in ABS part II scores — all in favour of controls where negative, and all non-significant. Ten (11%) of 88 participants in the memantine group and six (7%) of 85 controls had serious adverse events (P=0.33); five participants in the memantine group and four controls died from serious adverse events (P=0.77). The authors conclude that despite promising indications, memantine is not an effective treatment, and that therapies effective for Alzheimer's disease are not necessarily effective in this group.
cards.watchOut: The trial's impetus included benefit in transgenic mice — animal data that did not survive the human test; it is noted here only as the trial's stated rationale and is not evidence on this shelf. The wide intervals mean 'not shown effective', not 'proven useless at every dose and stage'.

shelves.title: Intermittent montelukast for episodic viral wheeze in preschool children (WAIT)
shelves.question: In children aged 10 months to 5 years with episodic viral wheeze, does parent-initiated intermittent montelukast vs placebo reduce unscheduled medical attendances for wheeze?
shelves.mesh: Acetates/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Anti-Asthmatic Agents/therapeutic use · Appointments and Schedules · Arachidonate 5-Lipoxygenase/drug effects · Asthma/drug therapy · Child, Preschool · Cyclopropanes · Cysteine/urine · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Genotype · Humans · Infant · Leukotrienes/urine · Male · Quinolines/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Respiratory Sounds/drug effects · Sulfides · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): One large multicentre randomised, placebo-controlled trial (WAIT, 1,358 children aged 10 months to 5 years with at least two wheeze episodes) found no significant overall difference in unscheduled medical attendances for wheeze over 12 months with parent-initiated intermittent montelukast versus placebo (mean 2.0 vs 2.3 attendances; incidence rate ratio 0.88 relative, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.01; p=0.06). A prespecified genotype stratum (ALOX5 promoter 5/5) showed a significant reduction (IRR 0.80 relative, 0.68 to 0.95; p=0.01) while the other stratum showed none (IRR 1.03 relative), but the interaction test was not significant (p=0.08) — so the genotype result is a subgroup signal inside an overall null trial, not a demonstrated responder group, and it is not promoted to the headline. One serious adverse event was recorded (a skin reaction, in a child on placebo).

cards.headline: WAIT (Nwokoro 2014): intermittent montelukast did not significantly reduce unscheduled wheeze attendances overall (IRR 0.88 relative; p=0.06); the ALOX5 5/5 subgroup signal had a non-significant interaction (p=0.08)
cards.summary: WAIT (Nwokoro 2014): intermittent montelukast did not significantly reduce unscheduled wheeze attendances overall (IRR 0.88 relative; p=0.06); the ALOX5 5/5 subgroup signal had a non-significant interaction (p=0.08)
cards.people: 1,358 children aged 10 months to 5 years with two or more wheeze episodes, at 21 primary-care and 41 secondary-care sites in England and Scotland (2010–13), stratified by ALOX5 promoter genotype (5/5 vs 5/x+x/x) and then randomised 1:1 to intermittent montelukast (669) or placebo (677) given by parents at each wheeze episode over 12 months; consent was withdrawn for 12 children and primary-outcome data were available for 1,308 (96%). Investigators and parents were masked to treatment and genotype strata. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: There was no difference in unscheduled medical attendances for wheezing episodes between montelukast and placebo (mean 2.0 [SD 2.6] vs 2.3 [2.7]; incidence rate ratio 0.88 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.77 to 1.01; p=0.06). In the 5/5 genotype stratum, attendances were reduced on montelukast (2.0 [2.7] vs 2.4 [3.0]; IRR 0.80 relative, 0.68 to 0.95; p=0.01), but not in the 5/x+x/x stratum (2.0 [2.5] vs 2.0 [2.3]; IRR 1.03 relative, 0.83 to 1.29; p=0.79), and the interaction was not significant (p-interaction=0.08). One serious adverse event was recorded — a skin reaction in a child allocated to placebo.
cards.watchOut: The 5/5-genotype finding is exactly the subgroup pattern this library fences: a significant within-subgroup result with a non-significant interaction test (p=0.08) does not establish a genotype-guided indication. The trial's own interpretation — 'no clear benefit' overall — is the headline; the overall confidence interval (0.77 to 1.01) also cannot exclude a modest benefit, which is why the null is graded POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY.

shelves.title: Dialectical behaviour therapy for adolescents with repeated suicidal and self-harming behaviour
shelves.question: In adolescents with repeated suicidal and self-harming behaviour, does dialectical behaviour therapy vs enhanced usual care reduce self-harm episodes?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Behavior Therapy/methods · Child · Female · Humans · Male · Self-Injurious Behavior/prevention & control · Single-Blind Method · Suicide, Attempted/prevention & control · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised trial (Mehlum 2014, Norway; 77 adolescents with recent and repetitive self-harm in community child and adolescent psychiatric outpatient clinics) found a shortened form of dialectical behaviour therapy for adolescents (DBT-A) superior to enhanced usual care in reducing self-harm, suicidal ideation and depressive symptoms over 19 weeks, with the authors reporting large effect sizes in the DBT-A group and small effect sizes in the control group — but the abstract prints no effect sizes, event counts or rates, so none are printed on the card, and the size of the benefit cannot be verified from the record. Treatment retention was generally good in both arms and emergency-service use was low. A single small trial whose abstract reports direction without numbers earns POSSIBLE. DBT in adult borderline personality disorder is Shelf #708 and is not re-opened here.

cards.headline: Mehlum 2014: DBT-A was superior to enhanced usual care for self-harm, suicidal ideation and depression in 77 adolescents — the abstract reports no effect sizes or event counts
cards.summary: Mehlum 2014: DBT-A was superior to enhanced usual care for self-harm, suicidal ideation and depression in 77 adolescents — the abstract reports no effect sizes or event counts
cards.people: 77 adolescents with recent and repetitive self-harm, treated at community child and adolescent psychiatric outpatient clinics in Norway, randomly allocated to DBT-A (a shortened form of dialectical behaviour therapy) or enhanced usual care; assessments at baseline and after 9, 15, and 19 weeks (end of treatment), with hospitalisations and emergency department visits recorded over the trial period. The abstract does not state the age range or sex mix.
cards.result: Treatment retention was generally good in both conditions, and use of emergency services was low. DBT-A was superior to enhanced usual care in reducing self-harm, suicidal ideation, and depressive symptoms. The authors state that effect sizes were large for treatment outcomes in patients who received DBT-A, whereas effect sizes were small for outcomes in patients receiving enhanced usual care; no numerical effect sizes, self-harm frequencies, or between-group statistics are printed in the abstract, so none are reproduced here. Total number of treatment contacts was a partial mediator of the association between treatment and changes in suicidal-ideation severity; no mediation effects were found for the other outcomes or for total treatment time.
cards.watchOut: This is the shelf where the record's weakness must be explicit: the card can certify the trial's direction and design (randomised, 77 adolescents, enhanced-usual-care comparator — a stronger control than waitlist) but not the magnitude of benefit, because the abstract prints no numbers. The mediation note (more treatment contacts partly explaining effect) also means DBT-A's advantage is entangled with contact intensity. Single country (Norway), single trial.

shelves.title: Oral dexamethasone vs oral prednisone for acute paediatric asthma in the emergency department
shelves.question: In children presenting to the emergency department with acute asthma, is a short course of oral dexamethasone vs oral prednisone non-inferior for relapse and admission outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Asthma/drug therapy · Child · Child, Preschool · Dexamethasone/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Humans · Male · Patient Compliance · Prednisone/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Prospective Studies · Recurrence · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — with a design caveat disclosed on the card's face: the record describes allocation by calendar day (prednisone on odd days, dexamethasone on even days), which is a quasi-random, predictable scheme despite the paper's 'randomized' label, so allocation concealment was not protected. Within that limit, the trial (533 children aged 2–18 years presenting to an emergency department with acute asthma) found 2 days of oral dexamethasone (0.6 mg/kg) gave outcomes similar to 5 days of oral prednisone/prednisolone: relapse within 10 days 7.4% vs 6.9%, hospitalisation from the ED 11% vs 12%, symptom persistence at 10 days 22% vs 21%. Dexamethasone had practical advantages: fewer children excluded for vomiting in the ED (0.3% vs 3%; P=.008), fewer noncompliant parents (0.4% vs 4%; P=.004), and fewer children missing at least 2 days of school (13.2% vs 19.5%; P=.05). The topic file notes later confirmatory RCTs exist; only this anchor is carded here. Long-term controller step-up therapy is Shelf #872.

cards.headline: Qureshi 2001: 2 days of dexamethasone matched 5 days of prednisone on relapse (7.4% vs 6.9%) in 533 children with acute asthma — allocated by odd/even calendar days, not concealed randomisation
cards.summary: Qureshi 2001: 2 days of dexamethasone matched 5 days of prednisone on relapse (7.4% vs 6.9%) in 533 children with acute asthma — allocated by odd/even calendar days, not concealed randomisation
cards.type: Prospective randomised trial as labelled by the authors — allocation by odd/even calendar day as described in the record (quasi-random, predictable allocation)
cards.people: Children aged 2 to 18 years presenting to an emergency department with acute asthma; 272 were analysed in the dexamethasone group and 261 in the prednisone group for the relapse outcome. Dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg (maximum 16 mg) was given on even days and prednisone 2 mg/kg (maximum 60 mg) on odd days in the ED; at discharge, the prednisone group received 4 further daily doses (1 mg/kg/day) and the dexamethasone group one prepackaged dose the next day — 2 doses versus 5 doses in total. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Relapse rates within 10 days were 7.4% (dexamethasone) versus 6.9% (prednisone); hospitalisation rates from the ED were 11% versus 12%, hospitalisation after relapse 20% versus 17%, and symptom persistence at 10 days 22% versus 21% — all similar. In the prednisone group, more children were excluded for vomiting in the ED (3% vs 0.3%; P=.008), more parents were noncompliant (4% vs 0.4%; P=.004), and more children missed 2 or more days of school (19.5% vs 13.2%; P=.05).
cards.watchOut: Alternate-day allocation is predictable and unconcealed: clinicians knew which drug a presenting child would receive, which can bias enrolment and co-interventions. The trial also excluded children for vomiting after allocation (3% vs 0.3%), a post-allocation exclusion that further softens the comparison. The similar relapse rates are reassuring but were not tested against a prespecified non-inferiority margin in this record.
cards.source: Qureshi F et al. Comparative efficacy of oral dexamethasone versus oral prednisone in acute pediatric asthma. J Pediatr. 2001. PMID: 11445789. shelves.title: Platelet transfusion thresholds in preterm infants (PlaNeT-2)
shelves.question: In preterm infants born before 34 weeks' gestation who develop severe thrombocytopenia, does a higher platelet-transfusion threshold (50 × 10⁹/L) versus a lower threshold (25 × 10⁹/L) change the rate of death or major bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Female · Hemorrhage/etiology/prevention & control · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Infant, Premature · Infant, Premature, Diseases/mortality/therapy · Male · Platelet Count · Platelet Transfusion · Thrombocytopenia/complications/mortality/therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY (harm) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: death is a component of the primary outcome). One large multicentre randomised trial, reported in its primary paper and a prespecified 2-year follow-up — one trial, counted once, stated on the face of the shelf. The question is corrected from the topic file, which described the population by birth weight (under 1500 g); the record enrolled infants born before 34 weeks' gestation with severe thrombocytopenia (platelets <50 × 10⁹/L; median birth weight 740 g). The liberal threshold caused harm: death or new major bleeding within 28 days occurred in 26% at the 50 × 10⁹/L threshold versus 19% at 25 × 10⁹/L (odds ratio 1.57 in relative terms, 95% CI 1.06–2.32; P=0.02), and at 2 years death or neurodevelopmental impairment remained higher (50% versus 39%; OR 1.54; P=0.017). The liberal arm was also transfused far more (90% versus 53% received at least one transfusion) — more product, more harm. Single trial, but large, multicentre and internally consistent across two timepoints; if the developer wants a second trial before any stamp, this shelf should be held rather than softened.

cards.headline: PlaNeT-2 (primary report): death or major bleeding in 26% at the higher transfusion threshold versus 19% at the lower (OR 1.57; P=0.02)

cards.result: The primary outcome — death or new major bleeding within 28 days of randomisation — occurred in 26% of the higher-threshold group (85/324) versus 19% of the lower-threshold group (61/329) (odds ratio 1.57 in relative terms, 95% CI 1.06–2.32; P=0.02). Serious adverse events did not differ significantly (25% versus 22%; OR 1.14, 95% CI 0.78–1.67).
cards.watchOut: This is a harm result for a prophylactic practice, from a single (though large) trial; bleeding was assessed with a validated tool and documented prospectively. The composite combines death and major bleeding — the record does not print the separate component rates in its abstract, and none are supplied here.

cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: PlaNeT-2 (Curley 2019 primary report; Moore 2023 two-year follow-up) — one trial, 660 infants, counted once.
cards.result: Transfusing preterm infants with severe thrombocytopenia at a platelet count of 50 rather than 25 × 10⁹/L increased death or major bleeding within 28 days (26% versus 19%) and death or neurodevelopmental impairment at 2 years (50% versus 39%). The restrictive threshold is the safer default on this evidence.
cards.watchOut: Single trial — the stamp rests on its size, its multicentre conduct and the consistency of the harm across two timepoints, and remains subject to the developer's Tier C verdict. Results concern prophylactic thresholds in preterm infants with severe thrombocytopenia, not therapeutic transfusion for active bleeding.
cards.source: Synthesis of Curley A et al. N Engl J Med. 2019 (PMID: 30387697) and Moore CM et al. Arch Dis Child Fetal Neonatal Ed. 2023 (PMID: 36810309). Registry ID ISRCTN87736839 as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Low-dose atropine slows children's myopia: a clear dose-response
shelves.question: In children with progressing myopia (shortsightedness), do nightly low-dose atropine eye drops slow progression — prescription change and eye lengthening — compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Atropine · Axial Length, Eye · Child · Disease Progression · Humans · Muscarinic Antagonists · Myopia · Ophthalmic Solutions · Refraction, Ocular
shelves.balance: Nightly low-dose atropine slows myopia progression in children, with a clear dose-response in the LAMP trial. In LAMP (438 children aged 4–12, 1 year), spherical-equivalent change was −0.27 D on 0.05%, −0.46 D on 0.025% and −0.59 D on 0.01%, versus −0.81 D on placebo, and axial length grew by 0.20, 0.29 and 0.36 mm versus 0.41 mm. The older ATOM1 trial of the much stronger 1% dose in one eye found progression of −0.28 versus −1.20 D over 2 years. In the phase 3 CHAMP trial (576 children, 3 years) of NVK002 (Vyluma), the 0.02% dose missed its primary responder endpoint (odds ratio 1.77, P = .37), while 0.01% met all its main endpoints: responder odds ratio 4.54 (a relative measure; the abstract does not report the responder proportions themselves), a spherical-equivalent difference of +0.24 D and axial length −0.13 mm relative to placebo. The endpoints throughout are progression and eye lengthening during childhood, not adult eye disease. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): consistent slowing across three randomised trials, with a concentration-dependent effect in LAMP and a 3-year phase 3 confirmation at the 0.01% dose.

cards.headline: LAMP 2019: a clean dose-response — spherical-equivalent change −0.27 D on 0.05% versus −0.81 D on placebo over 1 year
cards.summary: LAMP 2019: a clean dose-response — spherical-equivalent change −0.27 D on 0.05% versus −0.81 D on placebo over 1 year
cards.people: 438 children aged 4 to 12 years with myopia of at least −1.0 diopter (D) and astigmatism of −2.5 D or less, randomly assigned 1:1:1:1 to 0.05%, 0.025% or 0.01% atropine eye drops or placebo, once nightly to both eyes for 1 year, in a randomised, placebo-controlled, double-masked trial.
cards.result: After 1 year, the mean spherical-equivalent change was −0.27 D in the 0.05% group, −0.46 D (0.025%), −0.59 D (0.01%) and −0.81 D (placebo) (P < 0.001), with a respective mean increase in axial length of 0.20, 0.29, 0.36 and 0.41 mm (P < 0.001). Accommodation amplitude was reduced and pupil size increased most in the 0.05% group, but visual acuity and vision-related quality of life were not affected in any group, and all concentrations were well tolerated; of the three concentrations, 0.05% was the most effective in controlling spherical-equivalent progression and axial elongation over 1 year.
cards.watchOut: One year of follow-up: this phase shows slowing during treatment, not what happens after stopping, and not adult eye outcomes. The effects on accommodation and pupil size were largest at the best-performing 0.05% dose. The record's databank fields list no registry ID.
cards.source: Yam JC et al.. Low-Concentration Atropine for Myopia Progression (LAMP) Study: A Randomized, Double-Blinded, Placebo-Controlled Trial of 0.05%, 0.025%, and 0.01% Atropine Eye Drops in Myopia Control. Ophthalmology. 2019. PMID: 30514630. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: ATOM1 2006: atropine 1% in one eye — progression −0.28 versus −1.20 D and axial length −0.02 versus +0.38 mm over 2 years
cards.summary: ATOM1 2006: atropine 1% in one eye — progression −0.28 versus −1.20 D and axial length −0.02 versus +0.38 mm over 2 years
cards.type: Parallel-group, placebo-controlled, randomised, double-masked trial (ATOM1; treated-eye design)
cards.people: 400 Asian children aged 6 to 12 years with refractive error of spherical equivalent −1.00 to −6.00 diopters and astigmatism of −1.50 D or less, assigned with equal probability to 1% atropine or vehicle eye drops once nightly for 2 years in a parallel-group, placebo-controlled, randomised, double-masked study; only one eye of each subject was chosen through randomisation for treatment, and 346 children (86.5%) completed the 2-year study.
cards.result: After 2 years, the mean progression of myopia in the atropine-treated eyes was −0.28 D, versus −1.20 D in the placebo-treated control eyes — a difference of −0.92 D (95% CI −1.10 to −0.77, P < 0.001) — and axial length changed by −0.02 mm versus +0.38 mm, a difference of 0.40 mm (95% CI 0.35 to 0.45, P < 0.001). No serious adverse events related to atropine were reported, and topical atropine was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: A high dose (1%) by modern low-dose standards, given in one eye only, so this is a treated-eye comparison — and the tolerability burden of 1% atropine is why the field moved to low doses. A pre-registration-era trial with no registry ID in the record.
cards.source: Chua WH et al.. Atropine for the treatment of childhood myopia. Ophthalmology. 2006. PMID: 16996612. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — pre-registration-era trial. cards.headline: CHAMP 2023: NVK002 0.01% met all main endpoints over 3 years, but the 0.02% dose missed its primary responder endpoint
cards.summary: CHAMP 2023: NVK002 0.01% met all main endpoints over 3 years, but the 0.02% dose missed its primary responder endpoint
cards.type: Randomised, double-masked, placebo-controlled, parallel-group phase 3 clinical trial (CHAMP)
cards.people: 576 participants aged 3 to 16 years with −0.50 to −6.00 D spherical equivalent refractive error and no worse than −1.50 D astigmatism, recruited from 26 clinical sites in North America and 5 countries in Europe and randomised (2:2:3) to once-daily placebo or low-dose atropine 0.01% or 0.02% (NVK002, Vyluma) for 36 months in a double-masked, placebo-controlled, parallel-group phase 3 trial; 573 received trial treatment (safety set) and the 489 participants aged 6 to 10 years at baseline formed the modified intention-to-treat set for the main efficacy endpoints.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was the proportion of participants' eyes responding to therapy (less than 0.50 D myopia progression at 36 months). At month 36, compared with placebo, low-dose atropine 0.02% did not significantly increase the responder proportion (odds ratio 1.77, 95% CI 0.50 to 6.26, P = .37 — a relative measure; the abstract does not report the responder proportions) or slow mean spherical-equivalent progression (difference 0.10 D, P = .10), though it did slow mean axial elongation (−0.08 mm, P = .005). The 0.01% dose significantly increased the responder proportion (odds ratio 4.54, 95% CI 1.15 to 17.97, P = .03), slowed mean spherical-equivalent progression (difference +0.24 D, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.37, P < .001) and slowed axial elongation (−0.13 mm, 95% CI −0.19 to −0.07, P < .001). There were no serious ocular adverse events and no serious event was judged associated with atropine.
cards.watchOut: The dose pattern is the reverse of LAMP's dose-response — here 0.01% succeeded on every main endpoint while the higher 0.02% dose missed its primary endpoint — and the confidence intervals on the responder odds ratios are wide. NVK002 is a novel, preservative-free, unapproved proprietary formulation from Vyluma, named here because the publication names it and it is not interchangeable with a compounded atropine drop; no pharmacologic therapy is approved for treating childhood myopia progression, per the record.
cards.source: Zadnik K et al.. Efficacy and Safety of 0.01% and 0.02% Atropine for the Treatment of Pediatric Myopia Progression Over 3 Years: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Ophthalmology. 2023. PMID: 37261839. Registry ID: NCT03350620. MeSH: none in the record.

cards.headline: Synthesis: consistent slowing across three randomised trials, with a dose-response in LAMP — LIKELY (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: consistent slowing across three randomised trials, with a dose-response in LAMP — LIKELY (benefit)
cards.people: 1,414 children across the three randomised trials above: LAMP 2019 (438, aged 4–12, 1 year), ATOM1 2006 (400, aged 6–12, 2 years) and CHAMP 2023 (576, aged 3–16, 3 years).
cards.result: Every trial slowed progression versus placebo: a concentration-dependent effect in LAMP with 0.05% most effective at 1 year, a large effect of 1% atropine in one eye in ATOM1, and significant benefit of NVK002 0.01% on responder proportion, spherical-equivalent progression and axial length over 3 years in CHAMP — tempered by CHAMP's 0.02% dose missing its primary responder endpoint. The endpoints are myopia progression and axial lengthening during childhood, not adult eye disease. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Rebound after stopping and long-term safety beyond these trials' horizons sit outside this evidence, and the doses and formulations are not interchangeable — a compounded 0.01% drop is not NVK002, and the high-dose ATOM1 result should not be read as a recommendation for 1% atropine.
cards.source: Synthesis of Yam JC et al. Ophthalmology. 2019 (PMID: 30514630); Chua WH et al. Ophthalmology. 2006 (PMID: 16996612); Zadnik K et al. JAMA Ophthalmology. 2023 (PMID: 37261839).

shelves.title: Steroid cream loosens a tight foreskin in most boys — no surgery
shelves.question: In boys with phimosis where treatment is wanted, does topical corticosteroid cream make the foreskin retractile and avoid circumcision, compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Phimosis · Betamethasone · Betamethasone Valerate · Glucocorticoids · Hyaluronoglucosaminidase · Child · Humans
shelves.balance: When a boy's tight foreskin needs treatment, a course of topical corticosteroid cream usually makes it retractile and avoids circumcision. Betamethasone cream twice daily for 4 weeks cured 74% of boys versus 44% on placebo (Lund 2005) — the high placebo figure stated plainly, because the gentle retraction that goes with applying any cream itself loosens many foreskins — and with a second course for non-responders, surgery was avoided in about 85% of cases; at 18 months, 79 of 92 boys re-examined were still cured and 13 had relapsed. Three betamethasone valerate formulations (0.1%, 0.2%, and 0.2% plus hyaluronidase) each beat placebo over 60 days, with total plus partial response of about 95% versus a 29% placebo success rate (Nascimento 2011). Potency is not the lever: high-potency betamethasone valerate 0.06% and moderate-potency clobetasone butyrate 0.05% produced near-identical responses (81.3% versus 77.4%, not significant; Yang 2005). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): two placebo-controlled trials agree, the effect is durable at 18 months, and no side-effects were reported in these trials.

cards.headline: Lund 2005: betamethasone cured 74% versus 44% on placebo at 4 weeks; about 85% avoided surgery and most cures held at 18 months
cards.summary: Lund 2005: betamethasone cured 74% versus 44% on placebo at 4 weeks; about 85% avoided surgery and most cures held at 18 months
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial with 18-month follow-up (Lund 2005)
cards.people: 137 boys with phimosis, randomly assigned to betamethasone cream or placebo applied twice daily for 4 weeks in a prospective, randomised, double-blind study; non-responders were offered steroid treatment for a further 4 weeks, and all patients were invited to follow-up examination after 18 months.
cards.result: At the 4-week follow-up, 49 boys (74%) in the steroid group were cured, compared with 31 (44%) in the control group. With the further course for non-responders, surgery could be avoided in 85% of cases. Of the 92 boys who took part in the 18-month follow-up, 79 had been cured and 13 had suffered a relapse; 26 patients did not take part in the follow-up investigation. No side-effects were noted.
cards.watchOut: The 44% cure rate on placebo is the standing caveat: applying any cream involves gentle retraction, which itself loosens many foreskins — part of what is being measured is the routine, not only the steroid.
cards.source: Lund L et al.. An 18-month follow-up study after randomized treatment of phimosis in boys with topical steroid versus placebo. Scandinavian Journal of Urology and Nephrology. 2005. PMID: 15764277. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — pre-registration-era trial. cards.headline: Nascimento 2011: all three betamethasone valerate formulations beat placebo — total plus partial response about 95% versus 29% success on placebo
cards.summary: Nascimento 2011: all three betamethasone valerate formulations beat placebo — total plus partial response about 95% versus 29% success on placebo
cards.people: 220 boys aged 3 to 10 years with a clinical diagnosis of phimosis, randomised to betamethasone valerate 0.2% plus hyaluronidase, betamethasone valerate 0.2%, betamethasone valerate 0.1%, or placebo, applied twice a day for 60 days; 195 patients were included in the final analysis (54, 51, 52 and 38 per group respectively).
cards.result: The three betamethasone valerate groups had similar success and improvement rates, all higher than placebo. After 60 days of treatment, total and partial response rates for the steroid groups were 54.8% and 40.1% respectively (about 95% combined), while placebo had a success rate of 29%. Success and improvement rates were significantly better at 60 days than at 30 days.
cards.watchOut: 25 of the 220 randomised boys were not in the final analysis. The three formulations were indistinguishable from each other — neither doubling the concentration nor adding hyaluronidase bought anything measurable.
cards.source: Nascimento FJ et al.. Topical betamethasone and hyaluronidase in the treatment of phimosis in boys: a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial. International Braz J Urol. 2011. PMID: 21756378. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Yang 2005: high-potency versus moderate-potency steroid — response 81.3% versus 77.4%, not significant; this is a potency comparison with no placebo arm
cards.summary: Yang 2005: high-potency versus moderate-potency steroid — response 81.3% versus 77.4%, not significant; this is a potency comparison with no placebo arm
cards.type: Prospective randomised single-blind potency-comparison trial — no placebo arm (Yang 2005)
cards.people: 70 boys aged 1 to 12 years with phimosis, randomly assigned to topical betamethasone valerate 0.06% (highly potent) or clobetasone butyrate 0.05% (moderately potent), applied over the stenotic opening of the prepuce twice daily for 4 weeks and for another 4 weeks if no improvement was achieved, with parents instructed to retract the foreskin gently.
cards.result: Response rates (improvement in retractibility score of more than 2 points) were 81.3% with betamethasone valerate and 77.4% with clobetasone butyrate (p=0.63, not significant). Mean retractibility score fell from 3.9 to 1.7 and from 4.2 to 1.9 in the two groups respectively; both steroids were effective in all age groups, and no adverse effect was encountered.
cards.watchOut: This card answers which potency, not whether steroids beat nothing: there is no placebo or untreated group, and the response definition was, in the authors' own word, arbitrarily defined. Its practical message is that a less potent steroid may be tried first.

shelves.title: Daily antibiotics halve reflux children's UTIs — but scars were not prevented
shelves.question: In children with vesicoureteral reflux after a urinary tract infection, does daily low-dose antibiotic prophylaxis prevent further UTIs — and does it prevent kidney scarring?
shelves.mesh: Vesico-Ureteral Reflux · Urinary Tract Infections · Antibiotic Prophylaxis · Trimethoprim, Sulfamethoxazole Drug Combination · Anti-Infective Agents, Urinary · Child · Humans
shelves.balance: Daily low-dose antibiotic prophylaxis prevents further urinary tract infections in children with vesicoureteral reflux — but in the best trial it did not prevent kidney scarring, and it bred resistant bacteria. In RIVUR (607 children with reflux after a first or second UTI, treated for 2 years), recurrence occurred in 39 of 302 children on trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis (12.9%) versus 72 of 305 on placebo (23.6%): hazard ratio 0.50, a 50% relative reduction, on those absolute rates of about 13% versus 24%. Renal scarring was 11.9% on prophylaxis versus 10.2% on placebo, not significantly different, and among breakthrough E. coli recurrences, 63% of isolates were resistant to the drug versus 19% on placebo. PRIVENT (576 children after at least one symptomatic UTI, 42% with known reflux) pointed the same way over 12 months: UTI in 13% versus 19%, hazard ratio 0.61 (a 39% relative reduction), an absolute reduction of 6 percentage points. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): two large placebo-controlled trials agree that infections are prevented; scarring — the outcome prophylaxis ultimately aims at — was not shown to improve, and resistance is the price.

cards.headline: RIVUR 2014: prophylaxis halved UTI recurrence — hazard ratio 0.50, a 50% relative reduction (12.9% versus 23.6%) — but renal scarring was not reduced
cards.summary: RIVUR 2014: prophylaxis halved UTI recurrence — hazard ratio 0.50, a 50% relative reduction (12.9% versus 23.6%) — but renal scarring was not reduced
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (RIVUR Trial Investigators 2014, RIVUR)
cards.people: 607 children with vesicoureteral reflux diagnosed after a first or second febrile or symptomatic urinary tract infection, in a 2-year, multisite, randomised, placebo-controlled trial of trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis (302 children) versus placebo (305 children); secondary outcomes were renal scarring, treatment failure, and antimicrobial resistance.
cards.result: Recurrent urinary tract infection developed in 39 of 302 children on prophylaxis (12.9%) compared with 72 of 305 on placebo (23.6%) — hazard ratio 0.50 (95% CI 0.34 to 0.74), a 50% relative reduction in the risk of recurrence. The occurrence of renal scarring did not differ significantly between the groups (11.9% prophylaxis versus 10.2% placebo). Among 87 children with a first recurrence caused by Escherichia coli, the proportion of isolates resistant to trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole was 63% in the prophylaxis group and 19% in the placebo group.
cards.watchOut: Funded by the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases and others. The infection benefit was particularly marked in children whose index infection was febrile (hazard ratio 0.41) and in those with baseline bladder and bowel dysfunction (hazard ratio 0.21) — but the scarring outcome, the long-term reason for prophylaxis, was a clear null.
cards.source: RIVUR Trial Investigators et al.. Antimicrobial prophylaxis for children with vesicoureteral reflux. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2014. PMID: 24795142. Registry ID: NCT00405704. cards.headline: PRIVENT 2009: UTI in 13% versus 19% over 12 months — hazard ratio 0.61 (a 39% relative reduction), an absolute reduction of 6 percentage points
cards.summary: PRIVENT 2009: UTI in 13% versus 19% over 12 months — hazard ratio 0.61 (a 39% relative reduction), an absolute reduction of 6 percentage points
cards.people: 576 children under 18 years at four Australian centres who had had one or more microbiologically proven urinary tract infections (median age at entry 14 months; 64% girls; 42% with known vesicoureteral reflux), randomly assigned to daily trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole suspension (2 mg trimethoprim plus 10 mg sulfamethoxazole per kilogram) or placebo for 12 months.
cards.result: Urinary tract infection developed in 36 of 288 patients (13%) in the antibiotic group and 55 of 288 (19%) in the placebo group — hazard ratio 0.61 (95% CI 0.40 to 0.93), a 39% relative reduction. The reduction in absolute risk was 6 percentage points and appeared consistent across all subgroups of patients.
cards.watchOut: The trial randomised 576 children of the 780 planned, and only 42% had known vesicoureteral reflux — the population is broader than reflux alone, so for the reflux question this is supportive rather than direct evidence; the authors describe the treatment effect as modest.

shelves.title: Steroids for glue ear: the 389-child OSTRICH trial found hearing recovered in 40% versus 33% on placebo — not a real difference
shelves.question: In children with persistent otitis media with effusion (glue ear) and hearing loss, does a short course of oral steroids restore acceptable hearing compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Audiometry · Child · Child, Preschool · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage/*therapeutic use · Hearing Loss/prevention & control · Humans · Male · Otitis Media with Effusion/complications/*drug therapy · Prednisolone/administration & dosage/*therapeutic use
shelves.balance: Glue ear — otitis media with effusion — is one of the commonest reasons children undergo surgery, so a cheap steroid course that restored hearing would change practice. Older small trials hinted at short-term benefit but were underpowered and poor quality. The OSTRICH trial did the question properly: 389 children aged 2–8 with at least three months of effusion symptoms and confirmed bilateral hearing loss, randomised double-blind to a short course of oral prednisolone or placebo across 20 UK centres. At five weeks, acceptable hearing was found in 40% on steroids versus 33% on placebo — an absolute difference of 7% (95% CI −3 to 17), an adjusted odds ratio of 1.36 (0.88–2.11), p=0.16 — with no differences in adverse events or quality of life. A point estimate that leans the right way, a confidence interval that comfortably includes nothing: not a treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: OSTRICH: acceptable hearing at 5 weeks in 40% on prednisolone versus 33% on placebo (difference 7%, −3 to 17; p=0.16)
cards.summary: OSTRICH: acceptable hearing at 5 weeks in 40% on prednisolone versus 33% on placebo (difference 7%, −3 to 17; p=0.16)
cards.people: 389 children aged 2–8 years with symptoms attributable to otitis media with effusion for at least 3 months and confirmed bilateral hearing loss, recruited from 20 ENT, paediatric audiology and audiovestibular departments in England and Wales, randomised double-blind to oral prednisolone (n=200) or placebo (n=189); hearing assessed at 5 weeks in 363 children.
cards.result: Acceptable hearing was observed in 73/183 (40%) on steroids versus 59/180 (33%) on placebo: absolute difference 7% (95% CI −3 to 17), adjusted odds ratio 1.36 (0.88–2.11), p=0.16. No significant differences in adverse events or quality of life. Registry ID: ISRCTN49798431 (verified in the record).
cards.watchOut: Five weeks is the horizon that matters for the 'avoid surgery' hope, and the trial was powered for it; longer-term hearing was not the claim tested. Most effusion resolves on its own — the placebo group's 33% recovery is that natural history showing.
cards.source: Francis NA et al.. Oral steroids for resolution of otitis media with effusion in children (OSTRICH): a double-blinded, placebo-controlled randomised trial. The Lancet. 2018. PMID: 30152390. Registry ID: ISRCTN49798431. shelves.title: Behavioural sleep training for infant sleep problems
shelves.question: Do behavioural sleep-training techniques (controlled crying / graduated extinction, and bedtime fading) improve infant sleep problems, and are they safe for the child in the long term?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Behavior Therapy · Depression, Postpartum · Family Health · Female · Humans · Infant · Infant Care · Male · Mother-Child Relations · Mothers · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Regression Analysis
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — benefit is consistent across trials for the first months (sleep problems resolved in 53 of 76 vs 36 of 76 families in the largest early trial), and a five-year follow-up plus a small trial's cortisol and attachment measures give reasonable reassurance on harm. Parent-reported, unblindable outcomes, and a benefit that fades by four months as control babies mature, hold the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: A nurse-taught controlled-crying programme resolved more sleep problems at two months
cards.summary: A nurse-taught controlled-crying programme resolved more sleep problems at two months
cards.people: 156 mothers of infants aged 6–12 months with severe parent-reported sleep problems, Melbourne, Australia; behavioural intervention (controlled crying) over three consultations vs written information about normal sleep
cards.result: At two months, sleep problems had resolved in 53 of 76 intervention families vs 36 of 76 controls (P = 0.005); by four months the groups were similar. Among mothers with high depression scores, problems resolved in 26 of 33 vs 13 of 33 (P = 0.001), and depression scores fell further in the intervention group at two and four months.
cards.watchOut: Outcomes are mothers' reports, and mothers cannot be blinded to a behavioural intervention; the sleep advantage had faded by four months.
cards.source: Hiscock H et al.. Randomised controlled trial of behavioural infant sleep intervention to improve infant sleep and maternal mood. BMJ. 2002. PMID: 11991909. cards.result: No differences between intervention and control families on any measured outcome: children's emotional scores (P = 0.8) and conduct scores (P = 0.6), sleep problems (9% vs 7%, P = 0.2), psychosocial functioning, chronic stress, parent–child closeness or conflict, or maternal depression, anxiety and stress (all non-significant).
cards.watchOut: This follows the programme's later population-based trial (ISRCTN48752250), not the 2002 trial carded above; 31% of families were lost to follow-up.

cards.result: Behavioural sleep training works in the short term — problems resolve faster and maternal mood improves — but the advantage washes out by about four months as control babies mature, and the best long-term follow-up finds no trace of harm at age six. It is a tool for exhausted families now, not an intervention with lasting effects in either direction.
cards.watchOut: All trials rely on parent-reported sleep; none can blind parents to the intervention.

shelves.title: Vapour rub for children's night cough: one trial says it helps the whole family sleep — parents could smell the treatment
shelves.question: Does rubbing a vapour rub ointment on a child's chest and neck ease night-time cough and cold symptoms?
shelves.mesh: Antitussive Agents · Child · Child, Preschool · Common Cold · Cough · Double-Blind Method · Emollients · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Petrolatum · Respiratory Therapy · Steam · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE, Tier C — one partially blinded trial of 138 children found a single bedtime application of vapour rub beat both petrolatum and no treatment on parent-rated cough, congestion and sleep, while plain petrolatum beat nothing at all. It is a single trial, the outcomes are parents' ratings, and parents could smell which ointment their child received — so the shelf is Tier C and the stamp stops at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: 138 children: vapour rub beat no treatment on nearly every outcome, and beat petrolatum on cough and sleep
cards.summary: 138 children: vapour rub beat no treatment on nearly every outcome, and beat petrolatum on cough and sleep
cards.people: 138 children aged 2–11 years with upper respiratory infection; a single application before bedtime of vapour rub ointment, petrolatum ointment, or no treatment, allocated by partially double-blinded randomisation; parents rated symptoms over two consecutive nights
cards.result: Vapour rub scored best, and no treatment worst, for cough, congestion and sleep difficulty. Pairwise, vapour rub was superior to no treatment for all outcomes except rhinorrhea, and superior to petrolatum for cough severity, child and parent sleep difficulty, and the combined symptom score. Petrolatum was not significantly better than no treatment for any outcome. Irritant adverse effects (burning sensations of skin, nose or eyes) were more common with vapour rub.
cards.watchOut: Partially blinded at best: the rub's smell unblinds parents, and every outcome is a parent rating. The abstract does not name the brand of vapour rub tested, so no brand is named here. Single trial — Tier C.
cards.source: Paul IM et al.. Vapor rub, petrolatum, and no treatment for children with nocturnal cough and cold symptoms. Pediatrics. 2010. PMID: 21059712. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Newborn pulse-oximetry screening: catches about three-quarters to five-sixths of critical heart defects before discharge at a false-positive rate near 1 in 700 — and cannot see aortic arch obstruction
shelves.question: In newborns, does universal pulse-oximetry screening detect critical congenital heart disease before collapse?
shelves.mesh: False Positive Reactions · Heart Defects, Congenital/diagnosis/epidemiology · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Neonatal Screening/methods · Oximetry/methods · Physical Examination · Pilot Projects · Prospective Studies · Sweden/epidemiology
shelves.balance: Yes — with a defined blind spot. The meta-analysis of 13 studies (Thangaratinam 2012, PMID: 22554860; 229,421 babies) gives pulse oximetry a sensitivity of 76.5% and a specificity of 99.9% for critical congenital heart defects, with a false-positive rate of just 0.14% — and only 0.05% when screening is done after 24 hours of age. The Swedish prospective study (de-Wahl Granelli 2009, PMID: 19131383; 39,821 babies) found that oximetry plus examination detected 82.8% of duct-dependent circulation before discharge, and that babies in unscreened regions were far more likely to leave hospital undiagnosed (28% versus 8%; relative risk 3.36) — five died of undiagnosed lesions, versus none in the screened region. The lesions it misses are concentrated in aortic arch obstruction, where saturations can stay normal while the ductus is open. PROPOSED LIKELY (Tier C: observational evidence only — no randomised trial exists — but large, consistent, and mechanistically coherent).

cards.headline: de-Wahl Granelli 2009: adding pulse oximetry to the newborn examination raised detection of duct-dependent circulation to 82.8% in the nursery cohort — and babies in unscreened regions were far more likely to go home undiagnosed (28% versus 8%)
cards.summary: de-Wahl Granelli 2009: adding pulse oximetry to the newborn examination raised detection of duct-dependent circulation to 82.8% in the nursery cohort — and babies in unscreened regions were far more likely to go home undiagnosed (28% versus 8%)
cards.type: Prospective screening study with regional cohort comparison (de-Wahl Granelli 2009)
cards.people: Prospective screening study of 39,821 newborns in West Götaland, Sweden, with a cohort comparison against Swedish regions not using pulse-oximetry screening; outcomes include deaths at home with undetected duct-dependent circulation.
cards.result: Of 29 babies in well-baby nurseries with duct-dependent circulation missed by the discharge examination, pulse oximetry (saturation ≤90%) flagged 13, and examination alone caught 10 of the remaining 16 — combined sensitivity 82.8% (95% CI 64.2 to 95.2), and 100% for duct-dependent lung circulation; all 5 missed cases had aortic arch obstruction. The false-positive rate was 0.17% for oximetry versus 1.90% for examination alone, and nearly half the oximetry 'false positives' had other pathology. In the regional comparison, 28% of babies with duct-dependent circulation left hospital undiagnosed in unscreened regions versus 8% in West Götaland (relative risk 3.36, 1.37 to 8.24); five babies died of undiagnosed duct-dependent circulation in the unscreened regions and none in West Götaland.
cards.watchOut: The regional comparison is observational — regions differed in more than their screening policy, and the mortality contrast rests on five deaths. The test's blind spot is anatomical, not incidental: lesions obstructing the aortic arch with a patent ductus can saturate normally, which is why screening complements rather than replaces the examination and clinical vigilance.
cards.source: de-Wahl Granelli A et al. Impact of pulse oximetry screening on the detection of duct dependent congenital heart disease: a Swedish prospective screening study in 39,821 newborns. BMJ. 2009. PMID: 19131383. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Thangaratinam 2012: across 13 studies and 229,421 babies, pulse oximetry detected 76.5% of critical congenital heart defects at 99.9% specificity — false positives 0.14%, and five times fewer after 24 hours of age
cards.summary: Thangaratinam 2012: across 13 studies and 229,421 babies, pulse oximetry detected 76.5% of critical congenital heart defects at 99.9% specificity — false positives 0.14%, and five times fewer after 24 hours of age
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 accuracy studies of pulse oximetry for critical congenital heart defects in asymptomatic newborn babies, totalling 229,421 infants.
cards.result: Summary sensitivity was 76.5% (95% CI 67.7 to 83.5) and specificity 99.9% (99.7 to 99.9), with a false-positive rate of 0.14% (0.06 to 0.33). Timing mattered: the false-positive rate was 0.05% when screening was performed after 24 hours from birth versus 0.50% before 24 hours (P = 0.0017). The reviewers conclude the performance meets criteria for universal screening.
cards.watchOut: A 2012 synthesis: later studies and modern oximeters may shift the estimates, and 'critical congenital heart defects' is a wider basket than the duct-dependent lesions of the Swedish study, so the two sensitivities (76.5% and 82.8%) are not measuring identical targets. Sensitivity near three-quarters means a negative screen must never override a symptomatic baby's examination findings.
cards.source: Thangaratinam S et al. Pulse oximetry screening for critical congenital heart defects in asymptomatic newborn babies: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Lancet. 2012. cards.headline: Synthesis: about three-quarters to five-sixths of critical lesions are caught before discharge, at a false-positive price of roughly 1–2 babies per 1,000 screened
cards.summary: Synthesis: about three-quarters to five-sixths of critical lesions are caught before discharge, at a false-positive price of roughly 1–2 babies per 1,000 screened
cards.people: One large prospective screening study with a regional comparison (39,821 babies) and one meta-analysis of 13 studies (229,421 babies). No randomised trial exists or is likely — the comparison is against the examination alone and against unscreened regions.
cards.result: Sensitivity 76.5% (meta-analysis) to 82.8% (combined with examination, Swedish study); specificity 99.9%; false-positive rate 0.14–0.17%, falling to 0.05% when screening is done after 24 hours. In the Swedish comparison, undiagnosed discharge fell from 28% to 8% (relative risk 3.36 for unscreened regions, absolute rates given), and no baby died of an undiagnosed duct-dependent lesion in the screened region versus five in the unscreened regions.
cards.watchOut: The evidence is observational by necessity, and the effect on the hardest outcome — death before diagnosis — rests on small numbers in one country's comparison. What is not in doubt is the direction and the cheapness of the intervention; what a negative screen can never do is exclude arch obstruction or a lesion that declares after discharge.
cards.source: Synthesis of de-Wahl Granelli A et al. BMJ. 2009 (PMID: 19131383); Thangaratinam S et al. Lancet. 2012 (PMID: 22554860).
