shelves.title: A suppository before the journey: rectal artesunate halved death or disability when referral took more than six hours — and showed nothing when care was quick, or when the referral chain broke down in routine practice
shelves.question: In young children with severe malaria who cannot reach hospital quickly, does pre-referral rectal artesunate reduce death and disability?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Rectal · Adolescent · Adult · Antimalarials/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Artemisinins/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Artesunate · Child · Child, Preschool · Persons with Disabilities/statistics & numerical data · Female · Humans · Infant · Malaria, Falciparum/complications/drug therapy/mortality · Malaria, Vivax/complications/drug therapy/mortality · Male · Placebos/administration & dosage · Rural Health Services/organization & administration · Suppositories · Young Adult
shelves.balance: One very large trial, one crucial subgroup, and one sobering implementation lesson. Gomes 2009 randomised 17,826 patients with suspected severe malaria who could not be treated orally in Bangladesh, Ghana and Tanzania to a single rectal artesunate suppository or placebo before referral (12,068 analysed after exclusions). Overall, mortality was 2.5% versus 3.0% (p = 0.1 — not significant on its own), permanent disability was much rarer with artesunate (2 versus 13 patients), and the composite of death or permanent disability was significantly reduced: 2.6% versus 3.2% (p = 0.0484) (PMID: 19059639). The benefit was concentrated where the logic of the intervention says it should be: in patients who reached a clinic within about 6 hours there was no significant effect (death or disability 1.6% versus 1.9%, risk ratio 0.86), while in those still not in clinic after more than 6 hours — half of them still travelling after 15 hours — death or disability was halved, 1.9% versus 3.8% (risk ratio 0.49, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.77). There was no reduction in deaths within the first 6 hours: the suppository buys time, it does not rescue the already-moribund. The trial population was mostly young children, and guidelines subsequently adopted the intervention for young children facing long referral delays. But the CARAMAL roll-out across DR Congo, Nigeria and Uganda, following more than 6,200 severely ill children in routine practice, found no survival advantage — most likely, its investigators concluded, because referral was often incomplete and post-referral treatment inadequate: a suppository cannot compensate for a broken chain of care (PMID: 36549311). PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit when referral to injectable treatment takes many hours) / LIKELY (the treatment made no difference when patients reached care within about 6 hours, or in routine-practice roll-out with incomplete follow-up care) (Tier C: the efficacy claim rests on a single trial and its delay subgroup, and the real-world evidence is observational). Treatment of severe malaria once in hospital — intravenous artesunate — is a different question, homed at shelf #510.

cards.headline: Gomes 2009: 12,068 patients — death or permanent disability 2.6% versus 3.2% overall, and halved (1.9% vs 3.8%) in those still travelling after 6 hours
cards.summary: Gomes 2009: 12,068 patients — death or permanent disability 2.6% versus 3.2% overall, and halved (1.9% vs 3.8%) in those still travelling after 6 hours
cards.people: Placebo-controlled randomised trial in Bangladesh, Ghana and Tanzania of patients with suspected severe malaria who could not be treated orally, allocated to a single artesunate suppository (n = 8,954 randomised) or placebo suppository (n = 8,872) before referral to clinics where injections could be given. After excluding patients who had received antimalarial injections or had negative blood smears before randomisation, 12,068 patients (6,072 artesunate, 5,996 placebo) were analysed. Primary endpoints: mortality at 7–30 days and permanent disability. The population was predominantly young children in rural areas, though all ages unable to take oral treatment were eligible.
cards.result: Mortality was 154 of 6,072 on artesunate versus 177 of 5,996 on placebo (2.5% versus 3.0%, p = 0.1). Permanent disability occurred in 2 versus 13 patients (0.03% versus 0.22%, p = 0.0020). The composite of death or permanent disability was 156 versus 190 (2.6% versus 3.2%, p = 0.0484). There was no reduction in early mortality (56 versus 51 deaths within 6 hours). In patients reaching clinic within 6 hours (median 3 hours), artesunate had no significant effect on death after 6 hours or permanent disability (71/4,450 [1.6%] versus 82/4,426 [1.9%]; risk ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.18). In patients still not in clinic after more than 6 hours — half of whom were still not there after more than 15 hours — artesunate significantly reduced death or permanent disability (29/1,566 [1.9%] versus 57/1,519 [3.8%]; risk ratio 0.49, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.77; p = 0.0013).
cards.watchOut: Three cautions belong on the face of this result. First, mortality alone did not reach significance (p = 0.1) — the significant endpoint is the composite with permanent disability, and disability events were few (2 versus 13). Second, the headline benefit lives in the more-than-6-hours subgroup: pre-specified by the intervention's logic, but a subgroup nonetheless. Third, about a third of randomised patients were excluded from analysis (prior injections or negative smears), and 'suspected' severe malaria in a community setting is not the same population as confirmed severe malaria in hospital.
cards.source: Gomes MF et al. Pre-referral rectal artesunate to prevent death and disability in severe malaria: a placebo-controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2009. PMID: 19059639. Registry ID: ISRCTN83979018, 46343627, and 76987662 (registered in all three study countries, as printed in the record). cards.headline: CARAMAL (reported by Hetzel 2023): in routine roll-out across three African countries, more than 6,200 severely ill children given rectal artesunate had no better survival — the referral chain, not the drug, failed
cards.summary: CARAMAL (reported by Hetzel 2023): in routine roll-out across three African countries, more than 6,200 severely ill children given rectal artesunate had no better survival — the referral chain, not the drug, failed
cards.type: Review and implementation analysis of an observational roll-out (Hetzel 2023, reporting CARAMAL)
cards.people: Summary and analysis of the Community Access to Rectal Artesunate for Malaria (CARAMAL) project: a carefully monitored roll-out of quality-assured rectal artesunate into established community-based health systems in DR Congo, Nigeria and Uganda, with more than 6,200 severely ill children followed up 28 days after treatment initiation. Observational design.
cards.result: Children treated with pre-referral rectal artesunate in routine clinical practice did not have an increased chance of survival. The investigators attribute this most likely to shortfalls along the continuum of care: a substantial proportion of children did not receive comprehensive severe malaria care, either because referral to a secondary facility was incomplete or because post-referral treatment was incomplete. Their conclusion: rectal artesunate can save lives if patients receive adequate post-referral care, but without improving the entire continuum of care, promising interventions will fail to meet their full potential.
cards.watchOut: This is an observational implementation study reported in a review article, not a randomised comparison — sicker children may have been more likely to receive the suppository, and health-system differences between sites confound any survival comparison. Its weight is not 'the drug does not work' but 'the drug's trial benefit did not survive contact with real referral systems', which is a claim about delivery, not pharmacology.
cards.source: Hetzel MW et al. Pre-referral rectal artesunate: no cure for unhealthy systems. The Lancet. Infectious diseases. 2023. PMID: 36549311. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the suppository works exactly where pharmacology says it should — in the long journey — and nowhere else
cards.summary: Synthesis: the suppository works exactly where pharmacology says it should — in the long journey — and nowhere else
cards.people: One placebo-controlled trial of 12,068 analysed patients (Gomes 2009) and one three-country observational implementation study of more than 6,200 children (CARAMAL, reported by Hetzel 2023).
cards.result: Death or permanent disability: 2.6% versus 3.2% overall (absolute reduction about 0.6 percentage points); 1.9% versus 3.8% (risk ratio 0.49) when arrival at injectable treatment took more than 6 hours; no significant effect (risk ratio 0.86, CI spanning 1) when it took less; no effect on deaths within the first 6 hours. In routine practice with incomplete referral and post-referral care, no survival advantage was detectable at all. The intervention is a bridge, and a bridge only helps if there is something on the other side.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the overall composite without the subgroup structure: averaged over all referral times the absolute gain is about 6 per 1,000 treated, concentrated entirely in long-delay journeys. Nor should the CARAMAL result be read as a reason to withhold the drug where referral is long and the receiving facility functions — it is a reason to fix the chain, and it post-dates and does not overturn the randomised evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gomes MF et al. Lancet. 2009 (PMID: 19059639); Hetzel MW et al. The Lancet Infectious Diseases. 2023 (PMID: 36549311).

shelves.title: Short antibiotics and early oral switch in childhood bone and joint infection: 10 days cured septic arthritis and 20 days cured osteomyelitis in the Finnish randomised trials, with intravenous treatment only for the first 2–4 days
shelves.question: In children with septic arthritis or acute osteomyelitis, are short antibiotic courses with an early switch from intravenous to oral treatment safe?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage*/therapeutic use* · Arthritis, Infectious/drug therapy* · C-Reactive Protein/analysis · Cephalosporins/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Child · Child, Preschool · Clindamycin/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Female · Finland · Haemophilus influenzae/isolation & purification · Humans · Infant · Male · Prospective Studies · Staphylococcus aureus/isolation & purification · Streptococcus pyogenes/isolation & purification · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (no difference, within the studied conditions): Two randomised trials from one Finnish programme tested shorter against conventional durations, with antibiotics stopped on clinical response plus a falling C-reactive protein (CRP). For septic arthritis, 130 culture-positive children received 10 or 30 days of clindamycin or a first-generation cephalosporin, intravenous for only the first 2–4 days; every child recovered without sequelae (Peltola H et al., PMID: 19323633). For acute haematogenous osteomyelitis, 131 culture-positive children received 20 or 30 days on the same template; all but one child in each group recovered entirely, the exceptions being one mild sequela in each group (Peltola H et al., PMID: 20842069). The programme's prospective cohort of 265 cases (1983–2005) shows the same approach in routine practice: mean intravenous duration 4 days, hospital stay falling from 13 to 9 days, and sequelae rates unchanged (Pääkkönen M et al., PMID: 22568753). The conditions matter: these were culture-positive infections in a setting where Staphylococcus aureus was overwhelmingly methicillin-susceptible (89% of the osteomyelitis cases, all MSSA), surgery was kept to a minimum, and stopping was CRP-guided — the results cannot simply be assumed for MRSA, neonates, immunocompromised children, or infections responding slowly. Tier C: a single research programme in one low-resistance setting.

cards.headline: Peltola 2009: 10 days of antibiotics cured childhood septic arthritis as completely as 30 days — all 130 children recovered without sequelae, with only 2–4 days intravenous
cards.summary: Peltola 2009: 10 days of antibiotics cured childhood septic arthritis as completely as 30 days — all 130 children recovered without sequelae, with only 2–4 days intravenous
cards.people: 130 children aged 3 months to 15 years with culture-positive septic arthritis in a Finnish multicentre randomised trial; 63 received 10 days and 67 received 30 days of clindamycin or a first-generation cephalosporin, given intravenously for the first 2–4 days. Staphylococcus aureus, Haemophilus influenzae and Streptococcus pyogenes caused 88% of cases. Antibiotics were discontinued when the clinical response was good and CRP had decreased to 20 mg/L; the primary endpoint was full recovery without further antibiotics for an osteoarticular indication during the 12 months after therapy.
cards.result: Median treatment durations were 10 and 30 days as assigned. Surgical procedures beyond percutaneous joint aspiration were performed in only 12% of patients, with no excess in hip or shoulder arthritis. Two late-onset infections occurred in one child in the long-term group; all patients recovered without sequelae. The authors conclude that large doses of well-absorbed antimicrobials for under 2 weeks (initially intravenous) and only one joint aspiration are sufficient for most childhood septic arthritis, provided the clinical response is good and CRP normalises shortly after treatment starts.
cards.watchOut: Culture-positive cases only, in a low-resistance setting and era (Haemophilus influenzae type b was still circulating and has since been vaccine-eliminated there). The trial does not cover neonates, MRSA, or children whose CRP falls slowly — the stopping rule was response-guided, not a fixed calendar promise.
cards.source: Peltola H et al. Prospective, randomized trial of 10 days versus 30 days of antimicrobial treatment, including a short-term course of parenteral therapy, for childhood septic arthritis. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2009. PMID: 19323633. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Peltola 2010: 20 days cured childhood osteomyelitis as completely as 30 days — one mild sequela in each group, intravenous phase again only 2–4 days
cards.summary: Peltola 2010: 20 days cured childhood osteomyelitis as completely as 30 days — one mild sequela in each group, intravenous phase again only 2–4 days
cards.people: 131 children aged 3 months to 15 years with culture-positive acute haematogenous osteomyelitis in a Finnish randomised trial; 67 received 20 days and 64 received 30 days of clindamycin or a first-generation cephalosporin, intravenous for the first 2–4 days, with surgery kept to a minimum. Staphylococcus aureus caused 89% of cases and all strains were methicillin-susceptible; 18% also involved the adjacent joint. Antibiotics were discontinued once most signs had subsided and CRP had decreased to ≤20 mg/L; the endpoint was full recovery without further antibiotics during 12 months.
cards.result: Except for one mild sequela in each treatment group, all patients recovered entirely. Most children underwent only diagnostic percutaneous aspiration or drilling, and 24% had no surgery at all. The authors conclude that most cases of childhood osteomyelitis can be treated for 20 days, including a short intravenous period, with large doses of a well-absorbed antimicrobial, provided the clinical response is good and CRP normalises within 7 to 10 days.
cards.watchOut: Every S. aureus strain was methicillin-susceptible — the trial's largest transportability limit. It also says nothing about culture-negative disease, chronic osteomyelitis, or slow responders: the protocol's safety came from its monitoring and stopping rules, not from the number 20 alone.
cards.source: Peltola H et al. Short- versus long-term antimicrobial treatment for acute hematogenous osteomyelitis of childhood: prospective, randomized trial on 131 culture-positive cases. The Pediatric Infectious Disease Journal. 2010. PMID: 20842069. Registry ID: ISRCTN38832979 (verified against the record). cards.headline: Pääkkönen 2012: the programme's 265-case prospective series — intravenous antibiotics averaged 4 days and hospital stay fell from 13 to 9 days with no rise in sequelae
cards.summary: Pääkkönen 2012: the programme's 265-case prospective series — intravenous antibiotics averaged 4 days and hospital stay fell from 13 to 9 days with no rise in sequelae
cards.type: Prospective cohort analysis of the same Finnish programme (Pääkkönen 2012)
cards.people: 265 prospectively collected culture-positive cases of bone and joint infection in Finnish children (1983–2005), managed under the same programme as the two trials (cards 1–2), with protocol-defined treatment durations, surgery extent, and CRP-guided discharge decisions. This is the trials' parent cohort, not an independent test of the durations.
cards.result: Staphylococcus aureus was the commonest causative agent throughout, while Haemophilus influenzae type b was eliminated soon after vaccination was introduced. The time from symptoms to presentation (4 days), disease severity, CRP and the rate of sequelae did not change significantly over the period; the mean duration of intravenous antibiotics was only 4 days, and average hospital stay shortened from 13 to 9 days (P = 0.0001).
cards.watchOut: A 22-year before-and-after practice analysis: shorter stays track the programme's simplified treatment, but secular changes in care cannot be separated from the protocol's effect. Its value is showing that the trial approach survived contact with routine practice.
cards.source: Pääkkönen M et al. Shortened hospital stay for childhood bone and joint infections: analysis of 265 prospectively collected culture-positive cases in 1983-2005. Scandinavian Journal of Infectious Diseases. 2012. PMID: 22568753. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: in culture-positive, promptly responding childhood bone and joint infection, 10 days (joint) and 20 days (bone) with 2–4 intravenous days matched 30-day courses — recovery was complete in both arms
cards.summary: Synthesis: in culture-positive, promptly responding childhood bone and joint infection, 10 days (joint) and 20 days (bone) with 2–4 intravenous days matched 30-day courses — recovery was complete in both arms
cards.people: Two randomised trials (130 children with septic arthritis; 131 with osteomyelitis) and the 265-case prospective programme cohort behind them.
cards.result: Septic arthritis: all 130 children recovered without sequelae on 10 or on 30 days. Osteomyelitis: one mild sequela in each arm (20 vs 30 days) and every other child recovered entirely. Programme-wide, intravenous treatment averaged 4 days and hospital stay fell by four days without more sequelae.
cards.watchOut: The whole evidence base is one Finnish programme in methicillin-susceptible staphylococcal disease, with CRP-guided stopping and minimal surgery. Which agent to use (clindamycin versus a first-generation cephalosporin) was tested in a companion quasi-randomised trial of the same programme (Peltola H et al., PMID: 22011265), cross-referenced here and not carded. Settings where MRSA is prevalent, and children who respond slowly, sit outside this evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Peltola H et al. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2009 (PMID: 19323633); Peltola H et al. The Pediatric Infectious Disease Journal. 2010 (PMID: 20842069); Pääkkönen M et al. Scandinavian Journal of Infectious Diseases. 2012 (PMID: 22568753).

shelves.title: Parent training in ADHD: parenting and conduct problems clearly improve — the effect on core symptoms fades when the raters are blinded
shelves.question: In children with ADHD, does parent behaviour training improve symptoms and parenting versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Attention Deficit Disorder with Hyperactivity/diagnosis/psychology/therapy* · Behavior Therapy · Central Nervous System Stimulants/therapeutic use* · Child · Child, Preschool · Cognition Disorders/diagnosis/psychology/therapy · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Combined Modality Therapy · Diet Therapy* · Fatty Acids, Nonesterified/administration & dosage · Food Coloring Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Food Hypersensitivity/complications/therapy · Humans · Neurofeedback · Psychotherapy* · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: SPLIT — what parent training changes depends on who is rating, and on what is being rated. The broadest synthesis (Sonuga-Barke EJ et al., PMID: 23360949) found psychological treatments, behavioural interventions among them, produced significant effects on ADHD symptoms when rated by those closest to treatment (standardised mean differences 0.40 to 0.64), but the effects attenuated to non-significance when the best probably blinded assessments were used. Daley D et al. (PMID: 25062591) show where the blinded evidence does hold: across 32 randomised trials, probably blinded ratings still showed improved positive parenting (SMD 0.63), less negative parenting (SMD 0.43) and fewer conduct problems (SMD 0.31), while the core-symptom effect did not persist. The Cochrane review of parent training specifically (Zwi M et al., PMID: 22161373) is the cautionary base: only five trials and 284 children, unclear-to-high risk of bias, a non-significant pooled effect on externalising behaviour (SMD −0.32, 95% CI −0.83 to 0.18) and a significant one on internalising behaviour (SMD −0.48, −0.84 to −0.13). PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit) for parenting quality and conduct problems, which survive blinding / MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) for core ADHD symptoms, where the blinded evidence is null. Stimulant-versus-behavioural treatment comparisons are homed at shelf #643.

cards.headline: Sonuga-Barke 2013: non-drug ADHD treatments look effective through unblinded eyes — with probably blinded ratings, the behavioural effect on core symptoms attenuates to non-significance
cards.summary: Sonuga-Barke 2013: non-drug ADHD treatments look effective through unblinded eyes — with probably blinded ratings, the behavioural effect on core symptoms attenuates to non-significance
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analyses of 54 RCTs (Sonuga-Barke 2013)
cards.people: Fifty-four randomised trials of dietary treatments (restricted elimination diets, artificial food colour exclusions, free fatty acid supplementation) and psychological treatments (cognitive training, neurofeedback, behavioural interventions) in people diagnosed with ADHD or meeting a validated rating-scale cutoff. Every outcome was analysed twice: as rated by those closest to the therapeutic setting, and by the best probably blinded assessment.
cards.result: With ratings from those closest to treatment, all dietary treatments (standardised mean differences 0.21 to 0.48) and all psychological treatments (0.40 to 0.64) produced statistically significant effects on ADHD symptoms. With probably blinded assessments, effects remained significant only for free fatty acid supplementation (SMD 0.16) and artificial food colour exclusion (SMD 0.42); for behavioural interventions, neurofeedback, cognitive training and restricted elimination diets the effects were substantially attenuated to non-significant levels. The authors conclude that better blinded evidence is required before behavioural interventions can be supported as treatments for core ADHD symptoms.
cards.watchOut: The blinded-versus-unblinded contrast is the whole story of this literature: the same trials read as clearly positive or as null depending on whether the rater knew the child had been treated. The food-colour result, the largest blinded effect, often came from children selected for food sensitivities, so it does not generalise to unselected ADHD.
cards.source: Sonuga-Barke EJ et al. Nonpharmacological interventions for ADHD: systematic review and meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials of dietary and psychological treatments. cards.headline: Daley 2014 (32 trials): behavioural interventions improve parenting and conduct even on probably blinded ratings — positive parenting SMD 0.63, conduct problems 0.31
cards.summary: Daley 2014 (32 trials): behavioural interventions improve parenting and conduct even on probably blinded ratings — positive parenting SMD 0.63, conduct problems 0.31
cards.people: Thirty-two randomised trials of behavioural interventions in children and adolescents diagnosed with ADHD (or meeting validated rating-scale cutoffs), analysed across a broader range of child and parent outcomes than symptoms alone: parenting quality and self-concept, conduct problems, social skills and academic performance.
cards.result: On ratings by those closest to treatment (usually unblinded), behavioural interventions improved positive parenting (SMD 0.68), negative parenting (0.57), parenting self-concept (0.37), child ADHD symptoms (0.35), conduct problems (0.26), social skills (0.47) and academic performance (0.28). With probably blinded assessments, significant effects persisted for positive parenting (SMD 0.63), negative parenting (0.43) and conduct problems (0.31) — but not for core ADHD symptoms. Parent mental well-being did not improve.
cards.watchOut: The blinded positives are parenting and conduct, not symptoms — and parenting outcomes are still largely reported by the parents who delivered the intervention, so 'probably blinded' is doing real work in that sentence. What this review establishes is that behaviour therapy changes the family's functioning around the child; whether it changes the child's core symptoms is the question it could not answer positively.

cards.headline: Zwi 2011 (Cochrane, 5 trials, 284 children): the parent-training trial base is thin and mixed — externalising behaviour SMD −0.32, not significant
cards.summary: Zwi 2011 (Cochrane, 5 trials, 284 children): the parent-training trial base is thin and mixed — externalising behaviour SMD −0.32, not significant
cards.people: Five randomised trials (284 participants aged 5 to 18 years with a specialist diagnosis of ADHD) comparing parent training with de facto treatment as usual; one study added a nondirective parent support group as a second control. Four trials targeted children's behaviour and one assessed parenting skills. Outcome assessors were most often the parents who had delivered the intervention, so assessor blinding was impossible.
cards.result: Meta-analysis of three studies (n = 190) for child externalising behaviour fell short of significance (SMD −0.32, 95% CI −0.83 to 0.18, I² = 60%); two studies (n = 142) for internalising behaviour favoured parent training (SMD −0.48, 95% CI −0.84 to −0.13). Parent stress improved on the 'child' domain (mean difference −10.52, 95% CI −20.55 to −0.48) but not the 'parent' domain. Individual trials disagreed with each other at home and at school. No study reported academic achievement or adverse events. Risk of bias was unclear at best and often high, and the reviewers conclude the evidence is not strong enough to form a basis for clinical practice guidelines.
cards.watchOut: Cochrane's caution and Daley's broader pool are reconciled by outcome and scope: Cochrane asked about child behaviour in five small parent-training trials, while Daley's blinded positives are parenting and conduct across 32 behavioural-intervention trials. Both agree on the point that matters most — no blinded demonstration of an effect on core ADHD symptoms.

cards.headline: Synthesis: blinded evidence supports better parenting and fewer conduct problems — core-symptom benefit unproven (SPLIT)
cards.summary: Synthesis: blinded evidence supports better parenting and fewer conduct problems — core-symptom benefit unproven (SPLIT)
cards.people: Three syntheses: 54 trials of all non-drug ADHD treatments (Sonuga-Barke 2013), 32 behavioural-intervention trials with a wide outcome net (Daley 2014), and the 5-trial Cochrane review of parent training specifically (Zwi 2011).
cards.result: Unblinded ratings say behavioural treatment works for symptoms (SMDs 0.35 to 0.64); blinded ratings say it works for parenting quality (positive parenting 0.63, negative parenting 0.43) and conduct problems (0.31), and are silent-to-null on core symptoms; the Cochrane pool of parent-training trials alone is small, mixed and at unclear-to-high risk of bias. PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit) for parenting quality and conduct problems / MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) for core ADHD symptoms.
cards.watchOut: Parent training is a family intervention with family-level evidence; it should not be sold to parents as a treatment for the core symptoms themselves. How behavioural treatment compares and combines with stimulant medication is a different question, homed at shelf #643. The trials describe behavioural parent-training programmes generically; no specific named programme is singled out by this evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Sonuga-Barke EJ et al. The American Journal of Psychiatry. 2013 (PMID: 23360949); Daley D et al. Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry. 2014 (PMID: 25062591); Zwi M et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2011 (PMID: 22161373).

shelves.title: Neurofeedback for ADHD: parent ratings improve, blinded ratings and sham controls say no — the effect lives where blinding doesn't
shelves.question: In ADHD, does neurofeedback improve core symptoms versus sham or medication?
shelves.mesh: Attention Deficit Disorder with Hyperactivity/therapy* · Humans · Neurofeedback/methods* · Outcome Assessment, Health Care/statistics & numerical data* · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic/statistics & numerical data*
shelves.balance: SPLIT — neurofeedback's evidence divides cleanly along the blinding line. Cortese S et al. (PMID: 27238063), pooling 13 trials and 520 participants, found significant effects on ADHD symptoms only on the least blinded ratings — total symptoms SMD 0.35 (95% CI 0.11 to 0.59) — with no significant effect on probably blinded ratings and none in trials with active or sham controls; laboratory measures of attention and inhibition were also null, and only 4 studies checked that children had actually learned the EEG skill. Micoulaud-Franchi JA et al. (PMID: 25431555) found the same shape in 5 trials: parent (probably unblinded) ratings improved across all domains (overall SMD −0.49), while teacher (probably blinded) ratings improved only for inattention (−0.30). The one double-blind placebo-controlled trial, Vollebregt MA et al. (PMID: 24168522; 41 children, 30 sessions), found no effect on any neurocognitive measure. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) on unblinded parent ratings / LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) on blinded ratings, against sham, and for neurocognitive outcomes. No carded trial compares neurofeedback with medication head-to-head, so the 'versus medication' half of the question has no direct evidence.

cards.headline: Cortese 2016 (13 trials, 520 participants): neurofeedback improves ADHD symptoms on the least blinded ratings (SMD 0.35) — not on probably blinded ratings, and not against sham controls
cards.summary: Cortese 2016 (13 trials, 520 participants): neurofeedback improves ADHD symptoms on the least blinded ratings (SMD 0.35) — not on probably blinded ratings, and not against sham controls
cards.people: Thirteen randomised controlled trials (520 participants with ADHD, children and adolescents) of neurofeedback, analysed by outcome-rater blinding: assessors most proximal to the treatment setting (the least blinded measure), probably blinded ratings, and trials with active or sham controls; laboratory measures of inhibition and attention were also pooled.
cards.result: Significant effects appeared only on the least blinded ratings: ADHD total symptoms SMD 0.35 (95% CI 0.11 to 0.59), inattention 0.36 (0.09 to 0.63), hyperactivity/impulsivity 0.26 (0.08 to 0.43). Effects were not significant when probably blinded ratings were the outcome, nor in trials with active/sham controls. Laboratory measures were null: inhibition SMD 0.30 (−0.10 to 0.70), attention 0.13 (−0.09 to 0.36). Only 4 of the 13 studies directly assessed whether the child had actually learned to regulate the trained EEG signal. The authors conclude that evidence from well-controlled trials with probably blinded outcomes currently fails to support neurofeedback as an effective treatment for ADHD.
cards.watchOut: The positive number and the null number in this review come from the same trials — the difference is entirely who held the rating scale. A treatment whose effect is visible only to people who know it was given has not separated itself from expectation, effort and attention-placebo effects, and most trials never verified the one thing that would make the mechanism credible: that the child learned the EEG skill.
cards.source: Cortese S et al. Neurofeedback for Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: Meta-Analysis of Clinical and Neuropsychological Outcomes From Randomized Controlled Trials. Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry. 2016. PMID: 27238063. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Micoulaud-Franchi 2014 (5 trials, 263 children): parent ratings improve across all symptom domains — teacher ratings improve only for inattention (SMD −0.30)
cards.summary: Micoulaud-Franchi 2014 (5 trials, 263 children): parent ratings improve across all symptom domains — teacher ratings improve only for inattention (SMD −0.30)
cards.people: Five randomised trials of EEG neurofeedback in 263 children with ADHD (146 trained with neurofeedback), restricted to trials with semi-active or sham-neurofeedback control groups. Outcomes were split by rater: parent assessment (probably unblinded) and teacher assessment (probably blinded). Negative standardised mean differences favour neurofeedback.
cards.result: On parent assessment, overall ADHD score improved (SMD −0.49, 95% CI −0.74 to −0.24), as did inattention (−0.46, −0.76 to −0.15) and hyperactivity/impulsivity (−0.34, −0.59 to −0.09). On teacher assessment, only the inattention score improved significantly (−0.30, −0.58 to −0.03); overall and hyperactivity/impulsivity scores did not. The authors highlight the inattention dimension and call for adequately blinded studies with carefully controlled protocols.
cards.watchOut: This is the most favourable fair reading of the neurofeedback literature, and even here the blinded (teacher) signal narrows to a single domain in five small trials. The record carries no MeSH terms — the card states that plainly rather than borrowing terms from neighbouring records.

cards.headline: Vollebregt 2014: the double-blind placebo-controlled trial — 41 children, 30 sessions of real versus placebo neurofeedback, no effect on any neurocognitive measure
cards.summary: Vollebregt 2014: the double-blind placebo-controlled trial — 41 children, 30 sessions of real versus placebo neurofeedback, no effect on any neurocognitive measure
cards.type: Double-blind placebo-controlled RCT with systematic review (Vollebregt 2014)
cards.people: Forty-one children aged 8 to 15 years with a DSM-IV-TR diagnosis of ADHD, randomised to EEG neurofeedback or placebo neurofeedback for 30 sessions twice a week, stratified by age, electrophysiological arousal state and medication use. Children, parents, teachers and researchers were all blind to allocation (only the neurofeedback therapist was not). Outcomes were pre/post neurocognitive tests of attention, executive functioning, working memory and time processing; the paper pairs the trial with a systematic review of neurocognition.
cards.result: No significant treatment effect was found on any neurocognitive variable. The accompanying systematic review likewise found no systematic beneficial effect of EEG neurofeedback on neurocognitive functioning. The authors conclude that the existing literature and this study fail to support any benefit of neurofeedback on neurocognitive functioning in ADHD, while noting small sample sizes and other limitations.
cards.watchOut: Forty-one children is a small trial, and absence of evidence here is not proof of absence — but this is the design the field's positive claims have to survive, and on objective cognitive outcomes nothing survived. Symptom ratings were not this trial's outcome; the symptom-rating question under blinding is answered by Cortese 2016, carded on this shelf, and it is also null.
cards.source: Vollebregt MA et al. Does EEG-neurofeedback improve neurocognitive functioning in children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder? cards.headline: Synthesis: the effect lives exactly where blinding doesn't — SPLIT (possible on parent ratings / no difference blinded and sham-controlled)
cards.summary: Synthesis: the effect lives exactly where blinding doesn't — SPLIT (possible on parent ratings / no difference blinded and sham-controlled)
cards.people: Two meta-analyses split by rater blinding (Cortese 2016, 13 trials, 520 participants; Micoulaud-Franchi 2014, 5 trials, 263 children) and the one double-blind placebo-controlled trial with objective outcomes (Vollebregt 2014, 41 children).
cards.result: Unblinded parent ratings improve (SMDs 0.35, or −0.49 on the reverse sign convention); probably blinded ratings are null for total symptoms in the larger analysis and narrow to inattention alone (−0.30) in the smaller; against sham controls the effect is not significant; objective neurocognitive testing under full double-blind conditions shows no effect at all. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (benefit) on unblinded parent ratings / LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) on blinded ratings, against sham, and for neurocognitive outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Neurofeedback is typically sold as a course of dozens of sessions at substantial cost, often positioned as an alternative to medication. The evidence carded here does not support that positioning: whatever families are buying, the blinded literature cannot distinguish it from the attention and expectation that surround it. Medication comparisons are not part of this shelf — no carded trial compares neurofeedback with stimulants head-to-head.

shelves.title: Tiotropium add-on in paediatric asthma: lung function improves by roughly 90–175 mL across four placebo-controlled trials — symptom-control gains are trends, not proof
shelves.question: In children and adolescents with asthma not controlled on standard inhalers, does tiotropium add-on improve lung function and control?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adrenal Cortex Hormones/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Anti-Asthmatic Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Area Under Curve · Asthma/diagnosis/drug therapy* · Child · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Forced Expiratory Volume/drug effects · Humans · Male · Risk Factors · Severity of Illness Index · Tiotropium Bromide/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The paediatric tiotropium programme is unusually complete: four double-blind placebo-controlled trials spanning ages 1 to 17, all as add-on to inhaled corticosteroids with or without other controllers. In adolescents with moderate asthma, peak FEV1 improved by 174 mL on 5 µg and 134 mL on 2.5 µg over placebo at 24 weeks (Hamelmann E et al., PMID: 26960245). In adolescents with severe asthma the primary endpoint was missed at 5 µg (90 mL, p = 0.104) and met at 2.5 µg (111 mL, p = 0.046), with numerical trough and control gains (Hamelmann E et al., PMID: 27811070). In children aged 6–11 with severe asthma, 5 µg improved peak FEV1 by 139 mL and trough FEV1 by 87 mL, while 2.5 µg did neither (Szefler SJ et al., PMID: 28189771). In children aged 1–5, an exploratory 102-child trial found symptom scores no different from placebo, with tolerability comparable to placebo (Vrijlandt EJLE et al., PMID: 29361462). PROPOSED LIKELY — benefit for lung function as add-on therapy in children aged 6–17; asthma-control effects are trends rather than demonstrated benefits, and efficacy under age 6 is unproven. The adult triple-therapy question is homed at shelf #1033.

cards.headline: Hamelmann 2016 (398 adolescents, 48 weeks): tiotropium added to inhaled corticosteroids improves peak FEV1 by 174 mL (5 µg) and 134 mL (2.5 µg) over placebo
cards.summary: Hamelmann 2016 (398 adolescents, 48 weeks): tiotropium added to inhaled corticosteroids improves peak FEV1 by 174 mL (5 µg) and 134 mL (2.5 µg) over placebo
cards.type: Phase III randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Hamelmann 2016)
cards.people: 398 patients aged 12 to 17 years with moderate symptomatic asthma, randomised double-blind to once-daily tiotropium 5 µg or 2.5 µg (Respimat inhaler, every evening) or placebo, each added to inhaled corticosteroid maintenance therapy with or without a leukotriene receptor antagonist; long-acting beta-agonists were not permitted. Primary endpoint: peak FEV1 within 3 hours after dosing at week 24 of the 48-week trial.
cards.result: Both doses significantly improved peak FEV1 at week 24 versus placebo: 5 µg by 174 mL (95% CI 76 to 272 mL) and 2.5 µg by 134 mL (34 to 234 mL). Trough FEV1 at week 24 improved significantly with the 5 µg dose only. Trends for improvement in asthma control and health-related quality of life were observed over 48 weeks. Tiotropium was safe and well tolerated; the larger responses were with the 5 µg dose.
cards.watchOut: The hard endpoint here is a spirometry number at 24 weeks, not exacerbations or hospitalisations — neither this trial nor its siblings were powered for the events families actually fear. The control and quality-of-life signals are described by the authors themselves as trends.
cards.source: Hamelmann E et al. Tiotropium add-on therapy in adolescents with moderate asthma: A 1-year randomized controlled trial. The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology. 2016. cards.headline: Hamelmann 2017 (392 adolescents with severe asthma, 12 weeks): the primary endpoint was missed at 5 µg (90 mL, p = 0.104) and met at 2.5 µg (111 mL, p = 0.046)
cards.summary: Hamelmann 2017 (392 adolescents with severe asthma, 12 weeks): the primary endpoint was missed at 5 µg (90 mL, p = 0.104) and met at 2.5 µg (111 mL, p = 0.046)
cards.people: 392 patients aged 12 to 17 years with severe symptomatic asthma, randomised double-blind to once-daily tiotropium 5 µg or 2.5 µg or placebo, added to inhaled corticosteroids plus one or more other controller therapies, for 12 weeks. Primary endpoint: change in peak FEV1 within 3 hours post-dosing; key secondary: trough FEV1.
cards.result: Tiotropium 5 µg gave numerical improvement in peak FEV1 response versus placebo (90 mL; p = 0.104 — the primary endpoint was not met), while 2.5 µg reached significance (111 mL; p = 0.046). Numerical improvements in trough FEV1 and asthma control were observed with both doses. Safety and tolerability were comparable with placebo. The authors describe positive trends for lung function and asthma control rather than a demonstrated control benefit.
cards.watchOut: An inverted dose pattern — the higher dose missing its endpoint while the lower dose makes it — is what sampling noise looks like, and it caps how confident anyone should be about dose selection in adolescents. The honest summary of this trial is 'direction consistent, endpoint missed', which is why this shelf's stamp rests on the programme as a whole rather than on any single trial.

cards.headline: Szefler 2017 (401 children aged 6–11 with severe asthma, 12 weeks): tiotropium 5 µg improves peak FEV1 by 139 mL (P < .001) and trough FEV1 by 87 mL — the 2.5 µg dose does neither
cards.summary: Szefler 2017 (401 children aged 6–11 with severe asthma, 12 weeks): tiotropium 5 µg improves peak FEV1 by 139 mL (P < .001) and trough FEV1 by 87 mL — the 2.5 µg dose does neither
cards.type: Phase III randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Szefler 2017)
cards.people: 401 participants aged 6 to 11 years with severe symptomatic asthma, randomised double-blind to once-daily tiotropium 5 µg or 2.5 µg or placebo (Respimat), added to high-dose inhaled corticosteroids with one or more controller medications, or medium-dose corticosteroids with two or more controllers, for 12 weeks. Primary endpoint: peak FEV1 within 3 hours after dosing; key secondary: trough FEV1.
cards.result: Tiotropium 5 µg improved peak FEV1 versus placebo by 139 mL (95% CI 75 to 203; P < .001) and trough FEV1 by 87 mL (19 to 154; P = .01). The 2.5 µg dose did not (peak 35 mL, −28 to 99, P = .27; trough 18 mL, −48 to 85, P = .59). Safety and tolerability were comparable with placebo. The authors conclude the 5 µg dose improved lung function and was well tolerated as add-on therapy.
cards.watchOut: The record for this trial carries no registry ID — the card says so rather than supplying one from outside the record. As with the adolescent trials, the demonstrated benefit is spirometric over 12 weeks; exacerbation prevention in children is not what these trials measured.
cards.source: Szefler SJ et al. A phase III randomized controlled trial of tiotropium add-on therapy in children with severe symptomatic asthma. The Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology. 2017. PMID: 28189771. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Vrijlandt 2018 (102 children aged 1–5): symptom scores do not differ from placebo in this small exploratory trial — exacerbations reported as adverse events were fewer on tiotropium (6–14% vs 29%)
cards.summary: Vrijlandt 2018 (102 children aged 1–5): symptom scores do not differ from placebo in this small exploratory trial — exacerbations reported as adverse events were fewer on tiotropium (6–14% vs 29%)
cards.type: Exploratory phase 2/3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Vrijlandt 2018)
cards.people: 102 children aged 1 to 5 years with at least a 6-month history of persistent asthmatic symptoms requiring inhaled corticosteroids, randomised double-blind at 32 centres in 11 countries to once-daily tiotropium 2.5 µg, tiotropium 5 µg or placebo (Respimat), added to corticosteroids with or without additional controllers, for 12 weeks. The trial was exploratory: endpoints were defined but analysed descriptively only.
cards.result: Weekly mean combined daytime asthma symptom scores did not differ significantly between groups: adjusted mean difference versus placebo −0.080 (95% CI −0.312 to 0.152) for 2.5 µg and −0.048 (−0.292 to 0.195) for 5 µg. Adverse events were less frequent on tiotropium (56% and 58%) than placebo (74%), with no formal statistical comparison; asthma exacerbations reported as adverse events occurred in 29% of the placebo group versus 14% (2.5 µg) and 6% (5 µg). All three serious adverse events were in the placebo group; no adverse event led to discontinuation or death. The authors stress the small sample and descriptive analysis and call for adequately powered trials in this age group.
cards.watchOut: This trial answers a safety question, not an efficacy one — it was designed and analysed descriptively, and its symptom outcome is null. The exacerbation gap (29% versus 6–14%) is the kind of unpowered, unadjusted signal that generates hypotheses; quoting it as protection would overstate a 102-child exploratory study.
cards.source: Vrijlandt EJLE et al. Safety and efficacy of tiotropium in children aged 1-5 years with persistent asthmatic symptoms: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. The Lancet Respiratory Medicine. 2018. PMID: 29361462. Registry ID: NCT01634113. cards.headline: Synthesis: a consistent spirometric benefit of about 90–175 mL in children 6 and over — LIKELY for lung function, unproven for control and for the under-6s
cards.summary: Synthesis: a consistent spirometric benefit of about 90–175 mL in children 6 and over — LIKELY for lung function, unproven for control and for the under-6s
cards.people: Four placebo-controlled trials in the paediatric tiotropium programme: 398 adolescents with moderate asthma over 48 weeks (Hamelmann 2016), 392 adolescents with severe asthma (Hamelmann 2017), 401 children aged 6–11 with severe asthma (Szefler 2017), and 102 children aged 1–5 in an exploratory safety trial (Vrijlandt 2018).
cards.result: In children aged 6 and over, add-on tiotropium improves peak FEV1 by roughly 90 to 175 mL over placebo across trials and severities, with the 5 µg dose the most consistent; trough FEV1 gains are smaller (87 mL where significant). Asthma-control and quality-of-life effects are trends, not demonstrated benefits, and one adolescent trial missed its primary endpoint at the higher dose. In 1–5-year-olds, tolerability matches placebo and efficacy is unproven. PROPOSED LIKELY — benefit for lung function as add-on therapy in children aged 6–17; control benefits and under-6 efficacy remain open.
cards.watchOut: Every carded trial was industry-run and spirometry-led; none was powered for exacerbations, hospitalisations or growth effects, and treatment durations were 12–48 weeks in a disease treated for years. The adult question — tiotropium within triple therapy for asthma uncontrolled on ICS-LABA — is homed at shelf #1033.

shelves.title: Metabolic surgery in adolescents with severe obesity: about a quarter of body weight lost and most diabetes remitted at 3–5 years — observational evidence, with real nutritional and reoperation costs
shelves.question: In adolescents with severe obesity, does metabolic surgery improve weight and comorbidities versus lifestyle care?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Bariatric Surgery*/methods · Body Mass Index · Dyslipidemias/complications/epidemiology · Female · Humans · Hypertension/complications · Male · Malnutrition/etiology · Obesity, Morbid/complications/surgery* · Postoperative Complications · Prevalence · Prospective Studies · Quality of Life* · Reoperation/statistics & numerical data · Risk Factors · Weight Loss* · Young Adult
shelves.balance: No randomised trial exists; the evidence is two prospective programmes followed 3–5 years. In Teen-LABS, 242 US adolescents (mean BMI 53) lost 27% of body weight by 3 years, with remission of type 2 diabetes in 95% of those affected, of prediabetes in 76%, of elevated blood pressure in 74% and of dyslipidaemia in 66% (Inge TH et al., PMID: 26544725). The same cohort at 5 years — a repeat report, not a second study — had kept off 26%, with diabetes remission of 86% against 53% in adults (Inge TH et al., PMID: 31116917). Sweden's AMOS study, prospective and controlled but NOT randomised despite sometimes being described that way, found BMI fell 13.1 kg/m² after bypass while rising 3.3 kg/m² in matched conservatively treated controls (Olbers T et al., PMID: 28065734). The costs are consistent across both programmes: nutritional deficiency in 57–72% (hypoferritinaemia 57% in Teen-LABS), additional abdominal surgery in 13–25%, and 3 deaths among 161 Teen-LABS adolescents over 5 years. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit); Tier C: the balance rests entirely on observational comparisons, and the intervention's consequences are lifelong.

cards.headline: Inge 2016 (Teen-LABS, 242 adolescents): weight down 27% at 3 years; type 2 diabetes remitted in 95% — against hypoferritinaemia in 57% and further abdominal surgery in 13%
cards.summary: Inge 2016 (Teen-LABS, 242 adolescents): weight down 27% at 3 years; type 2 diabetes remitted in 95% — against hypoferritinaemia in 57% and further abdominal surgery in 13%
cards.people: 242 adolescents undergoing weight-loss surgery at five US centres, prospectively enrolled; the analysis covers 161 who had Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and 67 who had sleeve gastrectomy. Mean age 17 years, mean BMI 53; 75% female, 72% white. There was no non-surgical control group — outcomes are changes from baseline through 3 years, in weight, coexisting conditions, cardiometabolic risk factors, quality of life and complications.
cards.result: At 3 years, mean weight had fallen 27% (95% CI 25 to 29) overall — 28% after gastric bypass, 26% after sleeve gastrectomy. Remission rates among those with the condition at baseline: type 2 diabetes 95% (85 to 100), abnormal kidney function 86% (72 to 100), prediabetes 76% (56 to 97), elevated blood pressure 74% (64 to 84), dyslipidaemia 66% (57 to 74). Weight-related quality of life improved significantly. Against this: hypoferritinaemia in 57% (50 to 65) at 3 years, and 13% (9 to 18) had undergone one or more additional intraabdominal procedures.
cards.watchOut: A cohort without a comparator cannot separate surgery's effect from selection, maturation and the intensive follow-up that surrounds a surgical programme — and remission percentages rest on the subsets who had each condition at baseline, some of them small. The 95% diabetes remission figure is real arithmetic on a selected group, not a promise to the next patient.
cards.source: Inge TH et al. Weight Loss and Health Status 3 Years after Bariatric Surgery in Adolescents. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2016. PMID: 26544725. Registry ID: NCT00474318. cards.headline: Inge 2019 (Teen-LABS at 5 years): the SAME cohort as the 2016 report, compared with adults — weight loss equal (−26% vs −29%), diabetes remission higher in adolescents (86% vs 53%), reoperations more frequent
cards.summary: Inge 2019 (Teen-LABS at 5 years): the SAME cohort as the 2016 report, compared with adults — weight loss equal (−26% vs −29%), diabetes remission higher in adolescents (86% vs 53%), reoperations more frequent
cards.type: Prospective cohort comparison, Teen-LABS 5-year report (Inge 2019) — same cohort as Inge 2016
cards.people: 161 adolescents from the Teen-LABS cohort carded above (enrolled 2006–2012) compared with 396 adults (enrolled 2006–2009) from a related but independent study, all after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, followed 5 years for weight and coexisting conditions, with death, reoperation and micronutrient comparisons. This is a later report of the same adolescent cohort, NOT an independent study — the two cards describe one group of teenagers.
cards.result: Percent weight change at 5 years did not differ significantly between adolescents (−26%, 95% CI −29 to −23) and adults (−29%, −31 to −27; P = 0.08). Adolescents were significantly more likely to have remission of type 2 diabetes (86% versus 53%; risk ratio 1.27, 1.03 to 1.57) and of hypertension (68% versus 41%; risk ratio 1.51, 1.21 to 1.88). Three adolescents (1.9%) and seven adults (1.8%) died within 5 years. Abdominal reoperations were significantly more frequent in adolescents (19 versus 10 per 500 person-years, P = 0.003), and low ferritin was more common (48% versus 29%, P = 0.004).
cards.watchOut: Counting this paper as a second study would double-count one cohort — it is flagged as a repeat report for exactly that reason. The adolescent-versus-adult comparison is also confounded by design: the adults were enrolled in a different study in different years, with longer-standing disease, which is the likeliest explanation of their lower remission rates.

cards.headline: Olbers 2017 (AMOS, Sweden): bypass versus matched conservatively treated adolescents — BMI −13.1 versus +3.3 kg/m² at 5 years; 25% needed further abdominal surgery and 72% had a nutritional deficiency
cards.summary: Olbers 2017 (AMOS, Sweden): bypass versus matched conservatively treated adolescents — BMI −13.1 versus +3.3 kg/m² at 5 years; 25% needed further abdominal surgery and 72% had a nutritional deficiency
cards.people: A prospective, non-randomised controlled nationwide Swedish study: 81 adolescents aged 13–18 underwent Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (mean age 16.5 years, mean BMI 45.5), compared with 80 matched adolescent controls undergoing conservative treatment and 81 matched adult surgical controls. Primary outcome: change in BMI over 5 years. Allocation was by treatment received, not by chance.
cards.result: Over 5 years, surgical adolescents lost 36.8 kg, a BMI reduction of 13.1 kg/m² (95% CI −14.5 to −11.8), while BMI in conservatively treated adolescent controls rose by 3.3 kg/m² (1.1 to 4.8); adult surgical controls lost a similar 12.3 kg/m². Comorbidities and cardiovascular risk factors improved in the surgical group compared with adolescent controls. But 20 of 81 surgical adolescents (25%) underwent additional abdominal surgery for complications or rapid weight loss, 58 (72%) showed some type of nutritional deficiency, and healthcare consumption was higher than in controls. A quarter of the control group (25%) crossed over to bariatric surgery during follow-up, and 11% of surgical patients lost less than 10% of body weight.
cards.watchOut: The slate described AMOS among randomised anchors; it is not randomised — adolescents and families chose, or were chosen for, surgery, so the comparison carries selection effects no matching can fully remove. The control group's 25% crossover to surgery also blurs the contrast in both directions: it shrinks the measured difference while testifying that conservative care was failing a quarter of the controls.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a quarter of body weight, most diabetes remitted, real surgical and nutritional costs — POSSIBLE on observational evidence (Tier C)
cards.summary: Synthesis: a quarter of body weight, most diabetes remitted, real surgical and nutritional costs — POSSIBLE on observational evidence (Tier C)
cards.people: Two prospective programmes: Teen-LABS in the US (242 adolescents; 3-year outcomes in Inge 2016 and the 5-year adolescent-versus-adult report in Inge 2019 — one cohort, two papers) and AMOS in Sweden (81 surgical adolescents against 80 matched conservatively treated controls, Olbers 2017). No randomised trial of metabolic surgery in adolescents exists in this evidence.
cards.result: Weight falls by about a quarter to a third and stays down at 5 years (−26% Teen-LABS; BMI −13.1 kg/m² AMOS, against +3.3 kg/m² on conservative care); type 2 diabetes remits in 86–95% of affected adolescents, hypertension in about two-thirds to three-quarters. The costs are structural, not incidental: nutritional deficiency in 57–72%, additional abdominal surgery in 13–25%, and deaths occurred in the surgical cohorts (1.9% of Teen-LABS adolescents over 5 years). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — large and durable effects in prospective cohorts, held at POSSIBLE and Tier C because no randomised comparison exists and the harms are lifelong commitments made at 16.
cards.watchOut: These are the most selected patients in paediatric medicine — screened, motivated, operated on at expert centres, and followed intensively. Nothing here estimates what surgery would do in an unselected clinic population, and nothing follows these patients into the decades (pregnancy, bone health, alcohol use, revision surgery) over which the bargain must hold. Lifestyle and pharmacological comparators were not randomised against surgery in any carded study.
cards.source: Synthesis of Inge TH et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2016 (PMID: 26544725); Inge TH et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2019 (PMID: 31116917); Olbers T et al. The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology. 2017 (PMID: 28065734).

shelves.title: Growth hormone for idiopathic short stature: about 4 cm of extra adult height on average — real, modest, and highly variable between children
shelves.question: In idiopathic short stature, does growth hormone increase adult height, and by how much?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Body Height/drug effects* · Child · Dwarfism/drug therapy* · Female · Human Growth Hormone/therapeutic use* · Humans · Male · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The randomised evidence is consistent and the effect is quantified. Deodati A et al. (PMID: 21398350), pooling the three randomised trials with adult-height outcomes (115 children), found treated children ended 0.65 SD score — about 4 cm — taller than controls, with a mean height gain of 1.2 SD against 0.34 SD untreated; seven non-randomised trials gave a smaller 0.45 SD (about 3 cm). The one double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Leschek EW et al., PMID: 15240584) found adult height 0.51 SD (3.7 cm; 95% CI 0.10 to 0.92 SD) greater on growth hormone after a mean 4.4 years of treatment. Dahlgren J (PMID: 21912164), reviewing six long-term studies narratively, reports gains of 0.5 to 1.3 SD, largest in younger children furthest below their parental height, with a dose-dependent pattern but only about 1.2 cm between the dose regimens in the randomised pool. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): roughly 4 cm of adult height on average — an average that conceals wide individual variation, which the reviewers themselves emphasise. Growth hormone in Turner syndrome is homed at shelf #1422.

cards.headline: Deodati 2011 (BMJ): across 3 randomised trials (115 children), growth hormone adds 0.65 SD — about 4 cm — to adult height in idiopathic short stature
cards.summary: Deodati 2011 (BMJ): across 3 randomised trials (115 children), growth hormone adds 0.65 SD — about 4 cm — to adult height in idiopathic short stature
cards.people: A systematic review of randomised and non-randomised controlled trials (1985 to April 2010) of growth hormone in children with idiopathic short stature — height more than 2 SD below the mean, growth hormone responses above 10 µg/L, prepubertal, no previous growth hormone treatment and no comorbid condition impairing growth — with height measured in adulthood (growth rate under 1.5 cm/year, or bone age 15 in girls and 16 in boys).
cards.result: Three randomised trials (115 children) met the criteria: adult height in growth-hormone-treated children exceeded controls by 0.65 SD score (about 4 cm); mean height gain was 1.2 SD score in treated children versus 0.34 SD in untreated children. The difference between the two dose regimens studied was small, about 1.2 cm. In seven non-randomised controlled trials the treated advantage was 0.45 SD (about 3 cm). The authors conclude growth hormone partially reduces the adult height deficit, that its average effect is less than in licensed indications, and that individual response is highly variable.
cards.watchOut: One hundred and fifteen randomised children is a small foundation for a treatment given by daily injection for years: the pooled 4 cm is an average over responders and non-responders, and this review cannot tell a family in advance which their child will be. Adult height is also a surrogate for what families actually want — the review measures centimetres, not wellbeing.
cards.source: Deodati A et al. Impact of growth hormone therapy on adult height of children with idiopathic short stature: systematic review. BMJ. 2011. PMID: 21398350. cards.headline: Leschek 2004: the placebo-controlled trial — adult height 0.51 SD (3.7 cm) greater on growth hormone in 68 peripubertal children with marked short stature
cards.summary: Leschek 2004: the placebo-controlled trial — adult height 0.51 SD (3.7 cm) greater on growth hormone in 68 peripubertal children with marked short stature
cards.people: 68 children aged 9 to 16 years (53 boys, 15 girls) with marked idiopathic short stature (height or predicted height at or below −2.5 SD score), randomised double-blind to growth hormone 0.074 mg/kg subcutaneously three times a week or placebo until near adult height. Adult height measurements were available for 33 patients after a mean treatment duration of 4.4 years; a modified intention-to-treat analysis covered 62 patients treated for at least 6 months.
cards.result: Adult height was greater on growth hormone: −1.81 ± 0.11 SD score versus −2.32 ± 0.17 on placebo, a difference of 0.51 SD (3.7 cm; P < 0.02; 95% CI 0.10 to 0.92 SD). The same effect appeared against baseline height and baseline predicted height. The modified intention-to-treat analysis gave a similar estimate (0.52 SD, 3.8 cm; P < 0.001; 95% CI 0.22 to 0.82 SD) with no important dropout bias. The authors conclude growth hormone increases adult height in peripubertal children with marked idiopathic short stature.
cards.watchOut: Only 33 of 68 randomised children contribute the headline adult-height comparison — the rest had not reached it at termination — so the trial's precision rests heavily on the intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis agreeing with it, which it does. The confidence interval (0.10 to 0.92 SD) spans from under a centimetre to nearly twice the headline effect; families should hear the range, not just 3.7 cm.
cards.source: Leschek EW et al. Effect of growth hormone treatment on adult height in peripubertal children with idiopathic short stature: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. cards.headline: Dahlgren 2011: narrative review of 6 long-term studies — height gains of 0.5 to 1.3 SD, dose-dependent, larger in younger children further below their parents' height
cards.summary: Dahlgren 2011: narrative review of 6 long-term studies — height gains of 0.5 to 1.3 SD, dose-dependent, larger in younger children further below their parents' height
cards.people: A literature review (explicitly not a meta-analysis) of all randomised and non-randomised studies of growth hormone in idiopathic short stature from prepubertal years to adult or near-adult height published over the preceding 10 years: six publications. Only two reported data from matched control subjects.
cards.result: Reported height improvement ranged from 0.5 to 1.3 SD score, and remained substantial (0.5 to 1 SD) after adjustment for spontaneous growth in untreated controls. Several studies showed a dose-dependent response. The younger the child at start, and the greater the gap between the child's height and parental height, the more substantial the gain. There was no difference in height gain between familial and non-familial short stature after adjustment for spontaneous growth in controls. The author concludes patients with idiopathic short stature can benefit from growth hormone with results maintained into adulthood.
cards.watchOut: A single-author narrative review sits below the BMJ systematic review and the placebo-controlled trial on this shelf's own evidence ladder, and its upper range (1.3 SD) comes from uncontrolled comparisons. Its useful contribution is the pattern of who gains most — younger starters with the largest deficit against parental height — not a bigger effect estimate.
cards.source: Dahlgren J. Growth outcomes in individuals with idiopathic short stature treated with growth hormone therapy. Hormone Research in Paediatrics. 2011. PMID: 21912164. cards.headline: Synthesis: three designs agree — about 4 cm of extra adult height on average (LIKELY), with wide individual variation
cards.summary: Synthesis: three designs agree — about 4 cm of extra adult height on average (LIKELY), with wide individual variation
cards.people: One systematic review of controlled trials (Deodati 2011: 3 RCTs, 115 children; 7 non-randomised trials), one double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Leschek 2004: 68 children), and one narrative review of the long-term literature (Dahlgren 2011: 6 publications).
cards.result: Every design points the same way: growth hormone increases adult height in idiopathic short stature. Randomised evidence puts the gain at 0.65 SD (about 4 cm) over untreated controls; the placebo-controlled trial at 0.51 SD (3.7 cm; 95% CI 0.10 to 0.92 SD); non-randomised comparisons at about 0.45 SD (3 cm). Response is highly variable, dose differences are small (about 1.2 cm between regimens), and gains are largest in younger children furthest below parental height. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — a real, modest average gain of roughly 4 cm of adult height.
cards.watchOut: The carded evidence answers a centimetre question. It does not measure whether taller adult height improves quality of life, self-esteem or functioning in idiopathic short stature, and it prices the gain at years of injections through childhood with adult height known only at the end. Growth hormone for a defined deficiency state (Turner syndrome) is a different question, homed at shelf #1422.

shelves.title: Prophylactic paracetamol at vaccination: fevers fall by about a quarter — and antibody levels fall too, though immunological memory survives
shelves.question: In infants, does prophylactic paracetamol given around vaccination reduce antibody responses to the vaccines?
shelves.mesh: Acetaminophen/administration & dosage* · Analgesics, Non-Narcotic/administration & dosage* · Antibody Formation/drug effects* · Chemoprevention · Female · Fever/etiology/prevention & control* · Humans · Infant · Male · Vaccination/adverse effects*
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the same intervention wins on the outcome parents see and loses on the outcome the vaccine is for. In two consecutive randomised trials in 459 infants, three prophylactic paracetamol doses in the first 24 hours cut fever of 38.0 °C or more after at least one dose from 66% to 42% after primary vaccination and from 58% to 36% after the booster — absolute reductions of about 24 and 22 percentage points — while fever above 39.5 °C was uncommon in both groups (Prymula R et al., PMID: 19837254). Antibody concentrations, however, were significantly lower with paracetamol for all ten pneumococcal serotypes and several other antigens after priming, and for most serotypes after boosting. The follow-up of the same children at age 4 (Prymula R et al., PMID: 23391599 — a repeat report of the same cohort, flagged on its card) found immunological memory intact and functional antibody titres not significantly different, and the authors judge the reduction transient. PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit) fewer febrile reactions / POSSIBLE (harm) lower antibody responses, apparently transient; Tier C: the harm judgement rests on a surrogate outcome from a single trial programme. The trialists' own conclusion stands as the practical summary: prophylactic antipyretics at vaccination should not be routinely recommended.

cards.headline: Prymula 2009 (459 infants, two randomised trials): prophylactic paracetamol cuts fever ≥38 °C from 66% to 42% — and lowers antibody levels to every pneumococcal serotype and several other antigens
cards.summary: Prymula 2009 (459 infants, two randomised trials): prophylactic paracetamol cuts fever ≥38 °C from 66% to 42% — and lowers antibody levels to every pneumococcal serotype and several other antigens
cards.type: Two consecutive open-label randomised controlled trials (Prymula 2009)
cards.people: 459 healthy infants at ten Czech centres, randomised open-label in two consecutive studies (primary vaccination and booster) to three prophylactic paracetamol doses every 6–8 hours in the first 24 hours (n = 226) or no prophylactic paracetamol (n = 233) after each vaccination with the ten-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PHiD-CV) co-administered with a hexavalent DTPa-HBV-IPV/Hib vaccine and oral rotavirus vaccine.
cards.result: Fever of 38.0 °C or more after at least one dose was significantly less common with prophylactic paracetamol: 42% (94/226) versus 66% (154/233) after primary vaccination, and 36% (64/178) versus 58% (100/172) after the booster — absolute reductions of about 24 and 22 percentage points. Fever above 39.5 °C was uncommon in both groups (under 1% versus 1% after primary; 2% versus 1% after booster). But antibody geometric mean concentrations were significantly lower in the paracetamol group after primary vaccination for all ten pneumococcal serotypes, protein D, anti-PRP, antidiphtheria, antitetanus and antipertactin; after boosting, lower levels persisted for antitetanus, protein D and all pneumococcal serotypes except 19F. The authors conclude prophylactic antipyretics at vaccination should not be routinely recommended.
cards.watchOut: The fever benefit is real but modest in what it prevents: high fever above 39.5 °C was rare with or without paracetamol, and febrile convulsions were not an outcome. The antibody reduction is a laboratory surrogate — no increase in vaccine-preventable disease was shown — but it was consistent across antigens and persisted after the booster, which is why the authors advise against routine prophylaxis rather than merely noting the finding.
cards.source: Prymula R et al. cards.headline: Prymula 2013 (follow-up of the SAME children at age 4): immunological memory is intact regardless of earlier paracetamol — the lower antibody levels look transient
cards.summary: Prymula 2013 (follow-up of the SAME children at age 4): immunological memory is intact regardless of earlier paracetamol — the lower antibody levels look transient
cards.type: Follow-up study of the Prymula 2009 cohort (Prymula 2013) — same cohort, flagged
cards.people: 220 children who had been primed and boosted with PHiD-CV in the 2009 trials — with prophylactic paracetamol (PP) or without (NPP) — received one PHiD-CV dose in their fourth year of life to test immunological memory, antibody persistence and nasopharyngeal carriage; 223 age-matched previously unprimed children served as the control for the memory assessment. This is a follow-up report of the same cohort carded above, not an independent trial.
cards.result: Induction of immunological memory was shown irrespective of whether paracetamol had been given at priming and boosting. Antibody concentrations remained lower in the PP group for pneumococcal serotypes 1, 4, 7F and 9V, but opsonophagocytic titres — the functional antibody measure — did not differ significantly between PP and NPP groups, and the impact of earlier PP on antibody persistence kinetics was minor. Carriage of vaccine serotypes was reduced in both primed groups versus controls, with no obvious PP/NPP difference. The authors conclude the lower immune responses seen with prophylactic paracetamol appear to be of a transient nature.
cards.watchOut: Transient is the authors' word and the functional data support it — but the follow-up cannot restore what was never measured: whether the lower antibody levels in the first two years of life, when pneumococcal disease risk is highest, carried any clinical cost. The reassurance is about memory at age 4, not about protection at age 4 months.
cards.source: Prymula R et al. Immunological memory and nasopharyngeal carriage in 4-year-old children previously primed and boosted with 10-valent pneumococcal non-typeable Haemophilus influenzae protein D conjugate vaccine (PHiD-CV) with or without concomitant prophylactic paracetamol. Vaccine. 2013. PMID: 23391599. Registry ID: NCT00950833. cards.headline: Synthesis: fewer fevers, lower antibodies, intact memory — SPLIT (benefit on reactions / possible transient harm to responses), Tier C
cards.summary: Synthesis: fewer fevers, lower antibodies, intact memory — SPLIT (benefit on reactions / possible transient harm to responses), Tier C
cards.people: Two consecutive open-label randomised trials in 459 infants (Prymula 2009) and their pre-school follow-up (Prymula 2013, 220 of the same children at age 4).
cards.result: Prophylactic paracetamol does what parents ask of it — fever ≥38 °C falls from 66% to 42% after primary vaccination and from 58% to 36% after the booster — but high fever is rare either way, and antibody concentrations fall across essentially every antigen measured, with lower levels for some serotypes still visible years later. Immunological memory and functional (opsonophagocytic) titres are preserved, and the authors judge the effect transient. PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit) for fewer febrile reactions / POSSIBLE (harm) for reduced antibody responses, apparently transient; Tier C: the harm side rests on a surrogate outcome in one trial programme.
cards.watchOut: This shelf is about paracetamol given before or at vaccination to a well infant. It says nothing about treating fever or distress after vaccination, which is a different decision with a different balance, and nothing about other antipyretics or other vaccine schedules — the carded programme is one pneumococcal conjugate vaccine with specific co-administered vaccines in Czech infants.
cards.source: Synthesis of Prymula R et al. The Lancet. 2009 (PMID: 19837254); Prymula R et al. Vaccine. 2013 (PMID: 23391599).
