shelves.title: Exclusive enteral nutrition in paediatric Crohn's disease: remission matches corticosteroids in children — and the one trial that scoped the bowel found the mucosa heals better
shelves.question: In children with Crohn's disease, does exclusive enteral nutrition induce remission as well as corticosteroids, with better growth and mucosal healing?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adrenal Cortex Hormones/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Child · Crohn Disease/therapy* · Enteral Nutrition* · Female · Gastrointestinal Agents/pharmacology/therapeutic use* · Humans · Male · Quality of Life/psychology · Remission Induction/methods · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT by outcome, and the paediatric answer differs from the adult one. In children, enteral nutrition (EN) and corticosteroids have never been separated on clinical remission: the paediatric meta-analysis pooled a relative risk of 0.97 (95% CI 0.7 to 1.4) (Dziechciarz P et al., PMID: 17767463), and the Cochrane child subgroup pointed, if anything, toward EN (83% versus 61% remission; RR 1.35, 0.92 to 1.97), even though Cochrane's adult-dominated overall pool favoured steroids (Narula N et al., PMID: 29607496). On mucosal healing, the only randomised trial that scoped the bowel found healing in 74% on a polymeric diet versus 33% on corticosteroids, with remission rates the same (79% versus 67%) (Borrelli O et al., PMID: 16682258). On growth — the third limb of the question — the carded syntheses could not pool growth data at all, so a growth advantage is not demonstrated by this evidence. PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for clinical remission versus corticosteroids / POSSIBLE (benefit) for mucosal healing; Tier C: the healing claim rests on one small open-label trial and the remission evidence is graded very low quality.

cards.headline: Dziechciarz 2007 (paediatric meta-analysis): enteral nutrition matches corticosteroids for remission — pooled relative risk 0.97 across 4 trials
cards.summary: Dziechciarz 2007 (paediatric meta-analysis): enteral nutrition matches corticosteroids for remission — pooled relative risk 0.97 across 4 trials
cards.people: Eleven randomised trials (394 children) of enteral nutrition (EN) in active paediatric Crohn's disease: seven trials (204 children) compared EN with corticosteroid therapy, and four (190 children) compared two EN regimens (total versus partial enteral nutrition). Outcomes were remission rates; data were too sparse to pool time to remission, duration of remission or growth.
cards.result: Pooling the four trials with combinable data (n = 144) found no significant difference in remission rates between EN and corticosteroids (relative risk 0.97, 95% CI 0.7 to 1.4, random-effects model). In the regimen comparison, one trial (n = 50) found total EN achieved remission more often than partial EN (relative risk 2.7, 95% CI 1 to 7.4). The authors conclude limited data suggest similar efficacy for EN and corticosteroids, and that future studies should measure growth and quality of life in detail.
cards.watchOut: The confidence interval (0.7 to 1.4) is wide enough to hide a clinically important advantage for either treatment — 'no significant difference' in 144 children is not proof of equivalence. This is also the oldest synthesis on the shelf; the Cochrane update carded below re-pools the question with adults included, which changes the answer, and the difference between the two is itself instructive.
cards.source: Dziechciarz P et al. Meta-analysis: enteral nutrition in active Crohn's disease in children. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2007. PMID: 17767463. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Borrelli 2006 (37 children, randomised): clinical remission the same (79% vs 67%), but mucosal healing clearly better on a polymeric diet (74% vs 33%)
cards.summary: Borrelli 2006 (37 children, randomised): clinical remission the same (79% vs 67%), but mucosal healing clearly better on a polymeric diet (74% vs 33%)
cards.people: 37 children with active, recently diagnosed (naive) Crohn's disease, randomised open-label to an oral polymeric formula alone or oral corticosteroids for 10 weeks. Clinical activity, nutritional and serum variables were checked every 2 weeks; intestinal mucosal inflammation was assessed by endoscopy and histology at weeks 0 and 10. Primary outcomes: clinical remission and mucosal healing, analysed intention-to-treat.
cards.result: Clinical remission at week 10 was comparable: 79% (15/19; 95% CI 56% to 92%) on polymeric diet versus 67% (12/18; 44% to 84%) on corticosteroids (P = .4, not significant). Mucosal healing was significantly more frequent on the polymeric diet: 74% (14/19; 51% to 89%) versus 33% (6/18; 16% to 57%) on corticosteroids (P < .05). Endoscopic and histologic scores decreased significantly only in the polymeric group (P < .001). The authors conclude a short course of polymeric diet is more effective than corticosteroids at healing gut inflammatory lesions.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-seven children, open-label, one centre's endoscopists: the mucosal-healing difference is large (74% versus 33%) but the trial is exactly the size at which large differences arise by luck, and it has never been replicated at scale. It is the only carded study that actually looked at the mucosa — which is why the healing claim sits at POSSIBLE, not higher.
cards.source: Borrelli O et al. Polymeric diet alone versus corticosteroids in the treatment of active pediatric Crohn's disease: a randomized controlled open-label trial. Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2006. PMID: 16682258. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Narula 2018 (Cochrane, 27 studies): overall pool favours steroids — but the children-only subgroup points the other way (remission relative risk 1.35; per-protocol 1.43)
cards.summary: Narula 2018 (Cochrane, 27 studies): overall pool favours steroids — but the children-only subgroup points the other way (remission relative risk 1.35; per-protocol 1.43)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 27 RCTs (Narula 2018, Cochrane)
cards.people: Twenty-seven randomised studies (1,011 participants, adults and children) of enteral nutritional therapy for induction of remission in Crohn's disease: 17 comparing EN formulations with each other and 10 comparing EN with corticosteroids. Only 3 studies were at low risk of bias; 7 were high and 17 unclear. Evidence quality for the primary outcome was graded very low.
cards.result: Across eight pooled trials (223 participants in the EN-versus-steroid intention-to-treat analysis), remission was 50% on EN versus 72% on steroids (relative risk 0.77, 95% CI 0.58 to 1.03; very low quality). The age split reverses the picture: in adults, steroids were clearly better (45% versus 73%; RR 0.65, 0.52 to 0.82), while in children EN was numerically better (83% versus 61%; RR 1.35, 0.92 to 1.97), and the per-protocol child analysis reached significance (RR 1.43, 1.03 to 1.97). Formula composition (elemental versus non-elemental) made no difference to remission (RR 1.02, 0.88 to 1.18). Patients on EN withdrew for adverse events more often (RR 2.95, 1.02 to 8.48), most commonly inability to tolerate the diet.
cards.watchOut: Read the headline pool and you would deny children a treatment the paediatric subgroup favours: the pooled 0.77 is an adult-dominated average. The child subgroup itself is tiny (57 children in the intention-to-treat split) and graded very low quality, so this card disciplines both directions of over-claiming — steroids are not proven better in children, and EN is not proven equal, let alone superior, on remission alone.
cards.source: Narula N et al. Enteral nutritional therapy for induction of remission in Crohn's disease. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2018. PMID: 29607496. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: remission equal to steroids in children, mucosa better in the one trial that looked — SPLIT, Tier C
cards.summary: Synthesis: remission equal to steroids in children, mucosa better in the one trial that looked — SPLIT, Tier C
cards.people: A paediatric-only meta-analysis (Dziechciarz 2007: EN versus steroids pooled RR 0.97 in children), the one randomised trial with endoscopic outcomes (Borrelli 2006: 37 children), and the Cochrane synthesis whose child subgroup reverses its adult-dominated headline (Narula 2018).
cards.result: For clinical remission in children, the paediatric evidence shows no demonstrated difference from corticosteroids (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.7 to 1.4; child subgroup RR 1.35, 0.92 to 1.97) — while in adults steroids are superior (RR 0.65). For mucosal healing, the single trial that looked found a large advantage to the polymeric diet (74% versus 33%). For growth — the third limb of the question — none of the carded syntheses could pool growth data, so a growth advantage is asserted by practice, not demonstrated here. PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for clinical remission versus corticosteroids / POSSIBLE (benefit) for mucosal healing; Tier C: very-low-quality graded evidence and a single small trial behind the healing claim.
cards.watchOut: The practical barrier is adherence: EN patients withdrew for intolerance more often than steroid patients (RR 2.95), and the formulas are commonly delivered by nasogastric tube for weeks. A treatment equal on remission and better on mucosa only helps the child who can actually complete it — trial completion rates flatter real-world completion.
cards.source: Synthesis of Dziechciarz P et al. Alimentary Pharmacology & Therapeutics. 2007 (PMID: 17767463); Borrelli O et al. Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2006 (PMID: 16682258); Narula N et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2018 (PMID: 29607496).

shelves.title: Infliximab for IVIG-resistant Kawasaki disease: fever breaks faster than with a second IVIG course in two small trials — coronary outcomes are untested at this size
shelves.question: In children with Kawasaki disease resistant to IVIG, does infliximab shorten fever and inflammation compared with a second IVIG course?

shelves.balance: Two small randomised trials in the target population point the same way on fever. In the phase 3 Japanese trial, defervescence within 48 hours occurred in 76.7% on infliximab versus 37.0% on a second IVIG course (p = 0.023), with earlier resolution overall (Mori M et al., PMID: 29386515). In the US pharmacokinetic trial, fever ceased within 24 hours in 11 of 12 children on infliximab versus 8 of 12 retreated with IVIG, with no significant differences in inflammatory markers or coronary echocardiography (Burns JC et al., PMID: 18672254). The largest infliximab trial in the disease (Tremoulet AH et al., PMID: 24572997) answers a different question — adding infliximab to FIRST treatment did not reduce IVIG resistance (11.2% versus 11.3%) — and is carded here as flagged context only; it does corroborate faster fever resolution (median 1 versus 2 days) under double-blind conditions. Coronary artery outcomes, the outcome that matters most, rest on 4 events across the refractory trials and are effectively untested. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit); Tier C: 55 randomised children in the target population, one trial open-label, no trial powered for coronary outcomes. Corticosteroids in high-risk primary Kawasaki treatment are homed at shelf #646.

cards.headline: Mori 2018 (phase 3, 31 children with IVIG-refractory Kawasaki disease): fever gone within 48 hours in 76.7% on infliximab versus 37.0% on a second IVIG course
cards.summary: Mori 2018 (phase 3, 31 children with IVIG-refractory Kawasaki disease): fever gone within 48 hours in 76.7% on infliximab versus 37.0% on a second IVIG course
cards.people: 31 Japanese children aged 1 to 10 years with Kawasaki disease and persistent fever after initial IVIG, randomised open-label to a single intravenous dose of infliximab 5 mg/kg or a second course of intravenous immunoglobulin (polyethylene glycol-treated human immunoglobulin, 2 g/kg). Primary outcome: defervescence rate within 48 hours of starting treatment; safety followed to day 56.
cards.result: Defervescence within 48 hours was greater with infliximab (76.7%) than with second IVIG (37.0%) (p = 0.023), and fever resolved earlier on infliximab (p = 0.0072). Coronary artery lesions by day 21 occurred in 1 of 16 infliximab patients (6.3%) versus 3 of 15 IVIG patients (20.0%) — too few events to compare. Discontinuation for worsening disease was common in both arms (31.3% infliximab, 60.0% IVIG). Adverse events occurred in 93.8% versus 100%; there were no serious adverse events on infliximab and one on IVIG. The trial is registered as NCT01596335, stated in the abstract; the record's databank list is empty.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-one children is a very small phase 3: the defervescence difference is statistically real but fragile, the trial was open-label with fever — a partly judgement-laden outcome — as its endpoint, and a third to two-thirds of children in both arms worsened enough to stop the assigned treatment. It establishes that infliximab breaks fever faster in refractory disease; it cannot establish that it protects coronary arteries.
cards.source: Mori M et al. Infliximab versus intravenous immunoglobulin for refractory Kawasaki disease: a phase 3, randomized, open-label, active-controlled, parallel-group, multicenter trial. Scientific Reports. 2018. PMID: 29386515. Registry ID: NCT01596335 (as stated in the abstract; the record’s databank list is empty). cards.headline: Burns 2008 (24 children, randomised): fever stopped within 24 hours in 11 of 12 on infliximab versus 8 of 12 retreated with IVIG — no other outcome separated the groups
cards.summary: Burns 2008 (24 children, randomised): fever stopped within 24 hours in 11 of 12 on infliximab versus 8 of 12 retreated with IVIG — no other outcome separated the groups
cards.people: 24 children with acute Kawasaki disease and fever after initial IVIG treatment, in a multicentre randomised prospective trial of a second IVIG infusion (2 g/kg) versus infliximab (5 mg/kg). Primary outcome measures were the safety, tolerability and pharmacokinetics of infliximab; secondary measures were duration of fever and changes in inflammatory markers.
cards.result: Fever ceased within 24 hours in 11 of 12 subjects treated with infliximab and 8 of 12 retreated with IVIG. No infusion reactions or serious adverse events were attributed to either treatment. No significant differences were observed between groups in change from baseline in laboratory variables, fever measures, or echocardiographic assessment of coronary arteries. The authors conclude both options were safe and well tolerated, and that the optimal management of IVIG-resistant Kawasaki disease remains to be determined.
cards.watchOut: A pharmacokinetic study wearing a trial's clothes: 24 children, powered for drug levels, not for fever or coronary outcomes. Its value is directional consistency with Mori 2018 and a clean safety read in the exact population of interest — not independent confirmation of efficacy at any quotable precision.
cards.source: Burns JC et al. Infliximab treatment of intravenous immunoglobulin-resistant Kawasaki disease. The Journal of Pediatrics. 2008. PMID: 18672254. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Tremoulet 2014 (196 children, double-blind): ADJACENT evidence — infliximab added to FIRST treatment did not reduce IVIG resistance (11.2% vs 11.3%), though fever lasted a day less
cards.summary: Tremoulet 2014 (196 children, double-blind): ADJACENT evidence — infliximab added to FIRST treatment did not reduce IVIG resistance (11.2% vs 11.3%), though fever lasted a day less
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Tremoulet 2014) — adjacent question, flagged
cards.people: 196 children aged 4 weeks to 17 years with acute Kawasaki disease at two US children's hospitals, randomised double-blind to infliximab 5 mg/kg or placebo added to standard primary therapy (IVIG plus aspirin). Primary outcome: treatment resistance, defined as temperature of 38.0 °C or higher between 36 hours and 7 days after the IVIG infusion. This trial answers the primary-therapy question, NOT the resistant-disease question of this shelf; it is carded as context because it is the largest and most rigorous infliximab trial in the disease.
cards.result: Treatment resistance did not differ: 11.2% on infliximab versus 11.3% on placebo (p = 0.81). Fever duration was shorter on infliximab (median 1 versus 2 days, p < 0.0001), C-reactive protein and sedimentation rate fell faster, and the left anterior descending coronary artery Z score fell more by week 2 (not significantly different by week 5). IVIG infusion reactions occurred in 0 infliximab patients versus 13.4% on placebo (p < 0.0001). No serious adverse events were directly attributable to infliximab. The authors conclude adding infliximab to primary treatment did not reduce resistance, though it reduced fever duration and some inflammatory markers.
cards.watchOut: Quoting this trial as evidence about resistant disease would be a category error, and the card is labelled so it cannot be. Its real contribution here is mechanistic reassurance: in the same disease, under double-blind conditions, infliximab reproducibly shortens fever and speeds inflammatory-marker falls — the same effects the small refractory-disease trials report — while failing the harder endpoint of preventing resistance when given to everyone.
cards.source: Tremoulet AH et al. Infliximab for intensification of primary therapy for Kawasaki disease: a phase 3 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. The Lancet. 2014. PMID: 24572997. Registry ID: NCT00760435. cards.headline: Synthesis: fever breaks faster on infliximab than on a second IVIG course — POSSIBLE (Tier C); coronary protection untested
cards.summary: Synthesis: fever breaks faster on infliximab than on a second IVIG course — POSSIBLE (Tier C); coronary protection untested
cards.people: Two small randomised trials in IVIG-resistant disease (Mori 2018: 31 children, open-label; Burns 2008: 24 children, pharmacokinetic focus) and one large double-blind trial in primary therapy carded as flagged context (Tremoulet 2014: 196 children).
cards.result: In resistant disease, infliximab breaks fever faster and more often than a second IVIG course (defervescence within 48 hours 76.7% versus 37.0%; fever cessation within 24 hours 11/12 versus 8/12), with no attributable serious adverse events in either small trial. Coronary outcomes — the outcome that decides lives in this disease — rest on 4 events in one trial and no difference in the other, so they are untested at this size. In primary therapy, infliximab did not reduce resistance but did shorten fever. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — faster defervescence in refractory disease; Tier C: 55 randomised children in the target population, one trial open-label, neither powered for coronary outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Steroids, the other main escalation option, are not compared here: corticosteroids added to IVIG in high-risk primary treatment are homed at shelf #646. Nor does this shelf compare infliximab with other biologics or with steroid rescue in resistant disease — no carded trial does. The choice among rescue options in a deteriorating child remains a specialist judgement that this evidence informs but does not settle.
cards.source: Synthesis of Mori M et al. Scientific Reports. 2018 (PMID: 29386515); Burns JC et al. The Journal of Pediatrics. 2008 (PMID: 18672254); Tremoulet AH et al. The Lancet. 2014 (PMID: 24572997).

shelves.title: Xylitol to prevent ear infections: episodes fall by about a quarter in healthy daycare children — but not in the otitis-prone children this question asks about
shelves.question: In children prone to recurrent otitis media, does xylitol syrup or gum prevent acute otitis media episodes?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Chewing Gum · Child · Child, Preschool · Female · Gels/therapeutic use · Humans · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Male · Otitis Media/prevention & control* · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Sweetening Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Xylitol/adverse effects/therapeutic use*
shelves.balance: SPLIT by population, and the split runs against the question as posed. The Cochrane synthesis (Azarpazhooh A et al., PMID: 27486835) pooled three trials of 1,826 healthy Finnish children attending daycare: xylitol in any form reduced acute otitis media from 30% to around 22% (relative risk 0.75, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.88 — a 25% relative reduction, about 8 percentage points absolute). The largest trial shows the same shape by formulation: at least one episode in 41% on control syrup versus 29% on xylitol syrup, with chewing gum effective and lozenges not significantly so (Uhari M et al., PMID: 9755259). But in otitis-prone children — the population named in this shelf's question — the pooled estimate is null (RR 0.90, 0.67 to 1.21), as it is when xylitol is given during a respiratory infection (RR 1.13, 0.83 to 1.53). PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit) in healthy daycare children / MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) in otitis-prone children; Tier C: the evidence is concentrated in a small number of trials from largely one research group, using dosing regimens of 8.4–10 g a day in divided doses. Tympanostomy tubes for established recurrent otitis media are homed at shelf #629.

cards.headline: Azarpazhooh 2016 (Cochrane): xylitol cuts acute otitis media from 30% to about 22% in healthy daycare children (RR 0.75) — no effect during respiratory infections (RR 1.13) or in otitis-prone children (RR 0.90)
cards.summary: Azarpazhooh 2016 (Cochrane): xylitol cuts acute otitis media from 30% to about 22% in healthy daycare children (RR 0.75) — no effect during respiratory infections (RR 1.13) or in otitis-prone children (RR 0.90)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 5 trials (Azarpazhooh 2016, Cochrane)
cards.people: Five clinical trials (3,405 children up to 12 years) of xylitol versus placebo or no treatment to prevent acute otitis media (AOM); one trial was reviewed but not pooled because of heterogeneity. The pooled trials were Finnish, of adequate methodological quality, and mostly from the same research group. Populations analysed separately: healthy children attending daycare, healthy children during a respiratory infection, and otitis-prone healthy children.
cards.result: In three trials of 1,826 healthy children attending daycare, xylitol in any form reduced AOM risk from 30% to around 22% versus control (relative risk 0.75, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.88; moderate quality evidence) — an absolute reduction of about 8 percentage points, i.e. a 25% relative reduction. Xylitol was not effective during a respiratory infection (RR 1.13, 0.83 to 1.53; moderate quality) or in otitis-prone children (RR 0.90, 0.67 to 1.21; low quality). Dropouts for abdominal discomfort and rash did not differ significantly between groups. The authors conclude prophylactic xylitol can reduce AOM in healthy daycare children, with inconclusive evidence in respiratory infection and otitis-prone children.
cards.watchOut: Nearly all the pooled evidence comes from one Finnish research group in one care setting — daycare in a country with high daycare attendance — and the regimen in those trials demanded dosing several times a day for months. A relative risk of 0.75 earned in that setting is a hypothesis about, not a measurement of, what happens in a British or American toddler dosed when a parent remembers.
cards.source: Azarpazhooh A et al. Xylitol for preventing acute otitis media in children up to 12 years of age. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2016. PMID: 27486835. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Uhari 1998 (857 healthy daycare children): at least one ear infection in 41% on control syrup versus 29% on xylitol syrup — gum worked too, lozenges did not reach significance
cards.summary: Uhari 1998 (857 healthy daycare children): at least one ear infection in 41% on control syrup versus 29% on xylitol syrup — gum worked too, lozenges did not reach significance
cards.people: 857 healthy children recruited from Finnish daycare centres, randomised to five groups for 3 months: control syrup (n = 165), xylitol syrup (n = 159), control chewing gum (n = 178), xylitol gum (n = 179) or xylitol lozenge (n = 176). Daily xylitol dose ranged from 8.4 g (gum) to 10 g (syrup). The trial was blinded within the syrup and gum comparisons. Main outcome: occurrence of acute otitis media whenever the child showed symptoms of a respiratory infection.
cards.result: At least one episode of AOM occurred in 41% (68/165) of children on control syrup versus 29% (46/159) on xylitol syrup — a 30% relative decrease (95% CI 4.6% to 55.4%). Xylitol chewing gum reduced occurrence by 40% relative (CI 10.0% to 71.1%) and lozenges by 20% relative (CI −12.9% to 51.4%, not significant). Children on xylitol syrup or gum required antimicrobials less often than controls. Xylitol was well tolerated. The authors conclude xylitol syrup or gum prevented AOM and decreased antimicrobial use.
cards.watchOut: Chewing gum is a delivery system only older children can use, and the syrup result depends on doses given repeatedly through the day for three months — adherence in the trial was supervised by daycare. The lozenge arm's null result is a quiet warning that the effect is regimen-dependent, not a property of the molecule at any dose.
cards.source: Uhari M et al. A novel use of xylitol sugar in preventing acute otitis media. Pediatrics. 1998. PMID: 9755259. Registry ID: none — pre-registration era. cards.headline: Synthesis: a real preventive effect in healthy daycare children, a null in the otitis-prone — SPLIT (Tier C)
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real preventive effect in healthy daycare children, a null in the otitis-prone — SPLIT (Tier C)
cards.people: One Cochrane review (Azarpazhooh 2016: 5 trials, 3,405 children) and its largest constituent trial (Uhari 1998: 857 children). The evidence base is Finnish, daycare-based and largely from one research group.
cards.result: In healthy children attending daycare, xylitol reduces acute otitis media from about 30% to about 22% of children (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.88; absolute reduction about 8 percentage points). In the two populations parents most often ask about — children prone to recurrent ear infections and children who already have a respiratory infection — the pooled estimates are null (RR 0.90 and RR 1.13). PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY (benefit) in healthy daycare children / MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) in otitis-prone children, where the trials show no effect; Tier C: a small, single-group-dominated evidence base with a demanding dosing regimen.
cards.watchOut: The question as posed asks about children prone to recurrent otitis media — precisely the group with the null result — so this shelf must not be quoted as supporting xylitol for them. Prevention is also a different question from treating recurrent disease once established: tympanostomy tubes for recurrent acute otitis media are homed at shelf #629.

shelves.title: Omega-3 supplements in ADHD: a small symptom effect in pooled trials (g ≈ 0.38) that the Cochrane review could not find in parent or teacher ratings
shelves.question: In children with ADHD, do omega-3 fatty acid supplements improve core symptoms?
shelves.mesh: Attention Deficit Disorder with Hyperactivity/blood/drug therapy* · Child · Eicosapentaenoic Acid/blood/therapeutic use* · Fatty Acids, Omega-3/blood/therapeutic use* · Humans
shelves.balance: The meta-analyses disagree in a way that tracks their methods. Bloch MH et al. (PMID: 21961774), pooling 10 placebo-controlled trials (699 children), found a small but significant effect on ADHD symptoms, with efficacy correlated with the EPA dose in the supplement. Chang JP et al. (PMID: 28741625) found the same direction with a number attached: symptom scores improved by g = 0.38 across 7 trials (534 youths), with attention-related cognitive measures improving more (g = 1.09) in only 3 small trials. The Cochrane review (Gillies D et al., PMID: 22786509), analysing parent and teacher ratings separately across 13 trials (1,011 participants), found no significant difference on any rated outcome — parent-rated symptoms SMD −0.17 (95% CI −0.38 to 0.03) — and concluded there is little evidence of benefit. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a small average improvement on pooled global scores, inconsistently found when outcomes are split by rater, and far smaller than the effect of stimulant medication. The trials' records name no specific product, brand or company — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: Bloch 2011 (10 trials, 699 children): omega-3 supplementation has a small but significant effect on ADHD symptoms, larger with higher EPA doses
cards.summary: Bloch 2011 (10 trials, 699 children): omega-3 supplementation has a small but significant effect on ADHD symptoms, larger with higher EPA doses
cards.people: Ten randomised placebo-controlled trials (699 children) of omega-3 fatty acid supplementation in children with ADHD symptomatology. Primary outcome: standardised mean difference in rating scales of ADHD severity; secondary analyses examined the dose of each omega-3 component (EPA, DHA) against efficacy.
cards.result: Omega-3 supplementation produced a small but significant improvement in ADHD symptoms. The eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) dose within the supplements was significantly correlated with efficacy — higher EPA, larger effect. No evidence of publication bias or heterogeneity between trials was found. The authors judge the effect modest compared with stimulants, atomoxetine or alpha-2 agonists, but note the benign side-effect profile and suggest supplementation may reasonably augment standard treatment or serve families who decline other pharmacological options.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports the effect as 'small but significant' without a pooled number, and this card does not supply one from outside the record. The included supplements vary in EPA/DHA content and the trials' records name no specific product, brand or manufacturer — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.headline: Chang 2018 (7 trials, 534 youths): symptom scores improve (g = 0.38) and attention-related cognitive measures improve more (g = 1.09) — in only 3 small trials
cards.summary: Chang 2018 (7 trials, 534 youths): symptom scores improve (g = 0.38) and attention-related cognitive measures improve more (g = 1.09) — in only 3 small trials
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 7 RCTs plus case-control studies (Chang 2018)
cards.people: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials of omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids in children and adolescents with ADHD (7 RCTs, 534 randomised youths for clinical symptoms; 3 RCTs, 214 youths for cognitive measures), together with case-control studies comparing omega-3 levels in blood and buccal tissue between youths with ADHD and controls.
cards.result: Omega-3 supplementation improved ADHD clinical symptom scores (g = 0.38, p < 0.0001) and cognitive measures associated with attention (g = 1.09, p = 0.001). In the case-control data, children and adolescents with ADHD had lower levels of DHA (g = −0.76), EPA (g = −0.38) and total omega-3 fatty acids (g = −0.58) than controls. The authors conclude the evidence supports omega-3 supplementation improving symptoms and cognition in ADHD, alongside a demonstrable deficiency in omega-3 levels.
cards.watchOut: The eye-catching number is the weakest one: g = 1.09 for cognition rests on 3 trials and 214 children, and effects of that size in samples that small almost always shrink on replication. The deficiency findings are cross-sectional — children with ADHD may eat differently — so low omega-3 levels cannot by themselves argue that supplementation treats the condition.

cards.headline: Gillies 2012 (Cochrane, 13 trials, 1,011 participants): no significant difference on any parent- or teacher-rated ADHD outcome — 'little evidence that PUFA supplementation provides any benefit'
cards.summary: Gillies 2012 (Cochrane, 13 trials, 1,011 participants): no significant difference on any parent- or teacher-rated ADHD outcome — 'little evidence that PUFA supplementation provides any benefit'
cards.people: Thirteen trials (1,011 children and adolescents) of polyunsaturated fatty acid supplements versus placebo or other treatment for ADHD symptoms, with supplements given for 4 to 16 weeks: five trials of omega-3 versus placebo, others of combined omega-3/omega-6, omega-6 alone, or omega-3 versus omega-6 or versus dexamphetamine. Outcomes were parent- and teacher-rated symptoms, behaviour, side effects and loss to follow-up.
cards.result: There were no statistically significant differences in parent-rated ADHD symptoms (5 trials, 413 participants; SMD −0.17, 95% CI −0.38 to 0.03), inattention (6 trials, 469; SMD −0.04, −0.29 to 0.21) or hyperactivity/impulsivity (5 trials, 416; SMD −0.04, −0.25 to 0.16), and teacher ratings were likewise null. The one positive result was a higher likelihood of 'improvement' with combined omega-3/omega-6 versus placebo in two trials (97 participants; risk ratio 2.19, 1.04 to 4.62). Behaviour, side effects and loss to follow-up did not differ. The authors conclude there is little evidence that PUFA supplementation benefits ADHD symptoms in children and adolescents, citing small samples, variable selection criteria, variable supplement type and dose, and short follow-up.
cards.watchOut: Cochrane and the later meta-analyses are not pooling identical things: Cochrane separates raters and includes omega-6-only and active-comparator trials, which dilutes any omega-3-specific signal; Bloch and Chang pool global symptom scores. The disagreement is therefore partly about method, not only about data — but a family buying fish oil is buying the claim as Cochrane tested it, rater by rater, and there it is null.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a small pooled benefit that Cochrane's rater-by-rater analysis cannot find — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: a small pooled benefit that Cochrane's rater-by-rater analysis cannot find — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Three syntheses of overlapping small trials: Bloch 2011 (10 trials, 699 children), Chang 2018 (7 trials, 534 youths) and the Cochrane review (Gillies 2012: 13 trials, 1,011 participants).
cards.result: Two meta-analyses pooling global symptom scores find a small significant benefit (Chang: g = 0.38; Bloch: small, EPA-dose-related), while the Cochrane review's rater-by-rater analyses find no significant effect on any parent- or teacher-rated outcome, with one positive global-impression result for combined omega-3/omega-6 (RR 2.19 in 97 children). The most defensible reading is a small average effect that is fragile to how outcomes are pooled. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — small symptom improvement on pooled scores, inconsistently found; no specific product or brand is named in any record, and products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.watchOut: Even taking the positive meta-analyses at face value, the effect (g ≈ 0.4) is a fraction of what stimulant medication achieves, and the trials run 4–16 weeks in a condition treated for years. Omega-3 is a reasonable low-risk adjunct for families who want it; the evidence does not support it as a substitute for established treatment, and no trial carded here tests it as one.

shelves.title: Oral vs IV rehydration for moderately dehydrated children: oral therapy rehydrates just as reliably, fails in about 1 child in 25, and gets children home sooner
shelves.question: In children with moderate dehydration from gastroenteritis, is oral rehydration as effective as intravenous fluids?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Child, Preschool · Dehydration/etiology, therapy* · Female · Fluid Therapy* · Gastroenteritis/complications, virology · Humans · Infant · Infusions, Intravenous · Male · Rehydration Solutions/administration & dosage* · Single-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for successful rehydration — and the surrounding outcomes mostly favour the oral route. The one trial designed exactly on this question (Spandorfer PR et al., PMID: 15687435) randomised 73 moderately dehydrated children in an emergency department and found oral rehydration noninferior: half of each group was successfully rehydrated at 4 hours (difference −1.2%, 95% CI −24.0 to 21.6), treatment started about 21 minutes sooner by mouth, and fewer oral-therapy children were admitted (30.6% vs 48.7%). The two syntheses agree on the shape of the trade. Fonseca BK et al. (PMID: 15123483), pooling 16 trials and 1,545 children, found enteral therapy carried fewer major adverse events than IV (relative risk 0.36, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.89) and a hospital stay about 21 hours shorter, with an overall enteral failure rate of 4.0%. The Cochrane review (Hartling L et al., PMID: 16856044), 17 trials and 1,811 children, puts the failure excess precisely: 4 more failures per 100 children treated orally (risk difference 4%, 95% CI 1 to 7; one extra failure for every 25 treated), balanced against a stay 1.2 days shorter, more phlebitis with IV lines, more paralytic ileus with oral therapy, and no difference in the subgroup given modern low-osmolarity solution. Nasogastric infusion performs like IV too (Nager AL et al., PMID: 11927697). PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): oral rehydration is the equal of IV fluids for moderate dehydration, with a small, plannable failure rate rather than a hidden one.

cards.headline: Spandorfer 2005: the head-to-head noninferiority trial — oral and IV rehydration succeeded equally at 4 hours, oral started 21 minutes faster, and fewer oral-therapy children were admitted (31% vs 49%)
cards.summary: Spandorfer 2005: the head-to-head noninferiority trial — oral and IV rehydration succeeded equally at 4 hours, oral started 21 minutes faster, and fewer oral-therapy children were admitted (31% vs 49%)
cards.people: 73 children aged 8 weeks to 3 years with moderate dehydration (validated 10-point score) from viral gastroenteritis, randomised in a US children's hospital emergency department to oral rehydration therapy or intravenous fluids over a 4-hour study period; treating physicians were masked to allocation when assessing outcomes.
cards.result: Oral rehydration was noninferior for the main outcome: half of both groups were successfully rehydrated at 4 hours (difference −1.2%, 95% CI −24.0 to 21.6). Therapy began sooner by mouth (19.9 vs 41.2 minutes from randomisation; difference −21.2 minutes). Improvement in dehydration score at 2 hours was the same (78.8% vs 80%). Hospitalisation was less frequent after oral therapy (30.6% vs 48.7%; difference −18.1%, 95% CI −40.1 to 4.0), and parents were as likely to say they would choose the same route again (61.3% vs 51.4%).
cards.watchOut: A small trial (73 children) with a wide noninferiority interval — the confidence interval for the 4-hour success difference (−24 to +22 percentage points) cannot exclude a clinically meaningful gap on its own; the verdict rests on this trial read together with the two meta-analyses. Children were 8 weeks to 3 years old with viral gastroenteritis and moderate (not severe) dehydration; the result does not extend to shock, severe dehydration, or surgical abdomens.

cards.headline: Fonseca 2004 meta-analysis: 16 trials, 1,545 children — enteral rehydration caused fewer major adverse events than IV (RR 0.36) and shortened hospital stay by about 21 hours; 4% of enteral therapy failed
cards.summary: Fonseca 2004 meta-analysis: 16 trials, 1,545 children — enteral rehydration caused fewer major adverse events than IV (RR 0.36) and shortened hospital stay by about 21 hours; 4% of enteral therapy failed
cards.people: 16 randomised or quasi-randomised trials of enteral (oral or nasogastric) versus intravenous rehydration in 1,545 children under 15 with gastroenteritis of less than a week's duration, conducted in 11 countries.
cards.result: Compared with IV rehydration, enteral therapy was associated with significantly fewer major adverse events, including death or seizures (relative risk 0.36, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.89), and a significantly shorter hospital stay (mean reduction 21 hours, 95% CI 8 to 35). Weight gain did not differ (mean −26 g, 95% CI −61 to 10). The overall failure rate of enteral therapy was 4.0% (95% CI 3.0 to 5.0). The authors conclude enteral rehydration is as effective as, if not better than, IV rehydration for childhood gastroenteritis.
cards.watchOut: 'Enteral' here pools oral and nasogastric routes, and the major-adverse-event advantage is driven by rare events (deaths and seizures) in a small number of trials — the relative risk of 0.36 has a wide interval (0.14 to 0.89). The review predates universal low-osmolarity oral solution; the later Cochrane subgroup on low-osmolarity solution found no significant difference from IV at all.

cards.headline: Hartling 2006 (Cochrane): 17 trials, 1,811 children — oral therapy failed 4% more often (one extra failure per 25 treated), but stays were 1.2 days shorter and the harms were route-specific, not one-sided
cards.summary: Hartling 2006 (Cochrane): 17 trials, 1,811 children — oral therapy failed 4% more often (one extra failure per 25 treated), but stays were 1.2 days shorter and the harms were route-specific, not one-sided
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 17 RCTs (Hartling 2006, Cochrane)
cards.people: 17 randomised and quasi-randomised trials (1,811 participants up to 18 years) comparing intravenous with oral rehydration for dehydration due to acute gastroenteritis; the reviewers rated the trials poor to moderate quality.
cards.result: Treatment failure was more common with oral therapy (risk difference 4%, 95% CI 1 to 7; number needed to treat 25). Deaths were few and split the other way (6 in the IV group, 2 in the oral groups, across 4 trials). There were no significant differences in weight gain, hyponatraemia, hypernatraemia, duration of diarrhoea, or fluid intake at 6 or 24 hours. Hospital stays were shorter with oral therapy (weighted mean difference −1.20 days, 95% CI −2.38 to −0.02). Phlebitis occurred more often with IV therapy (number needed to harm 50) and paralytic ileus more often with oral therapy (number needed to harm 33). In the subgroup using low-osmolarity oral solution — the modern WHO formulation — there was no significant difference from IV therapy (729 participants, 6 trials).
cards.watchOut: The 4% failure excess is the number to plan around, not a reason to start IV: 'failure' in these trials means crossing over to IV fluids, which is a routine rescue, not a catastrophe. Trial quality was poor to moderate and the literature is now old — practice, oral solutions, and ondansetron use have moved on — but no newer trial has reversed the direction of the findings.

cards.headline: Nager 2002: rapid nasogastric rehydration matched rapid IV rehydration in 96 moderately dehydrated toddlers — and routine blood tests added nothing
cards.summary: Nager 2002: rapid nasogastric rehydration matched rapid IV rehydration in 96 moderately dehydrated toddlers — and routine blood tests added nothing
cards.people: 96 children aged 3 to 36 months with uncomplicated acute moderate dehydration from vomiting and/or diarrhoea (presumed viral gastroenteritis) in an urban paediatric emergency department, randomised to rapid nasogastric hydration with oral rehydration solution or rapid IV hydration with normal saline, each 50 mL/kg over 3 hours; 90 were analysed.
cards.result: Both routes were safe and efficacious: only 3 children failed treatment for intractable vomiting (2 IV, 1 nasogastric) and were admitted. Electrolytes, urea, creatinine and glucose measurements were not found to be of value on an intention-to-treat basis in these uncomplicated cases. Both rapid regimens were substantially cheaper than standard inpatient IV deficit therapy, and the nasogastric route was the more cost-effective of the two in the outpatient setting, with fewer complications and no greater nursing burden.
cards.watchOut: The comparison is nasogastric infusion, not drinking — it answers the question for children who cannot keep fluid down or refuse to drink, and it should not be quoted as a trial of oral intake itself. Failed treatments were excluded from the main analysis rather than carried in an intention-to-treat denominator, which flatters both arms slightly.
cards.source: Nager AL et al. Comparison of nasogastric and intravenous methods of rehydration in pediatric patients with acute dehydration. Pediatrics. 2002. PMID: 11927697. cards.headline: Synthesis: oral rehydration is the equal of IV fluids for moderate dehydration — the honest price is a ~4% crossover rate, the honest gain is no drip, a faster start, and a shorter stay
cards.summary: Synthesis: oral rehydration is the equal of IV fluids for moderate dehydration — the honest price is a ~4% crossover rate, the honest gain is no drip, a faster start, and a shorter stay
cards.people: One noninferiority trial in the emergency department (73 children), two meta-analyses spanning 16–17 trials and 1,545–1,811 children, and a randomised comparison of the nasogastric fallback route (96 children).
cards.result: Successful rehydration: no demonstrated difference (Spandorfer 2005 noninferiority; Fonseca 2004 and Hartling 2006 concordant). Failure needing IV rescue: about 4 in 100 with oral/enteral therapy (risk difference 4%, NNT 25 in the Cochrane pooling). Major adverse events: fewer with enteral therapy in the earlier meta-analysis (RR 0.36, 0.14 to 0.89), with deaths numerically fewer on oral therapy in the Cochrane data (2 vs 6). Hospital stay: roughly a day shorter by the enteral route. Harms split by route — phlebitis belongs to IV lines, paralytic ileus to oral therapy. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: This shelf covers moderate dehydration from gastroenteritis in otherwise well children. It says nothing about severe dehydration or shock (where IV resuscitation is standard), dehydration from other causes, or infants under 8 weeks. The trials are old enough that none used today's low-osmolarity solution plus ondansetron as the default package — the modern package plausibly performs better than the oral arms pooled here, not worse.
cards.source: Synthesis of Spandorfer PR et al. Pediatrics. 2005 (PMID: 15687435); Fonseca BK et al. Archives of Pediatrics & Adolescent Medicine. 2004 (PMID: 15123483); Hartling L et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2006 (PMID: 16856044); Nager AL et al. Pediatrics. 2002 (PMID: 11927697).

shelves.title: Gluten-free, casein-free diets in autism: the one positive trial had no placebo and parents who knew the diet — both double-blind tests found nothing
shelves.question: In children with autism spectrum disorder, does a gluten-free, casein-free diet improve behaviour or cognition?
shelves.mesh: Aging · Attention · Caseins/administration & dosage, adverse effects* · Child · Child Development · Child Development Disorders, Pervasive/diagnosis, diet therapy*, urine · Child, Preschool · Diet, Gluten-Free* · Diet, Protein-Restricted · Female · Glycine/analogs & derivatives, urine · Humans · Hyperkinesis · Male · Reproducibility of Results · Severity of Illness Index · Single-Blind Method · Statistics as Topic · Time Factors
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the benefit claim rests on the weakest design in the set. The ScanBrit trial (Whiteley P et al., PMID: 20406576) randomised 72 Danish children and reported significant improvement on some ADOS, GARS and ADHD-IV sub-domains by 12 months — but it was single-blind with no placebo diet, analysed per protocol (26 diet vs 29 control children at 12 months), and its adaptive 'catch-up' design then moved the control group onto the diet, dissolving the comparison for the 24-month data. The two double-blind studies found nothing: Hyman SL et al. (PMID: 26343026) kept 14 children on the diet and challenged them blind with gluten, casein, both, or placebo snacks — no significant effect on behaviour problems or autism symptoms; Elder JH et al. (PMID: 16555138), in a double-blind crossover of 15 children, likewise found no statistically significant effect, even though several parents reported improvement. The Cochrane review (Millward C et al., PMID: 18425890) had only two small trials (n = 35) to work with and concluded the evidence for efficacy is poor. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): where the raters cannot know the diet, the effect disappears; where they can, it appears — the signature of expectation, not of gluten or casein.

cards.headline: ScanBrit (Whiteley 2010): 72 children, some rating-scale sub-domains improved on the diet at 12 months — in a single-blind trial with no placebo diet and a control group that was then switched onto the diet
cards.summary: ScanBrit (Whiteley 2010): 72 children, some rating-scale sub-domains improved on the diet at 12 months — in a single-blind trial with no placebo diet and a control group that was then switched onto the diet
cards.people: 72 Danish children aged 4 years to 10 years 11 months with autism spectrum disorders, assigned by stratified randomisation to a gluten- and casein-free diet or no diet in a two-stage, 24-month trial with an adaptive 'catch-up' design; per-protocol data at 12 months were available for 26 diet and 29 control children, and at 24 months for 18 and 17.
cards.result: At 12 months there was a significant time-by-treatment interaction favouring the diet group on sub-domains of the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule, the Gilliam Autism Rating Scale, and the ADHD-IV inattention/hyperactivity scale. Because the diet group crossed the pre-set improvement thresholds, control children were re-assigned to the diet for stage 2; 24-month analyses suggested some sustained group improvement, possibly a plateau. The authors state plainly that, without a placebo condition, they cannot exclude effects arising from the intervention experience rather than the dietary change itself. The trial was registered as NCT00614198.
cards.watchOut: Every safeguard that separates a diet effect from an expectation effect is missing or weakened here: parents and children knew the allocation (only assessors were blinded, and the significant outcomes lean on rating scales), there was no placebo diet, the analysis was per protocol rather than intention-to-treat, and the design deliberately destroyed its own control group after 12 months. A positive result from this design is the weakest form a positive result can take.
cards.source: Whiteley P et al. The ScanBrit randomised, controlled, single-blind study of a gluten- and casein-free dietary intervention for children with autism spectrum disorders. cards.headline: Hyman 2016: the double-blind challenge test — 14 children kept on the diet, then secretly challenged with gluten, casein, both, or placebo; nothing happened on any measure
cards.summary: Hyman 2016: the double-blind challenge test — 14 children kept on the diet, then secretly challenged with gluten, casein, both, or placebo; nothing happened on any measure
cards.people: 14 children with autism aged 3 to 5 years, placed on a gluten-free, casein-free diet for 4 to 6 weeks with nutritional counselling, then entered into a 12-week double-blind, placebo-controlled challenge phase (weekly snacks containing gluten, casein, both, or placebo) while continuing the diet, with 12 weeks of follow-up.
cards.result: The diet itself was safe and well tolerated with nutritional counselling. The blinded dietary challenges had no statistically significant effects on measures of physiologic functioning, behaviour problems, or autism symptoms. The authors caution that the sample is small, but conclude the study provides no evidence to support general use of the gluten-free, casein-free diet.
cards.watchOut: Fourteen children cannot exclude a small effect, and a challenge design tests whether re-exposure worsens symptoms in children already on the diet — a slightly different question from whether starting the diet helps. But this is the only design in the literature where nobody knew who was eating gluten or casein, and its answer was null on every measure taken.
cards.source: Hyman SL et al. The Gluten-Free/Casein-Free Diet: A Double-Blind Challenge Trial in Children with Autism. Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders. 2016. PMID: 26343026. cards.headline: Elder 2006: double-blind crossover, 15 children, 12 weeks — no significant effect on autistic symptoms, though several parents believed their child had improved
cards.summary: Elder 2006: double-blind crossover, 15 children, 12 weeks — no significant effect on autistic symptoms, though several parents believed their child had improved
cards.people: 15 children aged 2 to 16 years with autism spectrum disorder in a randomised, double-blind, repeated-measures crossover trial of the gluten-free, casein-free diet, with symptom and urinary peptide data collected in the children's homes over 12 weeks on the diet.
cards.result: Group data showed no statistically significant findings for the diet on autistic symptoms or urinary peptide levels. Several parents nonetheless reported improvement in their children — the gap between unblinded parental impression and blinded measurement that runs through this whole literature. The authors present the study as preliminary and as a demonstration that a controlled trial of the diet can be done.
cards.watchOut: A pilot of 15 children over 12 weeks is powered to find only very large effects; its null result is weak evidence of no effect taken alone. Its weight comes from pointing the same way as the other double-blind study (Hyman 2016) and the opposite way from the unblinded one (ScanBrit).
cards.source: Elder JH et al. The gluten-free, casein-free diet in autism: results of a preliminary double blind clinical trial. Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders. 2006. PMID: 16555138. cards.headline: Millward 2008 (Cochrane): the whole randomised literature was two small trials and 35 children — 'current evidence for efficacy of these diets is poor'
cards.summary: Millward 2008 (Cochrane): the whole randomised literature was two small trials and 35 children — 'current evidence for efficacy of these diets is poor'
cards.people: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials eliminating gluten, casein, or both in autistic spectrum disorder; only two small trials (n = 35, the Knivsberg studies) met inclusion, with no common outcome measures, so no meta-analysis was possible.
cards.result: Three outcomes significantly favoured the diet, all from the Knivsberg reports: overall autistic traits (mean difference −5.60, 95% CI −9.02 to −2.18), social isolation, and overall ability to communicate and interact (mean difference 1.70, 95% CI 0.50 to 2.90). Three outcomes showed no significant difference, ten could not be calculated because the data were skewed, and no trial reported harms or disbenefits. The reviewers note the high use of exclusion diets by families and conclude that the evidence for efficacy is poor and that large, good-quality randomised trials are needed.
cards.watchOut: This review predates ScanBrit and the Hyman challenge trial, so its two-trial base is not the whole current literature — but the trials published since have not repaired the problem it identified: the positive results still come from designs without adequate blinding or placebo control. One confidence interval in the review's abstract is internally inconsistent as printed and is not quoted on this shelf.
cards.source: Millward C et al. Gluten- and casein-free diets for autistic spectrum disorder. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2008. PMID: 18425890. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: an unproven diet — benefit appears only where families know the diet is in place, and disappears under double-blind challenge
cards.summary: Synthesis: an unproven diet — benefit appears only where families know the diet is in place, and disappears under double-blind challenge
cards.people: Four randomised studies in total across the shelf: one single-blind 24-month trial (72 children), two double-blind studies (14 and 15 children), and a Cochrane review of the two earliest small trials (35 children).
cards.result: Unblinded/single-blind evidence: improvement on some rating-scale sub-domains (ScanBrit, per-protocol, no placebo). Double-blind evidence: no significant effect on behaviour, symptoms, or physiology (Hyman 2016; Elder 2006). Harms: none reported in the trials, though the diet is restrictive, socially costly, and was only shown safe with nutritional counselling. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — a family that wants to try the diet is not defying strong negative evidence, but no family should be told the evidence says it works.
cards.watchOut: Small blinded trials cannot prove a zero effect in every subgroup — a genuine responder subgroup (for example, children with coeliac disease or true milk allergy, who should be on the diet for those reasons anyway) would be invisible in samples of 14–15. What the evidence does exclude is a general effect large enough to justify recommending the diet to all children with autism.
cards.source: Synthesis of Whiteley P et al. Nutritional Neuroscience. 2010 (PMID: 20406576); Hyman SL et al. Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders. 2016 (PMID: 26343026); Elder JH et al. Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders. 2006 (PMID: 16555138); Millward C et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2008 (PMID: 18425890).

shelves.title: Immunostimulants to prevent children's respiratory infections: about 1.1 fewer infections per child in pooled trials — a 39% relative reduction built on low-quality, heterogeneous evidence
shelves.question: In children prone to respiratory tract infections, do immunostimulants (including bacterial lysates such as OM-85) prevent acute respiratory infections compared with placebo?
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the pooled effect looks substantial and the foundations look soft. The systematic review (Berber A et al., PMID: 36185547) gathered 72 placebo-controlled trials in 12,229 children; the 38 trials with usable data (4,643 children) showed a mean of 1.12 fewer acute respiratory infections per child (95% CI −1.39 to −0.85) and a ratio of means of 0.61 (0.54 to 0.69) — a 39% relative reduction, with the absolute difference of about one infection printed alongside. But the reviewers themselves graded the efficacy evidence low: heterogeneity was considerable to substantial, risk of bias was unclear in every domain in 32 of the 72 trials, only 14 trials reported adverse events at all, and publication bias is plausible. The best-known single product trial (Gutiérrez-Tarango MD et al., PMID: 11399700) randomised just 54 susceptible children and found large effects (about three fewer infections over 12 months) of a size that small trials produce more often than large ones confirm. The review's record carries no MeSH terms and no registered protocol number. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): immunostimulants may prevent roughly one respiratory infection per susceptible child per season — a claim the current trial base is too weak to carry with confidence, and safety reporting is thinner still.

cards.headline: Berber 2022 (systematic review): 72 trials, 12,229 children — mean 1.12 fewer infections (95% CI −1.39 to −0.85), ratio of means 0.61, on evidence the reviewers graded low
cards.summary: Berber 2022 (systematic review): 72 trials, 12,229 children — mean 1.12 fewer infections (95% CI −1.39 to −0.85), ratio of means 0.61, on evidence the reviewers graded low
cards.people: 72 placebo-controlled trials of immunostimulants (any agent, any route) to prevent acute respiratory tract infections in children under 18 without immunodeficiency, anatomical, genetic or allergic conditions, totalling 12,229 children; 38 trials (4,643 children) contributed data on mean number of infections to the meta-analysis.
cards.result: Immunostimulants reduced the mean number of acute respiratory infections (mean difference −1.12, 95% CI −1.39 to −0.85) with a ratio of means of 0.61 (95% CI 0.54 to 0.69), corresponding to a 39% relative reduction (95% CI 31% to 46% relative), the absolute difference being about one infection per child. The reviewers describe the estimate as moderate-quality data in one analysis but graded the overall quality of evidence for efficacy low, citing considerable to substantial heterogeneity and unclear risk of bias in all domains in 32 of the 72 trials. Only 14 trials reported adverse events. The review was unfunded and has no registered number, per its record.
cards.watchOut: A class-level pool of many different agents, doses and populations, dominated by small old trials with unclear bias protection: the 39% relative figure is exactly the kind of number such pools overstate. With safety reported in barely a fifth of trials, the review can support 'may work' and almost nothing about 'is safe'. The record carries no MeSH terms.

cards.headline: Gutiérrez-Tarango 2001 (OM-85 BV): 5.0 versus 8.0 infections over 12 months in 54 susceptible children — and half the antibiotic courses (2.5 versus 4.5)
cards.summary: Gutiérrez-Tarango 2001 (OM-85 BV): 5.0 versus 8.0 infections over 12 months in 54 susceptible children — and half the antibiotic courses (2.5 versus 4.5)
cards.people: 54 susceptible children aged 1–12 in Chihuahua City, Mexico, randomised to the bacterial lysate OM-85 BV (named in the publication as OM-85 BV, Broncho-Vaxom; the publication names no company in this record) or placebo — one capsule daily for 10 days a month for 3 months, repeated at 6 months — and followed for 12 months.
cards.result: Mean acute respiratory infections numbered 5.04 (±1.99) on OM-85 BV versus 8.0 (±2.55) on placebo — a mean difference of −2.96 (95% CI −4.22 to −1.7). Antibiotic courses were 2.46 (±2.08) versus 4.46 (±2.08), a difference of −2.0 (−3.14 to −0.86), and total illness duration was 35.23 (±17.64) versus 60.75 (±25.44) days, a difference of −25.52 days (−37.56 to −13.47), p<0.001 for all three. Four treated children had five adverse events (one skin rash judged related to the medication); six control children had six adverse events. No company is named for the tested product in this record, and current bacterial-lysate products may differ in safety and effectiveness from the preparation tested in 1997–99.
cards.watchOut: Fifty-four children, one centre, one product, conducted 1997–99: effects of this size (roughly 37% relative fewer infections, with absolute counts printed alongside) from trials of this size routinely shrink on replication. It is the illustrative product trial behind the class-level review, not independent confirmation of it.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a consistent-looking pooled benefit that the reviewers themselves would not grade above low — prevention of about one infection per child is a hope with numbers attached
cards.summary: Synthesis: a consistent-looking pooled benefit that the reviewers themselves would not grade above low — prevention of about one infection per child is a hope with numbers attached
cards.people: A 72-trial systematic review (12,229 children; 38 trials meta-analysed) and the best-known single-product randomised trial (54 children, OM-85 BV) — the evidence base for immunostimulants to prevent childhood respiratory infections.
cards.result: Infections: mean difference −1.12 per child (95% CI −1.39 to −0.85); ratio of means 0.61, a 39% relative reduction. Single-product trial: 5.04 versus 8.0 infections and 2.46 versus 4.46 antibiotic courses over 12 months. Safety: reported in only 14 of 72 trials in the review; one drug-related rash in the product trial. Evidence quality: low, with substantial heterogeneity and unclear bias in most trials. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: 'Immunostimulants' is a shelf of unlike products — bacterial lysates and synthetic agents pooled as one class — so a class-level average may describe no actual product a parent can buy; the one product trial names OM-85 BV (Broncho-Vaxom) without naming a company in its record, and current products may differ. What is missing is one large, well-blinded, safety-reporting trial of a named product. Tier C is not set: the base is a systematic review, however weak its contents.
cards.source: Synthesis of Berber A et al. The World Allergy Organization Journal. 2022 (PMID: 36185547); Gutiérrez-Tarango MD et al. Chest. 2001 (PMID: 11399700).

shelves.title: Statins in children with familial hypercholesterolaemia: LDL falls at every time point across nine placebo trials, carotid wall thickness regressed over two years on pravastatin — long-term safety still not firmly established
shelves.question: In children and adolescents with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, do statins lower LDL cholesterol safely compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Child · Cholesterol, LDL/blood · Female · Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Hyperlipoproteinemia Type II/blood/drug therapy/genetics · Male · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for cholesterol and the artery wall, with event prevention inferred, not shown. The Cochrane review (Vuorio A et al., PMID: 31696945) pooled nine randomised placebo-controlled studies in 1,177 participants up to 18 years old with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia: statins reduced mean LDL cholesterol at all time points (high-quality evidence), with little or no difference in liver enzymes, creatine kinase, myopathy measures, or clinical adverse events, though follow-up was short (median 24 weeks, range 6 weeks to 2 years). The largest single trial (Wiegman A et al., PMID: 15265847) randomised 214 children aged 8–18 to pravastatin 20–40 mg daily or placebo for 2 years: LDL cholesterol fell 24.1% on pravastatin versus a 0.3% rise on placebo (p<0.001), carotid intima-media thickness trended to regression on pravastatin (−0.010 mm) versus progression on placebo (+0.005 mm; between-group difference significant, p=0.02), and there were no differences in growth, maturation, hormone levels, or muscle and liver enzymes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): statins lower LDL substantially and appear safe over up to two years in children with familial hypercholesterolaemia; whether starting in childhood prevents adult heart attacks is biologically plausible but has never been tested in a trial with clinical events.

cards.headline: Vuorio 2019 (Cochrane): nine placebo-controlled trials, 1,177 children — LDL reduced at all time points (high-quality evidence); safety outcomes little or no different
cards.summary: Vuorio 2019 (Cochrane): nine placebo-controlled trials, 1,177 children — LDL reduced at all time points (high-quality evidence); safety outcomes little or no different
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Vuorio 2019, Cochrane review)
cards.people: Nine randomised placebo-controlled studies including 1,177 participants up to 18 years old with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, comparing a statin with placebo or diet alone; intervention and follow-up were short (median 24 weeks; range 6 weeks to 2 years).
cards.result: Statins reduced the mean LDL cholesterol concentration at all time points (high-quality evidence). There may be little or no difference between statin and placebo in liver function tests (aspartate and alanine aminotransferase, and creatine kinase; low-quality evidence), in myopathy measures (low-quality evidence), or in clinical adverse events (moderate-quality evidence). No studies reported rhabdomyolysis or death due to rhabdomyolysis. The review concludes that while statins seem safe and well tolerated in children, their long-term safety in this age group is not firmly established.
cards.watchOut: Every endpoint here is a blood test or a safety laboratory value over weeks to two years — no trial in children can or did measure heart attacks. The shelf's benefit claim is LDL lowering, and the leap to lifetime event prevention rests on the causal role of LDL and on adult trial evidence, not on anything measured in these children.
cards.source: Vuorio A et al. Statins for children with familial hypercholesterolemia. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2019. PMID: 31696945. cards.headline: Wiegman 2004: pravastatin for 2 years — LDL −24.1% vs +0.3%, carotid intima-media thickness regressed (−0.010 mm) vs progressed (+0.005 mm), no effect on growth or maturation
cards.summary: Wiegman 2004: pravastatin for 2 years — LDL −24.1% vs +0.3%, carotid intima-media thickness regressed (−0.010 mm) vs progressed (+0.005 mm), no effect on growth or maturation
cards.people: 214 children with familial hypercholesterolaemia aged 8–18 years at an academic medical referral centre in the Netherlands, after a fat-restricted diet run-in, assigned to pravastatin 20–40 mg daily (n=106) or placebo (n=108) for 2 years.
cards.result: Carotid intima-media thickness showed a trend toward regression with pravastatin (mean change −0.010 mm; p=0.049 versus baseline) and toward progression with placebo (+0.005 mm; p=0.28); the between-group difference in change (0.014 mm) was significant (p=0.02). Pravastatin reduced mean LDL cholesterol by 24.1% versus a 0.3% increase on placebo (p<0.001). No differences were observed for growth, muscle or liver enzymes, endocrine function, Tanner staging, onset of menses, or testicular volume.
cards.watchOut: Carotid thickness is a surrogate measured in millimetre fractions, and two years is a small slice of a treatment intended to run for decades. The reassuring growth and maturation data are the trial's most durable contribution; they cover puberty only partially and say nothing about safety into adulthood.
cards.source: Wiegman A et al. Efficacy and safety of statin therapy in children with familial hypercholesterolemia: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2004. PMID: 15265847. cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: Nine randomised placebo-controlled trials totalling 1,177 children and adolescents with heterozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia (Cochrane review), anchored by a 2-year pravastatin trial in 214 children.
cards.result: LDL cholesterol: reduced at all time points across trials; −24.1% vs +0.3% over 2 years on pravastatin. Carotid intima-media thickness: −0.010 mm vs +0.005 mm change (p=0.02 between groups). Safety: no differences in growth, maturation, hormones, or muscle/liver enzymes over the periods studied. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Tier C is not set: the base is a Cochrane meta-analysis of nine randomised trials plus a concordant 2-year trial. The honest limit is duration — 'safe for two years in childhood' is what the evidence says; 'safe and event-preventing for a lifetime started at age 8' is extrapolation.

shelves.title: Direct oral anticoagulants in children with VTE: rivaroxaban recurrence 1% versus 3% on standard care, dabigatran noninferior on the composite (46% versus 42%) — bleeding no higher in either trial
shelves.question: In children and adolescents with venous thromboembolism, do direct oral anticoagulants match standard anticoagulation for recurrence and bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Anticoagulants/therapeutic use · Child · Child, Preschool · Female · Humans · Infant · Male · Risk Factors · Rivaroxaban/therapeutic use · Venous Thromboembolism/drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — which, for a child facing injections and INR checks, is the win. EINSTEIN-Jr (Male C et al., PMID: 31699660) randomised 500 children aged 0–17 with acute venous thromboembolism to bodyweight-adjusted rivaroxaban or standard anticoagulants: symptomatic recurrence occurred in 4 children (1%) on rivaroxaban versus 5 (3%) on standard care (hazard ratio 0.40; 95% CI 0.11–1.41), thrombotic burden on repeat imaging improved more with rivaroxaban (p=0.012), and major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding occurred in 3% versus 2% (hazard ratio 1.58; 95% CI 0.51–6.27), with no major bleed on rivaroxaban and no treatment-related deaths. DIVERSITY (Halton J et al., PMID: 33290737) randomised 267 analysed children to dabigatran by an age- and weight-adjusted nomogram or standard care: the composite of complete thrombus resolution, freedom from recurrence, and freedom from VTE-related death was met by 46% on dabigatran versus 42% on standard care (weighted difference −0.04; 90% CI −0.14 to 0.07; p<0.0001 for noninferiority), with major bleeding in 2% of each group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): two randomised trials, two DOACs, efficacy and bleeding statistically indistinguishable from the heparin-and-warfarin standard they replace.

cards.headline: Male 2020 (EINSTEIN-Jr): recurrence 1% on rivaroxaban versus 3% on standard anticoagulants (HR 0.40); bleeding 3% versus 2%, all rivaroxaban bleeds non-major; thrombus burden improved more (p=0.012)
cards.summary: Male 2020 (EINSTEIN-Jr): recurrence 1% on rivaroxaban versus 3% on standard anticoagulants (HR 0.40); bleeding 3% versus 2%, all rivaroxaban bleeds non-major; thrombus burden improved more (p=0.012)
cards.type: Randomised open-label phase 3 trial with blinded central outcome assessment (Male 2020, EINSTEIN-Jr)
cards.people: 500 children aged 0–17 years with documented acute venous thromboembolism who had started heparin, enrolled at 107 paediatric hospitals in 28 countries, randomised 2:1 to bodyweight-adjusted rivaroxaban (tablets or suspension, 20-mg-equivalent dose; 335 children) or standard anticoagulants (heparin, or switch to vitamin K antagonist; 165); main treatment period 3 months (1 month for catheter-related VTE in children under 2).
cards.result: Symptomatic recurrent venous thromboembolism occurred in 4 children (1%) on rivaroxaban and 5 (3%) on standard anticoagulants (hazard ratio 0.40; 95% CI 0.11–1.41). Repeat imaging showed a significantly better effect of rivaroxaban on thrombotic burden (p=0.012). Major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding occurred in 10 of 329 children (3%, all non-major) on rivaroxaban and 3 of 162 (2%; two major, one non-major) on standard care (hazard ratio 1.58; 95% CI 0.51–6.27). There were no treatment-related deaths.
cards.watchOut: Nine recurrences and thirteen bleeds in total: the confidence intervals (recurrence HR up to 1.41; bleeding HR up to 6.27) admit differences that matter, and the trial was open-label with blinded adjudication doing the protective work. Event rates this low mean 'matched' is a statement about a 3-month horizon in mostly older children — infants and catheter-related clots are thin slices of the enrolment.
cards.source: Male C et al. Rivaroxaban compared with standard anticoagulants for the treatment of acute venous thromboembolism in children: a randomised, controlled, phase 3 trial. The Lancet Haematology. 2020. PMID: 31699660. Registry ID: NCT02234843. randomised open-label phase 3 trial with blinded central outcome assessment (male 2020, einstein-jr) 500 children aged 0–17 years with documented acute venous thromboembolism who had started heparin, enrolled at 107 paediatric hospitals in 28 countries, randomised 2:1 to bodyweight-adjusted rivaroxaban (tablets or suspension, 20-mg-equivalent dose; 335 children) or standard anticoagulants (heparin, or switch to vitamin k antagonist; 165); main treatment period 3 months (1 month for catheter-related vte in children under 2). symptomatic recurrent venous thromboembolism occurred in 4 children (1%) on rivaroxaban and 5 (3%) on standard anticoagulants (hazard ratio 0.40; 95% ci 0.11–1.41). repeat imaging showed a significantly better effect of rivaroxaban on thrombotic burden (p=0.012). major or clinically relevant non-major bleeding occurred in 10 of 329 children (3%, all non-major) on rivaroxaban and 3 of 162 (2%; two major, one non-major) on standard care (hazard ratio 1.58; 95% ci 0.51–6.27). there were no treatment-related deaths. nine recurrences and thirteen bleeds in total: the confidence intervals (recurrence hr up to 1.41; bleeding hr up to 6.27) admit differences that matter, and the trial was open-label with blinded adjudication doing the protective work. event rates this low mean 'matched' is a statement about a 3-month horizon in mostly older children — infants and catheter-related clots are thin slices of the enrolment. male c et al. rivaroxaban compared with standard anticoagulants for the treatment of acute venous thromboembolism in children: a randomised, controlled, phase 3 trial. the lancet haematology. 2020. pmid: 31699660. registry id: nct02234843. mesh: adolescent · anticoagulants/therapeutic use · child · child, preschool · female · humans · infant · male · risk factors · rivaroxaban/therapeutic use · venous thromboembolism/drug therapy

cards.headline: Halton 2021 (DIVERSITY): composite efficacy endpoint met by 46% on dabigatran versus 42% on standard care (noninferiority p<0.0001); major bleeding 2% in both groups
cards.summary: Halton 2021 (DIVERSITY): composite efficacy endpoint met by 46% on dabigatran versus 42% on standard care (noninferiority p<0.0001); major bleeding 2% in both groups
cards.type: Randomised open-label phase 2b/3 non-inferiority trial (Halton 2021, DIVERSITY)
cards.people: 267 children younger than 18 years with acute venous thromboembolism, initially treated with parenteral anticoagulation for 5–21 days and needing at least 3 months of therapy, randomised at 65 centres in 26 countries to dabigatran dosed by an age- and weight-adjusted nomogram (177 children) or standard care (low-molecular-weight or unfractionated heparin, vitamin K antagonists, or fondaparinux; 90 children); median exposure ~85 days in both groups.
cards.result: The primary composite efficacy endpoint (complete thrombus resolution, freedom from recurrent venous thromboembolism, and freedom from VTE-related death) was met by 81 children (46%) on dabigatran and 38 (42%) on standard care (Mantel–Haenszel weighted difference −0.04; 90% CI −0.14 to 0.07; p<0.0001 for noninferiority against a 20% margin). On-treatment bleeding occurred in 22% on dabigatran versus 24% on standard care (hazard ratio 1.15; 95% CI 0.68 to 1.94); major bleeding in 4 children (2%) versus 2 (2%) (hazard ratio 0.94; 95% CI 0.17 to 5.16).
cards.watchOut: A 20-percentage-point noninferiority margin on a composite whose largest component is imaging resolution is generous — 'noninferior' here tolerates dabigatran being meaningfully worse on the composite before the label fails. The dosing nomogram, not a fixed dose, is the intervention; results travel with the algorithm, and the youngest age stratum is small.
cards.source: Halton J et al. Dabigatran etexilate for the treatment of acute venous thromboembolism in children (DIVERSITY): a randomised, controlled, open-label, phase 2b/3, non-inferiority trial. The Lancet Haematology. 2021. PMID: 33290737. Registry ID: NCT01895777.
