cards.headline: Synthesis: two DOACs, two trials, 767 children — the standard is matched, the needles are optional
cards.summary: Synthesis: two DOACs, two trials, 767 children — the standard is matched, the needles are optional
cards.people: Two randomised open-label trials in children aged 0–17 with acute VTE: EINSTEIN-Jr (rivaroxaban, 500 children, recurrence primary) and DIVERSITY (dabigatran, 267 children, composite noninferiority primary), each against heparin/vitamin-K-antagonist standard care over ~3 months.
cards.result: Recurrence: 1% versus 3% (rivaroxaban; HR 0.40, NS). Composite resolution/recurrence/death: 46% versus 42% (dabigatran; noninferior). Major bleeding: no major bleed on rivaroxaban versus 2 on standard care; 2% versus 2% in DIVERSITY. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: Both trials were powered for noninferiority-style conclusions on small event counts, and neither addresses treatment beyond ~3 months, cancer-associated clots in children specifically, or adherence once the trial's scaffolding is removed. Tier C is not set: two concordant randomised trials carry the equivalence.

shelves.title: Severely obese adolescents with type 2 diabetes: surgery cohorts' HbA1c fell 6.8%→5.5% over two years while medical cohorts' rose 6.4%→7.8% — a non-randomised comparison, with reoperation in 23%
shelves.question: In adolescents with severe obesity and type 2 diabetes, does metabolic surgery produce diabetes remission more often than medical therapy over five years?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Anthropometry/methods · Bariatric Surgery/methods · Blood Glucose/metabolism · Body Mass Index · Child · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/blood/etiology/therapy · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin/metabolism · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · Longitudinal Studies · Male · Metformin/therapeutic use · Obesity, Morbid/blood/complications/surgery
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — large glycaemic separation, observational design, and a question trimmed to what the record actually covers: two years, not five. Comparing the Teen-LABS surgical cohort with the TODAY medical-therapy cohort (Inge TH et al., PMID: 29532078), mean HbA1c over 2 years fell from 6.8% to 5.5% in 30 surgical adolescents while rising from 6.4% to 7.8% in 63 medically treated adolescents; BMI fell 29% with surgery and rose 3.7% with medical therapy. The surgical price inside the same window: 23% of Teen-LABS participants required a subsequent operation within the 2-year follow-up. This is a secondary analysis comparing two separately enrolled cohorts — not a randomised trial — and baseline ages differed (16.9 vs 15.3 years). The candidate question's five-year frame is not in this record; the five-year Teen-LABS report is already carded on the live adolescent-surgery shelf, so this shelf is anchored on the uncarded head-to-head comparison instead (declared as a swap in the part summary). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): surgery outperformed medical therapy on glycaemia over two years in the only direct comparison, at a real reoperation cost; Tier C — observational evidence throughout.

cards.headline: Inge 2018 (Teen-LABS vs TODAY): HbA1c 6.8%→5.5% with surgery versus 6.4%→7.8% with medical therapy at 2 years; BMI −29% versus +3.7%; subsequent operation in 23%
cards.summary: Inge 2018 (Teen-LABS vs TODAY): HbA1c 6.8%→5.5% with surgery versus 6.4%→7.8% with medical therapy at 2 years; BMI −29% versus +3.7%; subsequent operation in 23%
cards.people: Secondary analysis of two consortia: 30 adolescents with severe obesity and type 2 diabetes who had metabolic/bariatric surgery in Teen-LABS (mean age 16.9 years, 70% female) and 63 who received medical therapy in the TODAY randomised trial (mean age 15.3 years) — metformin alone or with rosiglitazone or lifestyle, insulin on progression. Outcomes compared over 2 years.
cards.result: Mean HbA1c decreased from 6.8% (95% CI 6.4–7.3) to 5.5% (4.7–6.3) in Teen-LABS and increased from 6.4% (6.1–6.7) to 7.8% (7.2–8.3) in TODAY. BMI decreased by 29% (95% CI 24–34) with surgery and increased by 3.7% (0.8–6.7) with medical therapy. Twenty-three percent of Teen-LABS participants required a subsequent operation during the 2-year follow-up. Blood pressure, dyslipidaemia, and kidney-function measures also favoured surgery in the authors' reporting.
cards.watchOut: Not randomised: families who chose surgery differ from trial volunteers, the surgical group was older, and the medical arm is a 2004–2009 treatment era (no GLP-1 agonists, no SGLT2 inhibitors). Two years is not the five years of the candidate question, and remission as a binary endpoint is not the outcome this record reports — HbA1c trajectories are.
cards.source: Inge TH et al. Comparison of Surgical and Medical Therapy for Type 2 Diabetes in Severely Obese Adolescents. JAMA Pediatrics. 2018. PMID: 29532078. shelves.title: Late parenteral nutrition in critically ill children (PEPaNIC): new infections 10.7% versus 18.5% and ICU stay 6.5 versus 9.2 days when parenteral nutrition was withheld for the first week — mortality similar
shelves.question: In critically ill children, does withholding parenteral nutrition for the first week in intensive care (late parenteral nutrition) improve recovery compared with starting it within 24 hours?
shelves.mesh: Child · Child, Preschool · Critical Illness/mortality/therapy · Enteral Nutrition · Female · Fluid Therapy · Humans · Infant · Infections/epidemiology · Intensive Care Units, Pediatric · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Length of Stay · Male · Parenteral Nutrition* · Respiration, Artificial · Time Factors · gamma-Glutamyltransferase/blood
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — withholding parenteral nutrition for the first week sped recovery in one large paediatric intensive care trial, without a mortality difference. In PEPaNIC (Fivez T et al., PMID: 26975590), 1,440 critically ill children were randomised to early parenteral nutrition, started within 24 hours of ICU admission (n=723), or late parenteral nutrition, not provided until the morning of the 8th day in the ICU (n=717); in both groups enteral nutrition was attempted early, intravenous micronutrients were provided, and fluid loading was similar. New infection acquired during the ICU stay — a primary endpoint — occurred in 10.7% of the late group versus 18.5% of the early group (adjusted odds ratio 0.48, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.66). The other primary endpoint, ICU dependency, also favoured late nutrition: mean ICU stay was 6.5±0.4 days versus 9.2±0.8 days, with a higher likelihood of earlier live discharge from the ICU at any time (adjusted hazard ratio 1.23, 95% CI 1.11 to 1.37). Late parenteral nutrition was also associated with a shorter duration of mechanical ventilatory support (P=0.001), a smaller proportion of patients receiving renal-replacement therapy (P=0.04), and a shorter hospital stay (P=0.001). Mortality was similar in the two groups — the record gives no mortality rates — so the benefit shown is faster recovery and fewer new infections, not survival. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in critically ill children, withholding parenteral nutrition for the first week (late parenteral nutrition) reduced new infections and shortened ICU stay in one large multicentre randomised trial, with mortality similar between groups.

cards.headline: Fivez 2016 (PEPaNIC): new infections 10.7% on late parenteral nutrition versus 18.5% on early (adjusted odds ratio 0.48) — ICU stay 6.5 versus 9.2 days, mortality similar
cards.summary: Fivez 2016 (PEPaNIC): new infections 10.7% on late parenteral nutrition versus 18.5% on early (adjusted odds ratio 0.48) — ICU stay 6.5 versus 9.2 days, mortality similar
cards.people: 1,440 critically ill children in the paediatric intensive care unit (ICU), randomised to early parenteral nutrition initiated within 24 hours after ICU admission (n=723) or late parenteral nutrition not provided until the morning of the 8th day in the ICU (n=717). In both groups, enteral nutrition was attempted early and intravenous micronutrients were provided; fluid loading was similar in the two groups. The two primary end points were new infection acquired during the ICU stay and the adjusted duration of ICU dependency, assessed by the number of days in the ICU and as time to discharge alive from ICU.
cards.result: Mortality was similar in the two groups (the record gives no mortality rates). The percentage of patients with a new infection was 10.7% in the late-parenteral-nutrition group, compared with 18.5% in the early-parenteral-nutrition group (adjusted odds ratio 0.48, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.35 to 0.66), the absolute rates printed alongside the adjusted effect. The mean (±SE) duration of ICU stay was 6.5±0.4 days on late parenteral nutrition, compared with 9.2±0.8 days on early parenteral nutrition, with a higher likelihood of an earlier live discharge from the ICU at any time in the late group (adjusted hazard ratio 1.23, 95% CI 1.11 to 1.37). Late parenteral nutrition was also associated with a shorter duration of mechanical ventilatory support (P=0.001), a smaller proportion of patients receiving renal-replacement therapy (P=0.04), and a shorter duration of hospital stay (P=0.001). Plasma γ-glutamyltransferase and alkaline phosphatase were lower on late parenteral nutrition (P=0.001 and P=0.04, respectively), while bilirubin (P=0.004) and C-reactive protein (P=0.006) were higher. The authors concluded that withholding parenteral nutrition for 1 week in the ICU was clinically superior to providing early parenteral nutrition.
cards.watchOut: One trial carries this shelf, and its abstract reports no mortality rates — only that mortality was similar — so no survival claim can be made either way. The comparison is also narrower than 'feeding versus starving': enteral nutrition was attempted early and intravenous micronutrients were given in both groups, so the result is about the timing of supplemental parenteral nutrition in children whose gut feeding was already being attempted, in paediatric intensive care. Several secondary advantages (ventilatory support, renal-replacement therapy, hospital stay) are reported in the record as P values without magnitudes, and two laboratory measures (bilirubin and C-reactive protein) moved in the opposite direction on late nutrition.
cards.source: Fivez T et al. Early versus Late Parenteral Nutrition in Critically Ill Children. N Engl J Med. 2016. PMID: 26975590. Registry ID: NCT01536275. cards.headline: Synthesis: one large multicentre trial — fewer new infections and a shorter ICU stay when parenteral nutrition was withheld for a week, mortality similar — with the re-card declared on the face of the shelf
cards.summary: Synthesis: one large multicentre trial — fewer new infections and a shorter ICU stay when parenteral nutrition was withheld for a week, mortality similar — with the re-card declared on the face of the shelf
cards.people: One multicentre randomised controlled trial of 1,440 critically ill children (PEPaNIC), testing parenteral nutrition started within 24 hours of ICU admission (n=723) against parenteral nutrition withheld until the morning of the 8th ICU day (n=717), with enteral nutrition attempted early and intravenous micronutrients provided in both groups.
cards.result: New infection during the ICU stay: 10.7% on late parenteral nutrition versus 18.5% on early (adjusted odds ratio 0.48, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.66). ICU stay: mean 6.5±0.4 days versus 9.2±0.8 days; earlier live discharge adjusted hazard ratio 1.23 (95% CI 1.11 to 1.37). Mortality: similar in the two groups, with no rates given in the record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Re-card declaration: PEPaNIC (Fivez T et al., PMID: 26975590) is also carded as a supporting card on live shelf #77 (When should parenteral nutrition start in the ICU?), where it serves as the paediatric card inside a general ICU question framed by the adult timing comparison — parenteral nutrition within two days, or not before day 8. This shelf asks the standalone paediatric question — in critically ill children, does withholding parenteral nutrition for the first week improve recovery compared with starting it within 24 hours — a genuinely different population and question, built under the Nov 15 #3104 (RACING) precedent, as applied at #3325 (STRENGTH), #3489 (CAROLINA), #3597 (PROPATRIA), #3628, #3753, #3812, #3833 and #3921: a study carded elsewhere as a supporting card may anchor a new shelf when the new question is genuinely different. Cross-point: see live shelf #77 for the general ICU parenteral-nutrition timing question. Tier C is set because a single trial carries the shelf and the claim touches recovery and infection outcomes in children.

synthesis one multicentre randomised controlled trial of 1,440 critically ill children (pepanic), testing parenteral nutrition started within 24 hours of icu admission (n=723) against parenteral nutrition withheld until the morning of the 8th icu day (n=717), with enteral nutrition attempted early and intravenous micronutrients provided in both groups. new infection during the icu stay: 10.7% on late parenteral nutrition versus 18.5% on early (adjusted odds ratio 0.48, 95% ci 0.35 to 0.66). icu stay: mean 6.5±0.4 days versus 9.2±0.8 days; earlier live discharge adjusted hazard ratio 1.23 (95% ci 1.11 to 1.37). mortality: similar in the two groups, with no rates given in the record. proposed possible (benefit). re-card declaration: pepanic (fivez t et al., pmid: 26975590) is also carded as a supporting card on live shelf #77 (when should parenteral nutrition start in the icu?), where it serves as the paediatric card inside a general icu question framed by the adult timing comparison — parenteral nutrition within two days, or not before day 8. this shelf asks the standalone paediatric question — in critically ill children, does withholding parenteral nutrition for the first week improve recovery compared with starting it within 24 hours — a genuinely different population and question, built under the nov 15 #3104 (racing) precedent, as applied at #3325 (strength), #3489 (carolina), #3597 (propatria), #3628, #3753, #3812, #3833 and #3921: a study carded elsewhere as a supporting card may anchor a new shelf when the new question is genuinely different. cross-point: see live shelf #77 for the general icu parenteral-nutrition timing question. tier c is set because a single trial carries the shelf and the claim touches recovery and infection outcomes in children. synthesis of fivez t et al. n engl j med. 2016 (pmid: 26975590).

shelves.title: MIS-C / PIMS-TS: methylprednisolone matched IVIG on hospital stay in both randomised trials (median 6.0 vs 6.0 days head-to-head; RECOVERY stay 6.9 days on steroid vs 7.6 on usual care, IVIG 7.4) — no winner, steroid far cheaper
shelves.question: In children with multisystem inflammatory syndrome (MIS-C / PIMS-TS), does methylprednisolone alone match intravenous immunoglobulin — alone or combined — for fever resolution and cardiac recovery?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · Child · Female · COVID-19/complications · SARS-CoV-2 · Interleukin 1 Receptor Antagonist Protein/therapeutic use · Immunoglobulins, Intravenous/therapeutic use · Bayes Theorem · Treatment Outcome · Methylprednisolone/therapeutic use · Inflammation · Immunomodulation · Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — head-to-head, the steroid matched the immunoglobulin on the outcome both trials measured, hospital stay. In the Swissped randomised trial (Welzel T et al., PMID: 36746174), median stay was 6.0 days on methylprednisolone and 6.0 days on intravenous immunoglobulin (effect size −0.037 of log10-transformed stay, 95% CI −0.13 to 0.065; p=0.42), although fewer methylprednisolone patients needed respiratory support (27% versus 55%, p=0.025). In RECOVERY's first randomisation (RECOVERY Collaborative Group, PMID: 38272046), mean stay was 6.9 days with methylprednisolone (difference from usual care −0.7 days, 95% credible interval −1.9 to 0.6) and 7.4 days with IVIG (difference −0.1 days, 95% CrI −1.3 to 1.0) against 7.6 days on usual care. Neither trial randomised a combined IVIG-plus-steroid arm, and neither record reports the fever-resolution or cardiac-recovery endpoints in the question — stay is the measured proxy, and that gap is stated plainly. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): methylprednisolone alone performed indistinguishably from IVIG on hospital stay in two open-label randomised trials.

cards.headline: Welzel 2023 (Swissped): median hospital stay 6.0 days on methylprednisolone vs 6.0 days on IVIG (p=0.42); respiratory support needed by 27% vs 55% (p=0.025)
cards.summary: Welzel 2023 (Swissped): median hospital stay 6.0 days on methylprednisolone vs 6.0 days on IVIG (p=0.42); respiratory support needed by 27% vs 55% (p=0.025)
cards.type: Open-label multicentre randomised trial (Welzel 2023, Swissped RECOVERY)
cards.people: 75 children younger than 18 years (median age 9.1 years) hospitalised with PIMS-TS at 10 Swiss hospitals, May 2021 to April 2022, randomised 1:1 to intravenous methylprednisolone 10 mg/kg per day for 3 days (n=37) or a single dose of intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg (n=38); primary outcome length of hospital stay censored at day 28.
cards.result: Median length of stay was 6.0 days (IQR 4.0 to 8.0) in the methylprednisolone group and 6.0 days (IQR 5.0 to 8.8) in the IVIG group (estimated effect size −0.037 of the log10-transformed times, 95% CI −0.13 to 0.065; p=0.42). Fewer methylprednisolone patients required respiratory support (10 of 37, 27%) than IVIG patients (21 of 38, 55%; p=0.025). Need and duration of inotropes, ICU admission, cardiac events after baseline, and major bleeding and thrombotic events did not differ significantly between groups.
cards.watchOut: Small (75 children) and open-label, with discharge decisions made by unblinded teams — exactly the outcome most open to bias. The respiratory-support difference is a secondary outcome in a small trial and should be read as a signal, not a result. Fever resolution and cardiac recovery, named in the question, are not reported on this record.

cards.headline: RECOVERY 2024: mean stay 6.9 days (methylprednisolone) and 7.4 days (IVIG) vs 7.6 days (usual care) — neither first-line treatment clearly shortened stay; second-line tocilizumab did (−3.3 days)
cards.summary: RECOVERY 2024: mean stay 6.9 days (methylprednisolone) and 7.4 days (IVIG) vs 7.6 days (usual care) — neither first-line treatment clearly shortened stay; second-line tocilizumab did (−3.3 days)
cards.type: Randomised open-label platform trial (RECOVERY Collaborative Group 2024)
cards.people: 237 children younger than 18 years admitted with PIMS-TS to 51 UK hospitals, May 2020 to January 2022 (mean age 9.5 years); first randomisation (214 patients): usual care (n=80), usual care plus methylprednisolone 10 mg/kg per day for 3 days (n=61), or usual care plus IVIG 2 g/kg single dose (n=73); second randomisation for refractory inflammation (70 children): tocilizumab, anakinra, or usual care. Primary outcome duration of hospital stay, analysed in a Bayesian framework.
cards.result: Mean duration of stay was 7.4 days with IVIG versus 7.6 days with usual care (difference −0.1 days, 95% credible interval −1.3 to 1.0; posterior probability of benefit 59%) and 6.9 days with methylprednisolone (difference −0.7 days, 95% CrI −1.9 to 0.6; posterior probability 87%). Second-line tocilizumab shortened stay by −3.3 days (95% CrI −5.6 to −1.0; posterior probability over 99%); anakinra did not (−1.4 days, 95% CrI −4.3 to 1.8). Two persistent coronary artery aneurysms were reported in the usual-care group of the first randomisation; two children died, neither death considered related to study treatment.
cards.watchOut: RECOVERY compared each drug with usual care, not steroid directly with IVIG, and usual care itself often included one of the study treatments at clinician discretion — the platform design blurs the contrast. The trial ran across changing viral variants and falling case severity, and stay is again the primary endpoint, not fever or cardiac recovery.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two open-label trials, one direct and one indirect, both land on equivalence for hospital stay — and neither answers the fever or cardiac limbs of the question
cards.summary: Synthesis: two open-label trials, one direct and one indirect, both land on equivalence for hospital stay — and neither answers the fever or cardiac limbs of the question
cards.people: Two randomised trials totalling 289 children in the relevant comparisons (Swissped 75 head-to-head; RECOVERY 214 in the first randomisation).
cards.result: Head-to-head median stay: 6.0 versus 6.0 days (p=0.42). Against usual care: methylprednisolone −0.7 days (95% CrI −1.9 to 0.6), IVIG −0.1 days (95% CrI −1.3 to 1.0). No combined IVIG-plus-steroid arm was randomised in either trial, and neither record reports fever-resolution time or cardiac-recovery endpoints. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) on the measured outcome, hospital stay.
cards.watchOut: MIS-C incidence and severity have fallen sharply since these trials recruited (2020–2022); the equivalence finding is the durable part, the absolute stay durations less so. Escalation therapy (tocilizumab, anakinra) appears in the RECOVERY card as context from the same trial, not as this shelf's claim.

shelves.title: Prednisolone for children's Bell's palsy (BellPIC): complete recovery at 1 month was 49% on prednisolone versus 57% on placebo — an underpowered trial, and most children recover anyway (93–99% by 6 months)
shelves.question: In children with Bell's palsy, does early prednisolone improve complete facial recovery compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Child · Humans · Prednisolone/therapeutic use · Bell Palsy/drug therapy · Australia · Glucocorticoids/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the one placebo-controlled trial in children found no benefit, and its point estimate at the primary timepoint favoured placebo. In BellPIC (Babl FE et al., PMID: 36008143), complete recovery at 1 month was 49% (43 of 87) on prednisolone versus 57% (50 of 87) on placebo (risk difference −8.1%, 95% CI −22.8 to 6.7; adjusted OR 0.7, 95% CI 0.4 to 1.3); by 3 months recovery was 90% versus 85% and by 6 months 99% versus 93%, neither significant. The 12-month follow-up of the same cohort (Babl FE et al., PMID: 38320457) found clinician-rated recovery in 96% versus 92% at 12 months (OR 3.12, 95% CI 0.61 to 15.98). The trial recruited 187 children against a target of 540, so it lacked the precision to exclude an important benefit or harm — a single underpowered trial, hence Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): early prednisolone has not been shown to improve complete recovery in children, most of whom recover without it.

cards.headline: BellPIC 2022: complete recovery at 1 month 49% (43/87) on prednisolone vs 57% (50/87) on placebo (adjusted OR 0.7, 0.4–1.3); at 6 months 99% vs 93%
cards.summary: BellPIC 2022: complete recovery at 1 month 49% (43/87) on prednisolone vs 57% (50/87) on placebo (adjusted OR 0.7, 0.4–1.3); at 6 months 99% vs 93%
cards.people: 187 children aged 6 months to younger than 18 years presenting to emergency departments in Australia and New Zealand with Bell's palsy within 72 hours of symptom onset, randomised to oral prednisolone approximately 1 mg/kg for 10 days (n=94) or placebo (n=93), October 2015 to August 2020; primary outcome complete recovery of facial function at 1 month on the House-Brackmann scale; target recruitment had been 540.
cards.result: At 1 month, complete recovery was 49% (43 of 87) in the prednisolone group versus 57% (50 of 87) in the placebo group (risk difference −8.1%, 95% CI −22.8 to 6.7; adjusted odds ratio 0.7, 95% CI 0.4 to 1.3). At 3 months the proportions were 90% (71 of 79) versus 85% (72 of 85) (risk difference 5.2%, 95% CI −5.0 to 15.3), and at 6 months 99% (77 of 78) versus 93% (76 of 82) (risk difference 6.0%, 95% CI −0.1 to 12.2). There were no serious adverse events and little evidence of group differences in secondary outcomes. The record states this is Class I evidence that prednisolone does not significantly change complete recovery at 1 month, while lacking precision to exclude an important harm or benefit.
cards.watchOut: Underpowered by design failure, not by analysis: 187 randomised of 540 planned, so the confidence interval at 1 month (−22.8 to +6.7 points) still contains a worthwhile benefit. Adult Bell's palsy trials show a clear steroid benefit — this shelf is children only, where spontaneous recovery is far more common and the room for any drug to add is small.
cards.source: Babl FE et al. Efficacy of Prednisolone for Bell Palsy in Children: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled, Multicenter Trial. Neurology. 2022. PMID: 36008143. cards.headline: BellPIC 12-month follow-up 2024: clinician-rated recovery 98% vs 93% at 6 months and (parent-rated) 96% vs 92% at 12 months — a few children still unrecovered at a year in both groups
cards.summary: BellPIC 12-month follow-up 2024: clinician-rated recovery 98% vs 93% at 6 months and (parent-rated) 96% vs 92% at 12 months — a few children still unrecovered at a year in both groups
cards.type: Cohort follow-up of a randomised trial (Babl 2024)
cards.people: The 187 children randomised in BellPIC (93 prednisolone, 94 placebo in this follow-up's accounting), assessed to 12 months after diagnosis with the clinician-administered House-Brackmann scale and a modified parent-administered version.
cards.result: At 6 months, clinician-rated recovery was 98% (78 of 80) in the prednisolone group versus 93% (76 of 82) in the placebo group; parent-rated recovery was 94% (75 of 80) versus 89% (72 of 81) at 6 months (OR 1.88, 95% CI 0.60 to 5.86) and 96% (75 of 78) versus 92% (73 of 79) at 12 months (OR 3.12, 95% CI 0.61 to 15.98). Some children in both groups still lacked full recovery at 12 months, regardless of prednisolone use.
cards.watchOut: A follow-up report of the same single trial, not independent evidence: it extends the timeline but cannot repair the original trial's imprecision, and the 12-month odds ratio's interval (0.61 to 15.98) is compatible with almost anything. Its real contribution is natural history — roughly 1 in 12 children still had incomplete recovery at a year on placebo.

cards.headline: Synthesis: no demonstrated benefit in the only trial, a high spontaneous recovery rate, and intervals too wide to close the question
cards.summary: Synthesis: no demonstrated benefit in the only trial, a high spontaneous recovery rate, and intervals too wide to close the question
cards.people: One randomised trial (187 children) and its own 12-month follow-up — a single evidence base, reported twice.
cards.result: Complete recovery: 49% versus 57% at 1 month, 90% versus 85% at 3 months, 99% versus 93% at 6 months, and about 96% versus 92% (parent-rated) at 12 months — no significant difference at any point. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), Tier C: a single, under-recruited trial carries the shelf.
cards.watchOut: Adult Bell's palsy — where prednisolone clearly improves recovery — is judged on its own shelf; do not import the adult verdict into paediatric practice or this shelf's verdict into adults. An adequately powered paediatric trial remains undone.
cards.source: Synthesis of Babl FE et al. Neurology. 2022 (PMID: 36008143); Babl FE et al. Pediatric neurology. 2024 (PMID: 38320457).

shelves.title: Amoxicillin for children's chest infections in primary care (ARTIC PC): moderately bad symptoms lasted a median 5 days on antibiotic versus 6 on placebo (HR 1.13, 0.90–1.42) — no benefit overall or in any prespecified subgroup
shelves.question: In children presenting in primary care with acute lower respiratory tract infection, does amoxicillin reduce symptom duration or severity compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Amoxicillin/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Child · Child, Preschool · Double-Blind Method · England · Female · Humans · Infant · Male · Primary Health Care · Respiratory Tract Infections/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the one large placebo-controlled trial found nothing worth prescribing for. In ARTIC PC (Little P et al., PMID: 34562391), 432 children aged 6 months to 12 years with uncomplicated, non-pneumonic lower respiratory tract infection in English primary care received amoxicillin 50 mg/kg per day or placebo for 7 days; the median duration of moderately bad or worse symptoms was 5 days (IQR 4 to 11) on amoxicillin versus 6 days (4 to 15) on placebo (hazard ratio 1.13, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.42). No difference appeared in any of the five prespecified subgroups in whom antibiotics are commonly prescribed — children with chest signs, fever, a physician rating of unwell, sputum or chest rattle, or shortness of breath — and complete-case and per-protocol analyses agreed with the primary analysis. A single trial, however large and well blinded, is Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): amoxicillin does not meaningfully shorten uncomplicated chest infections in children when pneumonia is not suspected.

cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Little 2021, ARTIC PC)
cards.people: 432 children aged 6 months to 12 years presenting at 56 general practices in England with acute uncomplicated (non-pneumonic) lower respiratory tract infection judged infective in origin, pneumonia not suspected clinically, symptoms under 21 days; randomised to amoxicillin 50 mg/kg per day in three divided doses for 7 days (n=221) or matched placebo suspension (n=211); complete primary-outcome data for 317 (73%), with imputation for the primary analysis.
cards.result: Median duration of symptoms rated moderately bad or worse was 5 days (IQR 4 to 11) in the antibiotics group versus 6 days (4 to 15) in the placebo group (hazard ratio 1.13, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.42). No differences were seen in the five prespecified clinical subgroups (chest signs, fever, physician rating of unwell, sputum or chest rattle, short of breath), and estimates from complete-case and per-protocol analyses were similar to the imputed primary analysis. The authors concluded amoxicillin is unlikely to be clinically effective overall or in the subgroups in whom antibiotics are commonly prescribed, and that unless pneumonia is suspected, safety-netting advice should replace prescribing for most children with chest infections.
cards.watchOut: One trial, and its population is the point: children in whom pneumonia was suspected were excluded, so the null does not extend to suspected pneumonia. Symptom duration came from parent diaries with 27% missing data handled by imputation — the concordant complete-case analysis limits, but does not erase, that concern.

shelves.title: Nebulised epinephrine for croup: croup scores improve at 30 minutes (SMD −0.94) but the effect is gone by 2 hours — a bridge treatment, pooled from just 225 children
shelves.question: In children with moderate-to-severe croup, does nebulised epinephrine shorten symptoms and reduce intubation or return visits compared with placebo or supportive care?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic alpha-Agonists/administration & dosage · Adrenergic beta-Agonists/administration & dosage · Child · Child, Preschool · Croup/drug therapy · Epinephrine/administration & dosage · Humans · Infant · Length of Stay · Nebulizers and Vaporizers · Racepinephrine/administration & dosage · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real, fast, and deliberately temporary effect. The Cochrane review (Bjornson C et al., PMID: 24114291) pooled 8 studies with 225 children, mostly under two years old with moderate-to-severe croup: nebulised epinephrine improved croup scores at 30 minutes (standardised mean difference −0.94, 95% CI −1.37 to −0.51, across 3 trials), but the effect was not significant at two or six hours, and one trial found a shorter hospital stay (mean difference −32.0 hours, 95% CI −59.1 to −4.9). No study in the review sought or reported data on adverse effects, and none reported the intubation or return-visit outcomes named in the question — those limbs are unanswered on this record, and the small total (225 children) is why the stamp is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY. Racemic and L-epinephrine did not differ at 30 minutes, and delivery by intermittent positive pressure breathing added nothing over simple nebulisation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): nebulised epinephrine relieves croup symptoms within 30 minutes for a couple of hours; evidence that it prevents intubation or return visits is absent from the pooled record.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2013: croup-score improvement at 30 minutes (SMD −0.94, −1.37 to −0.51), not significant at 2 or 6 hours; hospital stay −32 hours in the one trial reporting it
cards.summary: Cochrane 2013: croup-score improvement at 30 minutes (SMD −0.94, −1.37 to −0.51), not significant at 2 or 6 hours; hospital stay −32 hours in the one trial reporting it
cards.people: 8 randomised or quasi-randomised studies with 225 children with croup (average age under two years in most studies; severity moderate to severe in all), evaluated in emergency departments or hospital (six inpatient, one ED, one unspecified); comparisons of nebulised epinephrine versus placebo, racemic versus L-epinephrine, and nebulisation with versus without intermittent positive pressure breathing. Six studies were at low risk of bias, two unclear.
cards.result: Nebulised epinephrine was associated with croup-score improvement 30 minutes after treatment (3 trials; standardised mean difference −0.94, 95% CI −1.37 to −0.51; I²=0%); the effect was not significant at two or six hours. Hospital stay was shorter than placebo in one trial (mean difference −32.0 hours, 95% CI −59.1 to −4.9). Racemic versus L-epinephrine showed no difference at 30 minutes (SMD 0.33, 95% CI −0.42 to 1.08); intermittent positive pressure breathing added no benefit at 30 minutes (SMD −0.14, 95% CI −1.24 to 0.95) or two hours. None of the studies sought or reported data on adverse effects.
cards.watchOut: 225 children across 8 mostly small, old studies: the 30-minute effect is consistent, but intubation, return visits and harms — the outcomes that decide whether the bridge leads anywhere — were simply not reported. The −32-hour stay figure rests on a single trial and should not be quoted as a pooled effect.
cards.source: Bjornson C et al. Nebulized epinephrine for croup in children. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2013. PMID: 24114291. shelves.title: Nebulised magnesium sulfate in children's acute severe asthma (MAGNETIC): severity score 4.72 versus 4.95 at 60 minutes — a statistically significant 0.25-point difference the trial itself judged not clinically significant, and no admission result in the record
shelves.question: In children with acute severe asthma, does nebulised magnesium sulfate added to standard bronchodilator therapy improve asthma severity and reduce hospital admission?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Administration, Inhalation · Adolescent · Albuterol/administration & dosage · Anticonvulsants/administration & dosage · Asthma/diagnosis/drug therapy*/physiopathology · Bronchodilator Agents/administration & dosage · Child · Child, Preschool · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Forced Expiratory Volume/drug effects/physiology* · Humans · Injections, Intravenous · Ipratropium/administration & dosage · Magnesium Sulfate/administration & dosage* · Male · Respiratory Muscles/drug effects/physiopathology* · Retrospective Studies · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real but small average effect on a severity score, below the difference the trial itself set as clinically significant, and with no admission result in the record. In MAGNETIC (Powell C et al., PMID: 24429155), 508 children aged 2–16 years with severe acute asthma who did not respond to standard inhaled treatment, enrolled at 30 hospitals in the UK, were randomly assigned to nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium bromide with either isotonic magnesium sulfate (2.5 mL, 250 mmol/L; 151 mg per dose; n=252) or isotonic saline placebo (n=256), on three occasions at 20-min intervals. The primary outcome, the mean Yung Asthma Severity Score (ASS) at 60 min post-randomisation, was 4.72 (SD 1.37) in the magnesium sulfate group versus 4.95 (SD 1.40) in the placebo group — an adjusted difference of −0.25 (95% CI −0.48 to −0.02; p=0.03). The trial had set a between-group ASS difference of 0.5 as the minimal clinically significant treatment effect, and the authors concluded that this difference was not clinically significant. The clinical effect was larger in children with more severe asthma exacerbation (p=0.03) and in those with symptoms present for less than 6 h (p=0.049), and no difference in the occurrence of adverse events was detected between groups. On the question's second half — hospital admission — the fetched record reports no admission outcome and no admission figures at all: every child was already recruited in hospital with a severe attack, so no admission benefit can be claimed from this trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one large masked randomised trial found a statistically significant but clinically sub-threshold average improvement in asthma severity score at 60 minutes from adding nebulised magnesium sulfate to standard bronchodilators, with the largest response in the most severe, earliest-presenting attacks; no admission effect is reported in the record.

cards.headline: Powell 2013 (MAGNETIC): asthma severity score at 60 min 4.72 on nebulised magnesium sulfate versus 4.95 on placebo (adjusted difference −0.25, 95% CI −0.48 to −0.02; p=0.03) — statistically significant, but below the trial's 0.5-point clinically significant threshold, and no admission outcome reported
cards.summary: Powell 2013 (MAGNETIC): asthma severity score at 60 min 4.72 on nebulised magnesium sulfate versus 4.95 on placebo (adjusted difference −0.25, 95% CI −0.48 to −0.02; p=0.03) — statistically significant, but below the trial's 0.5-point clinically significant threshold, and no admission outcome reported
cards.people: 508 children aged 2–16 years with severe acute asthma who did not respond to standard inhaled treatment, enrolled from 30 hospitals in the UK between Jan 3, 2009, and March 20, 2011, and randomly assigned (1:1) to nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium bromide with either 2.5 mL of isotonic magnesium sulfate (250 mmol/L; 151 mg per dose; n=252) or 2.5 mL of isotonic saline (placebo group; n=256), on three occasions at 20-min intervals. Randomisation used a computer-generated sequence with random block sizes of two to four; both patients and researchers were masked to treatment allocation; analysis was by intention to treat.
cards.result: The primary outcome measure was the Yung Asthma Severity Score (ASS) at 60 min post-randomisation: mean ASS was 4.72 (SD 1.37) in the magnesium sulfate group versus 4.95 (SD 1.40) in the placebo group (adjusted difference −0.25, 95% CI −0.48 to −0.02; p=0.03). The trial had regarded a between-group difference in ASS of 0.5 as the minimal clinically significant treatment effect, and the authors concluded that this difference, however, was not clinically significant. The clinical effect was larger in children with more severe asthma exacerbation (p=0.03) and those with symptoms present for less than 6 h (p=0.049). No difference in the occurrence of adverse events was detected between groups. The record reports no hospital-admission outcome and no admission figures.
cards.watchOut: The headline result is a 60-minute severity-score difference, not a patient-important outcome: at −0.25 points it is half the size the investigators themselves set as the minimal clinically significant effect, and the larger effects in the most severe attacks and in symptoms under 6 h are subgroup findings from this one trial. The record also reports no admission outcome, so this trial cannot answer whether nebulised magnesium keeps children out of hospital — all participants were already in hospital with attacks that had not responded to standard inhaled treatment.

cards.watchOut: Re-card declaration: MAGNETIC (Powell C et al., PMID: 24429155) is also carded as a supporting card on live shelf #238 (Magnesium in acute asthma), which asks generically whether magnesium improves outcomes in acute asthma — the intravenous, all-ages evidence. This shelf asks a genuinely different question — nebulised magnesium sulfate, by the inhaled route, in children with acute severe asthma, added to standard bronchodilator therapy — built under the Nov 15 #3104 (RACING) precedent, as applied at #3325 (STRENGTH), #3489 (CAROLINA), #3597, #3628, #3753, #3812, #3833 and #3921: a study carded elsewhere as a supporting card may anchor a new shelf when the new question is genuinely different. shelves.title: Preemptive high-dose fluticasone at the first sniffle: rescue oral steroid courses fell from 18% to 8% of colds (OR 0.49) — at the cost of measurably less height and weight gain in one trial
shelves.question: In preschool children with virus-induced wheezing, does preemptive high-dose inhaled fluticasone at the first sign of an upper respiratory infection reduce rescue oral corticosteroid courses?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Androstadienes/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Asthma/prevention & control · Bronchodilator Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Child · Child, Preschool · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fluticasone · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage · Growth/drug effects · Humans · Infant · Male · Respiratory Sounds/drug effects/etiology · Respiratory Tract Infections/complications/epidemiology/virology · Virus Diseases/complications
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — with the growth price printed on the same line. In the one randomised trial (Ducharme FM et al., PMID: 19164187), 129 children aged 1 to 6 years with recurrent virus-induced wheezing took fluticasone propionate 750 µg twice daily or placebo from the onset of each upper respiratory infection, for up to 10 days, over 6 to 12 months: 8% of infections in the fluticasone group led to rescue systemic corticosteroids, versus 18% on placebo (odds ratio 0.49, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.83). Children on fluticasone gained less height (z-score difference from baseline to endpoint −0.24, 95% CI −0.40 to −0.08) and less weight (z-score difference −0.26, 95% CI −0.41 to −0.09), with no significant differences in basal cortisol, bone mineral density, or adverse events. The trial's own authors concluded the approach should not be adopted in practice until long-term adverse effects are clarified — a single-trial benefit with a measured harm, hence Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): preemptive high-dose fluticasone roughly halves rescue steroid courses per cold, and slows growth velocity while it is used.

cards.headline: Ducharme 2009: rescue systemic corticosteroids after 8% of colds on fluticasone vs 18% on placebo (OR 0.49, 0.30–0.83); height-gain z-score difference −0.24, weight −0.26
cards.summary: Ducharme 2009: rescue systemic corticosteroids after 8% of colds on fluticasone vs 18% on placebo (OR 0.49, 0.30–0.83); height-gain z-score difference −0.24, weight −0.26
cards.people: 129 children aged 1 to 6 years with recurrent virus-induced wheezing, randomised to fluticasone propionate 750 µg (ex-valve dose) twice daily or placebo, started at the onset of each upper respiratory tract infection and continued for a maximum of 10 days, over 6 to 12 months (median follow-up 40 weeks); primary outcome rescue oral corticosteroid use.
cards.result: Over the study period, 8% of upper respiratory tract infections in the fluticasone group led to rescue systemic corticosteroid treatment, versus 18% in the placebo group (odds ratio 0.49, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.83). Mean height gain was 6.23 cm on fluticasone versus 6.56 cm on placebo (z-score difference from baseline to endpoint −0.24, 95% CI −0.40 to −0.08) and weight gain 1.53 kg versus 2.17 kg (z-score difference −0.26, 95% CI −0.41 to −0.09). There were no significant differences in basal cortisol level, bone mineral density, or adverse events. The authors concluded that, given the potential for overuse, this preventive approach should not be adopted in clinical practice until long-term adverse effects are clarified.
cards.watchOut: A single trial of 129 children using a dose far above ordinary maintenance inhaled-steroid doses, given episodically. The benefit is counted per infection, not per child, and the growth signal appeared within a single season — whether height is recovered after stopping is not answered by this record.

shelves.title: Azithromycin for asthma-like episodes in 1–3-year-olds (COPSAC): episodes lasted 3.4 days on azithromycin versus 7.7 on placebo — a 63% shortening in one single-centre trial, with resistance never measured
shelves.question: In young children aged 1–3 years with episodes of asthma-like symptoms, does a short course of azithromycin shorten the episode and reduce treatment escalation?
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Cortex Hormones/therapeutic use · Adrenergic beta-2 Receptor Agonists/therapeutic use · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Asthma/drug therapy/immunology · Azithromycin/therapeutic use · C-Reactive Protein/immunology · Child, Preschool · Cough/drug therapy/immunology · Denmark · Double-Blind Method · Dyspnea/drug therapy/immunology · Early Medical Intervention · Female · Hospitalization · Humans · Infant · Male · Respiratory Sounds · Time Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a large effect on episode duration from a single, small, single-centre trial. In COPSAC (Stokholm J et al., PMID: 26704020), 158 episodes of asthma-like symptoms in 72 children aged 1 to 3 years were randomised to a 3-day course of azithromycin 10 mg/kg per day or placebo: mean episode duration after treatment was 3.4 days on azithromycin versus 7.7 days on placebo, a shortening of 63.3% (95% CI 56.0 to 69.3; p<0.0001), larger when treatment began before day 6 of the episode (83% reduction) than on or after day 6 (36%). Clinical adverse events did not differ (23% of azithromycin episodes versus 30% of placebo episodes, p=0.30), but bacterial resistance after treatment was not investigated. The record does not report the treatment-escalation outcomes named in the question, and episodes rather than children were the unit of randomisation — Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): azithromycin substantially shortened asthma-like episodes in toddlers in one trial; whether it reduces escalation, and what it costs in resistance, is unmeasured.

cards.headline: COPSAC 2016: episode duration 3.4 days on azithromycin vs 7.7 days on placebo (63.3% shortening, 95% CI 56.0–69.3); 83% if started before day 6, 36% if later
cards.summary: COPSAC 2016: episode duration 3.4 days on azithromycin vs 7.7 days on placebo (63.3% shortening, 95% CI 56.0–69.3); 83% if started before day 6, 36% if later
cards.people: 72 children aged 1 to 3 years with recurrent asthma-like symptoms from the Copenhagen Prospective Studies on Asthma in Childhood 2010 birth cohort; 158 episodes lasting at least 3 days were independently randomised (79 to azithromycin, 79 to placebo) to a 3-day course of azithromycin oral solution 10 mg/kg per day or placebo, November 2010 to January 2014; children with clinical signs of pneumonia at assessment were excluded before each treatment; primary outcome episode duration from prospective daily diaries, analysed per protocol.
cards.result: Mean duration of the episode after treatment was 3.4 days on azithromycin versus 7.7 days on placebo — a shortening of 63.3% (95% CI 56.0 to 69.3; p<0.0001). The effect was larger with earlier treatment: an 83% reduction in duration when treatment began before day 6 of the episode versus 36% when begun on or after day 6 (p<0.0001 for the contrast). Clinical adverse events occurred in 18 of 78 azithromycin episodes (23%) versus 24 of 79 placebo episodes (30%; p=0.30). Bacterial resistance patterns after treatment were not investigated.
cards.watchOut: One centre, one birth cohort, 72 children contributing 158 episodes — episodes within the same child are not independent children, and the per-protocol analysis excludes episodes without outcome data. A 63% shortening is implausibly large for an antibiotic in largely viral illness, which is precisely why replication matters before the stamp can rise; the unmeasured resistance cost is the standing objection to routine use.
cards.source: Stokholm J et al. Azithromycin for episodes with asthma-like symptoms in young children aged 1-3 years: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. The Lancet. shelves.title: Antibiotics for sore throat: sore throat at day 3 falls (RR 0.70) and rheumatic fever was cut in the old trials (OR 0.36) — but 82% are better by a week anyway, and the complication data come from the 1950s
shelves.question: In children and adults with sore throat, do antibiotics shorten illness and prevent suppurative complications and acute rheumatic fever compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Child · Fever/drug therapy · Humans · Infant · Otitis Media/drug therapy · Pain/drug therapy · Pharyngitis/drug therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — a small, real symptom benefit and a real complication benefit, both resting largely on trials from an era when complications were common. The Cochrane review (Spinks A et al., PMID: 34881426) pooled 29 trials with 15,337 cases of sore throat: antibiotics reduced sore throat at day three (risk ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.80; 16 studies, 3,730 participants; number needed to treat for one fewer sore throat under six) and at one week (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.75; NNTB 18), although 82% of the placebo group were symptom-free by one week. Headache at day three fell (RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.70); fever at day three did not significantly (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.07). Antibiotics reduced acute otitis media within 14 days (Peto OR 0.21, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.40), quinsy within two months (Peto OR 0.16, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.35), and acute rheumatic fever within two months (Peto OR 0.36, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.50; 18 studies, 12,249 participants) — but the majority of included studies were conducted in the 1950s, when rheumatic fever rates were far higher than today, and harms were too poorly reported to quantify. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): antibiotics modestly shorten sore throat and prevent suppurative complications; the rheumatic-fever protection is proven in high-incidence settings and unquantifiable where the disease is now rare.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2021: sore throat RR 0.70 at day 3 and 0.50 at week 1; otitis media OR 0.21, quinsy OR 0.16, rheumatic fever OR 0.36 — 29 trials, 15,337 cases, most from the 1950s
cards.summary: Cochrane 2021: sore throat RR 0.70 at day 3 and 0.50 at week 1; otitis media OR 0.21, quinsy OR 0.16, rheumatic fever OR 0.36 — 29 trials, 15,337 cases, most from the 1950s
cards.people: 29 randomised or quasi-randomised trials with 15,337 cases of sore throat in children and adults (ages under one year to over 50, mostly adults) seeking medical care for sore throat symptoms, comparing antibiotics with placebo or no treatment; few studies distinguished bacterial from viral cause; the majority were conducted in the 1950s, when serious complications, especially acute rheumatic fever, were much more common.
cards.result: Sore throat was reduced at day three (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.60 to 0.80; 16 studies, 3,730 participants; moderate-certainty) with a number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome under six, and at one week (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.75; 14 studies, 3,083 participants; NNTB 18), by which time 82% of the placebo or no-treatment group were symptom-free. Headache at day three fell (RR 0.49, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.70; high-certainty); fever at day three did not significantly (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.07; high-certainty). Antibiotics reduced acute otitis media within 14 days (Peto OR 0.21, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.40; 10 studies, 3,646 participants), quinsy within two months (Peto OR 0.16, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.35; 8 studies, 2,433 participants), and acute rheumatic fever within two months (Peto OR 0.36, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.50; 18 studies, 12,249 participants; moderate-certainty), but not acute sinusitis within 14 days (Peto OR 0.46, 95% CI 0.10 to 2.05); there were too few cases of acute glomerulonephritis to judge. Harms were poorly or inconsistently reported and were not quantified.
cards.watchOut: The relative effects are solid; the absolute stakes have moved. Rheumatic fever was common enough to count in 1950s trial populations and is rare in most high-income settings now, so the same OR of 0.36 buys far fewer prevented cases today — while in high-incidence populations it remains the strongest reason to treat. Unblinded and unclearly allocated older trials may also inflate the symptom effects.
cards.source: Spinks A et al. Antibiotics for treatment of sore throat in children and adults. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2021. PMID: 34881426. shelves.title: Antibiotics for children's acute sinusitis: cure 50% versus 14% in the strict 2009 trial, but only a small average symptom gain in 2023 — and almost none in children without bacterial pathogens in the nose
shelves.question: In children with acute sinusitis, do antibiotics improve clinical cure compared with placebo — and which presenting features identify the children who benefit?
shelves.mesh: Child · Humans · Male · Acute Disease · Amoxicillin/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Anti-Bacterial Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Clavulanic Acid/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Common Cold/diagnosis · Sinusitis/diagnosis/drug therapy/etiology/microbiology · Female · Child, Preschool · Nasopharynx/microbiology · Streptococcus pneumoniae/isolation & purification · Haemophilus influenzae/isolation & purification · Moraxella catarrhalis/isolation & purification
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the benefit is real but concentrated, and the two trials show its two faces. In the strictly diagnosed 2009 trial (Wald ER et al., PMID: 19564277), high-dose amoxicillin-clavulanate cured 50% of children versus 14% on placebo, with treatment failure in 14% versus 68%. In the larger 2023 trial (Shaikh N et al., PMID: 37490085), mean symptom scores were modestly lower on amoxicillin-clavulanate (9.04 versus 10.60 on a 0–40 scale; between-group difference −1.69, 95% CI −2.07 to −1.31) and symptoms resolved at 7.0 versus 9.0 days — but children without nasopharyngeal bacterial pathogens benefited much less (difference −0.88, 95% CI −1.63 to −0.12) than those with pathogens detected (−1.95, 95% CI −2.40 to −1.51), and the colour of nasal discharge made no difference to efficacy (interaction P=.52). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): antibiotics help children with acute sinusitis, most clearly when bacterial pathogens are present; coloured discharge does not identify the beneficiaries.

cards.headline: Shaikh 2023: symptom score 9.04 on amoxicillin-clavulanate vs 10.60 on placebo (difference −1.69 on a 0–40 scale); resolution 7.0 vs 9.0 days; without nasal pathogens the gain shrank to −0.88
cards.summary: Shaikh 2023: symptom score 9.04 on amoxicillin-clavulanate vs 10.60 on placebo (difference −1.69 on a 0–40 scale); resolution 7.0 vs 9.0 days; without nasal pathogens the gain shrank to −0.88
cards.people: 515 children aged 2 to 11 years diagnosed with acute sinusitis on clinical criteria at primary care offices affiliated with 6 US institutions, February 2016 to April 2022; oral amoxicillin 90 mg/kg per day with clavulanate 6.4 mg/kg per day (n=254) or placebo (n=256) for 10 days; prespecified subgroups by nasopharyngeal culture for Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae or Moraxella catarrhalis and by presence of coloured nasal discharge; primary outcome symptom burden over 10 days on a validated 0–40 scale.
cards.result: Mean symptom scores were 9.04 (95% CI 8.71 to 9.37) in the antibiotic group and 10.60 (95% CI 10.27 to 10.93) in the placebo group (between-group difference −1.69, 95% CI −2.07 to −1.31), and time to symptom resolution was 7.0 versus 9.0 days (P=.003). Children without nasopharyngeal pathogens benefited less (difference −0.88, 95% CI −1.63 to −0.12) than those with pathogens detected (−1.95, 95% CI −2.40 to −1.51). Efficacy did not differ by coloured discharge (−1.62 with coloured versus −1.70 with clear discharge; P=.52 for interaction). The authors concluded testing for specific bacteria on presentation may be a strategy to reduce antibiotic use in this condition.
cards.watchOut: Clinically diagnosed sinusitis overlaps heavily with viral colds — that dilution is the likely reason the average effect is small. The pathogen subgroup was prespecified but nasopharyngeal testing is not routine practice, so the trial identifies who benefits more reliably than it tells clinics how to find them today.
cards.source: Shaikh N et al. Identifying Children Likely to Benefit From Antibiotics for Acute Sinusitis: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2023. PMID: 37490085. Registry ID: NCT02554383. cards.headline: Wald 2009: cured 50% (14/28) on amoxicillin-clavulanate vs 14% (4/28) on placebo; treatment failure 14% vs 68% — in stringently diagnosed bacterial sinusitis
cards.summary: Wald 2009: cured 50% (14/28) on amoxicillin-clavulanate vs 14% (4/28) on placebo; treatment failure 14% vs 68% — in stringently diagnosed bacterial sinusitis
cards.people: 56 children aged 1 to 10 years with a clinical presentation compatible with acute bacterial sinusitis, stratified by age and clinical severity; only 139 of 2,135 screened children with respiratory complaints (6.5%) met the sinusitis picture, 89% presenting with persistent symptoms and 57% classified severe; high-dose amoxicillin 90 mg/kg with potassium clavulanate 6.4 mg/kg or placebo, with outcomes rated cured, improved or failed to day 30.
cards.result: Of 28 children receiving the antibiotic, 14 (50%) were cured, 4 (14%) improved, 4 (14%) experienced treatment failure and 6 (21%) withdrew. Of 28 receiving placebo, 4 (14%) were cured, 5 (18%) improved and 19 (68%) experienced treatment failure. Children receiving the antibiotic were significantly more likely to be cured and less likely to fail than those receiving placebo, on parental report of time to resolution of symptoms.
cards.watchOut: Tiny (56 children) with a 21% withdrawal rate in the antibiotic arm, and a highly selected population — 6.5% of screened children — which is exactly why its cure gap dwarfs the 2023 trial's average effect. Read together, the pair argue the diagnosis, not the drug, is the variable: strict bacterial sinusitis responds; the broader clinical label mostly does not need treating.
cards.source: Wald ER et al. Effectiveness of amoxicillin/clavulanate potassium in the treatment of acute bacterial sinusitis in children. Pediatrics. 2009. PMID: 19564277. Registry ID: NCT00132275. cards.headline: Synthesis: two concordant trials, one lesson — benefit tracks bacterial likelihood, not discharge colour
cards.summary: Synthesis: two concordant trials, one lesson — benefit tracks bacterial likelihood, not discharge colour
cards.people: Two randomised trials, 571 children aged 1 to 11 years with clinically diagnosed acute sinusitis (US primary care and referral settings).
cards.result: Cure 50% versus 14% and failure 14% versus 68% in the strict 2009 trial; symptom-score difference −1.69 (of 40) and resolution 2 days sooner in 2023, shrinking to −0.88 without nasopharyngeal pathogens and unchanged by discharge colour. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): direction is consistent across both trials; size depends on how bacterial the presentation is.
cards.watchOut: Adult acute sinusitis — where the placebo-controlled verdict is considerably weaker — is judged on its own shelf. Neither trial here tested shorter courses, different antibiotics, or watchful-waiting-with-backup-prescription strategies.
cards.source: Synthesis of Shaikh N et al. JAMA. 2023 (PMID: 37490085); Wald ER et al. Pediatrics. 2009 (PMID: 19564277).

shelves.title: Adjuvant adenoidectomy for persistent glue ear (TARGET): no extra hearing gain over grommets in the first 6 months, but +4.2 dB through the second year and repeat-surgery eligibility halved (31% to 14%)
shelves.question: In children with persistent bilateral otitis media with effusion, does adjuvant adenoidectomy improve hearing and reduce later surgery compared with watchful waiting or grommets alone?
shelves.mesh: Adenoidectomy/methods · Child · Child, Preschool · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Hearing · Hearing Tests · Humans · Male · Middle Ear Ventilation/methods · Otitis Media with Effusion/physiopathology/surgery · Otoscopy · Reoperation/methods · Retrospective Studies · Treatment Outcome · Tympanic Membrane/physiopathology/surgery
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the adenoidectomy dividend arrives late, after the grommets have stopped working. In the TARGET trial (MRC Multicentre Otitis Media Study Group, PMID: 22443163), 376 children with persistent bilateral effusion and hearing level at least 20 dB were randomised to observation, ventilation tubes alone, or tubes plus adenoidectomy: adenoidectomy added nothing to the tubes' hearing benefit of 8.8 dB (95% CI 7.1 to 10.5) averaged over 3–6 months, but averaged over 12, 18 and 24 months adenoidectomy provided 4.2 dB of benefit (95% CI 2.6 to 5.7) while tubes alone gave none, and it halved the proportion meeting the 25 dB cut-off for repeat tube surgery — 31% to 14% at 12 months and 33% to 15% at 18 months — with an absolute reduction in actual re-insertion surgery of 21%. One of 165 children having adenoidectomy (0.6%) had haemorrhage requiring return to theatre. The earlier randomised trial (Maw R et al., PMID: 8490338) agrees on durability: a single grommet resolved effusion for a mean of 9.5 months, while the effect of adenoidectomy was sustained throughout follow-up, and combined treatment resolved fluid fastest. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): adding adenoidectomy to grommets extends better hearing into the second year and roughly halves later repeat surgery, at a small operative risk.

cards.headline: TARGET 2012: adenoidectomy added 0 dB at 3–6 months but 4.2 dB (2.6–5.7) averaged over 12–24 months; repeat-surgery eligibility 14% vs 31% at 12 months; re-insertion surgery absolute reduction 21%
cards.summary: TARGET 2012: adenoidectomy added 0 dB at 3–6 months but 4.2 dB (2.6–5.7) averaged over 12–24 months; repeat-surgery eligibility 14% vs 31% at 12 months; re-insertion surgery absolute reduction 21%
cards.type: Randomised controlled three-arm trial (MRC Multicentre Otitis Media Study Group 2012, TARGET)
cards.people: 376 children (of 425 eligible) aged 3.25 to 6.75 years with persistent bilateral otitis media with effusion and better-ear hearing level at least 20 dB persisting 3 months, at 11 UK ENT departments, randomised to observation, short-stay ventilation tubes, or ventilation tubes with adjuvant adenoidectomy, with five follow-up visits over 2 years (loss to follow-up 2%, 6% and 5% at 3, 12 and 24 months; 253 children with complete data).
cards.result: Adenoidectomy did not add to the hearing benefit of ventilation tubes of 8.8 dB (95% CI 7.1 to 10.5) averaged over 3–6 months postoperatively. Averaged over 12, 18 and 24 months, adenoidectomy provided 4.2 dB of benefit (95% CI 2.6 to 5.7) whilst ventilation tubes gave no benefit; standardised effect sizes through two years were 0.50 SD for tubes and 0.61 SD for adenoidectomy, additive at 1.11 SD combined. Adenoidectomy halved the numbers meeting a 25 dB bilateral cut-off for eligibility for repeat tube surgery, from 31% to 14% at 12 months and from 33% to 15% at 18 months, and the actual reduction in re-insertion surgery (absolute risk difference) was 21%. In tubed ears, tympanosclerosis occurred in 27%, otorrhoea in under 2% and permanent perforations in under 1%; one of 165 children having adenoidectomy (0.6%) had haemorrhage requiring return to theatre.
cards.watchOut: The hearing gain is a group average of 4.2 dB in the second year — meaningful for a population, modest for an individual child — and the trial's tube type (short-stay) sets the timetable: with longer-acting tubes the adenoidectomy advantage would start later or shrink. Children under 3.25 years and those with hearing better than 20 dB were not studied.
cards.source: MRC Multicentre Otitis Media Study Group. cards.headline: Maw 1993: combined adenoidectomy plus grommet resolved glue ear fastest; a single grommet's effect lasted a mean 9.5 months, adenoidectomy's was sustained through years of follow-up
cards.summary: Maw 1993: combined adenoidectomy plus grommet resolved glue ear fastest; a single grommet's effect lasted a mean 9.5 months, adenoidectomy's was sustained through years of follow-up
cards.people: 228 children aged 2 to 9 years with pronounced hearing loss from severe chronic otitis media with effusion, with persistent bilateral effusions confirmed on three occasions over three months, randomised to adenotonsillectomy, adenoidectomy, or neither (the two operated groups combined for analysis), with a Shepard ventilation tube inserted in one randomly chosen ear in all groups; follow-up annually for five years and then less often, up to 7 years 4 months.
cards.result: Survival analysis showed appreciable otoscopic and tympanometric resolution of fluid with ventilation tubes alone and adenoidectomy alone compared with no surgery, with further improvement when both treatments were combined; mean audiometric hearing thresholds improved as fluid resolved. A single Shepard tube insertion resolved the glue for a mean (SD) period of 9.5 (5.2) months, whereas the effect of adenoidectomy was sustained throughout follow-up. Resolution was delayed in younger children and in those whose parents smoked, irrespective of treatment.
cards.watchOut: A 1993 trial reported without the numerical hearing thresholds a modern reader would want — its contribution is the durability pattern, which TARGET later quantified. Adenotonsillectomy and adenoidectomy were combined for analysis, so the tonsillectomy component cannot be separated out.
cards.source: Maw R et al. Spontaneous resolution of severe chronic glue ear in children and the effect of adenoidectomy, tonsillectomy, and insertion of ventilation tubes (grommets). BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 1993. PMID: 8490338. cards.summary: Synthesis: grommets win the first year, adenoidectomy wins the second — doing both buys the whole curve and halves the return trips to theatre
cards.people: Two randomised trials, 604 children aged 2 to 9 years with persistent bilateral otitis media with effusion and significant hearing loss (UK).
cards.result: TARGET: tubes +8.8 dB at 3–6 months with no adenoidectomy addition; adenoidectomy +4.2 dB averaged over 12–24 months when tubes alone gave none; repeat-surgery eligibility 14% versus 31% at 12 months; actual re-insertion absolute reduction 21%; adenoidectomy haemorrhage requiring theatre 0.6%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): two concordant randomised trials, with the benefit explicitly time-shifted.

shelves.title: Oral antibiotics first for febrile infant UTI (Hoberman 1999): urine sterile within 24 hours in every child either way, fever gone in 25 vs 24 hours, kidney scarring at 6 months 9.8% oral versus 7.2% IV — at half the cost
shelves.question: In young febrile children with urinary tract infection, is initial oral antibiotic therapy as effective as initial intravenous therapy for cure and kidney scarring?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Administration, Oral · Cefixime · Cefotaxime/administration & dosage/analogs & derivatives · Cephalosporins/administration & dosage · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Female · Humans · Infant · Infusions, Intravenous · Logistic Models · Male · Patient Compliance · Pyelonephritis/etiology/prevention & control · Recurrence · Urinary Tract Infections/drug therapy/microbiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — route did not matter; the drug did the work in both arms. In the multicentre randomised trial (Hoberman A et al., PMID: 10390264), 306 children aged 1 to 24 months with fever and urinary tract infection received either oral cefixime for 14 days or intravenous cefotaxime for 3 days followed by oral cefixime: repeat urine cultures were sterile within 24 hours in all children, mean time to defervescence was 25 hours oral versus 24 hours intravenous, symptomatic reinfections occurred in 4.6% versus 7.2%, and renal scarring at 6 months was 9.8% oral versus 7.2% intravenous, with mean extent of scarring approximately 8% in both groups. Mean costs were at least twofold higher for initial intravenous therapy ($3,577 versus $1,473). One trial from 1999, with scarring confidence limits the abstract does not print — Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): initial oral therapy matched initial intravenous therapy on sterilisation, fever, reinfection and scarring in febrile infants with UTI.

cards.headline: Hoberman 1999: sterile urine within 24 h in all 306 children; defervescence 25 h (oral) vs 24 h (IV); scarring at 6 months 9.8% vs 7.2%; costs $1,473 vs $3,577
cards.summary: Hoberman 1999: sterile urine within 24 h in all 306 children; defervescence 25 h (oral) vs 24 h (IV); scarring at 6 months 9.8% vs 7.2%; costs $1,473 vs $3,577
cards.people: 306 children aged 1 to 24 months with fever and urinary tract infection in a multicentre trial, randomised to oral cefixime for 14 days (double dose on day 1) or initial intravenous cefotaxime for 3 days followed by oral cefixime for 11 days; outcomes included urine sterilisation and defervescence, reinfection, and incidence and extent of renal scarring on 99mTc-dimercaptosuccinic acid scans at 6 months; bacteraemia was present in 3.4% of the oral group and 5.3% of the intravenous group.
cards.result: Repeat urine cultures were sterile within 24 hours in all children, and mean time to defervescence was 25 hours for oral therapy and 24 hours for intravenous therapy. Symptomatic reinfections occurred in 4.6% of children treated orally and 7.2% of children treated intravenously. Renal scarring at 6 months was noted in 9.8% of the oral group versus 7.2% of the intravenous group, with mean extent of scarring approximately 8% in both groups. Mean costs were at least twofold higher for intravenous therapy ($3,577 versus $1,473). The authors concluded oral cefixime can be recommended as a safe and effective treatment for children with fever and urinary tract infection, with substantial savings.
cards.watchOut: A single 1999 trial, and the scarring comparison (9.8% versus 7.2%) numerically favours the IV arm without the abstract printing confidence intervals — equivalence on scarring is asserted from a trial not powered as a scarring noninferiority study. Children too unwell to take or absorb oral medication, and those with urinary-tract obstruction, are outside this evidence.
cards.source: Hoberman A et al. Oral versus initial intravenous therapy for urinary tract infections in young febrile children. Pediatrics. 1999. PMID: 10390264. shelves.title: Circumcision to prevent urinary infections in boys: febrile UTI risk 3% with circumcision plus prophylaxis versus 20% on prophylaxis alone in the CIRCUP randomised trial — in posterior urethral valves, with observational data (OR 0.23) for reflux
shelves.question: In boys with vesicoureteral reflux or recurrent urinary tract infection, does circumcision reduce further urinary tract infections compared with no circumcision?
shelves.mesh: Antibiotic Prophylaxis · Child · Circumcision, Male/adverse effects · Female · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Male · Proportional Hazards Models · Urinary Catheterization · Urinary Tract Infections/etiology/prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the one randomised trial is dramatic and narrow in equal measure. In CIRCUP (Harper L et al., PMID: 34563412), 91 newborn boys with posterior urethral valves were randomised to neonatal circumcision plus antibiotic prophylaxis or prophylaxis alone: the probability of a febrile urinary tract infection over 2 years was 3% with circumcision versus 20% without (hazard ratio for the uncircumcised group 10.3, 95% CI 1.3 to 82.5). No randomised trial in boys with vesicoureteral reflux — the population named in the question — was found on the record; for reflux the evidence is observational, pooled in a meta-analysis of boys with antenatal hydronephrosis (Chan JY et al., PMID: 37563014): circumcision was associated with reduced odds of UTI overall (OR 0.26, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.32) and in the vesicoureteral reflux subgroup specifically (OR 0.23, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.42), across 23 studies and 9,093 boys. The candidate anchor for this shelf, a Pennesi randomised trial of circumcision in reflux, could not be verified on PubMed — no such record exists — so the shelf is built on CIRCUP plus the meta-analysis and is Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): circumcision substantially reduces febrile UTI in high-risk boys, randomised in posterior urethral valves and observational in reflux.

cards.headline: CIRCUP 2022: febrile UTI probability 3% (circumcision + prophylaxis) vs 20% (prophylaxis alone) over 2 years; HR 10.3 (1.3–82.5) for the uncircumcised group
cards.summary: CIRCUP 2022: febrile UTI probability 3% (circumcision + prophylaxis) vs 20% (prophylaxis alone) over 2 years; HR 10.3 (1.3–82.5) for the uncircumcised group
cards.people: 91 boys aged 1 to 28 days with posterior urethral valves confirmed by voiding cystogram, at 13 French paediatric urology referral centres, August 2012 to July 2017, randomised to neonatal circumcision plus antibiotic prophylaxis (n=49) or antibiotic prophylaxis alone (n=42) and followed for 2 years; febrile UTI defined as fever above 38.5 °C with pyuria and culture-proven infection on catheter or suprapubic urine; 64 children (70.3%) completed full 2-year follow-up.
cards.result: The probability of presenting a febrile UTI was 20% in the prophylaxis-alone group versus 3% in the circumcision-plus-prophylaxis group; the hazard ratio for presenting a febrile UTI within 2 years in the prophylaxis-alone group compared with the circumcision group was 10.3 (95% CI 1.3 to 82.5). The authors concluded circumcision significantly decreases the risk of febrile UTI in boys with posterior urethral valves.
cards.watchOut: The population is posterior urethral valves, not the vesicoureteral reflux or recurrent-UTI boys named in the question — the nearest randomised evidence, declared as a swap on the face of this shelf. Ninety-one boys, few events, and a confidence interval from 1.3 to 82.5: the direction is clear, the size is not, and 30% of children lacked complete 2-year follow-up.
cards.source: Harper L et al. Circumcision and Risk of Febrile Urinary Tract Infection in Boys with Posterior Urethral Valves: Result of the CIRCUP Randomized Trial. European urology. 2022. cards.headline: Chan 2023 meta-analysis: circumcised boys with antenatal hydronephrosis had lower UTI odds (OR 0.26, 0.21–0.32); in the reflux subgroup OR 0.23 (0.13–0.42) — all observational
cards.summary: Chan 2023 meta-analysis: circumcised boys with antenatal hydronephrosis had lower UTI odds (OR 0.26, 0.21–0.32); in the reflux subgroup OR 0.23 (0.13–0.42) — all observational
cards.people: 23 comparative studies describing 9,093 boys with antenatal hydronephrosis (4,677 uncircumcised, 4,416 circumcised), searched to December 2022; outcomes included any UTI, UTI on continuous antibiotic prophylaxis, renal outcomes and circumcision complications, pooled with random-effects models and stratified by cause of hydronephrosis.
cards.result: Circumcised boys had significantly reduced odds of developing any UTI (OR 0.26, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.32; p<0.001), and of UTI when circumcised and on continuous antibiotic prophylaxis (OR 0.19, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.30). By cause, circumcision reduced UTI odds in isolated hydronephrosis (OR 0.33, 95% CI 0.16 to 0.68), vesicoureteral reflux (OR 0.23, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.42) and posterior urethral valves (OR 0.29, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.64). The authors noted varied UTI definitions and inconsistent reporting of renal outcomes and circumcision complications across studies.
cards.watchOut: Observational throughout: boys who are circumcised differ from boys who are not in ways no pooling removes, and an odds ratio of 0.26 from such data should be read as an upper bound on benefit. This card is also where the reflux-specific claim lives — there is no reflux randomised trial behind it.
cards.source: Chan JY et al. The role of circumcision in preventing urinary tract infections in children with antenatal hydronephrosis: Systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of pediatric urology. 2023. PMID: 37563014.
