shelves.title: Phentermine/topiramate in adolescents with obesity: BMI fell 10.4 percentage points more than placebo at the top dose and 8.1 points at the mid dose over 56 weeks — one trial, with two serious adverse events at the top dose
shelves.question: In adolescents with obesity, does once-daily phentermine/topiramate reduce BMI compared with placebo on top of lifestyle therapy?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a large weight effect in a single trial. In the 56-week randomised double-blind trial (Kelly AS et al., PMID: 36968652), 223 adolescents aged 12 to under 17 years with obesity received lifestyle therapy plus placebo (n=56), mid-dose phentermine/topiramate 7.5 mg/46 mg (n=54), or top-dose 15 mg/92 mg (n=113): the difference from placebo in mean percent change in BMI at week 56 was −10.44 percentage points (95% CI −13.89 to −6.99; P<0.001) at the top dose and −8.11 percentage points (95% CI −11.92 to −4.31; P<0.001) at the mid dose. Triglyceride and HDL-cholesterol changes nominally favoured the drug at both doses. At least one adverse event was reported by 51.8% on placebo, 37.0% on mid dose and 52.2% on top dose, and serious adverse events were reported for two participants in the top-dose group. One trial only — Tier C — and the record carries no MeSH terms. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): phentermine/topiramate produces substantial BMI reduction in adolescents over a year, on single-trial evidence.

cards.headline: Kelly 2022: BMI percent-change difference vs placebo −10.44 points (top dose) and −8.11 points (mid dose) at week 56, both P<0.001; serious adverse events in 2 top-dose participants
cards.summary: Kelly 2022: BMI percent-change difference vs placebo −10.44 points (top dose) and −8.11 points (mid dose) at week 56, both P<0.001; serious adverse events in 2 top-dose participants
cards.people: 223 adolescents aged 12 to less than 17 years with obesity (mean age 14.0 years, mean BMI 37.8 kg/m², 54.3% female), randomised 1:1:2 to placebo (n=56), phentermine/topiramate 7.5 mg/46 mg (n=54) or 15 mg/92 mg (n=113) once daily for 56 weeks, all with lifestyle therapy; primary endpoint mean percent change in BMI from randomisation to week 56. Funded by the manufacturer.
cards.result: The difference from placebo in percent change in BMI at week 56 was −10.44 percentage points (95% CI −13.89 to −6.99; P<0.001) for the top dose and −8.11 percentage points (95% CI −11.92 to −4.31; P<0.001) for the mid dose. Differences in percent change in triglycerides nominally favoured the drug (about −21% at both doses) as did HDL cholesterol (about +9 to 10%). The incidence of at least one adverse event was 51.8% (placebo), 37.0% (mid dose) and 52.2% (top dose); serious adverse events were reported for two participants in the top-dose group.
cards.watchOut: A single industry-funded trial with no post-treatment follow-up on this record: what happens to BMI when a sympathomimetic-plus-topiramate combination is stopped in a 14-year-old is unanswered, and the abstract does not itemise the two serious adverse events or the class-typical effects (paraesthesia, mood, cognition, birth-defect risk with topiramate) that dominate real-world counselling. This record carries no MeSH terms.
cards.source: Kelly AS et al. Phentermine/Topiramate for the Treatment of Adolescent Obesity. NEJM evidence. 2022. PMID: 36968652. Registry ID: NCT03922945. MeSH: none in the record

shelves.title: Orlistat in adolescents with obesity: BMI fell 0.55 while placebo gained 0.31 over a year — 26.5% versus 15.7% lost at least 5% of BMI, paid for in gastrointestinal adverse events in 9–50%
shelves.question: In adolescents with obesity, does orlistat reduce weight and BMI compared with placebo, and at what gastrointestinal cost?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Anti-Obesity Agents/therapeutic use · Behavior Therapy · Blood Glucose · Blood Pressure · Body Composition/drug effects · Body Mass Index · Combined Modality Therapy · Diet, Reducing · Double-Blind Method · Enzyme Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Exercise · Female · Humans · Insulin/metabolism · Lactones/therapeutic use · Lipase/antagonists & inhibitors · Lipid Metabolism · Male · Obesity/drug therapy/metabolism/therapy · Orlistat · Weight Loss
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a statistically solid, clinically modest effect, with the cost itemised. In the multicentre randomised trial (Chanoine JP et al., PMID: 15956632), 539 adolescents aged 12 to 16 years took orlistat 120 mg three times daily or placebo for a year, all with a mildly hypocaloric diet, exercise and behavioural therapy: BMI changed by −0.55 on orlistat versus +0.31 on placebo (P=.001), weight by +0.53 kg versus +3.14 kg (P<.001), and 26.5% on orlistat versus 15.7% on placebo achieved at least a 5% BMI decrease (P=.005), with at least a 10% decrease in 13.3% versus 4.5% (P=.002). Waist circumference fell 1.33 cm on orlistat and rose 0.12 cm on placebo (P<.05), and dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry attributed the weight difference to fat mass. Generally mild-to-moderate gastrointestinal adverse events occurred in 9% to 50% of the orlistat group versus 1% to 13% on placebo. One trial — Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): orlistat adds a small BMI advantage over lifestyle therapy alone in adolescents, and most users will feel why it works.

cards.headline: Chanoine 2005: BMI −0.55 on orlistat vs +0.31 on placebo (P=.001); ≥5% BMI loss in 26.5% vs 15.7%; gastrointestinal adverse events 9–50% vs 1–13%
cards.summary: Chanoine 2005: BMI −0.55 on orlistat vs +0.31 on placebo (P=.001); ≥5% BMI loss in 26.5% vs 15.7%; gastrointestinal adverse events 9–50% vs 1–13%
cards.people: 539 obese adolescents aged 12 to 16 years (BMI at least 2 units above the 95th percentile) at 32 centres in the US and Canada, randomised to orlistat 120 mg three times daily (n=357) or placebo (n=182) for 54 weeks (August 2000 to October 2002), all receiving a mildly hypocaloric diet (30% fat calories), exercise and behavioural therapy; primary measure change in BMI.
cards.result: BMI decreased by 0.55 with orlistat but increased by 0.31 with placebo (P=.001). A decrease in BMI of 5% or more occurred in 26.5% on orlistat versus 15.7% on placebo (P=.005), and of 10% or more in 13.3% versus 4.5% (P=.002). Weight increased 0.53 kg with orlistat versus 3.14 kg with placebo (P<.001), explained by fat-mass changes on dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry; waist circumference changed by −1.33 cm versus +0.12 cm (P<.05). Generally mild-to-moderate gastrointestinal adverse events occurred in 9% to 50% of the orlistat group and 1% to 13% of the placebo group. The authors concluded orlistat significantly improved weight management in obese adolescents without major safety issues, with gastrointestinal events more common on the drug.
cards.watchOut: In growing adolescents the placebo group's BMI rise is partly natural history, so the honest framing is divergence, not loss: the average orlistat teenager ended the year barely lighter than they began. One trial, from 2000–2002, before modern comparators existed; adherence to a three-times-daily drug with these side effects outside a trial is the open question.
cards.source: Chanoine JP et al. Effect of orlistat on weight and body composition in obese adolescents: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2005. PMID: 15956632. shelves.title: Metformin for childhood obesity: pooled BMI fell by about 1.07 kg/m² across 38 trials — but the best-stratified trial found the BMI z-score benefit only before puberty
shelves.question: In children and adolescents with obesity, does metformin reduce BMI and insulin resistance compared with placebo or lifestyle alone?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Biomarkers/blood · Body Mass Index · Cardiovascular Diseases/etiology/prevention & control · Child · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Inflammation/etiology/prevention & control · Male · Metformin/therapeutic use · Pediatric Obesity/blood/complications/drug therapy · Prospective Studies · Puberty · Sex Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a consistent small pooled effect that dissolves by pubertal stage when one trial looks carefully. The meta-analysis (Sadeghi A et al., PMID: 32068434) pooled 38 trials with 2,199 children and adolescents: metformin reduced BMI by a weighted mean difference of −1.07 kg/m² (95% CI −1.43 to −0.72), body weight by −2.51 kg (95% CI −3.14 to −1.89) and waist circumference by −1.93 cm (95% CI −2.69 to −1.16). The stratified randomised trial (Pastor-Villaescusa B et al., PMID: 28759403) gave metformin 1 g daily or placebo for 6 months to 160 prepubertal and pubertal children: BMI z score fell more on metformin only in the prepubertal group (−0.8 versus −0.6; difference 0.2; P=.04), alongside better insulin-sensitivity and adiponectin-leptin measures in that group, while no differential effect between prepubertal and pubertal children was formally demonstrated and the authors caution that dose per kilogram may explain the pattern. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): metformin produces a small average BMI reduction in children with obesity, clearest before puberty; an insulin-resistance benefit is shown only in subgroup measures, not as a pooled clinical endpoint.

cards.headline: Pastor-Villaescusa 2017: BMI z score fell −0.8 on metformin vs −0.6 on placebo in prepubertal children (P=.04), with better insulin-sensitivity index — no significant benefit shown in pubertal children
cards.summary: Pastor-Villaescusa 2017: BMI z score fell −0.8 on metformin vs −0.6 on placebo in prepubertal children (P=.04), with better insulin-sensitivity index — no significant benefit shown in pubertal children
cards.people: 160 nondiabetic children with obesity aged 7 to 14 years (80 prepubertal, 80 pubertal; BMI above the 95th percentile) at 4 Spanish hospitals, stratified by pubertal stage and sex, randomised to metformin 1 g per day or placebo for 6 months; 140 children completed the study (72 boys); primary outcome reduction in BMI z score; secondary outcomes insulin resistance, cardiovascular risk and inflammation biomarkers.
cards.result: Metformin decreased BMI z score versus placebo in the prepubertal group (−0.8 versus −0.6; difference 0.2; P=.04). In prepubertal children, metformin also improved the quantitative insulin sensitivity check index (0.010 versus −0.007; difference 0.017; P=.01) and the adiponectin-leptin ratio (0.96 versus 0.15; difference 0.81; P=.01), and lowered interferon-γ and total plasminogen activator inhibitor-1. No serious adverse effects were reported. The authors noted that a differential effect of metformin between prepubertal and pubertal children was not formally observed, and that the dose per kilogram administered may have influenced the apparent pattern.
cards.watchOut: The headline subgroup contrast is fragile: the prepubertal difference is 0.2 z-score units at P=.04, the pubertal null may be a dosing artefact (a fixed 1 g is less per kilogram in bigger adolescents), and 20 of 160 children did not complete. This trial supports 'small and early' rather than 'works before puberty, not after'.
cards.source: Pastor-Villaescusa B et al. Metformin for Obesity in Prepubertal and Pubertal Children: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Pediatrics. 2017. PMID: 28759403. cards.headline: Sadeghi 2020 meta-analysis: BMI weighted mean difference −1.07 kg/m² (−1.43 to −0.72), weight −2.51 kg, waist −1.93 cm across 38 trials and 2,199 participants
cards.summary: Sadeghi 2020 meta-analysis: BMI weighted mean difference −1.07 kg/m² (−1.43 to −0.72), weight −2.51 kg, waist −1.93 cm across 38 trials and 2,199 participants
cards.people: 38 clinical trials including 2,199 children and adolescents (39.75% male, 60.25% female) examining metformin against control for obesity indices, from literature searched to September 2018; outcomes pooled as weighted mean differences for BMI, weight, waist circumference, fat mass and lean body mass.
cards.result: Metformin significantly reduced BMI (weighted mean difference −1.07 kg/m², 95% CI −1.43 to −0.72), body weight (−2.51 kg, 95% CI −3.14 to −1.89) and waist circumference (−1.93 cm, 95% CI −2.69 to −1.16). It reduced body fat mass in participants with overweight or obesity (−1.90%) and in those with chronic diseases (−1.41%), but not in those with growth problems; lean body mass was not significantly affected in the overweight/obesity and growth-problem groups, though it fell in the chronic-disease subgroup (−1.49 kg, 95% CI −2.69 to −0.30).
cards.watchOut: Thirty-eight mostly small, short trials pooled into one average: the −1.07 kg/m² is a mean of heterogeneous doses, durations and populations (including children treated for other conditions), and the record reports no pooled insulin-resistance endpoint — the question's second limb rests on the single stratified trial's biomarker measures, not on this pooling.
cards.source: Sadeghi A et al. Metformin Therapy Reduces Obesity Indices in Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials. Childhood obesity (Print). 2020. PMID: 32068434. shelves.title: Family-based behavioural treatment in primary care: children's percentage above median BMI changed 0.00% on treatment versus +6.48% on usual care over 24 months — and untreated siblings improved too
shelves.question: In children with obesity treated in primary care, does family-based behavioural treatment reduce BMI compared with usual care?
shelves.mesh: Child · Female · Humans · Male · Behavior Therapy/methods · Body Mass Index · Overweight/psychology/therapy · Pediatric Obesity/psychology/therapy · Primary Health Care · Family Therapy/methods · Pediatrics · Siblings/psychology · Parents/psychology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the treated children held their trajectory while usual-care children gained, in one large pragmatic trial. In the primary-care trial (Epstein LH et al., PMID: 37314275), 452 children aged 6 to 12 years with overweight or obesity, their parents and 106 siblings were randomised to family-based behavioural treatment (a goal of 26 coached sessions over 24 months) or usual care: at 24 months the difference in change in percentage above median BMI favoured treatment by −6.21 percentage points (95% CI −10.14 to −2.29), with 0-to-24-month changes of 0.00% on treatment versus +6.48% on usual care in children, −1.05% versus +2.92% in parents, and 0.03% versus +5.35% in siblings who were not directly treated. Benefits were evident by 6 months and maintained through 24 months. A single trial, however pragmatic — Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): family-based treatment delivered in paediatric primary care prevents the BMI rise seen under usual care, with spillover to parents and siblings.

cards.headline: Epstein/Wilfley 2023: difference in change in percentage above median BMI −6.21 points (95% CI −10.14 to −2.29) at 24 months; siblings not treated also diverged (0.03% vs +5.35%)
cards.summary: Epstein/Wilfley 2023: difference in change in percentage above median BMI −6.21 points (95% CI −10.14 to −2.29) at 24 months; siblings not treated also diverged (0.03% vs +5.35%)
cards.people: 452 children aged 6 to 12 years with overweight or obesity (mean age 9.8 years, 53% female, mean percentage above median BMI 59.4%), their parents, and 106 siblings, at 4 US paediatric primary-care settings, November 2017 to August 2021; family-based treatment (behavioural techniques for eating, activity and parenting, delivered by a trained coach; goal 26 sessions over 24 months, individualised by family progress) versus usual care, followed for 24 months; primary outcome change in the child's percentage above the median BMI for age and sex.
cards.result: At 24 months, children receiving family-based treatment had better weight outcomes than usual care (difference in change in percentage above median BMI −6.21%, 95% CI −10.14% to −2.29%). Longitudinal models showed advantages evident at 6 months and maintained through 24 months: 0-to-24-month changes in percentage above median BMI were 0.00% (95% CI −2.20 to 2.20) versus +6.48% (95% CI 4.35 to 8.61) for children, −1.05% versus +2.92% for parents, and 0.03% versus +5.35% for siblings. The authors concluded family-based treatment was successfully implemented in paediatric primary care and improved weight outcomes for children and parents, with untreated siblings also benefiting.
cards.watchOut: Read the metric honestly: treated children on average ended where they began relative to the median — the win is preventing the usual-care rise, not producing weight loss, and the outcome (percentage above median BMI) is unfamiliar enough that the −6.21 points cannot be converted into kilograms from this record. One trial, delivered by trained coaches in four resourced US settings; ordinary practices without a coach are untested.
cards.source: Epstein LH et al. Family-Based Behavioral Treatment for Childhood Obesity Implemented in Pediatric Primary Care: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2023. PMID: 37314275. shelves.title: Clonidine extended-release for ADHD: symptoms improved significantly more than placebo both alone (8-week fixed-dose trial) and added to a stimulant (week-5 difference CI −7.83 to −1.13) — somnolence the commonest cost
shelves.question: In children and adolescents with ADHD, does clonidine extended-release — alone or added to a stimulant — reduce ADHD symptoms compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adrenergic alpha-2 Receptor Agonists/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Attention Deficit Disorder with Hyperactivity/drug therapy · Child · Clonidine/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Delayed-Action Preparations · Double-Blind Method · Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions · Female · Humans · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two placebo-controlled trials, one for each way the drug is used, both positive. As monotherapy (Jain R et al., PMID: 21241954), clonidine extended-release 0.2 mg/day and 0.4 mg/day each improved ADHD Rating Scale-IV total scores significantly more than placebo at week 5 in 236 children and adolescents, with significant gains on both inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity subscales and on global-impression measures; the most common treatment-emergent adverse event was mild-to-moderate somnolence, and electrocardiogram changes were minor. Added to a stimulant in children with an inadequate stimulant response (Kollins SH et al., PMID: 21555501), clonidine extended-release improved the ADHD Rating Scale-IV total score more than placebo at week 5 (95% CI for the difference −7.83 to −1.13; P=.009), with concordant parent-rating and global-impression results and generally mild adverse events. Neither abstract prints the point estimate of symptom change — magnitudes rest on the add-on trial's confidence interval — a declared gap that, with symptom scores rather than functional outcomes, keeps the stamp at POSSIBLE. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): clonidine extended-release reduces ADHD symptom scores versus placebo, alone and as stimulant add-on, with somnolence the principal cost.

cards.headline: Jain 2011 (monotherapy): both 0.2 mg/day and 0.4 mg/day beat placebo on ADHD-RS-IV total score at week 5, from week 2 onward; somnolence the commonest adverse event
cards.summary: Jain 2011 (monotherapy): both 0.2 mg/day and 0.4 mg/day beat placebo on ADHD-RS-IV total score at week 5, from week 2 onward; somnolence the commonest adverse event
cards.people: 236 patients aged 6 to 17 years with ADHD, randomised to clonidine extended-release 0.2 mg/day (n=78), 0.4 mg/day (n=80) or placebo (n=78) for 8 weeks including 3 weeks of dose escalation; primary endpoint mean change in ADHD Rating Scale-IV total score from baseline to week 5 (last observation carried forward); secondary endpoints included subscales, Conners Parent Rating Scale, and Clinical Global Impression measures.
cards.result: Improvement from baseline in ADHD-RS-IV total score was significantly greater in both clonidine groups than placebo at week 5, with significant separation from week 2 maintained throughout treatment, and significant improvements on the inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity subscales, the Conners Parent Rating Scale-Revised, Clinical Global Impression of Improvement and Severity, and Parent Global Assessment in both treatment groups. The most common treatment-emergent adverse event was mild-to-moderate somnolence; electrocardiogram changes were minor and consistent with clonidine's known pharmacology. The record reports significance levels rather than the numerical size of the score changes.
cards.watchOut: Declared gap: this record gives no point estimate or confidence interval for the symptom-score difference, so the size of the monotherapy effect cannot be quoted from it — only its direction and significance. Eight weeks, industry-era phase 3 design, last-observation-carried-forward analysis: durability and functional outcomes (school performance, family function) are outside the record.
cards.source: Jain R et al. Clonidine extended-release tablets for pediatric patients with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry. 2011. PMID: 21241954. Registry ID: NCT00556959. cards.headline: Kollins 2011 (add-on): clonidine ER plus stimulant beat placebo plus stimulant on ADHD-RS-IV at week 5 (difference 95% CI −7.83 to −1.13; P=.009) in stimulant partial responders
cards.summary: Kollins 2011 (add-on): clonidine ER plus stimulant beat placebo plus stimulant on ADHD-RS-IV at week 5 (difference 95% CI −7.83 to −1.13; P=.009) in stimulant partial responders
cards.people: 198 children and adolescents with hyperactive- or combined-subtype ADHD who had an inadequate response to a stable stimulant regimen (methylphenidate or amphetamine), randomised to clonidine extended-release (n=102) or placebo (n=96) added to their baseline stimulant; efficacy evaluated as change from baseline to week 5; safety from adverse events, vital signs, electrocardiograms and laboratory values.
cards.result: At week 5, greater improvement in ADHD-RS-IV total score was seen with clonidine plus stimulant versus placebo plus stimulant (95% CI for the difference −7.83 to −1.13; P=.009), with significant advantages on the hyperactivity (P=.014) and inattention (P=.017) subscales, Clinical Global Impression of Severity (P=.021) and of Improvement (P=.006), and Parent Global Assessment (P=.001); Conners Parent Rating Scale differences did not reach significance (P<.062 as reported). Adverse events and vital-sign changes in the clonidine group were generally mild.
cards.watchOut: A partial-responder population: the add-on gain applies to children already failing a stimulant, not to first-line use. As with the monotherapy record, the abstract gives a confidence interval for the difference without the groups' own mean changes, and five weeks is the whole horizon — blood-pressure and rebound effects of stopping are not addressed.

shelves.title: AKL-T01 digital therapeutic for ADHD (STARS-ADHD): objective attention index improved by a median 0.88 versus 0.03 mean change on control (p=0.006) — a computerised attention gain, with symptom change not the primary outcome
shelves.question: In children with ADHD, does the prescription digital therapeutic AKL-T01 improve objective attention compared with a control digital activity?
shelves.mesh: Attention · Attention Deficit Disorder with Hyperactivity/therapy · Behavior Therapy/methods · Child · Cognition · Digital Technology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Pediatrics · Play and Playthings · Severity of Illness Index · Software · Video Games
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the attention test it was built to move, in the one trial that exists. In STARS-ADHD (Kollins SH et al., PMID: 33334505), 348 children aged 8 to 12 years with confirmed ADHD and impaired Test of Variables of Attention (TOVA) Attention Performance Index scores (−1.8 or below), taking no ADHD medication, played AKL-T01 or a control digital activity for 25 minutes a day, 5 days a week, for 4 weeks: the median change in TOVA Attention Performance Index was 0.88 (95% CI 0.24 to 1.49; p=0.0060) on AKL-T01, with mean change 0.93 (SD 3.15) versus 0.03 (SD 3.16) on control. There were no serious adverse events or discontinuations; treatment-related adverse events were mild — frustration in 5 of 180 children (3%) and headache in 3 (2%) — and children completed a mean of 83 of 100 expected sessions. The primary outcome is a computerised attention measure, not ADHD symptoms or school function, and the trial was sponsored by the product's maker, Akili Interactive Labs — a named programme/product tested as specified, single-trial, hence Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): AKL-T01 improves objectively measured attention over 4 weeks versus a control game, with minimal adverse events; whether that becomes symptom or classroom benefit is not shown here.

cards.headline: STARS-ADHD 2020: TOVA Attention Performance Index median change 0.88 (0.24–1.49; p=0.0060) on AKL-T01; mean change 0.93 vs 0.03 on control; no serious adverse events
cards.summary: STARS-ADHD 2020: TOVA Attention Performance Index median change 0.88 (0.24–1.49; p=0.0060) on AKL-T01; mean change 0.93 vs 0.03 on control; no serious adverse events
cards.people: 348 children aged 8 to 12 years with confirmed ADHD and TOVA Attention Performance Index scores of −1.8 or below, not taking disorder-related medications, at 20 US research institutions, randomised 1:1 to AKL-T01 (n=180; mean age 9.7 years) or a digital control intervention (n=168; mean age 9.6 years): 25 minutes of at-home play per day, 5 days per week, for 4 weeks; primary outcome mean change in TOVA Attention Performance Index from pre- to post-intervention, analysed by intention to treat; sponsored by Akili Interactive Labs, the product's maker.
cards.result: The non-parametric estimate of the population median change in TOVA Attention Performance Index was 0.88 (95% CI 0.24 to 1.49; p=0.0060) in the AKL-T01 group; mean (SD) change was 0.93 (3.15) on AKL-T01 versus 0.03 (3.16) on control. There were no serious adverse events or discontinuations. Treatment-related adverse events were mild and included frustration (5 of 180, 3%) and headache (3 of 180, 2%). Compliance was a mean of 83 (SD 29.2) of 100 expected sessions played.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is performance on a computerised attention test closely related to the training task itself — near-transfer is the standing criticism of cognitive training, and symptom ratings, teacher reports and academic outcomes are not the primary outcome on this record. Four weeks, unmedicated children with objectively impaired attention scores, industry sponsorship: each narrows the claim. AKL-T01 is a specific tested product of Akili Interactive Labs, named here as the publication names it; other games or apps cannot borrow this result.
cards.source: Kollins SH et al. A novel digital intervention for actively reducing severity of paediatric ADHD (STARS-ADHD): a randomised controlled trial. The Lancet. Digital health. 2020. PMID: 33334505. Registry ID: NCT02674633. shelves.title: Aripiprazole cuts irritability scores in autistic disorder in two 8-week trials — with weight gain of 1.3–2.0 kg and sedation the price
shelves.question: In children and adolescents with autism, does aripiprazole reduce irritability and aggression compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Antipsychotic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Aripiprazole · Autistic Disorder/diagnosis/drug therapy/psychology · Child · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Irritable Mood/drug effects · Male · Personality Assessment · Piperazines/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Quinolones/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Weight Gain/drug effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two concordant 8-week placebo-controlled trials. In Owen et al. (PMID: 19948625), flexibly dosed aripiprazole beat placebo on the Aberrant Behavior Checklist irritability subscale from week 1 through week 8, with mean weight gain 2.0 kg versus 0.8 kg on placebo and extrapyramidal symptom-related events in 14.9% versus 8.0%. In Marcus et al. (PMID: 19797985), all three fixed doses improved irritability scores more than placebo at week 8 (-12.4, -13.2 and -14.4 points for 5, 10 and 15 mg/day versus -8.4 on placebo; all p<.05), with mean weight change +1.3 to +1.5 kg versus +0.3 kg on placebo. The benefit is real but short-term and symptom-scored, and clinically significant residual symptoms may persist. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): aripiprazole reduces irritability in autistic disorder over 8 weeks, at the cost of weight gain and sedation.

cards.headline: Owen 2009: flexibly dosed aripiprazole beat placebo on irritability from week 1 to week 8 — weight gain 2.0 kg versus 0.8 kg, extrapyramidal events 14.9% versus 8.0%
cards.summary: Owen 2009: flexibly dosed aripiprazole beat placebo on irritability from week 1 to week 8 — weight gain 2.0 kg versus 0.8 kg, extrapyramidal events 14.9% versus 8.0%
cards.people: 98 children and adolescents aged 6–17 years with autistic disorder and tantrums, aggression, self-injurious behaviour or a combination, randomised to flexibly dosed aripiprazole (target 5, 10 or 15 mg/day; n=47) or placebo (n=51) for 8 weeks.
cards.result: Mean improvement in Aberrant Behavior Checklist irritability subscale score was significantly greater with aripiprazole than placebo from week 1 through week 8, and Clinical Global Impression-Improvement scores also favoured aripiprazole. Discontinuation for adverse events was 10.6% on aripiprazole versus 5.9% on placebo; extrapyramidal symptom-related adverse events 14.9% versus 8.0%; no serious adverse events were reported. Mean weight gain at week 8 was 2.0 kg on aripiprazole versus 0.8 kg on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Eight weeks only, in children pre-selected for severe irritability behaviours; the record does not give the absolute point difference on the irritability subscale, and the authors note clinically significant residual symptoms may persist for some patients.
cards.source: Owen R et al. Aripiprazole in the treatment of irritability in children and adolescents with autistic disorder. Pediatrics. 2009. PMID: 19948625. Registry ID: NCT00332241. cards.people: Two randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials totalling 316 children and adolescents aged 6–17 years with autistic disorder and prominent irritability behaviours, each 8 weeks long.
cards.result: Both trials found significantly greater irritability reduction on aripiprazole than placebo (fixed-dose trial: -12.4 to -14.4 versus -8.4 points at week 8). shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the one large randomised trial missed its primary endpoint. In Benninga et al. (PMID: 33838349), overall spontaneous bowel movement response was 18.5% on lubiprostone versus 14.4% on placebo (P=.2245) in 606 children aged 6–17 years. The 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of pharmacological therapies for functional constipation in children (PMID: 41101321), covering 59 randomised trials and 7,045 participants, found polyethylene glycol probably more effective than placebo (RR 1.74, 95% CI 1.25–2.41, moderate certainty) — a contrast that underlines lubiprostone's null rather than rescuing it. Tolerability was acceptable in both records. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): lubiprostone has not been shown to increase spontaneous bowel movements over placebo in children.

cards.headline: Benninga 2022: spontaneous bowel movement response 18.5% on lubiprostone versus 14.4% on placebo (P=.2245) in 606 children
cards.summary: Benninga 2022: spontaneous bowel movement response 18.5% on lubiprostone versus 14.4% on placebo (P=.2245) in 606 children
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial with open-label extension (Benninga 2022)
cards.people: 606 patients aged 6–17 years with pediatric functional constipation randomised to lubiprostone 12 µg twice daily, 24 µg twice daily (doses weight-based; n=404 combined) or placebo (n=202) for 12 weeks, with an open-label extension for completers.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — overall spontaneous bowel movement (SBM) response, defined as an increase of at least 1 SBM/week over baseline and at least 3 SBMs/week for at least 9 weeks including 3 of the final 4 weeks — occurred in 18.5% on lubiprostone versus 14.4% on placebo, a difference that was not statistically significant (P=.2245). Both doses were well tolerated, with a safety profile consistent with adult studies.
cards.watchOut: A single trial carries this shelf's drug-specific claim; the response definition is stringent, and a small true effect below the trial's detection threshold cannot be excluded — but no significant benefit was shown on the endpoint the trial itself chose.
cards.source: Benninga MA et al. Lubiprostone for Pediatric Functional Constipation: Randomized, Controlled, Double-Blind Study With Long-term Extension. Clinical gastroenterology and hepatology : the official clinical practice journal of the American Gastroenterological Association. 2022. PMID: 33838349. Registry ID: NCT02138136, NCT02042183. cards.headline: 2025 meta-analysis (59 trials, 7,045 children): polyethylene glycol beat placebo (RR 1.74) — lubiprostone, in 2 trials, earned no such result
cards.summary: 2025 meta-analysis (59 trials, 7,045 children): polyethylene glycol beat placebo (RR 1.74) — lubiprostone, in 2 trials, earned no such result
cards.people: 59 randomised controlled trials with 7,045 participants younger than 18 years with functional constipation, comparing pharmacological therapies (including lubiprostone in 2 trials) with placebo, no treatment or other interventions, with at least 2 weeks of follow-up.
cards.result: For treatment success, polyethylene glycol was probably more effective than placebo (RR 1.74, 95% CI 1.25–2.41, moderate certainty of evidence) and may be more effective than lactulose (RR 1.35, 95% CI 1.11–1.64, low certainty). Linaclotide showed no clear difference in treatment success versus placebo (RR 1.21, 95% CI 0.69–2.13, low certainty) and prucalopride was not clearly more effective than placebo (RR 1.68, 95% CI 0.77–3.68). The review names polyethylene glycol, not lubiprostone, as the therapy with placebo-beating evidence and recommends it as first-line standard of care.
cards.watchOut: The meta-analysis pools many drugs and definitions of success; its value here is comparative context — it shows the field can detect a working drug against placebo, which makes lubiprostone's null harder to dismiss as a methods artefact.
cards.source: de Geus A et al. Efficacy and safety of pharmacological therapies for functional constipation in children: a systematic review and meta-analysis. The Lancet. Child & adolescent health. 2025. PMID: 41101321. cards.headline: Synthesis: one large null trial, and a field-wide review that finds a winner elsewhere
cards.summary: Synthesis: one large null trial, and a field-wide review that finds a winner elsewhere
cards.people: One randomised placebo-controlled phase 3 trial of lubiprostone in 606 children aged 6–17 years, read alongside a 2025 systematic review of 59 pharmacotherapy trials (7,045 children) in functional constipation.
cards.result: Lubiprostone response 18.5% versus 14.4% on placebo (P=.2245); in the same evidence field, polyethylene glycol beat placebo with RR 1.74 (95% CI 1.25–2.41). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: Absence of demonstrated benefit is not proof of zero effect in every subgroup; children with intractable constipation after standard therapy were not the population randomised here.

shelves.title: Tricyclics dry the bed while the child takes them — 78% versus 95% fail to reach 14 dry nights on imipramine versus placebo — then 96% are wet again after stopping, and alarms beat them
shelves.question: In children with nocturnal enuresis that alarms and desmopressin have not settled, do tricyclic drugs such as imipramine produce dryness — and does it last after stopping?
shelves.mesh: Antidepressive Agents, Tricyclic/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Child · Child, Preschool · Clinical Alarms · Enuresis/drug therapy · Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: SPLIT — tricyclics work during treatment and stop working when treatment stops. The Cochrane review (Caldwell et al., PMID: 26789925; 64 trials, 4,071 children) found imipramine gave one fewer wet night per week than placebo (mean difference -0.95, 95% CI -1.40 to -0.50; 4 trials, 347 children), with 78% failing to achieve 14 consecutive dry nights versus 95% on placebo (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.61 to 0.90; 12 trials, 831 children). After treatment ceased, 96% on imipramine were wetting again versus 97% on placebo. Alarms beat imipramine head-to-head: 67% failed to achieve 14 consecutive dry nights on imipramine versus 17% on alarms (RR 4.00, 95% CI 1.06 to 15.08; 1 trial, 24 children), with a more sustained alarm effect after stopping (100% versus 58% wetting at follow-up). Minor adverse effects were common across 30 reporting trials. PROPOSED SPLIT: a real on-treatment effect, no cure, and a better non-drug alternative.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2016 (64 trials, 4,071 children): imipramine — one fewer wet night per week, 78% versus 95% failing to reach 14 dry nights — but 96% wet again after stopping
cards.summary: Cochrane 2016 (64 trials, 4,071 children): imipramine — one fewer wet night per week, 78% versus 95% failing to reach 14 dry nights — but 96% wet again after stopping
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Cochrane review, Caldwell 2016)
cards.people: 64 randomised and quasi-randomised trials involving 4,071 children with nocturnal enuresis, comparing tricyclic or related drugs with placebo, other drugs, alarms or behavioural therapies; trials of daytime wetting were excluded.
cards.result: Versus placebo, imipramine produced one fewer wet night per week (mean difference -0.95, 95% CI -1.40 to -0.50; 4 trials, 347 children) and fewer children failing to achieve 14 consecutive dry nights (78% versus 95%; RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.61 to 0.90; 12 trials, 831 children). Amitriptyline and desipramine also beat placebo; nortriptyline and mianserin did not. Most tricyclics had no sustained effect after treatment stopped: at follow-up 96% on imipramine were wetting versus 97% on placebo. Minor adverse effects (dizziness, headache, mood changes, gastrointestinal discomfort, neutropenia) were common and reported in 30 trials; more serious side effects can occur but were not reported in the trials.
cards.watchOut: Many included trials were poor quality and most comparisons rest on single small studies; the review's own framing is short-term symptom control, and tricyclics carry a well-known danger in overdose that trial adverse-event tables understate.
cards.source: Caldwell PH et al. Tricyclic and related drugs for nocturnal enuresis in children. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2016. PMID: 26789925. cards.headline: Synthesis: on-treatment dryness is real, cure is not — and the alarm comparison reverses the verdict on value
cards.summary: Synthesis: on-treatment dryness is real, cure is not — and the alarm comparison reverses the verdict on value
cards.people: The Cochrane review of 64 trials (4,071 children) of tricyclic and related drugs for nocturnal enuresis, including its head-to-head comparisons with alarm therapy.
cards.result: On treatment: imipramine -0.95 wet nights/week versus placebo and 78% versus 95% failing to achieve 14 consecutive dry nights. After stopping: 96% versus 97% wetting — no sustained benefit. Against alarms: 67% failed to achieve 14 dry nights on imipramine versus 17% on alarms, and at follow-up 100% versus 58% were wetting. PROPOSED SPLIT (benefit while taken; the treatment made no difference after stopping).
cards.watchOut: The alarm comparison rests on one 24-child trial, so the size of the alarm advantage is imprecise even though its direction matches the relapse pattern seen across the review.
cards.source: Synthesis of Caldwell PH et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2016 (PMID: 26789925).

shelves.title: Succimer lowered blood lead by 4.5 µg/dL but bought no cognition: IQ 1 point lower (not significant) at 36 months, and still no benefit at age 7
shelves.question: In toddlers with raised blood lead levels, does chelation with succimer improve neuropsychological development compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Chelating Agents/therapeutic use · Chelation Therapy · Child Behavior/drug effects · Child Development/drug effects · Child, Preschool · Cognition/drug effects · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Infant · Intelligence/drug effects · Lead/blood · Lead Poisoning/drug therapy · Male · Neuropsychological Tests · Poverty Areas · Succimer/therapeutic use · Urban Population
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — one large, well-run trial programme, reported twice, with the same answer. In the Treatment of Lead-exposed Children trial (Rogan et al., PMID: 11346806), succimer lowered mean blood lead by 4.5 µg/dL (95% CI 3.7 to 5.3) over the first six months, yet at 36 months the succimer group's mean IQ was 1 point lower than placebo and parent-rated behaviour slightly worse, with slightly better scores on one neuropsychological battery — all differences small and none statistically significant. The age-7 follow-up of the same cohort (Dietrich et al., PMID: 15231903; 647 children remaining) again found no benefit in cognitive, behavioural or neuromotor endpoints. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): chelation cleans the blood test, not the brain outcome, at blood lead levels of 20–44 µg/dL.

cards.headline: Rogan 2001 (TLC): blood lead fell 4.5 µg/dL on succimer — IQ at 36 months was 1 point lower than placebo, no difference significant
cards.summary: Rogan 2001 (TLC): blood lead fell 4.5 µg/dL on succimer — IQ at 36 months was 1 point lower than placebo, no difference significant
cards.people: 780 children aged 12–33 months living in deteriorating inner-city housing, with blood lead levels of 20–44 µg/dL, randomised to up to three 26-day courses of oral succimer or placebo, with cognitive, motor, behavioural and neuropsychological testing over 36 months.
cards.result: During the first six months, mean blood lead was 4.5 µg/dL lower on succimer than placebo (95% CI 3.7 to 5.3). At 36 months, mean IQ in the succimer group was 1 point lower than placebo and parent-rated behaviour slightly worse, while scores on the Developmental Neuropsychological Assessment were slightly better; all differences were small and none statistically significant. The authors concluded chelation is not indicated at these blood lead levels.
cards.watchOut: One trial programme carries this shelf (Tier C): the result applies to blood lead 20–44 µg/dL in toddlers — it does not address severe poisoning at much higher levels, where chelation has other indications.
cards.source: Rogan WJ et al. The effect of chelation therapy with succimer on neuropsychological development in children exposed to lead. The New England journal of medicine. 2001. PMID: 11346806. cards.headline: Dietrich 2004 (TLC at age 7): 647 children retested — still no cognitive, behavioural or neuromotor benefit from succimer
cards.summary: Dietrich 2004 (TLC at age 7): 647 children retested — still no cognitive, behavioural or neuromotor benefit from succimer
cards.type: Randomised trial long-term follow-up (Dietrich 2004, TLC cohort)
cards.people: 647 of the original 780 TLC children remaining at age 7 years, originally randomised at 12–33 months of age with blood lead 20–44 µg/dL to oral succimer (up to three 26-day courses) or placebo, all with residential lead hazard control and daily multivitamins.
cards.result: Chelation lowered average blood lead for approximately six months but resulted in no benefit in cognitive, behavioural and neuromotor endpoints at age 7. The authors state the follow-up confirms the earlier finding and that succimer cannot be recommended for children with blood lead levels between 20 and 44 µg/dL.
cards.watchOut: This is the same randomised cohort as the 36-month report, not an independent replication — attrition from 780 to 647 children also leaves room for bias, though the null is consistent at both time points.
cards.source: Dietrich KN et al. Effect of chelation therapy on the neuropsychological and behavioral development of lead-exposed children after school entry. Pediatrics. 2004. PMID: 15231903. shelves.title: Iron-fortified formula in infancy tracked with lower scores a decade later: every 10-year outcome lower, and 16-year-olds scored lower on visual memory, arithmetic and reading
shelves.question: In infancy, does iron-fortified formula, compared with low-iron formula, change cognitive and developmental outcomes into adolescence in non-anaemic infants?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Anemia, Iron-Deficiency/prevention & control · Chile · Cognition/drug effects · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Food, Fortified · Humans · Infant · Infant Formula/classification · Infant Nutritional Physiological Phenomena · Iron/administration & dosage · Longitudinal Studies · Male · Motor Skills/drug effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — a single randomised cohort followed twice, pointing the same way. At 10 years (Lozoff et al., PMID: 22064877), children randomised as infants to iron-fortified formula (12.7 mg/L) scored lower than the low-iron group (2.3 mg/L) on every outcome measured — 1.4–4.6 points lower, significantly so for spatial memory and visual-motor integration — with the deficit concentrated in infants whose 6-month haemoglobin was high (>12.8 g/dL: 10.7–19.3 points lower), while infants with low haemoglobin (<10.5 g/dL) scored better on iron-fortified formula. At 16 years (Gahagan et al., PMID: 31253407), the iron-fortified group again scored lower on visual memory, arithmetic achievement and reading comprehension. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): in iron-replete infants, the higher-iron formula was followed by poorer long-term cognitive scores; infants who were iron-deficient may still need the iron.

cards.headline: Lozoff 2012 (10-year follow-up): iron-fortified group lower on every outcome (1.4–4.6 points); infants with high haemoglobin scored 10.7–19.3 points lower
cards.summary: Lozoff 2012 (10-year follow-up): iron-fortified group lower on every outcome (1.4–4.6 points); infants with high haemoglobin scored 10.7–19.3 points lower
cards.people: 473 of 835 Chilean infants who completed a randomised trial (1991–1994) of iron-fortified formula (mean 12.7 mg/L) versus low-iron formula (mean 2.3 mg/L) given from 6 to 12 months of age, assessed at 10 years with examiners masked to group; the infants were healthy, full-term and non-anaemic at entry.
cards.result: Compared with the low-iron group, the iron-fortified group scored lower on every 10-year outcome — significant for spatial memory and visual-motor integration, suggestive for IQ, arithmetic achievement, visual perception and motor coordination — by 1.4–4.6 points (effect sizes 0.13–0.21). Children with high 6-month haemoglobin (>12.8 g/dL; 5.5% of the sample, n=26) scored 10.7–19.3 points lower if they had received iron-fortified formula (effect sizes 0.85–1.36), while children with low haemoglobin (<10.5 g/dL; 18.4%, n=87) scored 2.6–4.5 points better on it.
cards.watchOut: A single cohort (Tier C), with only 56.6% of completers assessed at 10 years; the headline average effect is small, and the large subgroup effects rest on 26 and 87 children — hypothesis-shaping, not settled dosing science.
cards.source: Lozoff B et al. Iron-fortified vs low-iron infant formula: developmental outcome at 10 years. Archives of pediatrics & adolescent medicine. 2012. PMID: 22064877. cards.headline: Gahagan 2019 (16-year follow-up): iron-fortified group lower on visual memory, arithmetic and reading comprehension
cards.summary: Gahagan 2019 (16-year follow-up): iron-fortified group lower on visual memory, arithmetic and reading comprehension
cards.people: 405 adolescents (mean age 16.2 years, 46% male) from the same Chilean randomised cohort, assigned as 6-month-old infants to iron-fortified formula (12 mg/L) or low-iron formula (2.3 mg/L) for 6 months, assessed for cognitive ability, visual perceptual ability, visual memory and achievement in math, vocabulary and comprehension.
cards.result: Adolescents randomised to iron-fortified formula had lower scores than the low-iron group for visual memory, arithmetic achievement and reading comprehension achievement. For visual motor integration, the direction depended on infancy haemoglobin: the iron-fortified group outperformed when 6-month haemoglobin was low and underperformed when it was high.
cards.watchOut: The same single cohort as the 10-year report — two looks at one experiment, not two experiments; the record gives directions of difference rather than absolute point gaps for the 16-year outcomes.

cards.result: At 10 years: iron-fortified group lower on all outcomes by 1.4–4.6 points; high-haemoglobin subgroup 10.7–19.3 points lower; low-haemoglobin subgroup 2.6–4.5 points better. shelves.title: Daily penicillin in toddlers with sickle cell anaemia cut pneumococcal septicaemia by 84% — 2 infections versus 13, and 0 deaths versus 3, in a trial stopped early
shelves.question: In infants and young children with sickle cell anaemia, does daily penicillin prophylaxis prevent pneumococcal septicaemia and death?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Anemia, Sickle Cell/complications · Child, Preschool · Clinical Trials as Topic · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Infant · Male · Penicillin V/administration & dosage · Pneumococcal Infections/prevention & control · Random Allocation · Sepsis/prevention & control
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — an early-stopped trial with a very large effect, backed by a Cochrane synthesis. In the PROPS trial (Gaston et al., PMID: 3086721), pneumococcal septicaemia occurred in 2 of 105 children on penicillin versus 13 of 110 on placebo — an 84% relative reduction (P=0.0025) — with no deaths from pneumococcal septicaemia on penicillin versus three deaths on placebo; the trial was terminated 8 months early. The Cochrane review of prophylactic antibiotics in sickle cell disease (Rankine-Mullings & Owusu-Ofori, PMID: 33724440) found an odds ratio of 0.37 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.86; 2 trials, 457 children) for pneumococcal infection when starting penicillin, graded low-certainty evidence. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): prophylactic penicillin prevents pneumococcal septicaemia in young children with sickle cell anaemia. Tier C is set because the shelf carries a mortality claim resting substantially on one trial.

cards.headline: Gaston 1986 (PROPS): pneumococcal septicaemia in 2 of 105 on penicillin versus 13 of 110 on placebo (84% relative reduction, P=0.0025); deaths 0 versus 3 — trial stopped 8 months early
cards.summary: Gaston 1986 (PROPS): pneumococcal septicaemia in 2 of 105 on penicillin versus 13 of 110 on placebo (84% relative reduction, P=0.0025); deaths 0 versus 3 — trial stopped 8 months early
cards.people: 215 children with sickle cell anaemia who were under 3 years of age at entry, randomised to oral penicillin V potassium 125 mg twice daily (n=105) or placebo (n=110), followed for an average of 15 months before the trial was terminated 8 months early.
cards.result: Documented pneumococcal septicaemia occurred in 2 of 105 children on penicillin versus 13 of 110 on placebo — an 84% relative reduction in incidence (P=0.0025), with the absolute rates printed alongside. No deaths from pneumococcal septicaemia occurred in the penicillin group, versus three deaths in the placebo group. The authors concluded that children with sickle cell anaemia should receive prophylactic penicillin by four months of age.
cards.watchOut: A 1986 trial from before modern pneumococcal conjugate vaccination, stopped early — early stopping can exaggerate effect size, and today's vaccine-covered serotypes change the baseline risk the 84% relative reduction applies to.
cards.source: Gaston MH et al. Prophylaxis with oral penicillin in children with sickle cell anemia. A randomized trial. The New England journal of medicine. 1986. PMID: 3086721. cards.summary: Cochrane 2021: starting penicillin prophylaxis gives odds ratio 0.37 (95% CI 0.16–0.86) for pneumococcal infection — low-certainty evidence
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Cochrane review, Rankine-Mullings 2021)
cards.people: Three eligible trials totalling 880 children with sickle cell disease, randomised between 3 months and 5 years of age in the USA and Kingston, Jamaica, comparing prophylactic antibiotics with placebo, no treatment or a comparator drug.
cards.result: In trials of starting penicillin prophylaxis, the odds ratio for pneumococcal infection was 0.37 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.86; 2 trials, 457 children), graded low-certainty evidence. cards.watchOut: Low-certainty grading, few trials and few events: the direction is consistent with PROPS, but the pooled estimate cannot sharpen the size of the benefit in a vaccinated modern cohort.

shelves.title: Early azithromycin did not prevent chronic lung disease of prematurity: survival without moderate or severe disease 42% versus 45% (adjusted OR 0.84, p=0.43) in 796 preterm infants
shelves.question: In preterm infants, does early azithromycin prevent chronic lung disease of prematurity (bronchopulmonary dysplasia) compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Azithromycin/therapeutic use/administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · Infant, Newborn · Female · Male · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use/administration & dosage · Infant, Premature · Chronic Disease · Infant, Premature, Diseases/prevention & control · Treatment Outcome · Lung Diseases/prevention & control · Gestational Age · Intensive Care Units, Neonatal · United Kingdom
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — one large, adequately powered trial settles what smaller conflicting reviews could not. In AZTEC (Lowe et al., PMID: 38679042), survival without moderate or severe chronic lung disease at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age occurred in 166 of 394 infants (42%) on azithromycin versus 179 of 402 (45%) on placebo (adjusted OR 0.84, 95% CI 0.55–1.29, p=0.43), and pulmonary Ureaplasma colonisation did not influence the treatment effect. Serious adverse events were reported in seven infants in the azithromycin group and six in the placebo group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): prophylactic azithromycin cannot be recommended to prevent chronic lung disease of prematurity.

cards.summary: Lowe 2024 (AZTEC): survival without moderate or severe chronic lung disease 42% versus 45% (adjusted OR 0.84, 95% CI 0.55–1.29, p=0.43)
cards.people: 796 preterm infants born at less than 30 weeks' gestation in 28 UK tertiary neonatal intensive care units, who had received at least 2 hours of respiratory support within 72 hours of birth, randomised to intravenous azithromycin (20 mg/kg/day for 3 days, then 10 mg/kg for 7 days; n=394 analysed) or placebo (n=402).
cards.result: The primary outcome — survival without physiologically defined moderate or severe chronic lung disease at 36 weeks' postmenstrual age — occurred in 166 (42%) of 394 infants on azithromycin versus 179 (45%) of 402 on placebo (adjusted OR 0.84, 95% CI 0.55–1.29, p=0.43). Pulmonary Ureaplasma spp colonisation did not influence the treatment effect. Seven serious adverse events were reported in the azithromycin group and six in the placebo group.
cards.watchOut: A single trial carries this shelf (Tier C), testing one intravenous regimen started within 72 hours; it does not test azithromycin given later, orally, or for documented Ureaplasma infection rather than prophylaxis.

shelves.title: Inhaled nitric oxide does not save preterm babies or prevent lung disease: death or bronchopulmonary dysplasia risk ratio 0.94 in every timing group in the Cochrane review
shelves.question: In preterm infants with respiratory failure, does inhaled nitric oxide reduce death or bronchopulmonary dysplasia compared with placebo or usual care?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia/mortality/prevention & control · Cerebral Hemorrhage/epidemiology/prevention & control · Humans · Incidence · Infant, Newborn · Infant, Premature · Infant, Premature, Diseases/prevention & control/therapy · Nitric Oxide/administration & dosage · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Respiratory Insufficiency/therapy · Salvage Therapy · Vasodilator Agents/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — 17 trials grouped three ways, all null on the outcome that matters. The Cochrane review (Barrington et al., PMID: 28045472) found no significant effect of inhaled nitric oxide on death or bronchopulmonary dysplasia in any group: early rescue treatment (typical RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.87–1.01; 958 infants), routine use with respiratory support (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.87–1.02; 1,924 infants), or later treatment for bronchopulmonary dysplasia risk (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.85–1.01; 1,075 infants), and no effect on neurodevelopmental impairment. The largest single trial (Kinsella et al., PMID: 16870914; 793 infants) likewise found death or bronchopulmonary dysplasia in 71.6% on nitric oxide versus 75.3% on placebo (P=0.24). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): inhaled nitric oxide is not an effective rescue or preventive therapy in preterm respiratory failure.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2017 (17 trials): death or bronchopulmonary dysplasia RR 0.94 (early rescue), 0.94 (routine) and 0.92 (later) — none significant, no neurodevelopmental effect
cards.summary: Cochrane 2017 (17 trials): death or bronchopulmonary dysplasia RR 0.94 (early rescue), 0.94 (routine) and 0.92 (later) — none significant, no neurodevelopmental effect
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Cochrane review, Barrington 2017)
cards.people: 17 randomised and quasi-randomised trials of inhaled nitric oxide versus control in preterm infants with respiratory disease, grouped post hoc as early rescue treatment on oxygenation criteria (8 trials), routine use alongside respiratory support (4 trials), and later treatment for infants at raised risk of bronchopulmonary dysplasia (3 trials in the later analysis).
cards.result: No group showed a significant effect on death or bronchopulmonary dysplasia: early rescue typical RR 0.94 (95% CI 0.87 to 1.01; 958 infants); routine use RR 0.94 (95% CI 0.87 to 1.02; 1,924 infants); later treatment RR 0.92 (95% CI 0.85 to 1.01; 1,075 infants). There was no clear effect on intraventricular haemorrhage overall, though early rescue was associated with a non-significant 20% increase in severe intraventricular haemorrhage, and no effect on neurodevelopmental impairment.
cards.watchOut: The three groupings were made post hoc because entry criteria varied so much between trials; a pooled overall analysis was deliberately not performed, so the shelf's claim is 'no group showed benefit', not a single pooled null.
cards.source: Barrington KJ et al. Inhaled nitric oxide for respiratory failure in preterm infants. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2017. PMID: 28045472. cards.headline: Kinsella 2006: death or bronchopulmonary dysplasia 71.6% on nitric oxide versus 75.3% on placebo (P=0.24) in 793 ventilated preterm newborns
cards.summary: Kinsella 2006: death or bronchopulmonary dysplasia 71.6% on nitric oxide versus 75.3% on placebo (P=0.24) in 793 ventilated preterm newborns
cards.people: 793 newborns at 34 weeks' gestation or less with respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation, randomised to inhaled nitric oxide 5 ppm or placebo gas for 21 days or until extubation, stratified by birth weight (500–749 g, 750–999 g, 1000–1250 g).
cards.result: There was no significant difference in the composite of death or bronchopulmonary dysplasia at 36 weeks: 71.6% on nitric oxide versus 75.3% on placebo (P=0.24). In the 1000–1250 g stratum, bronchopulmonary dysplasia alone was lower on nitric oxide (29.8% versus 59.6%), and the combined endpoint of intracranial haemorrhage, periventricular leukomalacia or ventriculomegaly was lower overall (17.5% versus 23.9%, P=0.03), as was periventricular leukomalacia alone (5.2% versus 9.0%, P=0.048). Pulmonary haemorrhage and other adverse events were not increased.
cards.watchOut: The brain-injury and heaviest-baby subgroup findings are secondary and subgroup results inside an overall null trial — exactly the pattern the Cochrane review's null group analyses warn against over-reading.
cards.source: Kinsella JP et al. Early inhaled nitric oxide therapy in premature newborns with respiratory failure. The New England journal of medicine. 2006. PMID: 16870914. Registry ID: NCT00006401. shelves.title: Cooling started 6–24 hours after birth for hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy: death or disability 24.4% versus 27.9% — a 76% Bayesian probability of benefit, not proof
shelves.question: In newborns with hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy who present late, does therapeutic hypothermia started between 6 and 24 hours of age reduce death or disability compared with normothermia?
shelves.mesh: Bayes Theorem · Developmental Disabilities/etiology/prevention & control · Female · Gestational Age · Humans · Hypothermia, Induced · Hypoxia-Ischemia, Brain/complications/mortality/therapy · Infant, Newborn · Male · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Complications · Time-to-Treatment
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — one trial, analysed Bayesianly precisely because it could not settle the question. In Laptook et al. (PMID: 29067428), death or moderate/severe disability at 18–22 months occurred in 19 of 78 cooled infants (24.4%) versus 22 of 79 noncooled infants (27.9%) — an absolute difference of 3.5% (95% CI -1% to 17%). Bayesian analysis with a neutral prior gave a 76% posterior probability of reduced death or disability with hypothermia (adjusted posterior risk ratio 0.86, 95% credible interval 0.58–1.29), and a 64% probability of at least a 2% absolute reduction. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): late cooling may help, with genuine uncertainty — the trial's own conclusion.

cards.headline: Laptook 2017: death or disability 24.4% cooled versus 27.9% noncooled (difference 3.5%, 95% CI -1% to 17%); 76% posterior probability of any benefit
cards.summary: Laptook 2017: death or disability 24.4% cooled versus 27.9% noncooled (difference 3.5%, 95% CI -1% to 17%); 76% posterior probability of any benefit
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial with prespecified Bayesian analysis (Laptook 2017)
cards.people: 168 infants at 36 weeks' gestation or later with moderate or severe hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy, enrolled at 6–24 hours after birth (mean randomisation about 15–16 hours) at 21 US Neonatal Research Network centres; 83 were cooled to 33.5°C for 96 hours and 85 maintained at 37.0°C, with the primary outcome assessed in 78 and 79 infants respectively.
cards.result: Death or moderate/severe disability at 18–22 months occurred in 19 of 78 cooled infants (24.4%) versus 22 of 79 noncooled infants (27.9%): absolute difference 3.5% (95% CI -1% to 17%). Bayesian analysis using a neutral prior indicated a 76% posterior probability of reduced death or disability (adjusted posterior risk ratio 0.86, 95% credible interval 0.58–1.29); the probability of at least a 1%, 2% or 3% absolute reduction was 71%, 64% and 56% respectively.
cards.watchOut: A single trial (Tier C) that was designed around Bayesian estimation because a conventionally powered trial was not feasible: the credible interval runs from substantial benefit to appreciable harm, and 11 randomised infants are missing from the primary-outcome denominators.
cards.source: Laptook AR et al. shelves.title: Procalcitonin guidance cut neonatal antibiotic courses by about 10 hours (55.1 versus 65.0 hours) — but non-inferiority for reinfection or death could not be shown
shelves.question: In neonates with suspected early-onset sepsis, does procalcitonin-guided decision-making safely shorten antibiotic therapy compared with standard care?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage · Biomarkers/blood · Calcitonin/blood · Decision Making · Drug Monitoring/methods · Early Diagnosis · Female · Gestational Age · Humans · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Infant, Newborn, Diseases/blood/diagnosis/drug therapy · Internationality · Male · Sepsis/blood/diagnosis/drug therapy · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for antibiotic exposure; the safety half of the question stays open. In the NeoPInS trial (Stocker et al., PMID: 28711318), procalcitonin-guided decision-making shortened antibiotic therapy versus standard care (intention-to-treat 55.1 versus 65.0 hours, p<0.0001; per protocol 51.8 versus 64.0 hours, p<0.0001) in 1,710 neonates. But reinfection or death was so rare — 5 of 866 (0.6%) versus 4 of 844 (0.5%), risk difference 0.1% (95% CI -4.6 to 4.8) against a 2.0% non-inferiority margin, with no sepsis-related deaths and 9 possible reinfections overall — that non-inferiority could not be shown. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): procalcitonin guidance safely-appearing but unproven-safe shortening of neonatal antibiotic courses, Tier C as a single trial.

cards.headline: Stocker 2017 (NeoPInS): antibiotic duration 55.1 versus 65.0 hours (p<0.0001); reinfection or death 0.6% versus 0.5%, non-inferiority not shown
cards.summary: Stocker 2017 (NeoPInS): antibiotic duration 55.1 versus 65.0 hours (p<0.0001); reinfection or death 0.6% versus 0.5%, non-inferiority not shown
cards.people: 1,710 neonates of gestational age 34 weeks or older with suspected early-onset sepsis requiring antibiotics, randomised in 18 hospitals in the Netherlands, Switzerland, Canada and the Czech Republic to procalcitonin-guided decision-making (n=866) or standard care (n=844), stratified by physician-assigned risk category; 1,408 underwent per-protocol analysis.
cards.result: Duration of antibiotic therapy was shorter with procalcitonin guidance (intention-to-treat: 55.1 versus 65.0 hours, p<0.0001; per protocol: 51.8 versus 64.0 hours, p<0.0001). For the co-primary non-inferiority outcome of reinfection or death in the first month, the risk difference was 0.1% (95% CI -4.6 to 4.8) intention-to-treat (5 [0.6%] of 866 versus 4 [0.5%] of 844) and 0.1% (-5.2 to 5.3) per protocol; no sepsis-related deaths occurred and 9 of 1,710 neonates (<1%) had possible reinfection, so non-inferiority against the 2.0% margin could not be shown.
cards.watchOut: A single trial (Tier C) in high-income settings where culture-proven early-onset sepsis prevalence is 0.1% or less: the safety question is statistically unanswerable at this event rate, and the result does not transfer to settings with higher true sepsis rates.
cards.source: Stocker M et al. shelves.title: Preschool vision screening finds amblyopia risk accurately — but no trial has ever compared screening with no screening, so better later vision is inferred, not shown
shelves.question: In preschool children, does vision screening detect amblyopia and improve later visual outcomes compared with no screening or later detection?
shelves.mesh: Amblyopia/diagnosis/therapy · Child, Preschool · Educational Status · False Positive Reactions · Female · Humans · Infant · Male · Mass Screening · Refractive Errors/diagnosis · Risk Assessment · Risk Factors · Strabismus/diagnosis · Vision Screening · Visual Acuity
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — detection is proven; the outcome chain is indirect. The US Preventive Services Task Force evidence report (Jonas et al., PMID: 28873167; 40 studies, 34,709 children) found no randomised trial comparing screening with no screening and no studies of school performance, function or quality of life, while test accuracy was genuinely good: positive likelihood ratios of 5–10 for amblyopia risk factors in most studies and above 10 for combinations of clinical tests. Treatment links the chain only part-way: patching improved the amblyopic eye by less than 1 line after 5–12 weeks in pretreated children, and 45% versus 21% achieved at least a 2-line improvement with patching versus no patching (P=.003; 1 trial, 180 participants). The Vision in Preschoolers studies (Kulp et al., PMID: 35044337) confirm which tests perform best and that children unable to perform the tests (<2%) are more likely to have vision disorders and should be referred. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): screening detects the right children; that population screening improves later vision has never been randomised.

cards.headline: Jonas 2017 (USPSTF evidence report, 40 studies, 34,709 children): no screening-versus-no-screening trial exists; test accuracy is good and patching works once children are found
cards.summary: Jonas 2017 (USPSTF evidence report, 40 studies, 34,709 children): no screening-versus-no-screening trial exists; test accuracy is good and patching works once children are found
cards.type: Systematic review and evidence report (Jonas 2017, for the USPSTF)
cards.people: 40 studies (N=34,709) in children aged 6 months to 5 years: 34 evaluating test accuracy for amblyopia, its risk factors and refractive error, plus randomised trials of treatment versus inactive controls and cohort studies of harms.
cards.result: No randomised trials compared screening with no screening, and no studies evaluated school performance, functioning or quality of life. Positive likelihood ratios were 5–10 for amblyopia risk factors or nonamblyogenic refractive error in most accuracy studies and greater than 10 for combinations of clinical tests; in low-prevalence settings (<10%) false-positive rates were usually above 75%. For treatment, patching improved visual acuity of the amblyopic eye by a mean of less than 1 line after 5–12 weeks in glasses-pretreated children (2 trials, 240 participants), and 45% versus 21% achieved at least a 2-line improvement with patching versus no patching (P=.003; 1 trial, 180 participants). The authors conclude studies directly evaluating screening effectiveness were limited and do not establish whether screening is better than no screening.
cards.watchOut: Tier C: the shelf's benefit claim is a chain of indirect evidence (accurate test + effective treatment) with the middle link — earlier detection changing outcomes at population level — supported only by limited, high-attrition studies.
cards.source: Jonas DE et al. Vision Screening in Children Aged 6 Months to 5 Years: Evidence Report and Systematic Review for the US Preventive Services Task Force. JAMA. 2017. PMID: 28873167. cards.headline: Kulp 2022 (VIP/VIP-HIP): refraction tests and Lea Symbols acuity identified disorders best; the under-2% who cannot perform the tests are likelier to have a disorder
cards.summary: Kulp 2022 (VIP/VIP-HIP): refraction tests and Lea Symbols acuity identified disorders best; the under-2% who cannot perform the tests are likelier to have a disorder
cards.type: Research programme summary (Kulp 2022, Vision in Preschoolers studies)
cards.people: Preschool children (including Head Start populations) in the Vision in Preschoolers (VIP) and VIP-Hyperopia in Preschoolers (VIP-HIP) studies, comparing screening tests (retinoscopy, Retinomax, SureSight, Lea Symbols visual acuity) against comprehensive examination, by lay and nurse screeners.
cards.result: Refraction tests (retinoscopy, Retinomax, SureSight) and Lea Symbols visual acuity performed best in identifying children with vision disorders; for lay screeners, single crowded Lea Symbols testing at 5 feet was significantly better than linear crowded testing at 10 feet. Children unable to perform the tests (<2%) were more likely to have vision disorders than children who passed and should be referred. Amblyopia and strabismus prevalence was similar across racial and ethnic groups, while hyperopia, astigmatism and anisometropia varied; uncorrected moderate hyperopia was associated with reduced near visual function and early-literacy deficits.
cards.watchOut: VIP measures how well tests classify children against a gold-standard examination — accuracy, not whether screening programmes improve vision years later; the outcome half of the question remains untested by any record on this shelf.
cards.source: Kulp MT et al. cards.people: The USPSTF evidence report (40 studies, 34,709 children aged 6 months–5 years) and the Vision in Preschoolers programme's test-performance studies.
cards.result: Test accuracy: positive likelihood ratios 5–10, above 10 for test combinations. Treatment once found: at least 2-line acuity improvement in 45% on patching versus 21% without (P=.003). shelves.title: Babies whose hearing loss was confirmed by 9 months had language 0.70–0.82 standard deviations higher at age 8 — the case for universal newborn hearing screening rests on this cohort
shelves.question: Does universal newborn hearing screening improve language development in children with permanent hearing loss compared with later, distraction-test detection?
shelves.mesh: Child · Child Language · Cohort Studies · Hearing Loss · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Neonatal Screening · Speech
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — consistent observational evidence from one large birth cohort, never randomised. In Kennedy et al. (PMID: 16707750), among 120 children with bilateral permanent hearing impairment assessed at a mean age of 7.9 years, confirmation of hearing impairment by 9 months of age was associated with higher adjusted language scores relative to nonverbal ability (receptive language adjusted mean difference 0.82, 95% CI 0.31 to 1.33; expressive language 0.70, 95% CI 0.13 to 1.26), and birth during periods with universal newborn screening was associated with higher receptive language scores (adjusted mean difference 0.60, 95% CI 0.07 to 1.13), though not significantly higher expressive language; speech scores did not differ significantly. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): earlier detection through universal screening is associated with better language — but not better speech — in mid-childhood. Tier C: observational evidence throughout.

cards.headline: Kennedy 2006: early confirmation by 9 months — receptive language +0.82 SD (95% CI 0.31–1.33), expressive +0.70 SD (0.13–1.26); screening-period birth — receptive +0.60 SD (0.07–1.13); speech not significantly different
cards.summary: Kennedy 2006: early confirmation by 9 months — receptive language +0.82 SD (95% CI 0.31–1.33), expressive +0.70 SD (0.13–1.26); screening-period birth — receptive +0.60 SD (0.07–1.13); speech not significantly different
cards.type: Cohort study within a controlled screening comparison (Kennedy 2006, Wessex cohort)
cards.people: 120 children with bilateral permanent hearing impairment identified from a large birth cohort in southern England, assessed at a mean age of 7.9 years; 61 were born during periods with universal newborn screening and 57 had hearing impairment confirmed by 9 months of age, with outcomes expressed as z scores against 63 age-matched children with normal hearing and adjusted for severity of impairment and maternal education.
cards.result: Confirmation of hearing impairment by 9 months of age was associated with higher adjusted mean z scores for language relative to nonverbal ability (receptive language adjusted mean difference 0.82, 95% CI 0.31 to 1.33; expressive language 0.70, 95% CI 0.13 to 1.26). Birth during universal-screening periods was also associated with higher receptive language scores (adjusted mean difference 0.60, 95% CI 0.07 to 1.13), but expressive language scores were not significantly higher, and speech scores did not differ significantly between groups.
cards.watchOut: Observational (Tier C): children were not randomised to screening, so families and services that achieve early confirmation may differ in other ways that also improve language, despite adjustment for severity and maternal education.

shelves.title: Early prednisolone does not prevent kidney involvement in IgA vasculitis: proteinuria at 12 months in 15% on prednisolone versus 10% on placebo (OR 1.46, not significant)
shelves.question: In children with IgA vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein purpura), does early prednisolone prevent kidney involvement compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Child · Child, Preschool · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Humans · IgA Vasculitis/complications/drug therapy · Incidence · Kidney/physiopathology · Kidney Diseases/complications/drug therapy/epidemiology · Logistic Models · Male · Prednisolone/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Proteinuria/complications/drug therapy/epidemiology · Treatment Outcome · United Kingdom
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the largest trial of the question found nothing, with the point estimate leaning the wrong way. In Dudley et al. (PMID: 23845696), proteinuria at 12 months was present in 18 of 123 children (15%) on prednisolone versus 13 of 124 (10%) on placebo (OR 1.46, 95% CI 0.68 to 3.14; adjusted OR 1.29, 95% CI 0.58 to 2.82), and there was no significant difference in time to needing additional renal treatment (HR 0.53, 95% CI 0.18 to 1.59). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): a 14-day course of prednisolone at presentation does not prevent nephropathy in IgA vasculitis.

cards.headline: Dudley 2013: proteinuria at 12 months 15% (18/123) on prednisolone versus 10% (13/124) on placebo (OR 1.46, 95% CI 0.68–3.14) — no benefit on any renal outcome
cards.summary: Dudley 2013: proteinuria at 12 months 15% (18/123) on prednisolone versus 10% (13/124) on placebo (OR 1.46, 95% CI 0.68–3.14) — no benefit on any renal outcome
cards.people: 352 children under 18 years of age with new-onset Henoch–Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis), randomised to prednisolone or placebo for 14 days, with proteinuria (urine protein:creatinine ratio >20 mg/mmol) at 12 months and need for additional renal treatment over 12 months as primary outcomes; 247 children had 12-month laboratory results.
cards.result: Proteinuria at 12 months was present in 18 of 123 children (15%) on prednisolone versus 13 of 124 (10%) on placebo (OR 1.46, 95% CI 0.68 to 3.14), unchanged after adjustment for baseline proteinuria and relevant medications (adjusted OR 1.29, 95% CI 0.58 to 2.82). Time to additional treatment did not differ significantly (HR 0.53, 95% CI 0.18 to 1.59; n=323). The authors identify this as the largest trial of steroids in this condition and report no evidence that early prednisolone reduces proteinuria at 12 months.
cards.watchOut: A single trial (Tier C), and 105 of 352 randomised children lack 12-month laboratory results; the confidence interval cannot exclude a modest protective effect, but the observed direction was toward more proteinuria on steroids.
cards.source: Dudley J et al. Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial to determine whether steroids reduce the incidence and severity of nephropathy in Henoch-Schonlein Purpura (HSP). Archives of disease in childhood. 2013. PMID: 23845696. Registry ID: ISRCTN71445600.
