shelves.title: Intranasal fentanyl matched intravenous morphine for children's fracture pain: pain scores indistinguishable at every time point, with a 10-minute difference of -5 mm (95% CI -16 to 7)
shelves.question: In children with acute limb-fracture pain, is intranasal fentanyl as effective as intravenous morphine for pain relief?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Administration, Intranasal · Adolescent · Analgesics, Opioid/administration & dosage/pharmacokinetics · Child · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Emergency Medicine/methods · Emergency Service, Hospital · Fentanyl/administration & dosage/pharmacokinetics · Fractures, Bone/complications · Humans · Injections, Intravenous · Morphine/administration & dosage/pharmacokinetics · Pain/diagnosis/drug therapy/etiology · Pain Measurement · Patient Satisfaction · Pediatrics/methods · Prospective Studies · Therapeutic Equivalency · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one small double-blind equivalence trial, with a concordant systematic review behind it. In Borland et al. (PMID: 17067720), 67 children aged 7–15 years with deformed closed long-bone fractures received intranasal fentanyl (mean total dose 1.7 µg/kg) or intravenous morphine (mean total dose 0.11 mg/kg) under double-dummy blinding; visual analogue pain scores did not differ significantly before analgesia or at 5, 10, 20 or 30 minutes (P=.333), the 10-minute between-group difference was -5 mm (95% CI -16 to 7 mm), and there were no serious adverse events. The systematic review of intranasal fentanyl in children (Mudd, PMID: 21867860) found all reviewed studies showed similar or improved pain scores compared with other opioids and routes, with no severe adverse outcomes reported. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): intranasal fentanyl relieves fracture pain as effectively as intravenous morphine, without needing a cannula first. Tier C: the head-to-head trial is single and small.

cards.headline: Borland 2007: no significant pain-score difference at 0, 5, 10, 20 or 30 minutes (P=.333) between intranasal fentanyl and intravenous morphine in 67 children with fractures
cards.summary: Borland 2007: no significant pain-score difference at 0, 5, 10, 20 or 30 minutes (P=.333) between intranasal fentanyl and intravenous morphine in 67 children with fractures
cards.people: 67 children aged 7–15 years (mean 10.9 years) presenting to a tertiary paediatric emergency department with clinically deformed closed long-bone fractures (79.1% radius or ulna), randomised to active intravenous morphine with intranasal placebo, or active intranasal concentrated fentanyl (150 µg/mL) with intravenous placebo; mean total doses were 1.7 µg/kg intranasal fentanyl and 0.11 mg/kg intravenous morphine.
cards.result: Visual analogue scale pain scores did not differ significantly between groups before analgesia or at 5, 10, 20 or 30 minutes after analgesia (P=.333); at 10 minutes the difference in mean score between morphine and fentanyl groups was -5 mm (95% CI -16 to 7 mm). Pain scores fell significantly within both groups over time, and there were no serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: A single small trial (Tier C) run as a superiority comparison, not a formal non-inferiority trial: the 95% CI at 10 minutes (-16 to 7 mm) includes differences many clinicians would call meaningful, and children under 7 and open or multiple injuries were not studied.
cards.source: Borland M et al. A randomized controlled trial comparing intranasal fentanyl to intravenous morphine for managing acute pain in children in the emergency department. shelves.title: Rituximab did not reduce proteinuria in resistant childhood nephrotic syndrome: -12% at 3 months (95% CI -73% to 110%, P=0.77) in the one randomised trial
shelves.question: In children with steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome, does rituximab induce remission compared with standard therapy?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Albumins/metabolism · Antibodies, Monoclonal/therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Murine-Derived/therapeutic use · Calcineurin Inhibitors · Child · Child, Preschool · Confidence Intervals · Creatinine/blood · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Resistance · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Kidney Function Tests · Male · Nephrotic Syndrome/diagnosis/drug therapy · Patient Selection · Prednisone/therapeutic use · Prospective Studies · Proteinuria/physiopathology · Reference Values · Risk Assessment · Rituximab · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the one randomised trial was frankly null, and the 2025 Cochrane review rates the rituximab evidence as very low certainty. In Magnasco et al. (PMID: 22581994), adding two doses of rituximab to prednisone plus calcineurin inhibitors in 31 children with resistant idiopathic nephrotic syndrome changed proteinuria by -12% at 3 months (95% CI -73% to 110%; P=0.77). The Cochrane review of interventions for idiopathic steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome in children (Liu et al., PMID: 40337980; 29 studies, 1,248 children) concludes it is uncertain whether rituximab combined with cyclosporin and prednisolone increases remission compared with cyclosporin and prednisolone, because the certainty of the evidence is very low. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): rituximab has no demonstrated remission benefit in steroid-resistant disease — a different picture from steroid-dependent disease.

cards.headline: Magnasco 2012: proteinuria change -12% at 3 months with rituximab added (95% CI -73% to 110%; P=0.77) in 31 resistant children
cards.summary: Magnasco 2012: proteinuria change -12% at 3 months with rituximab added (95% CI -73% to 110%; P=0.77) in 31 resistant children
cards.people: 31 children (mean age 8 years, range 2–16) with idiopathic nephrotic syndrome unresponsive to combined calcineurin inhibitors and prednisone; all continued prednisone and calcineurin inhibitors, and one group additionally received two intravenous rituximab doses of 375 mg/m².
cards.result: Rituximab did not reduce proteinuria at 3 months: change -12% (95% confidence interval -73% to 110%; P=0.77 in the analysis of covariance adjusted for baseline proteinuria), and additional adjustment for previous remission and interaction terms did not change the results. The authors conclude the data do not support adding rituximab to prednisone and calcineurin inhibitors in resistant idiopathic nephrotic syndrome.
cards.watchOut: Small (31 children) and open-label (Tier C): the confidence interval is wide enough to hide a moderate effect in either direction, and 3 months is a short window for an antibody whose B-cell effects last longer.
cards.source: Magnasco A et al. Rituximab in children with resistant idiopathic nephrotic syndrome. Journal of the American Society of Nephrology : JASN. 2012. PMID: 22581994. cards.headline: Cochrane 2025 (29 studies, 1,248 children): whether rituximab improves remission in steroid-resistant disease is uncertain — very low-certainty evidence
cards.summary: Cochrane 2025 (29 studies, 1,248 children): whether rituximab improves remission in steroid-resistant disease is uncertain — very low-certainty evidence
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Cochrane review, Liu 2025)
cards.people: 29 randomised and quasi-randomised studies evaluating 1,248 children aged 3 months to 18 years with idiopathic steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome, comparing immunosuppressive and non-immunosuppressive interventions with placebo, prednisone or another agent.
cards.result: For rituximab, the review states it is uncertain whether rituximab/cyclosporin/prednisolone compared with cyclosporin/prednisolone increases the likelihood of remission or reduces adverse events, because the certainty of the evidence is very low, and kidney failure was not reported. By contrast, calcineurin inhibitors may increase complete or partial remission compared with placebo/no treatment or cyclophosphamide, and compared with intravenous cyclophosphamide may increase complete remission (RR 3.43, 95% CI 1.84 to 6.41; 2 studies, 156 children).
cards.watchOut: The review pools a spectrum of diseases under 'steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome'; genetic forms — a large share of resistant cases — would not be expected to respond to any immunosuppression, diluting every drug's signal including rituximab's.
cards.source: Liu ID et al. Interventions for idiopathic steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome in children. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2025. PMID: 40337980. shelves.title: Amitriptyline did not beat placebo for children's functional abdominal pain: 63% versus 57.5% felt better (P=.63), and the Cochrane pooled risk ratio is 1.17 (95% CI 0.87–1.56)
shelves.question: In children with functional abdominal pain or irritable bowel syndrome, does amitriptyline improve pain and quality of life compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Abdominal Pain/prevention & control/psychology · Activities of Daily Living · Adolescent · Amitriptyline/therapeutic use · Analgesics, Non-Narcotic/therapeutic use · Anxiety/etiology/prevention & control · Child · Dyspepsia/drug therapy/psychology · Female · Gastrointestinal Agents/therapeutic use · Humans · Irritable Bowel Syndrome/drug therapy/psychology · Logistic Models · Male · Medication Adherence · Pain Measurement · Prospective Studies · Severity of Illness Index · Surveys and Questionnaires · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · United States
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a multicentre trial and a Cochrane meta-analysis agree. In Saps et al. (PMID: 19596010), 63% of children on amitriptyline reported feeling better versus 57.5% on placebo (P=.63), with excellent or good pain relief in 50% versus 45% (P=.85) and no difference on logistic regression (P=.83) — while both groups improved substantially. The Cochrane review of antidepressants for functional abdominal pain disorders in children (de Bruijn et al., PMID: 33560523) pooled treatment success at RR 1.17 (95% CI 0.87 to 1.56; 2 studies, 205 participants), low-certainty evidence of no difference. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the large placebo response in this condition is the story; amitriptyline adds nothing measurable to it.

cards.headline: Saps 2009: feeling better in 63% on amitriptyline versus 57.5% on placebo (P=.63); excellent/good relief 50% versus 45% (P=.85) — both groups improved a lot
cards.summary: Saps 2009: feeling better in 63% on amitriptyline versus 57.5% on placebo (P=.63); excellent/good relief 50% versus 45% (P=.85) — both groups improved a lot
cards.people: 90 children with irritable bowel syndrome, functional abdominal pain or functional dyspepsia randomised to 4 weeks of amitriptyline (10 mg/day if under 35 kg, 20 mg/day if over) or placebo at multiple US centres; 83 completed (40 placebo, 43 amitriptyline).
cards.result: Overall response: 63% on amitriptyline reported feeling better and 5% worse, versus 57.5% better and 2.5% worse on placebo (P=.63). Pain relief was excellent in 15% and good in 35% on amitriptyline versus excellent in 7% and good in 38% on placebo (P=.85); logistic regression for excellent/good versus fair/poor/failed response showed no difference (P=.83). Children with more severe baseline pain did worse in both groups (P=.0065); amitriptyline reduced anxiety scores (P<.0001).
cards.watchOut: Four weeks at low dose in a mixed group of three functional diagnoses; the trial was powered for a larger drug-placebo gap than this condition usually leaves, because the placebo response itself was so large.
cards.source: Saps M et al. Multicenter, randomized, placebo-controlled trial of amitriptyline in children with functional gastrointestinal disorders. Gastroenterology. 2009. PMID: 19596010. cards.headline: Cochrane 2021: treatment success RR 1.17 (95% CI 0.87–1.56) for antidepressants versus placebo — low-certainty evidence of no difference
cards.summary: Cochrane 2021: treatment success RR 1.17 (95% CI 0.87–1.56) for antidepressants versus placebo — low-certainty evidence of no difference
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Cochrane review, de Bruijn 2021)
cards.people: Three randomised trials (223 participants) in children aged 4–18 years with functional abdominal pain disorders: two using amitriptyline and one citalopram, compared with placebo, with treatment success as the primary outcome.
cards.result: Meta-analysis of the two studies with comparable success definitions found low-certainty evidence of no difference between antidepressants and placebo (RR 1.17, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.56; 2 studies, 205 participants), downgraded for imprecision from extremely sparse data. The third study reported significantly more children on an antidepressant achieving at least 15% improvement in overall quality-of-life score at 10 and 13 weeks (P=0.007 and P=0.002; absolute figures not given). Withdrawals due to adverse events did not differ (RR 3.17, 95% CI 0.65 to 15.33, very low certainty).
cards.watchOut: Only three small trials exist for the whole drug class in this condition; the pooled confidence interval (0.87–1.56) still admits a moderate benefit, so this is 'no demonstrated difference', not proof of exact equivalence.
cards.source: de Bruijn CMA et al. Antidepressants for functional abdominal pain disorders in children and adolescents. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2021. PMID: 33560523. shelves.title: Internet-delivered family CBT reduced pain and activity limitations in two randomised trials — significantly greater activity-limitation reduction than education control at 6 months in 273 adolescents
shelves.question: In children and adolescents with chronic pain, does internet-delivered cognitive behavioural therapy improve pain and disability compared with waiting list or education control?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Child · Chronic Disease · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy/methods · Depression/etiology/psychology · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Internet · Male · Motor Activity · Pain/psychology · Pain Management · Pain Measurement · Patient Acceptance of Health Care · Patient Compliance · Patient Satisfaction · Sample Size · Socioeconomic Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two randomised trials from one programme, both positive on function. In Palermo et al. 2009 (PMID: 19695776), 48 children aged 11–17 with chronic pain showed significantly greater reductions in activity limitations and pain intensity on internet-delivered family CBT than wait-list control, maintained at 3-month follow-up, with a greater rate of clinically significant improvement in pain. In the larger multicentre trial (Palermo et al. 2016, PMID: 26335910; 273 adolescents), internet CBT produced significantly greater reduction in activity limitations from baseline to 6 months than internet education (b=-1.13, P=0.03), with benefits also on sleep quality (b=0.14, P=0.04) and parent behaviours. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): internet-delivered CBT improves function and pain modestly, and reaches families far from pain centres.

cards.headline: Palermo 2009: internet family CBT beat wait-list on activity limitations and pain intensity, maintained at 3 months, in 48 children aged 11–17
cards.summary: Palermo 2009: internet family CBT beat wait-list on activity limitations and pain intensity, maintained at 3 months, in 48 children aged 11–17
cards.people: 48 children aged 11–17 years with chronic headache, abdominal or musculoskeletal pain and associated functional disability, plus their parents, randomised to 8 weeks of internet-delivered family CBT modules (relaxation, cognitive strategies, parent operant techniques, communication, sleep and activity) alongside medical care, or wait-list with medical care only; outcomes via online daily diary.
cards.result: The internet treatment group showed significantly greater reduction in activity limitations and pain intensity at post-treatment than the wait-list group, with effects maintained at 3-month follow-up, and a greater rate of clinically significant improvement in pain. There were no significant group differences in parental protectiveness or child depressive symptoms. All children and parents rated internet treatment as acceptable.
cards.watchOut: Small (48 children) and wait-list controlled — wait-list comparisons inflate effects because the control group receives nothing new; the record gives significance and direction rather than absolute effect sizes.
cards.source: Palermo TM et al. Randomized controlled trial of an Internet-delivered family cognitive-behavioral therapy intervention for children and adolescents with chronic pain. Pain. 2009. PMID: 19695776. cards.headline: Palermo 2016 (273 adolescents, multicentre): activity limitations fell significantly more on internet CBT than internet education by 6 months (b=-1.13, P=0.03)
cards.summary: Palermo 2016 (273 adolescents, multicentre): activity limitations fell significantly more on internet CBT than internet education by 6 months (b=-1.13, P=0.03)
cards.people: 273 adolescents aged 11–17 years (205 female, 68 male) with mixed chronic pain conditions and their parents, randomised to internet-delivered CBT (n=138) or internet-delivered education (n=135), with all assessment and treatment online and follow-up to 6 months.
cards.result: Internet CBT produced significantly greater reduction in the primary outcome, activity limitations, from baseline to 6-month follow-up than internet education (b=-1.13, P=0.03). Secondary benefits included sleep quality (b=0.14, P=0.04), reduced parent miscarried helping (b=-2.66, P=0.007) and protective behaviours (b=-0.19, P=0.001), and higher treatment satisfaction; exploratory outcomes favoured CBT for parent depression, anxiety and self-blame about the adolescent's pain.
cards.watchOut: An active education control makes this the more credible of the two trials, and its primary-outcome effect is correspondingly modest (P=0.03); pain intensity itself is not among the significant between-group results reported in this record.
cards.source: Palermo TM et al. Internet-delivered cognitive-behavioral treatment for adolescents with chronic pain and their parents: a randomized controlled multicenter trial. Pain. 2016. shelves.title: Trauma-focused CBT is the best-supported treatment for childhood PTSD: largest symptom reductions in a 70-trial network meta-analysis (g=1.06 versus passive control), and a head-to-head win over child-centred therapy
shelves.question: In children and adolescents with PTSD, does trauma-focused CBT reduce symptoms versus usual care or waitlist?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Analysis of Variance · Child · Child Abuse, Sexual/psychology · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy/methods · Female · Humans · Male · Stress Disorders, Post-Traumatic/etiology/therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — a large network meta-analysis plus a rigorous head-to-head trial. The 2025 network meta-analysis (Hoppen et al., PMID: 39630422; 70 randomised trials, 5,528 patients) found trauma-focused CBTs produced the largest short-term reductions in paediatric PTSD versus passive controls (Hedges g 1.06, 95% CI 0.86–1.26, P<.001), were superior to both passive and active controls across sensitivity analyses, and held their effects at mid-term and long-term follow-up; 52 of the 70 trials (74%) examined trauma-focused CBTs. In the multisite randomised trial (Cohen et al., PMID: 15187799; 229 children aged 8–14 with sexual-abuse-related PTSD), trauma-focused CBT produced significantly more improvement than child-centred therapy in PTSD, depression, behaviour problems, shame and abuse-related attributions, with parents also improving more. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): trauma-focused CBT reduces PTSD symptoms in children and adolescents more than waiting, usual or non-trauma-focused care.

cards.summary: Hoppen 2025 network meta-analysis (70 trials, 5,528 patients): trauma-focused CBT g=1.06 (95% CI 0.86–1.26) versus passive control — largest effect, durable to 6–24 months
cards.people: 70 randomised trials with 5,528 children and adolescents (19 years or younger) with full or subthreshold PTSD, comparing psychological interventions with control conditions; 52 trials (74%) examined trauma-focused cognitive behaviour therapies.
cards.result: At treatment end, trauma-focused CBTs were associated with significantly larger PTSD reductions than passive controls (Hedges g 1.06, 95% CI 0.86–1.26, P<.001) — the largest effect among intervention classes — and outperformed both passive and active controls across all sensitivity analyses; in trials with parent involvement, trauma-focused CBT also beat non-trauma-focused interventions (g 0.35, 95% CI 0.04–0.66, P=.03). Mid-term (up to 5 months) and long-term (6–24 months) results were similar for trauma-focused CBT.
cards.watchOut: Network estimates lean heavily on comparisons with passive controls, which flatter any active therapy; the margin over other active therapies is much smaller (g 0.35 in the parent-involvement analysis) than the headline 1.06.
cards.source: Hoppen TH et al. Psychological Interventions for Pediatric Posttraumatic Stress Disorder: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis. JAMA psychiatry. 2025. PMID: 39630422. shelves.title: First-line stimulants in childhood ADHD: amphetamines lead on clinician ratings (SMD -1.02 versus -0.78 for methylphenidate) — but methylphenidate is the authors' first choice in children, on teacher ratings and tolerability
shelves.question: In children with ADHD, do methylphenidate and amphetamine formulations differ in efficacy and tolerability as first-line stimulant treatment?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adrenergic alpha-2 Receptor Agonists/therapeutic use* · Adult · Attention Deficit Disorder with Hyperactivity/drug therapy* · Bupropion/therapeutic use* · Central Nervous System Stimulants/therapeutic use* · Child · Clonidine/therapeutic use* · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Humans · Methylphenidate/therapeutic use* · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two stimulant classes split by outcome: amphetamines win on clinician-rated efficacy, methylphenidate wins on tolerability and teacher ratings, and the authors name methylphenidate the preferred first choice in children and adolescents. In the Cortese 2018 network meta-analysis (Cortese S et al., PMID: 30097390) of 133 double-blind randomised controlled trials (81 in children and adolescents), the efficacy analysis closest to 12 weeks covered 10,068 children and adolescents and the tolerability analysis 11,018. On clinicians' ratings of ADHD core symptoms versus placebo, amphetamines had the largest effect (standardised mean difference -1.02, 95% CI -1.19 to -0.85), ahead of methylphenidate (-0.78, 95% CI -0.93 to -0.62), and head-to-head efficacy differences favoured amphetamines over methylphenidate (standardised mean differences -0.46 to -0.24). The picture reverses on the other measures: on teachers' ratings, only methylphenidate (-0.82, 95% CI -1.16 to -0.48) among the stimulants was more efficacious than placebo, and on tolerability amphetamines were inferior to placebo in children and adolescents (odds ratio for dropout because of side-effects 2.30, 95% CI 1.36 to 3.89), whereas methylphenidate was listed as less well tolerated than placebo in adults only. Taking efficacy and safety together, the authors concluded that the evidence supports methylphenidate in children and adolescents as the preferred first-choice medication for the short-term treatment of ADHD — with no sufficient data at 26 or 52 weeks. PROPOSED SPLIT: short-term clinician-rated efficacy favours amphetamines, but tolerability and teacher ratings favour methylphenidate, which the synthesis names first choice in children and adolescents.

cards.headline: Cortese 2018: in children and adolescents amphetamines lead on clinician ratings (SMD -1.02) over methylphenidate (-0.78) — but only methylphenidate beats placebo on teacher ratings, and amphetamines double dropout for side-effects (odds ratio 2.30)
cards.summary: Cortese 2018: in children and adolescents amphetamines lead on clinician ratings (SMD -1.02) over methylphenidate (-0.78) — but only methylphenidate beats placebo on teacher ratings, and amphetamines double dropout for side-effects (odds ratio 2.30)
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of double-blind randomised controlled trials (Cortese 2018)
cards.people: 133 double-blind randomised controlled trials (81 in children and adolescents, 51 in adults, and one in both) comparing oral amphetamines (including lisdexamfetamine), atomoxetine, bupropion, clonidine, guanfacine, methylphenidate, and modafinil with each other or placebo. In children and adolescents, the efficacy analysis closest to 12 weeks was based on 10,068 participants and the tolerability analysis on 11,018. Primary outcomes were efficacy (change in severity of ADHD core symptoms on teachers' and clinicians' ratings) and tolerability (proportion of patients who dropped out of studies because of side-effects), at timepoints closest to 12 weeks, 26 weeks, and 52 weeks. This card reports the children-and-adolescents stratum only.
cards.result: For ADHD core symptoms rated by clinicians in children and adolescents closest to 12 weeks, all included drugs were superior to placebo: amphetamines standardised mean difference -1.02 (95% CI -1.19 to -0.85), methylphenidate -0.78 (-0.93 to -0.62), and atomoxetine -0.56 (-0.66 to -0.45). By contrast, on teachers' ratings, only methylphenidate (-0.82, 95% CI -1.16 to -0.48) and modafinil (-0.76, -1.15 to -0.37) were more efficacious than placebo. On tolerability in children and adolescents, amphetamines were inferior to placebo (odds ratio for dropout because of side-effects 2.30, 95% CI 1.36 to 3.89), as was guanfacine (2.64, 1.20 to 5.81); methylphenidate was listed as less well tolerated than placebo in adults only, not in children and adolescents. In head-to-head comparisons, only differences in efficacy (clinicians' ratings) were found, favouring amphetamines over modafinil, atomoxetine, and methylphenidate in children and adolescents (standardised mean differences -0.46 to -0.24). Confidence in the estimates varied from high or moderate (for some comparisons) to low or very low (for most indirect comparisons), and there were not sufficient data for the 26-week and 52-week timepoints. The authors' interpretation: taking into account both efficacy and safety, the evidence supports methylphenidate in children and adolescents as the preferred first-choice medication for the short-term treatment of ADHD, and new research should be funded urgently to assess long-term effects.
cards.watchOut: A network synthesis, not a head-to-head trial programme: the methylphenidate-versus-amphetamine comparison in children rests largely on indirect comparisons, most of them graded low or very low confidence, and the underlying trials are short — outcomes closest to 12 weeks, with insufficient data at 26 and 52 weeks, so nothing here speaks to long-term treatment. Tolerability in this record means only dropout because of side-effects, not the full adverse-effect profile, and the efficacy answer depends on the rater: clinicians' ratings favour amphetamines, teachers' ratings separate only methylphenidate (and modafinil) from placebo. Tier C is set because a single network synthesis carries the shelf, its key comparison is indirect, and its trials are short.
cards.source: Cortese S et al. shelves.title: Outpatient care for low-risk febrile neutropenia in children looks as safe as inpatient care: treatment failure RR 1.04 (95% CI 0.55–1.99) and mortality RR 0.63 (0.15–2.70) in the Cochrane child trials
shelves.question: In children at low risk with febrile neutropenia, is outpatient oral antibiotic therapy as safe as inpatient intravenous therapy?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Ambulatory Care · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Child · Febrile Neutropenia/chemically induced/drug therapy/mortality · Female · Fever/etiology · Hospitalization · Humans · Length of Stay · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasms/complications · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Quality of Life · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Time Factors · Treatment Failure
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — two systematic reviews find no clear safety penalty for stepping down care in carefully selected low-risk children. The Cochrane review (Rivas-Ruiz et al., PMID: 30887505) found, in children, no clear difference between outpatient and inpatient treatment in treatment failure (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.99; 4 studies) or mortality (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.15 to 2.70; 3 studies, 329 participants), both moderate-certainty evidence, with hospital stay shorter by 3.9 days in the one child study measuring it (mean difference -3.90, 95% CI -5.37 to -2.43). The systematic review of reduced-therapy regimens (Morgan et al., PMID: 26757936; 37 studies, 3,205 episodes) found odds ratios for treatment failure of 0.98 (95% CI 0.44–2.19) for outpatient treatment and 1.05 (95% CI 0.74–1.48) for oral treatment in the randomised trials, with only four safety events (two deaths, two intensive care admissions) across all included studies. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): in low-risk children, outpatient/oral strategies have not been shown to cost treatment failures or lives.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2019 (child trials): treatment failure RR 1.04 (95% CI 0.55–1.99), mortality RR 0.63 (0.15–2.70) for outpatient versus inpatient — hospital stay 3.9 days shorter
cards.summary: Cochrane 2019 (child trials): treatment failure RR 1.04 (95% CI 0.55–1.99), mortality RR 0.63 (0.15–2.70) for outpatient versus inpatient — hospital stay 3.9 days shorter
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Cochrane review, Rivas-Ruiz 2019)
cards.people: Ten randomised trials comparing outpatient with inpatient treatment for low-risk febrile neutropaenia in people with cancer: six in adults (628 participants) and four in children (366 participants); outpatient care included both exclusively outpatient treatment and early discharge to complete antibiotics at home.
cards.result: In children there was no clear evidence of a difference in treatment failure (RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.99; 4 studies) or mortality (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.15 to 2.70; 3 studies, 329 participants), both moderate-certainty evidence. Duration of fever in children did not clearly differ (mean difference -0.6, 95% CI -0.84 to 0.71 as reported; 3 studies, 305 participants), nor did days of antimicrobial treatment (mean difference -0.07, 95% CI -1.26 to 1.12). Hospital stay was lower with outpatient treatment by 3.9 days in the one child study reporting it (mean difference -3.90, 95% CI -5.37 to -2.43; 119 participants).
cards.watchOut: The confidence intervals are wide — the failure interval (0.55–1.99) admits anything from halving to doubling — so the verdict is 'no difference shown in selected low-risk children', with the risk stratification doing much of the safety work.

cards.headline: Morgan 2016 (37 studies, 3,205 episodes): randomised-trial failure OR 0.98 for outpatient and 1.05 for oral therapy; four safety events in total
cards.summary: Morgan 2016 (37 studies, 3,205 episodes): randomised-trial failure OR 0.98 for outpatient and 1.05 for oral therapy; four safety events in total
cards.people: 37 studies (13 randomised trials and 24 prospective observational cohorts) involving 3,205 episodes of low-risk febrile neutropenia in people younger than 18 years treated for cancer, examining location of therapy and route of antibiotic administration.
cards.result: In the randomised trials, the odds ratio for treatment failure (persistence, worsening or recurrence of fever or infection, antibiotic modification, new infection, readmission, critical care admission or death) was 0.98 (95% CI 0.44–2.19) for outpatient treatment and 1.05 (95% CI 0.74–1.48) for oral treatment. Across all studies, four safety events occurred (two deaths and two intensive care admissions). Pooled failure risk was 11.2% (95% CI 9.7–12.8%) for outpatient therapy and 10.5% (8.9–12.3%) for oral antibiotics, and failure was higher when reduced-intensity therapy started immediately after assessment rather than after 48 hours.
cards.watchOut: Most included evidence is observational cohorts with high heterogeneity in the pooled failure rates (I² about 77–78%), and 'low risk' was defined differently across studies — the timing signal (worse results when stepping down immediately) is a practical caution inside the reassuring headline.
cards.source: Morgan JE et al. Systematic review of reduced therapy regimens for children with low risk febrile neutropenia. shelves.title: Walnut oral immunotherapy desensitised 89% (49/55) versus 0% (0/18) on avoidance in a non-randomised cohort — with cross-desensitisation to pecan in all co-allergic patients and cashew in part
shelves.question: In children with cashew or walnut allergy, does oral immunotherapy raise the tolerated dose compared with avoidance or placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Allergens/administration & dosage/immunology/therapeutic use · Child · Child, Preschool · Desensitization, Immunologic/methods · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Juglans · Male · Nut Hypersensitivity/diagnosis/immunology/therapy · Nut Proteins/administration & dosage/immunology/therapeutic use · Prospective Studies · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — one prospective cohort, allocated by order of presentation rather than randomisation, with a very large effect. In the Nut CRACKER study (Elizur et al., PMID: 30926371), 49 of 55 patients (89%) on walnut oral immunotherapy were desensitised to walnut (passing a 4,000 mg walnut protein challenge) versus none of 18 in the avoidance control group. Cross-desensitisation followed for co-allergies: all 46 patients co-allergic to pecan were desensitised to pecan, and 18 of 30 patients (60%) co-allergic to hazelnut or cashew were fully desensitised or responded. The cost was reactions: 47 of 55 patients (85%) had an adverse reaction during clinic up-dosing (mostly grade 1–2) and eight required intramuscular epinephrine for a dose taken at home. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): walnut oral immunotherapy probably desensitises most treated children — randomised, placebo-controlled confirmation for tree nuts does not yet exist in this record.

cards.headline: Elizur 2019 (Nut CRACKER): walnut desensitisation 49/55 (89%) versus 0/18 on avoidance; pecan cross-desensitisation 46/46; hazelnut-or-cashew response 18/30 (60%)
cards.summary: Elizur 2019 (Nut CRACKER): walnut desensitisation 49/55 (89%) versus 0/18 on avoidance; pecan cross-desensitisation 46/46; hazelnut-or-cashew response 18/30 (60%)
cards.type: Prospective cohort study with non-randomised control group (Elizur 2019, Nut CRACKER)
cards.people: 73 patients aged 4 years or older with walnut allergy (with or without co-allergy to pecan, hazelnut and cashew) at a single Israeli centre, assigned to walnut oral immunotherapy (n=55) or observation with strict dietary exclusion (n=18) on the basis of order of presentation to the clinic; oral immunotherapy escalated over monthly visits to 4,000 mg walnut protein, then 1,200 mg daily for 6 months as maintenance.
cards.result: Walnut desensitisation (passing an oral food challenge with 4,000 mg walnut protein) was achieved by 49 of 55 patients (89%) on oral immunotherapy versus none of 18 controls. All patients co-allergic to pecan (n=46) were also desensitised to pecan; 18 of 30 patients (60%) co-allergic to hazelnut or cashew, and 14 of 15 (93%) co-allergic to hazelnut alone, were fully desensitised or responded. Adverse reactions occurred in 47 of 55 patients (85%) during clinic up-dosing (mostly grade 1 or 2); eight patients required intramuscular epinephrine for a dose at home. Of 45 patients with maintenance-phase follow-up, all maintained walnut desensitisation and one required epinephrine.
cards.watchOut: Not randomised and not placebo-controlled (Tier C): allocation by presentation order invites selection bias, desensitisation is a supervised-challenge threshold rather than freedom from real-world reactions, and cashew-specific desensitisation is reported only inside a combined hazelnut-or-cashew subgroup.
cards.source: Elizur A et al. Walnut oral immunotherapy for desensitisation of walnut and additional tree nut allergies (Nut CRACKER): a single-centre, prospective cohort study. The Lancet. Child & adolescent health. 2019. PMID: 30926371. shelves.title: Intramuscular vitamin K at birth nearly abolishes late bleeding (pooled RR 0.02 versus none); a single oral dose leaves risk 24.5-fold higher than intramuscular, while weekly oral dosing in Denmark recorded zero cases
shelves.question: In newborn infants, does vitamin K prophylaxis prevent vitamin K deficiency bleeding — and does a single intramuscular dose beat oral dosing?
shelves.mesh: Antifibrinolytic Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Humans · Incidence · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Observational Studies as Topic · Prospective Studies · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Retrospective Studies · Risk · Vitamin K/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Vitamin K Deficiency Bleeding/epidemiology/prevention & control
shelves.balance: SPLIT — prophylaxis works, and the route decides how completely. The systematic review (Sankar et al., PMID: 27109090) puts the median burden of late vitamin K deficiency bleeding at 35 per 100,000 live births (interquartile range 10.5–80) in infants who received no prophylaxis, and surveillance data show intramuscular or subcutaneous prophylaxis reduces late bleeding versus none (pooled RR 0.02, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.10). Against intramuscular dosing, a single oral dose increased the risk of vitamin K deficiency bleeding (RR 24.5, 95% CI 7.4 to 81.0), while multiple oral doses did not clearly differ (RR 3.64, 95% CI 0.82 to 16.3). Denmark's weekly oral regimen performed at the intramuscular level in practice (Hansen et al., PMID: 12892158): among about 396,000 infants given oral prophylaxis within 507,850 live births, no cases of vitamin K deficiency bleeding were found (incidence 0–0.9 per 100,000), with 94% of surveyed infants completing the course. PROPOSED SPLIT: one intramuscular dose is the reliable single-act protection; oral dosing protects only as a completed multi-dose course.

cards.headline: Sankar 2016 systematic review: late bleeding median 35 per 100,000 without prophylaxis; IM versus none pooled RR 0.02; single oral versus IM RR 24.5; multiple oral versus IM RR 3.64 (not significant)
cards.summary: Sankar 2016 systematic review: late bleeding median 35 per 100,000 without prophylaxis; IM versus none pooled RR 0.02; single oral versus IM RR 24.5; multiple oral versus IM RR 3.64 (not significant)
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials and observational surveillance studies (Sankar 2016)
cards.people: Randomised trials of intramuscular vitamin K and observational and population surveillance studies of vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB) in newborn infants across high-income and low- and middle-income countries.
cards.result: The median burden of late VKDB in infants who had not received prophylaxis was 35 per 100,000 live births (interquartile range 10.5 to 80), higher in low- and middle-income countries (80 per 100,000) than high-income countries (8.8 per 100,000). Four surveillance studies indicate intramuscular/subcutaneous prophylaxis significantly reduces late VKDB versus no prophylaxis (pooled RR 0.02, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.10). Compared with intramuscular prophylaxis, a single oral dose increased VKDB risk (RR 24.5, 95% CI 7.4 to 81.0) but multiple oral doses did not clearly differ (RR 3.64, 95% CI 0.82 to 16.3). In randomised trials of intramuscular prophylaxis, one trial reported reduced incidence of any bleeding (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.96) and moderate to severe bleeding (RR 0.19, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.46). No randomised trial evaluated prophylaxis against late VKDB directly; the authors grade the intramuscular evidence low quality but recommend it for all neonates.
cards.watchOut: Tier C: the decisive late-bleeding comparisons rest on observational surveillance, not randomisation — no trial has randomised babies to no prophylaxis for late bleeding, and none will; the single-oral-dose RR of 24.5 comes with a wide interval (7.4–81.0).
cards.source: Sankar MJ et al. Vitamin K prophylaxis for prevention of vitamin K deficiency bleeding: a systematic review. Journal of perinatology : official journal of the California Perinatal Association. 2016. PMID: 27109090. cards.headline: Hansen 2003 (Denmark, 507,850 births): weekly oral vitamin K — zero cases of deficiency bleeding found (incidence 0–0.9 per 100,000), 94% course completion
cards.summary: Hansen 2003 (Denmark, 507,850 births): weekly oral vitamin K — zero cases of deficiency bleeding found (incidence 0–0.9 per 100,000), 94% course completion
cards.people: 507,850 live births in Denmark from November 1992 to June 2000, of whom about 396,000 (78%) received oral prophylaxis (2 mg at birth, then weekly 1 mg doses given by parents while mainly breastfeeding) and 22% received intramuscular prophylaxis; cases ascertained by repeated questionnaires to all Danish paediatric departments and the National Patient Register, with compliance surveyed in parents of 274 infants.
cards.result: No cases of vitamin K deficiency bleeding were revealed in the oral-prophylaxis population: incidence 0–0.9 per 100,000 (95% CI). Compliance was good, with 94% of surveyed infants completing the prophylaxis course (at least 9 doses, counting a week as covered if the drop was given or the infant was mostly formula-fed).
cards.watchOut: A national programme evaluation without a concurrent control group: zero observed cases is powerful but depends on complete case ascertainment and on a health system that achieves 94% completion of a 3-month weekly course — the regimen, not the route alone, is what matched intramuscular results.
cards.source: Hansen KN et al. Weekly oral vitamin K prophylaxis in Denmark. Acta paediatrica (Oslo, Norway : 1992). 2003. PMID: 12892158. shelves.title: Escalating treatment in children's acute asthma: intravenous magnesium is the only option with high-certainty evidence of shorter stay and fewer admissions — aminophylline mainly adds vomiting, and almost every comparison rests on one to three tiny trials
shelves.question: In children with acute asthma exacerbations not responding to first-line therapy, which escalation treatment — intravenous salbutamol, aminophylline, or magnesium — works best?

shelves.balance: SPLIT — the three named options do not stand equal, and 'best' can only be answered by elimination. A Cochrane overview of 13 reviews (67 trials) of second-line treatment for children with acute asthma found intravenous magnesium sulfate was the only intervention shown to reduce hospital length of stay (high-certainty evidence) and one of the interventions reducing hospital admission (also high-certainty); no intervention was shown to reduce intensive care admission. Aminophylline increased vomiting compared with placebo (moderate-certainty evidence) and nausea compared with intravenous beta2-agonists (low-certainty), with no compensating benefit finding highlighted. A 2025 meta-analysis of intravenous magnesium specifically (nine randomised trials, 473 children) found lower hospitalisation and less need for non-invasive ventilation (risk ratio 0.17, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.54 as printed) at low certainty, with asthma scores, intensive care admission, invasive ventilation, and length of stay similar. Crucially, there are no adequate head-to-head trials between the options — most comparisons involve one to three trials and fewer than 100 children — so intravenous salbutamol's place is 'unproven', not 'disproven'. PROPOSED SPLIT: magnesium — supported; aminophylline — harm without shown benefit; intravenous salbutamol — no demonstrated advantage in this evidence.

cards.headline: Craig 2020 (Cochrane overview of 13 reviews, 67 trials): intravenous magnesium alone reduced length of stay (high certainty) and cut admissions; aminophylline increased vomiting; nothing reduced intensive care admission
cards.summary: Craig 2020 (Cochrane overview of 13 reviews, 67 trials): intravenous magnesium alone reduced length of stay (high certainty) and cut admissions; aminophylline increased vomiting; nothing reduced intensive care admission
cards.people: Thirteen Cochrane reviews reporting results for children alone, covering 67 randomised trials of second-line treatments for acute asthma exacerbations after first-line therapy (titrated oxygen, inhaled short-acting beta2-agonists, and oral corticosteroids) had failed; most individual comparisons involved one to three trials and fewer than 100 participants, with review populations ranging from 40 to 2,630 children.
cards.result: Intravenous magnesium sulfate was the only intervention shown to reduce hospital length of stay (high-certainty evidence), and hospital admission was reduced by intravenous magnesium sulfate (high-certainty), by adding inhaled anticholinergics to inhaled beta2-agonists (moderate-certainty), and by inhaled heliox (low-certainty). No evidence suggested any intervention reduced intensive care admission (low- to very low-certainty). Aminophylline increased vomiting compared with placebo (moderate-certainty) and increased nausea and nausea/vomiting compared with intravenous beta2-agonists (low-certainty). The overview states plainly that, for lack of comparative studies between options, firm practice recommendations cannot be made.
cards.watchOut: An overview is only as current as its component reviews — most had search dates more than four years old at publication, and four of the 13 reviews were rated at high risk of bias on study identification and selection. 'High certainty' for magnesium applies to length of stay and admission, not to intensive care or ventilation outcomes, where nothing worked.
cards.source: Craig SS et al. Interventions for escalation of therapy for acute exacerbations of asthma in children: an overview of Cochrane Reviews. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2020. PMID: 32767571. cards.headline: Hamud 2025: nine randomised trials of intravenous magnesium in children (473 participants) — hospitalisation and non-invasive ventilation lower (RR 0.17, 0.15 to 0.54 as printed), stay and invasive ventilation similar, no serious adverse events
cards.summary: Hamud 2025: nine randomised trials of intravenous magnesium in children (473 participants) — hospitalisation and non-invasive ventilation lower (RR 0.17, 0.15 to 0.54 as printed), stay and invasive ventilation similar, no serious adverse events
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Hamud 2025)
cards.people: Nine randomised trials totalling 473 children with acute asthma exacerbations, comparing intravenous magnesium sulfate added to standard first-line treatment (inhaled or nebulised short-acting beta2-agonist and systemic steroids) with standard treatment, searched to May 2024.
cards.result: Hospitalisation rate and the need for non-invasive ventilation were lower with intravenous magnesium (mean difference 0.70, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.90 for hospitalisation as printed in the record; risk ratio 0.17, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.54, p=0.003, for non-invasive ventilation). Asthma severity scores, length of hospital stay (mean difference −78.86, 95% CI −200.37 to 42.66, with I² of 99%), need for invasive ventilation (RR 0.35, 95% CI 0.11 to 1.17), and intensive care admission (p=0.43) were similar. Peak expiratory flow improved (p<0.001, in only 20 children). No serious adverse events were reported. The authors grade their own evidence as low certainty.
cards.watchOut: This focused review rates the magnesium evidence low certainty where the Cochrane overview rated its (older) component review high — the discrepancy itself is information about fragility. Several printed effect measures are internally odd (a 'mean difference' for a hospitalisation rate; extreme heterogeneity of 99% on length of stay), so the direction is more trustworthy than any single number.
cards.source: Hamud AA et al. Use of intravenous magnesium sulfate in addition to standard first-line treatment with inhaled/nebulised short-acting beta 2 agonist and systemic steroids in the management of acute asthma exacerbations in children: a systematic review and meta-analyses of randomised controlled trials. Archives of Disease in Childhood. 2025. PMID: 40562459. cards.headline: Synthesis: if a second-line drip is chosen for a child still struggling after first-line therapy, magnesium has the evidence — the others have habit, side effects, or silence
cards.summary: Synthesis: if a second-line drip is chosen for a child still struggling after first-line therapy, magnesium has the evidence — the others have habit, side effects, or silence
cards.people: A Cochrane overview of 13 reviews (67 trials) plus a focused 2025 meta-analysis of the nine randomised magnesium trials (473 children), in children with acute asthma exacerbations failing first-line therapy.
cards.result: Magnesium: only intervention reducing length of stay (high-certainty in the overview; low-certainty in the focused review), admission reduced in both syntheses, non-invasive ventilation RR 0.17 (0.15 to 0.54) in the focused review. Aminophylline: vomiting increased versus placebo, nausea increased versus intravenous beta2-agonists, no benefit finding. Intravenous salbutamol: no demonstrated advantage on the overview's primary outcomes. Intensive care admission: reduced by nothing. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C: the shelf carries a harm claim (aminophylline) resting on review-level evidence, which the developer reviews personally.
cards.watchOut: There are no head-to-head trials between the three named drugs, so the ranking is built from separate placebo comparisons of very different sizes — a network the overview's authors explicitly say cannot support firm recommendations. Dosing, age bands, and severity thresholds vary across the underlying trials.
cards.source: Synthesis of Craig SS et al. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2020 (PMID: 32767571); Hamud AA et al. Archives of Disease in Childhood. 2025 (PMID: 40562459).

shelves.title: Probiotics for preterm infants: necrotising enterocolitis roughly halved in the pooled trials and in ProPrems — late-onset sepsis and mortality not moved by the one large named-product trial
shelves.question: In preterm infants, do probiotics prevent necrotising enterocolitis, late-onset sepsis and death compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Enterocolitis, Necrotizing/prevention & control · Infant, Premature · Lactoferrin/therapeutic use · Morbidity · Oligosaccharides · Prebiotics · Probiotics/therapeutic use · Sepsis/prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — strongest for necrotising enterocolitis (NEC), the outcome that kills. A network meta-analysis of 106 trials in 25,840 preterm infants (Wang Y et al., PMID: 37782505) found multiple-strain probiotics associated with less severe NEC than placebo (risk ratio 0.38, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.50; absolute risk difference -3.7%) and with lower all-cause mortality (RR 0.69, 0.56 to 0.86; risk difference -1.7%), at moderate-to-high certainty. The largest single named-product trial, ProPrems (Jacobs SE et al., PMID: 24249817), randomised 1,099 very preterm infants to a three-strain combination or placebo: NEC of Bell stage 2 or more occurred in 2.0% versus 4.4% (relative risk 0.46, 0.23 to 0.93), but definite late-onset sepsis (the primary outcome) and mortality did not differ. Products, strains and doses vary across the pooled trials, and probiotics for preterm infants are not regulated as medicines in many countries — strain identity is the intervention, so this shelf names the ProPrems combination (Bifidobacterium infantis, Streptococcus thermophilus and Bifidobacterium lactis) exactly as published, and the pooled result should not be read onto any other product. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real NEC reduction across two evidence layers, with sepsis unproven and the mortality signal resting on the pooling — Tier C because a mortality benefit is among the claims.

cards.headline: Wang 2023 network meta-analysis (106 trials, 25,840 infants): multiple-strain probiotics — severe NEC RR 0.38, mortality RR 0.69 versus placebo
cards.summary: Wang 2023 network meta-analysis (106 trials, 25,840 infants): multiple-strain probiotics — severe NEC RR 0.38, mortality RR 0.69 versus placebo
cards.people: 106 randomised trials involving 25,840 preterm infants, comparing probiotics, prebiotics, lactoferrin and combination products against placebo or each other for prevention of mortality and morbidity; outcomes included all-cause mortality, severe necrotising enterocolitis and culture-proven sepsis.
cards.result: Only multiple-strain probiotics were associated with reduced all-cause mortality versus placebo (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.56 to 0.86; risk difference -1.7%, 95% CI -2.4% to -0.8%). For severe NEC, multiple-strain probiotics alone (RR 0.38, 0.30 to 0.50; RD -3.7%) and multiple-strain probiotics with oligosaccharides (RR 0.13, 0.05 to 0.37; RD -5.1%) were among the most effective interventions. Certainty was graded moderate to high for the multistrain mortality and NEC findings.
cards.watchOut: A network meta-analysis leans on indirect comparisons across dozens of small trials with different strains, doses and eras of neonatal care; small-trial effects in this literature have historically shrunk when large trials report. The mortality claim is exactly the kind this library sends to the developer personally — hence Tier C.
cards.source: Wang Y et al. Probiotics, Prebiotics, Lactoferrin, and Combination Products for Prevention of Mortality and Morbidity in Preterm Infants: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis. JAMA pediatrics. 2023. PMID: 37782505. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: ProPrems (Jacobs 2013): NEC 2.0% vs 4.4% (RR 0.46) with a named three-strain product — but the primary outcome, late-onset sepsis, did not differ
cards.summary: ProPrems (Jacobs 2013): NEC 2.0% vs 4.4% (RR 0.46) with a named three-strain product — but the primary outcome, late-onset sepsis, did not differ
cards.people: 1,099 very preterm infants (born before 32 weeks, birth weight <1500 g) in Australia and New Zealand, randomised to a daily probiotic combination — Bifidobacterium infantis, Streptococcus thermophilus and Bifidobacterium lactis, 1 × 10⁹ total organisms — or maltodextrin placebo. Control-group rates were low (sepsis 16.2%, NEC 4.4%, mortality 5.1%) with 96.9% breast-milk feeding.
cards.result: Definite late-onset sepsis did not differ between groups. NEC of Bell stage 2 or more occurred in 2.0% on probiotics versus 4.4% on placebo (relative risk 0.46, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.93; p=0.03; number needed to treat 43). All-cause mortality did not differ significantly. Treatment appeared safe.
cards.watchOut: The NEC result is a secondary outcome in a trial whose primary outcome was null, in a population with unusually high breast-milk feeding and low baseline NEC — the absolute benefit (2.4 percentage points) may not transfer to units with different feeding and NEC rates. The tested product is named because probiotic effects are strain-specific; the publication does not name a commercial brand in the record, and current products may differ.
cards.source: Jacobs SE et al. Probiotic effects on late-onset sepsis in very preterm infants: a randomized controlled trial. Pediatrics. 2013. PMID: 24249817. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: NEC prevention is the claim the evidence carries; sepsis prevention is not, and mortality sits between
cards.summary: Synthesis: NEC prevention is the claim the evidence carries; sepsis prevention is not, and mortality sits between
cards.people: A 106-trial network meta-analysis (25,840 preterm infants) and the 1,099-infant ProPrems randomised trial of a named three-strain combination.
cards.result: Severe NEC: RR 0.38 in the pooling for multistrain products; 2.0% vs 4.4% (RR 0.46) in ProPrems. Late-onset sepsis: no difference in ProPrems. Mortality: RR 0.69 in the pooling, no significant difference in ProPrems. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C for the mortality component and the strain-generalisability problem.
cards.watchOut: Regulatory status is part of the honest picture: in several countries these products are sold as supplements without pharmaceutical-grade strain verification, and rare probiotic sepsis in preterm infants is reported in the wider literature — a unit adopting this evidence is adopting a product-quality problem too.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wang Y et al. JAMA Pediatrics. 2023 (PMID: 37782505); Jacobs SE et al. Pediatrics. 2013 (PMID: 24249817).

shelves.title: Lactoferrin for very preterm infants split: sepsis cut from 17.3% to 5.9% in a 472-infant Italian trial — and no effect at all (29% vs 31%) in the 2,203-infant UK ELFIN trial
shelves.question: In very preterm infants, does enteral bovine lactoferrin supplementation prevent late-onset infection and sepsis compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Infective Agents/administration & dosage · Cross Infection/prevention & control · Female · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Infant, Premature · Infant, Premature, Diseases/prevention & control · Lactoferrin/administration & dosage · Male · Sepsis/prevention & control · Treatment Outcome · United Kingdom
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the small trial said yes, the large trial said no, and size wins arguments in this library. Manzoni P et al. (PMID: 19809023) randomised 472 very-low-birth-weight infants in Italy to bovine lactoferrin, lactoferrin plus Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG, or placebo: first late-onset sepsis occurred in 5.9% and 4.6% in the lactoferrin groups versus 17.3% on placebo (risk ratios 0.34 and 0.27). The ELFIN trial (PMID: 30635141) randomised 2,203 very preterm infants in 37 UK hospitals to lactoferrin 150 mg/kg/day or sucrose: late-onset infection occurred in 29% versus 31% (adjusted risk ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.04) — no effect, with serious adverse events numerically more frequent on lactoferrin (16 vs 10, two assessed as possibly related). Differences in baseline infection rates (17.3% placebo sepsis in Italy vs a broader 31% infection outcome in the UK), product, dose and case mix could explain part of the split, but a clinician choosing today faces the larger, null trial. PROPOSED SPLIT: benefit claimed by one moderate trial, refuted for routine use by one large trial — the honest shelf keeps both on its face.

cards.headline: ELFIN 2019: late-onset infection 29% on lactoferrin vs 31% on sucrose (adjusted RR 0.95, CI 0.86 to 1.04) in 2,203 very preterm infants
cards.summary: ELFIN 2019: late-onset infection 29% on lactoferrin vs 31% on sucrose (adjusted RR 0.95, CI 0.86 to 1.04) in 2,203 very preterm infants
cards.people: 2,203 very preterm infants born before 32 weeks' gestation in 37 UK hospitals, randomised within 72 hours of birth to enteral bovine lactoferrin (150 mg/kg/day, maximum 300 mg/day) or sucrose placebo until 34 weeks' postmenstrual age. Primary outcome: microbiologically confirmed or clinically suspected late-onset infection after 72 hours; data for 2,182 infants.
cards.result: Late-onset infection occurred in 316 of 1,093 infants (29%) in the lactoferrin group versus 334 of 1,089 (31%) in the control group (adjusted risk ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.04; p=0.233). Serious adverse events numbered 16 in the lactoferrin group and 10 in the control group; two events in the lactoferrin group (one case of blood in stool, one death after intestinal perforation) were assessed as possibly related to the intervention. The authors conclude the data do not support routine use.
cards.watchOut: ELFIN's outcome bundles suspected with confirmed infection, diluting any effect on proven sepsis; its control-group event rate (31%) is far above Manzoni's placebo sepsis rate (17.3%) partly for that reason. The trial is nonetheless the largest and most applicable test, and its confidence interval excludes the effect size Manzoni reported.

cards.headline: Manzoni 2009: first late-onset sepsis 5.9% on lactoferrin and 4.6% on lactoferrin plus probiotic vs 17.3% on placebo (RR 0.34 and 0.27)
cards.summary: Manzoni 2009: first late-onset sepsis 5.9% on lactoferrin and 4.6% on lactoferrin plus probiotic vs 17.3% on placebo (RR 0.34 and 0.27)
cards.people: 472 very-low-birth-weight infants (<1500 g) in 11 Italian neonatal intensive care units, randomised to oral bovine lactoferrin 100 mg/day alone (n=153), lactoferrin plus Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (n=151), or placebo (n=168), from birth to day 30 (day 45 if <1000 g). Primary outcome: first episode of late-onset sepsis with a pathogen isolated from blood, peritoneal or cerebrospinal fluid.
cards.result: Late-onset sepsis occurred in 9 of 153 infants (5.9%) on lactoferrin alone and 7 of 151 (4.6%) on lactoferrin plus LGG, versus 29 of 168 (17.3%) on placebo (risk ratio 0.34, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.70; p=0.002, and 0.27, 0.12 to 0.60; p<0.001). The reduction covered bacterial and fungal sepsis. No adverse effects or intolerances were reported.
cards.watchOut: A strong result in a single-country trial a fifth ELFIN's size, with a culture-proven endpoint but a much lower dose (100 mg/day fixed) than ELFIN's weight-based regimen — dose, product preparation, feeding practices and baseline risk all differ. When a small positive and a large null trial disagree, replication — not averaging — is the missing step.

cards.headline: Synthesis: do not average these two trials into a shrug — the large pragmatic trial governs practice, the small trial governs the research agenda
cards.summary: Synthesis: do not average these two trials into a shrug — the large pragmatic trial governs practice, the small trial governs the research agenda
cards.people: Two randomised placebo-controlled trials of enteral bovine lactoferrin in very preterm infants: 472 infants in Italy (culture-proven sepsis endpoint) and 2,203 in the UK (confirmed or suspected infection endpoint).
cards.result: Late-onset sepsis/infection: 5.9% vs 17.3% (RR 0.34) in Manzoni; 29% vs 31% (adjusted RR 0.95) in ELFIN. PROPOSED SPLIT, with ELFIN's null the operative result for routine supplementation.

shelves.title: Umbilical cord milking versus delayed clamping in preterm infants: the trial was stopped early — severe brain bleeding was higher with milking (8% vs 3%), and 22% vs 6% in babies born before 28 weeks
shelves.question: In preterm infants, is umbilical cord milking as safe as delayed cord clamping for death or severe intraventricular haemorrhage?
shelves.mesh: Cerebral Intraventricular Hemorrhage/prevention & control · Constriction · Early Termination of Clinical Trials · Female · Gestational Age · Humans · Infant · Infant Death · Infant, Newborn · Infant, Premature · Infant, Premature, Diseases/mortality/prevention & control · Male · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Pregnancy · Umbilical Cord
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — a safety signal from a trial that had to stop. Katheria A et al. (PMID: 31742630) randomised preterm infants born at 23–31 weeks to cord milking or delayed clamping in a noninferiority design, but enrolment was halted at the first interim analysis (474 of a planned 1,500 infants) because severe intraventricular haemorrhage was imbalanced: 8% (20/236) with milking versus 3% (8/238) with delayed clamping (risk difference 5%, 95% CI 1% to 9%; p=0.02), concentrated in the youngest stratum — 22% (20/93) versus 6% (5/89) at 23–27 weeks (risk difference 16%). The composite of death or severe haemorrhage did not differ significantly (12% vs 8%; p=0.16) and death alone did not differ. The earlier meta-analysis of seven small trials (Al-Wassia H et al., PMID: 25365246) had found no mortality difference and less intraventricular haemorrhage of all grades with milking (RR 0.62) — the large trial's severe-haemorrhage signal in the most immature infants reverses the reassurance for exactly the babies at highest risk. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm), Tier C: one stopped-early trial, post hoc analysis, but a harm signal the developer should see personally.

cards.headline: Katheria 2019: severe intraventricular haemorrhage 8% vs 3% (p=0.02) — trial stopped at first interim analysis; in infants 23–27 weeks, 22% vs 6%
cards.summary: Katheria 2019: severe intraventricular haemorrhage 8% vs 3% (p=0.02) — trial stopped at first interim analysis; in infants 23–27 weeks, 22% vs 6%
cards.people: 474 preterm infants born at 23–31 weeks' gestation (mean 28 weeks) at 9 centres in 4 countries, randomised to umbilical cord milking (n=236) or delayed umbilical cord clamping (n=238). Planned enrolment was 750 per group; the data and safety monitoring board stopped enrolment after a severe intraventricular haemorrhage imbalance at the first interim analysis, so the noninferiority analysis could not be performed and comparisons are post hoc.
cards.result: Death or severe intraventricular haemorrhage occurred in 12% (29/236) with milking versus 8% (20/238) with delayed clamping (risk difference 4%, 95% CI -2% to 9%; p=0.16). Severe intraventricular haemorrhage alone was significantly higher with milking: 8% (20/236) versus 3% (8/238) (risk difference 5%, 1% to 9%; p=0.02). The interaction with gestational age was significant (p=0.003): at 23–27 weeks, severe haemorrhage occurred in 22% (20/93) versus 6% (5/89) (risk difference 16%, 6% to 26%; p=0.002). Death alone did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: Early termination and post hoc analysis inflate effect estimates and forbid definitive conclusions — the authors say so. But a stopped-for-safety trial is not ignorable either: the signal is biologically plausible (rapid volume shifts in the most immature infants) and concentrated where the physiology predicts.
cards.source: Katheria A et al. Association of Umbilical Cord Milking vs Delayed Umbilical Cord Clamping With Death or Severe Intraventricular Hemorrhage Among Preterm Infants. JAMA. 2019. PMID: 31742630. Registry ID: NCT03019367. cards.headline: Al-Wassia 2015 meta-analysis (7 small trials, 501 infants): no mortality difference, less intraventricular haemorrhage of all grades with milking (RR 0.62) — the pre-2019 picture
cards.summary: Al-Wassia 2015 meta-analysis (7 small trials, 501 infants): no mortality difference, less intraventricular haemorrhage of all grades with milking (RR 0.62) — the pre-2019 picture
cards.people: 7 randomised trials involving 501 full-term and preterm infants comparing umbilical cord milking with other cord-handling strategies; preterm subgroup analyses for infants under 33 weeks.
cards.result: In infants under 33 weeks, milking showed no difference in mortality (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.35 to 1.64) or hypotension requiring volume expanders, higher initial haemoglobin (mean difference 2.0 g/dL), less oxygen requirement at 36 weeks (RR 0.42, 0.21 to 0.83) and less intraventricular haemorrhage of all grades (RR 0.62, 0.41 to 0.93). The authors called for further studies of neonatal and long-term outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Seven small trials cannot see a harm concentrated in a subgroup (23–27 weeks) that most of them barely enrolled; 'all grades' of haemorrhage pools trivial with severe bleeds. This card is kept on the shelf precisely to show how the evidence read before the large trial — and why it changed.
cards.source: Al-Wassia H et al. Efficacy and safety of umbilical cord milking at birth: a systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA pediatrics. 2015. PMID: 25365246. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: milking raises haemoglobin as promised — and, in the only large trial, raised severe brain bleeding in the youngest infants
cards.summary: Synthesis: milking raises haemoglobin as promised — and, in the only large trial, raised severe brain bleeding in the youngest infants
cards.people: One stopped-early randomised trial of 474 infants born at 23–31 weeks, read against a prior meta-analysis of 7 small trials (501 infants).
cards.result: Severe intraventricular haemorrhage: 8% vs 3% overall and 22% vs 6% at 23–27 weeks (milking vs delayed clamping) in the large trial; all-grade haemorrhage RR 0.62 favouring milking in the earlier small-trial pooling. Death: no significant difference in either source. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm), Tier C.
cards.watchOut: The comparison is milking versus delayed clamping — not versus immediate clamping. Nothing here argues against placental transfusion; it argues about the method, in the most immature infants.

shelves.title: Preventive zinc in children: diarrhoea and pneumonia episodes fell by about 13–19% in the pooled trials — all-cause mortality did not reach significance in either major review
shelves.question: In children in low- and middle-income countries, does preventive zinc supplementation reduce diarrhoea, pneumonia, malaria and death compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Child · Developing Countries · Diarrhea/epidemiology/mortality/prevention & control · Dietary Supplements · Humans · Malaria/epidemiology/mortality/prevention & control · Pneumonia/epidemiology/mortality/prevention & control · Trace Elements/therapeutic use · Zinc Compounds/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for illness episodes; the mortality claim is where two big reviews part company with the headline version of this story. Yakoob MY et al. (PMID: 21501441), pooling the preventive trials in under-5s, found diarrhoea incidence reduced by 13% in relative terms (RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.81 to 0.94) and pneumonia incidence by 19% (RR 0.81, 0.73 to 0.90), with a non-significant 9% lower all-cause mortality (RR 0.91, 0.82 to 1.01) and no effect on malaria. The Cochrane review of 80 trials in 205,401 children aged 6 months to 12 years (Mayo-Wilson E et al., PMID: 24826920) similarly found all-cause mortality compatible with benefit or slight harm (RR 0.95, 0.86 to 1.05), diarrhoea incidence reduced (RR 0.87, 0.85 to 0.89), no clear effect on lower respiratory infection incidence (RR 1.00) or malaria (RR 1.05), a very small height gain, and more vomiting (RR 1.29). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): episodes of diarrhoea clearly fewer; pneumonia and mortality unsettled between reviews — the shelf prints both.

cards.headline: Yakoob 2011: diarrhoea incidence RR 0.87, pneumonia incidence RR 0.81 — all-cause mortality RR 0.91, not significant; no malaria effect
cards.summary: Yakoob 2011: diarrhoea incidence RR 0.87, pneumonia incidence RR 0.81 — all-cause mortality RR 0.91, not significant; no malaria effect
cards.people: Randomised trials of preventive zinc supplementation for more than 3 months in children under 5 in developing countries; mortality data from 8 trials, cause-specific mortality from 5.
cards.result: Zinc was associated with a statistically insignificant 9% relative reduction in all-cause mortality (RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.01). Diarrhoea incidence fell 13% (RR 0.87, 0.81 to 0.94) and pneumonia incidence 19% (RR 0.81, 0.73 to 0.90). Cause-specific mortality estimates were non-significant: diarrhoea RR 0.82 (0.64 to 1.05), pneumonia RR 0.85 (0.65 to 1.11), malaria RR 0.90 (0.77 to 1.06); malaria incidence RR 0.92 (0.82 to 1.04). The authors adopted conservative 13% and 15% mortality-effect estimates for LiST modelling.
cards.watchOut: The LiST estimates used for policy (13% diarrhoea-mortality and 15% pneumonia-mortality reductions) were chosen by rule from morbidity data, not measured as significant mortality effects — a modelling convention that has a way of hardening into a fact downstream. This shelf keeps the measured and the modelled separate.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2014 (80 trials, 205,401 children): mortality RR 0.95 (CI 0.86 to 1.05), diarrhoea incidence RR 0.87, respiratory infection incidence RR 1.00, vomiting RR 1.29
cards.summary: Cochrane 2014 (80 trials, 205,401 children): mortality RR 0.95 (CI 0.86 to 1.05), diarrhoea incidence RR 0.87, respiratory infection incidence RR 1.00, vomiting RR 1.29
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Mayo-Wilson 2014, Cochrane)
cards.people: 80 randomised trials with 205,401 children aged 6 months to 12 years, of preventive zinc supplementation versus no intervention, placebo or waiting list, excluding hospitalised and chronically ill children and therapeutic zinc use.
cards.result: All-cause mortality: RR 0.95 (95% CI 0.86 to 1.05; 14 studies, high-quality evidence) — compatible with a reduction and with a small increase. Diarrhoea incidence fell (RR 0.87, 0.85 to 0.89; 26 studies). Lower respiratory tract infection incidence did not change (RR 1.00, 0.94 to 1.07) and malaria incidence did not fall (RR 1.05, 0.95 to 1.15). Height improved very slightly (SMD -0.09 for the deficit). Vomiting increased (RR 1.29, 1.14 to 1.46). The authors judged benefits to outweigh harms where zinc deficiency risk is high.
cards.watchOut: The pneumonia-incidence disagreement with Yakoob (RR 0.81 vs 1.00) reflects different age ranges, inclusion rules and outcome definitions — a live example of two competent reviews of overlapping trials reaching different secondary conclusions while agreeing on diarrhoea and on mortality's non-significance.

cards.headline: Synthesis: zinc prevents some diarrhoea, probably; whether it saves lives at population scale is not established by the randomised record
cards.summary: Synthesis: zinc prevents some diarrhoea, probably; whether it saves lives at population scale is not established by the randomised record
cards.people: Two systematic reviews of the preventive zinc trial literature: 8 mortality trials in under-5s (Yakoob) and 80 trials with 205,401 children aged 6 months to 12 years (Cochrane).
cards.result: Diarrhoea incidence: RR 0.87 in both reviews. Pneumonia incidence: RR 0.81 (Yakoob) vs LRTI RR 1.00 (Cochrane). All-cause mortality: RR 0.91 and 0.95, both non-significant. Malaria: no effect in either. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — for morbidity, with mortality explicitly unproven.
cards.watchOut: Therapeutic zinc for acute diarrhoea is a different question with a different (stronger) record and is not what this shelf answers; nor does this shelf cover zinc combined with other micronutrients.
cards.source: Synthesis of Yakoob MY et al. BMC Public Health. 2011 (PMID: 21501441); Mayo-Wilson E et al. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2014 (PMID: 24826920).

shelves.title: Routine iron and folic acid for preschool children where malaria is intense: the 24,000-child Pemba trial was stopped early — death or hospital admission was 12% higher on iron
shelves.question: In preschool children in a high malaria-transmission setting, does routine preventive iron and folic acid supplementation (with or without zinc) increase or decrease death and hospital admission?
shelves.mesh: Anemia, Iron-Deficiency/drug therapy · Child Mortality · Child, Preschool · Enzyme Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Female · Folic Acid/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Hematinics/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Infant · Iron/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Malaria/prevention & control/transmission · Male · Protoporphyrins/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — one of the most consequential safety trials in child health, with an important modern qualification. In Pemba, Zanzibar, Sazawal S et al. (PMID: 16413877) randomised 24,076 children aged 1–35 months to iron plus folic acid, iron plus folic acid plus zinc, or placebo; the iron-containing arms were stopped early on the data safety board's recommendation because children receiving iron and folic acid (with or without zinc) were 12% more likely in relative terms to die or need hospital treatment for an adverse event (95% CI 2% to 23%; p=0.02) and 11% more likely to be admitted (p=0.03), with 15% more deaths (CI -7% to 41%, non-significant). The Cochrane review of oral iron in malaria-endemic areas (Neuberger A et al., PMID: 26921618; 35 trials, 31,955 children) reframed the finding: overall, iron did not increase clinical malaria (RR 0.93, 0.87 to 1.00), and where malaria prevention and treatment services were provided, iron may reduce clinical malaria (RR 0.91) — while where such services were unavailable, iron may increase it (RR 1.16, 1.02 to 1.31). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm), Tier C: the harm claim rests on one very large stopped-early trial in one service context, and the Cochrane subgroup reading is the condition attached to it.

cards.headline: Pemba (Sazawal 2006): iron arms stopped early — death or hospital treatment 12% relatively higher (p=0.02), admissions 11% higher, deaths 15% higher (NS)
cards.summary: Pemba (Sazawal 2006): iron arms stopped early — death or hospital treatment 12% relatively higher (p=0.02), admissions 11% higher, deaths 15% higher (NS)
cards.type: Community-based randomised placebo-controlled trial, stopped early (Sazawal 2006)
cards.people: 24,076 children aged 1–35 months in Pemba, Zanzibar (high malaria transmission), assigned to daily iron (12.5 mg) plus folic acid (50 µg; n=7,950), iron plus folic acid plus zinc (n=8,120), or placebo (n=8,006); children 1–11 months received half doses. Primary endpoints: all-cause mortality and hospital admission. The iron-containing groups were stopped on 19 August 2003 on the data and safety monitoring board's recommendation, after 25,524 child-years of follow-up.
cards.result: Children receiving iron and folic acid, with or without zinc, were 12% more likely in relative terms to die or need hospital treatment for an adverse event (95% CI 2% to 23%; p=0.02) and 11% more likely to be admitted to hospital (1% to 23%; p=0.03); deaths were 15% higher (95% CI -7% to 41%; p=0.19, not significant). The authors concluded that universal supplementation in high-malaria settings can increase severe illness and death, that iron-deficient and anaemic children benefit when infections are actively detected and treated, and that guidelines for universal supplementation should be revised.
cards.watchOut: The harm signal is for the composite (death or admission) in a population supplemented without screening, in a setting with intense malaria transmission and the service level of Pemba in 2001–2003. It does not show that treating a diagnosed iron-deficient child is harmful — the trialists themselves carve that out — and early stopping can exaggerate the size of a real effect.
cards.source: Sazawal S et al. Effects of routine prophylactic supplementation with iron and folic acid on admission to hospital and mortality in preschool children in a high malaria transmission setting: community-based, randomised, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2006. PMID: 16413877. Registry ID: ISRCTN59549825.
