cards.headline: Cochrane 2016 (35 trials, 31,955 children): iron did not increase clinical malaria overall (RR 0.93) — but may where malaria services are unavailable (RR 1.16) and may reduce it where they are provided (RR 0.91)
cards.summary: Cochrane 2016 (35 trials, 31,955 children): iron did not increase clinical malaria overall (RR 0.93) — but may where malaria services are unavailable (RR 1.16) and may reduce it where they are provided (RR 0.91)
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Neuberger 2016, Cochrane)
cards.people: 35 randomised trials (31,955 children under 18) of oral iron, iron with folic acid, or iron with antimalarial treatment versus placebo or no treatment in hyperendemic or holoendemic malaria regions, with subgroup analyses by baseline anaemia, age, and availability of malaria prevention or management services.
cards.result: Overall, iron did not cause an excess of clinical malaria (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.00; 14 trials, high-quality evidence) or severe malaria (RR 0.90, 0.81 to 0.98). Where malaria services were provided, iron with or without folic acid may reduce clinical malaria (RR 0.91, 0.84 to 0.97; low-quality evidence); where services were unavailable, iron may increase malaria incidence (RR 1.16, 1.02 to 1.31; low-quality evidence). No difference in deaths was observed (control event rate 1%). Iron plus antimalarial treatment reduced clinical malaria (RR 0.54, 0.43 to 0.67).
cards.watchOut: The reassuring overall estimate pools across exactly the variable — functioning malaria services — that Pemba suggests decides safety; subgroup claims are low-quality evidence and trial-level, so individual children cannot be sorted by them. The two sources agree more than they appear to: both say context is the intervention's safety condition.
cards.source: Neuberger A et al. Oral iron supplements for children in malaria-endemic areas. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2016. PMID: 26921618. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: iron is not 'dangerous' or 'safe' in malaria country — it is conditional, and Pemba is the price of ignoring the condition
cards.summary: Synthesis: iron is not 'dangerous' or 'safe' in malaria country — it is conditional, and Pemba is the price of ignoring the condition
cards.people: One 24,076-child community trial stopped early for harm in a high-transmission, low-service setting, and a 35-trial Cochrane review stratified by malaria-service availability.
cards.result: Pemba: death or hospital treatment +12% in relative terms on routine iron/folic acid (p=0.02). Cochrane: clinical malaria RR 0.93 overall, 0.91 where services exist, 1.16 where they do not. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm), Tier C — the stamp attaches to unscreened universal supplementation without malaria services, not to iron treatment itself.
cards.watchOut: Folic acid dose, zinc co-administration and the era's malaria control (pre-widespread bednets and artemisinin therapy in Pemba) all bound the generalisability. Modern programmes pair supplementation with malaria control precisely because of this trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Sazawal S et al. Lancet. 2006 (PMID: 16413877); Neuberger A et al. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2016 (PMID: 26921618).

shelves.title: Universal newborn hearing screening finds deaf babies months earlier: 71 more babies per 100,000 referred before 6 months in the Wessex controlled trial — detection proven, better life outcomes inferred
shelves.question: Does universal neonatal hearing screening, added to the later distraction test, increase early identification, confirmation and management of permanent childhood hearing impairment?
shelves.mesh: England/epidemiology · Evoked Potentials, Auditory, Brain Stem · Feasibility Studies · Hearing Loss, Bilateral/classification/congenital/diagnosis/epidemiology · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Neonatal Screening/methods · Risk Factors · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the outcome the trial measured: finding the babies early. The Wessex controlled trial (PMID: 9872244) alternated periods with and without universal neonatal screening across hospitals between 1993 and 1996, covering 53,781 babies (25,609 born in screening periods). Screening achieved 87% coverage with a 1.5% false-alarm rate and a yield of 90 cases of bilateral permanent hearing impairment of 40 dB or more per 100,000 babies — about 80% of expected prevalence. Seventy-one more babies per 100,000 with moderate or severe impairment were referred before 6 months of age during screening periods, early confirmation and management increased significantly, and the screening test's false-negative rate was lower than the distraction test's (4% vs 27%). What the trial does not show is the downstream claim — better language, education and employment — which rests on the plausible, separately studied link between early management and development. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a single controlled (non-randomised) trial whose endpoint is detection, carrying a programme adopted worldwide.

cards.headline: Wessex 1998: 53,781 babies — screening periods yielded 71 more early referrals per 100,000, 87% coverage, 1.5% false alarms, false negatives 4% vs 27% for the distraction test
cards.summary: Wessex 1998: 53,781 babies — screening periods yielded 71 more early referrals per 100,000, 87% coverage, 1.5% false alarms, false negatives 4% vs 27% for the distraction test
cards.type: Controlled trial with alternating screening periods (Wessex Universal Neonatal Hearing Screening Trial Group 1998)
cards.people: 53,781 babies born in four UK hospitals between 1993 and 1996; two teams moved between hospital pairs to create four periods with universal neonatal screening (transient evoked otoacoustic emissions, then automated auditory brainstem response the same day for failures) plus the standard health-visitor distraction test, and four periods with the distraction test alone. 25,609 babies were born during screening periods.
cards.result: Neonatal screening achieved 87% coverage of births, a false-alarm rate of 1.5%, and an overall yield of 90 cases of bilateral permanent childhood hearing impairment ≥40 dB per 100,000 target population (about 80% of expected prevalence). During screening periods, 71 more babies per 100,000 with moderate or severe impairment were referred before age 6 months than during non-screening periods; early confirmation and management were significantly increased. False-negative rate: 4% for neonatal screening versus 27% for the distraction test (p=0.041).
cards.watchOut: Not individually randomised — periods, not babies, were allocated, in one English region in the 1990s — and the endpoints are referral, confirmation and management, not language or quality of life. The benefit claim for life outcomes is an inference chain (earlier management → better development) that this trial documents only at its first link.

cards.summary: Synthesis: the detection case for universal newborn hearing screening was made in one trial and has never needed remaking

shelves.title: Screening newborns' hips with ultrasound: no trial shows fewer late dislocations or less surgery — universal ultrasound mainly increases the number of babies treated
shelves.question: Do screening programmes for developmental dysplasia of the hip (universal or targeted ultrasound, versus clinical examination alone) reduce late-diagnosed hip dislocation and surgery in infants?
shelves.mesh: Delayed Diagnosis/adverse effects · Hip Dislocation, Congenital/diagnosis/diagnostic imaging/therapy · Humans · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Mass Screening/methods · Physical Examination/methods · Program Evaluation · Remission, Spontaneous · Splints · Time Factors · Ultrasonography
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — an entrenched programme whose randomised record is, on inspection, nearly empty. The Cochrane review (Shorter D et al., PMID: 21901691) found no study at all comparing screening with early treatment against no screening with later treatment. Universal ultrasound versus clinical examination alone did not significantly reduce late-diagnosed dysplasia or surgery but did significantly increase treatment; targeted ultrasound likewise showed no significant reduction in late diagnosis or surgery. Meta-analysis of two studies found universal versus targeted ultrasound also did not significantly change late diagnosis or surgery rates. For infants with unstable or mildly dysplastic hips, delayed ultrasound with targeted splinting reduced treatment without significantly increasing late diagnosis, compared with immediate splinting. The trials are substantially underpowered for the rare outcome that matters (late dislocation), so this is absence of evidence in both directions — but the treatment increase is the one effect that is demonstrated. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): screening strategy choice currently rests on tradition and observational data, not on randomised proof of better hips.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2011: no trial of screening vs no screening exists; universal ultrasound raised treatment without significantly reducing late DDH or surgery
cards.summary: Cochrane 2011: no trial of screening vs no screening exists; universal ultrasound raised treatment without significantly reducing late DDH or surgery
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised and quasi-randomised trials (Shorter 2011, Cochrane)
cards.people: Randomised, quasi-randomised and cluster trials comparing screening programmes for developmental dysplasia of the hip in newborn infants (clinical examination, targeted ultrasound, universal ultrasound, and splinting strategies), with late-diagnosed DDH and surgery as the clinical outcomes of interest.
cards.result: No study examined screening (clinical and/or ultrasound) with early treatment versus not screening with later treatment. Universal ultrasound versus clinical examination alone: no significant reduction in late-diagnosed DDH or surgery, but a significant increase in treatment. Targeted ultrasound versus clinical examination alone: no significant reduction in late DDH or surgery and no significant difference in treatment. Universal versus targeted ultrasound (2 studies): no significant difference in late DDH or surgery. Delayed ultrasound with targeted splinting versus immediate splinting of unstable hips (2 studies): no significant difference in late DDH, with a significant reduction in treatment; neither group required surgery in the mild-dysplasia study.
cards.watchOut: The review's central limitation is power: late-diagnosed DDH is uncommon, and the included studies are substantially underpowered to detect differences in it — so 'not significant' cannot be read as 'no effect exists'. What is demonstrated is the harm-side asymmetry: more babies in splints, with their own risks and costs, for unproven late-outcome gain.

shelves.title: A synbiotic for newborns in rural India: sepsis or death reduced by 40% relative (RR 0.60) in one 4,556-baby trial — driven by fewer sepsis cases, not fewer deaths (6 versus 4)
shelves.question: In healthy newborn infants in a low-resource community setting, does a daily oral synbiotic (Lactobacillus plantarum plus fructooligosaccharide) for the first week of life prevent sepsis and death over the first 60 days?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · India · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Lactiplantibacillus plantarum · Oligosaccharides/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Sepsis/diet therapy/microbiology/mortality/prevention & control · Synbiotics/administration & dosage · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one large, well-blinded community trial, with the mortality caveat on its face. In rural India (Panigrahi P et al., PMID: 28813414), 4,556 newborns (birth weight at least 2,000 g, at least 35 weeks' gestation, no signs of sepsis) received an oral synbiotic — Lactobacillus plantarum (the strain named in the record is ATCC-202195) plus fructooligosaccharide — or placebo, and were monitored for 60 days. The primary outcome, the combination of sepsis and death, fell with a risk ratio of 0.60 (95% CI 0.48–0.74), a 40% relative reduction; culture-positive sepsis, culture-negative sepsis and lower respiratory tract infections were also significantly reduced. Deaths themselves were few and not fewer on the synbiotic: 6 in the synbiotic arm versus 4 on placebo — the composite is carried by sepsis episodes prevented, not lives shown to be saved. The wider neonatal probiotic literature in low- and middle-income countries points the same way (Imdad A et al., PMID: 32192165: neonatal sepsis RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.70–0.86, across 33 mostly hospital-based trials), but those trials used other organisms in mostly preterm, hospitalised babies. The record names the strain but no manufacturer or commercial product, so none is stated — and strain identity is the whole intervention here, so other probiotic products cannot borrow this result. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a one-week synbiotic course prevented sepsis episodes in community newborns in a single large trial; a mortality benefit was not shown. Tier C: single trial, and the composite touches mortality.

cards.result: The primary outcome — the combination of sepsis and death — was significantly reduced in the treatment arm, risk ratio 0.60 (95% confidence interval 0.48–0.74), a 40% relative reduction. Significant reductions were also observed for culture-positive sepsis, culture-negative sepsis and lower respiratory tract infections. Deaths were few and numerically higher on the synbiotic: 6 versus 4 on placebo. The abstract does not report the absolute percentages for the composite outcome, so none are quoted here.
cards.watchOut: The composite's engine is sepsis diagnoses in a setting where most sepsis is culture-negative and clinically defined; the trial's own death counts (6 versus 4) forbid reading this as a mortality result. One trial, one strain, one region — replication with the same preparation has not been carded anywhere in this library.

cards.headline: Imdad 2020 meta-analysis: across 33 neonatal probiotic trials in low- and middle-income countries, sepsis RR 0.78 and mortality RR 0.80 — mostly hospital preterm populations, other organisms
cards.summary: Imdad 2020 meta-analysis: across 33 neonatal probiotic trials in low- and middle-income countries, sepsis RR 0.78 and mortality RR 0.80 — mostly hospital preterm populations, other organisms
cards.people: Thirty-three randomised trials of probiotic supplementation during the neonatal period in low- and middle-income countries, mostly conducted in hospital settings; analysed separately from the same review's sixteen vitamin A trials.
cards.result: Probiotics reduced neonatal sepsis (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.70–0.86), all-cause mortality (RR 0.80, 0.66–0.96) and necrotizing enterocolitis (RR 0.46, 0.35–0.59), with GRADE ratings of high for these three outcomes. (The same review found neonatal vitamin A supplementation did not reduce mortality at 1, 6 or 12 months.)
cards.watchOut: This is context, not confirmation of the Panigrahi preparation: the pooled trials used varied organisms, doses and mostly preterm hospitalised infants — a different population from healthy community newborns, and probiotic effects are strain-specific, so the pooled ratio cannot be assigned to the synbiotic on the anchor card.

shelves.title: Recurrent staph skin infections in children: decolonising the whole household cut recurrence in cases from 72% to 52% over a year — though carriage eradication was no better, and targeting only previously infected members later proved non-inferior
shelves.question: In households of children with community-associated Staphylococcus aureus skin infections, does decolonising every household member prevent recurrent skin and soft tissue infections better than decolonising the affected child alone — and can the effort be narrowed to members with a prior infection?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage · Anti-Infective Agents, Local/administration & dosage · Axilla/microbiology · Baths · Carrier State/drug therapy · Child · Child, Preschool · Chlorhexidine/administration & dosage · Combined Modality Therapy · Community-Acquired Infections/drug therapy · Family Characteristics · Female · Groin/microbiology · Humans · Infant · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Mupirocin/administration & dosage · Nose/microbiology · Patient Compliance · Patient Education as Topic · Soft Tissue Infections/drug therapy/prevention & control/therapy · Staphylococcal Skin Infections/drug therapy/prevention & control/therapy · Staphylococcus aureus · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — infections fell even though carriage did not, in one open-label trial programme. In St Louis (Fritz SA et al., PMID: 22198793), 183 children with community-onset S. aureus skin abscesses and colonisation were randomised to a 5-day decolonisation regimen (hygiene education, twice-daily intranasal mupirocin, daily chlorhexidine body washes) performed by the index child alone or by all household members. Eradication of carriage did not differ — 50% versus 51% at one month (p=1.00) and 54% versus 66% at 12 months (p=0.28) — but recurrent skin and soft tissue infection over 12 months was reported in 52% of cases in household households versus 72% in index-only households (p=0.02), and infection incidence in household contacts was significantly lower in the first six months. The follow-on HOME2 trial (Hogan PG et al., PMID: 32521007) then showed the burden can be trimmed: decolonising only household members who had an infection in the prior year was non-inferior to decolonising everyone for 3-month cumulative infection (9.7% versus 10.8%; difference −1.1 percentage points, 95% CI −6.7 to 4.5). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): household-wide decolonisation prevents recurrent infections in this setting, and the targeted version keeps the benefit with less work — Tier C, because the anchor comparison is a single open-label trial with self-reported infections.

cards.headline: Fritz 2012: eradication of carriage identical (50% versus 51% at 1 month), but recurrent SSTI over 12 months 52% with household decolonisation versus 72% with index-only
cards.summary: Fritz 2012: eradication of carriage identical (50% versus 51% at 1 month), but recurrent SSTI over 12 months 52% with household decolonisation versus 72% with index-only
cards.people: 183 paediatric patients with community-onset Staphylococcus aureus skin abscesses and colonisation of the nares, axillae or inguinal folds, enrolled 2008–2009 at primary and tertiary centres in St Louis, randomised to a 5-day regimen (hygiene education, twice-daily intranasal mupirocin, daily chlorhexidine body washes) performed by the case alone or by all household members; colonisation and infections ascertained at 1, 3, 6 and 12 months.
cards.result: Among 147 cases with 1-month data, S. aureus eradication was 50% in the index group and 51% in the household group (p=1.00); among 126 completing 12 months, eradication was 54% versus 66% (p=0.28). Over 12 months, recurrent skin and soft tissue infection was reported in 72% of cases in the index group versus 52% in the household group (p=0.02). Infection incidence in household contacts was significantly lower in the household group during the first 6 months, a trend that continued at 12 months.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, with infections self-reported — the group that did more washing may also have reported differently; and the dissociation between carriage (unchanged) and infections (reduced) is biologically odd enough to want replication before treating the 20-point gap as settled.
cards.source: Fritz SA et al. Household versus individual approaches to eradication of community-associated Staphylococcus aureus in children: a randomized trial. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2012. cards.headline: HOME2 (Hogan 2021): decolonising only members with a prior-year infection was non-inferior to decolonising everyone — 3-month SSTI 9.7% versus 10.8%
cards.summary: HOME2 (Hogan 2021): decolonising only members with a prior-year infection was non-inferior to decolonising everyone — 3-month SSTI 9.7% versus 10.8%
cards.people: 102 households of paediatric index patients with community-associated MRSA skin and soft tissue infection (plus their contacts and pets), enrolled after a 12-month observational study and randomised 1:1 to a personalised approach (5-day decolonisation — hygiene education, twice-daily intranasal mupirocin, daily bleach-water baths — only by members who had an infection during the observational year) or the household approach (everyone decolonises); 12-month trial with home follow-up visits.
cards.result: Non-inferiority of the personalised approach was established for the primary outcome of 3-month cumulative SSTI: 23 of 212 participants (10.8%) in household-approach households versus 23 of 236 (9.7%) in personalised-approach households reported infection (difference −1.1 percentage points, 95% CI −6.7 to 4.5). In multivariable analyses, prior-year infection and baseline MRSA colonisation were associated with cumulative infection.
cards.watchOut: HOME2 has no untreated or index-only control — it compares two active household strategies, so it refines the anchor trial's answer rather than independently confirming that decolonisation beats none; the primary outcome is again reported infection at 3 months.
cards.source: Hogan PG et al. HOME2 Study: Household Versus Personalized Decolonization in Households of Children With Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus Skin and Soft Tissue Infection-A Randomized Clinical Trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: treat the household, not just the child — and the household can be narrowed to the members who have actually been infected
cards.summary: Synthesis: treat the household, not just the child — and the household can be narrowed to the members who have actually been infected
cards.people: Two randomised trials from one St Louis programme: 183 index children (household versus index-only decolonisation, 12 months) and 102 households (personalised versus whole-household decolonisation, 3-month primary outcome).
cards.result: Recurrent infection in cases over 12 months: 52% (household) versus 72% (index-only), p=0.02, despite indistinguishable carriage eradication (50% versus 51% at 1 month). Narrowing treatment to previously infected members: 9.7% versus 10.8% cumulative infection at 3 months, non-inferior. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C — one programme, open-label designs, self-reported outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Both trials come from a single research group in one US region during the community-MRSA epidemic years; mupirocin resistance, chlorhexidine tolerance and different household structures elsewhere could all move the result, and no trial here compares household decolonisation with hygiene education alone.
cards.source: Synthesis of Fritz SA et al. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2012 (PMID: 22198793); Hogan PG et al. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2021 (PMID: 32521007).

shelves.title: Dengue shock syndrome fluids: Ringer's lactate matched both colloids for moderate shock (rescue-colloid risk ratio 1.08) — colloids recovered children marginally faster, dextran caused more reactions, and mortality was under 0.2% on any fluid
shelves.question: In children with dengue shock syndrome, does initial resuscitation with a colloid (dextran or hydroxyethyl starch) improve outcomes compared with the crystalloid Ringer's lactate — and does the answer change with shock severity?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Blood Coagulation Tests · Child · Child, Preschool · Dextrans/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fluid Therapy/adverse effects · Humans · Hydroxyethyl Starch Derivatives/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Infusions, Intravenous · Isotonic Solutions/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Male · Rehydration Solutions/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Resuscitation/methods · Ringer's Lactate · Severe Dengue/therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for the choice between crystalloid and colloid in moderate shock, which is where most children sit. In the double-blind Vietnamese trial (Wills BA et al., PMID: 16135832), 383 children with moderately severe dengue shock were randomised to Ringer's lactate, 6% dextran 70 or 6% hydroxyethyl starch, and 129 with severe shock to one of the colloids. Only one patient died (mortality under 0.2%). The primary outcome — needing rescue colloid — was similar across fluids: relative risk 1.08 (95% CI 0.78–1.47) for Ringer's lactate versus either colloid in moderate shock, and 1.13 (0.74–1.74) for dextran versus starch in severe shock. Ringer's lactate improved the haematocrit less rapidly and took marginally longer to initial recovery, but no other response measure differed; bleeding, coagulation derangement and fluid overload were similar, while dextran caused significantly more adverse reactions than starch. The earlier four-fluid trial (Ngo NT et al., PMID: 11170909) in 230 children likewise found no survivor difference (all children survived) and no clear advantage to any fluid, with the longest recovery times on Ringer's lactate and a suggestion that colloids helped most in children presenting with the narrowest pulse pressures. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): with prompt resuscitation, the fluid brand matters far less than giving fluid — crystalloid first for moderate shock is the trial-supported default.

cards.headline: Wills 2005: rescue colloid needed equally on Ringer's lactate and colloids in moderate shock (RR 1.08, 0.78–1.47); one death in 512 children
cards.summary: Wills 2005: rescue colloid needed equally on Ringer's lactate and colloids in moderate shock (RR 1.08, 0.78–1.47); one death in 512 children
cards.people: 512 Vietnamese children with dengue shock syndrome: 383 with moderately severe shock randomised to Ringer's lactate, 6% dextran 70, or 6% hydroxyethyl starch, and 129 with severe shock randomised to one of the two colloids; primary outcome requirement for rescue colloid after the study fluid.
cards.result: Only one patient died (mortality <0.2%). Requirement for rescue colloid was similar across fluids in both severity groups: relative risk 1.08 (95% CI 0.78–1.47; p=0.65) for Ringer's lactate versus either colloid in moderate shock; 1.13 (0.74–1.74; p=0.59) for dextran versus starch in severe shock; and 0.88 (0.66–1.17; p=0.38) for dextran versus starch combined. Ringer's lactate produced less rapid haematocrit improvement and a marginally longer time to initial recovery, with no differences in other response measures; bleeding manifestations, coagulation derangements and fluid-overload severity were similar for all groups, but significantly more dextran recipients than starch recipients had adverse reactions.
cards.watchOut: Conducted in a single expert Vietnamese centre where overall mortality was under 0.2% — far below the 1–5% the authors cite for dengue shock generally — so the trial compares fluids inside excellent supportive care, and its null may not travel to settings where resuscitation is later or monitoring thinner.
cards.source: Wills BA et al. Comparison of three fluid solutions for resuscitation in dengue shock syndrome. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2005. PMID: 16135832. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ngo 2001: four fluids, 230 children, all survived — no clear advantage to any; longest recovery on Ringer's lactate, colloid benefit hinted only at the narrowest pulse pressures
cards.summary: Ngo 2001: four fluids, 230 children, all survived — no clear advantage to any; longest recovery on Ringer's lactate, colloid benefit hinted only at the narrowest pulse pressures
cards.people: 230 Vietnamese children with dengue shock syndrome randomised to one of four initial resuscitation fluids: dextran, gelatin, lactated Ringer's, or normal saline; clinical response analysed against presenting pulse pressure.
cards.result: All the children survived, and there was no clear advantage to using any of the four fluids, although the longest recovery times occurred in the lactated Ringer's group. The most significant factor determining clinical response was the pulse pressure at presentation; comparing colloid with crystalloid groups suggested benefits in children presenting with lower pulse pressures who received one of the colloids.
cards.watchOut: The colloid-at-low-pulse-pressure signal is a subgroup suggestion the authors themselves flag as needing larger stratified trials — it is a hypothesis the shelf records, not a finding; and with zero deaths, the trial can say nothing about mortality differences between fluids.
cards.source: Ngo NT et al. Acute management of dengue shock syndrome: a randomized, double-blind comparison of 4 intravenous fluids in 230 children. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2001. PMID: 11170909. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: two blinded trials, 742 children, no fluid winner — speed of resuscitation and severity at the door decide outcomes, not the bag
cards.summary: Synthesis: two blinded trials, 742 children, no fluid winner — speed of resuscitation and severity at the door decide outcomes, not the bag
cards.people: Two double-blind randomised trials in Vietnamese children with dengue shock syndrome (512 and 230 children), comparing Ringer's lactate, dextran, hydroxyethyl starch, gelatin and saline for initial resuscitation.
cards.result: Mortality: one death across both trials' crystalloid/colloid comparisons in Wills (<0.2%), zero in Ngo. Rescue-colloid requirement RR 1.08 (0.78–1.47) for crystalloid versus colloids in moderate shock. Consistent secondary pattern: marginally slower haematocrit and recovery response on Ringer's lactate; more adverse reactions on dextran than starch. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for fluid choice in moderate shock, with colloids a reasonable reserve for severe presentations on the trials' own subgroup hints.
cards.watchOut: Hydroxyethyl starch has since accumulated safety concerns in other critical-care populations that postdate these trials; nothing here should be read as a general endorsement of starch resuscitation outside dengue shock in children.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wills BA et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2005 (PMID: 16135832); Ngo NT et al. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2001 (PMID: 11170909).

shelves.title: Routine antibiotics with therapeutic food in severe acute malnutrition: recovery 88.7% (amoxicillin) and 90.9% (cefdinir) versus 85.1% (placebo) — and mortality 4.8% and 4.1% versus 7.4%
shelves.question: For children with uncomplicated severe acute malnutrition treated as outpatients with ready-to-use therapeutic food, does adding a routine 7-day antibiotic (amoxicillin or cefdinir) improve recovery and survival compared with therapeutic food alone?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Amoxicillin/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Anti-Bacterial Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Cefdinir · Cephalosporins/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Child, Preschool · Combined Modality Therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Infant · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Protein-Energy Malnutrition/diet therapy/drug therapy/mortality · Risk · Treatment Outcome · Weight Gain
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — one large, rigorous trial is the evidence, and it is a mortality trial, which is why it is Tier C for the developer. In Malawi (Trehan I et al., PMID: 23363496), 2,767 children aged 6–59 months with severe acute malnutrition were randomised double-blind to amoxicillin, cefdinir or placebo for 7 days, all with ready-to-use therapeutic food as outpatients. Nutritional recovery was 88.7% with amoxicillin, 90.9% with cefdinir and 85.1% with placebo — relative risks of treatment failure with placebo of 1.32 (95% CI 1.04–1.68) versus amoxicillin and 1.64 (1.27–2.11) versus cefdinir. Mortality was 4.8%, 4.1% and 7.4% respectively — relative risk of death with placebo 1.55 (1.07–2.24) versus amoxicillin and higher still versus cefdinir (the record's text is truncated at that point, so only the amoxicillin comparison is quoted). In absolute terms, placebo cost about 2.6–3.3 extra deaths per 100 children treated. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): routine antibiotics alongside therapeutic food improved both recovery and survival in the only large trial — a single-trial mortality claim, held as Tier C.

cards.headline: Trehan 2013 (Malawi, n=2,767): recovery 88.7% amoxicillin, 90.9% cefdinir, 85.1% placebo; mortality 4.8%, 4.1%, 7.4% — placebo death risk 1.55× amoxicillin (1.07–2.24)
cards.summary: Trehan 2013 (Malawi, n=2,767): recovery 88.7% amoxicillin, 90.9% cefdinir, 85.1% placebo; mortality 4.8%, 4.1%, 7.4% — placebo death risk 1.55× amoxicillin (1.07–2.24)
cards.people: 2,767 Malawian children aged 6 to 59 months with severe acute malnutrition treated as outpatients with ready-to-use therapeutic food, randomly assigned to amoxicillin, cefdinir, or placebo for 7 days; primary outcomes were the rate of nutritional recovery and the mortality rate. The record does not name the manufacturers of the antibiotic products used, so none is stated.
cards.result: Recovery: 88.7% (amoxicillin), 90.9% (cefdinir), 85.1% (placebo) — relative risk of treatment failure with placebo versus amoxicillin 1.32 (95% CI 1.04–1.68) and versus cefdinir 1.64 (1.27–2.11). Mortality: 4.8%, 4.1% and 7.4% respectively — relative risk of death with placebo versus amoxicillin 1.55 (1.07–2.24); the record's abstract text is truncated before the cefdinir mortality comparison, which is therefore not quoted. Severe acute malnutrition contributes to about 1 million child deaths annually (context given in the record).
cards.watchOut: One trial, one country, uncomplicated outpatient cases — children with clinical infection or complications were a different pathway, and the result does not by itself settle which antibiotic, or whether the benefit survives today's resistance patterns; the mortality claim rests on this single trial, hence Tier C.
cards.source: Trehan I et al. Antibiotics as part of the management of severe acute malnutrition. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2013. PMID: 23363496. Registry ID: NCT01000298. cards.headline: Synthesis: in the only large trial, skipping routine antibiotics cost roughly 3 lives per 100 children treated — the strongest single-trial case in this corner of the library
cards.summary: Synthesis: in the only large trial, skipping routine antibiotics cost roughly 3 lives per 100 children treated — the strongest single-trial case in this corner of the library
cards.people: One double-blind placebo-controlled trial of 2,767 children with uncomplicated severe acute malnutrition in Malawi, all receiving therapeutic food.
cards.result: Recovery 88.7% (amoxicillin) and 90.9% (cefdinir) versus 85.1% (placebo); mortality 4.8% and 4.1% versus 7.4%. PROPOSED LIKELY, Tier C — a single-trial mortality benefit is precisely the class the developer reviews personally, and replication in other settings remains the open question.
cards.watchOut: The comparison is antibiotics versus none in children without overt infection signs, added to full nutritional therapy — not a licence to substitute antibiotics for therapeutic food, and not evidence about complicated or inpatient malnutrition.
cards.source: Synthesis of Trehan I et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2013 (PMID: 23363496).

shelves.title: Melatonin advances sleep onset by about 27 minutes and adds about 20 minutes of sleep in children with ADHD and chronic sleep-onset insomnia — with no effect on behaviour, cognition, or ADHD symptoms
shelves.question: In children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and insomnia, does melatonin improve sleep onset and total sleep time compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Attention Deficit Disorder with Hyperactivity/diagnosis/drug therapy/psychology · Child · Child Behavior Disorders/diagnosis/drug therapy/psychology · Chronic Disease · Circadian Rhythm/drug effects · Cognition Disorders/diagnosis/drug therapy/psychology · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Melatonin/adverse effects/blood/therapeutic use · Quality of Life/psychology · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders/diagnosis/drug therapy/psychology · Wakefulness/drug effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for sleep timing only, in two concordant double-blind trials. Van der Heijden 2007 (PMID: 17242627) randomised 105 medication-free children aged 6–12 years with ADHD and chronic sleep-onset insomnia to melatonin 3 or 6 mg (by body weight) or placebo for 4 weeks: sleep onset advanced by 26.9 minutes on melatonin and was delayed by 10.5 minutes on placebo (p < .0001), dim-light melatonin onset advanced by 44.4 minutes versus a 12.8-minute delay (p < .0001), and total time asleep increased by 19.8 minutes versus a 13.6-minute decrease (p = .01) — with no significant effect on behaviour, cognition, or quality of life. Weiss 2006 (PMID: 16670647), in 27 stimulant-treated children with ADHD and initial insomnia, found melatonin 5 mg reduced initial insomnia by 16 minutes relative to placebo in the crossover phase (effect size 0.6), after sleep hygiene alone had resolved insomnia in 5 children; improved sleep had no demonstrable effect on ADHD symptoms. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): melatonin modestly advances and lengthens sleep in children with ADHD and sleep-onset insomnia; it is not a treatment for ADHD itself.

cards.headline: Van der Heijden 2007: sleep onset 26.9 minutes earlier on melatonin versus 10.5 minutes later on placebo (p < .0001); total sleep +19.8 versus −13.6 minutes (p = .01)
cards.summary: Van der Heijden 2007: sleep onset 26.9 minutes earlier on melatonin versus 10.5 minutes later on placebo (p < .0001); total sleep +19.8 versus −13.6 minutes (p = .01)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Van der Heijden 2007)
cards.people: 105 medication-free children aged 6 to 12 years with rigorously diagnosed ADHD and chronic sleep-onset insomnia, randomised to melatonin 3 or 6 mg (depending on body weight) or placebo for 4 weeks; outcomes by actigraphy and salivary dim-light melatonin onset.
cards.result: Sleep onset advanced by 26.9 ± 47.8 minutes with melatonin and was delayed by 10.5 ± 37.4 minutes with placebo (p < .0001). Dim-light melatonin onset advanced by 44.4 ± 67.9 minutes on melatonin versus a delay of 12.8 ± 60.0 minutes on placebo (p < .0001). Total time asleep increased by 19.8 ± 61.9 minutes on melatonin versus a decrease of 13.6 ± 50.6 minutes on placebo (p = .01). There was no significant effect on behaviour, cognition, or quality of life, and no significant adverse events occurred.
cards.watchOut: Four weeks is short, the standard deviations are larger than the mean gains (responses vary widely between children), and the children were medication-free — most children with ADHD in practice take stimulants, which the second trial covers.
cards.source: Van der Heijden KB et al. Effect of melatonin on sleep, behavior, and cognition in ADHD and chronic sleep-onset insomnia. Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry. 2007. PMID: 17242627. cards.headline: Weiss 2006: in stimulant-treated children, melatonin cut initial insomnia by 16 minutes versus placebo after sleep hygiene had already helped 5 of 27
cards.summary: Weiss 2006: in stimulant-treated children, melatonin cut initial insomnia by 16 minutes versus placebo after sleep hygiene had already helped 5 of 27
cards.people: 27 stimulant-treated children aged 6–14 years with ADHD and initial insomnia (>60 minutes), who first received a sleep-hygiene intervention; nonresponders entered a 30-day double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial of 5 mg pharmaceutical-grade melatonin provided by the study's sponsor (no sponsor or product name is given in the record).
cards.result: Sleep hygiene reduced initial insomnia to under 60 minutes in 5 cases, with an overall effect size of 0.67 in the group as a whole. In the evaluable crossover data, melatonin reduced initial insomnia by 16 minutes relative to placebo (effect size 0.6). The combined sleep-hygiene plus melatonin effect from baseline to 90 days post-trial was an effect size of 1.7, a mean decrease in initial insomnia of 60 minutes. Adverse events were generally mild and not different from placebo, and improved sleep had no demonstrable effect on ADHD symptoms.
cards.watchOut: Very small, and the crossover analysis rests on the subset whose data could be evaluated; the headline 60-minute combined figure mixes the sleep-hygiene effect with the drug effect and is not a placebo-controlled estimate.
cards.source: Weiss MD et al. Sleep hygiene and melatonin treatment for children and adolescents with ADHD and initial insomnia. Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry. 2006. PMID: 16670647. randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial (weiss 2006) 27 stimulant-treated children aged 6–14 years with adhd and initial insomnia (>60 minutes), who first received a sleep-hygiene intervention; nonresponders entered a 30-day double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial of 5 mg pharmaceutical-grade melatonin provided by the study's sponsor (no sponsor or product name is given in the record). sleep hygiene reduced initial insomnia to under 60 minutes in 5 cases, with an overall effect size of 0.67 in the group as a whole. in the evaluable crossover data, melatonin reduced initial insomnia by 16 minutes relative to placebo (effect size 0.6). the combined sleep-hygiene plus melatonin effect from baseline to 90 days post-trial was an effect size of 1.7, a mean decrease in initial insomnia of 60 minutes. adverse events were generally mild and not different from placebo, and improved sleep had no demonstrable effect on adhd symptoms. very small, and the crossover analysis rests on the subset whose data could be evaluated; the headline 60-minute combined figure mixes the sleep-hygiene effect with the drug effect and is not a placebo-controlled estimate. weiss md et al. sleep hygiene and melatonin treatment for children and adolescents with adhd and initial insomnia. journal of the american academy of child and adolescent psychiatry. 2006. pmid: 16670647. mesh: adolescent · arousal/drug effects · attention deficit disorder with hyperactivity/diagnosis/drug therapy · child · circadian rhythm/drug effects · cross-over studies · double-blind method · education · female · health education · humans · male · melatonin/adverse effects/therapeutic use · sleep initiation and maintenance disorders/diagnosis/drug therapy · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Synthesis: sleep onset and total sleep improve modestly in both trials; daytime ADHD outcomes improve in neither
cards.summary: Synthesis: sleep onset and total sleep improve modestly in both trials; daytime ADHD outcomes improve in neither
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind trials totalling 132 children with ADHD and sleep-onset insomnia (105 medication-free; 27 stimulant-treated), 4 weeks and 30 days of treatment.
cards.result: Sleep onset: advanced 26.9 minutes versus a 10.5-minute delay on placebo (p < .0001); initial insomnia reduced by 16 minutes versus placebo in the crossover trial. Total sleep: +19.8 versus −13.6 minutes (p = .01). Behaviour, cognition, quality of life, and ADHD symptoms: no significant effect in either trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for sleep onset and total sleep time only.
cards.watchOut: Both trials are short and neither addresses long-term safety, dose choice (3 vs 6 mg was weight-based, not compared head-to-head), or whether sleep gains persist after stopping. Tier C per this band's rule.
cards.source: Synthesis of Van der Heijden KB et al. Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry. 2007 (PMID: 17242627); Weiss MD et al. Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry. 2006 (PMID: 16670647).

shelves.title: Closing a significant ductus in preterm infants: high-dose oral ibuprofen ranked best across 68 trials; paracetamol matched ibuprofen head-to-head (81.2% versus 78.8% closure) with less hyperbilirubinaemia and gut bleeding
shelves.question: In preterm infants with a haemodynamically significant patent ductus arteriosus, how do ibuprofen, indomethacin and paracetamol compare for duct closure and adverse events?
shelves.mesh: Acetaminophen/administration & dosage · Administration, Intravenous · Administration, Oral · Bayes Theorem · Cerebral Hemorrhage/etiology · Ductus Arteriosus, Patent/complications/drug therapy/mortality · Enterocolitis, Necrotizing/chemically induced/prevention & control · Hemodynamics · Humans · Ibuprofen/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Indomethacin/administration & dosage · Infant, Newborn · Infant, Premature · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Risk Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the drugs close the ductus; they differ in dose, route and side-effects, not in the hard outcomes. A Bayesian network meta-analysis of 68 randomised trials in 4,802 preterm infants (Mitra S et al., PMID: 29584842) found the overall closure rate was 67.4% (2,867 of 4,256), and that a high dose of oral ibuprofen beat a standard dose of intravenous ibuprofen (odds ratio 3.59, 95% credible interval 1.64–8.17; 199 more closures per 1,000 infants) and standard-dose intravenous indomethacin (odds ratio 2.35, 95% credible interval 1.08–5.31; 124 more per 1,000), ranking first for closure and for avoiding surgical ligation — while no treatment, including placebo, differed significantly on mortality, necrotising enterocolitis or intraventricular haemorrhage. Head-to-head, oral paracetamol closed the ductus in 81.2% versus 78.8% on oral ibuprofen, within the non-inferiority margin, with significantly less hyperbilirubinaemia and gastrointestinal bleeding (Dang D et al., PMID: 24223740). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for closure itself, high-dose oral ibuprofen has the strongest randomised support and paracetamol is a credible gentler alternative; no regimen has shown a mortality or brain-injury advantage.

cards.headline: Mitra 2018 network meta-analysis (68 trials, 4,802 infants): high-dose oral ibuprofen beat standard IV ibuprofen (OR 3.59) and standard IV indomethacin (OR 2.35) for closure; mortality, NEC and IVH did not differ between any treatments, placebo included
cards.summary: Mitra 2018 network meta-analysis (68 trials, 4,802 infants): high-dose oral ibuprofen beat standard IV ibuprofen (OR 3.59) and standard IV indomethacin (OR 2.35) for closure; mortality, NEC and IVH did not differ between any treatments, placebo included
cards.type: Systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis of randomised trials (Mitra 2018)
cards.people: Preterm infants (gestational age under 37 weeks) with a clinically or echocardiographically diagnosed haemodynamically significant patent ductus arteriosus, in 68 randomised trials (4,802 infants) of intravenous or oral indomethacin, ibuprofen or acetaminophen (paracetamol) against each other, placebo or no treatment; 14 treatment variations in total.
cards.result: Overall PDA closure rate was 67.4% (2,867 of 4,256 infants). High-dose oral ibuprofen was associated with significantly higher odds of closure than standard-dose intravenous ibuprofen (odds ratio 3.59; 95% credible interval 1.64–8.17; absolute risk difference 199 more per 1,000 infants, 95% credible interval 95–258) and standard-dose intravenous indomethacin (odds ratio 2.35; 95% credible interval 1.08–5.31; 124 more per 1,000, 14–188). High-dose oral ibuprofen ranked best for closure (mean SUCRA 0.89) and for preventing surgical ligation (0.98). There was no significant difference in the odds of mortality, necrotising enterocolitis or intraventricular haemorrhage with placebo or no treatment compared with any other treatment.
cards.watchOut: Rankings from a network meta-analysis lean heavily on indirect comparisons and on closure — an echocardiographic endpoint. The same analysis is the honest counterweight: closing the ductus faster has not been shown to change death, gut or brain outcomes, which is why conservative management keeps gaining ground.
cards.source: Mitra S et al. cards.headline: Dang 2013: oral paracetamol closed the ductus in 81.2% versus 78.8% on oral ibuprofen — non-inferior, with significantly less hyperbilirubinaemia and gastrointestinal bleeding
cards.summary: Dang 2013: oral paracetamol closed the ductus in 81.2% versus 78.8% on oral ibuprofen — non-inferior, with significantly less hyperbilirubinaemia and gastrointestinal bleeding
cards.people: 160 premature infants (gestational age 34 weeks or less) with echocardiographically confirmed patent ductus arteriosus, randomised to oral paracetamol (n=80) or oral ibuprofen (n=80), with a second course given if echocardiography showed the ductus remained open.
cards.result: The ductus closed in 65 of 80 (81.2%) infants on paracetamol versus 63 of 80 (78.8%) on ibuprofen; the 95% confidence interval of the difference (−0.080 to 0.128) demonstrated non-inferiority of paracetamol. The incidence of hyperbilirubinaemia and gastrointestinal bleeding was significantly lower in the paracetamol group. No significant differences in other side effects or complications were noted.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre, non-blinded trial of 160 infants — its non-inferiority verdict is consistent with the network picture but cannot carry paracetamol's case alone, and closure, again, is the endpoint rather than survival or neurodevelopment.
cards.source: Dang D et al. Comparison of oral paracetamol versus ibuprofen in premature infants with patent ductus arteriosus: a randomized controlled trial. PloS one. 2013. PMID: 24223740. Registry ID: ChiCTR-TRC-12002177. cards.summary: Synthesis: closure is a drug-contest the ductus drugs win at different prices; the outcomes that matter most have never separated them — or separated any of them from doing nothing
cards.people: 68 randomised trials (4,802 preterm infants) in network meta-analysis, plus a 160-infant head-to-head non-inferiority trial of oral paracetamol versus oral ibuprofen.
cards.result: Closure: high-dose oral ibuprofen ranked first (OR 3.59 versus standard IV ibuprofen; OR 2.35 versus standard IV indomethacin); paracetamol 81.2% versus ibuprofen 78.8% head-to-head, non-inferior, with less hyperbilirubinaemia and gastrointestinal bleeding. cards.watchOut: The stamp is for the closure question as asked. A shelf claiming these drugs improve survival or brain outcomes would not survive its own evidence — the network analysis says the opposite comparison (against placebo) is null on those outcomes.

shelves.title: Cooling encephalopathic newborns in low-resource settings (HELIX): death or disability 50% versus 47% — no benefit — and death alone significantly higher with hypothermia (42% versus 31%)
shelves.question: In term infants with hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy in low-resource settings, does therapeutic hypothermia improve survival without disability compared with usual care (HELIX)?
shelves.mesh: Bangladesh/epidemiology · Brain Diseases/mortality/therapy · Developing Countries · Female · Humans · Hypothermia, Induced · India/epidemiology · Infant, Newborn · Intensive Care, Neonatal · Male · Severity of Illness Index · Sri Lanka/epidemiology · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — the intervention that helps in high-income nurseries did not transfer. In HELIX (Thayyil S et al., PMID: 34358491), 408 term infants with moderate or severe neonatal encephalopathy in India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh were randomised to whole-body hypothermia at 33.5°C for 72 hours or usual care, in tertiary units with ventilation, cardiovascular support and MRI. Death or moderate or severe disability at 18–22 months occurred in 50% (98 of 195) on hypothermia versus 47% (94 of 199) on usual care (risk ratio 1.06, 95% CI 0.87–1.30, p=0.55) — and death alone was significantly higher with cooling: 42% versus 31% (p=0.022), including neonatal hospital deaths of 36% versus 24% (p=0.0087). The trial's own conclusion: therapeutic hypothermia should not be offered for neonatal encephalopathy in low-income and middle-income countries, even where tertiary intensive care is available. This is a different question from the high-resource cooling trials homed at live shelves #145 and #260. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): in low-resource settings, cooling encephalopathic newborns increased death without reducing disability.

cards.headline: Thayyil 2021 (HELIX): death or disability 50% versus 47% (RR 1.06, p=0.55); death alone 42% versus 31% (p=0.022) — cooling harmed where the high-income trials had helped
cards.summary: Thayyil 2021 (HELIX): death or disability 50% versus 47% (RR 1.06, p=0.55); death alone 42% versus 31% (p=0.022) — cooling harmed where the high-income trials had helped
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, open-label with masked outcome assessment (Thayyil 2021, HELIX)
cards.people: 408 infants born at or after 36 weeks of gestation with moderate or severe neonatal encephalopathy (continued resuscitation or Apgar under 6 at 5 minutes, or no cry by 5 minutes for home births) at seven tertiary neonatal intensive care units in India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh, randomised within 6 hours of birth to whole-body hypothermia (33.5°C for 72 hours, servo-controlled device; n=202) or usual care (n=206); primary outcome data available for 195 and 199 infants.
cards.result: Death or moderate or severe disability at 18–22 months: 98 of 195 (50%) on hypothermia versus 94 of 199 (47%) on usual care (risk ratio 1.06; 95% CI 0.87–1.30; p=0.55). Death alone: 84 infants (42%) on hypothermia versus 63 (31%) on usual care (p=0.022), of whom 72 (36%) versus 49 (24%) died during neonatal hospitalisation (p=0.0087). Five serious adverse events were reported (three hypothermia, two control); none was judged causally related to the intervention.
cards.watchOut: Single-trial flag: one large, well-run multicountry trial carries this shelf. It was open-label (cooling cannot be masked) though outcome assessors were masked, and its population — later presentations, more infection and growth restriction in the background — differs from the high-income trials, which is precisely the point of the question.
cards.source: Thayyil S et al. shelves.title: Prednisolone versus dexamethasone for croup: three head-to-head trials, including a 1,252-child noninferiority trial, found no clinically important difference
shelves.question: In children with croup, is oral prednisolone equivalent to dexamethasone for symptom relief, return visits and length of stay?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Child, Preschool · Croup/drug therapy · Dexamethasone/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Emergency Service, Hospital · Equivalence Trials as Topic · Female · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Humans · Infant · Male · Prednisolone/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Prospective Studies · Western Australia
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — between the two steroids. Three randomised head-to-head trials compared single-dose oral prednisolone with dexamethasone in childhood croup. The largest (Parker CM et al., PMID: 31416827) enrolled 1,252 children and demonstrated noninferiority of prednisolone 1 mg/kg and of low-dose dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg against standard dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg: adjusted Westley score differences at 1 hour were 0.05 (95% CI −0.07 to 0.17) for prednisolone, and unscheduled re-attendance within 7 days was 21.7% on prednisolone versus 17.8% on standard-dose dexamethasone (not significant). Two smaller trials agree: Fifoot AA et al. (PMID: 17305661, n=99) found no significant differences between prednisolone 1 mg/kg and either dexamethasone dose, and Garbutt JM et al. (PMID: 24092872, n=87) found no differences in additional care (7% versus 2%), symptom duration or parent outcomes. An earlier trial suggesting prednisolone inferiority (Sparrow & Geelhoed 2006) is already carded at live shelf #239 and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): prednisolone performs equivalently to dexamethasone for croup in the direct comparisons.

cards.headline: Parker 2019: prednisolone and low-dose dexamethasone both noninferior to standard dexamethasone — re-attendance 21.7% versus 17.8%
cards.summary: Parker 2019: prednisolone and low-dose dexamethasone both noninferior to standard dexamethasone — re-attendance 21.7% versus 17.8%
cards.people: 1,252 children (age >6 months, maximum weight 20 kg) with croup presenting to one tertiary paediatric emergency department and one urban district emergency department in Perth, Western Australia, randomised to dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg (n=410), low-dose dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg (n=410) or prednisolone 1 mg/kg (n=411), single oral dose.
cards.result: Mean baseline Westley Croup Score was 1.4–1.5 across groups. Adjusted difference in scores at 1 hour, compared with standard dexamethasone, was 0.03 (95% CI −0.09 to 0.15) for low-dose dexamethasone and 0.05 (95% CI −0.07 to 0.17) for prednisolone. Unscheduled re-attendance within 7 days was 17.8% (dexamethasone), 19.5% (low-dose dexamethasone) and 21.7% (prednisolone), not significant. Noninferiority was demonstrated for both low-dose dexamethasone and prednisolone.
cards.watchOut: Most children had mild croup (mean Westley score ~1.5), so equivalence is best shown where the stakes are lowest; the trial excluded children with a high suspicion of an alternative diagnosis and those recently given steroids. Re-attendance ran numerically highest on prednisolone (21.7% versus 17.8%) without reaching significance — a small real disadvantage cannot be excluded.

cards.headline: Fifoot 2007: no significant difference between prednisolone 1 mg/kg, dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg and dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg in 99 children
cards.summary: Fifoot 2007: no significant difference between prednisolone 1 mg/kg, dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg and dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg in 99 children
cards.people: 99 children aged 6 months to 6 years (mean age 1.7 years) presenting to a paediatric tertiary emergency department with croup and a Westley croup score of 2 or more, randomised to a single oral dose of prednisolone 1 mg/kg (n=34), dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg (n=34) or dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg (n=31); 86 (87%) were followed up by telephone at 1 week.
cards.result: There were no significant differences in primary or secondary outcome measures between the three treatment groups: magnitude and rate of reduction in Westley croup score, rate of return for medical care with ongoing croup, further steroid treatment in the following week, admission, or salvage therapy such as nebulised adrenaline during the index presentation. The authors concluded that prednisolone 1 mg/kg and low-dose dexamethasone did not differ in efficacy from dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg.
cards.watchOut: A 99-child trial can miss modest differences; its value is concordance with the much larger Parker trial rather than standalone proof of equivalence. Children had mild-to-moderate croup by design (Westley score ≥2 at entry, in an emergency department).

cards.headline: Garbutt 2013: community trial found no difference in extra care, symptom duration or parent stress between prednisolone and dexamethasone
cards.summary: Garbutt 2013: community trial found no difference in extra care, symptom duration or parent stress between prednisolone and dexamethasone
cards.people: 87 children aged 1 to 8 years with croup symptoms for 48 hours or less (42% mild, 58% moderate), randomised in community practice to prednisolone 2 mg/kg/day for 3 days (n=41) or a single dose of dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg plus 2 doses of placebo (n=46).
cards.result: There were no differences between dexamethasone and prednisolone for additional health care for croup (2% versus 7%, P=.34), duration of croup symptoms (2.8 versus 2.2 days, P=.63), non-barky cough (6.1 versus 5.9 days, P=.81), nights with disturbed sleep for the parent (0.68 versus 1.21 nights, P=.55), or days with stress (1.39 versus 1.56 days, P=.51).
cards.watchOut: The prednisolone regimen here (2 mg/kg/day for 3 days) differs from the single 1 mg/kg dose in the other two trials, and the sample is small; the trial speaks to real-world community use rather than to emergency-department equivalence testing.
cards.source: Garbutt JM et al. The comparative effectiveness of prednisolone and dexamethasone for children with croup: a community-based randomized trial. Clinical pediatrics. 2013. PMID: 24092872. cards.headline: Synthesis: whichever oral steroid is at hand works — the direct trials show no clinically important gap
cards.summary: Synthesis: whichever oral steroid is at hand works — the direct trials show no clinically important gap
cards.people: Three randomised head-to-head trials totalling over 1,400 children with croup (Parker 2019, n=1,252; Fifoot 2007, n=99; Garbutt 2013, n=87), comparing oral prednisolone with oral dexamethasone at standard and low doses.
cards.result: Westley scores at 1 hour differed by 0.05 points or less between prednisolone and standard dexamethasone (Parker); 7-day re-attendance was 21.7% versus 17.8% (not significant). Neither smaller trial found a significant difference on any outcome. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) between prednisolone and dexamethasone. The one discordant earlier trial (Sparrow & Geelhoed 2006, re-presentation 29% versus 7%) lives at live shelf #239 and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Equivalence is demonstrated mainly in mild-to-moderate croup; severe croup with airway compromise was not the population studied, and dexamethasone versus placebo itself is settled at live shelf #239 — this shelf answers only the head-to-head question.

shelves.title: Heliox in bronchiolitis: distress scores ease within an hour in small trials, but the 319-infant phase III trial found no shorter treatment overall — benefit only by tight facemask or CPAP
shelves.question: In children with moderate-to-severe croup or bronchiolitis, does helium–oxygen (heliox) reduce respiratory distress and intubation compared with oxygen alone?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Bronchiolitis/therapy · Continuous Positive Airway Pressure · Double-Blind Method · Female · Helium/therapeutic use · Humans · Infant · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Masks · Nitrogen/therapeutic use · Oxygen/therapeutic use · Oxygen Inhalation Therapy/instrumentation/methods · Respiratory Therapy/instrumentation/methods · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — scores versus hard outcomes, and delivery route decides. The phase III trial (Chowdhury MM et al., PMID: 23509160) randomised 319 infants with bronchiolitis to heliox or a nitrogen–oxygen control gas (airox): median length of treatment was 1.90 versus 1.87 days (P=.41), and the proportion needing CPAP was 17% versus 19% (OR 0.87). Benefit appeared only where the gas was actually delivered undiluted — by tight-fitting facemask (1.46 versus 2.01 days, P=.03) or CPAP (1.55 versus 2.26 days, P=.02) — and not by nasal cannula. Small intensive-care trials split: Cambonie G et al. (PMID: 16537867, n=20) found the respiratory distress score lower after 1 hour on heliox (3.05 versus 5.5, P<.01), while Liet JM et al. (PMID: 16356437, n=39) found positive-pressure ventilation was needed in 22.2% on heliox versus 19.0% on control gas (RR 1.17). No randomised trial of heliox in croup against oxygen alone with usable outcome data was found; the croup heliox record is a small pilot and a comparison against racemic epinephrine. PROPOSED SPLIT: heliox may ease distress scores and shorten treatment when delivered by facemask or CPAP in bronchiolitis, but it has not reduced ventilation or overall treatment length.

cards.headline: Chowdhury 2013 (phase III): length of treatment 1.90 versus 1.87 days overall — shorter only in the facemask (P=.03) and CPAP (P=.02) subgroups
cards.summary: Chowdhury 2013 (phase III): length of treatment 1.90 versus 1.87 days overall — shorter only in the facemask (P=.03) and CPAP (P=.02) subgroups
cards.people: 319 infants with bronchiolitis in a multicentre trial, randomised to heliox (helium–oxygen) or airox (21% oxygen with 79% nitrogen) delivered by facemask, nasal cannula if facemask-intolerant, or CPAP; 281 completed the study (140 heliox, 141 airox). Severe cases received CPAP from the start.
cards.result: Median length of treatment was 1.90 days (IQR 1.08–3.17) on heliox versus 1.87 days (IQR 1.11–3.34) on airox (P=.41). In the facemask-tolerant subgroup, length of treatment was 1.46 versus 2.01 days (P=.03); by nasal cannula, 2.51 versus 2.81 days (P=.53); in the subgroup started on CPAP, 1.55 versus 2.26 days (P=.02). The proportion needing CPAP was 17% versus 19% (OR 0.87, 95% CI 0.47–1.60, P=.76). Heliox reduced the respiratory distress score after 8 hours (P<.001).
cards.watchOut: The headline result is null; the positive findings are delivery-route subgroups, and nasal-cannula heliox — the easiest way to give it — was ineffective, plausibly because room air dilutes the helium. Subgroup wins inside a null phase III trial are hypothesis-grade, not proof.
cards.source: Chowdhury MM et al. Heliox therapy in bronchiolitis: phase III multicenter double-blind randomized controlled trial. Pediatrics. 2013. PMID: 23509160. Registry ID: ISRCTN18238432. cards.headline: Cambonie 2006: respiratory distress score 3.05 on heliox versus 5.5 on control gas after 1 hour in 20 PICU infants
cards.summary: Cambonie 2006: respiratory distress score 3.05 on heliox versus 5.5 on control gas after 1 hour in 20 PICU infants
cards.people: 20 infants under 3 months old admitted to a university paediatric intensive care unit with moderate-to-severe acute respiratory syncytial virus bronchiolitis, randomised to inhale heliox or an air–oxygen mixture (airox) for 1 hour under an oxyhood.
cards.result: After 1 hour, the respiratory distress score was significantly lower in the heliox group than in the airox group (3.05 versus 5.5, P<.01), with a significant reduction in accessory muscle use (P<.05) and expiratory wheezing (P<.01). Inspiratory breath sounds and cyanosis did not differ significantly between groups.
cards.watchOut: Twenty infants and a 1-hour score outcome: this shows heliox can ease the work of breathing briefly in a PICU, not that it changes intubation, stay or any outcome a family would count. Ex-premature infants started with higher distress scores.
cards.source: Cambonie G et al. Clinical effects of heliox administration for acute bronchiolitis in young infants. Chest. 2006. PMID: 16537867. cards.headline: Liet 2005: positive-pressure ventilation needed in 22.2% on heliox versus 19.0% on control gas (RR 1.17) in severe bronchiolitis
cards.summary: Liet 2005: positive-pressure ventilation needed in 22.2% on heliox versus 19.0% on control gas (RR 1.17) in severe bronchiolitis
cards.people: 39 non-intubated infants with severe respiratory syncytial virus bronchiolitis in 4 paediatric intensive care units, randomised within 8 hours of admission to a helium–oxygen mixture (n=18) or an air–oxygen mixture (n=21) through an inflatable head hood.
cards.result: Positive-pressure ventilation was judged necessary for 4 of 18 infants (22.2%) in the helium group and 4 of 21 (19.0%) in the control group (relative risk 1.17, 95% CI 0.34–4.01). No differences were detected between the groups for the rate of positive-pressure ventilation.
cards.watchOut: With 39 infants and 8 events, the confidence interval (0.34–4.01) excludes almost nothing — the trial is consistent with sizeable benefit or harm. It is carded because it is the only trial besides Chowdhury to test a hard endpoint, and its point estimate does not favour heliox.
cards.source: Liet JM et al. Noninvasive therapy with helium-oxygen for severe bronchiolitis. The Journal of pediatrics. 2005. PMID: 16356437. shelves.title: Antibiotics for glue ear: the founding trial said effusion cleared twice as often, its own reanalysis said the result was measurement bias — and hearing, the outcome that matters, remains unproven
shelves.question: In children with otitis media with effusion, do antibiotics improve hearing and effusion resolution compared with placebo or watchful waiting?
shelves.mesh: Child · Humans · Child, Preschool · Anti-Bacterial Agents/adverse effects · Otitis Media with Effusion/drug therapy · Quality of Life · Anaphylaxis/chemically induced/drug therapy · Hearing Loss/etiology/chemically induced
shelves.balance: SPLIT — effusion on paper versus hearing in the child. The founding double-blind trial (Mandel EM et al., PMID: 2880294) randomised 518 children with otitis media with effusion to 2 weeks of amoxicillin, with or without a decongestant–antihistamine, or placebo: effusion resolution at 4 weeks was twice as high on amoxicillin (P<.001), yet 69.8% of amoxicillin-treated children still had effusion, and about half of those who cleared relapsed within 3 months in both groups. A published reanalysis of the same trial (Cantekin EI et al., PMID: 1683673) concluded the apparent benefit rested on biased otoscopic judgement: by tympanometry the estimated efficacy was 4.8% (P=.171), recurrence after treatment was two to six times higher in the amoxicillin group (P=.001), and resolution at about 10 weeks was 13.6% versus 11.3% (P=.477). The 2023 Cochrane review (Mulvaney CA et al., PMID: 37870130; 19 studies, 2,581 children) rated the evidence low to very low certainty: return to normal hearing at 2 months rested on a single study (20/49 versus 0/37), persistent effusion at 6–12 months was 48% versus 54% against placebo (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.68–1.17), and against no treatment effusion resolved more by 3 months (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.50–0.80) with little to no difference in hearing threshold. PROPOSED SPLIT: antibiotics may clear effusion a little sooner; a hearing benefit is unproven and the flagship result is contested by its own reanalysis.

cards.headline: Mandel 1987: effusion resolution twice as high on amoxicillin at 4 weeks (P<.001) — but 69.8% still had effusion, and half of clearances relapsed
cards.summary: Mandel 1987: effusion resolution twice as high on amoxicillin at 4 weeks (P<.001) — but 69.8% still had effusion, and half of clearances relapsed
cards.people: 518 infants and children with otitis media with effusion ('secretory' otitis media), randomised to a 2-week course of amoxicillin 40 mg/kg/day, with or without a 4-week oral decongestant–antihistamine combination, or placebo; 474 were evaluated at the 4-week endpoint.
cards.result: The rate of resolution of middle-ear effusion at 4 weeks was twice as high in those treated with amoxicillin, with or without the decongestant–antihistamine, as in those who received placebo (P<.001) — but 69.8% of amoxicillin-treated subjects still had effusion. Resolution was more likely with initially unilateral effusion, effusion of 8 weeks or less, and no upper respiratory infection at 4 weeks. Among subjects without effusion at 4 weeks, recurrent effusion developed in approximately half of both the amoxicillin and placebo groups during the subsequent 3 months. Side effects were reported more often with the decongestant–antihistamine.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is fluid behind the eardrum at 4 weeks, judged otoscopically — not hearing, language or development. A doubling of a low clearance rate still left most treated children with effusion, and the benefit did not survive the following 3 months.
cards.source: Mandel EM et al. Efficacy of amoxicillin with and without decongestant-antihistamine for otitis media with effusion in children. Results of a double-blind, randomized trial. The New England journal of medicine. 1987. PMID: 2880294. cards.headline: Cantekin 1991: reanalysis of the same trial — efficacy 4.8% by tympanometry (P=.171), recurrence two to six times higher after amoxicillin
cards.summary: Cantekin 1991: reanalysis of the same trial — efficacy 4.8% by tympanometry (P=.171), recurrence two to six times higher after amoxicillin
cards.type: Reanalysis of a randomised trial (Cantekin 1991, of Mandel 1987)
cards.people: Re-examination of the Mandel 1987 double-blind placebo-controlled trial dataset: 518 infants and children with otitis media with effusion given a 2-week course of amoxicillin with or without decongestant–antihistamine, or placebo.
cards.result: At 4 weeks, amoxicillin efficacy by a tympanometric criterion was insignificant (P=.121), as was improvement in hearing (P=.311); only otoscopic judgement — shown to contain a systematic bias as used in this trial — supported marginal efficacy. Estimated efficacy of antibiotic treatment was 12.3% by otoscopy (P=.014) and 4.8% by tympanometry (P=.171). Six weeks after the end of amoxicillin therapy, recurrence of effusion was two to six times higher in amoxicillin-treated children than in placebo-treated children (P=.001), and resolution of effusion did not differ significantly (13.6% versus 11.3%; P=.477). The authors concluded amoxicillin is not effective for persistent asymptomatic middle-ear effusion.
cards.watchOut: A reanalysis is only as good as its own assumptions, and its authors were methodological critics of the original trial — but the dispute is the evidence: the same dataset supports opposite conclusions depending on how effusion is measured, which is why this shelf is SPLIT rather than positive or null.
cards.source: Cantekin EI et al. Antimicrobial therapy for otitis media with effusion ('secretory' otitis media). JAMA. 1991. PMID: 1683673. cards.headline: Cochrane 2023: 19 studies, 2,581 children — hearing evidence very uncertain; persistent effusion 48% versus 54% against placebo at 6–12 months
cards.summary: Cochrane 2023: 19 studies, 2,581 children — hearing evidence very uncertain; persistent effusion 48% versus 54% against placebo at 6–12 months
cards.people: 19 randomised and quasi-randomised trials (2,581 children aged 6 months to 12 years with unilateral or bilateral otitis media with effusion) comparing oral antibiotics (mostly 10–14 day courses) with placebo or no treatment; searches to 20 January 2023.
cards.result: Against placebo, return to normal hearing by 2 months rested on one study (20/49 on antibiotics versus 0/37 on placebo; Peto OR 9.59, 95% CI 3.51–26.18; very low-certainty evidence). Persistent effusion at 6–12 months was 48% versus 54% (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.68–1.17; 2 studies, 324 participants; very low certainty). Against no treatment, antibiotics may reduce persistent effusion at up to 3 months (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.50–0.80; 6 studies, 542 participants; low certainty), with little to no difference in final hearing threshold at 3 months in the single reporting study (mean difference −5.38 dB HL, 95% CI −9.12 to −1.64). No study reported anaphylaxis data directly; no study assessed disease-specific quality of life.
cards.watchOut: Every estimate is low or very low certainty, the hearing signal comes from single small studies, and the review could pool only a fraction of its 19 trials for any outcome. Spontaneous resolution is common in this condition, which shrinks any drug effect over time.
cards.source: Mulvaney CA et al. Antibiotics for otitis media with effusion (OME) in children. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2023. PMID: 37870130. Registry ID: NCT00539149. cards.headline: Synthesis: a contested surrogate win, a hearing question still open after 36 years
cards.summary: Synthesis: a contested surrogate win, a hearing question still open after 36 years
cards.people: One founding randomised trial (Mandel 1987, n=518) and its published reanalysis (Cantekin 1991), within a 2023 Cochrane review of 19 trials and 2,581 children with otitis media with effusion.
cards.result: Effusion resolution at 4 weeks: twice as high on amoxicillin by otoscopy (P<.001); 4.8% estimated efficacy by tympanometry on reanalysis (P=.171). Persistent effusion at 6–12 months versus placebo: 48% versus 54% (RR 0.89). Return to normal hearing: one small study only (20/49 versus 0/37), very low certainty. PROPOSED SPLIT, as stamped.
cards.watchOut: Steroids for this condition are a separate shelf (live #2496, OSTRICH) and adenoidectomy a separate pack (#3891); this shelf covers antibiotics only. Antibiotic harms and resistance are real costs against an unproven hearing benefit.
