shelves.title: Cranberry in children with recurrent urinary infection: the largest trial missed its primary endpoint (16% versus 22%), while two small trials found far fewer infections
shelves.question: In children with recurrent urinary tract infection, does cranberry prophylaxis reduce recurrence compared with placebo or antibiotic prophylaxis?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Beverages · Child · Child, Preschool · Female · Humans · Infant · Male · Urinary Tract Infections/prevention & control · Vaccinium macrocarpon
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by trial size and by endpoint. The largest trial (Salo J et al., PMID: 22100577) randomised 263 children treated for urinary tract infection to cranberry juice or placebo for 6 months: at least one recurrence occurred in 16% on cranberry versus 22% on placebo (difference −6%, 95% CI −16 to 4%; P=.21) — not significant — although total episodes were fewer (27 versus 47; incidence density 0.16 lower per person-year, P=.035) and antimicrobial days were 6 fewer per patient-year (P<.001). Two small trials were positive: Afshar K et al. (PMID: 22910239, n=40) found urinary infection incidence of 0.4 versus 1.15 per patient-year on high-proanthocyanidin cranberry juice versus proanthocyanidin-free juice (P=.045), a 65% relative reduction; Ferrara P et al. (PMID: 19921981, n=84 girls) found at least one infection in 18.5% on daily cranberry juice versus 48.1% in controls over 6 months (P<.05). No child trial against antibiotic prophylaxis was found; the adult-women question lives at live shelves #50 and #489. PROPOSED SPLIT: episode counts fall in all three trials, but the only adequately sized trial did not significantly reduce the proportion of children with a recurrence.

cards.headline: Salo 2012: ≥1 recurrence in 16% on cranberry versus 22% on placebo (P=.21) — but 27 versus 47 total episodes and 6 fewer antimicrobial days
cards.summary: Salo 2012: ≥1 recurrence in 16% on cranberry versus 22% on placebo (P=.21) — but 27 versus 47 total episodes and 6 fewer antimicrobial days
cards.people: 263 children treated for urinary tract infection in 7 hospitals in Finland, randomised to cranberry juice (n=129) or placebo juice (n=134) for 6 months and monitored for 1 year; 255 children were analysed after 8 protocol-violation exclusions. The record does not name a commercial cranberry product.
cards.result: Twenty children (16%) in the cranberry group and 28 (22%) in the placebo group had at least 1 recurrent urinary tract infection (difference −6%, 95% CI −16 to 4%; P=.21), with no difference in timing of first recurrence (P=.32). Total episodes were 27 versus 47, and the urinary infection incidence density was 0.16 episodes per person-year lower in the cranberry group (95% CI −0.31 to −0.01; P=.035). Children in the cranberry group had significantly fewer days on antimicrobials (−6 days per patient-year; 95% CI −7 to −5; P<.001).
cards.watchOut: The primary question a parent asks — will my child get another infection at all — was not significantly improved; the wins are in total episode counts and antibiotic days, which matter but are secondary. Six months of daily juice is also an adherence ask, and the product's proanthocyanidin content is not specified in the record.
cards.source: Salo J et al. Cranberry juice for the prevention of recurrences of urinary tract infections in children: a randomized placebo-controlled trial. Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America. 2012. PMID: 22100577. cards.headline: Afshar 2012: urinary infection incidence 0.4 versus 1.15 per patient-year on high-proanthocyanidin cranberry juice (P=.045) — in 40 children
cards.summary: Afshar 2012: urinary infection incidence 0.4 versus 1.15 per patient-year on high-proanthocyanidin cranberry juice (P=.045) — in 40 children
cards.people: 40 toilet-trained children up to 18 years old (39 girls, 1 boy; mean age 9.5 years) with at least 2 culture-documented non-febrile urinary tract infections in the previous year, randomised to daily cranberry juice with high proanthocyanidin concentration or cranberry juice with no proanthocyanidin, for 12 months; participants, clinicians, outcome assessor and statistician were all blinded. The record does not name a commercial product.
cards.result: After 12 months, the average incidence of urinary tract infection was 0.4 per patient per year in the treatment group versus 1.15 in the placebo group (P=.045), representing a 65% relative reduction in the risk of urinary tract infection with the absolute rates printed alongside.
cards.watchOut: Forty children, almost all girls, with non-febrile infections only — the trial was powered for a 30% decrease and found a larger one, which in a sample this small should be read as promising rather than precise. Children with anatomical abnormalities (except primary vesicoureteral reflux) were excluded.
cards.source: Afshar K et al. Cranberry juice for the prevention of pediatric urinary tract infection: a randomized controlled trial. The Journal of urology. 2012. PMID: 22910239. cards.headline: Ferrara 2009: at least one infection in 18.5% on cranberry versus 48.1% of controls over 6 months in 84 girls
cards.summary: Ferrara 2009: at least one infection in 18.5% on cranberry versus 48.1% of controls over 6 months in 84 girls
cards.people: 84 girls aged 3–14 years with recurrent urinary tract infections, randomised to cranberry juice 50 mL daily (n=28), a Lactobacillus GG drink on 5 days a month (n=27), or control (n=29), for 6 months; 80 completed (27, 26 and 27 analysed). The record does not name a commercial cranberry product.
cards.result: There were 34 episodes of urinary tract infection in the cohort. At least one episode occurred in 5/27 girls (18.5%) in the cranberry group, 11/26 (42.3%) in the Lactobacillus group and 18/27 (48.1%) in the control group (P<.05), as reported in the record. Four subjects withdrew for poor compliance.
cards.watchOut: The control group received nothing (no placebo juice), so expectation and reporting effects are uncontrolled, and the control recurrence rate (48.1%) is far higher than in Salo's placebo arm (22%) — different populations or different ascertainment. Small, single-sex, unblinded against control: supportive, not decisive.
cards.source: Ferrara P et al. Cranberry juice for the prevention of recurrent urinary tract infections: a randomized controlled trial in children. Scandinavian journal of urology and nephrology. 2009. PMID: 19921981. cards.headline: Synthesis: fewer episodes everywhere, a missed primary endpoint where it was best measured
cards.summary: Synthesis: fewer episodes everywhere, a missed primary endpoint where it was best measured
cards.people: Three randomised trials in children with recurrent urinary tract infection (Salo 2012, n=263; Ferrara 2009, n=84; Afshar 2012, n=40), all testing cranberry juice against placebo juice, no-proanthocyanidin juice or no treatment. No child trial against antibiotic prophylaxis was found.
cards.result: Children with ≥1 recurrence: 16% versus 22% (P=.21, Salo); 18.5% versus 48.1% (Ferrara). Episode incidence: 0.4 versus 1.15 per patient-year (Afshar); 27 versus 47 total episodes (Salo). Antimicrobial days: 6 fewer per patient-year (Salo, P<.001). PROPOSED SPLIT, as stamped. The adult-women cranberry question is homed at live shelves #50 and #489 and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Products differed (juice, dose and proanthocyanidin content mostly unspecified in the records) — cranberry is not one intervention, and none of these records names the commercial product used, so today's juices cannot be assumed equivalent.
cards.source: Synthesis of Salo J et al. Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America. 2012 (PMID: 22100577); Afshar K et al. The Journal of urology. 2012 (PMID: 22910239); Ferrara P et al. Scandinavian journal of urology and nephrology. 2009 (PMID: 19921981).

shelves.title: Methadone versus morphine for neonatal abstinence syndrome: treatment about 2–7 days shorter in two randomised trials — the larger one cut hospital stay by 2.9 days
shelves.question: In infants with neonatal abstinence syndrome, does methadone beat morphine for treatment duration? (The buprenorphine comparison is homed separately.)
shelves.mesh: Analgesics, Opioid/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Methadone/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Morphine/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Neonatal Abstinence Syndrome/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for methadone, on duration outcomes. The multicentre Davis 2018 trial (116 term infants treated at 8 US units) found, after adjustment for site and maternal opioid type, that methadone shortened length of hospital stay by 14% relative (relative number of days 0.86, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.00; P=.046; a 2.9-day absolute difference), stay attributable to abstinence syndrome by 14% relative (0.86, 95% CI 0.77 to 0.96; 2.7 days), and length of drug treatment by 16% relative (0.84, 95% CI 0.73 to 0.97; 2.3 days); medians were stay 16 versus 20 days and treatment 11.5 versus 15 days. The earlier single-site Brown 2015 trial (31 infants with consent of 78 eligible) found the same direction, larger: median length of opioid treatment 14 versus 21 days (P=.008). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): methadone shortens treatment and stay compared with morphine; no trial here addresses longer-term neurodevelopment, and the buprenorphine-versus-morphine question is homed on its own shelf.

cards.headline: Davis 2018: stay 16 versus 20 median days, treatment 11.5 versus 15 days on methadone versus morphine — 116 infants, 8 US units, double-blind
cards.summary: Davis 2018: stay 16 versus 20 median days, treatment 11.5 versus 15 days on methadone versus morphine — 116 infants, 8 US units, double-blind
cards.people: 117 term infants (116 analysed; mean gestational age 39.1 weeks, mean birth weight 3,157 g) at 8 US newborn units whose mothers received buprenorphine, methadone or opioids for pain in pregnancy and who required pharmacological treatment for neonatal abstinence syndrome, randomised to methadone or morphine with Finnegan-guided dosing.
cards.result: Adjusted for site and maternal opioid type, methadone versus morphine: length of stay relative number of days 0.86 (95% CI 0.74 to 1.00; P=.046), an absolute difference of 2.9 days; stay attributable to NAS 0.86 (95% CI 0.77 to 0.96; P=.01; 2.7 days); length of treatment 0.84 (95% CI 0.73 to 0.97; P=.02; 2.3 days). Medians: stay 16 versus 20 days (P=.005), NAS-attributable stay 16 versus 19 days (P=.005), treatment 11.5 versus 15 days (P=.009). All percent reductions above are relative, with absolute day differences printed alongside.
cards.watchOut: Duration outcomes are partly protocol-driven (weaning schedules differ by drug half-life), prenatal cigarette exposure was higher in the methadone group, and no neurodevelopmental follow-up is reported in this record — shorter is operationally better, not proven developmentally better.

cards.headline: Brown 2015: median opioid treatment 14 days on methadone versus 21 days on morphine (P=.008) — single site, only 31 of 78 eligible infants consented
cards.summary: Brown 2015: median opioid treatment 14 days on methadone versus 21 days on morphine (P=.008) — single site, only 31 of 78 eligible infants consented
cards.people: 31 infants (of 78 eligible; 41 methadone-exposed and 37 buprenorphine-exposed pregnancies) at a single US site, adjusted gestational age ≥35 weeks and medically stable, randomised prospectively to methadone or morphine for neonatal abstinence syndrome, stratified by maternal treatment.
cards.result: Length of opioid treatment was significantly shorter with methadone: median 14 versus 21 days (P=.008) — a 7-day absolute difference in medians.

shelves.title: Posterior urethral valves in newborns: vesicostomy versus primary valve ablation — no kidney-outcome difference in any comparison, more surgery with diversion, and bladder studies that disagree
shelves.question: What are the treatments for urine blockage in newborns (posterior urethral valves) — in newborn boys with posterior urethral valves, how do initial vesicostomy and primary valve ablation compare on kidney outcomes, bladder function and burden of surgery?
shelves.mesh: Child · Child, Preschool · Creatinine/urine · Cystostomy · Electrocoagulation · Humans · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Kidney Function Tests · Postoperative Period · Treatment Outcome · Ureterostomy · Urethra/abnormalities · Urethra/surgery · Urethral Obstruction/congenital · Urethral Obstruction/surgery · Urinary Bladder/physiopathology · Urinary Diversion · Urodynamics
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the two operations made no difference to kidney outcomes) — every comparison fetched is observational, and on kidney outcomes they agree: no significant difference between initial vesicostomy and primary valve ablation. In the matched newborn cohort (Weitzner 2025, PMID: 40750022; 12 versus 12 matched neonates), creatinine did not differ at 6 weeks (P = .74) or 1 year (P = .89) and time to renal replacement therapy did not differ (hazard ratio 1.32, 95% CI 0.32–5.45; P = .70). In the London comparison (Godbole 2007, PMID: 18947754; 54 boys), adjusted GFR and 1-year creatinine did not differ (P = 0.16 and P = 0.87). In the 100-patient long-term series (Smith 1996, PMID: 8627873), 13% had end-stage renal disease by age 15 with no statistical difference in age at end-stage disease between initial treatments — but diversion meant significantly more surgery. Bladder function is where the studies pull apart: one comparative urodynamic study (Puri 2002, PMID: 12415375; 67 patients) found vesicostomy bladders smaller and less compliant (mean maximal cystometric capacity 62% of normal versus 96% after fulguration; P = 0.002). Observational-only evidence caps this shelf at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Weitzner 2025 (matched newborns, 12 versus 12): no difference in creatinine at 6 weeks (P = .74) or 1 year (P = .89), and no difference in time to renal replacement therapy (HR 1.32, 95% CI 0.32–5.45; P = .70)
cards.summary: Weitzner 2025 (matched newborns, 12 versus 12): no difference in creatinine at 6 weeks (P = .74) or 1 year (P = .89), and no difference in time to renal replacement therapy (HR 1.32, 95% CI 0.32–5.45; P = .70)
cards.type: Retrospective matched cohort, primary valve ablation versus vesicostomy (Weitzner 2025)
cards.people: 24 neonates with posterior urethral valves treated at two institutions between 1995 and 2021 — 12 by primary valve ablation (with or without progressive urethral dilation, which made ablation feasible in infants previously too small) and 12 by primary vesicostomy — matched on creatinine at intervention, gestational age, and age/weight at intervention.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in serum creatinine at 6 weeks (P = .74) or 1 year (P = .89). Kaplan-Meier analysis showed no significant difference in time to renal replacement therapy between groups (HR 1.32, 95% CI 0.32–5.45; P = .70), and the findings persisted after adjustment for clinical covariates (OR 1.24, 95% CI 0.10–15.9; P = .87). The authors concluded renal outcomes were comparable, while noting vesicostomy may impose greater surgical burden and disrupt bladder cycling.
cards.watchOut: Matching removes the oldest bias in this literature — that the smallest, sickest babies got vesicostomies — but 12 babies per arm leaves confidence intervals wide enough (HR 0.32–5.45) to hide a large effect in either direction. 'No significant difference' here means 'not measured precisely', not 'proven equal'.
cards.source: Weitzner AS, Broadwell NH, Diah J, Sholklapper T, Griggs-Demmin A, Mudalegundi S, Smith EA, Wu CQ. cards.headline: Godbole 2007 (54 boys): adjusted GFR and 1-year creatinine did not differ between vesicostomy and primary fulguration (P = 0.16 and P = 0.87); dryness 79% versus 64% (P = 0.43)
cards.summary: Godbole 2007 (54 boys): adjusted GFR and 1-year creatinine did not differ between vesicostomy and primary fulguration (P = 0.16 and P = 0.87); dryness 79% versus 64% (P = 0.43)
cards.type: Retrospective comparison, vesicostomy versus primary fulguration (Godbole 2007)
cards.people: 54 boys with posterior urethral valves over 1 year of age who had not undergone renal transplant — 23 managed by initial vesicostomy and 31 by primary valve fulguration — assessed on ultrasound findings, continence status, glomerular filtration rate and 1-year creatinine.
cards.result: Ultrasound examinations were normal in 9 of 19 (47.4%) of the vesicostomy group and 11 of 24 (45.8%) of the fulguration group, with graded results not significantly different (P = 0.24). Vesicostomy patients were more often dry (79% versus 64%, P = 0.43). The vesicostomy group had on average higher GFR (95.26 versus 85.79) and lower 1-year creatinine values (49.58 versus 52.46, units as printed in the record), but after accounting for age differences between groups there was no significant difference in GFR or 1-year creatinine (P = 0.16 and P = 0.87). The authors concluded the major outcomes tended to favour vesicostomy, but confidence intervals were wide and differences of clinical importance could not be discounted.
cards.watchOut: Unadjusted numbers favour the vesicostomy group, but the vesicostomy boys were older — once age is accounted for, every advantage disappears into non-significance. Ultrasound denominators (19 and 24) are smaller than the group sizes (23 and 31), so some boys contribute no imaging outcome.
cards.source: Godbole P, Wade A, Mushtaq I, Wilcox DT. Vesicostomy vs primary ablation for posterior urethral valves: always a difference in outcome? Journal of Pediatric Urology. 2007. cards.headline: Smith 1996 (100 patients, median follow-up 11.2 years): 13% end-stage renal disease by age 15, no difference by initial treatment — but diversion meant significantly more operations
cards.summary: Smith 1996 (100 patients, median follow-up 11.2 years): 13% end-stage renal disease by age 15, no difference by initial treatment — but diversion meant significantly more operations
cards.type: Retrospective long-term case series with treatment comparison (Smith 1996)
cards.people: 100 patients with posterior urethral valves treated before 1985 with primary valve ablation (74%), vesicostomy (13%) or high diversion (9%), reviewed with median follow-up of 11.2 years; outcomes included end-stage renal disease, later diversion procedures, bladder storage capacity and continence.
cards.result: Overall 13% of patients had end-stage renal disease by age 15 years. Kaplan-Meier analysis indicated no statistical difference between treatments in patient age at end-stage renal disease development. Secondary diversion rarely helped: 3 patients initially treated with valve ablation and 3 initially treated with vesicostomy later underwent high diversion but none benefited, and of 4 ablation patients who subsequently underwent vesicostomy only 1 benefited. Bladder storage capacity was well preserved; diurnal continence developed in 46% of patients by age 10 and only 1 remained incontinent after age 20. Comparing the treatment groups revealed a significant increase in the amount of surgery in infants with diversion. The authors concluded their results were equivalent to the best published series advocating high diversion, and that avoiding diversion preserves bladder function and decreases the need for bladder augmentation.
cards.watchOut: A pre-1985 treatment era: neonatal intensive care, ablation instruments and dialysis have all changed since these boys were treated, and treatment was allocated by the practice of the time, not by chance — the 74/13/9 split means the diversion groups are small (13 and 9 patients). Its durable contributions are the 13% end-stage figure and the extra-surgery cost of diversion.

cards.headline: Puri 2002 (67 patients, urodynamics in all): vesicostomy bladders were smaller and less compliant — maximal cystometric capacity 62% of normal versus 96% after fulguration (P = 0.002)
cards.summary: Puri 2002 (67 patients, urodynamics in all): vesicostomy bladders were smaller and less compliant — maximal cystometric capacity 62% of normal versus 96% after fulguration (P = 0.002)
cards.type: Comparative urodynamic study by initial treatment (Puri 2002)
cards.people: 67 patients with posterior urethral valves treated between 1985 and 2000, grouped by initial surgical treatment — fulguration (n = 38), vesicostomy (n = 25) and ureterostomy (n = 4) — all undergoing urodynamic studies of flow rates, residual volume, maximal cystometric capacity (MCC), compliance, detrusor activity and pressure-specific bladder volume at 30 cm water.
cards.result: Mean percent MCC was 62%, 96% and 100% of normal in the vesicostomy, fulguration and ureterostomy groups respectively (P = 0.002); vesicostomy adversely affected bladder capacity and compliance (P = 0.007). Pressure-specific bladder volume was decreased in 48% of the vesicostomy group (mean 75% of normal versus 95% and 96%; P = 0.01), and uninhibited contractions were present in 21 patients, 14 of them in the vesicostomy group (P = 0.01). The predominant patterns were a good-capacity compliant bladder after fulguration and a small-capacity hyperreflexic bladder after vesicostomy. The authors concluded primary valve ablation is associated with better bladder function than vesicostomy and should be the treatment of choice.
cards.watchOut: This card conflicts in spirit with the Godbole card's dryness trend (79% vesicostomy versus 64%) — urodynamic capacity and day-to-day dryness are different outcomes measured in different eras and centres, and neither study randomised. Boys chosen for vesicostomy may have had worse bladders to begin with; the study cannot separate the operation's effect from the reason it was chosen.
cards.source: Puri A, Grover VP, Agarwala S, Mitra DK, Bhatnagar V. Initial surgical treatment as a determinant of bladder dysfunction in posterior urethral valves. Pediatric Surgery International. 2002. PMID: 12415375. Registry ID: none in the record (comparative study). cards.headline: Synthesis: kidneys do not separate the operations in any comparison; the argument is about bladders and burden of surgery
cards.summary: Synthesis: kidneys do not separate the operations in any comparison; the argument is about bladders and burden of surgery
cards.people: Weitzner 2025 (24 matched neonates), Godbole 2007 (54 boys), Smith 1996 (100 patients, median 11.2 years), Puri 2002 (67 patients with urodynamics). All observational; no randomised trial exists in the records fetched.
cards.result: Renal outcomes: no significant difference between initial vesicostomy and primary valve ablation in the matched cohort (creatinine P = .74/.89; renal replacement therapy HR 1.32, 95% CI 0.32–5.45), the London comparison (adjusted GFR P = 0.16; creatinine P = 0.87), or the long-term series (13% end-stage renal disease by age 15, no difference in age at end-stage disease). Burden: diversion significantly increased the number of operations (Smith 1996). Bladder: one urodynamic comparison favoured ablation (capacity 96% versus 62% of normal, P = 0.002; Puri 2002), while reported dryness in another favoured vesicostomy non-significantly (79% versus 64%; Godbole 2007). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the two operations made no difference to kidney outcomes) — observational evidence only, with wide intervals in the best-matched study.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Nothing here covers antenatal intervention, clean intermittent catheterisation, overnight drainage or bladder-neck procedures, which had no comparative records with extractable numbers in this session's fetch. Where a newborn is too small or too sick for ablation, vesicostomy remains the fallback the cohorts were built around — the shelf answers which first operation the evidence separates, and on kidneys it separates neither.

shelves.title: Auditory processing disorder in children: three small randomised trials, all positive on questionnaires or trained tasks and null or untested on blinded behaviour — 120 children is the whole evidence base
shelves.question: How is auditory processing disorder treated — in children diagnosed with auditory processing disorder, do auditory training programmes, language training, FM systems or remote-microphone hearing aids improve listening, and how strong is the trial evidence?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Age Factors · Analysis of Variance · Auditory Perception · Auditory Perceptual Disorders/diagnosis · Auditory Perceptual Disorders/psychology · Auditory Perceptual Disorders/therapy · Awareness · Child · Child Language · Cues · Discrimination, Psychological · Female · Hearing Aids · Humans · Language Therapy/instrumentation · Male · Mental Recall · Neuropsychological Tests · New Zealand · Pitch Discrimination · Predictive Value of Tests · Reading · Severity of Illness Index · Speech Perception · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — three small randomised trials exist, and each is positive on some outcomes and null on others, with the gains concentrated in trained tasks and parent/teacher questionnaires rather than in blinded real-world measures. Computer-based speech auditory training added to standard school strategies improved all its outcome measures in the trained group only, with effect sizes of 0.76 to 1.7, and speech-in-noise gains that persisted at 3 months (Loo 2016, PMID: 26418044; 39 children). A five-arm trial of bottom-up training, top-down language training and FM systems reported positive outcomes on several measures with an unchanged control group, but published no extractable effect sizes in its record (Sharma 2012, PMID: 22512470; 55 children). Remote-microphone hearing aids improved children's self-reported classroom listening at 3 and 6 months (mean difference 7.31 points at 3 months, P = 0.014) while behavioural listening-in-noise and attention measures did not change significantly (Stavrinos 2020, PMID: 32973443; NCT02353091; 26 children). Total randomised evidence: 120 children across three trials, no blinded outcome assessment in any, and the diagnosis itself remains contested. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): something in these interventions moves questionnaire and trained-task scores; whether auditory processing disorder treatment changes real-world listening is unproven.

cards.headline: Loo 2016 (prospective RCT, 39 children): 12 weeks of home computer-based speech training improved every outcome measure (effect sizes 0.76–1.7) in the trained group only, with speech-in-noise gains kept at 3 months
cards.summary: Loo 2016 (prospective RCT, 39 children): 12 weeks of home computer-based speech training improved every outcome measure (effect sizes 0.76–1.7) in the trained group only, with speech-in-noise gains kept at 3 months
cards.type: Prospective randomised controlled trial of computer-based auditory training (Loo 2016)
cards.people: 39 children aged 7–11 years diagnosed with auditory processing disorder — 19 controls receiving standard school-based listening strategies and 20 receiving the same strategies plus a 12-week home computer-based speech auditory training programme, practised 5 days a week.
cards.result: All outcome measures improved significantly after intervention in the intervention group only, with effect sizes ranging from 0.76 to 1.7; in the trained group, gains in speech-in-noise perception correlated significantly with gains on the Children's Auditory Performance Scale questionnaire, while no such correlation appeared in controls. Speech-in-noise improvement was sustained in the intervention group at retest 3 months later (only the intervention group was retested). The authors concluded the training might be a necessary adjunct for these children, whose auditory deficits did not resolve with school strategies alone.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-nine children, no blinding, and outcomes measured largely on tasks resembling the training itself — improvement on trained-style tasks is the weakest form of evidence for a training intervention, and the control group's flat scores may reflect receiving nothing new to practise rather than a true contrast. The 3-month durability claim rests on retesting only the trained group.
cards.source: Loo JHY, Rosen S, Bamiou DE. Auditory Training Effects on Speech-in-Noise Perception and Auditory Processing in Children with Auditory Processing Disorder: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Ear and Hearing. 2016. PMID: 26418044. cards.headline: Sharma 2012 (RCT, 55 children, five arms): bottom-up training, top-down language training and FM systems each showed positive outcomes on several measures, control group unchanged — but the record reports no effect sizes
cards.summary: Sharma 2012 (RCT, 55 children, five arms): bottom-up training, top-down language training and FM systems each showed positive outcomes on several measures, control group unchanged — but the record reports no effect sizes
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial of auditory/language training and FM systems (Sharma 2012)
cards.people: 55 children aged 7–13 years diagnosed with auditory processing disorder, randomised across bottom-up auditory training, top-down language training, each with or without a personal FM system, and a no-intervention control group; interventions ran 6 weeks with weekly 1-hour clinic sessions plus 1–2 hours of weekly homework.
cards.result: The authors report positive outcomes for both the bottom-up and top-down interventions, and for the FM system, on several outcome measures, with no change on retest in the control group. The published record gives no numerical effect sizes, confidence intervals or per-arm outcome values — the quantitative content extractable from it is the design itself: 55 children across five arms, 6 weeks of intervention. This card is included because it is one of only three randomised trials in the field; its evidentiary weight is correspondingly limited to 'a small multi-arm trial reported benefit'.
cards.watchOut: Five arms over 55 children means roughly 11 children per arm, and a results section the abstract summarises only qualitatively — treat this as a feasibility-grade signal, not an effect estimate. With several outcome measures and several arms, 'positive on several measures' is also the pattern multiple testing produces by chance.
cards.source: Sharma M, Purdy SC, Kelly AS. A randomized control trial of interventions in school-aged children with auditory processing disorders. International Journal of Audiology. 2012. PMID: 22512470. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Stavrinos 2020 (RCT, 26 children): remote-microphone hearing aids improved self-reported classroom listening at 3 months (mean difference 7.31, P = 0.014) and 6 months (5.00, P = 0.016) — behavioural listening and attention measures did not change
cards.summary: Stavrinos 2020 (RCT, 26 children): remote-microphone hearing aids improved self-reported classroom listening at 3 months (mean difference 7.31, P = 0.014) and 6 months (5.00, P = 0.016) — behavioural listening and attention measures did not change
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial of remote-microphone hearing aids (Stavrinos 2020)
cards.people: 26 children aged 7–12 years with auditory processing disorder — 13 fitted with remote-microphone hearing aids (a transmitter worn by the teacher streaming speech to ear-level receivers) and 13 controls — followed for 6 months, with self-reported classroom listening (LIFE-R questionnaire), behavioural listening-in-noise and attention measures as outcomes.
cards.result: Self-reported listening ability on the LIFE-R improved significantly in the intervention group at 3 months (mean difference 7.31, standard error 2.113; P = 0.014) and at 6 months (mean difference 5.00, standard error 1.468; P = 0.016). Behavioural measures of listening in noise and attention did not significantly change. The authors concluded remote-microphone aids improved perceived classroom listening without measurable change on the behavioural tests used.
cards.watchOut: The outcome that moved is the child's own report while wearing a visible device the child knows is meant to help — the classic setup for expectation effects, with 13 children per arm and no blinded assessment. The dissociation (questionnaire improves, behaviour does not) is the single most informative pattern on this shelf.
cards.source: Stavrinos G, et al. Remote Microphone Hearing Aids and Auditory Processing Disorder in Children: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Frontiers in Neuroscience. 2020. PMID: 32973443. Registry ID: NCT02353091. MeSH: not rendered in the record as fetched this session — see build flag in the part summary.

cards.headline: Synthesis: 120 randomised children in total, gains on trained tasks and questionnaires, nulls on blinded-style behavioural measures — the field's evidence is real but weak
cards.summary: Synthesis: 120 randomised children in total, gains on trained tasks and questionnaires, nulls on blinded-style behavioural measures — the field's evidence is real but weak
cards.people: Loo 2016 (39 children, auditory training), Sharma 2012 (55 children, training and FM arms), Stavrinos 2020 (26 children, remote-microphone aids).
cards.result: Auditory training: significant improvement on all measures in the trained group only, effect sizes 0.76–1.7, speech-in-noise gains sustained at 3 months in the trained group (Loo). Training/FM multi-arm trial: positive outcomes reported on several measures, no extractable effect sizes (Sharma). Remote-microphone aids: self-reported classroom listening improved (mean difference 7.31 at 3 months, P = 0.014; 5.00 at 6 months, P = 0.016) with no significant change in behavioural listening-in-noise or attention (Stavrinos). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — small samples, no blinding, surrogate and self-report outcomes, and a contested diagnosis underneath all three trials.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Auditory processing disorder's diagnostic validity is itself disputed in the literature; this shelf cards only the treatment trials and takes no position on the diagnosis. Commercial brain-training programmes marketed for APD had no qualifying randomised records with extractable numbers in this session's fetch and are not carded.

shelves.title: Cradle cap: no treatment has been shown to beat the rash's own course — Cochrane found six tiny trials (310 infants, all very low-certainty) and no randomised test of antifungals, oils or salicylic acid at all
shelves.question: My baby has cradle cap (infantile seborrhoeic dermatitis) — do antifungal creams, steroid creams or any other treatment clear it faster than leaving it alone?
shelves.mesh: Dermatitis, Seborrheic/therapy · Emollients/therapeutic use · Humans · Infant · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Scalp Dermatoses/therapy
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — cradle cap (infantile seborrhoeic dermatitis) is benign and self-limiting, and its trial record is exceptionally thin. The Cochrane review (Victoire 2019, PMID: 30828791) found just six randomised trials with 310 children (297 analysed), rated every comparison very low-certainty, and found NO trials of the treatments actually used — mineral oils, salicylic acid or antifungals. Within the trials that exist: a non-steroidal proprietary cream scored 96% success versus 92% on placebo at day 14; a moisturising gel plus shampoo reduced lesional score by 81.4% versus 70.2% for shampoo only (P=0.0092); hydrocortisone 1% lotion cured 95.8% versus 97.1% for licochalcone lotion — no difference; and oral biotin versus placebo (35 children in two trials) produced no reportable severity benefit. The one direct antifungal comparison is a non-randomised split-side study of 48 infants (Wannanukul 2004, PMID: 16083165): lesions cleared in 31% on the ketoconazole 2% side versus 35% on the hydrocortisone 1% side at one week, with all lesions in both groups cleared by the end of week two — the natural history of the condition doing most of the work. No trial measured quality of life. The honest summary: nothing has been shown to beat time, and the commonly recommended antifungal and oil treatments have never been randomised in infants.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2019: six trials, 310 infants, every result very low-certainty — and no trials at all of mineral oils, salicylic acid or antifungals
cards.summary: Cochrane 2019: six trials, 310 infants, every result very low-certainty — and no trials at all of mineral oils, salicylic acid or antifungals
cards.people: Six randomised trials (one cross-over) randomising 310 children and reporting outcomes for 297, mostly aged under seven months, with clinician-diagnosed infantile seborrhoeic dermatitis (including cradle cap) up to 24 months; two trials compared oral biotin with placebo, two compared proprietary products with placebo cream or control shampoo, and two compared topical corticosteroids with other products; treatment lasted 10–42 days.
cards.result: All results were based on very low-quality evidence, with unclear risk of bias in most domains and high risk of performance, detection or attrition bias in several trials. No study measured quality of life. The reviewers found no trials testing commonly used treatments such as mineral oils, salicylic acid, or antifungals. Their conclusion: the review identified only a limited number of studies, there is uncertainty regarding the effectiveness and safety of the studied treatments due to the very low-certainty evidence for all comparisons and outcomes, and in most studies the prognosis for the condition was favourable regardless of intervention.
cards.watchOut: A review whose main finding is an absence — of trials of the standard treatments, and of certainty in the trials that exist — cannot be turned into a treatment recommendation in either direction. It does not show that antifungals or oils do not work in infants; it shows they have never been properly tested in infants, which is a different and more uncomfortable statement.
cards.source: Victoire A, Magin P, Coughlan J, van Driel ML. Interventions for infantile seborrhoeic dermatitis (including cradle cap). Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2019. PMID: 30828791. cards.headline: What the six Cochrane trials actually tested: biotin no reportable benefit (n=35); a proprietary cream 96% versus 92% over placebo; a gel-plus-shampoo 81.4% versus 70.2%; hydrocortisone versus licochalcone 95.8% versus 97.1% cured
cards.summary: What the six Cochrane trials actually tested: biotin no reportable benefit (n=35); a proprietary cream 96% versus 92% over placebo; a gel-plus-shampoo 81.4% versus 70.2%; hydrocortisone versus licochalcone 95.8% versus 97.1% cured
cards.type: Constituent randomised comparisons within the Cochrane review (Victoire 2019)
cards.people: The constituent randomised comparisons inside the Cochrane review (Victoire 2019): oral biotin versus placebo in two trials (n=35); proprietary products versus placebo cream or control shampoo in two trials (n=160); topical corticosteroids versus other products in two trials (n=102). Treatment durations of one to three weeks; all results very low-quality evidence.
cards.result: Biotin versus placebo: one trial reported only a change in rash duration, the other only 'no statistically significant difference' in severity at three weeks, with no raw data; neither reported adverse events. Proprietary products: a non-steroidal cream (Promiseb — the proprietary product named in the review) achieved 96% success versus 92% on placebo at day 14, with no adverse events; lactamide MEA gel plus shampoo reduced lesional score (surface area covered) by 81.4% versus 70.2% for shampoo only (P=0.0092) at day 21. Steroid comparisons: hydrocortisone 1% lotion versus licochalcone 0.025% lotion cured 95.8% versus 97.1% (no significant difference) at day 14; flumethasone pivalate 0.02% ointment versus eosin 2% aqueous solution left 9% versus 7% of body surface affected at day 10, with all infants under 10% involvement and no adverse events.
cards.watchOut: The near-identical cure rates in the steroid comparisons (95.8% vs 97.1%) mostly show that almost every infant's rash clears within two weeks whatever is applied — a self-limiting condition makes weak treatments look effective and head-to-head trials nearly uninformative without a no-treatment arm. The proprietary-product results come from single small trials of named commercial preparations and should not be generalised to other creams.
cards.source: Victoire A, Magin P, Coughlan J, van Driel ML. Interventions for infantile seborrhoeic dermatitis (including cradle cap). Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2019. PMID: 30828791. cards.headline: Wannanukul 2004: ketoconazole 2% cream versus hydrocortisone 1% cream, split-side in 48 infants — cleared in 31% versus 35% at one week, and everything had cleared by two weeks
cards.summary: Wannanukul 2004: ketoconazole 2% cream versus hydrocortisone 1% cream, split-side in 48 infants — cleared in 31% versus 35% at one week, and everything had cleared by two weeks
cards.people: 48 infants aged 2 weeks to 2 years with a clinical diagnosis of infantile seborrheic dermatitis at King Chulalongkorn Memorial Hospital, Bangkok (December 2001 to November 2003), treated with 2% ketoconazole cream on the left side of the lesion and 1% hydrocortisone cream on the right side, twice daily; severity scored for erythema, scale and crust (0 = none to 3 = severe).
cards.result: Responses to ketoconazole and hydrocortisone did not differ significantly at 2–3 days or at 4–7 days. By one week both sides had improved significantly; lesions were cleared in 31% of the ketoconazole group and 35% of the hydrocortisone group. All skin lesions were cleared by the end of the second week. The authors concluded the two creams' efficacy was not significantly different, and that ketoconazole is an option that avoids the side effects of topical corticosteroid used long-term or over a large surface area.
cards.watchOut: Not a randomised trial — every infant received both creams, so spread between sides and the condition's own resolution blur the comparison, and with no untreated side the study cannot show either cream beats doing nothing: universal clearance by week two is exactly what untreated cradle cap does. It was also not among the randomised trials in the Cochrane review. Its value is narrow: no sign that the steroid side cleared faster than the antifungal side.
cards.source: Wannanukul S, Chiabunkana J. Comparative study of 2% ketoconazole cream and 1% hydrocortisone cream in the treatment of infantile seborrheic dermatitis. Journal of the Medical Association of Thailand. 2004. PMID: 16083165. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a self-limiting rash, six small randomised trials of other things, and no randomised test of the treatments parents are actually advised to use
cards.summary: Synthesis: a self-limiting rash, six small randomised trials of other things, and no randomised test of the treatments parents are actually advised to use
cards.people: The Cochrane review of six randomised trials (310 children; Victoire 2019) and one non-randomised split-side comparative study of 48 infants (Wannanukul 2004).
cards.result: Tested treatments: oral biotin — no reportable benefit over placebo (n=35); a proprietary non-steroidal cream — 96% versus 92% success over placebo; a moisturising gel plus shampoo — 81.4% versus 70.2% lesional-score reduction over shampoo alone; hydrocortisone versus licochalcone — 95.8% versus 97.1% cured, no difference. Untested in randomised trials: mineral oils, salicylic acid and antifungals — the mainstays of advice. Ketoconazole versus hydrocortisone (non-randomised): 31% versus 35% cleared at one week, all cleared by two weeks in both. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): no treatment for cradle cap has been shown, at usable certainty, to beat the condition's own course.
cards.watchOut: Tier C. Adult seborrhoeic dermatitis and dandruff have a separate, stronger antifungal trial record homed elsewhere in this library (see the ketoconazole shampoo shelf, #2494) — none of it transfers to infants, in whom the Cochrane review explicitly found no antifungal trials. Widespread, infected, weeping or persistent rash in an infant is a different clinical problem from ordinary cradle cap and is outside this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Victoire A et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2019 (PMID: 30828791); Wannanukul S & Chiabunkana J. Journal of the Medical Association of Thailand. 2004 (PMID: 16083165).

shelves.title: Developmental co-ordination disorder (dyspraxia): CO-OP and task-oriented therapy improve the goals children practise — but the Cochrane review found no motor-performance effect in the randomised trials alone, and rated the evidence very low to low quality
shelves.question: My child has developmental co-ordination disorder (dyspraxia) — do task-oriented therapy or the CO-OP approach actually improve their motor skills?
shelves.mesh: Child · Humans · Motor Skills Disorders/therapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic/statistics & numerical data · Task Performance and Analysis
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — children with developmental co-ordination disorder (DCD, dyspraxia) are usually offered task-oriented therapy, and the best synthesis is unusually candid about how little certainty it provides. The Cochrane review of task-oriented interventions (Miyahara 2017, PMID: 28758189; 15 studies, 649 children aged 5–12) found its main pooled analysis — two RCTs plus four quasi-RCTs, 169 children — favoured task-oriented intervention over no intervention for motor performance (mean difference −3.63, 95% CI −5.88 to −1.39; P=0.002), but rated that very low-quality evidence; restricted to the two true RCTs (51 children), there was no effect (mean difference −2.34, 95% CI −7.50 to 2.83; P=0.38). The largest single trial of the flagship approach, CO-OP (Cognitive Orientation to daily Occupational Performance), randomised 78 children aged 8–12 to immediate treatment or a waitlist (Izadi-Najafabadi 2022, PMID: 35466705; NCT02597751): goal performance and movement quality improved markedly after treatment in children with DCD with and without ADHD (both P<0.001) and gains were maintained at three months, but transfer to overall motor skills appeared only in the DCD-only group. The original CO-OP pilot (Miller 2001, PMID: 11471396) compared CO-OP with contemporary therapy in just 20 children, with greater improvement on self-rated and observer-rated goal measures but not on the standardised motor test. Stamp is held at MAYBE (weak evidence): goal-specific gains are repeatedly seen, a general motor-performance effect is not established.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2017: pooling everything favoured task-oriented intervention (mean difference −3.63; P=0.002) — but the two true RCTs alone showed no effect, and the evidence was very low to low quality
cards.summary: Cochrane 2017: pooling everything favoured task-oriented intervention (mean difference −3.63; P=0.002) — but the two true RCTs alone showed no effect, and the evidence was very low to low quality
cards.people: 15 studies (eight RCTs and seven quasi-RCTs) with 649 children and adolescents aged 5–12 years with developmental co-ordination disorder, from Australia, Canada, China, Sweden, Taiwan and the UK, comparing task-oriented interventions (5–50 sessions of 30–90 minutes, mostly under six months) with inactive or active controls; outcomes were standardised motor-performance measures, with GRADE quality ratings.
cards.result: A meta-analysis of two RCTs and four quasi-RCTs found in favour of task-oriented interventions for improved motor performance versus no intervention (mean difference −3.63, 95% CI −5.88 to −1.39; P=0.002; I²=43%; 6 trials, 169 children; very low-quality evidence — lower scores denote better performance on the pooled measure as reported). A meta-analysis of the two RCTs alone found no effect (mean difference −2.34, 95% CI −7.50 to 2.83; P=0.38; I²=42%; 51 children; low-quality evidence). Risk of bias was moderate to high across studies, no meta-analysis of secondary (psychosocial, activity, participation) outcomes was possible, and two studies reported no adverse effects. The authors concluded: 'We have very little confidence in the effect estimate: the true effect is likely to be substantially different from the estimate of effect', and that their conclusions are inconsistent with previous reviews that unanimously reported benefit.
cards.watchOut: The headline pooled result leans on quasi-randomised studies; remove them and the effect disappears into a wide interval on 51 children. Blinding of children and therapists is impossible in these interventions, so expectation and effort effects are baked in. The review's own authors explicitly disown confidence in the estimate — any shelf stamp stronger than MAYBE would misrepresent it.
cards.source: Miyahara M, Hillier SL, Pridham L, Nakagawa S. Task-oriented interventions for children with developmental co-ordination disorder. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2017. PMID: 28758189. Registry ID: none in the record (systematic review). cards.headline: CO-OP waitlist RCT (Izadi-Najafabadi 2022): goal performance rose from 2.7 to 7.0 after treatment (P<0.001) and held at 3 months — but transfer to overall motor skills occurred only in children without ADHD
cards.summary: CO-OP waitlist RCT (Izadi-Najafabadi 2022): goal performance rose from 2.7 to 7.0 after treatment (P<0.001) and held at 3 months — but transfer to overall motor skills occurred only in children without ADHD
cards.people: 78 children aged 8–12 years at BC Children's Hospital, Vancouver — 37 with developmental co-ordination disorder and 41 with DCD plus ADHD — randomised to treatment or waitlist groups in a randomised waitlist-control trial; intervention was one hour of Cognitive Orientation to daily Occupational Performance (CO-OP) once weekly for 10 weeks; outcomes included the Performance Quality Rating Scale (PQRS) for child-chosen goals and standardised motor testing, with three-month follow-up.
cards.result: Both diagnostic groups improved significantly (P<0.001) in motor performance of their goals after CO-OP (DCD: pre 2.7 ± 2.2, post 7.0 ± 1.0; DCD+ADHD: pre 2.3 ± 1.7, post 7.0 ± 1.5) and in movement quality (DCD: pre 3.0 ± 1.5, post 6.3 ± 1.7; DCD+ADHD: pre 3.0 ± 1.9, post 5.7 ± 2.3). Three months after treatment, children maintained their gains, but only children with DCD alone showed transfer of learning to overall motor skills (follow-up comparison P<0.001 as reported). The authors concluded CO-OP was similarly effective for children with DCD with or without ADHD in achieving and maintaining functional motor goals, with transfer limited to the DCD-only group.
cards.watchOut: A waitlist control cannot separate CO-OP's specific effect from attention, practice and expectation — children knew whether they were being treated, and the headline outcomes are ratings of the very goals the child practised, where improvement is easiest to show. The PubMed page for this report could not be opened this session, so its MeSH is recorded as not captured; the figures and registry ID are from the trial report as reproduced in this session's fetched sources, and the author list is given in abbreviated form for the same reason.

cards.headline: The original CO-OP pilot (Miller 2001): in 20 children, CO-OP improved self-rated and observer-rated goal performance more than contemporary therapy — but not the standardised motor proficiency test
cards.summary: The original CO-OP pilot (Miller 2001): in 20 children, CO-OP improved self-rated and observer-rated goal performance more than contemporary therapy — but not the standardised motor proficiency test
cards.type: Pilot comparative trial, CO-OP versus contemporary treatment (Miller 2001)
cards.people: 20 children with developmental coordination disorder (mean age 9.05 years, SD 1.23; normal intelligence; below the 15th percentile on a standardised motor test) in a pilot trial comparing the Cognitive Orientation to daily Occupational Performance (CO-OP) — problem-solving strategies and guided discovery of child- and task-specific strategies — with the Contemporary Treatment Approach (CTA: neuromuscular, multi-sensory and biomechanical methods); goals were child-chosen in both groups; measures included the Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM), Performance Quality Rating Scale (PQRS), Vineland scales and the Bruininks-Oseretsky Test of Motor Proficiency (BOTMP).
cards.result: Both treatments improved COPM self-ratings of performance and satisfaction, with greater improvements in the CO-OP group; the same pattern appeared in PQRS scores and Vineland motor scores, but not in BOTMP measures. Follow-up suggested greater long-term maintenance of goals and strategies after CO-OP, and parents rated CO-OP more useful. The authors state plainly that the outcome needs replication: there was no untreated control group, and the groups differed on relevant measures before treatment.
cards.watchOut: Twenty children (n=20, printed here because small samples govern how this card may be read), pre-treatment group differences, and no untreated control: this card is carded as the origin of the CO-OP approach and an early statement of the pattern the whole shelf shows — goal measures move, standardised motor proficiency does not — not as evidence of efficacy on its own.

PMID: 11471396. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era pilot trial). cards.headline: Synthesis: children get better at the goals they practise — whether task-oriented therapy improves underlying motor performance is unproven on the randomised record
cards.summary: Synthesis: children get better at the goals they practise — whether task-oriented therapy improves underlying motor performance is unproven on the randomised record
cards.people: A Cochrane review of 15 studies (649 children; Miyahara 2017), the 78-child randomised waitlist trial of CO-OP (Izadi-Najafabadi 2022) and the 20-child CO-OP pilot (Miller 2001).
cards.result: Goal-specific performance: improved after CO-OP in the waitlist trial (PQRS-type scores roughly 2.7 → 7.0; P<0.001), maintained at three months, with transfer to overall motor skills only in DCD without ADHD. General motor performance: pooled quasi-inclusive analysis favoured task-oriented intervention (MD −3.63; P=0.002, very low-quality), the RCT-only analysis did not (MD −2.34; P=0.38, 51 children), and the pilot found no advantage on the standardised proficiency test. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — task-oriented and CO-OP therapy plausibly help children achieve chosen functional goals; a dependable effect on measured motor ability has not been shown.
cards.watchOut: Tier C. This shelf covers task-oriented approaches including CO-OP for children roughly 5–12 years old. It does not cover process-oriented therapies, supplements, or interventions for the co-occurring conditions (ADHD, language and learning disorders) that often drive referral, and no long-term follow-up beyond three months was carded.
cards.source: Synthesis of Miyahara M et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2017 (PMID: 28758189); Izadi-Najafabadi S et al. Clinical Rehabilitation. 2022 (PMID: 35466705); Miller LT et al. Human Movement Science. 2001 (PMID: 11471396).

shelves.title: GnRH analogues for central precocious puberty: treated girls end about 4.8 cm taller than untreated girls in the comparative pooling — from observational studies, with no randomised trial
shelves.question: In children whose puberty has started too early (central precocious puberty), do GnRH analogue injections suppress puberty and leave them taller as adults than they would have been without treatment?
shelves.mesh: Body Height · Child · Female · Gonadotropin-Releasing Hormone · Humans · Male · Puberty, Precocious/drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — there has never been a randomised placebo-controlled trial of GnRH analogues in central precocious puberty (CPP); the entire case rests on comparative observational studies, which caps this stamp at POSSIBLE. The systematic review and meta-analysis (Luo X et al., PMID: 33387371; 98 studies, 5,475 individuals) found, in its comparative studies, that GnRH analogue treatment increased final adult height in girls with idiopathic CPP versus no treatment by a mean difference of 4.83 cm (95% CI 2.32 to 7.34; 4 studies, n=242; I² = 49%) and decreased BMI by 1.01 kg/m² (95% CI −1.64 to −0.37; 3 studies, n=334), with no significant difference in polycystic ovary syndrome incidence (risk ratio 1.21, 95% CI 0.46 to 3.15; 3 studies, n=179); the reviewers graded the evidence very low to moderate and called the evidence for other long-term outcomes very weak. A direct treated-versus-untreated comparison (Poomthavorn P et al., PMID: 21501002) found adult height 158.6 (SD 5.2) cm in 47 treated girls versus 154.8 (5.6) cm in 11 untreated girls (P < 0.05), a 4.7 cm gain over pre-treatment predicted adult height in the treated group, and menstruation resuming 0.9 (0.5) years after stopping treatment — pubertal suppression is reversible. A large treated-only series (Yang EH et al., PMID: 37015776; 246 girls) shows predicted adult height rising on treatment in both CPP and early-puberty (onset 8–9 years) girls, but with no untreated comparator it cannot separate drug effect from prediction drift. BOUNDARY: delayed puberty is a different question — constitutional delay in boys is homed on Shelf #2907 (letrozole/testosterone) — and adding growth hormone to a GnRH analogue is not covered here. The height benefit is best supported for girls treated young with rapidly progressive CPP; for slowly progressive or borderline early puberty the comparative data are thinnest.

cards.headline: Luo 2021 (systematic review & meta-analysis, 98 studies, 5,475 children): final adult height +4.83 cm (95% CI 2.32 to 7.34) and BMI −1.01 kg/m² for GnRH analogue versus no treatment in girls with idiopathic CPP; PCOS not increased (RR 1.21, 0.46 to 3.15)
cards.summary: Luo 2021 (systematic review & meta-analysis, 98 studies, 5,475 children): final adult height +4.83 cm (95% CI 2.32 to 7.34) and BMI −1.01 kg/m² for GnRH analogue versus no treatment in girls with idiopathic CPP; PCOS not increased (RR 1.21, 0.46 to 3.15)
cards.people: 98 comparative and single-arm studies including 5,475 children with idiopathic central precocious puberty treated with gonadotropin-releasing hormone analogues (GnRHa), searched in PubMed, EMBASE and the Cochrane Library; protocol registered on PROSPERO (CRD42018102792). The pooled comparative estimates are for girls with idiopathic CPP, GnRHa versus no treatment.
cards.result: Evidence-based comparative studies showed GnRHa treatment increased final adult height (4 studies, n=242; mean difference 4.83 cm; 95% CI 2.32 to 7.34; I² = 49%) and decreased body mass index (3 studies, n=334; mean difference −1.01 kg/m²; 95% CI −1.64 to −0.37; I² = 0%) in girls with idiopathic CPP compared with no treatment. Polycystic ovary syndrome incidence did not significantly differ with and without treatment (3 studies, n=179; risk ratio 1.21; 95% CI 0.46 to 3.15; I² = 48%). Overall risk of bias across studies ranged from critical to moderate, quality of evidence per outcome ranged from very low to moderate, evidence for other long-term outcomes was very weak, and evidence in boys was limited.
cards.watchOut: The +4.83 cm is a mean difference from four non-randomised comparative studies totalling 242 girls — treated and untreated girls in such studies differ in ways statistics cannot fully remove (families who accept years of injections, and clinicians who offer them, are not random). I² of 49% says the studies also disagree with each other by a moderate amount. This is the best comparative estimate available and it is genuinely uncertain; it should not be quoted to a family as a promised 4.8 cm.
cards.source: Luo X, Liang Y, Hou L, Wu W, Ying Y, Ye F. Clinical Endocrinology. 2021. PMID: 33387371. Registry ID: none in the record (systematic review; PROSPERO CRD42018102792). cards.headline: Poomthavorn 2011 (treated vs untreated girls): adult height 158.6 cm versus 154.8 cm (P < 0.05); treated girls gained 4.7 cm over their predicted adult height, and periods returned 0.9 years after stopping
cards.summary: Poomthavorn 2011 (treated vs untreated girls): adult height 158.6 cm versus 154.8 cm (P < 0.05); treated girls gained 4.7 cm over their predicted adult height, and periods returned 0.9 years after stopping
cards.type: Comparative cohort study, treated versus untreated (Poomthavorn 2011)
cards.people: Girls with idiopathic central precocious puberty at a Bangkok hospital: 47 treated with a GnRH analogue (mean age at start 8.5 (SD 1.0) years) and 11 untreated, compared on adult height, BMI and time of menarche. At diagnosis the groups did not differ in age, bone age, height, weight, BMI z-scores, predicted adult height or target height.
cards.result: Mean (SD) adult height was greater in the treated group: 158.6 (5.2) cm versus 154.8 (5.6) cm in the untreated group (P < 0.05) — an absolute difference of 3.8 cm. Adult-height gain over pre-treatment predicted adult height in the treated group was 4.7 cm. BMI z-score in treated girls was 1.26 (0.95) before treatment and returned to normal (0.16 (1.0)) by the time adult height was reached. Menstruation occurred 0.9 (0.5) years after GnRH analogue discontinuation, with a regular pattern. The authors conclude long-term GnRHa therapy has a modest beneficial effect on adult height gain in girls with idiopathic CPP, with no detrimental effect on BMI or on hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis reactivation.
cards.watchOut: Eleven untreated girls is a very small comparator, and why those 11 were untreated (milder disease? family choice? late presentation?) is exactly the kind of difference that can manufacture a height gap. The reassuring half of this card — suppression reversing, with menarche about a year after the last injection and no lasting BMI penalty — is the part least vulnerable to that bias, and it matches the wider literature.
cards.source: Poomthavorn P, Suphasit R, Mahachoklertwattana P. Adult height, body mass index and time of menarche of girls with idiopathic central precocious puberty after gonadotropin-releasing hormone analogue treatment. Gynecological Endocrinology. 2011. PMID: 21501002. Registry ID: none in the record (observational study). cards.headline: Yang 2023 (246 treated girls, no untreated group): predicted adult height rose from 153.7 to 158.5 cm in CPP and from 154.8 to 159.3 cm in early puberty (onset 8–9 years) over treatment and follow-up
cards.summary: Yang 2023 (246 treated girls, no untreated group): predicted adult height rose from 153.7 to 158.5 cm in CPP and from 154.8 to 159.3 cm in early puberty (onset 8–9 years) over treatment and follow-up
cards.people: 246 girls treated with a GnRH agonist (leuprolide acetate or triptorelin acetate 90 µg/kg every 4 weeks) at Pusan National University Hospital, Korea, 2013–2021: 40 with central precocious puberty (breast development before age 8, advanced bone age, pubertal GnRH stimulation test) and 206 with early puberty (onset at 8–9 years), treated until chronological age 11 years or bone age 12–12.5 years.
cards.result: Predicted adult height (PAH) at baseline did not differ between the CPP group (153.67 ± 4.95 cm) and the early-puberty group (154.77 ± 3.72 cm). In the CPP group PAH rose significantly at treatment completion (156.01 ± 4.61 cm) and at final follow-up (158.52 ± 6.04 cm) versus baseline (both P < 0.001); in the early-puberty group it rose likewise (157.27 ± 3.60 cm at completion; 159.31 ± 4.26 cm at final follow-up; both P < 0.001). The amount of PAH increase did not differ significantly between the CPP and early-puberty groups. The authors conclude GnRH agonist treatment can help increase final height even in early puberty diagnosed after age 8.
cards.watchOut: There is no untreated girl in this study, and the outcome is predicted — not measured final — adult height: predictions are computed from bone age, and because treatment slows bone-age advance, the prediction mechanically improves on treatment whether or not final height does. This card shows the on-treatment pattern in a large modern series, including girls treated at 8–9 years; the causal claim rests on the comparative cards above, and it is weakest exactly in this older, borderline group.
cards.source: Yang EH, Jo HY, Park SJ, Yoo HW, Choi SH, Kim HY, Park KH, Kim YM, Kwak MJ. Effect of gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonist treatment on near final height in girls with central precocious puberty and early puberty. Annals of Pediatric Endocrinology & Metabolism. 2023. PMID: 37015776. Registry ID: none in the record (retrospective study). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: suppression works and reverses; the height dividend is about 4–5 cm in comparative data that were never randomised
cards.summary: Synthesis: suppression works and reverses; the height dividend is about 4–5 cm in comparative data that were never randomised
cards.people: A systematic review/meta-analysis of 98 studies (5,475 children; Luo 2021), one treated-versus-untreated cohort (47 vs 11 girls; Poomthavorn 2011), and one large treated-only series (246 girls; Yang 2023).
cards.result: Final adult height, treated versus untreated girls with idiopathic CPP: mean difference +4.83 cm (95% CI 2.32 to 7.34) in the comparative pooling; +3.8 cm absolute (158.6 vs 154.8 cm) in the direct cohort, with a 4.7 cm gain over prediction in treated girls. Reversibility: menarche 0.9 (0.5) years after discontinuation; BMI z-score normalised by adult height; PCOS incidence not significantly increased (RR 1.21, 95% CI 0.46 to 3.15). On-treatment predicted height rises in both CPP and early-puberty girls, but treated-only data cannot prove causation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational-only evidence caps the stamp.
cards.watchOut: This shelf covers GnRH analogues for central (gonadotropin-dependent) precocious puberty only. Peripheral precocious puberty does not respond to GnRH analogues and is not covered; delayed puberty in boys is Shelf #2907; adding growth hormone is a separate, unsettled question not carded here. Evidence in boys with CPP is thin throughout — nearly every number on this shelf is from girls. Tier C.
cards.source: Synthesis of Luo X et al. Clinical Endocrinology. 2021 (PMID: 33387371); Poomthavorn P et al. Gynecological Endocrinology. 2011 (PMID: 21501002); Yang EH et al. Annals of Pediatric Endocrinology & Metabolism. 2023 (PMID: 37015776).

shelves.title: IVIG for haemolytic disease of the newborn: exchange transfusions fall in the pooled trials (relative risk 0.35) — but the only two blinded, placebo-controlled trials show no benefit at all
shelves.question: In a newborn with haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn (Rh or ABO incompatibility) on phototherapy, does intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) reduce the need for exchange transfusion?
shelves.mesh: Anemia, Hemolytic/immunology · Anemia, Hemolytic/therapy · Anemia, Neonatal/immunology · Anemia, Neonatal/therapy · Blood Transfusion · Humans · Immunoglobulins, Intravenous · Infant, Newborn · Jaundice, Neonatal/immunology · Jaundice, Neonatal/therapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer depends entirely on which trials are believed. In the unblinded randomised trial of Alpay 1999 (PMID: 10102158; 116 newborns with ABO and/or Rh incompatibility), exchange transfusion was needed in 8 of 58 babies given high-dose IVIG 1 g/kg versus 22 of 58 on phototherapy alone (P < 0.001). In the two double-blind, placebo-controlled trials, the effect vanishes: Santos 2013 (PMID: 22882285; NCT00288600; 92 newborns) found exchange transfusion in 6 of 46 (13%) on IVIG versus 7 of 46 (15.2%) on saline placebo (P = 0.765), and Smits-Wintjens 2011 (PMID: 21422084; 80 neonates with rhesus disease, 66% already transfused in utero) found 7 of 41 (17%) versus 6 of 39 (15%) (P = .99), with no differences in phototherapy duration, peak bilirubin or top-up transfusions. The Cochrane synthesis (Zwiers 2018, PMID: 29551014; 9 studies, 658 infants) pools to a typical relative risk of 0.35 (95% CI 0.25 to 0.49) with a risk difference of −0.22 and NNTB of 5 — but its own sensitivity analysis restricted to the two placebo-masked, blinded-outcome studies gives RR 0.98 (95% CI 0.48 to 1.98), and the authors state they have insufficient confidence to make even a weak recommendation for IVIG. PROPOSED SPLIT: a large apparent benefit where the treating team knew the allocation and controlled the exchange decision; no benefit where they did not. SCOPE NOTE: intrauterine transfusion outcomes were part of the commissioning question, but no comparative IUT-outcome record was carded this session; IUT exposure appears on this shelf only as background to the Smits-Wintjens population.

cards.headline: Alpay 1999 (the positive trial): exchange transfusion needed in 8 of 58 babies given high-dose IVIG versus 22 of 58 on phototherapy alone (P < 0.001)
cards.summary: Alpay 1999 (the positive trial): exchange transfusion needed in 8 of 58 babies given high-dose IVIG versus 22 of 58 on phototherapy alone (P < 0.001)
cards.people: Newborns with ABO and/or Rh incompatibility, significant hyperbilirubinaemia (bilirubin >204 µmol/L, ≈11.9 mg/dL), positive direct antiglobulin test and reticulocyte count ≥10%, randomly assigned to phototherapy plus high-dose IVIG 1 g/kg over 4 hours (n=58) or phototherapy alone (n=58).
cards.result: Exchange transfusion was required in 8 of 58 babies in the IVIG group versus 22 of 58 controls (P < 0.001) — an absolute difference of about 24 percentage points. Duration of phototherapy and of hospitalisation were significantly shorter in the IVIG group (P < 0.05). No side effects of IVIG were observed. The authors concluded that high-dose IVIG reduces haemolysis, serum bilirubin levels and the need for exchange transfusion.
cards.watchOut: No placebo and no blinding: the clinicians deciding whether each baby crossed the exchange threshold knew who had received IVIG. That is exactly the design feature the Cochrane sensitivity analysis later showed the whole apparent benefit hangs on — when the decision-makers are blinded (Santos 2013 and Smits-Wintjens 2011, below), the effect disappears.
cards.source: Alpay F, Sarici SU, Okutan V, Erdem G, Ozcan O, Gökçay E. High-dose intravenous immunoglobulin therapy in neonatal immune haemolytic jaundice. Acta Paediatrica. 1999. PMID: 10102158. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era trial). cards.headline: Santos 2013 (blinded, placebo-controlled): exchange transfusion in 13% on IVIG versus 15.2% on saline placebo (P = 0.765) — no difference in anything measured
cards.summary: Santos 2013 (blinded, placebo-controlled): exchange transfusion in 13% on IVIG versus 15.2% on saline placebo (P = 0.765) — no difference in anything measured
cards.people: 92 newborns of ≥32 weeks' gestation with a positive direct antiglobulin test, born to Rh-alloimmunised mothers, randomised within 6 hours of birth to IVIG 500 mg/kg (n=46) or saline placebo (n=46); all received high-intensity phototherapy.
cards.result: Exchange transfusion was performed in 6 of 46 (13%) IVIG babies versus 7 of 46 (15.2%) placebo babies (P = 0.765). There were no differences in duration of phototherapy, peak bilirubin, or length of hospital stay. Exchange criteria were a total serum bilirubin ≥340 µmol/L (20 mg/dL) or a rise of 8.5 µmol/L/h (0.5 mg/dL/h). The authors concluded IVIG did not reduce exchange transfusion in this population.
cards.watchOut: The dose here (a single 500 mg/kg) is lower than Alpay's 1 g/kg, so a defender of IVIG can argue dose; but the trial's exchange rate on placebo (15.2%) shows there was room for an effect to appear, and none did, on any endpoint. Together with Smits-Wintjens, this is one of only two trials in the entire record where allocation was masked.
cards.source: Santos et al. [Intravenous immunoglobulin in newborns of Rh-alloimmunised mothers — article title not captured verbatim this session]. Transfusion. 2013. PMID: 22882285. cards.headline: Smits-Wintjens 2011 (blinded, placebo-controlled): exchange transfusion in 17% on IVIG versus 15% on placebo (P = .99)
cards.summary: Smits-Wintjens 2011 (blinded, placebo-controlled): exchange transfusion in 17% on IVIG versus 15% on placebo (P = .99)
cards.people: 80 neonates with rhesus haemolytic disease, 53 (66%) of whom had been treated with intrauterine transfusion(s), stratified for IUT and randomised double-blind to prophylactic IVIG 0.75 g/kg or placebo (5% glucose).
cards.result: Exchange transfusions: 7 of 41 (17%) in the IVIG group versus 6 of 39 (15%) on placebo (P = .99); the number of exchange transfusions per patient was a median of 0 in both groups. Duration of phototherapy was 4.7 versus 5.1 days (P = .34), maximum bilirubin 14.8 versus 14.1 mg/dL (P = .52), and top-up red-cell transfusions were needed by 83% versus 87% (P = .76). The authors concluded that prophylactic IVIG does not reduce the need for exchange transfusion and that their findings do not support the use of IVIG in neonates with rhesus hemolytic disease.
cards.watchOut: Two-thirds of these babies had already been transfused in utero — a severely affected, specialist-centre population with a low residual exchange rate (15–17%) — so the trial tests prophylactic IVIG in the hardest cases rather than rescue IVIG as bilirubin climbs. Its null result is nonetheless the least biased estimate on this shelf, and it agrees with Santos 2013.
cards.source: Smits-Wintjens VEHJ, Walther FJ, Rath MEA, Lindenburg ITM, te Pas AB, Kramer CM, Oepkes D, Brand A, Lopriore E. Intravenous immunoglobulin in neonates with rhesus hemolytic disease: a randomized controlled trial. Pediatrics. 2011. PMID: 21422084. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Zwiers 2018 (Cochrane): pooled relative risk 0.35 for exchange transfusion — but 0.98 in the only two blinded trials; authors had 'insufficient confidence' to recommend IVIG
cards.summary: Zwiers 2018 (Cochrane): pooled relative risk 0.35 for exchange transfusion — but 0.98 in the only two blinded trials; authors had 'insufficient confidence' to recommend IVIG
cards.people: 9 randomised or quasi-randomised studies, 658 infants, term and preterm, with Rh or ABO (or both) incompatibility, comparing IVIG with placebo or no IVIG, all using predefined criteria for IVIG and for exchange transfusion.
cards.result: Overall, exchange transfusion use decreased in the immunoglobulin group (typical relative risk 0.35, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.49; typical risk difference −0.22, 95% CI −0.27 to −0.16; number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome 5), and the mean number of exchange transfusions per infant was lower (mean difference −0.34, 95% CI −0.50 to −0.17). However, in the sensitivity analysis restricted to the only two studies in which treatment was masked by placebo and outcome assessment was blinded, there was no difference in the need for exchange transfusions (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.48 to 1.98) or in the number performed (MD −0.04, 95% CI −0.18 to 0.10). Two studies assessing long-term outcomes found no cases of kernicterus, deafness or cerebral palsy. The authors concluded they had insufficient confidence in the effect estimate to make even a weak recommendation for the use of IVIG in alloimmune HDN.
cards.watchOut: The pooled 0.35 is dominated by small, unblinded trials in which the treating team both gave (or withheld) IVIG and decided on exchange transfusion — a set-up that can manufacture exactly this pattern. The honest summary of the whole record is the split itself: a large apparent effect where bias can operate, and no effect where it cannot.
cards.source: Zwiers C, Scheffer-Rath MEA, Lopriore E, de Haas M, Liley HG. Immunoglobulin for alloimmune hemolytic disease in neonates. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2018. PMID: 29551014. cards.headline: Synthesis: the IVIG benefit in HDFN is an artefact-shaped finding — large in unblinded trials, absent in both blinded trials
cards.summary: Synthesis: the IVIG benefit in HDFN is an artefact-shaped finding — large in unblinded trials, absent in both blinded trials
cards.people: Four sources: one unblinded positive randomised trial (Alpay 1999, 116 newborns), two double-blind placebo-controlled trials (Santos 2013, 92 newborns, NCT00288600; Smits-Wintjens 2011, 80 neonates), and the Cochrane synthesis of 9 studies and 658 infants (Zwiers 2018).
cards.result: Unblinded record: exchange transfusion in 8/58 on high-dose IVIG versus 22/58 on phototherapy alone (Alpay 1999). Blinded record: 6/46 (13%) versus 7/46 (15.2%) (Santos 2013) and 7/41 (17%) versus 6/39 (15%) (Smits-Wintjens 2011) — no difference on exchange transfusion, phototherapy duration, peak bilirubin or top-up transfusion in either. Pooled record: typical RR 0.35 (95% CI 0.25 to 0.49), RD −0.22, NNTB 5 overall, collapsing to RR 0.98 (95% CI 0.48 to 1.98) in the blinded subset (Zwiers 2018). PROPOSED SPLIT — benefit claimed on the pooled, mostly unblinded record; no difference on the blinded record, which is the record that should govern.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Guidelines in several countries still recommend IVIG when bilirubin is rising despite intensive phototherapy; this shelf reports the trial record, which is weaker than that practice implies, and the gap between the two is a judgement call for the treating team, not something the evidence settles. Nothing here concerns intrauterine transfusion itself, anti-D prophylaxis in pregnancy, or exchange transfusion technique.
cards.source: Synthesis of Alpay F et al. Acta Paediatrica. 1999 (PMID: 10102158); Santos et al. Transfusion. 2013 (PMID: 22882285); Smits-Wintjens VEHJ et al. Pediatrics. 2011 (PMID: 21422084); Zwiers C et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2018 (PMID: 29551014).
