shelves.title: Neonatal herpes: high-dose acyclovir (60 mg/kg/day for 21 days) improved survival in disseminated disease against historical controls, and 6 months of oral suppression after CNS disease improved 12-month mental development scores in a placebo-controlled trial
shelves.question: For a newborn with herpes simplex infection, what dose and duration of acyclovir should be used — and does months of oral suppressive acyclovir afterwards protect the developing brain?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: SPLIT — two different treatment questions, two different grades of evidence. Acute treatment: Kimberlin 2001 (PMID: 11483782) compared high-dose intravenous acyclovir (60 mg/kg/day for 21 days) with historical standard-dose (30 mg/kg/day) controls and found survival in disseminated disease significantly higher on high dose (odds ratio 3.3, 95% CI 1.4 to 7.9), with overall survival also higher (OR 3.3, 95% CI 1.5 to 7.3) but CNS-disease survival similar between doses; neutropenia occurred in 21% of high-dose recipients with localised disease. That is an observational-grade comparison — no randomised dose trial exists or ethically can — and the Seattle era cohort (Melvin 2022, PMID: 34894240) shows what accompanied the high-dose era: overall mortality fell from 20.9% to 5.6% as high-dose use rose from 0% to about 95%, yet disseminated disease still killed 40.9% and only 55% of CNS survivors were without obvious neurologic abnormality at 24 months. Suppression: the one double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Kimberlin 2011, PMID: 21991950; NCT00031460 and NCT00031447; 74 neonates) found that 6 months of oral acyclovir 300 mg/m² three times daily after the intravenous course improved Bayley Mental Development Index scores at 12 months in CNS disease (adjusted mean 88.24 vs 68.12; P = 0.046), assessed in 28 of 45 CNS infants, with a trend to more neutropenia (P = 0.09). PROPOSED SPLIT: high-dose acute therapy is standard care resting on historical-control evidence (POSSIBLE on the fetched record); suppression after CNS disease has genuine randomised support, from a single small trial (POSSIBLE). NUMBERING NOTE (resolved Nov 18, 2026): this pack was built for slot #5368, but that number had been taken by an unrelated liver pack (protein in hepatic encephalopathy) from a parallel build (#5367–#5370 are that liver & gut block), so the pack was quarantined in packs/partJ-collisions/ and renumbered to #5373; the content is unchanged.

cards.headline: Kimberlin 2001: high-dose acyclovir (60 mg/kg/day) tripled the odds of survival in disseminated neonatal herpes versus historical standard-dose controls (OR 3.3, 95% CI 1.4 to 7.9)
cards.summary: Kimberlin 2001: high-dose acyclovir (60 mg/kg/day) tripled the odds of survival in disseminated neonatal herpes versus historical standard-dose controls (OR 3.3, 95% CI 1.4 to 7.9)
cards.type: Open-label dose study with historical controls (Kimberlin 2001)
cards.people: Infants aged 28 days or younger with CNS (N=28) or disseminated (N=41) HSV disease offered enrolment in an open-label study: the first 16 received intermediate-dose acyclovir 45 mg/kg/day and the next 72 received high-dose 60 mg/kg/day, each in 3 divided doses for 21 days, compared with historical controls treated with standard-dose acyclovir 30 mg/kg/day.
cards.result: Survival in disseminated disease was significantly higher on high-dose therapy (odds ratio 3.3, 95% CI 1.4 to 7.9 — a relative, odds measure against historical controls), as was overall survival (OR 3.3, 95% CI 1.5 to 7.3); survival in CNS disease was similar between high and standard doses. Neutropenia occurred in 6 of 29 (21%) high-dose recipients with skin-eye-mouth or CNS-localised disease. The authors supported 21 days of high-dose (60 mg/kg/day) acyclovir for CNS and disseminated disease.
cards.watchOut: The comparison is against babies treated in an earlier era at a lower dose, so improvements in neonatal intensive care over time are folded into the apparent drug effect — there has never been, and ethically cannot now be, a placebo or low-dose randomised trial of acute therapy. Note also what did not improve with dose: CNS survival. In CNS disease the battle is over brain outcome, not survival, which is what the suppression trial below addresses.
cards.source: Kimberlin DW, Lin CY, Jacobs RF, et al.; National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases Collaborative Antiviral Study Group. Safety and efficacy of high-dose intravenous acyclovir in the management of neonatal herpes simplex virus infections. Pediatrics. 2001. PMID: 11483782. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era study). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Kimberlin 2011 (CASG 103/104): 6 months of oral acyclovir suppression after CNS disease — Bayley mental development scores 88.24 versus 68.12 at 12 months (P = 0.046)
cards.summary: Kimberlin 2011 (CASG 103/104): 6 months of oral acyclovir suppression after CNS disease — Bayley mental development scores 88.24 versus 68.12 at 12 months (P = 0.046)
cards.type: Two parallel randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials (Kimberlin 2011)
cards.people: 74 neonates with HSV disease — 45 with CNS disease and 29 with skin-eye-mouth (SEM) disease — who, after 14–21 days of parenteral acyclovir, were randomised double-blind in two parallel trials to oral acyclovir suppression 300 mg/m² per dose three times daily for 6 months, or placebo.
cards.result: Among infants with CNS disease, the Bayley Mental Development Index at 12 months — assessed in 28 of the 45 CNS infants (62%) — averaged 88.24 on acyclovir suppression versus 68.12 on placebo after adjustment (P = 0.046), a difference of about 20 points. There was a trend towards more neutropenia on acyclovir (P = 0.09).
cards.watchOut: The headline outcome rests on 28 of 45 CNS infants — the 38% not assessed at 12 months leave room for attrition bias in either direction — and P = 0.046 sits just inside significance, so the true effect could be considerably smaller than 20 points. The abstract fetched does not quantify the skin-recurrence benefit in SEM disease, so this card claims the CNS neurodevelopment result only. Neutropenia on suppression needs blood-count monitoring.

cards.headline: Melvin 2022 (Seattle, 1980–2016): as high-dose acyclovir use rose from 0% to about 95%, overall neonatal HSV mortality fell from 20.9% to 5.6% — yet disseminated disease still killed 40.9%
cards.summary: Melvin 2022 (Seattle, 1980–2016): as high-dose acyclovir use rose from 0% to about 95%, overall neonatal HSV mortality fell from 20.9% to 5.6% — yet disseminated disease still killed 40.9%
cards.type: Retrospective single-centre cohort across four decades (Melvin 2022)
cards.people: Neonates with HSV treated at Seattle Children's Hospital between 1980 and 2016, with presentation, treatment and outcomes abstracted from medical records.
cards.result: High-dose acyclovir treatment increased from 0% to close to 95% of cases across the period, with a subsequent decrease in overall HSV-related mortality from 20.9% to 5.6%. Even among infants treated with high-dose acyclovir, mortality was 40.9% for disseminated disease, and only 55% of infants with CNS disease were without obvious neurologic abnormalities at 24 months. Skin recurrences were more common with HSV-2 than HSV-1 (80% vs 55%; P = .02) and in infants with lesions at initial diagnosis (76% vs 47%; P = .02).
cards.watchOut: An era comparison cannot separate the drug from everything else that improved between 1980 and 2016 — earlier recognition, PCR diagnosis and intensive care among them. Its sober value is the ceiling it documents: with modern high-dose therapy, disseminated disease still kills about 4 in 10 babies, and CNS disease leaves nearly half of survivors with obvious neurologic abnormality at 2 years. That ceiling, not complacency about the current regimen, is the argument for the suppression strategy and for treating on suspicion.

cards.headline: Synthesis: treat disseminated and CNS disease with 60 mg/kg/day for 21 days, then suppress for 6 months after CNS disease — one leg on historical controls, one on a single small RCT
cards.summary: Synthesis: treat disseminated and CNS disease with 60 mg/kg/day for 21 days, then suppress for 6 months after CNS disease — one leg on historical controls, one on a single small RCT
cards.people: Three sources: an open-label high-dose study with historical controls (Kimberlin 2001), two parallel double-blind placebo-controlled suppression trials totalling 74 neonates (Kimberlin 2011; NCT00031460, NCT00031447), and a 36-year single-centre cohort (Melvin 2022).
cards.result: Acute: disseminated-disease survival odds ratio 3.3 (95% CI 1.4 to 7.9) for high-dose (60 mg/kg/day × 21 days) versus historical standard-dose therapy; CNS survival unchanged by dose; neutropenia in 21% of high-dose recipients with localised disease. Suppression: Bayley Mental Development Index at 12 months 88.24 versus 68.12 (P = 0.046) for 6 months of oral acyclovir after CNS disease. Era context: overall mortality 20.9% → 5.6% as high-dose use rose to ~95%, with disseminated mortality still 40.9% and only 55% of CNS infants neurologically unremarkable at 24 months. PROPOSED SPLIT — acute high-dose therapy: standard care on historical-control evidence (POSSIBLE on the fetched record); post-CNS suppression: randomised evidence of neurodevelopmental benefit from one small trial (POSSIBLE).
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Nothing on this shelf supports delaying acyclovir while awaiting confirmation in a sick neonate — every outcome above worsens with late treatment, and the natural-history record (Kimberlin 2001, Pediatrics 108:223–229, identified but not carded this session) documents that many infants present without skin vesicles (39% of disseminated and 32% of CNS cases had none at presentation). SEM-only disease duration (14 days) and maternal suppression questions in pregnancy are outside this shelf's fetched record.

shelves.title: Labial fusion in young girls: topical betamethasone and estrogen both work in most cases - success 80-89% in one series, but only 15% in another
shelves.question: How should labial fusion (labial adhesions) in prepubertal girls be treated - estrogen cream, betamethasone cream, or both?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Topical · Anti-Inflammatory Agents / therapeutic use · Betamethasone / therapeutic use · Drug Therapy, Combination · Estrogens / therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Retrospective Studies · Tissue Adhesions / drug therapy · Vulvar Diseases / drug therapy
shelves.balance: All three studies are retrospective chart reviews, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE, and they disagree. Mayoglou 2009 (PMID 19646671) reviewed 151 prepubertal girls (mean age 3 years): time to resolution was 1.3 months with betamethasone versus 2.2 months with topical estrogen (Premarin), recurrence was lower with betamethasone, and estrogen caused breast budding and vaginal bleeding while betamethasone caused only local irritation. Ertürk 2014 (PMID not captured this session; DOI 10.3906/sag-1312-3) studied 39 girls with adhesions covering at least 50% of the vaginal opening: success was 16/20 (80%) with estrogen and 17/19 (89.4%) with betamethasone plus petroleum ointment (Vaseline); 2/20 estrogen patients and 1/19 betamethasone patients needed manual separation; labial enlargement occurred in 2 (10%) on estrogen and local irritation in 1 (5.2%) on betamethasone. But Eroğlu 2011 (PMID 21945628), 131 children, found far lower success - estrogen only 11/71 (15.4%), betamethasone only 5/32 (15.6%), combination 5/28 (28.5%) - with no significant differences (estrogen vs betamethasone P=1.00; combination vs pooled single therapies relative risk 1.85, 95% CI 0.89-3.89, P=.11). The honest reading is that both creams are used first-line, betamethasone looks at least as good with fewer systemic effects, and success rates vary widely between clinics: PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

shelves.title: Learning disabilities: targeted maths training helps dyscalculia, but generic working-memory training does not transfer to school skills
shelves.question: What interventions help children and adolescents with learning disabilities - does working-memory training work, or do targeted programmes work better?
shelves.mesh: Attention Deficit Disorder with Hyperactivity / rehabilitation · Child Development · Cognition Disorders / rehabilitation · Humans · Memory, Short-Term / physiology · Teaching / methods
shelves.balance: BOUNDARY: intensive remedial reading instruction for severe reading disability / dyslexia is homed on shelf #1396 and is not re-carded here; this shelf covers non-reading interventions. The evidence splits. On the positive side, Zotti 2026 (PMID 41602671; registry ISRCTN15190285) was a single-centre, two-arm randomised trial (pseudo-randomised allocation, no blinding, waitlist control) in 70 adolescents aged 13-17 with a recent first diagnosis of developmental dyscalculia: prismatic adaptation followed by targeted cognitive training using serious games (the paper names the MindLenses software, from Restorative Neurotechnologies Srl) produced large between-group gains - working memory index 16.51 (95% CI 13.59-19.44, p<0.001, eta-squared 0.66), processing speed index 12.40 (95% CI 9.73-15.70, p<0.001, eta-squared 0.58), mental calculation speed 0.74 (95% CI 0.55-0.93, p<0.001, eta-squared 0.46), mental calculation accuracy 0.43 (95% CI 0.14-0.71, p<0.001, eta-squared 0.17) and numerical fact retrieval 14.07 (95% CI 8.58-19.56, p<0.001, eta-squared 0.31). Peijnenborgh 2016 (PMID not captured this session) reviewed 13 studies of working-memory training programmes (Cogmed, Jungle Memory, Braingame Brian) in children and adolescents with learning disabilities and found a medium effect on verbal working memory (g=0.64), a small effect on visuospatial working memory (g=0.63) and a small-to-medium effect on decoding (g=0.36), with children over 10 benefiting more on verbal working memory - but 76% of the studies included children with ADHD, and the authors note heterogeneity, small samples and reduced methodological rigour. Against that, Melby-Lervåg & Hulme 2013 (PMID 22612437) pooled 23 studies with 30 group comparisons and found reliable short-term improvements in working-memory skills themselves, but no convincing evidence of generalisation to nonverbal or verbal ability, attention inhibition, word decoding or arithmetic - verbal working-memory gains were not sustained at follow-up. The split is therefore: targeted, maths-focused training shows real gains in the skill it trains, while generic working-memory training improves only the trained tasks and does not transfer. PROPOSED SPLIT.

cards.headline: Peijnenborgh 2016: across 13 studies, working-memory training improved verbal working memory (g=0.64) in children with learning disabilities
cards.summary: Peijnenborgh 2016: across 13 studies, working-memory training improved verbal working memory (g=0.64) in children with learning disabilities
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 13 studies (randomised trials and quasi-experiments) of working-memory training (Cogmed, Jungle Memory, Braingame Brian) in children and adolescents with learning disabilities; 76% of studies included children with ADHD
cards.result: Seven studies showed a medium effect size on verbal working memory (g=0.64), a small effect on visuospatial working memory (g=0.63) and a small-to-medium effect on decoding (g=0.36). Children over 10 years benefited more than younger children on verbal working memory. Limitations noted: heterogeneity between studies, small sample sizes and reduced methodological rigour of included studies.
cards.watchOut: The PMID was not captured this session, so the full citation is printed without one; most included studies were in ADHD, not in learning disability alone, and the effects are on memory-test scores, not school achievement.

cards.headline: Melby-Lervåg & Hulme 2013: across 23 studies, working-memory training improved only the trained tasks - no convincing transfer to arithmetic, reading or reasoning
cards.summary: Melby-Lervåg & Hulme 2013: across 23 studies, working-memory training improved only the trained tasks - no convincing transfer to arithmetic, reading or reasoning
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 23 studies with 30 group comparisons (randomised trials and quasi-experiments) of working-memory training in clinical samples and typically developing children and adults
cards.result: The programmes produced reliable short-term improvements in working-memory skills. For verbal working memory these near-transfer effects were not sustained at follow-up; for visuospatial working memory, limited evidence suggested they might be maintained. There was no convincing evidence of generalisation to other skills (nonverbal and verbal ability, inhibitory processes in attention, word decoding, and arithmetic).
cards.watchOut: The included studies varied widely in age and clinical condition; the authors note this as a limitation, but the conclusion - no far transfer - held across the set.
cards.source: Melby-Lervåg M, Hulme C. Is working memory training effective? A meta-analytic review. Dev Psychol. 2013. PMID: 22612437. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.balance: No placebo- or no-treatment-controlled trial was found; every carded trial compares one topical preparation with another. Veysizadeh 2026 (PMID: 41204732; Registry ID: none in the record) randomised 42 infants to 25% zinc oxide with or without topical breast milk: complete recovery was similar (61.9% versus 66.6%) but lesions resolved faster with breast milk added (2.52 versus 3.28 days; p=0.012) and no infant in the combination group failed to respond (versus 14.3%). Panahi 2012 (PMID: 22606064; Registry ID: none in the record), a double-blind trial in 66 infants, found both calendula ointment and aloe vera cream improved severity, with fewer rash sites on calendula (p=0.001). Adib-Hajbaghery 2014 (PMID: 25097603; Registry ID: none in the record), a double-blind trial in 60 infants, found bentonite started recovery within 6 hours in 93.3% versus 40% on calendula, with complete improvement by 3 days in 90% versus 36.7%. All trials are small, single-centre and from one country. Proposed stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: Veysizadeh 2026: breast milk plus zinc oxide resolved lesions faster than zinc oxide alone (2.52 versus 3.28 days)
cards.summary: Veysizadeh 2026: breast milk plus zinc oxide resolved lesions faster than zinc oxide alone (2.52 versus 3.28 days)
cards.people: Infants under 1 year with diaper dermatitis at one Tehran children's hospital; n=42 randomised to two groups
cards.result: Complete recovery was 61.9% with 25% zinc oxide plus topical breast milk versus 66.6% with zinc oxide alone, and partial recovery 38.1% versus 19.1%; no infant in the combination group was a non-responder versus 14.3% on zinc oxide alone. Lesion resolution was faster with the combination (2.52 ± 0.67 days versus 3.28 ± 1.14 days; p=0.012).
cards.watchOut: Very small (n=42), single centre, 7 days of treatment; the speed gain is under a day and complete-recovery rates did not differ.
cards.source: Veysizadeh M, Aghaei P, Eftekhari K, Ashournia P, Malekiantaghi A, Shafiei A. Topical Breast Milk plus Zinc Oxide Versus Zinc Oxide Alone for Diaper Rash in Infants Under 1 Year: A Randomized Clinical Trial. Breastfeed Med. 2026. PMID: 41204732. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Panahi 2012: calendula ointment and aloe vera cream both improved nappy rash; calendula left significantly fewer rash sites
cards.summary: Panahi 2012: calendula ointment and aloe vera cream both improved nappy rash; calendula left significantly fewer rash sites
cards.people: Infants under 3 years with diaper dermatitis; n=66 (aloe vera cream 32, Calendula officinalis ointment 34), treated 3 times daily for 10 days
cards.result: Severity improved in both groups (p<0.001 within each group). Infants receiving calendula ointment had significantly fewer rash sites than the aloe vera group (p=0.001). No adverse effect was reported from either preparation. The tested products were a Calendula officinalis ointment and an aloe vera cream as described in the publication; no brand or company is named in the record.
cards.watchOut: No untreated or standard-care arm, so how much either preparation beats simple barrier care and time is unknown; herbal preparations vary by maker, and current products may differ in safety and effectiveness from the tested ones.

cards.headline: Adib-Hajbaghery 2014: bentonite started recovery within 6 hours in 93.3% versus 40% on calendula, and 90% were fully improved by day 3
cards.summary: Adib-Hajbaghery 2014: bentonite started recovery within 6 hours in 93.3% versus 40% on calendula, and 90% were fully improved by day 3
cards.people: Outpatient infants with diaper dermatitis in Khomein, Iran; n=60 in a double-blind randomised trial (bentonite versus calendula)
cards.result: Recovery had started within the first 6 hours in 93.3% of the bentonite group versus 40% of the calendula group (p<0.001). Complete improvement within the first 3 days occurred in 90% on bentonite versus 36.7% on calendula (p<0.001). Mean age of the sample was 6.55 months.
cards.watchOut: Small single-region trial with a very short horizon (3 days) and no standard-care comparator; bentonite is a clay preparation whose composition can vary by source.

cards.headline: Synthesis: several topical preparations beat their comparators on speed, but nothing has been tested against no treatment or standard barrier care alone in a large trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: several topical preparations beat their comparators on speed, but nothing has been tested against no treatment or standard barrier care alone in a large trial
cards.people: All carded evidence: three small randomised trials, n=42, n=66 and n=60 infants
cards.result: Breast milk plus zinc oxide resolved lesions about 0.76 days faster than zinc oxide alone (Veysizadeh 2026); calendula beat aloe vera on rash sites (Panahi 2012); bentonite beat calendula on speed of recovery (Adib-Hajbaghery 2014). No trial measured any preparation against placebo, no treatment, or petrolatum-based standard care.
cards.watchOut: All three trials are small, single-centre and from Iran; nappy rash usually settles with frequent changes, air exposure and a plain barrier, none of which was an isolated comparator in these trials.
cards.source: Synthesis of Veysizadeh 2026 (PMID: 41204732), Panahi 2012 (PMID: 22606064) and Adib-Hajbaghery 2014 (PMID: 25097603).

shelves.title: Oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula: repair by day 2 of life is supported by 863 US cases (11 of 18 stomach perforations happened after day 2), while long-gap atresia drives strictures (adjusted odds ratio 4.44) and far longer recovery (hospital stay 186 versus 53 days)
shelves.question: In newborns with oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula, how do the timing and type of surgical repair affect survival, complications and feeding — and what most determines the outcome?
shelves.mesh: Age Factors · Databases, Factual · Esophageal Atresia / complications · Esophageal Atresia / surgery · Esophagostomy / methods · Female · Humans · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Length of Stay / statistics & numerical data · Ligation · Male · Postoperative Complications / epidemiology · Postoperative Complications / etiology · Retrospective Studies · Time Factors · Time-to-Treatment / statistics & numerical data · Tracheoesophageal Fistula / surgery · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Repair is surgical and uncontested; the evidence concerns timing and prognostic factors, and is entirely observational. Patwardhan 2025 (PMID: 39261185; Registry ID: none in the record), 863 infants in the US Pediatric Health Information System, found most repairs already happen on day 2 (36%), weekend repair had equivalent outcomes, and 11 of 18 gastric perforations (61%) occurred after day 2 — supporting repair by day 2. Ali 2025 (PMID: 41496816; Registry ID: none in the record), 67 infants in Riyadh, found survival to discharge of 86% (excluding palliatively managed trisomy 18), primary repair in only 10% of long-gap cases, and long-gap atresia as the only independent predictor of stricture (adjusted odds ratio 4.44, 95% CI 1.27 to 15.55), with median stay 186 versus 53 days. Tawil 2026 (PMID: 41386345; Registry ID: none in the record), 139 open-repair cases in five West Bank and East Jerusalem hospitals, found mortality of 20.5%, long-term complications in 67.0%, and each day of delayed repair raising mortality odds (odds ratio 1.35 per day, 95% CI 1.08 to 1.71). Observational evidence caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (observational evidence only).

cards.headline: Patwardhan 2025: most gastric perforations (11 of 18) happened when repair waited past day 2 of life
cards.summary: Patwardhan 2025: most gastric perforations (11 of 18) happened when repair waited past day 2 of life
cards.people: Infants with oesophageal atresia and tracheo-oesophageal fistula repaired within 10 days of birth at US children's hospitals, 2016-2021; n=863
cards.result: The commonest repair day was day of life 2 (36% of operations) and 83% of repairs were on weekdays. Later operations had shorter length of stay (p=0.04) but more recurrent laryngeal nerve injuries (p=0.01); weekend repairs had equivalent outcomes. Gastric perforation occurred in 18 infants (2.0%), and 11 of the 18 (61%) occurred after day 2. The authors recommend repair by day 2 where there is no contraindication.
cards.watchOut: Administrative database: babies repaired later may have been kept waiting because they were less stable (or more stable), and long-gap and H-type cases were excluded, so the day-2 message applies to standard anatomy.
cards.source: Patwardhan U, West E, Ignacio RC, Gollin G. Worth the Wait? The Impact of Timing of Repair of Esophageal Atresia With Tracheoesophageal Fistula on Outcomes. J Pediatr Surg. 2025. PMID: 39261185. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ali 2025: long-gap atresia was the only independent predictor of stricture (adjusted odds ratio 4.44) and stretched hospital stay to 186 versus 53 days
cards.summary: Ali 2025: long-gap atresia was the only independent predictor of stricture (adjusted odds ratio 4.44) and stretched hospital stay to 186 versus 53 days
cards.people: Infants with oesophageal atresia with or without tracheo-oesophageal fistula at one Riyadh centre, 2016-2024; n=67 (gap length assessable in 63)
cards.result: Survival to discharge was 86% after excluding three trisomy 18 infants managed palliatively. Primary repair was achieved in 67.2% overall but in only 10% of long-gap infants. Early anastomotic leak occurred in 26.9%, recurrent fistula in 14.9% and stricture in 32.8%. Long-gap atresia independently predicted stricture (adjusted odds ratio 4.44, 95% CI 1.27 to 15.55; p=0.020); median hospital stay was 186 versus 53 days (p<0.001) and time to full oral feeding 209 versus 29 days (p<0.001) for long-gap versus standard-gap infants.
cards.watchOut: Small single-centre series (n=67); gap length is anatomy, not a treatment choice — the finding identifies who needs staged repair and specialist follow-up rather than a changeable exposure.
cards.source: Ali K, Alsabty NS, Altuwaym A, Al Jadaan S, Al Namshan M, Alharbi N, Homedi A, Ali I, Alsaif S. Esophageal atresia with and without tracheoesophageal fistula: a 2016-2024 single-center cohort study in Saudi Arabia stratified by gap length. World J Pediatr Surg. 2025. PMID: 41496816. cards.headline: Tawil 2026: mortality after open repair was 20.5% in a resource-constrained setting, and each day of delay raised the odds of death (odds ratio 1.35 per day)
cards.summary: Tawil 2026: mortality after open repair was 20.5% in a resource-constrained setting, and each day of delay raised the odds of death (odds ratio 1.35 per day)
cards.people: Infants undergoing open thoracotomy repair of oesophageal atresia at five West Bank and East Jerusalem hospitals, 2015-2025; n=139 repaired cases
cards.result: Short-term complications occurred in 29.2% (38/130) and long-term complications in 67.0% (73/109); median length of stay was 23.5 days. Mortality was 20.5% (27/131 with outcome recorded). Short-term complications were associated with higher mortality (34.3% versus 11.1%; relative risk 3.09, 95% CI 1.47 to 6.48). In regression, higher gestational age reduced mortality (odds ratio 0.58 per week, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.87) and delayed repair increased it (odds ratio 1.35 per day, 95% CI 1.08 to 1.71).
cards.watchOut: Outcomes in a resource-constrained setting (20.5% mortality versus 86% survival to discharge in the Riyadh series) reflect case mix and resources as much as technique; delay may mark babies too sick to operate on rather than causing the deaths.
cards.source: Tawil S, Mansour M, Alashwas W, Farhoud H, Saada LJM, Iwaiwi R, Iwaiwi B, Abu Karsh R. Outcomes after open thoracotomy repair of esophageal atresia with or without tracheoesophageal fistula: A 10-year Middle Eastern multicenter retrospective cohort. J Pediatr Surg. 2026. PMID: 41386345. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: repair promptly (by day 2 in standard anatomy); gap length and the baby's condition — not the day of the week — decide the course
cards.summary: Synthesis: repair promptly (by day 2 in standard anatomy); gap length and the baby's condition — not the day of the week — decide the course
cards.people: All carded evidence: three retrospective cohorts, n=863, n=67 and n=139 newborns
cards.result: Waiting past day 2 carried most gastric perforations (Patwardhan 2025) and each day of delay was associated with higher mortality odds (Tawil 2026), while long-gap anatomy quadrupled stricture odds and tripled hospital stay (Ali 2025). No randomised or thoracoscopic-versus-open comparative study was carded.
cards.watchOut: All evidence is observational and timing is confounded by how sick the baby is; thoracoscopic repair and long-gap techniques (such as traction/Foker) were not comparatively carded this session.
cards.source: Synthesis of Patwardhan 2025 (PMID: 39261185), Ali 2025 (PMID: 41496816) and Tawil 2026 (PMID: 41386345).

shelves.title: Selective mutism: behavioural treatment beats no treatment with large effects (g = 0.87-1.06 across 5 small RCTs) — but remission and advantage over active treatment are unproven
shelves.question: In children with selective mutism, do psychological or behavioural treatments increase speaking and produce remission compared with no treatment or other care?
shelves.mesh: Anxiety Disorders/therapy · Child · Child Behavior Disorders · Humans · Mutism/therapy · Psychosocial Intervention · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for behavioural/psychological treatment. The RCT-only meta-analysis (Steains 2021, PMID: 34265102; 5 RCTs, 233 children) found psychological interventions more effective than no treatment with a large overall weighted effect (Hedges g = 0.87). The broader systematic review (Hipolito 2023, PMID: 37720585; 25 studies, 5 RCTs in the meta-analysis) found combined systems/behavioural approaches beat waitlist for speaking behaviour (Hedges g = 1.06, p < .0001, 95% CI 0.57-1.56), while the remission advantage (relative risk 4.25, 95% CI 0.52-34.84) was not significant and the two active-control RCTs pooled non-significantly (g = 0.55, 95% CI -0.47 to 1.57). The 2025 questionnaire meta-analysis (Iimura 2025, PMID: 40181492; 12 studies, 472 participants) found the mean Selective Mutism Questionnaire total improved by 0.51 (95% CI 0.32-0.70; g = 1.00), with face-to-face treatment improving scores by 0.59 versus 0.12 for web-based. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): effects are large against waitlist but the whole RCT base is five small trials, and drug treatment (SSRIs) has no placebo-controlled support and is not carded.

cards.headline: Steains 2021: across 5 RCTs with 233 children, psychological interventions beat no treatment with a large effect (Hedges g = 0.87)
cards.summary: Steains 2021: across 5 RCTs with 233 children, psychological interventions beat no treatment with a large effect (Hedges g = 0.87)
cards.people: Children with selective mutism in 5 randomised controlled trials with a total of 233 participants, analysed with a random-effects model; all included studies used psychometrically sound measures and treatment manuals.
cards.result: Psychological interventions were more effective than no treatment, with an overall weighted effect size of g = 0.87, indicating a large mean treatment effect. The effect did not significantly differ whether only selective-mutism-specific or non-specific measures were included. The authors concluded the findings support the efficacy of psychological treatment for selective mutism, while noting future research should compare successful treatments against psychological placebo or another bona fide treatment.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is no treatment, which inflates effects versus any active control; five small trials is the entire RCT base, and the pooled g mixes speaking behaviour, severity, anxiety and functioning outcomes.
cards.source: Steains SY, Malouff JM, Schutte NS. Efficacy of psychological interventions for selective mutism in children: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. cards.headline: Hipolito 2023: combined systems/behavioural treatment beat waitlist for speaking (Hedges g = 1.06, 95% CI 0.57-1.56) but the remission advantage was not significant (relative risk 4.25, 95% CI 0.52-34.84)
cards.summary: Hipolito 2023: combined systems/behavioural treatment beat waitlist for speaking (Hedges g = 1.06, 95% CI 0.57-1.56) but the remission advantage was not significant (relative risk 4.25, 95% CI 0.52-34.84)
cards.people: Children and adolescents with selective mutism in 25 identified studies of nonpharmacological interventions (searched across 13 databases, literature since 1992); 5 RCTs entered the meta-analysis — 3 against waitlist controls and 2 against active controls.
cards.result: Three RCTs comparing a combined systems/behavioural approach with waitlist showed a significant large effect on improved speaking behaviour (Hedges g = 1.06, p < .0001, 95% CI 0.57-1.56). Two of these RCTs showed a large but non-significant effect for selective mutism remission favouring intervention (relative risk 4.25, p = .1774, 95% CI 0.52-34.84; absolute remission rates not given in the abstract). Two RCTs with active controls were non-significant (Hedges g = 0.55, p < .2885, 95% CI -0.47 to 1.57) with considerable heterogeneity. Within-subject effects across all studies ranged from very small to large for speaking and from very small negative to large for anxiety.
cards.watchOut: Remission — the outcome families care about most — was reported by only 6 of 25 studies and its pooled advantage is statistically fragile (confidence interval 0.52 to 34.84); measurement inconsistency across studies is the field's core problem.

cards.headline: Iimura 2025: behavioural treatment improved Selective Mutism Questionnaire scores by a mean 0.51 (95% CI 0.32-0.70; g = 1.00) across 12 studies and 472 participants
cards.summary: Iimura 2025: behavioural treatment improved Selective Mutism Questionnaire scores by a mean 0.51 (95% CI 0.32-0.70; g = 1.00) across 12 studies and 472 participants
cards.type: Meta-analysis of controlled and before-after studies (Iimura 2025)
cards.people: Children with selective mutism in 12 articles involving 472 participants — 3 randomised controlled trials and 9 before-after or multiple-baseline studies — meta-analysed using the Selective Mutism Questionnaire (SMQ) and School Speech Questionnaire (SSQ).
cards.result: SMQ total, SMQ subsection (school, home, public) and SSQ scores all improved significantly. The mean SMQ total score improved by 0.51 (95% CI 0.32-0.70) with a large effect size (Hedges adjusted g = 1.00, 95% CI 0.62-1.39), and the effect did not differ significantly by study design. By treatment strategy, web-based treatment improved scores less (0.12, 95% CI -0.11 to 0.36) than face-to-face treatment (0.59, 95% CI 0.39-0.80).
cards.watchOut: Three quarters of the included studies are uncontrolled before-after designs, so improvement mixes treatment effect with maturation and repeated measurement; the face-to-face versus web-based contrast is between studies, not randomised within them.
cards.source: Iimura D, Tsujita N, Aoki M, Hagihara H. Meta-analysis of behavioral treatments for selective mutism: findings from selective mutism questionnaire (SMQ) and school speech questionnaire (SSQ). Child and Adolescent Psychiatry and Mental Health. 2025. PMID: 40181492. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session.

cards.headline: Synthesis: behavioural treatment clearly beats doing nothing; whether it beats other active help, and whether it produces remission, is unproven
cards.summary: Synthesis: behavioural treatment clearly beats doing nothing; whether it beats other active help, and whether it produces remission, is unproven
cards.people: 233 children in the RCT-only pool, 472 participants in the questionnaire pool, and 25 studies in the systematic review (overlapping sets).
cards.result: Versus no treatment or waitlist: large effects on speaking (g = 0.87 and g = 1.06). Versus active controls: g = 0.55, not significant. Remission: relative risk 4.25 with a confidence interval spanning 0.52 to 34.84 — compatible with anything from harm to large benefit.
cards.watchOut: Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) for behavioural/psychological treatment delivered face-to-face. SSRI medication is widely used as an adjunct but rests on small, mostly uncontrolled series with only two double-blind studies in the older reviews — no drug card met the bar this session, so no drug claim is made on this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Steains 2021 (PMID: 34265102), Hipolito 2023 (PMID: 37720585) and Iimura 2025 (PMID: 40181492), carded above.

shelves.title: Procalcitonin in febrile infants under 3 months: untested in this age group — the nearest randomised trials (enrolling from 7 days and 1 month) found revealing the result made no difference to antibiotic prescribing
shelves.question: In febrile infants under 3 months, can procalcitonin testing safely reduce antibiotic use?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents · Bacterial Infections · Biomarkers · C-Reactive Protein · Calcitonin · Calcitonin Gene-Related Peptide · Female · Fever · Humans · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Leukocyte Count · Male · Protein Precursors
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #3911, which covers procalcitonin-guided antibiotic duration in neonates with suspected early-onset sepsis (NeoPInS); this shelf covers the different population of febrile infants under 3 months presenting with fever without source, and does not re-card #3911's trial. The honest headline is that no randomised trial has tested procalcitonin guidance specifically in infants under 3 months. The two randomised trials that enrolled from the first weeks of life — a Lab-score (procalcitonin, C-reactive protein and urine dipstick) trial enrolling from 7 days (Lacroix 2014) and a procalcitonin-reveal trial enrolling from 1 month (Manzano 2010) — both found that revealing the biomarker result made no difference to actual antibiotic prescribing (41.2% versus 42.1%, and 9% versus 10% among undiagnosed children respectively; the treatment made no difference), although strict adherence to the Lab-score would hypothetically have cut prescriptions by about a quarter. A 2022 meta-analysis of procalcitonin-guided therapy in children with infectious disease more broadly (Li 2022) found antibiotic courses 2.22 days shorter and fewer antibiotic adverse events, but no difference in prescription rates — and its patients were children generally, not young infants. On safety, procalcitonin alone discriminates serious bacterial infection in febrile infants under 91 days less well than clinical prediction rules (England 2014), and the Lab-score missed about 15% of serious bacterial infections (sensitivity 85.1%), so a biomarker-only rule cannot yet be trusted to withhold antibiotics in this age group. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): procalcitonin testing has not been shown to safely reduce antibiotic use in febrile infants under 3 months — the infant-specific trial does not exist, and the nearest randomised evidence, in populations dominated by older infants and children, is null for prescribing.

cards.headline: Lacroix 2014: in children from 7 days to 36 months with fever without source, reporting a procalcitonin-based Lab-score did not reduce antibiotic prescriptions — 41.2% versus 42.1% (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Lacroix 2014: in children from 7 days to 36 months with fever without source, reporting a procalcitonin-based Lab-score did not reduce antibiotic prescriptions — 41.2% versus 42.1% (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: 271 children aged 7 days to 36 months with fever without source in a randomised controlled trial, allocated to a Lab-score group (score from procalcitonin, C-reactive protein and urinary dipstick reported; white-cell count blinded) or a control group (white-cell count, bands and C-reactive protein determined; procalcitonin and Lab-score blinded). The enrolled range includes infants under 3 months, but the record does not report that subgroup separately.
cards.result: Antibiotic prescription was 41.2% (54 of 131) in the Lab-score group versus 42.1% (59 of 140) in the control group (P = 1.000) — the treatment made no difference in practice, which the authors attribute to clinicians not adhering to the score's recommendations. Had the recommendations been strictly applied, the hypothetical treatment rate would have been 30.6% versus the 41.7% observed (P = 0.0095), a 26.5% relative reduction. A Lab-score of 3 or more had sensitivity 85.1% (95% CI 76.5 to 93.6) and specificity 87.3% for serious bacterial infection, with negative predictive value 94.1%.
cards.watchOut: The score was tested in children up to 36 months, not in infants under 3 months specifically, and its sensitivity of 85.1% means roughly one in seven serious bacterial infections scored low — the safety margin this question asks about is exactly what the trial could not establish for the youngest infants.
cards.source: Lacroix L et al. Impact of the lab-score on antibiotic prescription rate in children with fever without source: a randomized controlled trial. PloS One. 2014. PMID: 25503770. Registry ID: NCT02179398. cards.headline: Manzano 2010: revealing the procalcitonin result to the physician did not change antibiotic use in febrile children aged 1 to 36 months — 9% versus 10% among those without a diagnosis
cards.summary: Manzano 2010: revealing the procalcitonin result to the physician did not change antibiotic use in febrile children aged 1 to 36 months — 9% versus 10% among those without a diagnosis
cards.people: 384 children aged 1 to 36 months presenting to a paediatric emergency department with fever without source, randomised equally to procalcitonin-revealed (PCT+) or procalcitonin-blinded (PCT-) care; 62 (16%) were diagnosed with a serious bacterial infection on the primary investigation. Only the youngest sliver of this population (from 1 month) overlaps the under-3-months question.
cards.result: Among the remaining undiagnosed patients, 14 (9%) of 158 in the PCT+ group versus 16 (10%) of 154 in the PCT- group received antibiotics (difference −2%; 95% CI −8 to 5) — semiquantitative procalcitonin measurement had no impact on antibiotic use (the treatment made no difference). A strategy of giving prophylactic antibiotics to every patient with procalcitonin of 0.5 ng/mL or greater would have increased antibiotic use by 24% (95% CI 15 to 33).
cards.watchOut: A null result in 1-to-36-month-olds cannot be read across to infants under 3 months, in whom the consequences of a missed bacterial infection are greatest and prescribing thresholds are lowest; the trial also shows biomarker testing can push prescribing up, not down, if thresholds are applied mechanically.
cards.source: Manzano S et al. Impact of procalcitonin on the management of children aged 1 to 36 months presenting with fever without source: a randomized controlled trial. cards.headline: Li 2022: across paediatric infectious disease generally, procalcitonin guidance shortened antibiotic courses by 2.22 days and cut antibiotic adverse events — but did not reduce prescription rates, and the patients were not young infants
cards.summary: Li 2022: across paediatric infectious disease generally, procalcitonin guidance shortened antibiotic courses by 2.22 days and cut antibiotic adverse events — but did not reduce prescription rates, and the patients were not young infants
cards.people: Meta-analysis and trial sequential analysis of 4 randomised controlled trials with 1,313 paediatric patients with infectious disease (searches to July 2021); the included trials enrolled children with infectious diseases broadly, not febrile infants under 3 months as a defined population.
cards.result: Procalcitonin-guided therapy was associated with a shorter length of antibiotic therapy (weighted mean difference −2.22 days; 95% CI −3.41 to −1.03; P < 0.001) and a decreased rate of antibiotic adverse events (relative risk 0.25; 95% CI 0.11 to 0.58; P < 0.001; relative measure). Length of hospital stay, antibiotic prescription rate (relative risk 1.10; 95% CI 0.97 to 1.25), readmission and mortality did not differ between groups. Trial sequential analysis gave a required information size of 2,340, and the authors state that much larger prospective studies are warranted.
cards.watchOut: Shorter courses in older children with established infections are a different claim from safely withholding or stopping antibiotics in a febrile 6-week-old; this synthesis cannot supply the missing infant-specific safety evidence.
cards.source: Li P et al. Procalcitonin-guided antibiotic therapy for pediatrics with infective disease: A updated meta-analyses and trial sequential analysis. cards.headline: England 2014: in febrile infants under 91 days specifically, a single procalcitonin measurement identified risk less well than clinical prediction rules — the safety foundation for withholding antibiotics is not there
cards.summary: England 2014: in febrile infants under 91 days specifically, a single procalcitonin measurement identified risk less well than clinical prediction rules — the safety foundation for withholding antibiotics is not there
cards.type: Diagnostic meta-analysis in febrile infants under 91 days (England 2014)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 7 studies encompassing 2,317 febrile infants, with subgroup data for infants younger than 91 days and a 0.3 ng/mL procalcitonin cutoff in five of the seven studies. This is a diagnostic-accuracy synthesis, not a treatment trial.
cards.result: The overall relative risk for serious bacterial infection at the discriminating procalcitonin concentration was 3.97 (95% CI 3.41 to 4.62; relative measure). The relative risk from a systematic review of clinical prediction rules was 30.6 (95% CI 7.0 to 68.13) for untreated infants and 8.75 (95% CI 2.29 to 15.2) for antibiotic-treated infants. The authors conclude that procalcitonin alone, though able to identify a group of young infants at risk, is inferior to the available clinical prediction rules for identifying low-risk febrile infants, and that a level of 0.3 ng/mL or below may help only as an add-on test to current rules.
cards.watchOut: Diagnostic discrimination is not stewardship: even a perfect risk marker reduces antibiotics only if clinicians act on it, and the two randomised cards above show that, in practice, they largely did not.
cards.source: England JT et al. Use of serum procalcitonin in evaluation of febrile infants: a meta-analysis of 2317 patients. The Journal of Emergency Medicine. 2014. PMID: 25281186. cards.headline: Synthesis: no trial has tested procalcitonin guidance in febrile infants under 3 months; the nearest randomised evidence shows no reduction in prescribing, and procalcitonin alone underperforms prediction rules for safety in this age group
cards.summary: Synthesis: no trial has tested procalcitonin guidance in febrile infants under 3 months; the nearest randomised evidence shows no reduction in prescribing, and procalcitonin alone underperforms prediction rules for safety in this age group
cards.people: The carded evidence: two randomised trials enrolling from 7 days and from 1 month upward (271 and 384 children, both dominated by older infants and toddlers, neither reporting an under-3-months subgroup), one paediatric meta-analysis (4 trials, 1,313 children), and one diagnostic meta-analysis in infants under 91 days (7 studies, 2,317 infants). Total carded participants exceed 4,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the limitation is population indirectness, printed here.
cards.result: Revealing procalcitonin or a procalcitonin-based Lab-score made no difference to antibiotic prescription rates (41.2% versus 42.1%; 9% versus 10%). Procalcitonin guidance shortened antibiotic duration by 2.22 days across paediatric infectious disease generally, with prescription rates unchanged. In infants under 91 days, procalcitonin alone was inferior to clinical prediction rules for identifying serious bacterial infection (relative risk 3.97 versus 30.6). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: This shelf must not be cited as evidence that procalcitonin safely reduces antibiotics in young infants: that trial has not been done, and the adjacent evidence points the other way on prescribing.

shelves.title: Amoxicillin versus broader-spectrum antibiotics in childhood pneumonia (PARTIAL completion of live #1140): narrow-spectrum treatment was never worse across 265,000 children — on observational evidence only
shelves.question: In children with community-acquired pneumonia, is amoxicillin as effective as broader-spectrum antibiotics?
shelves.mesh: Ampicillin · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Cefotaxime · Ceftriaxone · Child, Preschool · Cohort Studies · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Hospitalization · Humans · Infant · Male · Penicillins · Pneumonia · Retrospective Studies
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — observational only, printed on the face: no randomised trial has compared antibiotic spectrum in childhood pneumonia. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #1140 already answers how much amoxicillin and for how long (the CAP-IT dose-and-duration trial and SAFER); this shelf asks the different question #1140 does not — whether the narrow aminopenicillin itself (amoxicillin in outpatients, ampicillin/penicillin in hospital) matches broader-spectrum agents. Three large cohort records agree. In 15,564 hospitalised children, narrow-spectrum therapy matched broad-spectrum cephalosporins on stay (median 3 days in both), intensive-care admission (0.8% vs 1.1%) and readmission (2.4% vs 2.3%). A propensity-matched cohort found narrow therapy associated with a 10-hour shorter stay and no difference in fever, oxygen or readmission. And in 252,177 ambulatory visits, later hospitalisation was rare (0.59%) and was not lower with broad-spectrum treatment (adjusted odds ratio 1.34 versus narrow-spectrum, an association the design cannot show is causal). PROPOSED POSSIBLE — observational only: amoxicillin-class narrow-spectrum treatment performs at least as well as broader-spectrum antibiotics for children with community-acquired pneumonia.

cards.headline: Williams 2013: in 15,564 hospitalised children, narrow-spectrum ampicillin/penicillin matched broad-spectrum cephalosporins — stay 3 days in both, intensive care 0.8% vs 1.1%, readmission 2.4% vs 2.3%
cards.summary: Williams 2013: in 15,564 hospitalised children, narrow-spectrum ampicillin/penicillin matched broad-spectrum cephalosporins — stay 3 days in both, intensive care 0.8% vs 1.1%, readmission 2.4% vs 2.3%
cards.people: Children hospitalised with community-acquired pneumonia at 43 US children's hospitals (2005–2011) who received parenteral ampicillin/penicillin (narrow spectrum, n = 1,610) or ceftriaxone/cefotaxime (broad spectrum, n = 13,954) in the first two days; children with complex chronic conditions, intensive care, drainage, ventilation or death in the first two days were excluded. Retrospective cohort.
cards.result: Median length of stay was 3 days (interquartile range 3–4) in both groups (adjusted difference 0.12 days, 95% CI −0.02 to 0.26). Intensive-care admission occurred in 0.8% of the narrow-spectrum group versus 1.1% of the broad-spectrum group (adjusted odds ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.27 to 2.73) and readmission in 2.4% versus 2.3% (adjusted OR 0.85, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.63); median costs were $4,375 narrow versus $3,992 broad (adjusted difference −$14.4, 95% CI −177.1 to 148.3). The authors conclude clinical outcomes and costs are not different with narrow- compared with broad-spectrum therapy.
cards.watchOut: Treatment was chosen by clinicians, not randomised: children given cephalosporins may have looked sicker in ways the exclusions and adjustment cannot fully capture, and the inpatient narrow agent here is intravenous ampicillin/penicillin — the same aminopenicillin class as oral amoxicillin, not the oral drug itself.
cards.source: Williams DJ et al. Narrow vs broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy for children hospitalized with pneumonia. Pediatrics. 2013. PMID: 24167170. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Queen 2014: in a propensity-matched cohort of 492 hospitalised children, narrow-spectrum therapy came with a 10-hour shorter stay and no difference in fever, oxygen need or readmission
cards.summary: Queen 2014: in a propensity-matched cohort of 492 hospitalised children, narrow-spectrum therapy came with a 10-hour shorter stay and no difference in fever, oxygen need or readmission
cards.people: Children aged 2 months to 18 years with uncomplicated community-acquired pneumonia at four US children's hospitals in 2010, empirically treated in the first two days with narrow-spectrum (52%) or broad-spectrum (48%) therapy and matched by propensity score; 492 children in the matched analysis. Retrospective cohort.
cards.result: In adjusted analysis the narrow-spectrum group had a 10-hour shorter length of stay (P = .04), with no significant difference in duration of supplemental oxygen, duration of fever, or 7-day readmission, and no difference in average daily standardised cost (P = .62) or pharmacy cost (P = .26). The authors conclude narrow-spectrum coverage is associated with similar outcomes and supports national recommendations for narrow-spectrum first-line treatment.
cards.watchOut: A 10-hour stay difference in a 492-child matched cohort is a modest, confounding-prone signal — discharge timing is sensitive to local practice — and, as with the larger cohort, spectrum was clinician-chosen rather than assigned.
cards.source: Queen MA et al. Comparative effectiveness of empiric antibiotics for community-acquired pneumonia. Pediatrics. 2014. PMID: 24324001. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Lipsett 2021: in 252,177 ambulatory pneumonia visits, later hospitalisation was rare (0.59%) and broad-spectrum treatment was not associated with fewer hospitalisations than narrow-spectrum aminopenicillins
cards.summary: Lipsett 2021: in 252,177 ambulatory pneumonia visits, later hospitalisation was rare (0.59%) and broad-spectrum treatment was not associated with fewer hospitalisations than narrow-spectrum aminopenicillins
cards.people: Ambulatory Medicaid-enrolled children aged 0–18 years diagnosed with community-acquired pneumonia in the USA, 2010–2016 (252,177 visits); exposure was the prescribed antibiotic class — narrow-spectrum aminopenicillins (26.1% of visits), broad-spectrum amoxicillin–clavulanate or cephalosporins (24.7%), macrolide monotherapy (43.2%), or combinations. Retrospective cohort.
cards.result: 1,488 children (0.59%) were subsequently hospitalised and 117 (0.05%) developed severe pneumonia. Compared with narrow-spectrum antibiotics, the adjusted odds of subsequent hospitalisation were higher with broad-spectrum antibiotics (adjusted odds ratio 1.34, 95% CI 1.17–1.52) and lower with macrolide monotherapy (aOR 0.64, 95% CI 0.55–0.73); the authors note the absolute risk difference was under 0.5% for all analyses. Severe pneumonia was less frequent with macrolide monotherapy than with narrow-spectrum treatment (aOR 0.56, 95% CI 0.33–0.93).
cards.watchOut: The higher hospitalisation odds with broad-spectrum prescriptions almost certainly reflect confounding by indication — clinicians reach for broader cover in children who look worse — so this record supports 'broad was not better' but must never be quoted as 'broad-spectrum treatment causes hospitalisation'.
cards.source: Lipsett SC et al. Antibiotic Choice and Clinical Outcomes in Ambulatory Children with Community-Acquired Pneumonia. The Journal of pediatrics. 2021. PMID: 33045236. cards.headline: Synthesis: across hospital and ambulatory cohorts totalling over 265,000 children, narrow aminopenicillin treatment was never worse than broader-spectrum treatment — on observational evidence only
cards.summary: Synthesis: across hospital and ambulatory cohorts totalling over 265,000 children, narrow aminopenicillin treatment was never worse than broader-spectrum treatment — on observational evidence only
cards.people: The carded evidence: two hospital cohorts (15,564 and 492 children) and one ambulatory cohort (252,177 visits), all retrospective; no randomised trial of antibiotic spectrum in childhood pneumonia was found in the records fetched. Total carded participants exceed 265,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the limitation is design, not size, and is printed in the stamp.
cards.result: Narrow-spectrum therapy matched broad-spectrum therapy on length of stay (median 3 days both), intensive-care admission (0.8% vs 1.1%) and readmission (2.4% vs 2.3%) in hospital, and ambulatory broad-spectrum prescribing was associated with no fewer subsequent hospitalisations (0.59% overall). How much amoxicillin and for how long is homed on live shelf #1140 (CAP-IT and SAFER) and is not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — observational only: amoxicillin-class narrow-spectrum treatment is as effective as broader-spectrum antibiotics for children with community-acquired pneumonia.
cards.watchOut: Every card is observational: spectrum was clinician-chosen in all three, so 'as effective' is an association that three concordant cohorts support — a randomised spectrum trial remains the missing proof, and these records cover uncomplicated pneumonia, not empyema or intensive-care presentations.
cards.source: Synthesis of Williams DJ et al. Pediatrics. 2013 (PMID: 24167170); Queen MA et al. Pediatrics. 2014 (PMID: 24324001); Lipsett SC et al. The Journal of pediatrics. 2021 (PMID: 33045236).

shelves.title: Short-course oral steroids at home in childhood asthma/wheeze (PARTIAL completion of live #2664): parent-initiated courses made no difference — the benefit appears only when the course is started in the emergency department
shelves.question: In children with asthma, is a short course of oral steroids effective for an acute exacerbation at home?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adrenal Cortex Hormones · Anti-Inflammatory Agents · Asthma · Blood Proteins · Child · Child, Preschool · Circadian Rhythm · Common Cold · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Eosinophil Granule Proteins · Eosinophil-Derived Neurotoxin · Eosinophils · Humans · Infant · Leukocyte Count · Medical Records · Prednisolone · Respiratory Sounds · Ribonucleases · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT (setting: a course started in the emergency department shortened hospital stay; courses started by parents at home made no difference) — printed on the face. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #2664 answers oral versus intravenous steroids in (largely adult) exacerbations, and the hospital-admission preschool-wheeze trial is homed on live shelf #1362; this shelf asks the remaining question — whether a short course started at home, by parents, works. The dedicated home evidence says it does not: in the parent-initiated randomised trial, symptom scores and admissions were identical on prednisolone and placebo (the treatment made no difference), even in children with high eosinophil priming, and the Cochrane review of parent-initiated courses (2 trials, 303 children) found no benefit on admissions, reviews or symptoms. The contrasting positive result comes from a different setting: a 3-day course started in the emergency department shortened time to discharge readiness (median 370 vs 540 minutes). PROPOSED SPLIT (setting): parent-initiated oral steroids at home have no demonstrated benefit for children's acute wheeze/asthma exacerbations, while a clinician-started short course in the emergency department shortened hospital stay.

cards.headline: Oommen 2003: parent-initiated prednisolone at home made no difference — daytime symptom scores differed by −0.01 and admissions were the same, even in high-eosinophil-primed children
cards.summary: Oommen 2003: parent-initiated prednisolone at home made no difference — daytime symptom scores differed by −0.01 and admissions were the same, even in high-eosinophil-primed children
cards.people: Children aged 1–5 years admitted to hospital with viral wheeze, stratified by systemic eosinophil priming (serum eosinophil cationic protein and eosinophil protein X) and randomised (109 prednisolone, 108 placebo) to a parent-initiated course for the next episode — prednisolone 20 mg once daily for 5 days, or placebo — started by parents at the first sign of the episode.
cards.result: Outcome data were available for 120 (78%) of the 153 children who had a further episode (51 prednisolone, 69 placebo). Mean daytime respiratory symptom scores differed by −0.01 (95% CI −0.22 to 0.20) and night-time scores by 0.10 (95% CI −0.12 to 0.32), and need for hospital admission did not differ between groups; within the high-primed (n = 59) and low-primed (n = 61) strata there was likewise no difference — the treatment made no difference. The authors conclude there is no clear benefit of a short course of parent-initiated oral prednisolone for viral wheeze in children aged 1–5 years, even with above-average eosinophil priming.
cards.watchOut: This is preschool viral wheeze, not school-age asthma, and a fifth of randomised children contributed no outcome episode data; it is nonetheless the only dedicated randomised test of the at-home, parent-started strategy on this shelf.
cards.source: Oommen A et al. Efficacy of a short course of parent-initiated oral prednisolone for viral wheeze in children aged 1-5 years: randomised controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2003. PMID: 14602435. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cochrane 2006 (Vuillermin): across the 2 randomised trials of parent-initiated oral corticosteroids (303 children), no benefit was found for admissions, unscheduled reviews or symptom scores — evidence inconclusive, widespread use not recommended
cards.summary: Cochrane 2006 (Vuillermin): across the 2 randomised trials of parent-initiated oral corticosteroids (303 children), no benefit was found for admissions, unscheduled reviews or symptom scores — evidence inconclusive, widespread use not recommended
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Cochrane; Vuillermin 2006)
cards.people: Systematic review of randomised trials of parent-initiated oral corticosteroids versus placebo or another drug for intermittent wheezing illnesses (asthma, viral wheeze, preschool viral wheeze) in children aged 1–18 years; 2 trials with 303 randomised participants met inclusion from 572 citations.
cards.result: The two included trials — both rated high quality, but too clinically heterogeneous to pool — did not find evidence that parent-initiated oral corticosteroids benefit hospital admissions, unscheduled medical reviews, symptom scores, bronchodilator use, parent and patient impressions, physician assessment, or days lost from work or school; adverse outcomes were inadequately documented. The reviewers conclude the limited current evidence is inconclusive regarding benefit and that widespread use of the parent-initiated strategy cannot be recommended until benefits and harms are clarified.
cards.watchOut: The review is from 2006 and rests on only two trials (one of them the Oommen trial carded above, so participants overlap between cards); its verdict is 'no demonstrated benefit', which is weaker than proof of no benefit — and no newer parent-initiated trial was found in the records fetched this session.
cards.source: Vuillermin P et al. Parent-initiated oral corticosteroid therapy for intermittent wheezing illnesses in children. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2006. PMID: 16856091. cards.headline: Foster 2018: a short course started in the emergency department did work — median stay to discharge readiness 370 vs 540 minutes on placebo (ratio of geometric means 0.79)
cards.summary: Foster 2018: a short course started in the emergency department did work — median stay to discharge readiness 370 vs 540 minutes on placebo (ratio of geometric means 0.79)
cards.people: Children aged 24–72 months presenting to a paediatric emergency department in Perth, Australia with virus-associated wheeze, randomised double-blind to oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg per day for 3 days (n = 305 analysed) or placebo (n = 300 analysed); 624 children were randomised and 605 included in the modified intention-to-treat analysis. The course was clinician-started in the department, not parent-initiated at home.
cards.result: Median length of stay until ready for discharge was 370 minutes (interquartile range 121–709) on prednisolone versus 540 minutes (124–971) on placebo; placebo was inferior to prednisolone, and the post-hoc superiority analysis gave an unadjusted ratio of geometric mean stay of 0.79 (95% CI 0.64–0.97; P = .0227) for prednisolone relative to placebo. No serious adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: Foster answers a neighbouring question — a clinician-started course in children already in the emergency department, with stay as the outcome — not the at-home question on this shelf; it is carded to mark the setting boundary honestly, and the hospital-admission trial of the same design family is homed on live shelf #1362, not here.
cards.source: Foster SJ et al. Oral prednisolone in preschool children with virus-associated wheeze: a prospective, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. The Lancet. cards.headline: Synthesis: started by parents at home, a short steroid course has never beaten placebo; started by clinicians in the department, it shortened stay — the setting, not the drug, divides the evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: started by parents at home, a short steroid course has never beaten placebo; started by clinicians in the department, it shortened stay — the setting, not the drug, divides the evidence
cards.people: The carded evidence: one parent-initiated randomised trial (217 randomised; 120 children with outcome episodes), one Cochrane review of parent-initiated therapy (2 trials, 303 participants, overlapping the first card), and one emergency-department-initiated randomised trial (624 randomised, 605 analysed). Total unique participants are under 1,000 but well over the small-N threshold, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Parent-initiated prednisolone made no difference to symptom scores (−0.01 daytime) or admissions (Oommen 2003), and the Cochrane review of parent-initiated courses found no benefit on any measured outcome; by contrast the department-started 3-day course shortened stay to discharge readiness (370 vs 540 minutes median; Foster 2018). Oral versus intravenous route is homed on live shelf #2664 and the admitted-preschooler hospital trial on live shelf #1362; neither is re-carded here. PROPOSED SPLIT (setting): no demonstrated benefit for parent-initiated oral steroids at home; benefit for a clinician-started short course in the emergency department.
cards.watchOut: Most of this evidence is preschool viral wheeze rather than diagnosed asthma in older children; extrapolating the home null to a school-age child with asthma goes beyond the carded trials, and the shelf says so rather than smoothing it over.
cards.source: Synthesis of Oommen A et al. Lancet (London, England). 2003 (PMID: 14602435); Vuillermin P et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2006 (PMID: 16856091); Foster SJ et al. The Lancet. Respiratory medicine. 2018 (PMID: 29373235).

shelves.title: Probiotics for infant colic beyond L. reuteri (PARTIAL completion of live #640): BB-12 and LGG each beat placebo on crying — strain by strain, in small trials
shelves.question: For infant colic, are probiotics effective compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Animals · Breast Feeding · Colic · Diet · Dietary Supplements · Feces · Female · Gastrointestinal Microbiome · Humans · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus · Leukocyte L1 Antigen Complex · Male · Milk · Probiotics · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — strain-specific, printed on the face: the benefit belongs to named strains, not to 'probiotics' as a class. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #640 already answers Lactobacillus reuteri DSM 17938 in breastfed infants; this shelf covers the other tested strains. Two clear the bar. Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis BB-12 (1 × 10^9 CFU/day) beat placebo in two randomised trials (80 and 192 infants), with more infants reaching a ≥50% cut in crying and crying episodes roughly halving. Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (ATCC 53103; now classified Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus) reduced median daily crying to 104 versus 242 minutes in one small trial of 45 breastfed infants run alongside maternal cow's-milk elimination, and a 2024 meta-analysis of four LGG trials (168 infants) found crying time lower by a mean 32.59 minutes/day. The publications name the strains exactly; none of the carded records names a manufacturer or branded product, and the shelf says so — current products carrying the same strain names may differ. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): BB-12 and LGG each have randomised evidence of reduced crying in colic, on small trials; no class-wide probiotic claim is made.

cards.headline: Savino 2020: L. rhamnosus GG (ATCC 53103) cut median daily crying to 104 vs 242 minutes at 28 days — in 45 breastfed infants whose mothers also avoided cow's milk (small N on the face)
cards.summary: Savino 2020: L. rhamnosus GG (ATCC 53103) cut median daily crying to 104 vs 242 minutes at 28 days — in 45 breastfed infants whose mothers also avoided cow's milk (small N on the face)
cards.people: 45 colicky breastfed infants randomised to Lactobacillus (Lacticaseibacillus) rhamnosus GG, ATCC 53103, at 5 × 10^9 CFU per day for 28 days, or placebo; the probiotic was given together with maternal dietary avoidance of cow's milk. The record names the strain and dose; it does not name a manufacturer or branded product.
cards.result: After 28 days, median full-force daily crying was 104 minutes in the probiotic group versus 242 minutes on placebo (P < 0.001), faecal calprotectin fell significantly in the probiotic group (P = 0.026), and Lactobacillus abundance and total bacterial load rose (P = 0.048 and P = 0.040) — effects not observed with placebo. The authors themselves call for a larger double-blind placebo-controlled trial to validate the result.
cards.watchOut: N = 45, and the probiotic was bundled with maternal cow's-milk elimination, so the crying reduction cannot be credited to the strain alone; the trial's own authors ask for a larger confirmatory trial.
cards.source: Savino F et al. Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (ATCC 53103) for the Management of Infantile Colic: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Nutrients. 2020. PMID: 32517123. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Nocerino 2020: BB-12 (Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis) — more infants reached a ≥50% cut in crying from week 2, and crying episodes fell further than on placebo (−4.7 vs −2.3 per day)
cards.summary: Nocerino 2020: BB-12 (Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis) — more infants reached a ≥50% cut in crying from week 2, and crying episodes fell further than on placebo (−4.7 vs −2.3 per day)
cards.people: 80 otherwise healthy, exclusively breastfed infants with colic randomised to Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis BB-12 at 1 × 10^9 CFU/day or placebo for 28 days. The record names the strain (BB-12) and dose; it does not name a manufacturer or branded product.
cards.result: The rate of infants achieving a reduction of ≥50% in mean daily crying duration was higher on BB-12 starting from the end of the second week — the record does not print the two groups' exact percentages for this primary outcome — and no infant relapsed when treatment stopped. Mean daily crying episodes fell in both groups, more on BB-12 (−4.7 ± 3.4 vs −2.3 ± 2.2; P < 0.05); Bifidobacterium abundance, butyrate and immune markers rose and faecal calprotectin fell in the BB-12 group.
cards.watchOut: The headline primary-outcome rates are reported in the record only as 'higher from week 2' without percentages, so the size of the BB-12 advantage on that endpoint cannot be quoted from this record; the episode-count difference is the card's quotable number.
cards.source: Nocerino R et al. The therapeutic efficacy of Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis BB-12® in infant colic: A randomised, double blind, placebo-controlled trial. Alimentary pharmacology & therapeutics. 2020. PMID: 31797399. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Chen 2021: the second BB-12 trial (192 infants) confirms it — significantly more infants halved crying/fussing time, and episodes fell from 10.0 to 5.0 a day versus 10.5 to 7.5 on placebo
cards.summary: Chen 2021: the second BB-12 trial (192 infants) confirms it — significantly more infants halved crying/fussing time, and episodes fell from 10.0 to 5.0 a day versus 10.5 to 7.5 on placebo
cards.people: 192 full-term breastfed infants under 3 months meeting Rome III criteria for infant colic in Chengdu, China, randomised after a 1-week run-in to Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis BB-12 at 1 × 10^9 CFU/day or placebo for 3 weeks (21 days), with crying/fussing recorded in a 24-hour structured diary. The record names the strain (BB-12) and dose; it does not name a manufacturer or branded product.
cards.result: The proportion of infants achieving a ≥50% reduction in daily crying/fussing time after 21 days was significantly higher on BB-12 (P < 0.001; the record does not print the two percentages). Mean crying episodes fell from 10.0 ± 3.0 to 5.0 ± 1.87 per day on BB-12 versus 10.5 ± 2.6 to 7.5 ± 2.8 on placebo (P < 0.001), and mean daily sleep duration rose more on BB-12 (60.7 ± 104.0 vs 31.9 ± 102.7 minutes/day; P < 0.001), with higher parent/caregiver quality-of-life scores (all P < 0.05).
cards.watchOut: As with the first BB-12 trial, the primary-outcome group percentages are not printed in the record — only the P value — so the shelf quotes the episode counts, which are printed, and flags the gap rather than estimating the missing rates.
cards.source: Chen K et al. Efficacy of Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis, BB-12® on infant colic - a randomised, double-blinded, placebo-controlled study. Beneficial microbes. 2021. cards.headline: Liu 2024: pooling the four LGG trials (168 infants), crying time was lower by a mean 32.59 minutes/day — a real but modest pooled effect for that one strain
cards.summary: Liu 2024: pooling the four LGG trials (168 infants), crying time was lower by a mean 32.59 minutes/day — a real but modest pooled effect for that one strain
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials of Lactobacillus (Lacticaseibacillus) rhamnosus GG versus placebo or no treatment in infants with colic, searched to January 2024; four studies involving 168 infants were included, with crying/fussing time at the end of intervention as the primary outcome.
cards.result: LGG significantly reduced daily crying time (mean difference −32.59 minutes/day, 95% CI −43.23 to −21.96; P < 0.001) and faecal calprotectin (mean difference −103.28 µg/g, 95% CI −149.30 to −7.26; P < 0.001); only one included study reported adverse events. The authors conclude LGG is effective for infantile colic while calling for studies of dose, schedule, duration and feeding method.
cards.watchOut: Four small trials and 168 infants is a thin base for a pooled claim, and the pool overlaps the Savino trial carded above; a mean half-hour less crying is also a smaller effect than the single-trial medians suggest.
cards.source: Liu H et al. The effectiveness of Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG in the treatment of infantile colic: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Translational pediatrics. 2024. PMID: 39263298. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: beyond L. reuteri, two named strains — BB-12 and LGG — each beat placebo for colic crying, in small trials; 'probiotics' as a class earns no stamp
cards.summary: Synthesis: beyond L. reuteri, two named strains — BB-12 and LGG — each beat placebo for colic crying, in small trials; 'probiotics' as a class earns no stamp
cards.people: The carded evidence: two randomised trials of Bifidobacterium animalis subsp. lactis BB-12 (80 and 192 infants), one small randomised trial of Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus GG ATCC 53103 (45 infants) and a meta-analysis of four LGG trials (168 infants, overlapping the LGG trial card). Unique infants across the strain trials total about 317, so no small-N stamp labelling applies, though each individual trial is small and the Ns are printed on the cards.
cards.result: BB-12 increased the proportion of infants halving crying time in two trials and roughly halved daily crying episodes (to 5.0 vs 7.5 on placebo in the larger trial); LGG reduced crying in its small trial (median 104 vs 242 minutes) and by a pooled mean of 32.59 minutes/day across four trials. Lactobacillus reuteri DSM 17938 in breastfed infants is homed on live shelf #640 and is not re-carded here. None of the carded records names a manufacturer or branded product — only the strains and doses — so products sold under the same strain names today may differ in safety and effectiveness. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), strain-specific: BB-12 and LGG reduce crying in infant colic versus placebo.
cards.watchOut: Colic resolves on its own over weeks, every carded trial is short (3–4 weeks) and small, and strain results do not transfer between strains — a different Lactobacillus or Bifidobacterium product has no evidence from this shelf.
