shelves.title: Five versus ten days for otitis media beyond the under-twos: older and mixed-age trials look close, but the pooled failure rate still favours longer courses and no dedicated trial in children 2 and older exists
shelves.question: In children aged 2 years and older with acute otitis media, is a 5-day antibiotic course as effective as a 10-day course?
shelves.mesh: Otitis Media/drug therapy · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Drug Administration Schedule · Age Factors · Child · Humans · Treatment Failure
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — this pack is a PARTIAL completion: pack #2948 homes the under-2s question, where the strict Hoberman trial found 5 days clearly worse (clinical failure 34% versus 16%); its two records are not re-carded here. The uncovered slice is children aged 2 and older — and the honest finding is that no trial has ever randomised only that age group to 5 versus 10 days. What exists is the wider-childhood literature in which older children predominate numerically: the Cochrane short-course review (49 trials, 12,045 children aged 1 month to 18 years) found treatment failure at one month modestly higher on courses under 7 days (21% versus 18% absolute; odds ratio 1.34, 95% CI 1.15 to 1.55 — the odds ratio is a relative measure, printed beside the absolute rates), with fewer gastrointestinal adverse events on short courses of short-acting antibiotics. The largest direct 5-versus-10-day comparison in this older-skewing literature (Gooch 1996; 719 children aged 3 months to 12 years, cefuroxime) found satisfactory outcomes of 69% on 5 days versus 70% on 10 days of the same drug. The oldest trial (Hendrickse 1988; 175 children) found no advantage to 10 days when the eardrum was intact (failure 10% versus 6% plus one relapse, not significant) — but a stark exception: with spontaneous perforation, failure was 53% on 5 days versus 8% on 10 days (p = 0.016). Two under-2 trials by Cohen (1998, 2000; mean ages 13–14 months) were deliberately NOT carded: their populations belong to the #2948 slice, and borrowing them here would mislabel the age evidence. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): for a child of 2 or older with an intact eardrum, 5 days looks close to 10 in the trials that include such children, but equivalence is inferred, not demonstrated, and perforation is a clear exception.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2010 (Kozyrskyj): across 49 trials and 12,045 children, short courses failed more often at one month — 21% versus 18% (odds ratio 1.34)
cards.summary: Cochrane 2010 (Kozyrskyj): across 49 trials and 12,045 children, short courses failed more often at one month — 21% versus 18% (odds ratio 1.34)
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (Kozyrskyj 2010)
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials of short-course (under 7 days) versus long-course (7 days or more) antibiotics for acute otitis media in children aged 1 month to 18 years: 49 trials, 12,045 participants. Treatment failure was absence of resolution, relapse or recurrence within one month. This 2010 Cochrane review is a separate, larger publication from the 1998 JAMA meta-analysis homed on pack #2948, which is not re-carded here.
cards.result: Risk of treatment failure was higher with short courses (odds ratio 1.34, 95% CI 1.15 to 1.55 — a relative measure) at one month, corresponding to absolute failure rates of 21% on short courses versus 18% on long courses, a 3-percentage-point difference. No failure difference was found for short-course ceftriaxone or azithromycin against long-course comparators. Gastrointestinal adverse events were significantly fewer with short courses of short-acting antibiotics and azithromycin.
cards.watchOut: The pooled population runs from 1 month to 18 years: the 3-point average penalty is driven substantially by the youngest children (the group pack #2948 covers), and the review's abstract prints no age-2-and-older subgroup — this card bounds the question; it does not answer it for older children alone.
cards.source: Kozyrskyj A et al. Short-course antibiotics for acute otitis media. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2010. PMID: 20824827. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — systematic review, not a single trial. cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (kozyrskyj 2010) cochrane systematic review of randomised trials of short-course (under 7 days) versus long-course (7 days or more) antibiotics for acute otitis media in children aged 1 month to 18 years: 49 trials, 12,045 participants. treatment failure was absence of resolution, relapse or recurrence within one month. this 2010 cochrane review is a separate, larger publication from the 1998 jama meta-analysis homed on pack #2948, which is not re-carded here. risk of treatment failure was higher with short courses (odds ratio 1.34, 95% ci 1.15 to 1.55 — a relative measure) at one month, corresponding to absolute failure rates of 21% on short courses versus 18% on long courses, a 3-percentage-point difference. no failure difference was found for short-course ceftriaxone or azithromycin against long-course comparators. gastrointestinal adverse events were significantly fewer with short courses of short-acting antibiotics and azithromycin. the pooled population runs from 1 month to 18 years: the 3-point average penalty is driven substantially by the youngest children (the group pack #2948 covers), and the review's abstract prints no age-2-and-older subgroup — this card bounds the question; it does not answer it for older children alone. kozyrskyj a et al. short-course antibiotics for acute otitis media. the cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2010. pmid: 20824827. registry id: none in the record's databank fields — systematic review, not a single trial. mesh: acute disease · age factors · anti-bacterial agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · azithromycin/therapeutic use · ceftriaxone/adverse effects,therapeutic use · child · drug administration schedule · humans · otitis media/drug therapy · time factors

cards.headline: Gooch 1996: 5 days of cefuroxime matched 10 days in 719 children up to age 12 — satisfactory outcomes 69% versus 70%
cards.summary: Gooch 1996: 5 days of cefuroxime matched 10 days in 719 children up to age 12 — satisfactory outcomes 69% versus 70%
cards.type: Two randomised, investigator-blinded multicentre trials reported together (Gooch 1996)
cards.people: Two independent investigator-blinded multicentre randomised trials reported together: 719 children aged 3 months to 12 years with acute otitis media received cefuroxime axetil suspension for 5 days (n = 242, with placebo on days 6–10) or 10 days (n = 235), or amoxicillin-clavulanate for 10 days (n = 242); one trial included tympanocentesis cultures.
cards.result: A satisfactory clinical outcome (cure or improvement) occurred in 69% (101/147) of clinically evaluable patients on 5 days of cefuroxime, 70% (121/173) on 10 days of cefuroxime and 74% (131/177) on 10 days of amoxicillin-clavulanate. Pathogen eradication or presumed eradication was 92%, 84% and 95% respectively. Drug-related adverse events, mainly gastrointestinal (diarrhoea 34% versus 17% and 12%), were significantly more frequent on amoxicillin-clavulanate than on either cefuroxime course (p < 0.001). The authors concluded 5 days of cefuroxime was equivalent to 10 days.
cards.watchOut: Ages ran from 3 months to 12 years with no older-child subgroup printed, the evaluable denominators (147–177 per arm) are well below the 719 enrolled, and the drug was cefuroxime — equivalence for one cephalosporin does not automatically transfer to amoxicillin regimens.
cards.source: Gooch WM et al. Effectiveness of five days of therapy with cefuroxime axetil suspension for treatment of acute otitis media. The Pediatric infectious disease journal. 1996. PMID: 8822290. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era trial). cards.headline: Hendrickse 1988: no advantage to 10 days with an intact eardrum (failure 10% versus 6%) — but with a perforated eardrum, 5 days failed 53% versus 8%
cards.summary: Hendrickse 1988: no advantage to 10 days with an intact eardrum (failure 10% versus 6%) — but with a perforated eardrum, 5 days failed 53% versus 8%
cards.people: Double-blind randomised trial of 175 children with acute otitis media (the record prints no age range — age composition N not documented in the record) assigned to 10 days of cefaclor 40 mg/kg/day or 5 days of cefaclor followed by 5 days of placebo; 151 were evaluable at 10 days, including 123 with both eardrums intact and 28 with spontaneous perforation.
cards.result: With intact eardrums, treatment failure was 6/59 (10%) on 5 days versus 4/64 (6%) failures plus 1 early relapse (2%) on 10 days — not significantly different — and reinfection and persistent effusion rates did not differ out to 90 days. With spontaneous perforation, failure was 8/15 (53%) on 5 days versus 1/13 (8%) on 10 days (p = 0.016). The authors concluded a 5-day course appears sufficient with intact membranes but not with purulent drainage through a perforation.
cards.watchOut: A 1988 trial of cefaclor — an agent little used for this indication now — with only 28 children in the perforation subgroup; the perforation signal is large but rests on 15 versus 13 children, and the record does not document the children's ages.
cards.source: Hendrickse WA et al. Five vs. ten days of therapy for acute otitis media. The Pediatric infectious disease journal. 1988. PMID: 3277153. cards.headline: Synthesis: for children 2 and older the short course looks close — inferred from mixed-age trials, never tested in the age group alone — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: for children 2 and older the short course looks close — inferred from mixed-age trials, never tested in the age group alone — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: The carded evidence: the Cochrane duration review (49 trials, 12,045 children aged 1 month–18 years), the Gooch cefuroxime trials (719 children aged 3 months–12 years) and the Hendrickse cefaclor trial (175 children, ages not documented in the record). The under-2 trial evidence is homed on pack #2948 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: Five days versus ten: satisfactory outcomes 69% versus 70% in the largest direct comparison enrolling older children; no significant difference with intact eardrums in the oldest trial; a pooled 3-percentage-point failure penalty for short courses across all childhood (21% versus 18%); and one clear exception — perforated eardrum, failure 53% versus 8%. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): probably close for an older child with an intact eardrum, unproven as stated, and not to be extended to perforation or to the under-twos.
cards.watchOut: Every card mixes ages: anyone quoting this shelf as proof that '5 days is enough over age 2' is claiming a subgroup result that none of these records prints. A dedicated duration trial in children 2 and older would replace this shelf's inference with evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kozyrskyj A et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2010 (PMID: 20824827); Gooch WM et al. shelves.title: Atomoxetine versus stimulants in children: non-inferiority was met in two analyses, but the blinded head-to-head trials favoured methylphenidate on response rates — close, not equal
shelves.question: In children and adolescents with ADHD, is atomoxetine as effective as stimulant medication for core symptoms?
shelves.mesh: Attention Deficit Disorder with Hyperactivity/drug therapy · Atomoxetine Hydrochloride · Methylphenidate/therapeutic use · Central Nervous System Stimulants/therapeutic use · Child · Adolescent · Humans · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — this pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #1390 homes atomoxetine versus placebo in children (one trial), and live shelf #707 homes the medication-class comparison in adults only; the child head-to-head against stimulants is the uncovered slice, and neither home's records are re-carded here. The child comparisons split by design. Where non-inferiority was the test, atomoxetine passed: Wang 2007 (double-blind, 330 outpatients aged 6–16) found response rates of 77.4% on atomoxetine versus 81.5% on methylphenidate, meeting the non-inferiority criterion, though with more anorexia, nausea, somnolence, dizziness and vomiting and slightly more weight loss (−1.2 kg versus −0.4 kg); and the Hazell 2011 direct-comparison meta-analysis (7 studies, 1,368 children and adolescents) found 6-week response rates of 53.6% versus 54.4% (difference −0.9%, 95% CI −9.2 to 7.5), within its −15% non-inferiority margin. Where superiority was the test, the stimulant won: Newcorn 2008 (516 children aged 6–16, double-blind, placebo-controlled) found response in 56% on osmotic-release methylphenidate versus 45% on atomoxetine versus 24% on placebo, the stimulant significantly superior — while also showing about 42–43% of non-responders to one drug responded to the other. Kemner 2005 (open-label, community-based, 1,323 children aged 6–12) likewise favoured OROS methylphenidate on symptom-score change (20.24 versus 16.0 points at 3 weeks), a design whose lack of blinding flatters the familiar drug. PROPOSED SPLIT: on average atomoxetine is somewhat less effective than methylphenidate for core symptoms over 3–8 weeks, close enough to meet generous non-inferiority margins, and a genuine alternative for the substantial minority who do not respond to, or do not tolerate, a stimulant.

cards.headline: Wang 2007: double-blind non-inferiority met — response 77.4% on atomoxetine versus 81.5% on methylphenidate in 330 children aged 6–16
cards.summary: Wang 2007: double-blind non-inferiority met — response 77.4% on atomoxetine versus 81.5% on methylphenidate in 330 children aged 6–16
cards.people: Randomised, double-blind comparison trial in 330 paediatric outpatients aged 6–16 with ADHD in China, Korea and Mexico: once-daily atomoxetine 0.8–1.8 mg/kg/day (n = 164) versus twice-daily methylphenidate 0.2–0.6 mg/kg/day (n = 166) for about 8 weeks. Response was a ≥40% fall in ADHD Rating Scale total score.
cards.result: Atomoxetine was non-inferior to methylphenidate on response rates (77.4% versus 81.5%; one-sided 95% lower confidence limit −11.7%, p = 0.404). Adverse effects significantly more frequent on atomoxetine included anorexia (37.2% versus 25.3%), nausea (20.1% versus 10.2%), somnolence (26.2% versus 3.6%), dizziness (15.2% versus 7.2%) and vomiting (11.6% versus 3.6%), mostly mild or moderate; mean weight loss was greater on atomoxetine (−1.2 kg versus −0.4 kg, p < 0.001).
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority here means 'not worse by more than the prespecified margin' — the lower confidence limit of −11.7% still allows atomoxetine to be up to about 12 response points worse. The methylphenidate comparator was immediate-release twice daily, not a long-acting stimulant.
cards.source: Wang Y et al. Atomoxetine versus methylphenidate in paediatric outpatients with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: a randomized, double-blind comparison trial. The Australian and New Zealand journal of psychiatry. 2007. PMID: 17464703. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era trial). cards.headline: Newcorn 2008: in the blinded placebo-controlled comparison, methylphenidate beat atomoxetine — response 56% versus 45% (placebo 24%)
cards.summary: Newcorn 2008: in the blinded placebo-controlled comparison, methylphenidate beat atomoxetine — response 56% versus 45% (placebo 24%)
cards.people: Large double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 516 patients aged 6–16 with ADHD of any subtype: atomoxetine 0.8–1.8 mg/kg/day (n = 222), osmotic-release (OROS) methylphenidate 18–54 mg/day (n = 220) or placebo (n = 74) for 6 weeks, with a subsequent double-blind switch phase for the methylphenidate group. Response was a ≥40% fall in ADHD Rating Scale total score.
cards.result: Response rates were 56% on OROS methylphenidate, 45% on atomoxetine and 24% on placebo; both drugs were markedly superior to placebo, and the response to OROS methylphenidate was significantly superior to atomoxetine. Completion rates and discontinuations for adverse events did not differ significantly from placebo for either drug. Crossover data showed differential response: of 70 methylphenidate non-responders, 30 (43%) later responded to atomoxetine, and 29 (42%) of 69 atomoxetine non-responders had previously responded to methylphenidate.
cards.watchOut: Six weeks is the acute phase only, and the comparison is against one long-acting methylphenidate formulation at fixed dose bands — it does not test atomoxetine against amphetamine stimulants or against individually optimised stimulant dosing.
cards.source: Newcorn JH et al. Atomoxetine and osmotically released methylphenidate for the treatment of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: acute comparison and differential response. The American journal of psychiatry. 2008. PMID: 18281409. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Kemner 2005: in open-label community practice (1,323 children), OROS methylphenidate improved symptom scores more than atomoxetine — 20.2 versus 16.0 points at 3 weeks
cards.summary: Kemner 2005: in open-label community practice (1,323 children), OROS methylphenidate improved symptom scores more than atomoxetine — 20.2 versus 16.0 points at 3 weeks
cards.people: Multicentre, prospective, open-label randomised community-based study in 1,323 children aged 6–12 with ADHD, randomised 2:1 to once-daily OROS methylphenidate (n = 850) or atomoxetine (n = 473) for 3 weeks, with investigator-rated ADHD Rating Scale and global-impression outcomes assessed in a practice-like setting.
cards.result: Mean ADHD Rating Scale decreases were 20.24 points on OROS methylphenidate versus 16.0 on atomoxetine (p < 0.001), with the between-treatment difference growing over time (2.77, 3.44 and 4.24 points at weeks 1, 2 and 3; p < 0.001); treatment response (≥25% score reduction) was significantly greater on methylphenidate at each evaluation. Withdrawals for adverse events were similar (4.8% versus 5.5%).
cards.watchOut: Open-label and only 3 weeks: families and raters knew the treatment, atomoxetine's slower onset (its effect builds over weeks) is structurally disadvantaged by a 3-week horizon, and expectation favours the established stimulant. Read this card as real-world short-term data, not as a fair efficacy race.
cards.source: Kemner JE et al. Outcomes of OROS methylphenidate compared with atomoxetine in children with ADHD: a multicenter, randomized prospective study. Advances in therapy. 2005. PMID: 16418159. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era trial). cards.headline: Hazell 2011: direct-comparison meta-analysis of 7 studies (1,368 children) — 6-week response 53.6% versus 54.4%, atomoxetine non-inferior within a −15% margin
cards.summary: Hazell 2011: direct-comparison meta-analysis of 7 studies (1,368 children) — 6-week response 53.6% versus 54.4%, atomoxetine non-inferior within a −15% margin
cards.people: Non-inferiority meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials directly comparing atomoxetine with methylphenidate in children and adolescents with ADHD, using ADHD Rating Scale response (≥40% reduction) at 6 weeks: 7 studies, 1,368 participants (811 atomoxetine, 557 methylphenidate).
cards.result: After 6 weeks, 53.6% (95% CI 48.6 to 58.4) of atomoxetine-treated patients had responded versus 54.4% (47.6 to 61.1) on methylphenidate — an absolute difference of −0.9% (95% CI −9.2 to 7.5), demonstrating non-inferiority against the prespecified −15% margin. The authors conclude the two had comparable efficacy for core symptoms at 6 weeks.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials include the open-label Kemner study carded above, response definitions and methylphenidate formulations vary across the seven studies, and a −15% non-inferiority margin is generous — 'non-inferior' here can still mean up to 9 points worse on the observed interval.

cards.headline: Synthesis: atomoxetine is a close second to methylphenidate on average — non-inferior by formal margins, beaten on response in the strictest blinded trial — SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: atomoxetine is a close second to methylphenidate on average — non-inferior by formal margins, beaten on response in the strictest blinded trial — SPLIT
cards.people: The carded evidence: two double-blind head-to-head trials (330 and 516 children), one open-label community randomised study (1,323 children) and one direct-comparison meta-analysis (7 studies, 1,368 children), all against methylphenidate formulations over 3–8 weeks. Atomoxetine versus placebo is homed on live shelf #1390 and adult class comparisons on live shelf #707; neither is re-carded here.
cards.result: Response rates across the blinded trials: 77.4% versus 81.5% (non-inferiority met) in Wang 2007 and 45% versus 56% (stimulant superior) in Newcorn 2008; pooled response 53.6% versus 54.4% in Hazell 2011. About 42–43% of non-responders to one drug responded to the other. PROPOSED SPLIT: atomoxetine is not the equal of methylphenidate on average core-symptom response, but the gap is modest, non-inferiority margins are met, and individual children clearly prefer one drug or the other.
cards.watchOut: All comparisons are against methylphenidate (immediate-release or OROS); there is no carded child head-to-head against amphetamine-based stimulants, and all horizons are 8 weeks or shorter — long-term comparative effectiveness is not answered here.

shelves.title: Ziresovir in hospitalised infants with RSV (AIRFLO): severity score fell 0.8 points more than placebo at day 3 — single-country (China) evidence, score endpoint, resistance mutations in 9%
shelves.question: In infants hospitalised with RSV lower respiratory tract infection, does oral ziresovir, compared with placebo, improve clinical severity scores and shorten illness?
shelves.balance: One development programme (Shanghai Ark Biopharmaceutical), conducted entirely in China — SINGLE-COUNTRY flag. Phase 2 (n=72): the 2 mg/kg twice-daily dose improved the Wang respiratory score more than placebo at 96 hours (PMID 37502622). Phase 3 AIRFLO (intention-to-treat n=244): the Wang bronchiolitis clinical score fell 0.8 points more on ziresovir than placebo at day 3 (P=0.002), with a larger viral-load fall (PMID 39321361); a prespecified subanalysis in infants 6 months or younger showed a 1.2-point difference (PMID 40246359, a second report of the same AIRFLO trial). FLAGS: the endpoint is a symptom/severity score, not mortality, ventilation or length of stay; resistance-associated mutations emerged in 9% of ziresovir-treated participants in AIRFLO. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one programme, one country, surrogate-score endpoint.

cards.headline: Phase 2 AK0529/ziresovir (Huang 2023): at 2 mg/kg twice daily, the Wang score fell 4.0 points vs 2.0 on placebo at 96 hours — in 72 infants
cards.summary: Phase 2 AK0529/ziresovir (Huang 2023): at 2 mg/kg twice daily, the Wang score fell 4.0 points vs 2.0 on placebo at 96 hours — in 72 infants
cards.people: Infants aged 1–24 months hospitalised with RSV infection: Part 1, 24 patients randomised 2:1 to a single dose of AK0529 (ziresovir) up to 4 mg/kg or placebo; Part 2, 48 patients randomised 2:1 to ziresovir 0.5, 1 or 2 mg/kg twice daily or placebo for 5 days (total N = 72).
cards.result: No safety or tolerability signals: grade 3 or higher treatment-emergent adverse events in 4.1% on ziresovir vs 4.2% on placebo, none leading to death or withdrawal. In Part 2, target exposure was reached at 2 mg/kg twice daily, with a numerically greater viral-load reduction than placebo at 96 hours; median Wang Respiratory Score change was −4.0 (95% CI −4.51 to −2.03) at 2 mg/kg vs −2.0 (95% CI −3.42 to −1.82) on placebo.
cards.watchOut: A 72-infant dose-finding study: the score difference is a point estimate from small dose groups, and 'numerically greater' viral-load reduction is the authors' own cautious wording. It set the dose for phase 3; it does not establish benefit.
cards.source: Huang LM et al. Safety and efficacy of AK0529 in respiratory syncytial virus-infected infant patients: A phase 2 proof-of-concept trial. Influenza and Other Respiratory Viruses. 2023. PMID: 37502622. Registry ID: NCT02654171. cards.headline: AIRFLO (Zhao 2024): Wang bronchiolitis score fell 3.4 vs 2.7 points at day 3 (difference −0.8, P=0.002); resistance mutations in 9%
cards.summary: AIRFLO (Zhao 2024): Wang bronchiolitis score fell 3.4 vs 2.7 points at day 3 (difference −0.8, P=0.002); resistance mutations in 9%
cards.people: Infants 1–24 months hospitalised with RSV infection in China, randomised 2:1 to oral ziresovir (10–40 mg by weight, twice daily, 5 days) or placebo. Intention-to-treat population 244; safety population 302. SINGLE-COUNTRY: all sites in China.
cards.result: Primary endpoint — change in Wang bronchiolitis clinical score (0–12, higher is worse) at day 3: −3.4 points (95% CI −3.7 to −3.1) on ziresovir vs −2.7 (95% CI −3.1 to −2.2) on placebo (difference −0.8 points, 95% CI −1.3 to −0.3, P=0.002). Viral load fell more by day 5 (−2.5 vs −1.9 log10 copies/mL; difference −0.6). Drug-related adverse events: 16% vs 13% (diarrhoea 4% vs 2%; raised liver enzymes 3% vs 3%; rash 2% vs 1%). Resistance-associated mutations were identified in 15 participants (9%) in the ziresovir group.
cards.watchOut: A 0.8-point difference on a 12-point symptom score is statistically real and clinically modest; the trial's endpoints are scores and viral load, not ventilation, length of stay or death. Emergent resistance mutations in 9% of treated infants are an early warning for a fusion inhibitor used at scale.
cards.source: Zhao S et al. AIRFLO: Ziresovir in Hospitalized Infants with Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infection. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2024. PMID: 39321361. Registry ID: NCT04231968. cards.headline: AIRFLO subanalysis in infants 6 months or younger (Zhang 2025): score difference −1.2 points (p=0.0004) — a prespecified second report of the same trial
cards.summary: AIRFLO subanalysis in infants 6 months or younger (Zhang 2025): score difference −1.2 points (p=0.0004) — a prespecified second report of the same trial
cards.people: Prespecified subanalysis of AIRFLO restricted to infants aged 6 months or younger: intention-to-treat infected population 150 (100 ziresovir, 50 placebo); safety population 188, across 28 hospitals in China, with 24-month follow-up. Explicitly labelled: second report of the AIRFLO trial (PMID 39321361), not an independent trial.
cards.result: Least-squares mean change in Wang bronchiolitis clinical score at day 3: −3.5 points (95% CI −3.9 to −3.1) on ziresovir vs −2.2 (−2.8 to −1.7) on placebo (difference −1.2, 95% CI −1.9 to −0.6, p=0.0004). Drug-related treatment-emergent adverse events in 18% on ziresovir vs 11% on placebo; no drug-related serious adverse events and no deaths.
cards.watchOut: Same trial, youngest subgroup: the larger point estimate in the subgroup does not add an independent replication, and subgroup effects of this size commonly shrink. It supports consistency in the highest-risk age band, nothing more.

cards.headline: Synthesis: ziresovir speeds symptom-score recovery in hospitalised infants with RSV — one programme, one country, a score endpoint
cards.summary: Synthesis: ziresovir speeds symptom-score recovery in hospitalised infants with RSV — one programme, one country, a score endpoint
cards.people: Phase 2 (72 infants), AIRFLO phase 3 (244 in the intention-to-treat population), and its prespecified 6-months-or-younger subanalysis (150 infants) — all conducted in China.
cards.result: Wang bronchiolitis score at day 3: −0.8 points vs placebo overall (P=0.002) and −1.2 points in infants 6 months or younger. shelves.title: Clesrovimab (Enflonsia, Merck): one dose cut medically attended RSV infection 60.4% relative and RSV hospitalisation 84.2% relative in healthy infants (CLEVER); in high-risk infants it matched palivizumab (SMART)
shelves.question: In infants entering their first RSV season, does a single dose of clesrovimab, compared with placebo, prevent medically attended RSV lower respiratory tract infection and hospitalisation?
shelves.balance: Standalone pack cross-pointed to live shelf #255 (preventing RSV in infancy), which cards palivizumab and nirsevimab only — clesrovimab is not carded there and none of #255's PMIDs is re-used here; placement (sibling shelf vs added cards on #255) is the developer's ruling at serve time. The product is clesrovimab (Enflonsia, Merck), named per the clarification exception as a single-manufacturer product. CLEVER (3,614 infants dosed): one 105 mg intramuscular dose before the first RSV season reduced medically attended RSV lower respiratory infection by 60.4% relative (2.6% vs 6.5%) and RSV hospitalisation by 84.2% relative (9/2,398 vs 28/1,201) through day 150 (PMID 40961446). SMART (997 high-risk, palivizumab-eligible infants): season-1 medically attended infection rates were comparable to monthly palivizumab (3.2% vs 3.4%) in a trial whose primary outcome was safety (PMID 42475081). A population pharmacokinetic analysis (2,942 infants) gives a 44.0-day half-life supporting the single fixed dose (PMID 41589687). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one manufacturer's programme — a large placebo-controlled trial plus an active-comparator safety trial, with no head-to-head against nirsevimab.

cards.headline: CLEVER (Zar 2025): one clesrovimab dose — medically attended RSV infection 2.6% vs 6.5% (60.4% relative efficacy), hospitalisation 84.2% relative efficacy
cards.summary: CLEVER (Zar 2025): one clesrovimab dose — medically attended RSV infection 2.6% vs 6.5% (60.4% relative efficacy), hospitalisation 84.2% relative efficacy
cards.people: 3,614 healthy preterm and full-term infants entering their first RSV season received one intramuscular injection: clesrovimab 105 mg (n=2,412) or placebo (n=1,202), randomised 2:1; efficacy followed through 150 days.
cards.result: RSV-associated medically attended lower respiratory infection: 60 of 2,398 (2.6%) on clesrovimab vs 74 of 1,201 (6.5%) on placebo — efficacy 60.4% relative (95% CI 44.1 to 71.9, P<0.001). RSV-associated hospitalisation: 9 of 2,398 vs 28 of 1,201 — efficacy 84.2% relative (95% CI 66.6 to 92.6, P<0.001). Serious adverse events: 11.5% on clesrovimab vs 12.4% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Relative efficacies on low absolute rates: hospitalisation fell from about 2.3% to about 0.4% in absolute terms (28/1,201 vs 9/2,398 as reported). One season, one dose, trial conditions — durability beyond 150 days and performance in routine programmes are separate questions.
cards.source: Zar HJ et al. CLEVER: Clesrovimab for Prevention of RSV Disease in Healthy Infants. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2025. PMID: 40961446. Registry ID: NCT04767373. cards.headline: SMART (Zar 2026): in 997 high-risk infants, clesrovimab's season-1 infection rate matched palivizumab (3.2% vs 3.4%) — a safety-primary trial, with a second-season dose
cards.summary: SMART (Zar 2026): in 997 high-risk infants, clesrovimab's season-1 infection rate matched palivizumab (3.2% vs 3.4%) — a safety-primary trial, with a second-season dose
cards.people: 997 palivizumab-eligible infants (prematurity, chronic lung disease of prematurity, or haemodynamically significant congenital heart disease) at 110 sites in 27 countries, randomised 1:1 to clesrovimab 105 mg once (plus a day-28 placebo) or monthly palivizumab 15 mg/kg (up to 5 doses) in season 1; 276 children received open-label clesrovimab 210 mg before season 2.
cards.result: The primary outcome was safety: proportions experiencing adverse events in season 1 were comparable between groups, and the season-2 210 mg dose was well tolerated. RSV-associated medically attended lower respiratory infection through day 150 in season 1: 3.2% (95% CI 1.8%–5.2%) on clesrovimab vs 3.4% (95% CI 2.0%–5.6%) on palivizumab. Total RSV-associated medically attended infection through day 180 after the season-2 dose was 7.3% (95% CI 4.4%–11.4%), with no season-2 comparator.
cards.watchOut: SMART was designed and powered around safety, not efficacy non-inferiority: 'comparable' infection rates in a safety trial do not prove equal protection. The earlier NEJM record for SMART (PMID: 40961423) is a letter with an abstract-empty record and is not carded; this JAMA Pediatrics report is the full trial publication. Palivizumab is homed at live #255 — only the comparison rates are reported here, not its own cards.

cards.headline: Population pharmacokinetics (2026): clesrovimab half-life 44.0 days across 2,942 infants — the basis for one fixed dose per season
cards.summary: Population pharmacokinetics (2026): clesrovimab half-life 44.0 days across 2,942 infants — the basis for one fixed dose per season
cards.people: Population pharmacokinetic modelling of 5,850 samples from 2,942 infants across three studies (phase 1b/2a MK-1654-002, CLEVER, and SMART), preterm and full-term.
cards.result: A two-compartment model with first-order absorption and elimination described clesrovimab concentrations; estimated half-life was 44.0 days. Body weight, maturation with age, and race were statistically significant covariates, but each changed exposure by less than 30% — supporting a single fixed intramuscular dose regardless of weight, as used in CLEVER and SMART.
cards.watchOut: Carded as pharmacology support for the fixed-dose claim, not as efficacy evidence: it pools the same programme's studies (including the two trials above) and measures concentrations, not infections prevented.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a single clesrovimab dose prevents RSV disease in healthy infants and is tolerated in high-risk infants — one programme, no nirsevimab comparison
cards.summary: Synthesis: a single clesrovimab dose prevents RSV disease in healthy infants and is tolerated in high-risk infants — one programme, no nirsevimab comparison
cards.people: CLEVER (3,614 infants dosed), SMART (997 high-risk infants), and a pooled pharmacokinetic analysis (2,942 infants). Cross-point: live shelf #255 cards palivizumab (IMpact-RSV, Feltes) and nirsevimab (Griffin, MELODY, HARMONIE); none of its PMIDs is used here.
cards.result: Against placebo: medically attended RSV lower respiratory infection reduced 60.4% relative and RSV hospitalisation 84.2% relative over 150 days. Against palivizumab in high-risk infants: comparable adverse events and similar season-1 infection rates (3.2% vs 3.4%) in a safety-primary trial. Half-life 44.0 days supports one fixed dose per season. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — single-programme evidence; there is no randomised comparison with nirsevimab.
cards.watchOut: Premise verified against live #255 before building: its five cards cover palivizumab and nirsevimab only, with no clesrovimab mention — the slice is genuinely uncovered. Choice between long-acting antibodies in practice will rest on programme factors (supply, timing, cost) that no trial here measures.

shelves.title: Serdexmethylphenidate/dexmethylphenidate (Azstarys) in ADHD: one laboratory-classroom trial showed SKAMP benefit across the school day, a small China phase 3 agreed, and a 1-year open-label study found stimulant-typical harms
shelves.question: In children 6–12 with ADHD, does once-daily serdexmethylphenidate/dexmethylphenidate, versus placebo, improve classroom behaviour (SKAMP) across the school day?
mesh: Attention Deficit Disorder with Hyperactivity / drug therapy
Central Nervous System Stimulants / adverse effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). The tested product is the specific prodrug co-formulation serdexmethylphenidate/dexmethylphenidate (Azstarys, named in the pivotal report); results do not transfer to other methylphenidate products, and the fetched records do not name the manufacturer. One pivotal dose-optimised laboratory-classroom trial (149 children completing) found a least-squares SKAMP-Combined advantage of −5.41 points versus placebo averaged over the classroom day (p<0.001), significant from 1 to 10 hours post-dose on the prespecified analysis; the often-quoted 0.5-to-13-hour duration comes from a post hoc analysis and is labelled as such on the card. A small China phase 3 bridging trial (n=55) pointed the same way on ADHD-RS-5 (−5.8 points at week 3, p=0.0292). A 12-month open-label safety study (282 enrolled) found the stimulant-typical profile — decreased appetite 18.5%, decreased weight 7.6%, irritability 6.7% — with 60.1% reporting at least one treatment-emergent adverse event and no unexpected cardiac signal. Adult evidence is open-label only and is not carded; this shelf answers the paediatric question only. Record note: the pivotal report's PubMed record carries no registry ID, so none is printed on its card.

cards.headline: Pivotal laboratory-classroom trial (Kollins 2021): SKAMP-Combined improved by −5.41 points vs placebo averaged over the school day (p<0.001), with effect from 1 to 10 hours post-dose
cards.summary: Pivotal laboratory-classroom trial (Kollins 2021): SKAMP-Combined improved by −5.41 points vs placebo averaged over the school day (p<0.001), with effect from 1 to 10 hours post-dose
cards.people: 149 children aged 6–12 with ADHD completed a 3-week open-label dose-optimisation phase (starting 39.2 mg/7.8 mg serdexmethylphenidate/dexmethylphenidate, titrated weekly to a maximum 52.3 mg/10.4 mg), then a 7-day double-blind phase on their optimal dose or placebo; efficacy was assessed on day 7 in a laboratory classroom with the SKAMP rating scale and the PERMP academic-productivity measure.
cards.result: The primary analysis favoured serdexmethylphenidate/dexmethylphenidate: least-squares mean treatment difference in SKAMP-Combined change averaged over the classroom day −5.41 (95% CI −7.10 to −3.71; p<0.001). A significant treatment effect was observed from 1 to 10 hours post-dose; a post hoc analysis constructed to match similar studies indicated onset and duration from 0.5 to 13 hours. PERMP-Attempted and PERMP-Correct changes also favoured treatment (p<0.001 for both). No serious adverse events were reported; during dose optimisation two-thirds of subjects reported adverse events, most commonly insomnia and decreased appetite.
cards.watchOut: A 7-day double-blind phase after open-label dose optimisation in children who had already tolerated titration is an enriched, best-case design: it prices neither long-term classroom benefit nor effects in stimulant-naive children starting at a fixed dose. The 13-hour duration figure is post hoc, not the prespecified analysis. The record carries no registry ID, so none is printed.

cards.headline: China phase 3 bridging trial (Liu 2026): ADHD-RS-5 improved by −5.8 points vs placebo at week 3 (p=0.0292) — n=55
cards.summary: China phase 3 bridging trial (Liu 2026): ADHD-RS-5 improved by −5.8 points vs placebo at week 3 (p=0.0292) — n=55
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 bridging trial (Liu 2026)
cards.people: 55 children aged 6–12 meeting DSM-5 criteria for ADHD, randomised at multiple Chinese centres to serdexmethylphenidate/dexmethylphenidate (n=28) or placebo (n=27); primary endpoint was least-squares mean change in ADHD Rating Scale-5 (ADHD-RS-5) total score at week 3.
cards.result: At week 3 the between-group least-squares mean difference in ADHD-RS-5 total score was −5.8 (standard error 2.58; p=0.0292), effect size 0.61, meeting the prespecified efficacy-consistency criterion (≥0.25). At week 4, differences also favoured treatment on ADHD-RS-5 total (−8.4), inattention (−4.4) and hyperactivity-impulsivity (−3.7) subscores, CGI-Severity (−0.8), CGI-Improvement (0.9) and evening/morning behaviour ratings. Most treatment-emergent adverse events were mild to moderate, with no new safety signals reported.
cards.watchOut: Fifty-five children is a bridging study, not an independent pivotal trial: it was designed to show consistency with the global programme in a Chinese population, and its week-4 secondary results rest on the same small sample. It corroborates direction; it does not add precision about uncommon harms.

cards.headline: 12-month open-label safety study (Childress 2023): 60.1% had a treatment-emergent adverse event; decreased appetite 18.5%, decreased weight 7.6% — no unexpected safety findings
cards.summary: 12-month open-label safety study (Childress 2023): 60.1% had a treatment-emergent adverse event; decreased appetite 18.5%, decreased weight 7.6% — no unexpected safety findings
cards.type: Open-label, dose-optimised 12-month safety study (Childress 2023) — no comparator
cards.people: 282 children aged 6–12 with ADHD enrolled (70 rolled over from the double-blind study, 212 new); 254 entered the 360-day treatment phase after dose optimisation and 155 completed the study. The treatment-phase safety population was 238 children who received at least one dose and had a post-dose safety assessment. Registered as NCT03460652.
cards.result: Of 238 children assessed, 143 (60.1%) had at least one treatment-emergent adverse event (15.1% mild, 39.9% moderate, 5.0% severe in the report's grading breakdown). The commonest were decreased appetite (18.5%), upper respiratory tract infection (9.7%), nasopharyngitis (8.0%), decreased weight (7.6%) and irritability (6.7%). There were no clinically meaningful trends in electrocardiograms, cardiac events or blood-pressure events, and none led to discontinuation; two subjects had eight serious adverse events judged unrelated to treatment. ADHD-RS-5 and CGI-Severity scores fell during treatment, as expected without a control group.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and uncontrolled: the symptom-score falls cannot be separated from expectancy, maturation and regression to the mean, and 127 of 282 enrolled children discontinued — tolerability in completers overstates tolerability in starters. The record's publication types label it a randomised trial, but its own abstract describes an open-label safety study, and the card follows the abstract.

cards.headline: Synthesis: serdexmethylphenidate/dexmethylphenidate improves classroom behaviour across the school day in children 6–12 — a single-programme answer with stimulant-typical harms
cards.summary: Synthesis: serdexmethylphenidate/dexmethylphenidate improves classroom behaviour across the school day in children 6–12 — a single-programme answer with stimulant-typical harms
cards.people: Synthesis of the three reports carded on this shelf: the pivotal laboratory-classroom trial (149 completers), the China phase 3 bridging trial (n=55) and the 12-month open-label safety study (282 enrolled) — the paediatric programme only.
cards.result: Efficacy is concordant across the two placebo-controlled reports (SKAMP-Combined −5.41 points; ADHD-RS-5 −5.8 points at week 3), and the safety profile over 12 months is the familiar methylphenidate profile — appetite and weight effects foremost — with no new signal in these reports.
cards.watchOut: POSSIBLE (benefit): one sponsor programme, one pivotal trial, a 55-child bridging study and uncontrolled long-term safety data. Nothing carded here addresses adults, head-to-head comparison with other methylphenidate formulations, or outcomes beyond symptom ratings.

shelves.title: Dasiglucagon in congenital hyperinsulinism (PARTIAL vs live #1777; FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 trials, N = 44): larger trial's primary MISSED; CGM signal post-hoc; infant crossover cut IV glucose need
shelves.question: In infants and children with congenital hyperinsulinism and persistent hypoglycaemia, does continuous subcutaneous dasiglucagon, added to standard care or compared with placebo, reduce hypoglycaemia and intravenous glucose requirements? FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 trials, N = 44 in total. PARTIAL beside live #1777, which homes dasiglucagon rescue use in type 1 diabetes — that question is not re-asked here.
shelves.mesh: Infant · Child · Humans · Glucagon · Blood Glucose · Blood Glucose Self-Monitoring · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1 · Congenital Hyperinsulinism · Hypoglycemic Agents · Insulin
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — FLOOR-RISK: exactly 2 trials, N = 44 children in total, printed on the face. PARTIAL beside live #1777, which homes dasiglucagon as severe-hypoglycaemia rescue in type 1 diabetes; only the congenital-hyperinsulinism (CHI) slice is carded here. The larger trial (32 randomised, open-label, dasiglucagon infusion plus standard care vs standard care alone for 4 weeks) MISSED its primary endpoint: self-monitored-glucose-detected hypoglycaemia event rate ratio 0.85 (95% CI 0.54 to 1.36, P = 0.5028). Its affirmative result — a 43% relative reduction in blinded continuous-glucose-monitoring-detected hypoglycaemia (event rate ratio 0.57, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.83, P = 0.0029) — is a POST-HOC analysis and is labelled post-hoc wherever it appears on this shelf. The smaller trial (12 infants, double-blind crossover) found intravenous glucose infusion rate over 48-hour periods was 4.3 mg/kg/min on dasiglucagon versus 9.5 mg/kg/min on placebo (P = 0.004) — a 48-hour surrogate in 12 infants. Skin and gastrointestinal events were more frequent on dasiglucagon in the larger trial. This row is kept at FLOOR-RISK because CHI is a rare disease with no competing randomised therapy base — not because the base is strong.

cards.headline: Phase 3 RCT in infants and children (Thornton 2024): the primary endpoint was NOT significantly different — self-monitored hypoglycaemia event rate ratio 0.85 (95% CI 0.54 to 1.36, P = 0.5028); the 43% relative CGM reduction is a POST-HOC analysis
cards.summary: Phase 3 RCT in infants and children (Thornton 2024): the primary endpoint was NOT significantly different — self-monitored hypoglycaemia event rate ratio 0.85 (95% CI 0.54 to 1.36, P = 0.5028); the 43% relative CGM reduction is a POST-HOC analysis
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised open-label trial, continuous subcutaneous dasiglucagon + standard care vs standard care alone
cards.people: 32 patients aged 0.6–10.9 years with congenital hyperinsulinism and persistent hypoglycaemia, randomised 1:1 (16 vs 16) to continuous subcutaneous dasiglucagon infusion (10–70 µg/h) plus standard care or standard care alone for 4 weeks, followed by 4 weeks in which all patients received dasiglucagon plus standard care.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — average self-monitored plasma glucose (SMPG)-detected hypoglycaemia episodes per week (SMPG below 3.9 mmol/L (≈ 70 mg/dL)) during weeks 2–4 — fell in both groups with no statistically significant difference (event rate ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.54 to 1.36, P = 0.5028). In a POST-HOC analysis, blinded continuous-glucose-monitoring-detected hypoglycaemia (below 3.9 mmol/L (≈ 70 mg/dL)) fell by 43% relative on dasiglucagon (event rate ratio 0.57, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.83, P = 0.0029), and other CGM measures of hypoglycaemia fell by 37% to 61% relative (also post-hoc analyses). Dasiglucagon appeared safe and well tolerated; skin and gastrointestinal events were more frequent with dasiglucagon plus standard care than with standard care only.
cards.watchOut: The trial missed its primary endpoint. Every affirmative number on this card comes from post-hoc continuous-monitoring analyses and is labelled post-hoc; post-hoc findings in a 32-patient trial are hypothesis-generating, not confirmatory.
cards.source: Thornton PS et al. Dasiglucagon for the Treatment of Congenital Hyperinsulinism: A Randomized Phase 3 Trial in Infants and Children. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2024. PMID: 37930757. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Infant crossover RCT (De Leon 2025): IV glucose infusion rate was 4.3 mg/kg/min on dasiglucagon versus 9.5 mg/kg/min on placebo over 48-hour periods (P = 0.004) in 12 infants dependent on IV glucose
cards.summary: Infant crossover RCT (De Leon 2025): IV glucose infusion rate was 4.3 mg/kg/min on dasiglucagon versus 9.5 mg/kg/min on placebo over 48-hour periods (P = 0.004) in 12 infants dependent on IV glucose
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial (48 hours per period) with a 21-day open-label extension
cards.people: 12 infants aged 7 days to 12 months with congenital hyperinsulinism who were dependent on intravenous glucose, at 4 centres in Germany, the UK and the USA, randomised to dasiglucagon or placebo for 48 hours and then crossed over to the other treatment for 48 hours (part 1), followed by 21 days of open-label dasiglucagon for all (part 2).
cards.result: The primary outcome — mean intravenous glucose infusion rate in the last 12 hours of each part-1 period — was significantly lower on dasiglucagon: least-squares mean 4.3 mg/kg/min (95% CI 1.04 to 7.60) versus 9.5 mg/kg/min (95% CI 6.24 to 12.81) on placebo (P = 0.004). The most frequent adverse events in both treatment groups were gastrointestinal, dermatological, and metabolism and nutritional disorders.
cards.watchOut: Twelve infants and a 48-hour surrogate (glucose infusion rate): the result shows dasiglucagon can substitute for intravenous glucose over two days in this tiny sample; it measures neither durable hypoglycaemia control, neurodevelopment, nor avoidance of surgery or other CHI outcomes.
cards.source: De Leon DD et al. Dasiglucagon in Children With Congenital Hyperinsulinism Up to 1 Year of Age: Results From a Randomized Clinical Trial. cards.people: No patients are carded on this card; it records where the rest of the dasiglucagon evidence lives in the library.
cards.result: Live shelf #1777 asks whether ready-to-use dasiglucagon restores plasma glucose faster than placebo, and how its speed compares with reconstituted glucagon, in people with type 1 diabetes and insulin-induced severe hypoglycaemia (rescue use, single-dose). That question, its trials and its PMIDs stay homed at #1777 under the one-home rule and none is re-carded here. This shelf asks the different question of continuous subcutaneous dasiglucagon infusion, added to standard care, in infants and children with congenital hyperinsulinism and persistent hypoglycaemia — a different population, formulation schedule, comparator and outcome set. Exactly 2 trials answer this shelf's question (N = 44 in total); there is no third trial to card.
cards.watchOut: This card carries no efficacy data and must not be counted as a third report: the shelf's base remains exactly 2 trials, N = 44, as printed on the face.
cards.source: Cross-point only: live shelf #1777, 'Dasiglucagon for severe hypoglycaemia' (rescue use in type 1 diabetes) — no source is carded on this card and no PMID from that shelf is used here.

cards.headline: Synthesis: FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 trials, N = 44 total: the larger trial missed its primary endpoint (post-hoc CGM signal only), and the smaller trial showed a 48-hour reduction in IV glucose requirement in 12 infants
cards.summary: Synthesis: FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 trials, N = 44 total: the larger trial missed its primary endpoint (post-hoc CGM signal only), and the smaller trial showed a 48-hour reduction in IV glucose requirement in 12 infants
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: In the 32-patient open-label trial, dasiglucagon plus standard care did not significantly reduce self-monitored hypoglycaemia versus standard care alone (rate ratio 0.85, P = 0.5028); a post-hoc blinded-CGM analysis found a 43% relative reduction (rate ratio 0.57, P = 0.0029), labelled post-hoc throughout this shelf. In the 12-infant crossover trial, dasiglucagon halved the intravenous glucose infusion rate needed to maintain euglycaemia over 48 hours (4.3 vs 9.5 mg/kg/min, P = 0.004). Skin and gastrointestinal events were more frequent on dasiglucagon. There is no third randomised trial of dasiglucagon in congenital hyperinsulinism — this shelf is, by design, a two-trial shelf, kept because the disease is rare and no competing randomised therapy base exists.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.
